title: Jack Fuller letters [07], 1970-2008

Homewood, Il
June 6, 1994.

My dear son:
I know I just finished talking to you and offering Congratulations from many people in church. As I said, that's what I like about St. Paul's - the people care -- they're happy when good things happen to people they know and sad when people are faced with trials & tribulations. They - show God is love. ----
I need not tell you how proud I am of you - & many times I look at your dad's picture & tell him about you. Sounds silly, but it isn't. I know he'd be glad you became a journalist & lawyer instead of some other profession -- even tho' he tried to talk you out of it! He did didn't he?
This letter might be unnecessary, but I had to write--and tell you again I'm proud and I love you--
Love
Mother.
I hope your cold is better.
Dorothy Fuller

Feb. 6, 1976
Dear Alyce and Jack,
With another 6 inches of snow outside our windows, I'm really hoping for an early end to winter. In any case, we've decided to seek out the warm sun by taking a much needed vacation to the Carribean. The three of us (not counting #4 on the way) leave for St. Thomas, Virgin Islands on Feb. 25 for a week's stay on a sandy beach. Jonathan has his pail and shovel ready, although he certainly will be surprised to learn that this beach is not a half-hour drive away. Of course we're very excited and looking forward to spending the time together.
Danny has been working very hard doing all the civil litigation at the firm. Hopefully before very long they'll have someone to help him out and take some of the pressure off.
Jonathan is growing up very fast. He's walking a lot more and that makes him more interesting and fun. Right now he's very much into fire-engines. He has a fireman hat that he even wears to sleep.

title: Jack Fuller letters [04], 1970-2008
transcription:
When we call him Jonathan, he says, "No, me fireman!" He has a whole fleet of firetrucks and spends much of every day waiting for an alarm to slide down the pole. I supposed like everything else, this too is only a phase.
We're really enjoying the house, especially the fireplace during this cold winter. We have a spare room and hope you'll be able to visit soon. We'd like to give you a chance to compare NY's culture to that of Chicago and Washington. More importantly we'd really like to see you, so keep us in mind, in case we're not able to come to you. It was a real treat speaking to you on New Year's Eve. It made an otherwise ordinary night very special, and is a nice tradition. Thanks again for your thoughts.
I've waited too long to write this letter, but did want to say hello and let you know we're all well.
Hi from me too. We often think and talk about you guys. We want and plan to come to Washington for a few days this spring, so that we can check up on you, the Rossiters and some other friends. My big news is that I've got a literary agent (who happens to be Learned Hand's

title: Jack Fuller letters [04], 1970-2008
transcription:
2interested in my prospective book on the 
granddaughter!) who is very interested in my prospective book on the unconstitutionality of inheritance and has lined up an editor at Random House for it. I'm working on an outline and an introduction, which will be the basis for an advance (substantial, I hope!). The other news--which Susan alluded to--is that I've been working pretty hard recently. The firm pushed out my boss to "of Counsel" status and brought in a criminal lawyer as the "litigation partner." He knows from nothing about civil litigation, given no aid, comfort or supervision on my civil cases (which after a year are finally starting to increase in number), and in fact has added to my workload by virtue of his criminal practice. I'm seeing a lot of action (last Monday I was supposed to have my first unsupervised trial, but a bad snow prevented the judge and the other side showing up!) but sometimes I feel like I'm ready to burst. One of the satisfying things is that I'm beginning to bring in business that pays well--referrals from Paul Weiss and other clients I've been servicing. The pressures of litigation are really  intense--last week I had to prepare a hurried "order to show cause" for an appellate

title: Jack Fuller letters [04], 1970-2008
transcription:
court to stay a judgment. We had the oral argument in chambers, and it made me feel like a real lawyer. Two days ago the guy who used to be my boss (now "of counsel") sounded me out on forming our own two-man partnership. It's interesting and I may do it.
The other day, I finished reading Bickel's Morality of Consent, and I think it was the best thing he wrote, really superb.
Love from all of us
Susan, Danny & Jon

title: Jack Fuller letters [03], 1970-2008
transcription:
WARSH, STEVE
Nov. 9
Dear Jack,
This is in the way of a thank you note for your concern, patience and kindnesses over the last year -- one which for me, in the Chinese vein, might be dubbed the year of the skids -- a year dominated by depression, interrupted briefly by a spot of Don Quixote-like euphoria, curtailed by a nervous breakdown and climaxed by a 2-month stay in the hospital which has put me back on my feet. My regrets, also, if I caused any difficulties.
Situations like mine tend to breed or encourage euphemisms. I feel no need for any. A breakdown by any other name is still the same. The split with Bonnie and some recurring Vietnam readjustment

title: Jack Fuller letters [03], 1970-2008
transcription:
problems proved to be too much to handle.
The business with Bonnie still hurts but it is fine, thank God. A few Vietnam nightmares persist but seem less awesome than they once were. I expect them to die hard. Over the last year, some of them have rippled though me like a string of frags or daymares, producing both despair and outrage.
For the time being, I intend to stay in the news business, preferably on the editing end, riding herd on reporters. I still enjoy reporting but I think I'll give it a break -- at least full-time reporting. Intend to do some grad courses and freelance writing on the side

title: Jack Fuller letters [03], 1970-2008
transcription:
After I clear myself financially -- which should take a few years -- I am seriously considering law school though close consideration of such a venture is a long way off.
On the whole, I have not known greater peace of  mind in over a year -- I'm no longer running on nervous energy and it's pleasant to not be scared shitless most of the time, of one thing or the other.
Again, Jack, thank you for being the first-rate human being that you are.
Steve

April 30, 1984
Dear Jack,
I read Fragments and enjoyed it. I read it in one day, using some multi-hour blocks between interviews.
With relief I learned that the village was not wiped out by the VC, in retribution. For some reason, that would've been too painful for me to read
Your resolution was less painful for me.
I detect much slimming down of the story. Am I right? That is, drafts #1 and #2 were longer?
"wiggle your ass" -- after the lower body wound. A realistic touch.
The story moved and was exciting.
The title "Fragments" has strong poetry. Your references to "fragments" (including the leftover steel in wounds) make strong poetry.
I detect the lawyer in you. Your search for the facts, the facts makes me think that Yale affected us in similar ways.
A a deeper level, there is a Melville quality to your book characters. These men encountered evil.
There are spiritual themes in FRAGMENTS. Morgan & Neumann: (This is just a small thing I noticed) Both German names. Translation: Morning and New Man. Post-resurrection? Who knows? You're the one who named them. I look forward to talking. Honi did my cover, too. Both are beautiful. Let's pitch in together & send her flowers.
Jack
[WHEELER]

In addition, all the paper's sports writers think they're funnier than Dennis Miller. Maybe they are, but they have not set the bar very high.

Dear Bob,
Payne has no single musical model. There's Coltrane and Eric [[?]], but neither played with fusion or Payne (Or were they as rotten as human beings as Payne sometimes was). There's Sonny Rollins and even Miles Davis. But he's really only himself.
As to the Orlando Sentinel, there are those who love it.
Best,

3rd - create the idea in the child that paintin is a pleasure to do & should be enjoyed by doing. This by the care of the materiels - Silence in the room - except as the child might wish to talk about something connected with the work - at the slightes sign of boredom or desire to talk about other things too much, work should be stopped or better still if you have clay to start working with that for a while - a small child has only short endurance which should not be strained but a switch to another medium will keep it in that train of thought and then later they will go back to the painting - and by the way when you make the switch do it simply - explanations and much movements confuse a child - the best way is when you see the signs to quietly get a piece of clay & simply say "Here work with this awhile" Also the word "work" should be used in preference to "paint" "model" etc. this eventually sinks into the child's conciousness in his attitude. 
Praise her - but only when she has done somehting you know is the best of her capabilities– this encourages her to reach out always –
The same with critizism - very good for child but she must feel it is just - you can keep on the line in this by critizing only from her point of view that is "that wasn't as well done as the other picture you made" - that kind of thing if you get what I mean- mostly I think it's important never to say "It doesn't

title: Ben Hecht letters [10], 1914-1979
transcription:
I don't have any books - I haven't kept up with the literature of teaching children, but all I ever saw written about it was eye wash anyway – there are a few very simple things to do -
1st - always create a feeling of respect toward the materiels - Dont ever talk about it but every time the paints are used let the child wash the brushes. If they are not thoroughly clean don't point it out, put them away - next time give them to her to place in the paint jars and if you see one that looks dirty withhold it and say "that didn't get clean enough did it – you'd better wash it over" This as routine until the child thinks that way
Spilled paint - never say anything - just get a rag and let the child wipe it up.
Wasting paper by scribbling all over. When this starts just take the paper away and say "that's not good enough for such a fine sheet of paper" but gently with no reproof in the voice. Then turn the paper over (not a new sheet) and say 'here try again'.
2nd - never suggest subject until child is stuck - then try to have the suggestion come from her by drawing her out - If child draws interestingly and with concentration never interrupt the train of though & never ask "what is it?" let her tell you if she wishes and accept it as that

title: Ben Hecht letters [10], 1914-1979
transcription:
prob like it" - not critizing and praise children used jointly as both are important - but very simply - phrases such as "that's a fine color" "what a good line" (for drawings) or "how beautiful " etc these encourage without becoming involved - and "that's a fine color - too bad that part isn't as good" sort of joint praise and critizism and if the child asks why isn't it good again be simple and say "it isn't as pleasing" This probably sounds like drivel to you, Rose, but there is a definite motive in this language - painting is primarily an emotion interpreted with skill by doing. 
If a child paints he is just as important as an adult in that experience - but he has his range in which he feels comfortable - Impose an adult rang and he's unhappy. For him to grow in this experiece the teacher has to be aware of the range and never forget it and also be aware of it's growth so the teaching changes with the enlargement of the range. The kind of language in relation to the work is important. the minimum talk is important as painting is between the child and the paper - what it is thinking and feeling and how it can do it - teaching the child is helping him with what he needs of your knowledge at that time and put so it is very matter of fact and nothing unusual- well I am rambling. This subject

Dear Rose,

No doubt you should relieve yourself of some responsibilities as running the house in Nyack and standing free of extra burdens no longer of consequence. Stay young at heart and stay loose. Now is the time too to visit all your friends as time goes by. Who the hell am I to give advice?? With your deep understanding of life I feel punny!
I'm going to finish my book inspired by you & Ben and I'm sure even if it never gets off the ground you & Ben will know I tried. I have seven chapters to go (they are in outline) making a good "door stopper" of 20 chapters. If you'd like to edit this endeavor I'd be honored with your help & critical assist.

title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979
transcription:
II
Rose do you intend to live permanently in N.Y.C. at the apt? Are you intending to come West in the future? Please let me know any plans including the Coast here!
Butch finished his 3rd year of college and managed to survive calculus  chem, genetics, German and Analytic Biol. He will probably go for a masters degree in Math.
Sister Mary Liniel[[?]] is finishing her teachers assignment in Cleveland and may get a post closer to the West. A calm lovable sister.
The twins are real popular in High School and are finishing their 2nd year as honor students.
Barbara finished 1st grade with straight A's in reading and etc.
Lu and I are still in the school of hard knocks. Doing excellent.
Lu goes in for female surgery the 15th of this month at our new Hospital called Tri-city.
Oceanside will have its own live theatre (seating capacity 3000), only known actors will perform? They are working in it this month. Preston Foster is the guiding light. He now is a resident of Oceanside and seems energetic and very persuasive.

title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979
transcription:
III
So the face of our small community is changing for the best and progress in arts is one of the main thrusts.

title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979
transcription:
9 Sept 64
Dear Rose,
I hope by the time you receive this you will be settled down to your new endeavor sans government vulchers and etc.
Marion and yours truly are again at it for the finish. We have some real interesting humorous and historic stories in the final chapters. I purposely omitted the horrors of war and leaned toward the lighter side of comedy of errors and human situations of the unusual in most places. A conformist I was not thus never rose to colonel as many of my friends who I felt had less to offer. Working with the men meant more to me than prestige or money. I lived to the fullest with no regrets.
Rose I hope its understood that anyone who you would chose to be the guiding agent would receive the usual renumerance for their assistance. I leave this to your control. I hope I did not cause you an additional worry and burden, this I don't wish. Your friendship is worth more to methan Fort Knox.

title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979
transcription:
II
I hope your problems are solved to your satisfaction and your worries diminished to caring for yourself.
With I could talk to you rather than write. Someday when my ship comes in I could afford to visit N. Y.  and we can sit down to a bull-session. I want to know your problems and successes and feel you are your "old self," a dynamo of ideas.
Again I wish to thank you from the bottom of my heart for your wonderful thoughts and assistance. Perhaps someday we should get our heads together as my book is only a smidgeon of the stories I have tucked away.
Take good care of yourself and have some fun with your work.
Lu and the children send their love.
Effectionately
Butch

title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979
transcription:
Dear Ben, Rose and Jenny
A small report of my lack of activity. For a few weeks, I've been relatively in luxury at the Naval Hospital in San Diego attempting to patch another duodenal ulcer and getting a few tests as to why my right hand goes numb. The mileu[[?]] is quiet and healing and an arthritic condition in the upper vertebrae & shoulder (my rt) is subsiding. I missed my great opportunity by not going into politics while my hand was numb as I could have out-lasted all opponents in shaking hands without paying the price of sore hand. I guess I'm not geared to progress as my timing is always screwed-up. (the election were last year) Anyhow while here they also have given me comprehensive tests on my damaged noggin & nerves for encephalitis. The only phase I dislike is the spinal-tap but then all is for the best. To my immediate knowledge my only deter[[?]]tion is in age. One good thing that occurred is my ability to be able to watch Col Glenn take the ride and this without interruption.

title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979

Dear Ben,
I'm out of the hospital and have been loafing now for four months. I have been replaced by a Prudential Ins Co's younger man, and will be on disability until the first of the year. title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979
transcription:
II
I'm going to attempt something in the way of writing. I'm going to record and tape and have a gal I know transpose to paper and see what kind of mish-mash comes out. title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979
transcription:
III
He is taking a heavy schedule for a Jr. German, Chemistry, Calculus, and Biology!! He has done very well so far and will probably lean toward Chem. Eng. He is living off the campus in S. D. with 5 boys in a huge house. He comes home week-ends to date and eat. All the girls are progressing well in school. Lu remains the same.
I'm free for awhile so if you wanted to take a gander at the far East I'm with you. There is a story there I'm sure.
Please call me when you get into town. I miss you.
My sincere best wishes & effection to Rose & Jenny from all of us
Your friend
Butch

title: Ben Hecht letters [09], 1914-1979

Reiner

Tuesday, April 21st, 1964
Dear Rose:
You have been constantly in my thoughts ever since I read the incredible news on Sunday. The deep sympathy that I feel comes from my heart and from my own experience these past six aching months.
I live quietly in the country taking care of unfinished details, but I do have to go into New York occasionally - staying at Essex House. If you should ever want to pick up the threads of an old friendship, I would be very happy.
Dear Ben -- the only thing I can say is thank God that he was spared the terrible indignity of a long illness, so terrifying for a great and vital man.
Sincerely,
Carlota Reiner

transcription:

but as neither of us had seen a copy of it since we went to Sunday school, we could not decide the question, while we were trying to improve on the druggests version we arrived at Montello, and in a few minutes proverbs had been driven from our minds by roast beaf, potatoes and pudding. And I would suggest to any one in doubt, that he eat a good hearty dinner. Soon after we got started for home Sam inquired if I had ever had the pleasure of seeing a man hung or lynched while I was on the plains. I replied that I had never witnessed either a hanging or a lynching, but I was in the vicinity where a man was hung, and on another occasion I could have seen a man lynched if I had wanted to do so. Sam asked if I knew what crimes these two men were charged with, I replied that one of them had shot a man, and the other man was a horse theif, he said I had better go ahead and tell the stories and get them off my mind. I was willing so I said "all right! here's to you." Now in the murder case I will have to tell it

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
"as it was told to me, because I had never met any of the people who were interested previous to the day of the hanging.
In the year 1852 there lived in one of the interior counties of Missouri a man by the name of Thomas Adler, he owned a 100 acres of good land which he lived on, he had a wife and two children both boys, the eldest John was 12 and his brother William was 7 years old. Opposite of the Adler farm lived a man by the name of Sutton who also owned a 100 acre farm, his family consisted of himself, a wife, and an 8 years old daughter named Sally. Both Adler and Sutton were in what is called good circumstances, and they had inherited the farms on which they had been born from their fathers, and the intercourse between the two families had always been of a friendly nature. Mrs. Sutton previous to her marriage had been a school teacher in an adjoining town. She had a brother by the a,e of James Penrose who was a bachelor, who made her house his home, and they had a cousin by the name of Isaac Penrose, who

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
was known by the name of peg-leg Ike, for the reason that he had to use a peg-leg, having lost his left leg below the knee, and he also made his home with the Suttons. During the fall of '52, three events occured that laid the foundation for a tragedy, the first event was the going of James Penrose to California via the [[?]] of Panama, the second was the death of Sutton, a few weeks later Mrs Adler died, and that gave the community something besides the weather to talk about. Two years afterwards the widow Sutton married Thomas Adler, but she retained control of the property that Sutton had left her a life lease of, and power to sell if she wished to do so. 
In 1856 James Penrose returned overland from California and took charge of her farm. In the spring of '58 Mrs Adler sold her farm for cash and invested the money in mortgages. Penrose had intended to go to California again that spring, but a fit of sickness prevented him from doing so, and peg-leg Ike was going with him. During the few years that he had spent in California,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
Penrose had apparently become enamoured with the charmes of a rural life in that climate, at all events his descriptions of the healthfull climate and the bountiful harvests of that region of country, awakened an interest in the minds of both his sister and her husband in the subject; and the result of their many consultations was that in the fall Adler sold his farm and during the following winter he made preperations to emigrate to California the next spring. As early in the spring of '59, as it was practicable Adler and a number of other emigrants joined forces and made up a large train of wagons the motive power of which was furnished by oxen with a nominal speed of two miles an hour, provided their feet did not get to sore, an ox with tender feet would sometimes delay a train for two or three days.
Adler fitted out two wagons with three yoke of young oxen to each of the wagons, and he laid in a supply of provisions to last them until they arrived at their destination. His brother in law James Penrose went with him as

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: a passenger, and he payed his passage before they started from home, and Peg-leg Ike also accompanied them, he worked his passage by driving one of the wagons. At the time they started from Missouri John Adler was 19, and his brother William was 14 years old and they took turnes in driving the wagon that their father and step mother and her daughter rode in. Sally Sutton at that date was 15 years old and she was the special pet of both her Uncle and peg-leg Ike. The domestic life of the party had always been a pleasant one, and there had never been any friction between any of the family, Penrose and Ike after Mrs Adlers marriage had made their homes with her, and they had been heartily welcomed by Adler as being a desireable addition to his family. Their journey to, and across the MIssouri river and up the north fork of the Platte river, was made without any incident of importance occurring, and it was about the same character that was experienced by thousands of other trains that crossed the plains during the Summer of 1859, to Pikes Peak and California.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: The Adler party all remained in the best of health, and the only thing that occured to mar the pleasant relations that existed between them all, was caused by John Adler, as a boy his disposition had been stubborn, willful and generally mean, his father had been obliged to use a rawhide on his person frequently as long as he could master him, but now John was the strongest of the two, and he was master of both his father and brother, and he kept them through fear for their own safety subjects of his whims, but he had a wholesome fear of both Penrose and Ike, and he was very careful not to cross either of them, or give them any back talk, he took every occasion that presented itself, to talk to his father against them both, and he urged his father to get rid of them in some way, even if he had to set their trunks out and leave them sitting by the side of the trail on them. His father told him that he had signed a contract to convey both of them to California, and it was stipulated that the contract should not be annulled

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: except by the consent of both parties, and he was sure that neither Penrose or Ike would consent to withdraw, but they would hold him to the contract until they arrived in California, and as for trying to force either of them to leave, that could not be thought of for a moment, because every man in the train -- or for that matter in other trains -- would side with them, and if it was necessary they would confiscate one of our wagons and teams, and turn them over to Penrose and Ike and I could not stop them from doing so. And that probably would have been the result if Adler had refused to take them farther, for there were hundreds of other men who had made like contracts, and a precedant of that kind might make trouble for many of them, and as the most of the questions that came up  between the men, were usually settled by calling in men of another train to arbitrate the question, Adler would have been left without a foot to stand on, and he had sense enough to know it; and not to take any chances

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
of that kind, but he kept right on upholding John in his numerous cussednesses. The emigration that year to Pike's Peak and California was immense, and much larger than it had been any previous year, or has been in any year since, and prairie schooners were as plentiful on the plains that summer, as were dead animals at every camping ground along that trail.
Horace Greely went by stage across the plains that summer and in one of his letters to the New York Tribune, he estimated that these would die between the Missouri and Sacramento rivers that season as many a one hundred thousand head of oxen, horses and mules, so that one can judge something of the magnitude of the emigration of that year. When John Adler found out that his father could not put Penrose and Ike out and drive off leaving them sitting by the side of the road, without their consent, he began to work a scheme that he hoped would make them both willing to cancel the agreement made with his father, he would compell his father

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
18
to start in the morning before the rest of the train was ready to move, and then travel alone for a couple of days before he would consent to their joining the train again, he did this four or five different times, but as niether Penrose or Ike seemed to care whether they traveled in company of the others or not, he gave that scheme up and turned his attention to trying to annoy Sally Sutton in any way that he could do so, and still keep within the bounds of decency, Penrose spoke sharply to him on two or three occasions after he had frightened her, and Ike threatened to take off his peg leg and break it over his ugly head if he did not stop bothering her. John Adler was a bully by nature and like the majority of that kind of vermin he was also a coward, and his cowardice kept him from committing any meanness that would be this cause for a quarrel with either Penrose or Ike, for he knew that both of them would be glad to give him a thrashing that would leave him with more bumps on his body than nature intended that he should have.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: 19 The train went through the South Pass of the Rocky Mountains, and when it arrived at Sublette's Cut-off, which rout was supposed to shorten the distance to Raft river 22 miles, Adler was in favor of taking that route, for the reason that they could gain one days travel over the train, which intended to follow the old trail, and by doing so they could stay in camp one day and give their oxen a needed rest, and join the train at Raft river. Neither Penrose or Ike made any objections to this arrangement, so Adler decided to take the Cut-off and a man and his wife by the name of Green, who had two yoke of oxen and a light wagon, joined the party. The Overland Stage route went through the Cut-off and there were several Stage Stations from 10 to 15 miles apart along the route. The Adler's and Green traveled along togather, and on the following Saturday they camped on a small creek about a quarter of a mile from a Stage Station. Adlers two wagons were on one side of the creek and close togather; Green's wagon was

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
20
the opposite side of the creek and about 30 yards distant from them. Sunday morning Mrs Green, Sally and William Adler went a berrying along the creek, they found a quantity of wild currants, and the Adlers and Green's had currant pie for their dinners.  Early that afternoon Adler, Penrose, Green and Ike went to the Stage Station and played a few games of 'Seven up', and they also indulged themselves by drinking a few glasses of Valley tan- that is-, Mormon whiskey made from potatoes and wheat. Sally Sutton, after failing to get Mrs Green to go with her, went alone down the creek in search of currants for supper, when she left the camp both John and William Adler were lieing in the shade of one of the wagons asleep. She had filled her bucket with currants, and was leisureally making her way back to the wagons, when she was startled by a rustling of the bushes behind her. She stopped to find out what had caused the noise, and she was almost paralyzed when she saw what she took to be either a wolf or a bear running towards

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: 21 her. She screamed and started on a run towards the wagons, after she had run a short distance She turned to see if the animal was following her, but instead of seeing either a bear or wolf, she saw John Adler a few rods behind her, she increased her speed and soon came out into an open spot, and ran sobbing into the arms of her Uncle James Penrose, who with his companions was returning from the Stage Station. Sally told her Uncle that John had scared her by running on all fours through the bushes, and then he had raised to his feet and chased her. Both Penrose and Ike indulged in some strong language in regard to his actions, and Ike suggested that Penrose get his rifle and shoot the _____whelp! and before the conversation ended a revolver was fired but not at John Adler, for as soon as he discovered the party he skulked back and disappeared into the bushes before he had been seen by any of them. Penrose swore that he would give him a pounding when he saw him that

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
22
he wouldn't get over for the rest of his life, and Ike was equally anxious to be the first one to meet the pup, but John kept away from camp until both Ike and Penrose were sound asleep in their blankets under a wagon, then he came sneaking back and he and his father held a long conversation togather before they went to their beds. As they intended to continue their journey the next day, they were all early risers the next morning. Penrose got up and went down to the creek for a morning bathe just as the sun began to show above the eastern horizon, Green came from his wagon and accompanied him to the camp fire where Mrs Adler and Sally were preparing breakfast. Penrose stopped near the fire and held first one hand then the other over the blaze while he continued his conversation with Green, until Adler called to Green to come to him as he wanted to ask his advice about some trumped up scheme. Ike at the time was on the opposite side of the wagons greasing the wheels. Green left the camp fire and started for the wagon where Adler was,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: 23 As he turned towards the wagons he saw a gun barrel resting on a wheel of the rear wagon, and he saw John Adler in the act of sighting it, befor he had had time to take but a step or two towards the boy, a bullet came whistling past his head, it startled him so badly that he sprang to one side, and at the same time he heard both Mrs Adler and Sally scream, he then turned towards the camp fire he had just left, and there he saw Mrs Adler kneeling by the side of Penrose who was lieing prostrate on the ground, and Sally was screaming with every breath she drew. Mrs Adler was wringing her hands and moaning, "My poor Jim they have killed you at last! and John done it with your own rifle." Green went to the fallen man but he could not help him in any way, for the bullet had passed through his heart heart killing him instantly. Sally threw herself down by the side of her Uncle and raised his head to her lap and cried, "Oh what will become of me now? for they have killed you, Uncle Jim, to get you out of the way." Ike came to the camp fire and after one glance at Penrose's body, he turned and started

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
24
towards his wagon without saying a word, Mrs Green came over to offer her assistance just as Adler appeared on the scene with a rifle in his hands, he ordered Green and his wife to go to their wagon and stay there until he was ready to leave the camp, and then he threatened to shoot both of them if either told any one how Penrose had lost his life. Green and his wife went to their wagon, and Green went to get his gun, but it was not in its accostomed place and he could not find it in the wagon; it had mysteriously disappeared. When Ike left the place where Penrose was lieing he went to his wagon to get his rifle, where he was confronted by John Adler with Penrose's rifle- which he had shot him with-, in his hands, John said to him, "I am the boss now, and you will have to do as I tell you, Your rifle is where you will never see it again, and Green's gun has also been taken care of, so you need not expect any help from him, Dad and me have the only two guns in the outfit in our own hands and we will see that

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: 25 they don't get out of our reach, and if you tell anybody how Jim Penrose met his death I will kill you." Adler also threatened to kill Mrs Adler and Sally if they ever said a word about Penrose's having been shot. Although Adler and John had been the prime movers in a tragedy, they finished the cooking of the interupted breakfast, which none of the others felt like eating. When John found that Ike did not want any breakfast he oredered him to get a shovel and dig a grave to put Jim Penrose's carcass in, continuing he said, "You can tell Greene to come and help you, and when you get it done throw Jim in and cover him up, for I wont help you, I have done my share in putting him out of the way and now you can do the rest, and then we will both have a hand in getting rid of a bad man." The young assassin indulged himself in giving full vent with his tongue, to his hatred of Penrose, until his father interfered and threatened to club him if he said another word before Mrs Adler and Sally about Penrose.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
26
Ike and Green were both in unfavorable possitions to oppose John Adler, for neither of them had a weapon, and they knew that his father would side with him in any controversy that might arise between them, so they concluded that the best they could do was to do as he bid them as cheerfully as they could, until they overtook a train, and then they would report the murder of Penrose. After they had dug a grave they wrapped Penrose's body in a blanket and Ike and Green lowered it into the ground. Mrs Adler was almost delerious from grief, but she managed between her paroxysm's of sobbing to repeat the Lord's Prayer over her brothers remains, and then the grave was filled and a mound of stones were piled on it, to protect it from being travelled over by the wagons of other campers on that spot. Neither Adler or John paid any attention to the burial of Penrose, they seated themselves on a wagon pole, with their backs turned twards the group around that lonely grave, and conversed togather until the services at the grave were completed.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
27
Chapter XXI
Life may be worth living and it may not, it all depends on whether it is your life or the other fellows.
The boy William had taken the oxen down the creek at day light and he knew nothing of the murder until he returned with them to camp, while they were burying Penrose. He inquired of his father what had happened, John answered his question by saying, "Jim Penrose shot at me last night with a revolver, and to protect my own life I shot him with his own rifle this morning, but if you ever tell any body that I shot him I will kill you too, now get your breakfast and remember what I have just told you for I mean just what I have said, so look out!, and I don't want to catch you a talking to Green and his wife, or Ike about this affair, for if you do I will give you such a pounding that you will wish you had't, dad and me are the bosses now, for both Green and Ike have lost their guns and they will never find them

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
28
again, so dad and me will run this show to suit ourselves." William knew that in the death of Penrose he had lost his best friend, for Penrose had oftern taken his part and saved him from the brutality of John, he knew that he need not look to his Father for any help in any controversy that he might have with John, wnd he also knew that neither Ike or Green could help him now, for they were both as much under the dominion of John as he himself was, So he decided to do what he was ordered to do, as [[?]] he could, and hope that he would soon be released from such degrading slavery. As soon as possible after the burial of Penrose they got ready for the road, Adler took the precaution to have Green's wagon between his own two wagons, where he could keep an eye on him and see that neither he or his wife held any conversation with any of the men at the Stage Stations on their route, and John kept a strict guard over Ike to keep him from having any intercourse with any one at the Stations either. Adler and John took turns in carrying their guns during the day, and at night

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
29
one or the other remained on guard to make sure that none of their prisoners escaped.
Three days passed without any incident worthy of note happening to them, but on Thursday, the fourth day since the murder of Penrose, they arrived at Raft River about 10 oclock in the forenoon. The trail through Sublette's Cut-off comes into the old emigrant trail a short distance east of Raft river. Adler's intention was to not make any stop at that point on the river, but to push onward as fast as he could, and put as much distance between his three wagons-for he had taken full control of the movements of the Green's-, and the train he had traveled with from Missouri. He felt sure that he would arrive at the river before that train did, and as he intended to travel alone in the future, and camp at some distance from any other wagons, by doing in this way he hoped that the murder of Penrose would not become known outside of his own party before they arrived in California, and once there he had no fear of the result of its becoming known. As early as it

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
30
was in the day there was already several large trains in camp on the river bottom, and the trail ran so near to some of the camps that Adlers wagons could not pass by without being seen by some one in the camps. When they had first sighted the river, Mrs Green, Mrs Adler and Sally were walking a short distance ahead of the wagons, Adler called to them to stop and when the wagons came up he oredered them to get into their wagons and keep out of sight, he had no fear that they would disobey him for they had been so badly terrorized by John's brutal conduct ever since the day of the murder, that they dared not disobey either him or his father. They passed two or three camps and from each came the hail, "Hello! neighbor! where do you hail from." Adler without stopping his wagons, replied to each question, "Missouri," and he was allowed to move on without hindrance, but unfortunately for his well laid plans, the next party that wanted to know where he hailed from, were also from Missouri, and when he replied that he was from Missouri, his wagons were

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
31 
immediately surrounded by a throng of men and women, all eager to hear the latest news from their dear old Missouri. So many gathered around the wagons that their progress was efectually bloked, by the chance meeting of those people 2,000 from their native homes, Mrs Adler was recognized by an old school mate, and in a short time she had told him the story of her brothers murder. Mrs Adler and Sally were taken in charge  by her friend, and Adler was ordered to go into camp immediately, he objected and he did some blustering in vigorous language against being stopped on the highway, and compelled to go into camp against his will, but the threatning attitude that some of those who surrounded his wagons assumed, convinced him that he had better comply to their demands without further protest, he told his two boys to drive down near the river and they woul camp for a while. As soon as they had been halted by the crowd, Green drove his wagon out to one side, and Ike-who was driving the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
32
last wagon-, deserted his post and mixed in with the crowd, he was soon surrounded by men and women who were anxious to hear all about the murder even to the smallest item.
About noon the train that Adler had left at the east end of the Cut-off arrived at the river and camped, in a few minutes the story that John Adler had shot James Penrose to death, was known by every person in the train, the most of the men and many of the women in the train, had known Penrose and his sister Mrs Adler all of their lives, and some of them were also well acquainted with the Adlers. As soon as the news that the train that Adler had started with from Missouri, had become generally known to have arrived, men from the other trains came flocking into their camp, some had advice to give, others were seeking information as to what it was best to do under the circumstances, and the excitement caused by this cold blooded murder ran high amongst those Southerners, and when a man joined the party in haste, and in a loud clear

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
33
voice said, "Men, I just now saw that skunk John Adler, a strutting round with his thumbs stuck in the arm holes of a vest that I know belonged to Jim Penrose, and the cur said-, Yes I'm the man that shot Jim Penrose, and I would like to have a chance to do it again." The crowd went nearly wild with excitement, some were for lynching the young assassin at once and some started to get ropes to hang him with, and others wanted him shot with the rifle he had killed Penros with, and it was suggested that he be burned at the stakes. That assemblage of men soon began to resemble a mob of frienzied men who only waited a signal to begin to burn, pllage and murder, but fortunately they had no leader to urge them on, and say follow me. Amongst the emigrants assembled there, there were several lawyers, also doctors and two or three ministers, as well as many other men who had been prominent in public affairs in the localities from which they came, and among the rest were two or three men who had served terms as county or circuit Judges.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
34
After a time several of these men succeeded in quieting the turbulance of the crowd, so that a proposition to hold a mass meeting and determine what it was best to do in the case could be heard, the proposition was received with cheers, and a mass meeting was called to meet at 1,30 P, M.  When the meeting convened a Chairman and Secritary were chosen and the meeting was declared ready for business, a motion was offered that an election be held to elect a Judge, Prosecuting Attorney, Sheriff and a Constable, the motion was unanimousely carried, the Chairman was then authorized to appoint three Inspectors to receive and count the ballots cast, then the meeting adjourned without date. Caucuses were at once held to nominate candidates for each of the four offices, After the election four of the candidates were declared duly elected, the oath of office was administered to the Judge elect by one of the ministers, and then the Judge administered the oath to the others according to the statutes of the State of Missouri. As soon as these

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: 35 ceremonies were concluded, Ike swore out a warrant against John Adler charging him with the willful murder of James Penrose, and also one against his father Thomas Adler as being an accessory both before and after the crime was committed. The two warrants were placed in the hands of the Sheriff with orders to arrest the two men. The Sheriff and Constable arrested the two Adllers, a tent for their use was secured and they were confined to its limited space. Then a jury of twelve men was drawn by writing the mames of 120 men  who were assembled on the grounds, on seperate slips of paper, ten of the slips were placed in each of twelve hats, and after the Sheriff had been blindfolded he drew one slip from each hat, and the owner of the name on the slip became a jury man. The Court was held in the open air and barrels, boxes, tubs, kegs and other articles that could be used for desks or seats were brought into use, The Jury were sworn and after they had chosen a foreman, the Court was declared ready for business. An ex-judge and

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
36
a lawyer to assist him, were appointed Counsel for John Adler, and another prominent lawyer was assigned to assist the prosecuting Attorney. John Adler was arrainged for the willful murder of James Penrose, he plead not guilty and his trial began. There was a strong array of witnesses against him, Mrs Adler and Sally, Mr and Mrs Green and Ike, and they each swore to the facts of the murder as they ahve already been related. The prisoner was allowed to testify in his own defence, he swore that Penrose had oftern threatened to kill him, and that on that Sunday evening he had shot at him with a revolver, that he had brought home with him from California two or three years before. Mrs Green was then called to the witness stand in rebuttal, She swore that the day before they started from home, James Penrose gave her a revolver and it only had one chamber loaded, he said he has lost the bullet moulds, and he then jokingly continued that if she ever had occasion to use it on some big Indian who insisted upon her going with him and be his squaw,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
37
after she had fired that one shot she could throw it at her assailants head and do him more damage thatn she was likely to do with it loaded. She then produced a small revolver which in those days was known by the name of Allen's pepper box, and holding it above her head she said, "I wish to testify that this is the identical revolver that James Penrose gave me before we started from Missouri, and that it has not been out of my possession since the day he gave it to me, and I also swear that it was me and not Penrose who fired that shot, and John Adler saw me when I fired into the air, and he pulled off his straw hat and swung it around his head." She was asked why she had fired the revolver. She replied that she had no reason for doing so, for it was just a momentary whim that caused her to do as she did, She  had heard Sally's screames and also the loud talking of the four men, and the thought had come to her to try and see if she could not scare them, and then have a laugh at their expense.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
38
The trial ended and the Counsel on both sides sumed up the case, and then the Judge charged the jury and they retired to deliberate on the matter. After an absence of ten minutes the jury returned with virdict of murder in the first degree against John Adler for the shooting of James Penrose, and they recommended that he pay the penalty for his crime of being hanged by the neck until he was dead. After giving the prisoner a chance to say whatever he wished to, the Judge sentenced him to remain in the custody of the Sheriff until 9 oclock the next morning, and then to be hanged by the neck until he was dead. As soon as sentence had been pronounced on John, the case of Thomas Adler as accessory to the act of Penrose's murder was called. A new jury was impounded in the same manner that the other jury had been chosen. The evidence taken in the other was gone over, and then the case was given to the jury, after deliberating for half an hour, the jury brought in a verdict of guilty of being an accessory after the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
39
deed had been committed, and they recommended that the Court impose a severe punishment on him. The Judge called to his assistance several men who had been prominent in public affairs of their native States, and after a lengthy consultation they came to the decision that Adler's punishment should be a severe one, and the Judge's sentence was that his best four yoke of oxen and best wagon should be given to Mrs Adler, and of the provisions and supplies that he still had, there should be given to her all in excess of a quantity sufficient to last him and his boy William until they arrived at Carson City Na, and that he should give all the money he had with him, more than 50 dollars to Mrs Adler, and he should also be barred from traveling with any of the wagons then in camp at that place.
The Judges sentence in Adlers case may seem to be somewhat arbitrary, especially the last clause of it, but we must bear in mind the fact that a human life had been taken in a cold blooded manner, and that the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
40
perpetraters of the crime were then in the hands of men who were terribly in earnest, and that the majority of them thought that Adler was as guilty of the murder of Penrose as his son was, and that he should also be hung, the Arbitration Committee undoubtedly knew that there was a feelilng antagonistic to Adler among the men in the different camps, when they decided that he should not be allowed to travel with any of the trains then in camp, and thus protected him the best they could, from a possibility of yet being lynched by some of Penrose's friends. The Judge appointed three men to carry out the provisions of the sentence. Adlers two wagons were unloaded, and in one of them they found Green and Ike's guns. After a division of the supplies had been made, the wagons were again loaded and the one intended for Adlers use was drawn to some distance from the other one. Adler was then ordered to produce all of the money he had with him; by that time he was so thoroughly frightened for his own

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
41
Safety, that he did so without making any protest, he gave up more than $5,000 in gold and nearly $400 in silver, 50 dollars was returned to him and the rest was given to his wife, Adler was then released from the custody of the Sheriff and told to look out for himself. That evening Mrs Adler sent for William Adler to come to her wagon; She gave him 500 dollars in gold after he had promised her that he would not let his father know that she had given it to him.
Adler prepaired a supper for John and carryed it to the tent where he was confined, he remained in conversation with John while he ate the supper, after he was done eating, Adler gathered up the few dishes he had used and while he was doing so, the Sheriff noticed that he slipped something into John's hand. After Adler had left the tent the Sheriff asked John what his father had handed him, John denied that he had handed him anything, but his denial did not satisfy the Sheriff, who began to search him

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
42
and he soon found a razor, he asked him what he intended to do with that razor, he replied. "Cut my throat before morning, and cheat this mob out of the pleasure of hanging me." The Sheriff notified the Judge of the incident, and he told him not to allow his father to meet him again until the hour set for his execution.
The following morning two wagons were placed with the front ends facing each other about eight feet apart, the pole of each was raised perpendicular and fastened securely in place, a third wagon pole was used for a cross beam to fasten the rope to, thus making an improvised gallows on which John Adler was hanged at 9 A.M, without any ceremony other that a prayer by one of the ministers. After he had been declared dead by the Doctors who were present, his body was taken down and buried in a grave already prepared to receive it, and this last act ended that tragedy, and those congregated there began at once to leave their camps.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
43
What I have told of this affair was told me by members of Adlers family and by a man who was a near neighbor of Adler in Missouri, but what follows will be my personal observation and knowledge. About 9 oclock on the morning that John Adler was hung, the train that I was with came in sight of Raft river, we noticed the large assemblage of wagons gathered togather, and there was considerable speculation amongst us as to the cause of so large a gathering, Some of our men who were walking ahead of the wagons thought that a beef had been killed for they could see an object hanging betwen two wagons, but it was so far away they could not make out what it was. By the time we had arrived on the scene all of that vast gathering of wagons had left the grounds except one, and a few yards from the trail there was a newly made grave, and a board at its head told us that the object seen hanging between the two wagons was a human being, and not a carcass of beef, for on the board there was carved in rude letters this inscription. "John Adler Aged 19 Hung for the Murder of James

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
44
Penrose." Below this inscription there was written with a lead pencil this date, "Aug 12 1859." We soon discovered that the lone wagon we found at the river belonged to the father of John Adler, but he would not give us any information in regard to the murder, in fact he would not talk about the matter neither would his son William who was the only person with him, and I never heard either of them mention the subject, we soon saw that they wished to be left to themselves, and we respected their wishes by keeping away from them, although we were just bursting from curiosity to learn of the particulars of that murder. Adler and his boy were like the proverbial Clam for they could both keep a closed mouth. Adler asked permission to travel in our company for a few days, and his request was granted.
When we left the camp about noon, Adler fell in behind the other wagons, and while he was with us he followed along in our rear, and at night he camped 10 or 15 rods from our wagons, and neither he or his boy sought any intercourse with any of us.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
45
It happened that my mess was short of flour, so I thought I would try Adler and see if he had any to sell, that evening I went to his wagon and asked him if he had any flour to sell, he replied, "I don't know but I will see how much I have got on hand, how much do you want?" I replied that I would take 50 pounds if he could spare it, he then said, "Come round in the morning and I will let you know, good night." The next morning I went to his wagon, he pointed to a grain bag partly filled and said. "There is 50 pounds of good flour in that bag, and I raised the wheat from which it was made, you can have it at my price." I asked him how much he wanted for it, he replied, "Ten dollars." I handed him a 10 dollar gold piece, and shouldered the bag, as I was leaving he said, "Empty that bag as soon as you can and bring it back." I carried my prize to the mess and mighty glad we were to get that flour even if we did have to pay ten cents a pound for it. This little business transaction with Adler did not help us

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
46
in learning any of the particulars of the murder or hanging, for he refused to be sociable and exchange lies with any of us, and he would not talk either on that subject or any other, so that when we camped four days later in the Thousand Springs Valley, we knew nothing more about that tragedy than the board at the head of the grave had told us. Three or four large trains were already in camp, and it happened that the train that Adler had left Missouri with was one of them. We were soon surrounded by men from those trains all anxious to know from what part of  "God's Country," we had come, and each one also hoped to hear some news from the vicinity of their dear old homes. Even the news that Sam Stubb's son Obediah had eloped with his step mother, and left old Sam to get in his crop alone, would have been welcomed by that news hungry crowd.
After supper I lighted my pipe and took a stroll through the several camps to see if I could find any body that I knew. I finally came to a camp fire near which were seated on camp stools two women, a girl, and two men,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
47
What had attracted my particular attention to the group was a liver colored greyhound that was standing near the girls stool, which I recognized for he had been in my possession for two or three weeks a couple of months before. I approached the party and said. "Don, old fellow! I did not expect to meet you here." At the sound of my voice the dog ran to me wagging his tail, and the girl after looking at me a moment, turned to one of the women and said, "O Ma! here is the man that had Don," then she turned to me and continued, "A'int you mister?" I replied, "yes I am the man that restored Don to you," but I will have to digress a bit. When we were in camp 10 or 12 miles west of Omaha waiting for our oxen to become used to living on grass and water only, without any mixed feed for desert, but they got plenty of desert later, when we were crossing it, for we had left civilization behind us and a thousand mile Journey had to be made before we could buy a postage stamp or a tomb stone. One day a returning Pikes Peak train stopped for an hour near

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
48
our camp, One of the men asked me if I wanted a dog, I asked him what kind of a dog he had to dispose of, he whistled and a liver colored greyhound came running to him, he was a fine looking, full grown animal, patting him on the head he said, "This is the dog, I dont want to take him home with me, and all I ask for him is that you treat him kindly."
I accepted the dog on the tearms he had proposed, and after telling me that the dog answered to the name of Don he left us. My pardners and I got some fun out of chasing Jack rabbits with Don, but we never saw him catch one for in a two mile race Joack would distance him about 40 rods every time and disappear.
Some three weeks afterwards we camped one evening on the Platte river a short distance below a large emigrant train. After we had had our suppers we discovered that Don was missing, I went up to the other camp to see if he was there, I found him apparently very much at home in a group eating their supper, the party consisted of a woman and a girl about 14, four men and a boy.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
49
I spoke to Don and he started to come to me, but the girl stopped him by throwing one arm over his neck, I approached nearer to the party and the woman asked me if I claimed to be the owner of that dog, I replied that I did, she asked, "Where did you get him." I told her how he had come into 
my possession. She replied, "Well the dog belongs to my daughter, and he was stolen from us one night when we were in camp on the Loup Fork, a train on its way east from Pikes Peak passed our camp some time during the night, and I suppose Don followed them a ways and then they kept him." The girl then approached me leading Don by his collar and said. "Uncle Jim gave Don to me when he was little puppy, and I have cared for him ever since that time, and I am sure you will not be so cruel as to insist upon taking him away from me now, will you?"
I told her that I would not deprive her of her pet, and I assured her that I was made very happy by being instrumental in restoring Don to her. Her mother said that

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
50
if Don had been any expense to me she would repay me. I replied that Don had not cost me anything, and I did not wish any pay for returning him. Both the Mother and daughter were profuse with their thanks, and when I had said good night, I started to return to my wagon carrying with me a distinct conviction that my mission on earth was to make others happy if-it did not cost me anything. The male members of the party had remained silent during our conversation, so I had not particularly noticed any of them, and as there had been no occasion for an interchange of names, I did not learn the name of any of them, but I was to know more about them later. 
Now having explained how I became acquainted with that dog, I will return to the Thousand Springs Valley and take up the broken thread of my story. As I have said the girl inquired if I was not the man that had her dog, and I replied that I was. The girl then said, "Ma this is the man that returned Don to us on the Platte river." Her mother greeted

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
51
me kindly and asked me to take a seat, then she said to the girl, "Sally get a stool for the gentleman." As I seated myself I noticed that one of the men wore a peg leg, and the thought flashed through my mind that I was in the presence of a portion of the Adler family, and my surmise was confirmed after I had given my name, by the woman's saying, "These are Mr and Mrs Greene, this is my cousin Ike Penrose, my daughter Sally and my name is Adler." After the introduction Ike said to Mrs Adler, "Do you see that wagon out there?"- pointing towards Adlers wagon which was at least a quarter of a mile distant from its nearest neighbors,- She answered "Yes." "Well," he continued, "Thats Tom Adlers wagon." She passionately replied, "Now Ike, I want you to promise me that you will keep away from him, and let him alone, for he has alrady done us all the harm that I can stand, and I do not want to ever meet him again, for fear that I might be tempted to avenge my brothers murder by killing him with the same weapon that he counseled John to kill poor Jim with. You must not

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
52
quarrel with him, for Sally and I have no protector but you now." After this outburst our conversation became general. They told me all of the incidents connected with the murder of James Penrose, and of the trial of John Adler and his execution, also of the trial of his father for the same crime, and of the punishment that he had met with by the confiscation of the larger portion of his property. From their conversation I could see that they all believed that the murder of Penrose was planed while the father and son were seated on the wagon pole the night before, and that Adler was equally guilty, and that he should have received the same punishment that was inflicted upon his son.
They informed me that their train was going to cross the Navada Mountains by the Truckee rout, which would take them into the northern part of the State. When I returned to my wagon and it became known that I had had an interview with Mrs Adler I soon became the centre of a group of men who were anxious to learn the particulars

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: of that tragedy, and it was long after the usual hour for retireing before any of us got to bed, when we got up the next morning, the Missouri train had broken camp, and the near wagons were barely in sight, and we did not overtake them again. When we left camp that morning, Adler had not yet yoked up his oxen, and I did not see  again until four or five days after my train arrived at Carson City where we disbanded and separated. In a few days we were spread out over that region of country in small parties in pursuit of that fickle jade Fortune. A number of the men remained in Nevada, where silver ore had been discovered, but a short time before, in large quantities at Virginia City and Gold Hill, but the most of the men crossed the Nevada mountains to California. Of the 51 men whom I had been associated with for four months, I have not met or heard of but two or three of them since we parted in Carson CIty in September 1859.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: One afternoon several days after our arrival at Carson City while returning from Washoe Valley I saw an emigrant wagon coming from the direction of the Carson river that I recognized as belonging to Adler, when I reached the emigrant trails I stopped and waited for him to overtake me, when he came up we entered into conversation, after a while he asked me if I knew of a good place where he could camp on the outskirts of the city, I told him that there was a good place not far from where I was camped, and before I left him I pointed out the direction he was to drive in order to reach it, but for some reason he did not seek that place but camped elsewhere. I did not see him again for several days, I inquired when he intended to cross the mountain over to Placerville, he replied that he intended to remain at Carson City and not go any further west at present, for he had got a job of hauling ore from a mine to the Stamp Mills, and he thought that he could do better at that than in California. I did not meet him again before I started over the mountains, but I met his son William several times before I went.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription: The first of November '61 found me stationed at Fort Churchill on the Carson river 32 miles east of Carson City, for I had enlisted in a Cavalry regiment a few months before. I was acting Hospital Steward at the Fort for several months, and one of my duties was to fill out discriptive blanks for men who came to the Fort to enlist. One morning I filled out the blank for a man by the name of Benton, after I got through he asked me if I hadn't crossed the plains in '59. I replied that I had, he then said, I thought I had seen you before somewhere, you are the man that had a dog which was stolen from a girl in a Missouri train are you not?" I replied that I was, and then I asked him if he knew those people. He answered that he had known them all his life, for he was born and raised within half a mile of Adlers home, he told me that he had seen Mrs Adler about two months before. She had bought a ranch near Red Bluffs [[?]], which Ike Penrose managed for her, and also that the Green's had also bought a small ranch in the vicinity, and they were all prospering and living in comfort. Berton asked me if I had seen or heard anything of Adler since we left Thousand Springs Valley. I told him about my seeing him in Carson City when he

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
58
arrived there, and also that I saw him and William in the crowd that was gazing at us when we came through Carson City on our march to Ft Churchill, the last of the previous Oct. Benton said that he had been in Carson City for two weeks before he came down to the Fort, but he did not meet Adler and he was glad that he did not but he would like to meet Will for he had always been a manly good natured boy, and he was liked by all who knew him.
During the following summer I was in Carson City several times, but I did not meet Adler, but I met William two or three times, he told me that his father was still hauling ore with the oxen he had brought from Missouri, and that he had bought a four mule team and wagon, and hired a man as driver. It looked to me as though Adler was prospering beyond his deserts, and it also looked very much as though the way of the Transgressor was usually smoothed for him and kept well greased. That fall my Troop of Cavalry was transfered to Utah, a week or so before we started, I met William Adler, he told me that his father was doing well and that he had bought another four mule team and wagon, and that is the last I have heard from any of those people.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
55
Chapter XXII
The worst use you can put a man to is to hang him; if he deserves a capital punishment marry him to a grass widow.
By the time my story was concluded we arrived at Sam's house, and I stopped with them for the night. After we had had supper the Sage's, Murray's, Carpenter's, Roger's, and Purdy's came in, and I have since thought that it was not wholly by accident that they all chose the same evening to make a friendly call upon Sam and his wife, but be that as it may, I had not been comfortably seated but a few minutes before Sam turned my cup of nectar to gall by saying, "Come Sergeant, you are having altogather to much comfort there in that corner, so tune up and tell us about that lynching affair that you were to tender hearted to witness, so go a head and make us all comfortable." The others- especially the ladies-, intreated me to relate the story. I replied that it was not much of a story, but such as it was I would try to make as interesting as I

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
58
could- afford to. I then related the following incident. In the Spring of '63, 25 men- of which number I was one-, of my troop of Cavalry under the command of 2d Lieutenant Bradley, were detailed to escort three Officers who had been commissioned to choose a site for a small Army Post on or near the Bear River in Idaho, a short distance from the Southern border of that territory. Our outfit consisted of a mule pack train loaded with twenty days rations, and also a four mule ambulance to carry the Officers baggage, mess kit and a tent for their use, as for the rest- well the open air and dry ground was all that we required, and it was all that we got in the way of sleeping quarters when on a march. We left the Fort one pleasant morning in early June and during the 25 days that the most of us were gone, we did not encounter a single rain storm. Our route lay over the same ground that we had marched over, 250 strong- the preceding January when the ground was covered with snow to a depth of 10 or 12 inches, and on that march we did not have any tents, or any other method of protecting ourselves from the severely cold

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
59
weather that we encountered other than our clothing and blankets. Each trooper was provided with two heavy woolen blankets and two men bunked togather, After they had chosen a place for their bed chamber, they cleared the frozen ground of all the snow, then two blankets were spread on it to lay on, and the other two and their large caped overcoats were used for covering, then with their saddles for pillows, and their guns lieling on the borders of the lower blankets to keep them dry, and their revolvers housed in their boots, they were ready to crawl into beds that even a tramp might envy-, where they could sleep soundly until the bugle sounded Reveille at day light, unles the bugle sounded Asemble and Boots and Saddles in the middle of the night, which it frequently had a way of doing, and turning us out from our sweet dreams of home and kindred, to face the stern realities which beset us. Bugles in appearance are harmeless looking instruments, but not the less they make lots of troubles for troopers, for bugles are like guns in the respect that they envaribly go off when you dont want them to. Mrs Sage wanted to know if the troopers ever

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
60
said any prayers before they went to bed. I replied that I had never witnessed a demonstration of their doing so, and that as a usual thing a troopers prayer was apt to be more profane than spiritual and they were always extempore, short and to the point; (Some people when they pray ask for so much that it would take all summer to deliver the goods.) Now the ostensible object of our January expedition was to attack and destroy an Indian Village on the Bear River 120 miles distant. We accomplished our task and incidently we also succeeded  in planting the seed for a crop of rheumatism, twinges of which would draw anathemas from a stoic or tears from a potatoe- bug-. That seed was in a sound state and evergreen, and it never has been winter killed, its harvests come early and stay late and they are always abundant, and the majority of those troopers who have not yet been mustered out and joined the great majority, have for the past 25 or 30 years, probably been applying liniment and profanity in alternate doses to their rheumatic limbs. As it has already been said;

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
61
there are two things to be done with rheumatism- grin and bear it, or bear it and not grin-.
But such is the fortune of war and all Soldiers have to swallow many other things besides Angel food. Our journey was without incident and we went into camp on the on the Bear river on the afternoon of the fourth day after we left the Fort. The following day we spent in riding over the adjacent country in search of a good location to establish a new Army Post. Before night came the officers completed their task by locating a government reservation at Soda Springs Idaho, which in honor of the General in command of that army district they named Camp Connor. The next morning the three Officers with their ambulance, and an escort of six troopers started on their return march to the Fort, where they arrived in safety. By previous orders the Lieutenant and the remainder of the detail were left behind to scout over the country adjacent to the Bear and Malad rivers, and locate any Indian Villages that we found, so that we could find them again afterwards.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
62
But our search proved fruitless, for we did not get a sight of an Indian during our Scout. After we had been out long enough to eat all of our rations except enough to last us until we got back to the Fort, we started on our return march and headed for the Stage road that ran from Brigham City Utah to Boise City Idaho, and that night we camped on the Malad river not far distant from a Stage Staion. About noon of the next day we halted at another Stage Station to bait our horses, and after picketing them on the bottom land near the river, we sought the shade of some Cotton Wood trees that stood about a hundred yards back of the Station house. While we were were eating our lunches of raw bacon and hard tack and washing the same down with Spring water, a party of 20 or 25 men rode up to the Station house with horses on a run and immediately surrounded it. Five or six of the men rode to the back of the house with their revolvers in their hands ready for use, two men covered each of the two back windows, and one man dismounted

[[Transcriber note: bait means to give food and drink to an animal especially on the road]]

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
63
and guarded the door, they had not been in possition more than three minutes before a man rode from the front of the house and spoke to them, they immediatley put up their revolvers and rode back with him, from our location we could not see what was taking place at the front of the house, and we asked each other what it all ment, until some one suggested that it was probably a posse of Vigilantes from Idaho, and that they had probably rounded up another horse thief, this surmise proved to be correct.
