The party remained in front of the house ten or fifteen minutes, and then they started in the direction of the river. As they rode past where we were standing we saw that they had a prisoner with them, he was a fine looking man of perhaps 35 years old, he was on foot and his arms were tied behing him, and to each arm there was tied a picket rope which the men on each side of him kept taut, and several men who rode near him carried their revolvers in their hands ready for instant use, so there was but little likelihood of his escaping with his life.
They had two or three pack animals and we

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
64
noticed that they carried both picks and shovels. When they came opposite of us, their Captain rode up and said to the Lieut, "If you and your men want to see a lynching, you can do so by going out there on the bluff," at the same time he pointed towards some Cotton wood trees whose tops we could see above the bluff-, "And you can all get front seats." The Lieut thanked him and then said, "I do not think that any of my men care to witness the scene, as for me I do not care to go." Then he asked the Capt what crime the man was guilty of, he replied, "Wholesale horse stealing, he was spotted more than two years ago, but he has escaped capture until now, a week ago we struck his trail and we have finally rounded him up with two stolen horses in his possession, and he will now have to pay the penalty that many others have had to do for their misdeeds, and in the same manner, and there are others that we have sworn to either capture and lynch or drive out of the country, and we will keep our oaths, but I must be going, you had better come and see how

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
65
humanely we do what we consider to be our duty." After saying this he put spur to his horse and joined his companions. There were two or three of our men who had a curiosity to witness that lynching, and one of them asked the Lieut if he had any objection to their going out to the bluffs and viewing it. The Lieut hesitated a moment before he answered, then he said. "I shall not order any of you men not to go, but I would prefer that none of you go out there just to witness that lynching. I had hoped that not one of men had a desire to see a human life taken without legal form of law, and for a man who is not in any way interested in the matter to connect himself with it merely to gratify an idle curiosity, manifests a morbid desire or craving to witness some thing more horrible than a head end collission of two locomotives. At first I was tempted to try and rescue that prisoner and hand him over to the civil authorities, but a moments reflection convinced me that an attempt to do so would be useless, for his captors would have riddled his body with bullets at

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
66
the first aggresive movement we made. Now any of you that want to go and see that man lynched can do so, but I think that the less that any of us see of that scene, the less he will have to regret in the future."
None of the men made a move towards the bluff after the Lieut had concluded his little homily, perhaps it was because his remarks had awaken sensibilities that had in the past laid dormant, which upon being arroused, had inserted themselves for the good of their possessor, and made him ashamed to show a desire to go and view the death struggles of a fellow man. At all events the few of us who had expressed a desire to see the lynching, declared afterwards that they were glad they had not seen it. The Vigilantes had been gone about half an hour when we heard the report of a revolver, down below the bluff, we asked each other what that ment, but none of us could tell. Ten or fifteen minutes later the party came riding back and they were leading two fine looking horses, they saluted us as they passed where we were standing,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
67
and they were soon out on the road headed in the direction of Boise City, and that was the last we saw of them. After they had been gone a few minutes the Station Keeper came out to see us and in answer to our many questions he said. "The man that they have just lynched was the Captain of one of the gangs of horse thieves who have their head quarters some where in northwestern Idaho, but none of the Vigilance Committes have as yet been able to locate their rendezvous, so they have been obliged to run them down one by one. Down there by those Cotton wood trees there are now four graves, each one of them was filled by a man who died with his boots on, and all of the four were lynched for horse stealing. The last victim came to the Station early this morning riding one horse and leading another. He asked me if he could get a breakfast, I replied, "Yes, if you have got the price!" He threw me a five dollar gold piece and said, "I shall also want dinner so you can keep the change until I leave for Ogden where I am due to morrow noon." Then he took his

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
68
horses out under the Bluff. He brought his blankets back with him, and after eating breakfast he rolled up in them, and after telling me to have his dinner ready by 12 o'clock, he went to sleep and he did not awaken until I called him to dinner. He had not been seated at the table more than three minutes before the station was surrounded as you saw, and he was immediately covered with a dozzen revolvers and ordered to throw up his hands. Now he probably did not suspect that a posse of Vigilantes was on his trails for he did not take his two revolvers out of his belt and lay them by the side of his plate, as he would have done if he had imagined that he was in any danger of being captured. He cast a hasty glance around him and threw up his hands, as he did so he said. "I surrender! for the jig is up." After he had been disarmed, the Captain told him that he could finish his dinner if he wanted to, he replied, "Thank you, will you join me?" The Captain declined his invitation. As he was leaving the house he turned to me and said. "You can keep that change and

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
69
those two blankets to remember me by, for I wont need them where I'm going, good bye until we meet again." In answer to my question of where he hailed from he replied. "From over on the Green river, where I have got a ranch," later events have proved that story to be a lie. No I have not witnessed any of the lynchings that have taken place down there, although I have been invited to all of them, but there was a hostler here last summer who wend down and saw two of the lynchings. He said that everything was done in a quit orderly manner, the men were given an opportunity to pray, and the party uncovered their heads during the time he was praying. As soon as the body was taken down a bullet was fired into the head, then the body was wrapped in canvas and buried, and he said that he did not hear a profane word spoken on either occasion." In answer to our inquiries if all of those men had been captured at his station, he replied. "No, that man to day was the only one of the four who was captured there. About a year ago the first one was captured

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
70
just below the corral, his horse was shot from under him and he got a bad fall, but he was game to the last, for he empted both his guns at his captors before he threw up his hands, but none of his shots did any harm. His leg was so badly hurt that he could not walk, they put him on a horse and rode down below the bluff up the bank of the river. I went down there and found a newly made grave, and that was all they had left to show that they had lynched their prisoner. The first of last July a posse of Vigilantes rode up to the station with a prisoner securely bound to a horse; the leader of the party was the man that was in command of the posse today. After a few minutes halt they rode down below the bluff. When they returned one of the men said. "That other fellow wont be so lonesome now, for he has got company." One day in October, a posse headed down the river passed the station, the next afternoon they returmed with a prisoner and they also rode down below the bluff, when they returend their prisoner was not with them, but they left them on more

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
71
graves, and now there are four down there, and it begins to look as though there would be a good sized grave yard ready planted within a stones throw of the station, if the Vigilantes continue in the business a few years longer."
We bade the Station keeper goodbye and mounted our horses, we rode down the bank of the river and halted a few minutes near those lonely graves, the four there were in one row, and earth had been heaped on each of them to make a low mound, but there was nothing left in sight to show whose remains reposed beneath either of the mounds, apparently the Vigilantes did not want any of them to ever be identified. We rode quietly away from the spot carying with us much to think about in the future. Ten minits later we were out of sight of the place where four horse thieves had been lynched and three days later we reported at our Post tired and dusty, but all in good healths, and that ends my story of that lynching that I did not witness 
Mrs Purdy asked me if I was tired o talking!, before I had time to reply Sam said

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
72
"No, he never gets tired talking or from talking either." Sam's remark cause considerable merryment among the men present,- but the ladies came manfully to my defense, with such expressions as-, "O! fie Sam;" "that was to bad of you Sam," and, "Sam, I'm ashamed of you," from his wife. As soon as I got the chance I said. "Don't be to hard on poor Sam, for once he is more than half right, because I am sure that I could never become tired while I was trying to entertain a company of as fair ladies as are present to night." My reply gave me the inside track once more, and I kept it to the finish. Mrs Purdy said. "Then if you are not tired Sergeant, and want to entertain us, please relate another reminiscence of your Army life." I replied that it would afford me pleasure to comply with her request, and I would do so by relating a short story about a man we called Goody Winters. 
It has been said, - "that there are times when the still small voice of conscience is as audible as a bass drum," and also- "tis conscience that doth make cowards of us all."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
73
I think that the most conscientious person, or the one with the most sensitive conscience that I ever knew was a man we calld Goody Winters. He belonged to the same troop of Cavalry that I did, he was a good Soldier and he made a fairly good comrade when his conscience was taken a rest. When the weather would permit our forenoon drills usually ended with a charge by platoons, of about a quarter of a mile down a slight descent. Across the course there had been built at equal distances a part, first a ditch four feet wide, next a stone wall four feet high, then a log fence and also a brush fence, and last another ditch, and our horses had to jump those obstructions while on a run. One day while charging down the course, Winters horse stumbled when he jumped the log fence and came down onto his knees and threw Winters over his head, and two platoons rode over to him but fortunately none of the horses stepped on him, as soon as his horse regained his feet he continued the charge without his rider. Winters right shoulder was dislocated by his fall, and he also received

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
74
several bad bruises. Now when he got up off of the ground, instead of first going to the Hospital and having his hurts dressed, he limped down to the stable to see if his horse was badly hurt, he found his horse in his stall, and he patted his neck while he told him how sorry he was that he had hurt his knees, then he was overheard to say, "But it was all my own fault, because I held the curb rein to tight, but I will be more careful for the future and try not to do so again,"- after a moment he continued-. "So forgive me this time old fellow!". After asking the stable police to see that the horses knees were bathed with liniment, he hobbled up to the hospital and had his shoulder yanked into place and his bruises dressed. After using up a yard or so of plasters, and a quart or two of liniment, he got well enough to returned to duty. But in the mean time a man by the name of Gotleib Schultz- he was a German-, whose horse had gone lame, was given Winters horse to ride until his own got well again. A few days before Winters returned to duty, his horse when on a charge

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
75
stumbled near the place where he did with Winters and broke his neck, His rider Schultz besides being badly bruised had his right arm broken, Schultz was helped to the Hospital and when he met Winters he said. "Gootty, dot horse vos some humbugs, both of us he kills mit some preaks and pains, and den he goes out und preaks his own tam neck, dot horse vos von Schackass alreaty, vosn't dot so?" 
Winters came near having a relapse when he heard that his horse had broken his neck, and for several days he was in a quandery whether to give the most sympathy to his dead horse, or to the bruised Schultz, but he compromised the matter by requesting that a mule should be isued to him instead of another horse.
The reason he gave for wanting a mule to ride, was that he could never  bring himself to the point again of riding a horse into any danger. A mule was was issued to him, but I never heard of his wasting any sympathy on him after he had kicked him a few dozzen times. Now perhaps I havn't got as tender a conscience as many people have, but never-the-

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
76
less it has never been the cause of my loosing any sleep on its account, for I have never had to lay awake nights to pull prickers out of it.
Goody Winters conscience would not allow him to ride a horse into any danger because his horse broken his neck, but it did not kick when he rode a mule. When I saw Winters pounding his mule with a club, a couple of months after he got him, I came to the conclusion that his conscience was now in a very healthy condition, and that if he continued associating with that mule a few months longer, it would never bother him any more, and with that prophecy my story ends.
I was immediately urged to tell another story, as I was feeling as jolly as though I had just arrived from Joliet, I complied and related the following incident.
A few days after we got back from out trip up to the Bear river country, of which I have already told you, my Troop of Cavalry was ordered out to guard the Overland Stageline from Indian depredations.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
77
After we had made good Indians of a number of hostiles, and driven the rest away from the Stage route, the troop was divided into three squads of about 20 men each, and we seperated and scouted independently of each other. I was in the squad commanded by our 2d Lieutenant, and during the next three months we rode over a large portion of western and southern Utah. We visited Mormon Settlements several times and bought such luxurys as vegetables, milk, butter, cheese and eggs, although our Army rations were sufficient to supply our needs in the eating line, but we wanted a change of diet once in a month or two. A friend of mine changed his boarding houses, after fried liver had been set before him every meal for three weeks, his landlady said to him, "I forgot to ask you Mr Jones, but you may not like liver." Jones replied, "I don't mind having it for five or six months, but I don't think I should like it for a steady diet." That is the way with a soldier and his Army rations, after a time he begins to hanker for some of his mothers cookery, until

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
78
his sleep is disturbed by visions of roast Turkeys, mince pies and nightmares. The last of Oct we received orders to report at headquarters and we at once begun our homeward march, a few days later we camped on a creek near a small Mormon Settlement, and the uninitiated would have said the the five or six houses that were within a quarter of a mile of our camp, judging from the number of children around each of them, were all school houses. As soon as we came in sight several women rushed out of the houses and down to the creek, and began to hustle a number of calves who were quietly feeding there, towards the barns where they probably thought they would be safe from the depredation of those ungodly Soldiers. Their efforts to drive and pull their unwilling charges was a source of amusement to us. 
When I was returning from picketing out my horse, I saw a woman coming towards camp holding her apron to her face. I stopped and as she came nearer I saw that she was crying, She came up to me and between her sobs said, "I want to see the Captain of you Thives." I asked her what the trouble was and why she

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
79
called us thieves, she replied, "Because you are for some of you men have already stolen one of my calves." It told her that if she would come with me I would take her to our Lieut, on the way I asked her what made her think that some of us had taken one of her calves, she replied, "Because I have got them all in the barn except two and they both had ropes on them, I led them to the door and pulled one of them into the barn, and while I was doing that the other calf run round the corner of the barn, and when I pulled the rope there was nothing hitched to it, for it had been cut, I dropped it and ran out to see what had become of the calf, but I could not see it anywhere and your men cut that rope and stole that calf."
Just then we met the Lieut and Mrs Sanders for that was the name she gave me-, related her tale of woe to him. He asked her how much her calf was worth, she replied, "Three dollars," and then she inquired if he would surely pay for it, the Lieut answered. "If any of my men have taken your calf or anything else I will see that they are paid for, but as yet you have no proof that you calf has been

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
80
taken by anyone, it may be down by the creek under the bank out of sight from your barn." Then he continued, "Several of my men have been to your houses and tried to buy vegetables and milk, butter, cheese and eggs, but at all of the houses they were told that they had nothing to sell them, now havn't you people got any vegetables or dairy products that you will sell us for the ready cash." Mrs Sanders replied, "Yes! we all have produce that we would be glad to exchange for money, but our husbands are away for a week to Tooele city on military duty and we woman are all alone, and we have always been told not to put any trust in soldiers, and we were afraid to say that we had anything to sell for fear that your men would take them any way whether they paid for them or not."
The Lieut replied, "Although we are Soldiers, we are also honorable men and not a gang of thieves, and none of you people need feel any alarm for your own safety, or the safety of your property while we stay here, or that you will not be paid for what

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
87
you sell us." while the Lieut was talking I saw Corporal Hayes coming towards us from the direction of the creek leading his horse, when he came up to us he said to the Lieut. "Begorry [[?]] jist as soon as Foley an Oi tuck the saddles off our horses, the bloody bastes broke away from us and runed down to the creek, an' down [[forninst?]] that barn"- pointing towards Mrs Sander's barn-. "and bedad phwat must one of thim be doin but run over a calf phwat wor in his road, the unmannerly baste!, whin three of the byes seen him do that they's run up to help the calf, poor crature!, an' they's found him wid a broken leg,, thin they's cut the rope phwat wor tied round his neck an' carried him down to the creek an' killed him to aise his aches, but afore they's wint wid the calf they tied a five dollar green back to the end of the rope so that his owner wod not be put to an inconvenience fromthe bad manners of that horse, bad luck to him!'" Now the Corporals story was invented for that occasion, for the truth of the matter was that the calf had been captured and taken down to the creek and killed before those horses ran down there, and the green back

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
82
incident was an afterthought of Hayes, and he put it there himself. Mrs Sanders asked Hayes if the green back was still tied to the rope, Hayes replied that he was sure that it was for none of the men would steel it, then she said, "I will go right back and see if it is there, but I can't yet believe but what you are lieing to me, for our Bishop had often told us that all soldiers are thieves and liars." She started to go home and the Lieut told me to go with her and be sure that she got the greenback. She said to me that they had always been told that the soldiers that were sent to Utah, were all robbers and that the most of them had been in prison, and she could not yet believe that they were honest men. Before I had a chance to reply she quickened her footsteps to a run, we were only a short distance from the barn-, I followed more slowly and when I overtook her she was standing with hands clasped and gazing at the end of the rope round which was wrapped a new green back tied with hair taken from the tail of her calf. After drawing a deep sigh she said, "I was so anxious to know whether that man told the truth or not, I could not wait any longer and ran away

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
83
from you, and now"- with another sigh-" that I have the proof before me that he did tell the truth I feel that I can believe all that your Lieut and you have told me, but,-" another sigh-"we have been shamefully deceived by those in authority over us I cut the green back loose and handed it to her, and she said, "Yes, it is truly a five dollar bill, but-" with another sigh-", it is more than the calf was worth." I told her not to let that bother her for it it was worth that to us, and if she had any more to sell we would take two or three more, and also buy what produce we needed, She said she would sell us all the produce she could spare, and the other women would be glad to sell us what they could spare. I went back to camp loaded down with supplies, and I spread the news that we could buy what we needed at the houses, and in a short time men were coming from those houses loaded with provisions of various kinds, and all kinds of untensils were pressed into service to carry our purchases to camp,- (there was no free delivery in those days)- such as nose-bags, haversacks, camp-kettles, soap and candle boxes, blankets [[?]] and we borrowed

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
84
bags, sacks, wash-tubs and buckets of the women, and I saw two men carrying a wash boiler full of onions, and another man with a churn half full of fresh buttermilk on his shoulder. We bought three more calves for we had been without any fresh meat for three or four days. When we left the Fort in June we took with us- (in the care of herders-), beef cattle enough to give us seven rations of fresh beef out of every ten, but the day before we started on our homeward march we killed our last steer, and now we wanted a change of diet-. Although fat bacon, beans, bread and black coffee, are mighty good company for a lonesome stomach to entertain, they prefer a change of callers often, and they seldom object to anything in the eating lilne, and they have even been known to receive roast-duck, fried oysters and strawberry short cake with pleasure. I need not say that we had a royal feast that night, but we did and we had enough uncooked provisions left to last us for the three days we were on the march before we arrived at the Fort. The next morning while the others were getting ready to break

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
85
camp I mounted my horse and rode over to Mrs Sanders to get two cakes she had promised that she would make, one for the Lieut and the other for me. We had supposed that our molasses keg was empty, but by taking the faucet out of it, I succeeded in squeezing nearly anouther pint out of it, as there was not enough of it to go round I suggested to the Lieut that we get Mrs Sanders make a couple of molasses cakes for us, he told me to go ahead and do so.
When Mrs Sanders promised to make the cakes, it was with a proviso that we should furnish the flour and molasses, and she would donate the other ingredients, the evening before I carried the molasses and about 20 pounds of flour down to her house, when she saw the sack of flour she said, "For goodness sake! what is all that flour for." I replied that it was to make two cakes with, she laughed as she said, "Why that is enough to make a dozzen cakes, and there is not near enough molasses to use up all of that flour." I replied that if that was the case, she could use the molasses and what flour she needed for two cakes, and keep what was

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
86
left to help repay her for her trouble. Mrs Sanders had the two cakes ready for me and they looked so tempting that- Well! if I had been alone I should have probably eaten one of them there and then. When I bade her good bye she made me promise to come and see her if I was ever in that section again. I carryed the two cakes very gingerly until I caught up with my comrades and then I put them in a safe place. Now it so happened that the next summer I was in the vicinity of that little Mormon Settlement for a month, and I called on the Sanders family several times. On one of my visits Sanders told me with a chuckle,"The first time the Bishop visited them after we were there, all of the women jumped on him rough shod, for the lies he had told them about you Soldiers, and since that time he is careful not to go near any of the houses, for fear that he will be mobbed." Now this is not much of a story, except to show that a lie when covered with a greenback, will bring more happiness to an empty stomach, than asscore of naked truths.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 4], 1903
transcription:
87
Chapter XXIII
The first time that we go out to have a good time with the boys, we leave behind us our morals and they never overtake us again.

The following summer Sam Browne, his cousins Robert and George Carpenter and Larry and Joe Murray with their families went out to Delavan lake, where each of them had secured cottages in the vicinity of Petersburgh for two months. Hugh Connor and I remained at home, but I should have gone with them if my financial condition had been in a healthy order, but Hugh could not be coaxed or badgered into going with them. He said, "Ye knows that me heart will be broken wid lonesomeness wid out ye here where Oi can see yere bonny faces ivery day, but Oi cant make meself belave that it wod be for the best to lave me an' Larry's farms to be mismanaged by hired help for so long a toime. But ye are all to go an' have a good toime an:

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
Chapter xix.
The latest news by pigeon post
Direct from Salt Lake City,
Is that each man has fourteen wives
And all deserve our pity.

Two years previous to the occurance of the incidents related in the last Chapter, gold was discovered in California, that is, in the year 1848.
Like magic the lonely trail from the Missouri river to Salt Lake City, became a great highway for travel and thousands of emigrant wagons followed its windings yearly, and the Mormons lost their exclusiveness, for Salt Lake City was on the line of travel and it soon became a market where the emigrants could exchange their sore footed and broken down horses, mules or oxen for stronger animals, and they could barter their surplus provisions for vegetables and meats. From Salt Lake City there was two principal trails to California, the one that was the most traveled was the Humboldt rout, which followed that river down to its sink in the Carson desert, and then to Genoa at the foot of the Nevada Mountains, thence

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[122]
through Strawberry Valley to Hangtown--now named Placerville--the most important place in the middle mining district. The other trail ran southwest from Salt Lake City down through Provo, Lemi, St George and through the mountain meadows into California. This was the most direct rout to the southern mines. This rout was generally taken by emigrants who arrived at Salt Lake City late in the season, not only on account of its passing through or near several settlements, but also because of the climate which was more mild and pleasant than it was likely to be at that season of the year on the more northernly route, down the Humboldt River. But I must now give Ben Rogers a chance to finish his story. "The Strongs tried to be cheerful but neither of them could be resigned to the fate that appeared to be awaiting them. The middle of Oct came without their having again been molested by the Elders, and then Strong had to go up to Salt Lake City to attend a semiannual conference of the Seventies, which convened on the 20th of the month. The house of the Strongs was 30 or 40 rods from any other dwelling, but that

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[123]
did not give either of them any uneasiness, for they lived in a quiet peaceful region, and they were surrounded by friends who would quickly come to their relief in time of need, and the genius hobo had not yet unfolded in its splendor of raiment and cheek, so they were under no apprehension of danger from their immediate surroundings. A stoical thick headed Swede who lived lived with two wives about a quarter of a mile from them, had taken care of the few head of stock that Strong kept which included 3 saddle horses, for the past year, and he had also kept the pile of stove wood from entirely disappearing. With Halver Larsen, the Swede, to look after the needs of his dumb animals, Strong had no anxiety in regard to the safety and comfort of his family during his absence of 10 days or two weeks. He bade his family a fond adieu and mounted his horse for his 60 miles ride to the City of the Saints, little dreaming of the momentous events that would occur before he met them again. At that time the Strongs had three children, the eldes Robby was 12, Charley was 10 and Nellie was 8 years old, they were all bright active

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[124]
and healthy children. On the afternoon of the second day after Strong started for Salt Lake City, an emigrant train went into camp on the creek about a quarter of a mile from the house of the Strong's.The train numbered 13 wagons and each wagon was drawn by 4 horses, the next morning the train did not leave camp, as the trains that camped there normally did, and Robby got permission from his mother to visit the emigrant camp, he had been absent two or three hours when he came rushing into the house all excitement, and short of breath, as soon as he could talk he cried "Mama who do you think I found down to the camp," his mother replied, "I am sure I don't know! Who was it?", Bobby answered, "Why! Uncle Charles of course!", his mother asked him, "What Uncle Charles, have you got more than one?", Robby ran to the front door and threw it wide open before he replied to his mother's question, then he said, "This Uncle Charles," his mother turned towards the open door and saw a stranger standing in door way, one glance at his face told her that her brother Charles Moore stood before her, with a

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[125]
glad cry of, "Oh Charley!", she sprang towards him and was at once enfolded in his arms, and the children completed the tableau by standing with eyes and mouths stretched to their fullest extent. When the excitement of their meeting had in a measure subsided so as to allow of rational conversation, the brother and sister found plenty to talk about, for they had not met before since the year after Mrs Strong's was married 14 years ago. Mrs Strong inquired how her brother had discovered that Robby was her son. Charles Moore replied, "I noticed a boy going round from one camp fire to another, and when he came to mine I asked him where he lived, he pointed to this house, and answered, "Up there in that house sir!", after a few more questions I asked him if he would like to go to California with me, he answered, "Yes sir!, but I can't go now for I have to stay at home now and take care of Mama and Charley and Nellie." Asked him if his father couldn't take care of them and let him go with me, he replied., "Why! no sir, Papa has gone up to Salt Lake City, and he won't be home for two or three weeks." I said, I understand how you are situated

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[126]
now, and you will have to stay and take care of the family until he comes back, he answered, "Yes sir!", I inquired, "what is your mothers name," he answered, "Mama, just mama, that is what Papa, and all of us call her, " then I asked, "What is your Papa's name," he replied, "Don't you know? why he is Bishop Strong." "Now this answer did not greatly surprise me, for I seemed to be expecting just such an answer, but wishing to be sure that I was right in my conjecture that he was my nephew Robby Strong, I asked him if his father did not sometimes call his Mama Hellen," he replied, "Yes sir he does, and when he went away he said, now don't worry about me Hellen, while I am gone." I asked what answer you made him, and he said that you replied, "I will try not to Henry." These answers banished any doubts that I may have had that he was not your son, and then I told him that I was your brother and also his Uncle Charles." Mrs Strong then acquainted him with the possition that her husband now stood in, in regard to his having to take another wife, and that their future life looked dark and dismal to both

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[127]
of them. Moore listened to her Story with close attention, and when she had concluded he abruptly said, "Well Hellen, I will go back to the camp now, but I will return within an hour, and I hope that I shall then have some good news to tell you." Robby and Charley both wanted to go to the camp with him, but he said that he would have to excuse their attendance at that time, but they could go with him the next time he went, and they contented themselves with this promise. Before he left them he cautioned them all not to tell any body that he was a relative of theirs, or that they knew any one in the train. Within the hour he returned, and almost the first question he asked his Sister was. "Hellen, have you a good riding horse and side saddle." She replied, " Yes, I have both, do you want me to take a ride with you?." he answered, "Not today, but I am very glad that you have got a side saddle, for that simplyfies matters and makes our project more easy of accomplishment." He then told her that two of their cousins, Harvey and Amos Moore, sons of their father's brother Thomas, were his partners and that they were now at the Camp.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: And that he had explained to them this possition in which she was placed, and they had decided between themselves that the best thing that she could do under the present circumstances was to leave her home, and with her children go with them to California, where she would be free from any persecution that the Mormon Elders might try to impose upon her in the future. When her brother proposed that she and the children go with him to California, Mrs Strong declared that she could not entertain an idea like that not for a minute, although she was anxious to get away from the Mormons and everything connected with them, but she could never consent to run away from her husband and leave him to fight the villianies of the Elders alone, and if she consented to do so, she knew that she would never see him again; for her running away from him would part them forever, and Henry would be taking other hateful wives, and then she gave many other reasons that in the first flush of excitement come so readily to the mind and find ready vent. But after her brother had explained to her a plan that he and their cousins had decided could be carried to a successful ending

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[129]
without probable danger to any of them, she became interested in its details, and before he had concluded she began to look at the matter in a more favorable light, and when he informed her that they would not only rescue her and the children, but also her husband she gave a willing consent to be guided by them in the matter. As soon as she had consented to go with him, Moore wrote a note to his cousin Harvey, telling him that his sister had consented to go with them, and also telling him and Amos to talk with the other members of the train, and find out if they would stand by them in case of need. He gave the note to Robby and told him to inquire for Harvey Moore when he reached the camp, and give it to him, and then wait and bring back the answer, Charley got permission to go with Robby and they were soon racing down the slope to the camp, and half an hour later they were racing back again. Charles Moore took the note from Robby's hand and read, "We are all right old man! every man in the train is with us in our undertaking, and they can all be depended upon to the end of the chapter."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: The plan that the Moores had decided to follow, was to have Mrs Strong and the three children come to the camp before daylight the next morning when a wagon would be ready to receive them, supplied with an abundance of beds and bedding for them, that had been brought down from the house, so that there could be no possibility of any of them suffering with cold during their journey. As Mrs Strong had already had some experience in travelling with an emigrant train, she would the sooner adapt herself to her new way of living and make herself comfortable. The wagon intended for her use had an inside cover that could be fastened down to the wagon box on both sides and the near end, and at the front end behind the drivers seat there was a curtain that could also be tightly closed, and over this cover there was another similar in every respect to those on the other wagons, so , that wagon would not attract special attention to it, and it would furnish Mrs Strong quite as much privacy as she would find in a sleeping car, for no prying eyes would be likely to see what was in the wagon under that cover. The Moore's were aware that there was

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: a spy in each of the Mormon settlements through which they had passed, and that his duty was to keep the Elders of the Church posted in regard to all emigrant trains that passed through his district, these spies were expected to report the number of wagons,mules, horses, oxen, men and women and children, and also the number and kind of fire arms there was in each train, and also the name of its Captain. They had been in Camp but a short time this evening before, when a man came to the Camp who they at once spotted as being a spy. He inquired for the Captain of the train and was directed to Charles Moore. Captain Moore answered his questions in a straight-forward manner, and he left them apparently satisfied that they were all right, and that the Mormon Church need not fear them, but before he left them, he informed the Captain that if he or his men wanted to buy or trade for any dairy products or vegetables, he thought they could get those articles over at that ranch, pointing towards a house on the other side of the creek 30 or 40 rods distant. Men from the camp visited the ranch and procured a supply of produce, later they

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[132]
discovered that their friendly spy was the owner of that ranch, and that he had been drumming up custom for himself while attending to his Church duties. He left them but he soon returned mounted on a mustang, he told Capt Moore that he was going up the creek a couple of miles, when an ox train was camped in which there was a man sick with mountain fever, as he was something of an herb doctor, they had sent down for him to come and see if he could help the man, as he did not give his name, the Train men dubbed him Doctor Ferret, and that was the only name they had for him. The next morning Dr Ferret stopped at the camp on his way home, and told Capt Moore that the man was a little better, and he was now going home to get some needed sleep, but he had promised to go back again in the evening and stay with him during the night. The prospect was that he would likely be engaged and out of their way, and there would not be any danger of his coming around spying during the night or the next morning when they broke camp. With Dr Ferret disposed of for that night, they considered their project sure of success, for Mrs Strong told her brother that she did not think

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
133
that the Swede Healver Loursen would discover that se was not at home for a week if left to himself, for he was so stupid that he never noticed any change in anything about the place, except in the size of the pile of fire wood, and in the summer when Strong rode one of his horses down to St. George, where he went on buisness, he had been gone three days before Healver made up his mind that one of the horses was missing, then he came to her and said that he couldn't find but two of the hroses, and he had looked all over the stables, then he added "and [[?]] him haf loose herself some times already". Capt Moore said that Robby and Charley could bring all the wood he had cut into the house, and then he would not have a wood pile to notice, unless he cut some more wood. Every night and morning Robby milked what milk the family needed from one of the three cows, and Healver carried the rest of the milk that the cows gave home, so that he did not have any occasion to visit the house, unless he found something wrong in his department that he could not right without assistance, and the situation began. To look to them as though they would not find any stumbling block in their path, and

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
134
now they had no fears in regard to their ability to rescue Mrs. Strong, for everything appeared to favor their carrying out their plan successfully. But the rescuing of her husband would require considerable more strategy, and they decided upon a scheme that they thought would be practable. Their plan was a bold one, and for that reason they expected if would more easily succeed. Their plan included the remaining of Amos Moore at Lemi with four of their poorest horses and a wagon until the next Spring. Providing he could find accommodations for himself and horses, with one of the mormon families during the winter, where he could pay part or all of their bo[[?]] in work. That afternoon Amos went over and called on Dr Ferret, he found him at home and he told him that four of their best horses had become so thin in flesh, that he and his pardners were afraid that they would not stand the journey that was yet before them, and as they were horses that would command a big price in California, they had concluded to let him remain with them there until spring, if accomodations could be found for them all, then he added, "I would like to find a good place where I

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
135
could do some work myself or with a team, to in part or wholly pay for our keeping, for [[?]] have something to busy myself with doing , it will help make the time slip away the faster, but if it is necessary I am prepared to pay the cash for half of our board. Now if you know of any body that would be likely to take me and my horses on those terms until - say the first of June, you will do me a great favor by directing me to his home. The Dr replied, "I am glad that you came to me in regard to this matter, for in the absence of Bishop Strong I am consulted about all such matters, and I am also glad because I think that I can make satisfactory arrangments for you accomodation with us, I have a small log home a few roads distant from this house, it is empty now and it is divided into two rooms, in one of which is a good fire place, you can make a bunk beds head for the beddign you have, and we will contrive to get a table and a chair or two for your use. I have plenty of stable room for your horses and also some hay and grain for them, you can eat your meals here at my first wifes table. Now in regards to the pay for your board, I do not think we will have any

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
136
trouble in regard to that, for there are no horse teams in the settlement, and I can get you jobs at hauling wood and goods to and from the tithing store, so that in the spring you will find that you have earned enough, if not more than enough, to pay your expenses. If you will excuse me for a moment I will go and get my wife, for it is always best to have the mistress of the house on our side." After an absence of five minutes the Dr returned accompanied by a pleasant appearing woman of about 45 who he introduced as Mrs Stanton, Amos gave his name as Albert Moreland, and the Dr said that his wife would be pleased to board him, after completing his arrangements Amos returned to the camp, and the next morning after the others has left the camp he drove his horses and wagon over to the doctors ranch and took up his quarters there, where I will leave him for the present and return to the Strong family. During that night Mrs Strong's and the Children's clothing was carried down to the wagon and also as many articles of furniture as they could find room for in the wagons. Before daylight Mrs Strong and the three children were hidden in the wagon, and of sunrise the train broke camp and continued its journey.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: Three days later the train passed through St George,  - the last of the Mormon settlements that they would see, and camped at the head of the defile leading into the mountain meadows, Capt Moore expected that he would be followed, and he chose this spot to meet his pursuers, because that day at St George, 8 mounted men had made their appearance coming from the direction of Salt Lake city, they rode to the head of the train and ranged themselves across the road, when the train came to a halt, the leader inquired who the train belonged to. Capt Moore said that he was the Captain of it, but he did not know as it was any of his business who the train belonged to, so he had better clear the road of his highwaymen before he got into trouble. The man took his advice and the train moved on without further molestation, but the Capt was sure that they had not yet seen the last of their visitors and his surmise was correct. The Capt was prepared for just such a contingency, and he did not intend to take any chances by waiting to learn what their next move would be. Before daybreak the next morning Mrs Strong and her two boys were mounted on the two horses that belonged to Strong which they had brought with them, and Nellie sat on a pillion behind Harvey Moore, adieu were

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
spoken and Mrs Strong escorted by Harvy and four men, began their long ride of 75 miles to San Leandro an old Spanish mission just across the border in California. They made the journey in safety in about 15 hours, Harvey found accommodations for the party where they remained until the train arrived.
The Capt was in no hurry to start that morning, but he had the horses hitched to the wagons, and everything made ready for a start. Soon after breakfast four or five of the men went out scouting in the bluffs on each side of the defile, they soon returned and reported that there was Indians in ambush on each side of the defile. Capt Moore sent up a heartfelt thanksgiving that his sister and her escort had started early enough to escape running into that ambush. Then he had the wagons drawn into a semicircle agross the road, and the horses unhitched and tied on the inside of the circle to the wagons, he then sent 10 men to each side of the defile and told them to get as close to the Indians as they could without being seen, and to wait until they heard firing at the wagons before they fired a shot. 
The Capt had hardly got his arrangements made before the same gang of horsemen that had stopped them at St George came galloping up, the leader asked, "Which of you is Capt Moore?", the Capt replied, "I am the man!

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: What do you want?", the leader replied, "I have a warrant here to search your wagons for a saddle that was stolen in Provo when you came through there." The Captain replied, "Produce your warrant," the man handed him a paper which he tore up without reading, while throwing the pieces onto the ground he said, "There are no saddles in this train but what have come with it from east of the Missouri river, and I shall not allow you to search my wagons," then he turned to his companions and said, "boys you had better get your guns," as soon as the 20 men had armed themselves, he turned to the leader and said, "Now Mr Danite or whatever name you are known by, About Face and ride back the same way you came and save yourselves and further trouble." Instead of doing as he told them the Mormons started to ride around one end of the circle of wagons towards the defile, but the Capt's stern command of "Halt! where you are, or will will fill your worthless carcases with lead," brought them to a stand still. Their leader raised his right hand and said, "We are in your power now, but we came on a lawful errand, without any intention of molesting or bothering you farther than to look for a stolen saddle, but you refuse

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: to let us search for it, and we started to return by the Valley trail to our homes, and you have ordered us to halt, what do you mean by treating us in such a manner." The Capt replied, "Come back here from where you started," after they had made back he told his men to cover them with their rifles, then he said to the leader, "I fully understand the innocent game you were trying to play, you started to join your Indian alies who are now lieing in ambush on each side of that defile yonder, but I have blocked your little game, and for your comfort I will tell you that there are 30 men from this train out there in the bluffs, and but few of those Indians will escape unhurt. Now if you had had good sense and rode back to St George the same way you came, we would have let you go unmolested, but now we will take your weapons away from you, and leave you without a sting for a time at least, " calling two men to his assistance they proceeded to disarm their prisoners, of their rifles, dragoon revolvers, hunting knives and ammunition, while doing this one of the men of the gang either from nervousness or carelessness let his revolver belt slip through his fingers just as he had unbuckled it, it fell to the ground and the jar exploded

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: one of the chambers of the revolver and the bullet entered the horse of one of his comrades back of the shoulder and killed him instantly, the horse fell on his rider and broke the mans leg above the knee, they rolled the horse off the man and placed him with this back against the horse. As soon as the men out in the bluffs heard the report of the revolver, they began to try to get into good possitions nearer to the Indians, in doing so several of them narrowly escaped being hit by Indian bullets. The emigrants opened fire on the Indians, and as the majority of them were fairly good marksmen, the most of their bullets hit the mark. Leaving 10 men to guard their prisoners the Capt with the other 10 men went out to reenforce their comrades, but the fight was about over when they arrived there, and a few minutes later there could not be an Indian seen except the killed and wounded ones. They found 16 dead and 12 wounded Indians, but fortunately none of the emigrants had been hit by a bullet, in their search for guns, knives and ammunition they discovered that four of the killed and two of the wounded were white men disguised as Indians. After gathering up the arms the emigrants returned to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: their wagons and put their captured arms into a wagon with those taken from the Mormons, and then they again hitched the horses to the wagons and straightened out the train ready for a start. Capt Moore rode up to the leader of the Mormons and said to him, "You are now free to go to your homes or to stay here, but I would suggest that you send a man or two back to St George after conveyances to take your companion and the 12 wounded Indians or white men laying out in the defile, where they can get surgical attendance, and in their absence you and your aids could employ your time to good advantage by doing what you could to relieve them of their pain. You will find four white men among the killed in the disguise of Indians, I recommend that they be buried there or in any out of the way hole in their disguise just as they are without having the paint washed off their faces, for it would be showing them to much respect to bury them like civilized beings; yes just bury them as you would any other brute. I hope your Elders won't pour out bottles of wrath upon your head, because of your failure to recover a saddle that had not been stolen, and take

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: the value of it out of your wages. But I must say good bye, for the closest friends have to part, and I trust that if we ever meet again, that I shall have the pleasure of leaving you and your gang dangling at the ends of ropes. Saying this the Capt made to the head of the train, and it started with a man on each side of a wagon with his rifle in his hands ready for instant use, and a man sitting by the driver with rifle in readiness, and the driver also had a rifle within his reach. The wagons entered the defile and 20 minutes later they emerged onto the meadows, without having seen but a few Indians, and they kept themselves at a safe distance out of the range of their death dealing rifles. The train had got a couple of miles out on the meadows, when the Capt espied a man sitting by the side of the trail a short distance ahead, the Capt drew his revolver and made towards him, when he came within a dozzen rods of him, the man jumped to his feet and threw up both of his hands and said, "Don't shoot, I surrender," the Capt demanded, "Who are you? and what are you doing here." The Stranger was a

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: young man about 24 or 25 years old, and although his face showed streaks of red paint that he had been unable to rub off, it had a preposessing appearance, and his clothing also showed an attempt at Indian disguise. In a straight forward manner he replied to the Captains questions. "I am your prisoner and in your power, and you find me here trying to escape from this cussed country, and I beg of you to let me accompany you to California, I have no money to pay you with, but I will bind myself to work for you when you reach your destination, until I have paid you in full for your kindness to a stranger. I have no clothes here except these that I stand in, and they are none to good, and I have no weapons except a pocket-knife, and I will add that every word I have told you is the truth." The men of the train had gathered around the Capt and the Stranger, and they heard what he had to say for himself, his manner apparently impressed them favorably, for when the Capt asked if they had any objections to his going along with them, there was not a dissenting voice. He was told to get into a wagon and make himself comfortable, then the train got under motion

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: once more, after a five hours drive the train halted at 1 p.m. for a two hours rest. The Stranger gave his name as being George Slocum a native of Canada, where he had been converted to the Mormone faith three years before, and he had been duped into coming to Utah the previous year. He said he had found work enough to keep him from actual suffering during the winter but no more, but he had not found one who he could count on for a friend, in the Spring he left Salt Lake City and he had worked his way to St George, where the Bishop gave him work at 25 cents a day and his board. He said that he witnessed the stopping of the train by the Danites, and the idea had come to him to try to escape to the train and beg to be taken along with it. After the Danites had failed in their attempt to hold up the train, their leader and the Bishop had a consultation which he had overheard. The Bishop said that he would immediately ride over to the camp of the [[?]]hoots, who were camped two miles from St George, and enlist their services by promising them all the plunder they could get, the Indians could lie in ambush on each side of the defile leading into the meadows, and attack the train there and capture the whole of

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: it, the men as well as the horses and wagons. While the Bishop was gone on his mission to the Indians, the Danite was to secure as many white men as he could, to go and help their Indian alies murder and plunder the train, the next morning as soon as it had got well into the defile. Slocum said that he thought that the opportunity he had been wishing for to get out of the country had come, so he offered his services to go and help the Indians. That night he accompanied a party of 12 white men, each armed with a rifle and a revolver, to the Indian camp, at midnight reenforced by 40 well armed Indians they started for the place where they were to ambush the train, and they arrived there about four o'clock, the early morning was dark and he had no trouble in stealing away from his companions without being seen, and when daylight came he was a mile from the defile out on the meadows, he found a hole and bunged the rifle and revolver because he prefered to take his chances without them, as for the fight he knew nothing, he could see puffs of smoke but he did not hear the reports of the guns. He said that when he saw the head of the train emerge from the defile, he

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
gave a shout of joy, for he knew that the Indians had been defeated, and he had hoped that the whole gang had been wiped out. When the train went into camp that night, they they had made 30 miles that day. Although they did not expect that they would be followed, a doubble guard was posted, and every man slept with his rifle within reach of his hand, the night passed without their being disturbed, and at sunrise they resumed their journey. About noon on the third day after their fight with the Indians they arrived at San Leandro, to be heartily welcomed by Harvey Moore and his companions. Mrs Strong and the children filled with joy by the arrival of the train, and the children could not get enough of Uncle Charles company to satisfy them without tagging him every where he went. The story of their fight with the Indians was told, and Harvey Moore and his four companions regretted that they were not present to have a hand in the fight, Harvey said that the battle deserved a distinctive name, and as it was mostly all on one side, he would suggest that it be called the battle of the Jug-handle.
When Mrs Strong was informed of how near she and the children had been to falling into an

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
ambush, and she realized how narrow an escape they had really had, she was almost paralized with terror. The next morning the train started for Logtown in the Southern mining district, which was their destination, the distance was about a 100 miles over a rough and hilly country without roads of any kind, and all the road they had to travel on was the trail of a pack train, but after overcoming many obstacles in their route, they arrived in safety at Logtown on the afternoon of the fifth day after leaving San Leandro.
The advent of a wagon train into their camp where there had never before been a wagon seen, set those handy miners half beside themselves with delight, but when they heard the startling news, that there was a real live white woman and three children with it, and their enthusiasm knew no bounds, and Mrs Strong and the children received a royal ovation from those men, many of whom had not seen a white woman or a child befor, for two years or longer. In a short time every man in Logtown had told Mrs Strong that if she needed anything, to let him know and he would get it for her or bust.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: The miners declared a holiday for the rest of that day and the day following, and they insisted upon being allowed to build a house for Mrs Strong to live in, so the next day they made a bee and before night they had put up a double log house with a fireplace and chimney all complete, and then they begged for the privilege of sending a man to San Francisco, and get a pack train load of furniture to furnish the house in a first class manner, but she goodnaturedly declined their offer, with what furniture she had brought from Lemi, she was enabled to furnish her two rooms so that they presented quite a home like appearance. Although there was a good fine place in one of the rooms, Mrs Strong prefered to do the most of her cooking out in a shack that her brother built for that purpose. The house had spaces cut out for doors and windows, but there were no doors or window sash to be found in a mining camp in those days. Mrs Strong covered the openings with canvas, and she soon began to feel as secure and safe from intrusion as she had behind a bolted at Lemi, for it did not take her but a short time to understand, that she was surrounded by men each of whom had

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: constituted himself her special protector and friend, and it would probably have went rough with the man who by word or deed, took any liberties with that family. Mrs Strong attended to the cooking for her brothers mess, with the assistance of George Slocum who had proved to be an honorable man, and a man that could be depended upon, and he was taken into full favor by all of the family. The Capt and Harvey located claims for their party, which consisted of themselves, Slocum, Mrs Strong, Robby, Charley and Nellie, the claims adjoined each other so there was little danger of any of them being jumped. As soon as they could do so they went to work washing out gold, for the winter season in most of the mining camps was the miners harvest time, for then they had a supply of water to wash dirt that often yielded from 5 to 10 dollars a pan. Mrs Strong and Nellie's claims were worked enough by the others to save them from being jumped, but both Robby and Charley worked like little beavers on their claims, and with a little help from the men they made big daily pay. The winter passed away and the first of May came, and the Capt and

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[151]
Harvey began to make preparations for a journey back to Utah in the interest of Henry Strong.Before they left Lemi, the Capt, Harvey and Amos, had agreed upon a plan to get Strong out of the clutches of the Mormons, by getting him out of the territory, their plan made it necessary that they should wait until the following summer before they could put it into practice with a hope of a successful issue. For it was then so late in the season that the weather could not be depended upon for 12 hours in advance, So they concluded not to make any attempt to rescue him at that time. Amos agreed to remain at Lemi during the winter, and have Henry Strong at the lower end of the defile leading to the mountain meadows, at 4 o'clock on the morning of the first day of June, and once there he would be escorted by the Capt and Harvey to Logtown, by what means Amos was to use in getting Strong to the rendezvous none of them could foretell, so they left that matter wholly to Amos. At that early date there was no mail between the eastern States, Salt Lake City and California, that crossed the plains, the mails were carried by sailing vessels around Cape Horn to and

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[152]
from San Francisco, a distance of more than 10,000 miles, and the voyage took from 5to 6 months. So that the Moore's had to perfect their plans while they were together, even if letters could have passed frequently between them, the chances were that they would have been opened and read by some Mormon Bishop or Spy, and their plans discovered and reported to the Elders, and in that case they could give up all hope of rescuing Strong, and his and also Amos Moore's lives would be in peril. Amos found his home with the Stanton's a pleasant one, and as for work, the Dr found him all he wanted to do so, that the time did not drag along on his hands. At the breakfast table on the morning that the emigrants had the fight with the Indians, Dr Ferret said, that the evening before it was discovered that Mrs. Strong and her children were missing, he had himself visited the house, and he had found it cold and deserted, and he thought from the looks of things, that some of the furniture and bedding had been removed, but no one appeared to know where she had gone, and he could not find any body that had seen her

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[153]
or her children since the day that the Moore train was in camp here, and both of their horses and her side saddle are also missing. Amos said that she would probably return in a few days, as he may have gone on a visit to some friend a few miles away, and as you say the horses and her saddle are also gone, it looks as though that was the case, for she and the little girl could have rode one of the horses, and the two boys the other one. But neither the Doctor or his wife were inclined to view the affair in that light, but neither of them had a better reason to offer for her absence A protracted search was made made for Mrs Strong, and Amos took just enough interest in the search to ward off any suspicion that he knew any thing in regard to their whereabouts, or that he had ever seen the woman. The search did not throw any light upon her mysterious disappearance. The following afternoon a rumor began to be whispered around the village, that Capt Moore's train had a fight with Indians at the head of the mountain meadows. The next morning Amos inquired of the Doctor if he had heard anything in regard to Capt Moore's train having a fight

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[154]
with Indians. The Dr replied. "Yes the report is true, a messenger brought the news from St George last night. It seems that a party of Goshoot Indians who have a camp near St George, were out early in the morning hunting for some of their ponies that had strayed, in the bluffs on each side of the canyon leading to the meadows, and when the train was passing through the canyon the emigrants discovered the Indians, and mistaking them for a war party in ambush, they fired on them and killed and wounded several Indians, but the Indians did not return their fire, and the train had passed through the defile without having been molested. A party of Mormons who were on their way from St George to Webber Canyon had just arrived on the ground as the emigrants opened fire on the Indians, they hastened to tell Capt Moore that the Indians were on a peaceful mission, and that they were not armed. The Capt replied that he was glad to hear that they were on a peaceable errand, and he very much regretted that any of them had been injured, and he offered any help that any of the train could render, but the party of Mormons thanked

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[155]
him for his offer of assistance, and then told him that he had better hasten his journey before the news of the accident spread abroad, and other Indians gathered together and attacked the train for revenge. During the excitement one of the Mormon's horse was shot and killed, the horse fell on his rider and broke the mans leg." Amos did not take much stock in the Doctors story, and he had an idea that the Dr was trying to get him to express an opinion of the affair, but he was to wary to be caught by him, so he answered the questions that the Dr asked him in an off handed manner that was both perplexing and misleading. Of one thing he was quite sure and that was that the men of the train had not been the aggressors, and that they had not fired on the Indians until they had themselves been shot at, but he thought it best to keep this opinion to himself. About a weet after this incident Amos inquired of the Doctor, if it was not about time for Bishop Strong to get back, the Dr replied that he had just been informed, that the Bishop had been sent on church business up to the northern Settlements and that he was not expected to be back to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[156]
Salt Lake City before sometime in February or the first of March. Amos was glad to hear this, for his absence from home would probably delay any action in regard to his taking another wife, but at the same time he was sorry that he could not get the news to Strong that his family had escaped to California, but there was no way by which he could communicate with him. He did not think that it was probable that Strong had been told of the disappearance of his family, for his Mormon masters wanted his services, and they were to clever to inform him of anything connected with his family, that would tend to unfit him for the work that they had planed for him to do. February and March had come and gone, but Bishop Strong had not returned to his home, but about the 20th of April Dr Ferret told Amos that he had received a letter from Bishop Strong, and he wrote that he would be home before the 20th of May, for on that day he would inspect the tithing books of Lemi. When the Dr made this announcement Amos had hard work to repress his feelings, for he had begun to be anxious that Strong

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[157]
Should return home, for the first day of June was but a few weeks away, and he wanted him there so that they could perfect their plan for his escape. Amos was positive that the Capt and Harvey would be at their posts ready to receive him, but if he did not return home before the first of June, they would have all their trouble for nothing, and he could not see that the prospect for spiriting him away in the future looked very promising. On the 10th of May Amos went up to Salt Lake City after a load of goods for the store at Lemi, a week later on his return trip when within four of five miles of Lemi, he was overtaken by a horseman, Amos had not met Henry Strong since his marriage to his cousin Helen Moore, more than 14 years preceding that time, but at the first glance at the strangers face, he recognized him as being Henry Strong. After passing the complements usual for such occasions, Amos got off his wagon and approached the stranger with one hand outstretched saying, "I am glad to meet you once more Henry Strong." The man clasped hands with him and replied. "You appear to know me, but you have the advantage of me there,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription: for I can not place you among my acquaintances. Amos replied, "Your name is Henry Strong is it not? and you are the Bishop of Lemi," the stranger replied, "Yes my name is Henry Strong, and now will you be kind enough to tell me your name." Amos replied, "Sure! my name at home is Amos Moore, but at Lemi I am known as Albert Moreland, I am from Wayne Co N.Y. and I have the honor of being a cousin of your wifes. As soon as Amos told his name Strong recognized him, and at once began to ply him with questions, all of which Amos answered, Amos told him that he had been staying a Lemi during the winter. Strong asked him if he knew how his family were getting along, Amos replied by asking him if he had heard from them often during his absence, Strong answered that he had not received a letter from his wife since he left home, although he had written to her every week, and heretofore their letters had been delivered by someone that was going to Lemi, or near his stopping place for the time. Amos then told him that his wife and children had gone to California with her brother Charles, and that he had remained a Lemi to assist

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
him in getting out of the country, then he told Henry of the plan that they had decided to follow, after he had made him familiar with all the details, Amos asked him if he wanted to escape and join his family in California, or remain where he was, with the prospect before him of never seeing them again.
Strong replied that he was anxious to cut loose from Mormonism and leave the country as soon as he possibly could, and he added that he was very glad to know that his family was safely out of the country, although is was a bitter disappointment to him, that he would not be able to meet them that evening as he had anticipated doing, after a seperation from them of 7 months. 
Bishop Strong took up his duties and to the many questions that were asked him, in regard to the absence of his wife and family, he had but one answer to give, and that was to the effect that when he left home he had expected to find them there on his return, for his wife had never in any way hinted to him that she intended to leave him, and he could not yet believe that she contemplated leaving him at that time, but he thought it probably that the idea had come

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
to her later, and she had at once acted upon it, and taken her children and fled to California, which she could have easily done for he had been informed that there had been several emigrant trains at Lemi about that time, and she might have been taken in by one of them, and carried beyond pursuit before her absence from home was discovered.
Amos began to be anxious to have a horse train put in its appearance, for he wanted to be on the road when Strong started. On the afternoon of May 27th he was gratified by seeing a horse train of 15 wagons go into camp on the creek. He visited the train, and he was surprised to find that its Capt was on old school mate, who he had not seen before since they were boys. Amos soon made the Capt acquainted with the reason of his being there, and then he asked him if he would allow him to join the train, the Capt told him that he was welcome to do so, and if he needed any assistance he could have it. Amos returned returned to the Doctor and told him and his wife that he was going to leave them, they both expressed regret at his going, and they made him promise to come and see them if he ever came to Utah again.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[161]
Amos drove his horses and wagon to the camp and during the night it was loaded with house hold goods brought from the Strong homestead. The next morning the train pulled out for California, and the following day Henry Strong bid a final adieu to Lemi.
