Strong had made arrangements to be at St George on the morning of June first, and on his way there he was to stop at Parawan and Milton Settlements, he stopped at both those places but when he left Milton late in the afternoon of the 31st of May, he was apparently in no hurry to reach St George 15 miles distant, for he allowed his horse to take his own gait until he had come come within about five miles of that place, then he stopped his horse and struck a match, for the night had set in sometime before, he found that it was 10 o'clock, and he had yet 6 hours in which to reach the rendezvous with Capt Moore, he turned his horses head to the left and rode some distance in that direction before he again turned to the right, and by that time he was a mile or more outside of any of the reanches in the vicinity of St George, he rode slowly in the direction of the trail he had left until he struck into it again, his watch told him that it was 3,30 a.m. He soon arrived at the defile and in

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[162]
a few moments he was traversing its lights and shades, when he emerged from it he was confronted by a mounted man with a led horse, the man rode across the trail and stopped. Neither of the men could distinguish the others features in the dim light of the early morning. The stranger broke the silence by asking. "Are you Henry Strong?"," Strong replied, "Yes! and you are Charles Moore." Five minutes later, Strong mounted on a fresh horse was speeding towards the next relay post 15 miles distant, where Harvey More would meet him with a fresh horse. An hour later Strong rode up to Harvey Moore, and after a few greetings had passed between them, he continued his flight on a fresh horse. A Mexican had the third relay horse in charge, and soon after Strong left him he overtook the train that Amos Moore was with. Strong at that time was about 60 miles from St George and out of danger of pursuit, by the request of Amos backed by Capt Daniels of the train, he consented to make the rest of his journey with the train. Early in the afternoon the train went into camp, and before evening it was overtaken by Capt and Harvey Moore and the Mexican. The rescue of Henry Strong proved to be a grand success, and he arrived with his companions at Logtown in

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.2], 1903
transcription:
[163]
Safety. The Capt and Harvey had left Logtown on the 20th of May, leaving George Slouch to take care of Mrs Strong and her family, at San Leandro they had hired three Mexicans with five extra horse, but as it turned out they did not have to use but three of them.
The Moores and Strong remained at the mines for the next two years, and then after they had gained a competency, they all returned to their old homes in the State of New York. George Slocum accompanied them as far as New York, where he left them and went to his home in Canada. Captain Moore and Henry Strong opened a private banking business, which I understand is conducted by their sons at the present time. Amos Moore became the owner of a fine farm, a few years ago he made a trip to Lemi and called on Doctor Ferret, who he found in good health and happy, because he was now a real live Bishop. It is probable that the escape of Henry Strong and family from the clutches of the Mormon Church, is the only instance of the kind that met with success, and of the scores of those who have attempted to escape, there has never anything been heard in regard to their fate.
End of Volume 3.

transcription:
came in sight of the Camp of the Troopers, then they parted, Little Neck going toward the Camp, and he continuing his way to his home, he said he had divided his dinner with Little Neck, but got no thanks from him for doing so.
The Major concluded the talk by saying he was sure Little Neck could not be very weak from the traveling or fasting he had endured that day, so but what he could go to the Indian Village that night; and get the boy, and return with him by sun rise the next morning, he said he would release him for the purpose of his doing so, but if he failed of executing his mission, they all knew what the consequences would be to them, and also what would befall the people in their Village.
Little Neck was given a supper, and after eating it-he had a short talk with his companions, and many of their words were emphasized with gestures, which were expressive

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
of the earnestness of their talk, they were soon through talking, and he again started for the Indian Camp.
Among the Troopers there was much talk and conjecture, and there were many different opinions as to what would be the result of Little Neck's visit to the Indian Camp; while some thought he would return with the boy, others were of the opinion he would not return at all, and if he did not return, the Major would order the two Chiefs hung, after their execution he would send a Courier to the Camp at Salt Lake City for reenforcements, and upon their arrival he would immediately march to the Indian Village or Camp, attack and destroy it, but he would save the life of the boy if possible; many claimed, that in case the Indian Village should be attacked, they would not find the boy alive, because as soon as the attack was made, the Indians would be sure to kill him, provided they had no way or place to secrete him, where he could not be found by the soldiers, but their talk was all conjecture, and the morrow would settle the question."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:

Chapter 12
"Mrs. Fogarty ad a few opinions to air, and she now made an opportunity to air them by saying.
"Sure! an' Oi did not know the Soljers wor required to do enny of the thinkin' at all, at all! For Oi belaved it wor the Captins an' Officers, phwat done the thinkin' for thim, while they's occupied their moinds wid smokin', an Slapein,' an' growlin'; be me faith! Oi beze sure that whin the Captins an' Officers inspicted the soljers in the ranks, they's had to often pass the growler, no matther whidder they's ivver took a taste thimselves or no. If its atein' ye wod be doin' ye will find a bite of pie an' cake, an' could biled cabbage, an' some could pertaties, in the "butth [[very?]]" there. Sure! ye can ate an' talk too, an' Oi dont be doubtin' that the atein will be the best loiked."
Thanking her for her kind offer I again resumed my story.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
117
"The Canadian and Miner were naturally somewhat excited, for the next few hours had much in them, which was fraught with benefit or disaster to them both; for it could possibly be, that the boy would prove not to be the Canadians Nephew, if such should prove to be the case, they would have to continue the search in some other direction and locality, without the accessories which they now had to help them; then there was the possibility that Little Neck would not bring the boy to Camp.
So taking it all in all, there was not much rest for them in the way of sleep that night, so they contented themselves by lounging around the guards Camp fire, and whiled the weary hours of waiting away in talking and smoking.
The Camp was early astir the next morning, for it needed no "Reveille" bugle call to awake the Troopers and bring them from their frost

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
118
covered blankets, for all of them had recovered from their fatigue of a few hours previous, and all of them were awaiting with eagerness the rising of the sun.
The Horses and Mules were fed and groomed, and breakfasts were hastily prepared and also hastily eaten, as the Troopers breakfasts only included coffee with out milk, hard tack, and bacon, it did not take them long to be through with them.
So that when the sun began to show above the eastern horizon, many anxious eyes were fixed upon the trail by which Little Neck was expected to return to Camp.
The troopers were all unquiet and restless, for they all realized that there would soon be either a drama or a tragedy enacted in their little camp, in which they would be called upon to fill the double role of both actors and spectators.
Which was it to be! tragedy or drama?."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
119
"About half an hour after sun rise, a shout startled the Camp, bringing all to their feet, then other voices joining in made it of such bulk and completeness, -for one of the pack mules added his base voice-as the "everlasting hills" of that country had never before reverberated too. 
The cause of the tumult was easily explained, for there on the trail, in plain sight of all the Troopers, could be seen Little Neck coming toward the Camp, and with him was a boy.
The cheering soon ceased, and they all felt relieved of the strain upon their nervous system, which they had been enduring in silance for several hours; Upon the arrival of Little Neck and the boy in Camp, they were taken in charge by the guard, and a substantial breakfast, consisting of coffee, raw bacon, and hard tack, was set before them. 
Although the boy was dressed in Indian garb, and his face and hands were tanned

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
120
to a copper hue, it was plain to be seen that he was of white parentage, and that no drop of Indian blood coursed through his veins.
The Troopers gathered around the guards Camp fire, each eager to get a look at the boy, and all equally anxious for the solution of the oft repeated question, - 'is he the Canadians Nephew?' -, with all their sympathy and hope in favor of an affirmative answer.
The Canadian was treated to many a friendly slap on his back, and he received many - "cheer up old man! it will come out all right" -, or -"I'm sure the boy is your Nephew!" - with the ready answer-, "of course he is! and just the right age too," -, and he received many more expressions of hearty sympathy and good will.
The Canadian had already told the Major, that the year before his brother left Canada, and started for California, he had pricked with India ink, a capital E upon the left

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
121
leg of his brothers boy, about mid way between the knee and thigh; the letter E was intended to stand for Edgar, the name which had been given to his brothers boy.
As soon as the boy was through eating his beakfast, he was taken to the Majors tent, or more strictly speaking-, to the place where his tent would probably have been pitched, provided he had had a tent with him to pitch.
The poor boy seemed to be in great fear, and it could be plainly seen that he was trembling, and that he did not appear to be at all reassured, by the kind and friendly words which were addressed to him, to let him know that there was no harm intended him, and that he was with friends; but this was accounted for when it was later discovered, that he could understand but a very few of the simpler English words, and that he could speak but very little English."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
122
"Neither the Canadian, nor the Miner could muster up courage enough to examine the boy's leg, to learn if there was a letter E upon it; although they might take their lives in their own hands, if occasion demanded it, and trail Indians for miles upon miles, but when it came to the immediate Solution of a question, which was of such importance to each of them, their hearts failed them, and they had to request the Major to have the Interpreter uncover the boys left leg.
A stillness as though the Death Angel was hovering just above their heads, comes over that little group of Soldiers; with bated breath and staring eyes, they anxiously awaited the uncovering of that tell tale leg.
As soon as it was uncovered, all in that group easily discerned a capital letter E between the knee and thigh, for the boys skin was as white and as fair, as any in that crowd could lay claim to having, where

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
123
it had been covered and has not been exposed to the weather of the changing seasons.
The Canadian dropped upon his knees, and with bared head and uplifted eyes, he in a voice tremulous from emotion said. "My God! I thank thee for this mercy." - Then catching the wondering boy in his arms, he gave him a close embrace, while his pent up feeling found relief in tears.
As soon as it was known for a certainty, that the boy was the Canadians Nephew, all was commotion in the Camp, cheer after cheer went out from the thankful throats, and the mule did not forgit to assist with his base voice.
The Canadian and Miner had made arrangements with the wife of a Settler, to let them bring the boy to her house, even if he should prove not to be the boy they were in search of, - and give him a good washing -, which he was sure to be in great need of -; and she had promised to sell them a suit of her own boys

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
124
clothing, which would fit him very well, as her boy was also about 12 years old.
As soon as the Canadian and Miner could get away from Camp, after received many hearty congratulations and kind wishes from the Troopers, - they took the boy to the home of the Settlers wife; After he had been thoroughly scrubbed and dressed in clean clothing from head to  feet, he looked to be a well buildt and sturdy young semi-savage.
The Major released the three Indians, as he had promised them he would when they boy had been brought to him; he told them they could now go to their Village, or where they might wish too, and they would not be molested by him or his soldiers; he then warned them not to attach any more emigrant trains, and after murdering the men and women, take the children prisoners and keep them in captivity; he told them that there were Soldiers now stationed

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
125
at Salt Lake City, and he could assure them, that those soldiers would kill the last one of the Indians in their band, if they ever attempted to attack another emigrant train, or any other white people again.
After a midday lunch, the bugle sounded "Boots and Saddles"; and soon thereafter the Troopers began their return march to the Camp at Salt Lake City. The boy was given the mule- which had assisted with his voice, in welcoming him back to civilization-, to ride, and he soon made it evident, that he was a good rider and equal to the difficult task, of staying on the back of a bucking Mule.
The boy soon got over much of his timidity, and by the time the Troopers had arrived at their Camp, he had recalled to memory so many words, that he could be made to understand what was wnated of him, and how he was to do it."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
126
Chapter 13.
"Upon the arrival of the Troopers at the Camp at Salt Lake City, they were accorded military honors by being received by the garrison with a "Present Arms". The Troopers were congratulated by their comrades who had remained at the Camp, for having accomplished so successful an ending to the campaign. The Colonel in, "General Orders"- thanked and congratulated the detachment for what it had accomplished in the rescuing of the boy. The Colonel forwarded to Department-Head Quarters, a report, that the expedition had been successful, that it had resulted in the rescuing of a white boy, who had been held in captivity by that band of Piute Indians, for the past seven years, and that those Indians killed his Father and Mother in 1855 on the Humboldt River, and they took the boy and his sister prisoners, and his sister if yet living, was a captive in one of the Indian

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
127
bands in Utah Territory; the Colonel further reported, that every year that same band of Indians committed many depredations and murdered emigrants by the score, leaving their bodies scalped and otherwise mutilated; and also that the Indians found ready purchasers among the Mormons, for all the plunder they secured on their raids. 
Not very long after the rescue of the boy, a rumor became current in the Camp, that the Indian Village on the Bear River was soon to be attacked and destroyed; subsequent events proved the rumor to have had a correct foundation, for orders were soon issued, for four Troops of Cavalry, and one Company of Infantry, a total of 260 Officers and men, to prepare to take up the line of March January 25th, for Bear River, near the Southern border of the Territory of Idaho, where the battle of Bear River was fought on the 29th of January 1863; the Colonel was in command, and he had two Majors as aids."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
128
The battle resulted in the killing of more than 267 Indians, and also of nearly as many Squaws and papooses, and the total destruction of the Indian Village; only a very few of the male Indians escaped, less than a score of them eluded the soldiers and got away, all the Squaws and children were spared that could be, for although there was no quarter given to bucks, there were no Squaws or Chidren wantonly or recklessly killed, those who were killed were hit by random bullets, in the indiscriminate shooting incident to a pitched battle, and also to the almost impossibility of distinguishing a buck from a Squaw by clothing. 
The soldiers did not gain their victory without having received in return, a heavy punishment in killed and wounded, and also frozen, for there were 21 killed, 49 wounded, and 79 frozen either hands or feet; butfortunately none were frozen to death on the expedition."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
129
Mrs. Fogarty had a reminiscence which she related. "Sure! Misfortunes niver  coom single! as Paddy Dooley's brodder Moike-phwat beze the husband of the Widdy Hogan-, said whin he had the two twin bye's borned to him, on the same day that his two horses wor killt by the cars. "But begorra!" says Moike. "Oi'll name thim Tom an' Ned afther they's betthers, an' iviry toime Oi bate thim, Oii can be rememberin' of me ould hosses Tom an Ned, an' that will be some consolation for the coomin' of this misfortunate day, so it will!." 
"An' sure! the poor burthened man had grate nade of sympathy an'- a nurse."
To which I replied. "I fully agree with you in your last remark Mrs. Fogary! but to resume the story."
"After the battle was over, the Troopers found the dead bodies of their three unwilling guests of a few weeks before, Bear Hunter, Sam Pete, and Little Neck; they had all been mounted on ponies at the beginning of the battle, and they

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
130
were found lieing near each other, as though they were all killed about the same time; Bear Hunters right hand still grasped the handle of a short spear, to the head of which was fastened the scalp of a white woman, with long wavy hair of a golden color, which the fiend had been waving at the beginning of the batle as though it were a banner around which the braves of the band would rally, and be encouraged by its presence to deeds of greater daring.
The Poney which Little Neck had ridden, was still alive, but it was in great agony from the pain caused by a broken shoulder blade; one of the Troopers shot it in the head and ended its sufferings, as the Trooper turned away, after doing that humane deed- an arrow struck him on his breast, his exclamation of -"I'm hit-" called the attention of his Comrades to him, a moment later another arrow hit him, and it had but barely reached its mark, before half a dozen carbines were

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
131
discharged in quick succession, and a poor unfortunate but revengeful Squaw, lay lifeless on the snow covered ground. It was found upon examination, that the two arrows had hit the Trooper on the breast-bone, one above the other and not more than two inches apart, the arrows were extracted by the Surgeon, and in a few weeks the Trooper returned to duty. He was the last man to be shot or wounded in that battle; the first man wounded in the battle, was in the act of dismounting, just as he threw his right leg over the cantle of his saddle, a bullet from a heavy rifle struck the foot and broke the ancle bone; and he was the only one of the seventy, who were either killed or wounded in this fight, that was hit below the waist-belt-evidently the Indians took time to aim and sight their guns.
It was a grand achievement for men in the midst of winter, without tents to shelter them from the inclemency of the weather when in Camp, to march four nights in succession

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
132
through snow which covered the ground to a depth of from sixteen inches to two feet, and with the mercury each night falling below the zero mark-, and then in the early morning, without having had any breakfasts, or any thing to eat since about four oclock of the previouse afternoon,- to attack and defeat a foe of double their effective number, who was entrenched in a naturally strong position.
But of such heroic material, the armies of our Country have ever been composed, always invincible! because they are always found for the right; and please God! they will always remain so. 
The day following the battle, the Troops bearing their dead and disabled comrades, began their return march to the Camp at Salt Lake City, when they arrived after an absence of ten days, in which time they had fully accomplished their mission, but it was by the sacrifice of many promising lives that it was done."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
133
""The "Morning Report"! of the Camp for the next day, reported 21 dead, 49 wounded, and 155 as frozen or sick in Hospital or quarters, and 35 for duty; that being the status or present condition of the 260 Officers and men who comprised the detachment.
When the Troopers who rescued the boy returned to Camp, he Canadian and Miner both enlisted in the same Troop Cavalry, and that Troop had in a measure adopted the boy, who soon began to recall to memory many events of his life previous to his capture, and in a short time he began to talk to his Uncle, about his sister and their capture by the Indians.
He related to his Uncle all he could remember about the murder of his Father and Mother, the details of which he and his sister were happily spared from witnessing. He said his father and Mother had their bed on the ground, by the side of the wagon, with a canvas cover over it, the ends of which were fastened to the ground by tent pins.
His sister and he slept on a bed in the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
134
wagon, and tghey had gone to bed early the night before, and his sister had never seen either of her parents since that night; the next morning very early they were awakened by yells and the reports of fire arms, which frightened them so badly, that they covered up their heads with the bed clothes, and kept very still although both of them were all in a tremble, in a short ime the shouting and shooting stopped, and it seemed to be very quiet, but just as he was agoing to raise up, the covers were pulled off of them, and they saw the paint daubed faces of four or five Indians, bending over them, his sister began to cry from fright, and one of the Indians raised his arm as though to hit her with a short club he held in his hand, but another Indian caught hold of his arm, and said something to him, which caused him to drop his arm, he then grasped the boy by his arm and pulled him out of the wagon, they then dragged the bed out with his sister still screaming, on it."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
135
Chapter 14.
"The Indians then threw the most of the things that were in the wagon out on the ground, then one of the Indians pointed to their clothes, and at the same time spoke some Indian words, the boy understood from the gesture, that he wanted them to put on their clothes, which they at once began to do, as soon as he had dressed himself, he helped his sister by buttoning and pining her clothes.
When the Indians pulled them out of the wagon it was on the opposite side from their Camp fire, and also from their parents bed, so that they had not then seen their father of Mother; as soon as they were dressed, the boy took his sister by the hand, and they started to go around the end of the wagon to the Camp fire where they expected to find their father and Mother, they had nearly passed the canvas which covered their bed, and they were in sight of the Camp fire, when they were stopped by one of the Indians and driven back to the other side of the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
136
wagon again, but the boy caught a sight of his father and Mother lieing near each other on the ground near their Camp fire, they were partly dressed, and he had wondered why they were lieing there so quietly, for he did not then know that they were both dead.
While he and his sister were dressing the Indians had been busy gathering such articles as were of most value to them, and making them into bundles which they could carry on their backs, for they had no horses with them.
After his sister and he were driven back to the other side of the wagon, they were taken by one of the Indians, a short distance from the Camp were they were kept until they were joined by the other Indians; the boy saw the Indians shoot the oxen, and then set fire to the wagon after they had put into it the things they did not want to take with them, they even threw the three ox yokes into the wagon, so they might be burned and thus become useless to other emigrants."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
137
"After the fire had got a good start on the wagon and its contents, the Indians shouldered their packs and started in a northernly direction, toward the foot hills, which were about twenty miles distant; the boy and his sister were made to walk and run, to keep up with the rest, until they gave out from exhaustion, then two of the Indians each took one of the children on his back, they carried them for a mile or more, then they were made to trot along until they again gave out, and this method was observed until the Indians arrived at their Camp in a Canyon of the foot hills, late in the afternoon of that day. 
As soon as the Indians had reached the Camp, they began to pack up, then seperating into small parties, they took their squaws and papooses, ponies and dogs, and went farther up in the mountain, where they stayed for several weeks, gathering pine nuts and fishing in the mountain streams for Salmon trout, which they cured for their winter food by

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
138
hanging them on poles and drying them in the sun.
Upon the arrival of the Indians at their Camp, the boy was given to Little Neck and his Squaw Minona, who had no children, his sister was given to an old Squaw by the name of Mahala, who lived in the family of her eldest son, his name was Mule Ears, and the name of his Squaw was Netonka.
The boy said the Indians treated him kindly the most of the time; he said he did not have to do much work, because the Squaws had to do all the drudgery of the Camp, so he spent the most of his time with the boys of the band in play, and in riding the young ponies, or shooting arrows at a mark. He said the Indians would not let him go alone, to any of the houses in the settlements, nor would they allow him to talk with any of the settlers, and the two or three times he had been whipped by Little Neck, was for running away and going to a house to try to talk with a boy who lived there; but, he said his sister had to do a good deal of work, in bringing water and gathering wook

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
139
for the fire, and old Mahala would often beat her, because she could not do as much as she wanted her too, on account of her being so small and weak, but at such times Netonka would take the girls part; and keep Mahala from hurting her very badly.
He said, that the most of the time they had plenty to eat, in the shape of Jack rabbits, fish, and pinenuts, and also potatoes and wheat occasionally, which the Indians got from the Mormons, in exchange for wagon covers, tents, harness, tools etc, which they had captured in successful raids upon emigrant trains; after a raid of that kind, the Indians would have flour, meat, rice, bacon, Sugar and Coffee, and other edibles which they would not trade to the settlers, but they would keep them for their own use.
While he and his sister were together in the band they talked English; he had found several books in the Indian Village, which the Indians had got on their raids and kept, because they had pictures in them, he would often take one of the books and read to his

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
140
Sister, and he had tried to teach her the letters, but he did not succeed very well, for he had no printed alphabet to assist him; one of the books he found was a copy of Robinson Crusoe, and he had read it through several times, he had told his boy companions about the life Crusoe lived with his goats, and his man Friday, and they were so much interested in the story, they would often leave their play to gather around him, and then bid him to tell them more of the story, which has been so often read and dreamed about, by so many thousands of young people, who have lived in each of the several generations which have been born since the story was written.
Mrs. Fogarty had a few casual remarks to make. "Sure now! dont Oi be mindin' the toime, whin Oi wor a slip of a girl, whin Oi used to stale away from me work, an' be radin' such books as Robinson Crusoe, Fox' book of Martyrs, the Arabian Nights, an' others of the loike; an' Oi'd be cryin' me two eyes out over the radin' of thim, whin Oi should be a doin' the work me

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
141
Mudder bade me do, an' thin wid me eyes all red an' swelled, an' me head achin' that bad! me Mudder wod bate me, an' Oi wod have to do me task, afore Oi got a bite or sup to ate or drink, nor a chance to lie down an' aise me achin' head.
Musha! but stolen [[swates?]] cooms dear, an' they's carry a sting wid thim!; an the thinkin' of them good ould days, brings to me moind recollections of many delights an'- batin's-so they do!"
For you and Mrs. Fogarty! those good old days of childhood are passed and gone, but their joys and pleasures, and also their sorrow and pain, still remain the inheritance of each succeeding generation."
"But to return again to the boys story."
He told his Uncle many incidents connected with Indian life, as he had learned the language, he could understand them when they were talking to each other.
He said, that the summer before, a party of bucks from the band with Sam Pete for leader, had gone down Humboldt river on a marauding expedition, they were

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
142
mounted on their ponies, and they were gone several weeks; when they returned to the Village, their ponies were loaded with things which they got on a raid on an emigrant train, and they had also a number of oxen, he said he had overheard an Indian by the name of Wolf Cub- who was one of the party- tell Little Neck, that they surprised an emigrant train of five wagons, one afternoon, just as the train was going into Camp, and they succeeded in capturing it without any of the Indians being hurt, but they killed thirteen of the emigrants, and took the remaining two prisoners, the prisoners were both girls, one was about eightenn, the other about sixteen years old, neither of the girls had been hurt during the fight, which was a one sided one, for the Indians had killed the whites without getting any shots in return. 
The Indians gathered all the plunder they could pack on their ponies and their own backs, and started with the girls and oxen, for their Village on the Bear River; but a few days later the girls became weak and foot-sore, from being compelled to travel over the rough country adjacent to the Mountain range, near

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
143
which the Indians, for their own safety, were keeping, and they were both killed one morning soon after leaving Camp, because they could not walk any farther, they were scalped and their bodies were left where they fell, then the Indians continued their home-ward flight, where they arrived with their spoils in safety: and later they traded the oxen they had captured, to the Mormon settlers for wheat and potatoes.
The boy said that during the time he was with the Indians, he had never heard of their taking any prisoners, excepting the two girls, and he had never seen a white prisoner in any of their Camps, and it was quite probable that if they had taken any on their raids, they had disposed of them as soon as they had become troublesome, or that there was a probability of their being overtaken by their pursuers, and their prisoners be rescued; because that was true in the case of the two girls they captured on the Humboldt river, when they murdered the rest of the emigrant train; for he heard Wolf Cub tell

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
144
tell Little Neck what had happened after the capture until the girls were disposed of.
Wolf Cub said that when the Indians moved from the scene of the massacre of the emigrants, he and Tom John had been left behind as rear guards, to signal the main body in case of danger. 
They hid their ponies in the willow bushes on the bank of the river, a few miles above the emigrant Camp. Wolf Cub then went back toward the Camp far enough to have that and the emigrant trail or road, up and down the river, - in full view; Tom John stationed himself on a rise of ground nearer their ponies, but in sight of him, so that they could signal each other if necessary; they remained on guard until sun down without having seen any trains, then they went up the river to their ponies and camped for the night; before going to sleep they signaled their comrades of the main party, who were over near the foot-hills, that there was no danger in sight."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
145
"They signaled by building a fire of the dry willow branches, on a rise of ground nearby, after allowing the fire to burn brightly for a few minutes, they smothered the flame with bunches of green sage bush for a moment, and then allowed it to blaze up again, this was repeated three times, then putting out the fire, they awaited an answering signal from the party ahead, they did not have long to wait before they saw a signal fire blaze up on a high point of the foot hills, and they knew their signal had been seen by their party. 
The next day was a repitition of the afternoon and evening before to him and Tom John, but on the second day soon after mid day, he discovered a band of horse soldiers - Cavalry - coming on the emigrant trail from down the river, he knew they would soon reach the despoiled Camp and discover the massacre; he realized that it was his duty to get to the main party of his friends as soon as it was possible for him

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
146
to do so, and notify them of the danger which now threatened them from their rear, for he full will knew that a scouting party of Troopers, would now be soon on their trail.
He and Tom John at once hurried back to their ponies; their ponies had had two days rest and they were fresh and they could travel with renewed vigor; they saddled and mounted their ponies, then lashing them into a run they started for that point of the foothills where they had seen the signal fires of the two preceding nights blaze up As the ground between the river and the foothills, was rough and broken into ravines, gullys, mounds, and knolls, the two Indians had no fear of the soldiers seeing them before they reached the friendly shelter of one of the gulches in the foothills, even if they should start in immediate pursuit, which it was not at all probable they would do before the next morning."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
Chapter 15.
"When the two fleeing scouts searched the point of the foot hills where the signal had been lighted, they were joined
by the scout who had been stationed there, they all con-
turned their flight until near morning, when they
had to stop and let their tired ponies rest for a 
few hours; during their flight they were joined
by three other scouts, who had been left behind to watch
for signals, and to forward them either by smoke
in the day time, or by fire at night.
On the morning of the second day Wolf Cub and
his companions overlook the main party just as
they were going to leave their camp I a Council
was at once held, and it was decided to kill the
two prisoners who had become through -- bru-
talith and abuse, unable to walk or even stand alone,
then they would continue their flight with all 
the haste possible, trusting that as they had
four days start of the soldiers, they could 
escape them and get back to their village.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
148
on the Bear River in Safety, with the twenty five or thirty oxen, and the other spoils which they had plundered the emigrant train of.
After killing and scalping the two girls, the Indians started to escape the danger which threatened them, but owing to their having the oxen to drive, they could not cover their trail, but they had decided that in case the Soldiers were likely to overtake and attack them, they would kill the Cattle, and then they would seperate into small parties, and each party would take a different route to their Village; but they did not have to adopt that last recourse, because the Soldiers did not overtake them, and they eventually arrived with their plunder in Safety at their Village in the Bear River range of Mountains.
The boy said that the wheat and potatoes which the Soldiers found in the Village, when they captured it the following winter, were procured from the Mormons in exchange for the oxen which

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
149
the Indians got on their raid on the emigrant train. The boys account of the Massacre of the emigrant train, and of the taking of the two girls prisoners, would seem to be a part of another story which my brother John told me, for each appears to be this continuation and sequel of the other.
John said that while his Command was on the March from California to Salt Lake City, in 1862 they came upon an emigrant train one day, on the Humboldt River which had been attacked by the Indians, and all of the people had been massacreed, it was a small train of only five wagons.
The Troopers found thirteen scalped and mutilated bodies, which they buried, the dead included four men, five women, and four small children; there was nothing left in the Camp which would disclose the names of any of the party, for the Indians had set fire to the wagons, after they had been plundered of their covers and such other articles as they could make use of."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
150
"Soon after the Troopers had discovered the murdered emigrants, another emigrant train arrived at the Camp; Many in that train recognized the bodies as being the remains of a party who had travelled with them, for the most of the time since they left the Missouri  river, but these emigrants said there were two young woman in the train, and they must now be in the hands of the Indians, unless they had escaped capture-, which was not probable, for there were fifteen in the party when they had  last parted company, and the bodies of those two young women were not among the others.
The Major in command of the Troopers, ordered a detail of 25 Troopers to move at daybreak the next morning, with five days rations, on the trail of the Indians, with orders to recapture the girls if it was possible.
The detail left the Camp the next morning with orders to follow the emigrant road up the river for thirty or forty miles, and then to turn to the right and strike the Indian trail near the foot-hills; this order was

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
151
given by the Major, because he reasoned that the Indians would move close to the foothills for many miles, before they entered them, as they could move faster in the open country, than they could among the hills; but this proved to be an unfortunate order.
After following the emigrant trail up the river for eight hours, and riding at a speed of about five miles an hour, the Troopers halted to rest their tired horses; late in the afternoon they again mounted their horses, and turned their head toward the foot hills, where they hoped to be able to strike the trail of the Indians before sun down; but they did not succeed in finding the trail that night, nor did they strike it until they had gone back along the border of the foot hills, for twenty miles or more, and not then until they had lost nearly 24 hours of valuable time.
The trail of the Indians was broad and easily seen, the Troopers pushed forward over divide and through gulch and defile, as fast as the nature of their road would permit them to; about four oclock in the afternoon of the fourth day, they reached the Camp

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
152
whcih the Indians had left the morning of the day before, in it they found the bodies of the two girls lieing side by side, scalped and otherwise mutilated.
The Troopers buried the two poor victims of Indian brutality, as best they could, with an ax and shovel for their only tools. As there was no probablility that the Troopers could overtake the Indians, and as they had but one days ration of food left, they reluctantly gave up the pursuit after the Indians, and began their return march to their command, which they rejoined two days later, both hungry and tired after their ride of more than 300 miles in seven days, over mountainous country; but the ride had been a success in as much as it had been the means of informing them of the final fate of the two young women. But those Troopers had the good fortune to meet those Indians, the next January at the battle of Bear River, and they fully revenged the Massacre of that emigrant train, and also many other murders and atrocities which those Indians had perpetrated on the whites, for many past years."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
153
The boy told his Uncle that in the summer of each year, after the grasshoppers and crickets had attained their growth, the Indians would have a hunt or drive for insects, which he described as being managed in the following manner; a piece of ground would be selected which was well covered with Sagebrush, greese wood, and bunch grass, a large pit would be dug in the ground near the middle of the plot, to a depth of two or three feet, the pit would be filled with brush and wood, and then set on fire, after the wood had been consumed, the pit and the ground close around it would be as hot as a bake overn; as soon as the fire had got low enough, the coals and ashes were scooped out, and then the pit was ready for business; then for the youngsters of the band the fun commenced; as large a patch of ground as could be encompassed by the Indians, both bucks and squaws, old and young, and yet be within a few feet of each other at the start, would then be surrounded, then at a signal they would all begin to shout and beat the bushes and ground near them with

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
154
sticks and steadily march toward the hot pit in the center of the field, driving before them all the bug and insect kind, soon the circle would become so contracted that there was but little chance for anything to pass to the rear, through that cordon of humanity, so the grasshoppers, crickets, horned toads, lizzards, and other "small deer," would be forced toward the pit, where, upon reaching it they would be soon roasted. The boy said, that sometimes a drive would result, in securing several bushels of bugs: he explained that the purpose of the drive, was to procure the insect for food; that after being roasted they were packed away for futures use, and they were prepared for eating, by being first pounded in a stone mortar, and then mixed with crushed pine nuts, or bunch grass seed, also flour and meal were used when they had a supply, the mass was moistened with water and kneaded into flat cakes which were baked on hot stone; the boy claimed the cakes were good eating, and that they were considered a great delicacy by the Indians.
But I doubt if our civilized appetites, could

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
155
be educated to partake of food which contained such a number of different ingredients, of both the cereal and insect species and call it good; but an Indian was never known to refuse anything to eat, no matter whether it be 'quail on toast,' or the offal of a slaughtered animal, this is a well known peculiarity of the taste of ''povr[[?]]." Yes! his taste is extremely low!
In regard to his sister, the boy said she and he had been togather in the same band of Indians, for the first four years of their captivity; he had helped her in bringing water and wood for old Mahala, which was a great help to her, and it saved her from many beatings by the old Squaw.
About three years before, the old Squaw had gone to live with another of her sons, who lived with a band of Pi-utes, that had their villages more than a 100 miles south of Salt Lake City; her sons name was Blue Dog, and his squaws name was Leonta; the old Squaw took his sister with her when she went; and he had not seen her since, but he had heard from her several times, the last time he had heard from her was the previous fall, then she was well and was still living with the old Squaw."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
156
"In the month of the following June, the Colonel sent the Troop of Cavalry, to which the Canadian and Miner belonged, down to the southern part of Utah, with orders to make every effort to rescue the boys sister. The Captain of the Troop executed his orders so well, that when he returned the first of Aug to the Camp, he had the girl with him, and he had rescued her through treaty, without having been compelled to fire a hostile shot.
As soon as the girl had been rescued, the Canadian began to be anxious to send the two children to their Grandparents in Canada, for the Miner and he had enough money to pay the necessary expenses to their old home.
Learning that a man in Salt Lake City was about to visit Boston, the Canadian and the Miner went to see him; they asked him to take charge of the children, and cross over into Canada at Detroit, and leave them at their Grandfathers, they offered him a Liberal sum of money to pay him for the extra trouble he would be put to; the man consented to take charge of the children, and he promised to care for them as well as he would if they were his own boy and girl."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
157
"About the first of September, the man with the children started by Overland Stage for Omaha Neb, en route for Canada; They arrived in Safety at Omaha, and there they changed to a Stage line which conveyed them to the terminus of a Rail Road in central Iowa: they then continued their journey by Rail Road, and they soon arrived at the home of their Grandfather, to whom their escort had the pleasure of delivering the children in good health, after their life of seven years among the Indians of the Western plains.
The first of the following Dec, the Canadian received a letter from his father, which informed him of the safe arrival of the children, and of the satisfaction it was to all the family to have them safely with them once more.
The father wrote the son, that his mother and he had taken a journey early that fall, over to the United States, and that they had visited several of the States during their journey, and they were both so well pleased with the climate, scenery, and residents of the state of Wisconsin, that they had decided to locate a new home, and as a result of that decision, he had purchased a fine farm in that state, near the city of Milwaukee, and in the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
158
Spring the family would all move to that place, for he had disposed of all his property in Canada, and in time he should become a Citizen of the United States.
He wrote the son to come and make his home with the rest of the family in Wisconsin, as soon as he was discharged from the Army: he also sent a special invitation to the Miner to come with the son and visit them, for they all now looked upon him as belonging to the family, and they were all impatiently awaiting an opportunity to repay him in part, by friendship and kindness for what he had done for them, by his assistance in the rescue of the children.
The father inclosed in his letter, a draft for one hundred dollars, as a contributation to the fund for the Monument, which the soldiers were erecting at the Camp at Salt Lake City, to perpetuate the memories of those of their Comrades who had fallen at the battle of Bear River, and in the several other engagements and skirmishes in which the Commands had been compelled to take an active part against the Indians who inhabited that county."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
159
"The Civil War ended in the spring of 1865, but the terms of enlistment of the Canadian and Miner, did not expire until Jan 1866, and that date found them both stationed at Fort Leavenworth Kansas; as soon as they were discharged and had received their pay, they started by rail for Chicago, where upon their arrival, they remained for several days.
Upon their arrival their first pleasure was in the exchange of their Army blue uniforms, for civilian garments which would make them less conspicuous when in public.
After seeing all that was intersting in the City, and having visited the site of Camp Douglas, they continued their journey, and in a few hours they arrived at the new home of the Canadians, where they received a hearty welcome.
They found the children much grown, and also much improved by their two years contact wit civilization; evidance of their formar namadic life was easily to be seen, and it would often crop out at the wrong time, but they all hoped that the evils of their early life, would soon be eradicated by kind judicious treatment, and good example.
The Miner was so well pleased with the Climate

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
160
and the family, and especially with one member of it-an unmarried daughter- that he decided to sell his interests in California, and buy a farm near the Canadians, and become a farmer.
The adult male Canadians had all delared their intentions of becoming citizens, by taking out their first naturaliztion papers, and when the next Presidential election occured they cast ballots as other citizens of this great Republic are wont to do. 
The following Christmas eve, the Miner led to the altar the sister of his Comrade, the ex Canadian- who had also found a prize, in the person of a neighbors daughter, and he was also married at the same time.
After the festivities incident to so joyous an event had become less in number, the newly wedded couples settled in homes of their own.
As soon as they could do so, the ex-Canadian and Miner, legally adopted the two orphan children the Miner adopted the girl, and the ex-Canadian adopted the boy.
With this happy outcome the story must end because my brother John has heard nothing since of any of the actors in these truthful events."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
163
wor small blame to thim, if all of the best men in the army desarted, an' wor then shot becase they's wor human an' cud not kape from getting hungry, an'-."
I interrupted her to say, that I doubted, that any of the Soldiers deserted during the early day of the war, for the reason that they did not get enough to eat, for there was generally plenty of rations, such as they were-no great variety it was true-, but of a quality which would ward off hunger-, except occasionally, when the supply trains were captured by the enimy, or a detachment got so far from its base of supplies, that their rations became short or exhausted: even in such a case the Soldiers always had a chance to forage for food in the country around them, and their forays were generally successful in the finding of something good to eat.
As for hard tack! if they were crushed between two big stones, and then soaked in water for 24 hours or longer- the longer the better-, and then immediately fried in bacon drippings, they made a dish which was not only palatable, but also one that was eagerly

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.2], 1903
transcription:
164
sought for by those who still retained strength enough, to masticate the mixture.
As regards the men deserting! it was probably more from the reason that many of the men had been accustomed to a free, and as I may say- go as you pliase- life, and the restrictions they met with upon enlistment, trended to make them dissatisfied with their new vocation, to such a degree, that they allowed themselves to forget principle, honor and country, and turn their backs to the Flag, under whose starry folds many of them had been born, but when they became sensible of the great wrong and crime they had been guilty of, to their credit be it said, the most of those who deserted during the first two years of the war, returned and surrendered themselves up to punishment; a few were punished but the larger portion were returned to duty, and they served the remainder of their original terms of enlistment, and they proved themselves as being as brave and self denying as any of the other men in the army.
Mrs Fogarty accepted my interuption easity and replied."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: [[Black Journal Book Cover with the number 3 on it of Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864]]

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
Then I started in and told the following story
The incidents I am about to relate took place in fall of 1862 and the locality where they occured was on or near the Humboldt river in the state of Nevada. The Indians in that region of [[?]] and also those in the vicinity of Salt Lake Utah, had become so bold and troublesome during the summer of '61,  that the Government had been compelled to send troops to eastern Utah and Nevada to protect the emigrants that were passing through the Indian's country enroute to the states on the Pacific coast, and also to protect the overland stages which carried the mails from the Missouri river to Sacramento Cal. Two companies owned the stage line, one company owned the line west of Salt Lake City, and the other the line east of that city. In the contracts for carrying the mail made withe these two companies, the Government had pledged its self, to protect the companies from attacks by the Indians on their Stages, and Stations, and to also repay to them all they lost from Indians depridations. In the summer of '62 an Infantry regiment, and also 5 troops of Cavalry from the regiment. I had the honor to be a member of,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
were ordered to proceed to Utah and take Station at Salt Lake City. Now troops H of which I was a member - and troop A, both of the 2d California cavalry had been ordered from San Francisco  to Fort Churchill [[?]] the last of Oct '61, and we had spent the interevening time before being joined by the Infantry and the three other troops from our regiment, in Scouting after Indians and kindred amusements.
On the first day of September '62, the Infantry and four troops of our cavalry took the line of march for Salt Lake City about 400 miles distant. We had a large wagon train, for we had to carry with us all our supplies for the coming winter. Nothing befell us until we arrived in Ruby Valley, about mid way between Churchill and Salt Lake City.
We halted in the Valley for 4 or 5 days to give the Infantry time to build log quarters large enough to accomodate comfortably an' Infantry company that was to be left there, a small Hospital and Officers quarters were also built. Two days before we were to take up the march again, an emigrant came into our camp and reported that a band of Indians had attacked a small emigrant train, near Gravelly ford on the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: Humboldt river emigrant trail, and killed 13 men, women and children, and they had taken two girls aged 15 and 17 prisoners, and gone in an easterly direction, towards the Bear River Mountains, taking with them between 30 and forty head of oxen, and all the plunder they could carry, and also their two prisoners, but before they left they set fire to everything they could not carry with them. As soon as this news became known in camp, every body wanted to be the one to rescue those two girls. The Colonel's tent was soon surrounded by men anxious to volunteer to go in pursuit of the Indians. The Colonel made the boy's a short speech, in which he thanked them for offering their services, and he commended them for the zeal they were now showing for the rescue of those two poor girls. He then informed them, that the massacre had occured four days before, and that the locality of the murder was two days march, or 40 miles, from Fort Ruby, and that the Indians would have six days the start of their pursuers by the time they could arrive at the scene of the tragedy, and they could not hope to overtake them on foot even by forced

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: marches, which they would not be able to stand longer than three days at the outside limit. The Colonel then said that he would do all that lay in his power to rescue the girls, by sending a troop of cavalry in pursuit of the Indians. With this promise the "doughboys" - as the Infantry is often jestingly called - had to be contented. That evening at retreat: - (sun set), general orders from the War Department were read, they ordered the Command to exterminate all the Indians that it found, and not to take any prisoners, then there was an order read detailing troop's H and K of the 2nd Calvalry, on detached service, with 40 days full rations, and also ammunition, transportation &, to move the next morning for the Humboldt river, and upon arriving there, to follow the emigrant trail and report at Salt Lake City as soon as practicable, and in the mean time do scouting duty, and to make every effort to overtake the Indians and rescue the two girls. Since leaving Fort Churchill our command had followed the overland stage road, which shortened the distance to the City of Salt Lake a good many miles, because the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: emigrant trail kept close to the rivers and followed their windings, for the emigrants had to depend upon the rivers for their food and drink their stock required, the former they found on the bottom lands through which the rivers and small streams sluggishly flowed, and their drink they found in their alkaline waters. As soon as those orders were read, all of us in troop's H and K, knew we were in for plenty of hard work, for the next months, but that fact did not give any of us nervous prostration, and we were all up half of that night busy loading the 21 wagons we were to take with us, with Quartermaster stores, and Commissary and Ordinance stores also. The next morning at sun rise troops H and K under the Command of a Major who had fought the Seminole Indians in two of their wars, were given the commands, "Forward! -- March!" and we were soon stretched out on the trail headed for Gravelly Ford on the Humboldt river about 45 miles distant. On the next day which happened to be the first day of October, we arrived at this ford. Up to that day we had had splended weather all the time since we left Fort Churchill,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: but we went into camp that afternoon as bedraggled, sorry looking lot of pilgrims, for the weather had changed the night before, and a fine drizzling rain set in about noon and it soon wet us to our skins. We soon had our Sibley tents pitched and fires burning in the center of each tent, this was our first experience with a fire in a tent, and it was not a success, but a decided failure, and for comfort deliver me from a Sibley tent with a open fire burning in in it, for although each of them has a large opening at the top for the smoke to escape through, I have never heard that any smoke was ever seen to issue from that opening, but it all m[[?]]ots upon remaining in the tent to blind the inmates, and the little that escapes does through the door, while the half blinded and weeping inmates are cussin' the day they first saw a Sibley tent. After boiling a camp kettle of coffee we kicked the fire out, and by the time we crawled between our blankets, we had become fairly comfortable, and I went to sleep and dreamed I was a charcoal burner, and that I fell into a milliners bleaching tank,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: from which I was with difficulty rescued, before I had quite lost my eyesight, by an old squaw on a yellow horse that blew smoke out of his nostrils all the time, the old squaw pulled me out of the tank and threw me across the back of the horse in front of her, just then the horse made a vicious jab at me with his mouth wide open, he struck me in the sides and --I awoke to find my bunkys elbow in my ribs, while he was growling because I had got all of the blankets. The next morning the weather was worse, for it had grown colder and the rain that continued to fall, had become sleet. The weather being so bad, the Major decided not to move that day, so we remained in camp, but we did all of our cooking outside of our tents. It began to look as though there would not be many bright days ahead of us, on our mark of 150 miles through an uninhabited country, but in the afternoon the weather changed for the better, the rain ceased falling, and soon after the sun burst through the clouds, and when the sun set that night there was not a cloud

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: to be seen in the sky, and we looked upon that bright sun and hoped that it was a harbinger of many brighter days that were in store for us, on our long march where we would not see either house, barn, church, pig-pen or even a schoolhouse until after we had reached the Mormon settlements 50 or 60 miles north of Salt Lake city, and (when we did arrive at the first settlement, we took it for granted from the number of children we saw around the houses, that we had struck a school section and we naturally supposed that the buildings were all school houses, but that idea was knocked out of our heads later.) By 7 o'clock that morning we were on the march. A scouting party with three days rations had left the camp with orders to find the place where the massacre occurred, and also the trail that the Indians had left behind them when they left the place with their prisoners and plunder. The Indians had now 7 days the start of us, but we knew they would have to travel slow, encumbered as they were with 30 or 40 head of oxen, that had been driven from east of the Missouri river, and were now

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: thin in flesh and weak, and they could not be urged to travel faster than two miles an hour at the outside. But none of thought that the Indians would be able to drive them more than 10 or 12 miles a day, and it was for their own advantage to keep the oxen in a good condition, because the better condition they were in when they arrived at the Mormon Settlements, the more wheat and potatoes they would get in exchange for them, from their Mormon friends who were always ready to exchange their produce for the spoils the Indians captured on their plundering expeditions. The trail the Indians would take would be over rough and stony ground, for the Indians would keep to the foothills and out of sight of the emigrant trail as much as possible and the oxen's feet would soon become so tender and sore, that it would be impossible to drive them fast. As we had not seen any signal fires or smoke, we concluded that the Indians had not left any picket guards behind them, and it was not probably that they had yet learned that there were soldiers in Ruby Valley, or as

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: near to them as our two troops were, which would account for our arrival in the Humboldt Valley not being signaled up and down the valley. On the third day following the scouting party returned, they reported they had found the scene of the tragedy, and that they had made the graves of the victims secure from coyotes by piling stones on each of them, this act of humanity done they had followed the trail of the Indians, without  discovering any sign of them, until they were obliged to turn back on account of want of rations. The following morning another party -- of which I was a member --, was sent out on a scout with two days rations. Our Command had marched 70 miles in the three days since we left Gravelly Ford, and the Major figured that the Indians had not made more than half that distance in the same length of time, travelling 12 miles a day, so we had virtually gained three days on them, and that it would take them at least two days more, with tender footed oxen to drive, to arrive at a point in the foothills opposite the camp we would occupy

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: at that time, for during those two days we would make at least 40 miles, so that we would be in striking distance of the Indians, for we were both travelling in parralell directions some 30 or 40 miles apart. The scouting party all belonged to H troop, and our 2nd Lieutenant was in command. We struck the Indian trail about 15 miles from camp, we followed it without any incident other than finding one or two places where the Indians had halted or camped. At sunset we camped in a small valley that made down in the direction of the Humboldt, it had a small stream of clear cold water running through the center of it. In the morning our sentinel's reported that they had not seen any signal fires during the night, which would show that our presence in the alley of the Humboldt, had not yet been discovered by the Indians, but the locality of our little camp might have made some difference in regard to seeing signal fires unless they were near [[?]], because the hills on each side of our camp were higher than were those in our rear. After eating a hearty breakfast of black coffee, and bacon - broiled on the end of a stick held

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
over the blaze of a fire- and bread, we saddled up and again started to follow the Indian's trail. At noon we halted to bait and rest our horses for half an hour, and enjoy the time in eating the last of the rations we had with us. Up to this time we had seen no Indians or any Indian signs except their trail, and as we had eaten the last of our two days ration for lunch, it looked as though we would soon have to head for our command. 
Soon after we started again one of our men by the name of Jones, got permission from the Lieutenant to ride a few miles ahead on the trail, and see if he could discover any Indian signs, at that time we were about to leave the trail and bear to the left in the direction of the river. The Lieut, ordered Jones to join us at a high ridge that was in sight about three miles distant, and then he said we would strike out and find the camp of our command, where grub was more plentyful that it was where we then were, and our comrades would be in camp long long before we got there anyway. When we arrived at the bridge, we had to wait more than an hour before Jones joined us. The Lieutenant

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: started in to give him a warm reception, but at the first hot blast Jones threw up both hands, and declared that he did not mean to do it. Then he informed us that he had followed that trail to its end, his statement met with ridicule from all of us, but notwithstanding our gibes and sneers, he stuck loyally to his assertion that he had followed the trail to its final end, which was about 5 miles distant from the place where he had parted from us, he also said he had not seen any Indian signs in the vicinity. It was now to late in the day for us to prove the truth or falsity of his story, for our Camp was,- we knew not how many miles from us-,  so we turned our backs to that trail and started in the direction of the river, and we arrived in camp about 9 p.m, with jaded horses, empty haversacks and stomachs, but not a bit discouraged. We found that our camp was about due south of the point where Jones claimed the trail ended, so that the Majors calculations of the gain we would make on the Indians, was not mistaken, which proved to be the case, and at that hour the Indians were

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: all of 25 miles ahead of us yet. The next morning my Captain was sent on a Scout with a detail of 15 men from his own troop. On the previous scout I had rode a mule, leaving my horse to follow the wagon train, as he was in a good condition for riding. I volunteered my services to the Captain and he accepted them, but before we had got back to the command again, I had occasion to wish I had been born with sense enough to know better than to fool with a buzz saw when there was an oyster stew within reach, and I vowed to myself that for the future I would not volunteer my services for any purpose, unless it might possibly be eating. After breakfast I saddled my horse and we were soon mounted and out of camp, with three days rations in our haversacks. Jones and three or four more who were on the previous Scout were of the party. Jones persuaded the Captain to head for a high foot hill about ten miles from where he claimed he had seen the end of the Indian trail. Jones gave for a reason for doing so, that if we found a new trail through the hills in that direction-which he was positive we would do-, we would be

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
some ten miles nearer the Indians, than we would be at the place where the trail had disappeared-which was quite true-, but if we did not find a new trail, we might just as well give the pursuit up and return to camp-which was equally wrong-. However he was the only one that I heard express any desire to ever give up the pursuit as long as we had a horse able to carry a man.
About 10 a, m, I got the Captain to consent to my making a short scout independent of the others, but I had to promise him, that I would not loose sight of him and the others for longer than 15 minutes at a time, and also that I would rejoin them at noon. After leaving them I made for a hill that was about half way between the hill the Captain was steering for and the place where Jones saw the end of the trail. I skirted the base of the hill and soon found myself on a gently rising plateau of many acres in extent, I rode up the slope a distance and I was just on the point of riding across to the opposite ridge, to be in view of the Captains party, when I discovered that I had stumbled onto a plainly defined Indian trail that had been made by pony's.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: The finding of a trail there nearly took my breath away, and it quite took my memory away, for I forgot all about my promise to the Captain, and also the many good resolutions I had thought it necessary to make in regard to a proper observance to the letter, of all orders of my superior officers, and by doing so keep out of trouble. Through my loss of memory I did not see my companions again until the next morning, but the finding of that trail had a heap to do with the scrape I got myself into. I dismounted and upon examination I found that the trail had been made by bare footed ponies only, for there was no tracks of oxen among the other hoof prints. The trail led up the slope in a northernly directions, I mounted my horse and followed it, after riding about a mile I began to notice that it was bearing towards the east, and I soon found it had turned to the south, and before another ten minutes had passed it was bearing to the west, and after going perhaps half a mile in that direction it began to circle to the north and up the slope. I was soon surprised by seeing the tracks my horse had made befor he had entered the trail.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
Chapter XV. Continued.
Don't take our troubles to bed with you- hang them on a chair with your trousers, or drop them in a glass of water with your teeth.
Here was a puzzle, and what it all ment I could not comprehend, but I at once determined to work out that puzzle if it took the rest of my enlistment to do it. I rode forward up the trail and when I came to the point in the trail where it began to bear to the east, I halted and dismounting I began an investigation of my surroundings, I soon discovered that the trail I had been following for two hours or more was a loop of a plain trail, and that the stem to that loop was a blind one, and that it had been made by leading ponies singley in parallel rows a few yards apart, until they had got to the head of the loop, and there they had joined to make a distinct trail that any one could see, and I found that after making that oval shaped trail, which I might liken to a mammoth  Summer Squash in shape, the Indians

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: had left the trail the same way they had entered it, that was singly. These discoveries whetted my appetite for more, leading my horse I followed two of the tracks that came from the west, the direction where Jones had lost the trail the day before, after crossing the plateau for some 500 yards they ascended a rise of ground, and I looked down into a ravine or small valley at least a 1000 yards wide, with a small stream of water running through its center down towards the river which I could faintly see some 12 or 15 miles distant. I started down the bluff and soon reached the creek, which I found to be shallow although from 20 to 30 feet wide, both up and down as far as I could see, I mounted my horse and forded the brook, and I was not much surprised when I discovered that I had stumbled onto the trail of the Indians where Jones had lost it, for there in the soft ground were to be seen not only the prints of pony hoofs, but also the prints of the split hoofs of Cattle. It did not take me many minutes to solve the mystery of why the trail became lost there or was apparantly lost or ended.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: The Indians had made a blind trail by taking to the water with their stock, and keeping both oxen and ponies in the water so that they could not leave any tell tale print of a hoof behind them. After satisfying myself that the Indians had gone up the creek, I recrossed the stream and retraced my steps to the point where I had left the other trail, then I started up the plateau in search of another trail, after riding about half a mile I came to the head of a narrow ravine which ran down to the ravine in which the lost trail was, I started down it and soon reached the brook, and a little farther up I found the place were the Indians had left the water and again taken to the land. Their trail soon became broad and plain, and it led in the direction of the Bear River Mountains to the north east. I followed the trail for a mile or two, but I made no new discoveries, then I turned my horses head towards the Humboldt river, for I had no desire to ride up and down those hills in search of the Captains party. I knew that the Captain would be quite likely to search for me towards Sun down, before he made his way down to the river to camp, which

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: I was quite possitive he would do, because I knew that from the direction he was going when I left him, he would not strike the trail, and when it began to get late in the day he would return to the river and make a fresh start in the morning.
