I was also positive that they would in the mean time be making use of language on my behalf, that he never learned in polite society, but I was in for it now, and all I had to depend on was my horse and myself with a carbine and 7 shooter revolver, and I did not fear that either one would fail me in time of need. When I got back to the place where that loop began, I understood the whole game that the Indians had tried to play. They evidently thought that in case they were followed, their pursuers would when they came to the brook become bewildered because of the disappearence of the trail, and as they would not find any hoff prints on the opposite side of the brook, they would likely go back on the trail a ways to look for tracks leading in that direction, and those Indians had prepared for just such a possibility.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: for they had driven or led the oxen an ponies back on the trail for a distance of near a half mile, and then led them singly back on the grass on both sides of the trail, and then taken to the water with them, for the trail ended a hundred feet from the bank of the creek and there was not a single hoofprint between the end of the trail and the bank of the creek. The Indians probably figured that when their pursuers found that the tracks led away from the brook, they would conclude that the Indians had turned back and were moveing in another direction, and then the pursuers would also take the back trails, and they - the Indians - could put many more miles between themselves and danger before their ruse was discovered. An the Indians had taken the trouble to make the trail on the plateau of 7 or 8 miles in circumference for the purpose of misleading those who saw it, into thinking it was made by a party of Indians that had gone down to the river to fish, and they would not investigate it more closely. But I did not stop there to reason all of this out, but I did so while on my way to the river, which I arrived at just as the sun disappeared below the horrison.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: I had not seen any fresh Indian signes in all my wanderings that day, and I did not see any of the Captains party or any signs of them on my ride to the river. Before I dismounted I looked up and down the river hoping to see some sign of them, but they were not in sight. At first I could not decide what it was best for me to do, for I had confidently expected to find the Captain with his men camped on the river,and I knew I could not be many miles from the camping ground we had started from in the morning, but whether I was above or below it I could not tell, for there was nothing in sight which I could locate my self. I dismounted and examined the road, but it gave me no information, for a wind had coverd any tracks that were there late in the afternoon with dry sand, and there had been no new tracks made since the wind had gone down. As daylight was fading away I concluded that the best thing for me to do was to find a good place and camp there. Nearby the river made a bend in the shape of a horse shoe, and the opposite back for some distance was lined

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: The machine slipped a cog here, I will fill it in with a story of a Missionary that many years ago went among the Crow Indians. He was admitted to an audience of the leading men, and he began through an interpreter, to tell them the story of how sin first came into the world, and how all men had become bad whether white or red. Then he proceeded to explain the principals of Christianity, telling the savages that he had come among them to do them good, and to show them how to be happy and he declared that unless they listened to him and worshipped the Good Spirit as he instructed them, they could never reach that happy country into which good people alone found admittance after death. A venerable Chiefthen arose and said. "My white brother is a stranger to us. He talks evil of us, and he talks evil of his own people. He does this because he is ignorant. He thinks my people, like his, are wicked. Thus far he is wrong. Who were they who killed the very good man of whom he tells us? None of them were red men! The red man will die for his friends- he will not kill them. Let my pale face brother talk to the white man. His own people they are very bad. He says he would do us good. He does us no good to chide us and say we are bad. True we are bad, and if we were as bad as the pale face's, it would become us to listen to him. Would my brother do us good? Then let him tell us how to make powder, and we will believe in the in the sincerity of his profession- but let him not belie us by saying we are bad like the pale face's.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: with small willow bushes that grew so close togather that they made a screen through which I could not see what was on the other side of them. I mounted my horse and after a little trouble, I found a fording place and crossed over to the other side, the water came up to my horses flanks, but as I wore long cavalry boots I did not get much wet. I found that the bend contained about half an acre of fine grazing ground, and also that I was completely hidden from the road, by that screen of willows. I began at once making preperations for camping, and like all good troopers my first care was for my horse, after attending to his wants, I could attend to my own but his needs and comfort was always my first care. I considered that my horse was the best friend in time of need, that I had in the troop, and I had especially thought so since one occasion, when we were both in a hurry to get away from half a dozzen yelling Indians. After I had attended to my horse I broke off some dry branches from the willows and made a smokeless fire, for I did not want any tell tale smoke going up into the air to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: be seen by either friend or foe, for I had become quite independent, and as I could not have the earth I had reconciled myself to that bend on the Humboldt river, and I did not want any trespassing. I boiled a pint cup of coffee, with that and raw bacon and bread I made my supper, then I lighted my pipe and turned my attention to the predicament I had unintentionally gotten myself into. I was quite positive that it could not be much worse unless I killed some one other than an Indian, and I was sorry that I had volunteered in the Army in the first place-why didn't I get myself sent to the penetentary and have done with it-, and I was specially sorry that I had been fool enough to volunteer to come on this dog-gasted scout, and I was also sorry for a great many other equally foolish things that I had done in the past which insisted upon being remembered. A second pipe put a little more nerve in me, and I began to tell myself that I would pull out of that scrape all right yet, I called to mind the sayings that the blackest cloud has lightning behind it,- and that- it was always lighter after sun up-, but they did not

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: seem to raise my spirits much. But in the mean time I did not overlook the fact that I was then in an enemy's country, and that I must take all the precautions that I could for the safety of myself and horse. I was both tired and sleepy, and I soon spread down my blankets on the ground and placed my saddle at one end for a pillow, and put my carbine and revolver under it, but before I rolled myself with boots on up in the blankets I knotted my neck handkerchief around my left wrist, and tied the loose end of my horses picket rope to the knot, as a safe guard against his breaking away without my knowing it, then I rolled up in my blankets feeling tolerabley comfortable for a pilgrim in a strange land. I was to tired and sleepy for my mind to have much time to dwell upon my present condition, and I was soon asleep, but I had not been asleep more than an hour-as I found out later- before I sprung to my feet wide awake and trembling in every limb. What had awakened me I did not know, it was not my horse for he had

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: stopped feeding and lain down, and he was apparantly asleep, and up to the present time I have formed no lucid idea of what awoke me that night. You may safely believe me when I say that my nerveous system was all in a tremor in an instant, for I had awakened so quickly that for a few moments I was actually scared, but I did not loose my head, my first act was to put my revolver in my belt and lay the carbine across the saddle. I knew that both weapons were in good order because I had examined them before I laid down. There was no moon but the night was bright star light, and I could see to a distance of several rods. I bent my body and listened intently for some sound or noise, and in a few moments I heard what sounded to me like the murmur of several human voices, I hastily caught up a blanket and ran to my horse and threw it over his head, and he soon got onto his feet an stood shaking his head to get rid of its unwelcome covering, but I soon quieted him with whispers and pats on his cheeks and neck. I covered his head for fear that if he heard the sound of voices, he

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: would whinney and betray our whereabouts. The murmurs became more distinct and I soon made out that it was a mounted party, for I could hear the tread of horses going up the river trail. The road was to far away for me to tell whether the party were Indians or whites, so I kept very quiet until they had passed and their voices had faded away in the distance. As soon as I had heard the last of my unwelcome visitors, I drew a long breath of relief, then I took the blanket off my horses head, and he rubbed his cheek against my shoulder, as if in mute inquiry as to what such foolishness was all about anyway. I went back to my bunking place with the blanket and hung it on the willows between me and my disappearing visitors for a screen, I struck a match and looked at my watch, and it told me that it was only 10 minutes after 9 oclock, so that I could not have been asleep long before I was so unceremoniously awakened. I lighted my pipe and before I had taken a dozzen whiffs, I had come to the conclusion that I was doing pretty

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
well where I was, and that I would stay there until morning unless I was driven away. After two or three more yawns I found the end of the picket rope- which I had untied-, and tied it again to my wrist, and again rolled up in my blankets, and I soon forgot all about Indians, burglers, midnight raiders, and the roasting I was sure to get when I again met the Captain, but I slept on in blissful forgetfulness of punishments for the present or in the future until sun rise, and it is probable that I would not have awoke then if my horse had not given my wrist a jerk in his search for fresher grass. 
As soon as I was fully awake the incidents of the night came vividly to my mind, and I at once became anxious to know whether the party that passed in the night, was a maraudering band of Indians, or the party of peacible whites to which I belonged. I made a hasty breakfast and saddled my horse and lashed my blankets and cooking utensils- a pint tin cup- on the pummel of the saddle and mounted. I forded the river and rode straight to the trail, one glance at it told me that the last party

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: that had passed were going up the river, and also that they rode large horses, for the hoof prints were all large ones, and also that the horses had shoes on their forward feet only. This discovery sent a thrill of pleasure through my body, for when we were first issued horses at San Francisco, we had had them shod all around, but in a short time those half broken half breeds had done so much damage by kicking each other and many of the men, that an order was issued to have the hind shoes pulled off the horses and not replaced again until further orders, but the time for the 'further orders,' never arrived in that regiment. So that this discovery was a great relief to me, for it told me that the party was a small squad of troopers, and I felt like blessing the man that first invented horse shoes. I thought that the party was another Scouting Squad that had been sent out after we had left the camp, for I could not get the idea out of my head but what my Captain had struck the river above me, for I could see no reason for his going so

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
far back to the west after I had left him. 
I mounted my horse and turned his head up the river, before I had ridden two miles, I saw th Captains party camped in a bend of the river. As soon as I got near enough I was hailed by the boys with cheers, and a dozzen questions were fired at me at long range. After I had attended to my horse I prepared another breakfast for myself more leisurely than I had the previous one, for my early ride had made me hungry. While I was disposing of it I found out that the Captain had become doubtful of Jones ability to guide them to the place where he had lost the trail, so an hour or so after I had left them, he began to shape their course more to the right and west, thinking that he would strike the old trail in a few miles, but they did not discover it and about 3 oclock they came in sight of the river, and by that time the Captain had become worried at my prolonged absence, he had sent a man to every highhill they came to, to see if I could be seen without success, and when they came in sight of the river he decided to ride down to it and camp, feeling sure that I was to the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: west of them, when in fact I was at least 5 miles east of his camp, for in his turnings to the right he had gradually taken a westerly direction, and on his route he had crossed the creek and the blind trail about half way from its two ends, and then crossed the ravine and rode to the top of the bluff, but seeing nothing inviting in the prospect before him, he and his men had recrossed that blind trail in the creek, and then they turned to the left and rode along the right bluff of the ravine for a couple of miles before again turning west, and by doing so he had rode passed the end of the lost trail within a distance of 700 or 800 yards without seeing it, and then he had rode directly away from it, as we discovered before noon of that day when we crossed the trail they had made. Several of the men had rode round in the foot hills in search of me, but they did not see either sign or track of me. My informant went on to say that about half past 7 the evening before, the Captain being very uneasy, had come to the conclusion

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: that perhaps I had made the river several miles further up the river than they had, so he had decided to move up the river a few miles and again camp and await for morning to come, and then they would find the trails we had made that morning and follow them to the place where I had left them, and then they would take my trail and follow it to its end, even if it led to the portals of hades, and the Captain had said that he heartily wished it would. The boys treated me to the gratuitous information that when the Captain got up, he would give me such a roasting that I wouldn't feel cold for the rest of that Scout. From what I had been told of the Captains remarks about me, and of the temper he was in, I did not feel any to comfortable when I presented myself to his notice, with a Salute and the information that I had the honor to report. He looked steadily at me for several moments,- and I fancied I saw a ball and chain back of that look-, before he spoke and the first words he said were, "You probably carry a stop watch, for your fifteen minutes are- long ones, and I have had no end of worry on your

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: account, now I have a good mind to have you bucked and gagged, for a couple of hours preliminary to having you court-martialed and drumed out of the __service. And it would be a warning to the other men of what a man may get for disobeying orders when on duty, and also breaking his word as you have done." When the Captain stopped to take breath, I said. Captain I am very sorry that I have unintentionally caused you and the men worry and trouble on my account but if you will kindly listen to me for a few minutes, I feel assured that you will not think my late conduct, so culpable as it now appears to you to be. In a gruff tone of voice he said. "What excuses have you ready made up, to offer, that could diminish or paliate your grave offence one particle, but if you have come in prepared with one, I want to hear it__ quick, and for your own good you had better stick closely to the truth, because if you tell me a __ lie, I will be __ if I don't have you court-martialed." With this encouragement I began my story by informing him at the start that I had found the continuation of the trail

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
that Jones said was lost, and that I had followed it for three or four miles. This news changed the Captains aspect materially, and by the time I had related my last nights experience in camping alone, he had quite thawed out, and he soon became his own genial self once more, which he proved by begging a pipe of tobacco of me. The Captain wanted to know how far I thought that trail was from where we were then. I told him that I should judge that it was between 15 and 20 miles, he then told me to tell Sergeant Kilgore to have the men saddle up and we would steer for that trail.
Before we mounted our horses, I suggested to the Captain, that we ride down the river to the place where I had camped the night before, and then take the trail I had made in coming down to the river, because if we followed it we would have an easy climb up to the plateau, where I rode in the circle, and also into the foot hills.
The Captain agreed to my suggestion and we started down the river. When we arrived opposite of my last nights camp, I pointed out the spot and they all expressed regret that they did not know that I was there, for if they had they

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: had they would have called on me and remained all night. I dismounted and after a short search I found the trail I had made in coming down from the hills, the Captain told me to take the lead and the rest of them would follow me as long as they could see me. After an hours ride we struck the loop trail on the plateau, I led them up the right hand trail to what I have called the stem, and then down to the brook for all of them were anxious to see the place where the trails apparently stopped. When we were going down to the brook we crossed the trail that the Captains party had made the day before near the bluff. I pointed it out to the Captain and remarked that when they were making that trail I was probably going back on the Indian trail to see how far back they had driven those oxen, and if I had not done that we would have met within half a mile of where we were at present, and now we would be 20 or 25 miles nearer those Indians than we were now, for if we had met I could have led them to the trail in less than half an hour and then we could pushed on after

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: the Indians. But if we had not lost all of the time we did, we could not have changed the final result. We rode down to the brook and crossed it and then for the first time Jones recognized the spot where he had lost the trail three days before. Poor Jones felt cheap enough, and the banter he got from the others did not tend to make him feel any the more comfortable, and from that day all that was necessary to close him up like a clam was to say - 'lost trail -'. We rode up the brook and found where they had crossed it the day before, and when we got to where the trail took to the land again, we halted for an hour to bait and rest our horses, and to have a lunch ourselves. When we again mounted our horses we had come to the conclusion that we were at the least fully 50 miles in the rear of the Indians, and we realized that we stood a mighty slim show for overtaking them, for we had now only one days ration and a half in our haversacks, but the Captain siad we would follow them as long as we could and hope that something might turn up in our favor. By this time I stood again all right with my comrades, and some of them

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
suggested that the Captain ought to recommend me to the Major for appointment as chief Scout of the expidition. If the Captain did so, I have not as yet received an official notice of the act. But I have no doubt but what, in case their votes could have elected me a pound master, Governor or something, I would have been elected. But Jones had lost prestige for not being able to recognize the locality of the lost trail the following day, when he was within 700 yards of its end. At sundown we camped in a small valley, after riding about 20 miles, we passed two of the Indian camping ground's, but they did not furnish us any information of our fleing foes.
By sun rise the next morning we wee again in our saddles and on the trail, for we were anxiously expecting to come to another of the Indian camp ground's within four or five miles. Our expectations were realized, for we not only found an' old camp, but we also found the bodies of two girls laying on the ground a few feet apart cold in death. The girls had both been scalped, but aside from that fiendish mutilation, they did not show any other

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: marks of violence on their bodies that would indicate thaty they had been killed, or even tortured in any manner, except that the bottoms of their feet presented a mass of skinless flesh, that showed that they must have endured great torture in walking over the flinty trail, and also that they must have spent their hours of rest in excruciating agony. From our cursory examination we came to the conclusion that they both had died natural deaths after their power's of endurance had become exhausted. With the only tools we had with us, an axe and a spade, we made a grave for them in that secluded valley, far away from kindred and friends, as reverently and tenderly as the situation would admit of, we laid them side by side in that lonely grave, where the young lives that had ended in unknown cruelties and anguish, would ever more rest in  peace. The Captain repeated as much of the burial service as he could call to mind. After we had filled in the grave, we made a mound of stones upon it to protect it from the ravages of the Coyotes, who fortunately had not yet been near the bodies, and this pile of

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: stones was all we could mark their grave with. When our sad task was finished it was about 10 a.m. We reconed that the Indians were still about two days marche's, or 20 miles from us yet, for every thing about the camp indicated that the Indians had camped there two nights before. As we only had enough rations left for lunch that day, and as we expected that we were then 25 or 30 miles from the place where our command would likely camp that evening, we were not in a very good condition to trail the Indians any father at that time. The Captain said, "We have found the girls, but unfortunatelhy to late to rescue them, we have discovered what their fate was, and we have done all for them that mortal men could do under the circumstances, and we wll now turn our faces towards the river, and try to find our command, and tomorrow if the Major is willing, we will start again after those cussed red skins and follow the last one of them if necessary, before we drop him, into Brigham Young's harem or into the inner portals of hades." This was a pretty long speech for our Captain

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: to make, but it was worthy of the occasion that called it forth, and it tersely expressed the sentiments of his audience. We were soon in the saddle again and headed for the river; about the middle of the afternoon we came in sight of our command going into camp, and an hour or so later we joined them. After dismissing us the Captain rode to the Majors tent to report the result of his scout, and the rest of us attended to our horses. Afte supper the Majors striker came to me and said that they Major wanted to see me. I grumbled some because I had just filled my pipe, and I was spoiling for the want of a smoke, the interview with the Major I was willing to postpone but I did feel that way inclined in regard to a smok, but I knew that my wishes in the matter would not be respected, so after brushing a little more dust off my clothes, I started for the Majors tent. I found gathered there besides the Major, our Surgeon, Capt Smith of K troop and four Lieutenants, and my own Captain. As soon as I had saluted the party, my Captain said to me that the Major wanted to hear my adventures while seeking for that lost trail, and also about my scare

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: while camping alone. The Major invited me to take a seat, but as each of the Officers occupied his own camp stool, which he had brought with him, and as there was not an extra one, I had no option but to take a seat on the grass which I did. I repeated the incidents connected with my search for the lost trail and of my experience in my horse camp, and then they pressed question after question upon me which I succeeded in answering somehow, after I had satisfied their curiosities and been pumped dry, I was dismissed to my quarters and pipe. The next morning we were told that the Major had decided not to send another party in pursuit of those Indians, but to push ahead for Salt Lake City as fast as our already jaded mules and horses could stand to travel, and also that he expected that during the coming winter or the spring following, we would all be given a chance to meet those Indians and avenge the wrongs and deaths of those two girls, and also the deaths of many others who had been plundered and killed by that same band

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: of Indians during the past 10 to 15 years. While on our further march to our station we were on scouting duty nearly every day, and the results of these scouts was that 25 or more bad Indians were sent to the 'happy hunting grounds' of their forefathers before they were fully prepared to start on the journey. We arrived at Salt Lake City on Nov 1st several days after our command had arrived there. This ends my true Indian story, in which I have not introduced an Indian in person, for the reason that in the several scouts in pursuit of the Indians who had captured the two girls, none of my companions or myself saw an Indian. When I had finished my story, Robert Carpenter said he would entertain us with a short one. A school teacher asked one of his scholars "Johnny Riley, why were you absent from school yesterday." "me Mother was sick," "me Mother was sick, such shocking grammar! what was the matter with your Mother." "I think she had the mumps," "Well don't you know the mumps are catching, your Mother might give you mumps, then the other scholars would catch the disease from you." "Awh; she would not give me nothin', she's me step mother."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
Chapter XVI
'Beware of the man who approaches you with the promise that he has come to do you a favor.'
A few days later I met Hugh Connor on the road with his horse and buggy, when we came abreast of each other he pulled up his horse with a, "Whoa there Icobod! now Serjint right oblique an' surmount obsticles- in other words climb into me carriage an' help yeresilf to a front sate." I inquired where he was bound for he replied that business took him to River View, and he was agoing there if the buggy held togather until he got there. I told him that I would go along, as I had no more objection to taking a ride with him, than I had for taking a dose of Spiritus [[frumenti?]], he replied. "Oi am plazed to hear ye say that Serjint, becase it shows that it wor only yere liver phwat wor ailin; ye, whin Oi wor thinkin' mebby ye wor throubled wid Softenin' of the brain, an' Oi wor jist agoin to advise ye not to rade enny of thim jokes phwat ye sees in the noosepapers, because thim jokes wod make

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
[[Oi?]] can tell ye that the ould man wor in no hurry about sayin' grace, an' Donal for once got his hearty [[fill?]] at that table enny how, an' so did he at night, an' the next mornin' also, an' whin he wor goin' back home that Monday mornin' he laped the mill race, an' Felix coom out an' gave him a cheer, Donal took Felix by both hands an' he shook thim right heartily. An ivery Monday mornin' afther that, for the three years that the ould man lived, Felix always saw Donal lape the mill race as [[?]] as a sparrow wod hop over a twig. At the end of the three years the ould died, an' Donal wint to live on the farm altogather, an' there wor no [[?]] and iver coom to see him that he more heartily welcomed than he did Felix the Miller."
[[?]] now! that's all of me fairy story, an does an' [[?]] be thinkin' it wor substantial enought to kape [[from?]]  bein' faint wid hunger afore we gits to thir homes agin.?, or will we stop at the Empire an' git some dinner to countheract enny possible faintin' spells phwat wod attack us [[?]] [[?]]." "Oi am hungry me silf, an' Oi knows of [[?]] wor falin' wake by the way Oi have to [[?]] on the lines to kape him from bein' run-

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: over by the buggy." I replied that I felt as though a good dinner would not come amiss to any of us, and as for myself, after listening to his story I felt the need of something to stimulate the inner man, which has become quite exhausted with hearing of so much food being wasted. After we had dinner Hugh left me to go and transact the business that had called him there. I spent the time of waiting until he was ready to start for home, in walking around the village, I inspected the Rolling Mills and several other industral plants, with which that busy suburb is well supplied- from a distance-. After we had got started for home, Hugh inquired if I hadn't an Army story or incident that I could while away the time by telling. I replied that there was an' incident that happened in the winter of '61 and '62 at the Fort where my troop of Cavalry was stationed at that date. I was at the time acting Hospital Steward at the Fort, at that time there was only two troops of Cavalry at the Fort A. and H., and there was 20 men from

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: each troop on detached service at Carson City for two months guarding the Territorial prison- Nevada at that date was a Territory-. from an expected raid and rescue of a notorous criminal who was confined within its walls. Along the last day of Feb '62, a man by the name of Booth, of A troop, who was one of the detail on guard at the prison, was taken sick, and he was sent back to the Fort, he was brought to the Hospital for treatment, he had a serious attack of inflamation of the lungs, or what is now know as pneumonia. He pulled through all right, and in a couple of weeks he was up and walking about the Hospital, and in a few days he was allowed to extend his walks to the parade ground outside. A few night after Booth had began to go out of doors, I went out to the wood pile in the rear of the Hospital a few minutes after 9 oclock, to get an armful of wood, there was a guard post a few yards distant, and I noticed that the Sentinel was coming from the farther end of his beat. I loaded [[up?]] with wood, and I had turned to go back [[when?]] I heard a trembling voice say- [[?]] Steward?.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: I turned towards the Sentinel- whom I recognized-, and asked, "What do you want Myers?" He replied hardly above his breath, "Com- Come here." From the way he was acting I thought that perhaps he had been taken suddenly ill. I threw down my load of wood and went to where he was standing, and said to him, "What is the trouble, are you sick Myers?', he replied, "n-o no, but look up there," pointing with his right hand towards the Cemetery, which was situated on the bluff about 600 yards from the Hospital. A full moon was shining brightly. I looked in the direction that Myers pointed and plainly saw a ghost, or something that resembled the traditional ghosts that we have heard about, ever since we were old enough to be scared half out of our lives, and wholly out of our senses by some imbacile who hadn't brains enough to furnish a square meal for a gnat. As far as I could see the Apparation was dressed all in white, and in the moon light it looked to be 7 or 8 feet it highth. I inquired of Myers how long it was since he had first seen it, and he answered, "A- about half an hour." I asked if

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: it had remained stationary all of that time, and he replied that it had disappeared into the ground three times for a few minits each time. When I first saw the apparation I will admit that I was startled and my pulse must have quickened its beats, for much that I had heard and read about ghosts visiting the earth and being seen in cemeteries in the night time, came to my memory and I thought that I was looking at a veritable ghost, but however this feeling was of short duration, for as soon as Myers told me that the apparation appeared and disappeared at pleasure, I was sure that a living agent was at the bottom of the mystery. I told Myers that I would go in and get my overcoat for I was getting cold. He begged of me not to go and leave him there alone, because he knew that that was Murphy's ghost, come back to haunt us for not giving him a Christian burial. I laughed at Myers for believing that there were so called ghosts who walked the earth at night, or any other time for that matter, I told him that he would be relieved in a few mintues, and then he and I would go  and capture that ghost, but he declared

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: that he would not go one step nearer the cemetery, even if he had to stay in the guard house the ballance of his enlistment. While we were talking the apparation disappeared two or three times to reappear after a few moments and remain motionless for a while. I went into the Hospital, taking an armfull of wood with me, and put on my overcoat, and I also took the precaution to buckle my revolver belt around me, for I did not know but what I might need it before that ghost was captured. Just as I reached the guards beat, the Sergeant of the guard with the relief arrived on the scene, After Myers had been relieved I told the Sergeant what we had seen up in the cemetery. When the Sergeant with the relief came round the corner of the Commissary building the apperation was in sight, but at their apperance it immediatley disappeared, so that none of the detail had as yet got a glimpse of it. I asked the Sergeant if he would take the three relieved guards and go with me up to the cemetery and capture the ghost, he answered, "yes, come along men and we will make it hot for his ghost ship." But Myers utterly refused to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: go, the Sergeant sent him back to the guard house with the information that he would attend to his case in the morning. Then we four started up the bluff for the cemetery, when we started the ghost was in sight, but we had not gone far before it disappeared from our view, as soon as we got within hearing distance of the cemetery we heard some one talking, we stopped to listen and then we could distinctly hear a voice in earnest prayer, but only for a few moments for the ghost, who we could now plainly see kneeling by the side of a grave-, changed from praying to cursing. I recognized the voice as belonging to Booth my patient in the Hospital, I walked to where he was still kneeling throwing out oaths by the yard, and slapping him on the shoulder, I inquired what he was doing there, he probably wanted me to think that he was either out of his head or else in a trance, for his first words were. "Is that you Steward? where am I" how did I get here" I went to bed but the spirits must have brought me here," then catching hold of my arm he continued, "See! there they are now," [[moving?]] towards the Sergeant and the two

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
men with him. I told him that they had come to take him back to the Hospital for they thought he had been out there in the cold long enough. We had no trouble in getting him back to the Hospital, for he walked quietly by my side with one hand grasping my arm. Af first I was inclined to send Booth to the guard house for safe keeping, but I feared that he might have a relapse after his exposure to the night air, so I took him to his bed and began to peel him.
I found that he had a sheet from off his bed, thrown loosely over his head and shoulders, that reached nearly to the ground, and under that he had wrapped a folded blanket over his clothes, around his body leaving both of his arms free, so that he had gone out well prepared to resist the cold. The next morning I reported the incident to the Surgeon, and he sent Booth to his troop, and before night his first Sergeant sent him to the guard house charged with shaming insanity. He got a guard house sentence, and for the next 30 days his only amusement was cutting wood for the use of the Hospital and Bakery, under the charge of a guard with a loaded gun, at the end of

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: 30 days he was wholly cured of his insanity. He confessed to his Captain that he had played the insanity role with the expectation that he would make it work, so that he would be declared crazy and discharged from the Army, but as it had not succeeded he had concluded to do his duty like a man the ballance of his enlistment. After he had served out his sentence, he returned to duty with his troop, and after that episode he was a good trusty soldier. The following fall we were transfered to Fort Douglas Utah, and a year later Booth married a Mormon girl, and at the expiration of his term of service he was honorably discharged. As soon as he was discharged, he and his wife went to Nevada and settled on a ranch in Carson Valley. Something like 15 years after he settled in Carson Valley, I was told by a comrade who had visited them at their home the year before, that Booth and his wife were living happily with their little family on the ranch, and that they were in comfortable circumstances. And he added that Booth told him, that as every thing had turned out, he was very thankful that his insanity dodge had not been a success, for if it had been he might not have a home now.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
Chapter XVII
"If you would win success in life, don't waste your time in reading maxims like this and taking advice from the successful. Just get busy yourself."
When I had concluded my story, Hugh remarked, "Now that wor phwat one cud call a rale live ghost Story, but Oi wor a bit sorry that yere man Booth didn't have a asy relapse of his distimper, for a punishment for giving ye the undacint scare phwat he did. Now be honest Sergint, didn't yere two knees knock togather like a pair of castinettes, an' yere lower jaw fall down onto yere breast, while ye wor holdin' yere cap on wid both hands to kape yere hair from lavin' yere head." I replied that it was not quite so bad as he represented, but as I had already stated, I was considerably startled when I first saw the apparation, but that feeling had soon changed to one of vexation toward the perpetrator of what I had concluded was intended as a hoax, and I felt more inclination to interview his ghost ship, than I did to run away from him. Hugh replied, "Ye make a brave diffince.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
[[?]] all anxious to hear you tell the whole of it, for Hugh says that it is more thrilling and awesome than Tommy's ghost was, and you are not to skip any of the details in relating it, and when you have told it, I promise that both [[?]] and I will forgive your breach of the peace."
With such an incentive in sight, I could not refuse her request, so I began and told the story as I have already told it in the previous chapter. After I had finished the story Mrs Norah Murray enquired what Myers had ment by saying that Murphy's ghost had come back to haunt us for not giving him a christian burial. I replied that I would have to tell another story to explain his remark. She asked me to relate it, and I was beset on all sides to tell the story, so that I had no option but to comply with their wishes, which I was quite willing to do. I should have mentioned that there were no children present, except two or three in arms, so that I felt more at liberty to tell the story as it had actually occured, than I should have [[?]] if there had been a number of little ears [[?]] to hear the grewsome tale.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: Before I began the story I was cautioned to not omit any of the details of the incident, for if I did it would be just to bad for anything, the ladys declared. I promised not to skip even an 'and' in the recital of Murphy's dersertion, which incident I related as follows. A man by the name of Murphy who was a member of troop A, of which troop I have spoken in my story of Myers ghost, as having been stationed at the same post that my troop was in Nevada during the winter of '61 and '62. About a month previous to the ghost incident, Murphy deserted from his troop quarters one night, takeing with him his carbine and revolver. The next morning when he did not present himself at roll call, it was soon discovered that he had deserted. A detail of troopers was sent in pursuit of him. He was found at a ranch about 8 miles from the Fort, he was captured while eating his breakfast, his revolver was lieing on the table at his right hand, and the carbine was resting against the table at his left, but he was not given an opportunity to use either weapon, for the door of the room suddenly opened and four troopers stepped into the room with their revolvers

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: pointed at his heart, and at the same moment outside of the house, at each of the three windows of the room, there appeared a trooper with his carbine pointed at his body. Probably the first intimation Murphy had of their presence, was when the Sergeant of the Squad ordered him to throw up his hands or he would be a dead man in a minute, one look around showed him the futility of attempting to escape, but his hands went up much quicker than the time I have used in telling this passed. Murphy was allowed to finish his breakfast, and Joe- the owner of the ranch-, and his wife, whom the troopers had kept under guard until Murphy was captured, were allowed to wait on him. When they were ready to start back to the fort, Murphy's wrists were bound togather with a handkerchief, and the end of a picket rope was passed around them and tied, and he was led back to the Fort, for they had no extra horse for him to ride. When the squard arrived within a half mile of the Fort, Murphy was tied to the tail of a horse, and led in that ignomineous manner to head quarters, where the Sergeant

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: was ordered to turn him over to the Officer of the guard, he was put in the guard house and kept in close confinement while awaiting trail for desertion. One morning three or four days before Booth played the role of ghost to an unappreciative audience-, when the guard unlocked Murphy's cell door, he found the cell empty, Murphy had escaped during the night through the window in his cell. He had sawed, with a saw made from a case knife and then tempered, two three quarter inch bars enough so that he could bend them and pull the ends out of their sockets, he had used terpentine as a lubricant to deaden the sound of his saw, having no farther use for the saw or small vial of turpentine he had left them behind. On investigation it was found that the knife was not taken from either of the mess rooms, and that there was not another like it at the Fort, and where and how he had procured it was a mystery. A squad of troopers was immeditately sent in pursuit of him, but they returned at night and reported that they had not found any trace of him.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: That morning when the mail ambulance left the Fort at 9 o'clock, for Carson City 32 miles distant, both the ambulance driver and the Surgeon, who was going as a passenger to Carson City, knew of Murphy's escape from the Guard house. During their drive to Carson they neither heard or saw anything of Murphy, and after their arrival there they did not hear anything of him. The next morning they started on their return trip to the Fort accompanied by a citizen of the name of Crosby, that supplied the Fort with beef cattle, who was goind down to the Fort on business connected with his contract. They had arrived within about 15 miles of the Fort when the driver saw Murphy dodge behind a ledge of rocks that ran paralell with the road for a few hundred feet, and about 400 yards distant from it. The driver told the Surgeon what he had seen, and he told him to stop his team and he would capture him. The Surgeon exchanged his 5 shooter for the drivers heavy 7 shooter, for he would have to remain with his team, for there was no hitching posts or trees within several miles of the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: place. The Surgeon armed with the drivers Colt's navy revolver, started in the direction that Murphy had been seen to hide, the citizen Crosby offered his services in capturing him, and they were accepted by the Surgeon who remarked that now we will make short work of capturing the renegade. They had not gone but a few steps when Murphy poked his head up above the rocks, the Surgeon ordered him to come out and surrender himself, Murphy answered that he would see him _____first, and then he wouldn't, the Surgeon told him that he would give him three minutes to surrender in, and if he had not at the end of that time he would shoot him. Murphy replied, "Shoot and be damned, if you want me come and get me," the Surgeon took out his watch and when the three minutes had passed, he and Crosby began to advance towards Murphy, they had not taken more than a dozzen steps, before Murphy brought a carbine into sight and rested its barrel on a rock, this action of his did not make them stop, seeing that it did not he took sight and without saying a word he pulled the trigger, the bullet

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: passed between the two men and then went through the cover of the ambulance. The Surgeon and driver had supposed that Murphy had no weapons with him, for he had taken none from the guard house when he escaped, and it was a mystery where he had got that carbine, and as far as I know it has never been cleared up. The Quartermaster Sergeant of his troop had the theory that a close friend of Murphy's in the troop, had stolen the carbine and ammunition out of his room, because a few days before he had missed 20 rounds of ammunition, and that this friend had hidden the carbine and cartrages in some secluded spot not far from the Fort, and then he had informed Murphy, - who he was allowed to visit in the guard house as often as he wished to-, where he would find them. Murphys friend was arrested but there could be nothing proven that would implicate him in any way in the matter, so he was released at once, and further investigation was soon suspended. But when Murphy opened fire on his would be

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
captors with the carbine, it complicated matters, for the Surgeon had assured Crosby that he was unarmed, but the knowledge that he was armed and ready to use his weapon, did not make them any the less determined to capture him, and they both proved themselves to be brave men. Murphy loaded and fired as rapidly as he could, and several shots had been fired by each side without any ones being hit, then a bullet from Murphy's carbine buryed itself in Crosby's head, and a few moments later the Surgeon sent a revolver ball through Murphy's heart, and he fell to the ground dead.
After the Surgeon had satisfied himself that Murphy was passed doing any more mischief, he turned his attention to his wounded companion, whom he found dangerously hurt and unconscious, he and the driver lifted him into the ambulance as carefully as they could and placed him in a reclining position on the back seat, then after getting Murphy's carbine and ammunition they started for the Fort, leaving Murphy's

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
body lieing where it fell. They drove as fast as it was possible to do under the circumstances, and about three hours after Crosby was wounded he was carried into the Hospital at the Fort.
The Surgeon probed for the bullet but he could not find it, everything that could be done for Crosby was done, but all the efforts in his behalf were in vain, for he never regained consciousness again, and death relieved him of all further pain and trouble two days after he was wounded. The afternoon before he died his wife was sent for, and she arrived from Carson City the next forenoon a short time after her husband died, the next day his remains were sent with an escort to Carson City where they were intered. When the ambulance arrived at the Hospital with the wounded citizen, the Surgeon told the driver to report the shooting of Murphy to the Commanding Officer, which he did, half an hour later a six mule team left the Fort with a detail of four men and a sergeant, with orders to bring in the body of Muphy, they returned with it sometime between midnight and daylight,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: The body was left in the wagon with a guard over it until the next morning, then the wagon was driven to the cemetery where a grave had already been prepared, the body was taken out of the wagon and placed in a rough board box and lowered into the grave and covered up with as little ceremony as a mongrel dog would have received. Murphy by his double crime of desertion had forfeited all of his rights to a military funeral, therefore he was buryed as an outcast, for there were none so poor as to do him reverence- as Shakespeare remarked on a certain occasion-, for neither his close friend or any of his chums took the trouble to be present at his interment, there was no one present but the detail that had been sent after the body, and when they left the cemetery it would have been tramped and leveled to corrispond with the ground surrounding it and its outlines had been obliterated. And this was the fate of Muphy the deserter.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
It was this incident that the guard Myers refered to when he said that it was Murphy's ghost come back to haunt us for not giving him a Christian burial. And now I will tell you what happened to Myers, and then both stories will be ended in proper form.
The next morning after the appearance of the ghost, the Sergeant reported Myers breach of discipline and cowardice to the Officer of the day, and he reported the same to the Commander of the Fort, and there the matter appeared to stop, for Myers was not kept under arrest, but he continued to do duty, but the duty he did was around the mess house and for the Officers of his troop when they had undesirable jobs for him to do, and he was not again detailed for guard duty. But as Myers continued to do duty of some kind we concluded that no further notice would be taken of his flagrant breach of discipline, but that he would be allowed to remain with his troop and used as a kind of Jack of all work. But the following Oct while we were on the march to Utah, we were surprised one

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: evening by having read to us at Retreat, an order from Headquarters, dishonorably discharging Myers without pay or allowance, for cowardice and uncleanliness. I suppose they thought this the easiest and cheapest way to get rid of him, because a Court Martial to try him would have been expensive, for 6 or 8 officiers would have to be sent from distant posts to try him, and then he would surely be found guilty when tried, and sentenced to work on the fortification on Alcatraz Island in the harbor of San Francisco, the ballance of his term of service. So taking it all round Myers got off with a mighty light punishment. The last time that I have ever heard from or seen Myers was the morning tht he left us on the Malad river in Utah, on his way to Boise City Idaho. And now my two stories are completed, and I have given you all of the details without reserve. Mrs George Carpenter inquired if Myers had any money to buy food with on his journey, and if there was any places where he could buy it if he had money. The others were all anxious to know what

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: the prospects of his reaching his destination were, and if he could travel in safety, and also what, without pay or allowance ment. I replied that it would give me pleasure to answer their questions to the best of my ability. Although Myers was discharged without pay or allowance, the members of his troop did not allow him to leave them with empty pockets, for they made up a purse that the Officers increased with generous donations, that would keep him for a month, even in that country where a meal of black coffee without milk, beans, bacon and hot biscuit, indigestible enough to create a mutiny before they were eaten, and bacon greese in the place of butter, cost from 50 cents to a dollar, and a lodging cost 50 cents and you had to furnish your own blankets, and spread them on the floor, but if you prefered to spread them under a tree or anywheres out of doors you were at liberty to do so, and no charge was made, but if you did the landlord would not be responsible for any valuables you might have about your person. A soldier honorably discharged receives

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: all the pay due him at that time, and also an allowance of 20 cents a day for mileage to the place where he enlisted, and rations to cover the the distance on a basis of 20 miles a day, the ration is commuted to its value in money, and the man is given money instead of food, and he is paid the actual cost of a daily ration at the post where he is discharged. For an illustration, a man honorably discharged say 600 miles from the place where he enlisted, would receive 6 dollars at one cent a mile for transportation, and supposing a days ration cost 40 cents, he would be paid 12 dollars for the 30 days rations he was entitled to receive for thirty days travel at 20 miles a day, so that he would get 18 dollars for expenses on a 600 mile journey. Little enough you say, that is true, but it is better than nothing, and a heap more than Myers received. However Myers was permitted to take all his clothing, and also his two blankets, so he did not leave us in a destitute condition. It was about 130 miles to Boise City from where he had to leave us, and

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
50 miles to the nearest Settlement, but there were Stage Stations every 12 to 15 miles along the road were he could find both food and shelter. 
As soon as I had concluded Mrs Purdy inquired whether I had ever had an opportunity to become acquainted with the domestic life of a Mormon family or not. I answered that I with 5 other troopers had stopped with a Mormon family, 70 miles north of Salt Lake City, for 6 or 8 days the last of Jan '63. The family comprised the husband and three wives and 9 children all living in the same house, but each wife had her own apartments. The mans name was Smart and he also had two other wives living on ranches or farmes a few miles distant. Two of the wives in the house where we stopped, were sisters and both of them were red headed, but I did not notice that that reality interfered with the harmony of the household.
All of us troopers had had our feet more or less badly frozen, and we were compelled to stop for a few days and doctor them until they would allow us to return to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
our head quarters at Fort Douglas. We were treated very kindly and our feet were cared for as well as they were after we got home.
We took all our meals with the first Mrs Smart, who apparently had general supervision over the whole house. The Sisters each had her own table and did the cooking for herself and children, and they were both 20 years and more younger than Mrs Smart number one. 
I had several conversations with Mrs Smart, in which she told me a little of the history of her life. Both she and her husband were born and raised in England, and soon after their marriage they were both converted to the Mormon faith, and three years later they concluded to come to the United States so that they would be nearer to the heads of their church. They converted their property into money and made all their arrangements to start on a certain date. Two weeks before they were to start her eldest child, a little girl of two years of age, was taken sick, and she did not appear to be getting any better when the day for

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: their departure arrived. As they had disposed of all their household goods and other property, they concluded to embark and leave her in the care of Mrs Smart's Mother which they did do, and with her husband and two months old baby boy in her arms, she left her little girl, life long friends and relatives to try the realities of what had proved to be almost a new existence. I asked her if she had ever seen her daughter since that day, she replied. "No! I have never seen her since the day I kissed her feverish lips, good bye-, more than 25 years ago, but her father has seen her twice when he was on Missionary duty in England, the last time was two years ago, he visited her at her home, for she has a home of her own, she married a wealthy young landed proprietor, and at that time she had a little son two years old. I inquired why they had not had her brought to them, after they had got settled in their present home, by some of the converts who arrive at Salt Lake City annually from England, or her father could have brought her with him when he returned

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: from his mission. After a pause of two or three minutes she replied. "Because I did not want her to come here, I will tell you that much but please do not ask me any more questions on that subject, after that in all of our conversations I was careful to keep away from thin ice, but at the same time I wanted to know whether her husband was willing that their daughter should remain in England or not, but I respected her wishes and curbed my curiosity, but I felt at the time as a fellow does after being chiated in a horse trade. Mrs Smart told me that she had three boys all grown to manhood, two of them were married and the youngest was teaching school, and then she exclaimed, "but my wee baby girl is away off there in England, and she has a baby of her own now." It was evident that the Mothers thoughts often turned to her absent daughter. I asked her if she really believed in a doctrine that taught that a man should have as many wives as he could support in comfort, she answered that when her husband first spoke to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: her about his taking another wife, she had objected to his doing so, but after careful thought and prayer, she had been shown that it was his duty to do so, for all male Mormons should have as many wives as they can support and help in the building up of Zion, and at the time her husband was abundently able to support two or three more wives, so she had given her consent, and he had taken wife No 2, and 6 months later he had taken wife No 3, and 3 years later he took wife No 4, and two years afterwards he took the sister of wife No 4 for his fifth wife. These last two wives she had requested him to marry, and now she had wife No 6 already picked out for him, she was a smart young woman of 20, healthy and a good worker but she was not very good looking- which I found to be the case with all that I saw-, she was poor and an orphan without a home, and she thought that she would consent to marry her husband soon, for a few days before she had told her that she had about made up her mind to accept

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: him and become his sixth wife. It did not look like a good day for proselyting so I dropped the subject. It has always been a mystery to me, why Mrs Smart having a belief in the Divine right of poligamy and of the righteousness of having a plurality of wives, should object to her daughters coming to Utah to live, where her belief was carried to its utmost limits, but then one can't fathom the depths of a Mothers feelings or her thoughts when the wellfare of her child is at stake, and I felt quite sure that her Mother heart sent out a prayer for the -, wee baby girl away off there in England-, a dozzen times a day, even after she had grown to womanhood, but I could not help but think that she was trying bravely to make the best of the situation that she found herself placed in, and I was convinced that she had discovered- when to late-, that all was not gold that glittered, even amongst the Later day Saints. I had an idea that discontent like a canker had been growing at her heart strings all the years since she left England, and the only way she could quiet is by action, therefore she had approved of, and also urged her husband to take other wives,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: hoping to then have something on her mind to distract her thoughts from the little baby girl in England. Mrs Smart informed me that she and her husband were living at Nauvoo Ill, at the time their prophet Joseph Smith and his brother Hyrum were shot by an angry mob, and that they were driven out of the State, they went to Missouri, and a few years afterwards when the Mormons departed for the Salt Lake Valley, under the direction and leadership of Brigham Young, they had come with them, and the next Spring after their arrival at Salt Lake, a Settlement was made at that place and named Box Elder, and her husband was made Bishop of the Colony, and they had lived there ever since, and they had greatly prospered for her husband was a Bishop and also the richest man in the county. I asked her how many children her husband was the father of, she replied, "That is something that don't concern you." I replied that she was mistaken, for I had a burning desire to know, and I feared that it would not be quenched until I was informed. She replied, "then ask Samrt for I won't gratify your curiosity by telling you." I did ask Smart if he had any objections to telling me how many children he had, and he replied. "None in the world,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
why should I have? when I am willing to acknowledge them all at any time, I have 28 childen, 16 of them are girls, and 12 are boys quite a nice little family hey!." When Mrs Smart told me about her being compelled to leave her baby girl in England, and that she had not seen her since, I had both pity and sympathy to spare for her in her trials, but after she had told me that she had been contented to have her husband take another wife, and that she had been instrumental in marrying him to three other women, and also that, at that time she had another woman in training for a wife for him, I transfered all of my sympathy to her husband, for I thought he needed it more than she did, for she appeared to be disposed to get him into all kinds of troubles, without having a twinge of conscience.
This was my only experience of the domestic life of the Mormon families, and this little insight into the workings of their polygamus belief left a bad taste in my mouth, that time has not wholly effeaced.
And now that I have done penance and purged myself of any offence I will take a back seat and try to feel resigned.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
Chapter XVIII.
Solomon must have got awful tired of walking with babies at night.
After I had made a final conclusion to my story telling, the ladies of the party wanted to learn more about the Mormon Sect, and they had many questions to ask in regard to them, and their questions received answers more or less unsatisfactory, for none of us were Seers or Soothsayers, and I doubt if a dozzen of each could have satisfied their curiosity.
During the conversation that followed it was discovered that Ben Rogers could tell us an incident of Mormon life that was founded on fact. As soon as this became known Mrs Purdy said. "I am glad to hear that you can tell us something about those people, for as yet I have heard nothing to their credit, and now I will invite all of you to a lawn party at my home next Saturday at 1 p.m. and there is to be no postponement on account of the weather either, for the house will shelter

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
us if it is stormy, and I will persuade Ben Rogers to tell us what he knows about Mormonism, and I am sure that the Sergeant will also be willing to entertain us with an incident connected with these people." We all promised to meet at her home- on time-, on the day mentioned, and as it was getting late in the evening we started for our homes like a lot of loitering school children with many last words to say. I walked with Hugh Connor as far as the corner of his street and he said to me. 
"Now Sergint, do yere duty like a soldier an' git yere wits to work an' be thinkin' up some incident phwat happined ye on the plains, an' the more ye bring into the story about the Mormons, the betther thes women folks will appreciate it, for Oi wor thinkin' that they's will be talkin' of little else for the next month. Now to plaze thim, Oi wor almost timptid to go out to Utah for a week an' see the people in their ivery day life an' wearin' they's workin' clothes, but [[meb?]] it wor betther for me to recave me knowledge of thim through a proxy, for wid me feelin's of riverince for all woman kind, Oi have

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
no call to go where woman become concubines, an' some of thim by their own wishes, for Oi wod be gitin' mesilf into all kinds of throubles an' hav me head broke a dozzen times a day, becaze Oi wod be that ignorant that Oi wod be askin' thim all sorts of unasy questions to answer, for wid the rheumatiz an' me pigs both breakin' out at the same time, Oi wor sure to have plinty of throuble 'till they's wor arristid agin." I assured him that I would come prepared to to entertain the company with a reminiscence of my adventures in Utah. The day for the lawn party at Mrs Purdy's arrived, and it was one of those gladsome days in early September, that seem to be made specially for the enjoyment of us mortals on such occasions.
And then with the accessaries of a blue sky above, and green turf beneath our feet, with hamocks, easy chairs and seats in the shade of the large oak trees with which the grounds were plentifully supplied, and then last but not least, the presence of several fair dames to complete the harmony, one could ask for nothing more for he was already in

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
paradise. After the guests had all arrived and got settled down comfortably, Sam Browne remarked that we were continually running up against something or other now-a-days, may be a head on collision of two trains of cars, or a barbed wire fence with the flavor of torn cloths still hanging about it, but there is nothing funny in either of those to common accidents, but an excuse that a School teacher received from the Mother of one of his pupils, had a spice of humor in its composition, of which fact the writer was probably blissfully ignorant, and he read it for our benefit. "Mr teacher. Please excuse James for being absent. We have got a pet goat and he et up his-James'es- pants. His father- James'es- couldn't git him any until yesterday. P. S. Wev'e tide up the goat."
As soon as Sam had finished his excuse story, Mrs Purdy hastened to request Ben Rogers to relate his story. Ben prefaced his story by saying that the story he was about to relate, would differ but slightly, as far as the treatment of the members of the church was concerned

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
from many other incidents that could be told of the Mormons since they had become a sect by themselves, and the priesthood had assumed unto themselves arbitrary powers of life and death over their deluded converts, which power they did assuredly assume, and for many years there was a band of unscrupulous men called Danites, but they were generally called the Distroying Angles, who were in the service of the leaders of the Church, and I do not know but what they have an organization of the same kind at the present day. The Danites had the pleasant duty of quietly making away with all disaffected ones within the Church.
And after their migration to Utah, the Danites were sent in pursuit of any one who had become dissatisfied with Mormonism, and was trying to escape from its tyranny by leaving the Territory, but with very few exceptions none of the large number of those who tried to escape, were ever heard from, and the Mormon Elders gave it out that the missing ones had either been killed by Indians, or else they had perished from hunger and exposure in the Mountains, for dilligent search had been

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
made for each one wth the hope of finding and saving them from death by exposure, but no trace could be found of the missing ones.
But as the remains of none of them were ever discovered, it was understood by the faithfull that the Distroying Angels had found the runaways and after killing them, they had disposed of the bodies in a way that would obliterate all traces of their crime. He continued. 
I have made this explination thinking that perhaps it would be a help in getting a clear understanding of the positon in which my hero and his wife  were placed, as my story unfolds its several different aspects." Then he said that a son of a near neighbor of his fathers in Wayne County New YOrk, had joined the Mormons soon after their self appointed prophet Joseph Smith made the claim that he had discovered in a cave, the tablets of brass upon which were engraved the words that are printed in their book of Mormon, and Joe Smith had also discovered that he had been given the power or gift of interpretation, which was lucky for the Mormons, for no one else could

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
read the tablets or make any sense out of them, and this young man had been very intimate with Smith up to the time of his death.
The young mans name was Henry Strong, and he was of a good family and well connected. At the time he was converted to Mormonism, he was a School teacher and taught the School in the district where my father lived, but I was not old enough to go to school at that time. At the time of Henry Strong's conversion to Mormonism he was engaged to be married to a charming young lady, they had been sweethearts from their childhood, but she was not of the Mormon faith and she would have none of it, the day for their marriage had been set and the invitations sent out, but she refused to marry him then, and at the time she declared that she would never marry him as long as he remained a Mormon. At that time Henry Strong's future prospects looked very bright, for he was about to marry an intelligent as well as a handsome young woman of as good a family as his own, and his father had promised to give him a deed of 80 acres of land with a good barn already on it, and also to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
assist him to build a house on the land, and his intended wife would bring dower enough with her to stock their farm, so that his prospects for the future looked bright indeed. But Henry prefered to be a disciple of Joe Smith and to follow his fortunes, than to have a comfortable home presided over by a charming wife. Henry and the young lady, whose name was Hellen Moore, remained on intimate terms, and finally constancy and persuasion backed by love triumphed, and they were married about three years afterwards, and they both went to the Mormon's Strong-hold some where in Ohio. They soon removed to Nauvoo Ill, and after Joe Smith's tragic death they had to flee to Missouri, and when the Mormons departed for Salt Lake Valley Utah, Mrs Strong walked by her husband's side or rode in a wagon drawn by oxen and driven by her husband.
At that time they had three children two boys and a girl baby a few weeks old. They were amongst the first pilgrims to arrive in the Salt Lake Vally, and before winter had set in Strong had buildt a comfortable adobe-sun dried brick- house for his famly where they lived

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
happy and contented during their first winter in the valley. The following Spring Strong was appointed one of the Council of 70- one of the Mormon inside organizations- and sent on a two years Missionary tour to England and Scotland. This was the first time that Strong and his wife had been parted for any length of time since they were married 7 years previous, and they both felt the seperation keenly, but they had to submit to this mandate of the Church, and Strong was to loyal to her demands to think of questioning them, or requesting that some other brother be sent on that mission in stead of him.
During the two years of his absence his family was taken care of by the Church, and their wants supplied as far as they could be with the limited means they had at hand, because they had to freight all of their food supplies from the Missouri river 1500 miles distant, in wagons drawn by from 3 to 6 yoke of oxen, until they could raise a crop of grain and vegetables. The Mormons had brought with them from the east, a large amount of vegetable seeds and also several hundred

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
bushell's of the cereals wheat, barley, oats and corn, and also potatoes; as soon as the ground was fit to work the next Spring, plowing began and the grain and seeds were planted and they produced a large crop, and after the next years harvest they had no need to send abroad for any supplies except dry good and groceries, and when the emigration to California set in they had a surplus to sell or to barter to the emigrants. It was not until after the death of Joseph Smith, that the heresy of a plurality of wives doctrine began to be talked of. But Brigham Young the new head of the Church, and also a full fledged prophet of the Church of Later Day Saints, had a bad dream or the night mare one night, which he claimed was a direct revelation from Heaven to him as the head of the Church, and to him had also been given the knowledge of interpritation. The revelation as he promulgated it was like this. 
"Thus spake the Angel of the Lord. My chosen people the later day Saints, shall multiply and become exceeding numerous and overrun the whole earth, and to them all things shall be possible. But they must seperate themselves

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: from the ungodly, and go out into the wilderness unto a valley overflowing with milk and honey. And there build a temple to my glory, and it shall be a covenant between Me and them for ever, that they multiply and replenish the earth. Ye hear My will! See that ye obey My commands." or words to the same purport.
