As Brigham Young had already sent out spies to the Salt Lake valley, who had returned with glowing accounts of the fertility of the soil of the valley, and now this timely revelation paved the way for a migration to that then distant land and but little known region, uninhabited except by Indians and rattle snakes, and it opened up a quick and practicable way for them to obey the mandate that they believed had come from Heaven to Brigham Young, at that way was to cut loose from the vicinity of their fellow man, and isolate themselves by migrating to the Salt Lake valley 1,500 miles distant from a Court of Justice or a State law, and there they could practice their abomnable doctrine of polygamy in peace, for there would be no hated Gentiles-the name they gave to all who were not members of their sect-.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
there to interfere with their pleasures, or to come to the rescue of any unfortunate female who might object to becoming the second, third or even the tenth wife of a brute in the garb of a man. Mrs Strong had never identified herself in any way with the Mormon dogma, although she was with them, she was not of them, and she was of a temperment that would not admit of her being coersed or coaxed from what she considered her line of duty. She had married Henry Strong because of her great love for him, and she could be happy in following his fortunes as long as her religious belief was not interfered with or in any way outraged.
As her husband had proved to be a very useful man in the church, she was allowed full liberty of thought and action. At the end of the two years Henry Strong returned from his mission, bringing with him a large number of new converts. A Settlement was founded in a fertile valley 60 miles south of Salt Lake City, and Strong was appointed Bishop of the new colony, to which the name of Lemi was given. Henry soon had a large adobe house built

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
for his family, where they lived for a season in perfect content, but a Serpent even entered the garden of Eden. Henry Strong had never been a believer in polygamy, and until he had become prosperous he had not been spoken to about taking another wife, but as soon as it was discovered that he was abundantly able to support more than one family, he was urged to take unto himself another wife, but he had declined doing so for the reason that he could not believe that he would be justified in doing so by his conscience.
A short time after this Heber C Kimball the first vice president of the Church visited Lemi on his annual inspecting tour of the settlements. He stopped with the Strong's while there, and it was but a short time before he began to sound Strong as to his opinion of the docterine of a plurality of wives. He frankly told Kimball that he could not conscientiously approve of the docterine, for the idea of dividing ones affections between several wives was repugnent to his feelings, and he could not bring himself to believe but what there must be a mistake somewhere, and that it was not a divine command from Heaven

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
that the Mormon's should have more than one wife. Kimball rather hotly retorted. "Then you don't believe that brother Brigham has been endowed with the knowledge of interpritation, or that he has interpreted the revelation corectly, but falsely." Strong quietly replied that he did not wish to be understood as making any such an accusation, for he believed that brother Brigham was convinced that he had given the true interpritation of all the revelations that he had received, but Brigham himself had publicly said, that he was only a mortal, and therefore he can not be infalible, and it was this remark of brother Brigham's that had brought out his remark, that he believed that there must be a mistake somewhere.
Henry's quiet tone and manner had a soothing effect on Kimball and he replied. That is all right as far as it goes, but it does not in the least release you from your obligation of obedience to the doctrines of the Church until they are proven to be wrong, and I doubt if you have a desire to enter into a controversy with the Elders, knowing as you do the power

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
that they wield in Church matters. Now that you are prosperous and able to support more than one family, it is a duty that you owe to our Church to take other wives and raise up children to the glory of Zion. And I think that after you have had a reasonable time in which to reflect upon this subject and aided by earnest prayer, that you will see your way clearly, and be ready and also anxious to do your whole duty to our Church, without its being necessary for the Elders to visit you and mark out the path that you must surely travel in. It is often said that a miss is as good as a mile to the game at the other end of a gun, and I trust that this hint of mine will bring forth fruit meet for righteousness by your ready obedience to the behests of your Church, and not turn out to be 'Apples of Sodom,' the eating of which will bring to you tribulation's and everlasting persecution while you are here on earth, and eternal damnation for your future life."
The afternoon of the day on which this conversation took place, Mrs Strong was taken with a severe attack of tooth ache, she bravely presided at the supper table until the wants of all were attended to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: and then she begged to be excused. Kimball replied, Certainly my dear Sister, but I very much regret that you find it necessary to leave us so soon, because I have that on my mind which I wished particularly to speak to you about, and as I must continue my journey in the morning, I fear I shall have no opportunity to do so during this visit, which I regret almost as much as I do that you are a sufferer from a tooth ache, that is depriving us of your charming company, but I will not detain you any longer, allow me!," and he opened the door for her to pass through. Now it is a question whether Kimball was sincere in what he said or not, but the chances are that he was really more chagrined that she had escaped him, and he had lost an opportuntiy to do some proselyting, than that he was sorry because his hostess was in distress, for he was a crafty old fox who had no use for complementary speach, except to further his own ends, but be that as it may, he did not again refer to the subject of the conversation that he and Strong had had in regard to the advisability of his taking another wife, during the time he remained with him. During the evening Kimball told several

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
anectdotes, one of which he considered a good joke on brother Brigham, to the effect that Brigham was walking one day on Temple Street Salt Lake City, when he came to a boy 7 or 8 years old, who was playing in a puddle of dirty water, he was barefooted and hatless, and what pants he had on were held up by one suspender, and what few other clothes he had on were wet and covered with the mud he was splashing around him. Brigham was shocked at the spectacle and ordered the boy to come out of that mud puddle. The boy waded ashore and Brigham asked, "Whose boy are you." the boy replied, "Brigham Young's," This answer confused Brigham for a moment, and then he said, "go home and tell your mother that Brigham Young says that she must put some clean clothes on you, and then keep you off the street."
He also told this one about himself. 
"Last year at St George, while on an inspecting tour, I visited a family in which was a girl of only 14 years of age, that had spun several hundred knots of yarn, and knit dozzens of pairs of socks and mittens during the past year, besides attending school daily

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
during the school terms, and she had also woven wollen cloth enough to make herself as dress and a petticoat. After my return to Salt Lake city, I related this incident of uncommon diligence in so young a girl, one Sunday at the Tabernacle, and I used it as a text from which I preached a powerful discourse, which stirred the Sisters to the bottom of their hearts. I ended my sermon by saying. 
"Now my young Sisters you should one and all take patern after this young country girl, and not dribble away- as many of you are disposed to do- your time in talking about each other and your clothes, work is the best antidote for your many real and imaginary ills. It is a duty you owe to the church, to learn to weave, spin, knit and sew, and then you can make all of your own clothes, and also those for the families that you are each destined to have, and then you will not be dependent upon the ungodly Gentiles for the covering upon your bodies, and you my Sisters who have blessed with families, owe your girls a duty as well as you owe it to the church, for it is your duty to teach your girls to be both frugal and industrious, and to see

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
that they don't fritter away the hours in idleness." As soon as I had taken my seat, a Sister arose and said, "Your remarks are timely brother Heber, and I am sure that all of the Sisters present will profit by them, but what we most need are more examples of the same kind of thrift that you have just told us of, and I would like to know brother Heber if your young daughters are also taught to weave, spin, knit, sew and make their own clothing from start to finish, how many of them can do this brother Heber?" 
"Her question was so unexpected that it stumped me for a moment to know what answer to make to it, for I had no answer already prepared, but I replied that I did not know how many of my daughters could make their own clothes, or spin, weave, knit and sew, for I left that matter to their mothers, but the truth is that I have so many daughters that I do not try to keep track of them all, or of their domestic perfections either." "After saying this I closed the meeting." One Sunday in Oct '63, the writer was present at the Tabernacle in Salt Lake City, when Heber C Kimball

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription:
related the foregoing incident, but instead of being asked by one of the Sisters present if his daughters worked and made their own clothes, he said, "Some of the Sisters may be anxious to know if my daughters are taught to weave, spin and knit, but I can't enlighten them on that point, for the truth of the matter is, I have so many daughters that I do not try to keep track of them all.
The next morning Kimball resumed his journey without having again met Mrs Strong, but he had left behind him the sting of a serpent. Henry Strong neither believed in or approved of the plurality of wives doctrine, he had embraced Mormanism from conscientious motives believing it to be the only true faith for one to live and die by, and for his conscience sake he had forsaken friends, comfort and home, but when the polygamy dogma was sprung upon the people of the Mormon faith, as a divine commandment, his faith received a shock from which it had never recovered. He had hoped that he would be sent on another mission, and in case he was he intended to insist that he be allowed

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: to take his family east and leave them with his parents while he was absent, but no such good luck had come to him, and now he found himself fast within the reach of the innumerable arms of the Church that he had thought to be immaculate, and he was counseled to obey her mandates, for the consequences of a refusal to do so would be disastrous to him. Neither her or his wife could see anything in the future but misery for them, without one little glimmer of hope. Heber C Kimball's visit to Lemi was in the second week in Sept, and the Strong's expected that soon after his return to Salt Lake City, they would be visited by one or more of the Elders, as the members of the council of 12 were called. Two weeks later Strong received a call from two of his fellow members of the Council of Seventy, who made the excuse for their call that they were in the neighborhood, and thought they would come and see him. Their conversation for the most part was in regard to polygamy, and each of them had only praise for its beneficial workings to offer, and they related many instances of its being the direct means of giving many poor and homeless girls, a comfortable home and also a loving husband.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: As each of these men had more than one wife they could not be considered as being impartial advocates of the doctrine. They did not question him directly in respect to this opinions in regard to the matter, but they questioned him in a way that they tried to make jocose, about his resources, and what he had made since he became a Bishop, and what it had cost him a year to support a family of five, and other questions of the same intent. When they bade him adieu they had in their possession almost as good a knowledge of his personal affairs as he had himself. During the first week of Oct Strong received a letter from the Council of twelve, which read. "From a reliable source the Council has become acquainted with your yearly income, and resources, and find that you are able to provide for another family, therefore the Council has decided to counsel you to take another wife, and it grants you until the first day of the coming year to comply with this counsel. It also suggests that Christmas would be an appropriate day for the ceremony, and the members of the Council will all try to be present and have the pleasure of dancing with your[[last?]] wife."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 3.1], 1903
transcription: The receipt of this letter completely prostrated Mrs Strong and she was quite ill for several days, and the wording of it showed Strong that he need not expect any farther clemency to be showed him by the heads of the Church until he complied with their demand, and also that if he did not soon obey this mandate and take another wife, he would subject himself to their wrath, and the consequences for doing this he hardly dare contemplate. At first he thought that if he was alone he might possibly make his escape from the Territory, but he was not alone, and he could not bring himself to think of deserting his family. The position in which Strong was placed made him almost crazy, and he could not see any way out of his troubles except to take another wife. But in a few days his wife was well enough to come to his aid, and her cheerfulness did much to raise his spirits. She told him that he had more than two months before he was required to obey the command of the Elders, and in that time something might happen that would help him to evade their mandate, and she was almost sure that there would, for she could not bilieve that they would be allowed to do as they liked always."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 2], 1903
transcription:
I need make no comments, the second
shows how highly my friends esteemed me.
But my friends as far as my imobility to distin
one note of music from another was concessed 
were not yet over, for the future had more in 
laid up for me. It was my fortune to be a mem-
ber of a Cavalry regiment in the Civil War.
As all known who have witnessed a regiment
of cavalry maneuver, on a troops of horse drill, 
the different commands are sounded on a
trumpet, and it is very necessary that each
trooper recognise and respond to the call im-
mediately. In camps I could get along very
well for these the calls were for the most part all regular ones. With sunch calls as breakfast,
dinner, stable, surgeons or sick, assemble, fatigue or boots and saddles, I could get along
all night by following the lead of my com-
paginons. The call that gave me the least tro-
ble to remember was taps - lights out- but
I was generally asleep when taps sounded.
But it was quite a different thing when 
I was on the drill ground mounted,
where I was expected to answer promptly,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 2], 1903
transcription:
to-night turn, -when the truth was that
I could not distinguish that call from
supper call. But to the intelligence of a horse
I was indebted for the success I achieved as
the best drilled man in my troop. By great 
good luck I had been issued a horse by the
Q master-master, that had two good ears,
one of which was a musical one. Now we never hear
the expression - two musical ears -, it is always
- a musical ear-, and as a, denotes an object
in the singular number, it stands to reason
that it don't mean two. My first mounted drill
do not furnish material for pleasant remem-
berance, as we were all now recruits, confu-
sion was to be expected, and that the comman-
ds would be misunderstood, but the drill
sergeant exercised a fair amount of patience
in handling us. But when a maneuver was 
balked by what he called my stupidity in
trusting to others to guide me anight, he was
sure to get red hot and address me by
epittets that he never had learned in a
sunday school. "Poor old Reiley!" he was
and killed by an Indian in '63, but I

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 2], 1903
transcription:
forgave him and the Indian long ago.
As I have said, I owed to my horse all of the
success I even achieved on the drill ground,
because within a month he knew the several
bugle calls by heart on ear, as the case maybe,
and by the time the last note of a call was sound-
did my horse was ready to obey it without being
prompted, and it was a wonder to me, how
that horse and many others could distingu-
ish one call from another when so many of the troopers could not tell one call from an-
other during their life time. My horse soon
learned - right turn, - left turn, - trot - forward
march - Gallop, - charge, - recall, - halt - and the
others that are used principally on the panacle
and drill grounds, and he always made
an effort to obey them, and I allowed him a
trust to the intelligence of my horse to save
me from disgrace when the trumpet soun-
did one of its diabolical solo's. That horse
was the best friend I had from the two years
and over that we were Comrades, and then
his death separated us. He was so badly

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 2], 1903
transcription:
kicked by another horse that death would
in a few days relieve him from his suffering.
But I did not want him to have to suffer any
longer than was necessary, as I knew he could not
recover I wanted him put out of his misery at
once. I went to my captain and asked him for 
an order to shoot him, he replied, the horse
should be shot at once and I will write you
an order to do so but -  you will have to get
it indorsed by the major. "I took the order to the
major who said, "Certainly the horse should be
shot and put out of his agony, and he would indorse the order, but - it would have to be approved by the regimental Qmaster master.
At that time our detatchment was in camp
about 160 miles from our headquarters where our Qmastermaster then was. I next went to
the adjustant and he told me that he would
forward the order to the headquarters by the
next Courier, who would leave camp on the 
third day following. As it would take that Courier 7 days to go and come, which with 
the three that would intervene before he start-
ed, would make 10 days before the horse

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 2], 1903
transcription:
could be legally put out of suffering.
Our horse were handed a mile or so from
camp, and mine was with or near the others.
After leaving the order with the Adjutant, I
went out to the herd and found one of my 
own mess on guard, after a few minutes con-
version with him I started for camp and I 
remember that his last words were, "Ill wait then
minutes, you'll by out of hearing by that time."
I stopped for a minute by the side of my horse
and after patting his neck I continued my walk
to camp, about half an hour later, when
that guard had been relieved, he came to me
and said that my horse had died without
a struggle a short time after I was [[?]]ut these.
Ten days after we had buried Harry I got an order
to shoot him. So much for army med tape.
My newt mount was a less intelligent beast
with a good moral character and but few
blemishes bassing a spiked tail, a mig bone
or two and a blind eye he was all right,
he also had two good ears and a voice
that awoke the the camp from its slumber
every night. From remarks that I overheard

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 2], 1903
transcription:
I do not think that thoughts or visions of 
paradise were very plentiful in the minds
of the men within half a mile of that mule.
In a few days that mule was banished nights to
the near with the wagons, and [[?]] of blistered
tongues soon got well. I rode that mule several
months, but I had to leave him with the wagons nights
when I was discharged from the army I turned the mule over to the Qmaster master department,
and for a week afterwards - while on my journey
to my distant home-, I would catch myself
listening for a pensive bray from that mule.
I have since learned  Jimis fate. He remained
in the service and while foraging in the
near of the Dullins tent one day, he found
some pickled artichokes, mistaking them for
brandy peaches - which he was very fond of - 
he tried to swallow one of them whole but it
stuck in his throat and could not be dislodged. He
fell to his knees and with a last attempt to bray
he fell over onto his right side dead, so that
the U.S. brand he had honourably worn for years
on his left shoulder was in view of all. Jim had 
been damned many a time and often,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 2], 1903
transcription:
but condemned he had never been. There
was no condemning letter C below the U.S. to show
that he had outlived his usefulness to the Gov-
ernment that he had served so long and faith-
fully, and as he had a good deal of mule
sense, he was probably proud of the fact that the
brand he has carried for many years,
had never been dishonoured by having ad-
ded to it the letter C. Jim was deserving
of an epitaph, and I was very much sat
isfied when I discovered some dozzen
or more years ago, that the following
tribute had been composed by one of
his many admirers.
To Jim.
Jim was a mule with a long pedigree
And ears that were nearly as long,
He had a voice that for a mile could be heard
Whenever he sang his evening song.

But by death at last he was corraled,
Our eyes are dim - our hearts are broke,
For the cause of this sad mischance
Was a pesky pickled artichoke.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 2], 1903
transcription:
Chapter IX.

Getting on is a slow process except 
when one is getting on in years.

Now that I have got that mule disposed of,
I am at liberty to return and try to enjoy
more of Kate Murrays singing. After she
had sung the 'Weaning of the g[[?]]un','Annie Laurie'
and "Marching through Georgia." Mrs Murray sat
down to the piano and played a few selections
of operatic music to the satisfaction of her
audience, if the encores she received could 
be taken for evidences of pleasure, al-
though not a judge of classical music, I
can tell when I am pleased with the music
I am listening to, and I had to acknowledge 
to myself, that I was greatly pleased with
Mrs Murrays playing, for I am not so dumb
that I cannot tell the music of a Cornet
from that made by a trom-bone. Sam
suggested that we dance a quadrille,
and the idea met with instant favour.

"An' sure Oi be knowin' the vexatious ways, phwat byes are always havin' wid thim? For din't me two byes Johnny an' Ned, pull all of me pay vines up whin they wor jist in flower, an' dig all the ground up a [[?]] for pay- nuts, becase they's larned in the book that pay-nuts growed in the ground on the roots of the pay vines?
Begorra! they's got a foine healthey bastin for their trouble, so they's did! phwat lasted thim until they's got well agin'
Thin one day Oi must be catchin thim a throwin' little pertaties at the head of me ould drake, phwat they's had buried in the ground all but his head and neck, an' they's wor peltin' at his head to make him dodge it from side to side, phwat no young gintlemen has no call to be doin' at all at all!
But sure Oi am! that nayther of thim dodged enny of the blows phwat the strap wod be givin' thim, they's caught thim all, so they's did!

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
18
An' thin one day phwat must they's be a doin' b barberin', an' Johnny wod be shampooin' Neds heas, usin' me ould scrub brush an' the wather phwat the pertaties wor biled wid, wid the soft soap to make the great lather; an' thin Johnny puts on the hair tonic phwat they's makes with lard an' mucilage, an' kereosine ile, wid half of me botthle of peppermint to give it the great flavor, an' Johnny made Neds head look slick an' dacint to both their eyes; but Oi had to cut the last hair off that gossoons head afore Oi cud get that mucilage an' kereosine ile oder away from it.
But, they's both got a dacint latherin of an' other koind, for they's impudince, so they's did! an' it wor a long toimme that whinever oither of thim byes sot down to the table to ate his males, he stood up. 
Sure! an' it wor more nor a year afore the good effects of that latherin' wore off.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
19
An' now, dont Oi be knowin' that byes beze great humbugs? an' always unsartin? an' they's causes us poor wimmin a dale of throuble an' unasiness all their indispensable lives, for sorry wor the fact! we cud'nt endure life widout thim."
Mrs. Fogarty now became very quiet, and I begun to think she had at last fallen asleep, but she had not been quiet but a very short time before she roused up and tried to put both of her feet on the floor, but without succedding, for with a cry of agony she hastily got them back into their former possition on the couch, and then she sobbed out.
"The matther phwat's got in me ph[[?]]! an' will it iver git out agin Oi dont know?"
Then turning to me she continued.
"Ye big spallpeen! wod ye be sthandin' there an' see a poor widdy woman die right [[?]] yeze two eyes, widout havin' the dacincy to be askin', wid yeze love! Sure! its yereself phwat

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
20
dont care whedder Oi dies or not, all along of the aighty foive cints ye beze owin' one for the wash; an' a foine hard toime Oi had amin' it to be sure! an' its the aighty foive dollars ye wod be owin' me this day, wod Oi have let ye, an' had Oi me jest dues, instid of the aighty foive cints; for phwat wid one taking the best bits out of me shates off me beds, to mind the ould shirts an' things of yeze, Oi have niver a shate to civver up wid the foine Album quilt phwat wor me great-great Gran'Modders afore me, phwat me own twin sister Kate, do be kapin' all the toime sure, an' it wor made wid the illigant bits of foine cloth, wid the names of scores of people wrote on thim; an' thim same names wod call to moind many incidents an' evints phwat happened in the past an' gone toimes.
Now there wor the Maid of Orleans, an' she a ridin' on the foine horse wid her sword on.
An' the Maid of Athens, an' she wid the haythin Apache wid her, phwat a good Christian

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
21
wod not be payin' enny attention too at all, at all!
An' the Maid of Perth, an' she wid the gould handled ridin' whip on her right writsl aisy to her hand.
An' the Maid of the Mist, a ridin' on the wather with her Bridal Veil on all the toime sure!
Thim there wor the Maid all Forlorn, who no body iver asked wod she have a ride? an' she wid out scarcely nothin' on, poor dear! Sure! there wor all the rest of the great folks of the day, phwat laved their names behind thim, an' not much of enny thing more but descindints.
An' me now wid me best tathe at the Dentists, since Brian Dooleys sisters brat of a bye Moikey, wod be havin' me break thim a bitin' on a pace of pie crust, phwat Bridget Gillhooleys sister Maggies bye Dennis gave him out of his dinner pail, phwat he beze a gittin' from the Widdy Maloney who he beze a boardin' wid.
An' the Widdy Maloneys husband Morris wor runned over an' killt, by one thim Board of Health

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
22
carts, phwat collects up all the smells in one Strate, an' thin distributes thim wid a remarkably impartial an' lavish hand, in the next Strate, so that the people wod all persave that the Board of Health, wor as usual attindin' to its bounden duties by proxy.
An' Morris'es own fourth cousin Jerry Madigan wor a sittin' on the sate of the cart, an' drivin' the ould horse, wid a wart on the side of the nose of him, as big as a duck egg, the blagguard! But he will niver run over enny body agin, for he cud not draw the cart enny longer wid the koind of food he wor gittin', so one day he must be atein' straw phwat had some pickled Arthichokes in it, an' he died from strangulation. 
An' the Widdy Maloney do be now kapin' the boarders, an' makin' money an' the piecrusts, phwat wod smash the tothe of a dacint body, whiniver they's wod be tryin' to ate it; an' she only a three months widdy yet."

transcription:
23
Chapter 3
By this time She had become so much exhausted from talking, that her tongue got a short rest.
I inquired if her son Ned would be home at supper time?, thinking that when he saw the condition his Mothers foot was in, he would insist upon her calling in a Doctor.
"No." She replied. " No he wont be here this blessed night for no supper! For sure! its the long shift he beze a workin' this day; for Daniel Brannigans bye Patsey, wor runned over an' killt the other day, by the illigant new Strate car, phwat the owners of the Rail Road, an' they's wives, an' their friends wor ridin in.
An' Patsey wor siven year ould, an' that big they's cud have seen him an' stopped the car an' got out, an' not bin so hard hearted as to ride over a little gossoon loike Patsey wor, an' he a half orphan, wid his own Mudder dead an buried these last foive year."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
24
They's hild an inquist on little Patsey, an' the vardict made it out that no body wor to blame but Patsey hisself, becase he runned away from school whin he had no lave to do so.
Mebby some of thim belaved it wor a visitation of a wise providence, becase had Patsey lived an' growed up, he might have been elected Alderman or Justice of the Pace, an' wint to the bad that way.
But sure! Oi beze a thinkin' it wor for sure a visitation of a Strate car, phwat killt little Patsey.
An' sure now! he beze a full orphan, wid out aither a fodder or a mudder to his name, an' may he have a paceful rist! For now his fadder Daniel has the illigant new wife an' baby, an' he will soon be forgittin of little Patsey, an' be givin' all the attintion an' considerashun to the new baby, phwat beze crosseyed, an' has got the rickets.
An' so it beze wid no all; we beze iver ready to declare that we cud not endure the loss of avin' a sickly kitten, or a mangy puppy,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
25
phwat had made us fraquint throuble, an' that same throuble wod becoom a pleasure whin it wor for their comfort; but whin they's be dead an' gone from our sight for iver, we soon lave off the sorrowin' an mournin' for thim, an' afther a toime- phwat our good friends call undacintly short-, we begin to notice an' care for other bastes or humans, an' soon we begin to wonder how it wor that, we cud iver have loiked or loved the one gone, as well as we now do the one phwat now looks up so friendly or smilingly in our faces.
Now me bye Ned beze a workin' this day for Daniel to kape his place in the shop, while they's be gone to the buryin.
An' Oi beze stoppin' at me home wid one phfut, whin Oi wor wantin' to go to the funeral an' see the new cloak phwat Maggie Conley has bin gittin trusted for at the store below, wid the big slaves an' thim illigant bagatelles, or phwat iver they's call thim things made of lace an jet, phwat they's put on the shoulders of the cloaks."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
26
"Maggie beze only recevin two dollars an' fifty cints a week for doin' the house work for Lawyer Smarts wife, wid her big family of siven childens, an' her havin' to kape a nurse girl to care for thim an' a blind pug dog.
An sure! Mistress Smart beze owin' me for the laundryin' of the bed clothes, iver since last August wod be a year, Afther they's all had the hay faver, phwat theys all ketched whin they were out to her fadders farm, durin' the hayin' sason.
Oh dear! an sure it do same as though Oi had more throubles than Oi cud stand, all along of the bit of wood phwat beze in me phfut-. Sure now! it wor a great disaster."
The pain in her foot had now become very severe; She sighed and moaned while great tears followed each other down her cheeks.
I felt very sorry for her, and heartily wished I could do somethin to aliviate her sufferings, or at least help her in some way to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
27
do so; the thought came to me, that although She would not take any laudanum to deaden the pain, She might be induced to take some liquor, which would act as a stimulant if no more, so I said to her. "I am very sorry you are in so much pain Mrs. Fogarty, and it seems cruel to me that you have to suffer as you are now doing, and I wish you would consent to see a Doctor, but as you say you will not, dont you think a little sup of Brandy or Whisky would do you good.
I know you do not often indulge in either, but at this time you need a little of something of that kind as a stimulant, for you are now weak from fasting and loss of sleep, and a drink of liquor at this time may do you a great deal of good, at all events it will do you no harm to try some; if you have none in the house I will go out and get some for you if you will promise to take a drink of it on my return."
She had remained very quiet all the time

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
28
I had been talking, her eyes being closed, I did not know but I had talked her to sleep; but as soon as I had stopped talking, she opened her eyes and looking intently at me for a moment before she answered, she finally said.
"Indade thin! is it the sup of whisky ye wants me to be takin'? Sure! Oi wod take a bit of a sup of that an Oi had it!; but Oi'll not be takin' the pizin' lodnum phwat ye iver recomminding me too, for phwat ye calls a stimulant.
For didn't me own sister Katie's girl Annie phwat beze own first cousin to me bye Ned, git hould of the botthle wid the pizin stuff in it, an' drink that much of the dirthy pizin, they's had to sind for the Docthor to come wid his pump-the baste-, an' stick it down her throat, an' pump the dirthy pizin up again; an' she a liein' there loike a little lamb, widout spakin' a word to enny body, an' wid the freckles on her face a showin' loike the patches on her fadders

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
29
breeches, an her little throat stretched that much, she cud have swallowed a hull dish of pertaties at one time had she tried, so she cud!.
An' she but the wee bit of a girleen three year ould, phwat's to be married to me bye Ned, whin her own sister Ellen has bin dead an' buried a year come Michaelmas Day; an' Oi beze thinkin'" 
I interupted her to say. I will not urge you any more Mrs. Fogarty, to take laudanum and as you have promised to take some whiskey, shall I go out and get some for you? For I am sure you are greatly in need of something of that discription."
She looked at me a moment before she answered, and then she said.
"Oi'd be thinkin' its the blarney ye wod be tratin' me too now, wid the soft word for meself; whin it wod be yeze own silf phwat wod be wishin' for a taste of the crature this minnit, so ye wod! an' ye wod be takin' that way to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
30
be gittin' it. Sure! ye be knowin' Oi cant abide a little taste of the whisky, widout it beze in the hot wather, wid the lump of sugar an' a bit of lemon, wid the gratin' of nutmeg on the top of it all, an' the foine silver tay spoon to stir it wid; phwat General Butter gave me second man Barney, afther he had captured the foight an' the spoon-, down there to New Orleans.
An' he wor the foine brave General! to be capturing silver tay spoons, an' givin one to aich of his soljers, whin they's cud jest as well take thim their own selves, afther theys had won a foight, an' not be a puttin' him to all that throuble.
An' there beze no fire in the stove now to hate the hot wather Oi wod be takin' the drop of whisky wid; an'___."
I interupted her to say, that I could start a fire in the stove, and put some water on to heat, and then it would not be many minutes before she could have some hot

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
31
water. She had not informed me whether she had any whisky in the house or not, or if she would like to have me go down street and get some for her; so I again asked her if she had any in the house.
Pointing toward a closet she replied. "Yes! Oi've a drop in the cubboard there! on the top shilf behind the box in which Oi kapes the illigant Sergeants stripes, phwat me man Hughey got whin he wor in the Army sick of the masles in the Hospital, phwat he do be capturing wid out enny orders, jest as soon as he rached the front, where they's do the foightin' wid guns, an cannon, an' swords, an' things phwat a true Oirishman wod scorn to be usein', so long as he wod have the two fists wid him to back up his spache.
An' Hughey wod have a relapse as soon as he recovered his health, an' be sick wid some odder disase, so he did not have to do enny of the foightin' at all at all! only jest enough to capture some of the nice dacint

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
32
food to ate, phwat the Sanitary Commission wod be havin' their agints out all over the country a askin' the poor folks to sind to the Hospitals enny thing they's wor willin' to deprive thimselves of-for the good of their country-, in the shape of articles phwat wod nourish an' presarve their clerks an' nurses, while theys wod be waitin' on the poor sick an' wounded soljers; an' Hughey cut the stripes off of the coat slave of a sick sergeant phwat died wid hunger, in the next bed from the one Hughey slaped on.
An' there also beze the foine spurs phwat me second man Barney, wod be gittin' whin he wor a soljer out there in the wild western country.
He took thim spurs off the phfuts of a wild Injin, phwat wod be tryin' to scalp the head of one of Barneys comrades,  who wor lashed on his horse an' cud'nt defind hisself, becase he wor sick wid mountain faver of some koind; an' Barney wid a blow of his sabre asked the Injin, wod

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
33
he quit that unaquil encounther? an' the Injin wod! thin Barney accepted his spurs, to prove he hild no resintment agin' him now for the cowardly assault phwat he had made on a definsless man, an' - becase the spurs wor all phwat he had that wor worth the takin'.
An' there beze in the box the illigant discharge phwat they's gave Hughey for lavin' the Army; an' the foine dacint ones, phwat Barney wod git for his three enlistments, an' his left hand an' the two toes of his right phfut.
Sure now! Hughey wor well desarvin' of a clane wholesome discharge, becase he kaped his head; an' there wor no call for him to enlist for his health, becase he had niver seen the toime whin he cud'nt get enough to ate at his home; but whin he stood face to face wid the inducement of a big bounty, Sure thin! he sinsed roight away, that his country had great an' urgent nade

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
34
for his sarvices, an' thin he made haste to enlist in his countrys definse; but by that toime the war beze almost through wid, so he did'nt have to do enny of the foightin at all, an' he wor not in so much rale danger as he wod have bin, had he gone to the Army whin the foightin first begun, whin they's did not give the poor soljers enny bounty at all, at all! nor much of enny thing else except the hard ground to slape on, wid out narry a fedder nor a shate beneath thim, an' the bread phwat theys call the hard tack for thim to ate, wid out enny butther or a drop of treacle to ate wid it, an' the male they's calls the salt horse, phwat wor jest as loikley to have bin the salt mule-, for thim to ate, whinever occasion wod give thim the oppertuntiy to cook it a bit, by holdin' it on the end of they's bayonets, over a slow fire, whin their attintion wor not all employed wid lookin' afther their inimies in the Rebel loines, nor afther those in their own loins."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
356
Chapter 4
"Now wor'nt that the undacint tratemint for the poor soljers to meet wid? an' they's wid no place to hide in, whin the shott an' the bullets wod be a bustin' all round thim; phwat wid the Captins an' the Officers in all of the holes, an' behind all the trees an' stones, there wor no places left for the poor soljers to git behind or hide in.
An' there wor nothin' betther they's cud do than jest lie down in the open an be killt.
An' Hughey wor saying', they's had to make the charge on the Pickets an' run thim in.
Sure now! that wor dangerous! Oi wod not be wishin' for thim to be makin' the charge on me pickets an' run thim in, for they's wod git stuck fast and hurted, an' they's wod muss up me fence that bad, Oi wod have to white wash it agin, an' Oi beze a white washin' it all clane an' tidy, only three year ago, wid the brush phwat Oi lost for Mary Ann

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
36
Rooney, an' phwat Oi had to pay her tin shilling' for doin'. Sure! Hughey said they's wod be shootin' the morthar, for phwat Oi dont know! but Oi beze a thinkin' the roight place for the morthar, wor on the sides of the house, an' not to be shooted at a body avin if he beze yere inimy, a spoilin' his clothes an' blindin' him wid it.
An' Hughey tould me they's had the big guns a ridin' on the two wheels, the sax pound there an' the sivin pound there, an' also the Parrots.
Now Oi've seen the men an' the byes, an' the women an' the girls, a ridin' on the two wheels, but Oi have niver seen enny Parrots ridin on two wheels.
But Oi do be thinkin' they's wod look jest as well ridin' on two wheels, as the woman an' girls does; wid the little cap stuck on the top of their heads, wid the sun a plantin' the foine crip of freckles on their faces the while, an' wid the chin of thim pushed up that high, they's cud part their hair wid the end of their noses,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
37
if they's wor to mislay their combs, an' they's loiked! an' they's wod be ridin' up behind a body wid out makin' a bit of noise, an' thin be ringin' the little bell, as much as to be askin' wod ye look out there? phwat wod give enny body the scare! whin they's cud jest as well go past, wid out flustratin their betthers.
An' thim avid the clothes an' things on thim, phwat dont belong to thim to wear at all, at all! phwat wid the caps an' coats, an' their undacint brodders br__."
I interupted her to ask if she had a lemon in the house? For I had started a fire in the stove, and the tea kettle was beginning to sing a song "of family glee."
"Yes". She answered. "Yes ye will find one an' nutmeg grather, on the shelf in the butthery there, an' the sugar phwat Oi buy's wid me ould duck eggs, beze in the box phwat me man Barney, do be gittin whin he wor a soljer, from the wild Injins, phwat wod be only covered with their nakedness, an' the dirthy bugs

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
38
an' things had luck to thim!.
Sure! Barney wor tellin' me that one day afther they's had had a foight wid the Injins, an' the blagguard Injins wor all runned away or killt, he found the box in one of their ta_ta_tagpols." I interupted her to suggest, that it was in a tepee that Barney found the box as many bands of Indians called their lodges or houses tepees. "Yes." She said. "Yes that's the haythin name Barney beze callin' it.
Well Barney found the box in the taypee an' in the inside of it wor a lot of bits of the scalps, phwat the murtherin Injins had cut off the heads of some dacint Christian bodies, who will niver foind thim enny more, for Barney buried thim in the ground, away out there on the desarted plains, where the Wolves, an' the Buzzards, an' the Buffalo, an' the Bears an' the Snakes, an' the Rabbits, do be all livin' togather in the one hole in the ground-."
I interrupted her to say she was mistaken about the Buffalo living in holes in the ground,"

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
39
that it was Prairie dogs, Rattlesnakes and a small horned Owl, who had been found living togather or inhabiting the same hole in the ground, but it was not probable they all dwelt togather in one burrow, but rather, that each species had its own individual burrow, while the opening at the surface of the ground was common to them all.  And as for the Buffalo, they were animals as large as our cows, and they resembled them in all of their good qualities, except their docility; whereas our Cows and Cattle were domesticated, and had been under the subjection of man for many centuries, the reverse was true of the Buffalo; for in this country they were in a wild state, and they were often found in bands of from five hundred to ten thousand or more in number, they were hunted and killed for their flesh and hides, their flesh was used for food by the Indians and the other dwellers upon the westerns plains, Although the flesh of the Buffalo resembled domestic beef in flavor, it was not

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
40
so juicy and tender; of their hides were made the warm robes, which are so comfortable to have snugly tucked around you on a cold day, when you are taking a drive-."
Mrs. Fogarty interupted me to enter a protest. 
"An' do ye mane to tell me? that the Buffalo beze goin' round wid the bands? makin the great noise an' as good as askin' the hunters to coom an' take their hides off an' kill thim? Sure thin! Oi wont belave a word of it! avin if the poor basties beze out there in that wild state, wid its Coyotes, an' Cowpunchers, an' Horned Toads, an' Alkalies, an' odder Calamities. Barney may not have said that the Buffalo lived in the holes in the ground, wid the Owls an' odder reptiles, but sure Oi am! he did not say that the Buffalo wint round wid the bands; for he wod scorn to repate such a misbelavin' story as that wod be, an' he well knowin' nobody wod belave him if he wor to do do.
For Barney wor a truthful man! not withstandin'

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
41
he wor a soljer in the Army for the long fourteen year an' ten months; an' he coomed back home the dacint man, barrin' the two toes he had to have cut off, phwat wor froze out there in the Rocky Mountains, whin he had to ride his horse saxty miles one night in the winter toime, wid out narry sup of whisky to warm thim wid; an' it wor that could the poor soljers had to kape smokin' they's pipes all the toime, to kape their two eye lids from being froze tight togather; an' the left hand wor cut off by the Docthor, afther he had it shot full of holes in a foight wid the dirthy Indians, away out there in the west, where they's be shootin' aich odder wid out takin' the toime to say-wid your lave-! An' Barney havin' only three weeks more to be a soljer, afore his toime wod expire agin, an' he wod be discharged wid lave to go away from the Army an' be a good man agin.
Now wor'nt that they mane way to be tratin' a man phwat had been a soljet for fourteen year an' more, to be makin' him go an' foight an' lose his hand,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
42
whin he had got almost through wid the Army an' its intolerance, whedder he wanted to go or no! an' they's wod be cuttin' off his hand an toes, wid out askin' wod he have it so! an' thin sindin' him away from the Army, out into the world wid out enny certificate of good character wid him, an' they's wod be expectin' he wod make a one handed livin' for himself in an honest manner, whedder he cud or not. Barney coomed back home here wid the rheumatiz, an' the indolence, an' the appertit, phwat all the soljers bring back wid thim from the Army; an' afther he beze gittin' the pinsion money, Oi felt that compassionate toward him, that Oi took him for me second man. 
And Barney wor a good husband to me an' the childer, until Oi laid him to rist in the lot in the buryin' ground beyont, wid the place resarved for meself between him an' Hughey, awaitin the toime whin Oi shall be called to meet thim agin."
With an "oh! ouch!" she continued. " Me odder phfut beze asleep now! wod ye give

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
43
me the stick in the corner there? Pointing to a small cane-. "While Oi see if Oi cant bate some dacincy into it." I handed her the cane and she tapped her foot with it for a minute or more, then handing the cane back to me she said.
"That fales a dale asyer now! as Moike Donnovan said to the Docthor afther he had cut off Moikes hand, phwat the buzz saw wod be cuttin' off afore, whin he wor sawin' the wood for the Widdy Barnes, an' she a askin' him to pay for the lost toime, an' the drop of blud phwat she claned off the floor.
Sure! She beze that close an' stingy, She wod be skimmin' the dish wather afore she wod give it to the pigs, an' they's behavin' loike the gintlemen phwat they's be. Oi well remimber the toime her man died; she sint for the Underthaker to coom an' make the bargin to bury him, she tould this Underthaker she wanted Barnes to have a foine dacint buryin', becase he owned the farm an' all there wor on it, whin he married her."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
44
"But." she said. "But oi have saved all the money, for Barnes wor so soft-hearted an' liberal he wod not have left me and the two childers, half so much as he did, wod Oi have let him give away an' ate as much as he wod be wantin' too." Thin she says. "Oi cudn't niver put but one piece of pie or cake for ache one of us on the table at males toime, or Barnes wod be atein' more than one piece, which beze enough for a man; but Barnes wor a great ater, for did'nt Oi catch him one day in me butthery, an' he jumped out of the windy atein' a fried cake, an' havin' three more of thim in his hands; an' he jest afther atein' a hearty dinner of Dandelion greens, an' corn male mush, wid butthermilk to drink, but Oi did not give him the chance to do the loikse of that agin, for Oi locked me pies an' cakes, an' sass up, so he cud not not get to thim, for Oi kaped the kay in one poclet durin' the day toime, an' Oi put the kay under me pillow whin it wor the night sason."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
45
Thin she wod be askin' the Underthaker phwat he wod be chargin' her for a foine black cloth Casket, wid the silver handles, an' the Hearse wid the plumes, an' tin carriages wid drivers, an' the Underthaker to pay the Minister for his sarvices.
The Underthaker tould her that a funeral of that character wod cost not a cint less than one hundred an' seventy foive dollars. 
"Oh!" She exclaimed, "Oh! Oi cud niver think of payin' all that money out for the buryin' of Barnes, although he wor a good man enough as far as men go, but it wod look to me loike flyin' right into the face of Providence, to spind so much money as that on one man, an' he a dead an' gone one. 
An' thin she asked the Underthaker how much it wod cost wid out the silver handles to the Casket?
The Underthaker tould her he wod do the buryin' wid Nickel handles on the Casket, for a hundred an' foifty dollars; but she declared that that amount wor more than she wor willin' to expind."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
46
"An' thin she begun to lave out, first a carriage, an' thin the handles on the Casket, an' thin an' odder carriage, an' the broad cloth for the Casket, an' so on- until she had dispinsed wid all of the Carriages an' the hearse as well as the foine Casket, an' bought a plain stained pine Coffin, for foive dollars, to be paid for in the fall wid Squash, Pumpkins, an' Turnips." Thin she says, "Oi am sure i cud niver slape at all in the nights, knowin' Oi had spint such a lot of money for the buryin' of Barnes; whin Oi have the foine one horse wagon on phwat can be used in the place of the hearse, an' also a dacint two sated Spring wagon, phwat me an' the two childer can ride in to the grave yard; an' if enny of Barnes friends wants to attind the buryin', theys can jest furnish their own conveyance or els go a foot."
"An' the Preacher can ride wid me an' the childer in the Spring wagon, an' drive the horses, an' Oi will tell him, that Oi intind to give his

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
47
wife a little lamb, an' so Oi will git oid of the bother of bringin' the lamb, whose mudder died this morning, up by hand, an' for the gift of that lamb, the Preacher will not be inclined to make enny charge for the funeral sarvices; an' the Saxton do be owin' Barnes two dollars for pertaties, which he wor to work out, an' now he can work the half of it out in diggin' a grave for Barnes.
An' Oi am sure Oi shall feel relaved an' betther satisfied, whin it beze all done wid an' Oi can coom home an' sit down all alone by meself, an' have the pleasure of takin' a cup of good strong tea; an' now it wod be black tay that Oi wod made to be drinkin! an' Oi am sure that will be the first bit of rale comfort that Oi will be havin' since Oi become a Widdy, an' it will assist in consoling me for the throuble Oi have jest endured in wakeness an' wid resignation.
 "Now worn't that the unblushin' way for her to be tratin the man phwat had married

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
48
her out of the Poor House, wid out the second shoe to her back, nor enny name to spake of? Wid all the illigant girls around the country jest waitin' to be asked,- wod they's be Mrs Barnes?-; Sure! an' it wod be small blame to thim if they's wod! for did'nt Barnes own the foine farm, wid the mortgage an' the cows, an' the horses, an' the shape, an' the pigs, an' a goat; an' he had the money in the bank, an' the respict an' estame of all his kindred an neighbors, an' also the consumption, phwat carried him off in his own one horse wagon-, jest about foive year afther he wor married to that woman, phwat wod not be lettin' him have aither a quiet an' paceful loife whin he wor livin', nor a dacint buryin' whin he died."
Sure! an' the talkin' beze fatiguein' to me now! wid all the throuble phwat beze on me, an' Oi will not beze discoursin' to ye enny more at all at all!"

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
49
Chapter 5
"Now." I said to her. " Now Mrs. Fogarty! if you wish and if you will kindly listen to me, I will try to entertain you by telling a true Indian story."
She gave a graceful assent, then closing her eyes she turned her face from me; thus encouraged I commenced the recital of the following tale.
"You are aware, Mrs. Fogarty, that through my brother John I can lay claim to some knowledge of Indian warfare and atrocities, for John served for more than three years in the army on the frontier and plains. I can believe what you tell me about Barneys service among the Indians, where he was stationed the most of the time he was in the Army.
John has told me a good deal about the time he was in the army out on the western plains, where all the service or fighting they had was against the Indians or Hostiles, as the army men call them.
John told me this story about a man and his family, which consisted of his wife and two children,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
50
the eldest was a boy aged about five years, and the youngest a girl of three or three and a half years old.
This family left Canada in the spring of the year 1855, for California, intending to locate and make a new home in that state.
They started on the overland route, by the way of Council Bluffs, Fort Laramie, and Salt Lake City. The Canadian had a considerable amount of money with him, and upon their arrival at Council Bluffs Iowa, he procured an outfit which was complete in all of its details; he was so fortunate as to find a large ox wagon train of emigrants nearly ready to start for the land of gold.
He joined this large train, and a few days later they had left civilization behind them and had had an introduction to the trials and perplexities of a nomadic life." Here a groom informed me that I had an attentive listener.
"All went well with the train, and also with the Canadian and his family, they had no

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
51
trouble except such as was incidental to an undertaking of that magnitude.
He and his wife, and also their children remained in good health and spirits, and the life they were now living appeared to agree with them all.
They arrived in safety at Salt Lake City, and there found awaiting them, letters from friends in Canada.
During the few days of their stay at the "City of the Saints", they purchased such necessary supplies as they needed to last them until they arrived in California, they also wrote and mailed letters to their friends at their old home in Canada.
After a weeks rest at Salt Lake City, the train resumed its slow march westward, and in a few weeks it had reached the head waters of the Humboldt river, an' Alkali stream whose banks even to its final disappearance into the sand of the desert, were dotted with stunted Cottonwood trees, Willows, old wagon irons, grave, ox chains, Buzzards, and grotesque heaps of domestic animals

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
52
in all stages of decomposition, and now the train was slowly and wearily journeying down its inhospitable and buzzard infested banks."
"One evening after the train had gone into camp, the Canadian had a difficulty with one of his companions of the train, although the quarrel was only a wordy one, the Canadian became so angry, that he declared he would no longer travel in the company of his antagonist, nor with anyone who sided with him in the late controversy;and he declared he would rather travel the remainder of the distance to California alone, than to longer remain in their company.
The Captain of the train and other cool headed men, tried to persuade him not to think of leaving the train at that time; they told him that it was extremely dangerous for one wagon to attempt to travel alone, they recalled to mind that many stories and

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
53
reports they had lately heard of Massacres and of other atrocities, which had been committed that season by the Piute Indians, who claimed and roamed at will over all the country lieing between the Green river on the east, and the Nevada Mountains on the west; they urged him to remain with the train, until they should overtake another train, or until they were overtaken by a train which was not but a few days journey behing them, and they also offered to remain in their present camp until a train should overtake them. they assured him that it would not be very long before a train would arrive probably not longer than the next afternoon.
But their friendly offers and advice, were were to no purpose, for he said he was not afraid of the Indians injuring him, or that they would molest him in any manner, and as for the many rumors and reports of massacres and rapine, which they had heard of, he for

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
54
one did not believe that one in ten of those reports were true; for they had met a large number of Indians since they started from the Missouri river, and all of them had been very friendly, and no one in the train had been molested in any way by them, and as far as his knowledge of Indians went, he must say that he believed the Indians at their best were nothing more than a cowardly, skulking, and thieving people who never made a hostile demonstration, or attempted to attack unless they were positive they had at the time, the advantage either of numbers or possition, and it was his opinion that one good resolute white man could defend himself from the attack of a dozen of the red fiends, and soon beat them off; he also said that although he appreciated the well ment and friendly efforts of many of his companions in trying to induce him to remain with the train, he

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
55
would have to refuse to do so, for he had decided, and the next morning he should leave them.
His wife joined her entreaties to the others, but with no better success, for with true John Bull obstinacy he refused her prayers, and ignored her wishes, then he checked her tears by brutally ordering her to stop whining and crying, and he thought it necessary at the same time to frurther humilitate her, by telling her that she never did look a bit pretty when she was crying."
"The remark-"The baste! why he wor the most disreputable man phwat Oi wor acquainted wid for this many a long year-." informed me that my audience were not all asleep."
"The Canadians wife visited the wagons or Camp fires, of all the women with whom she had been the most intimate, since the train left Council Bluffs, and with

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
56
aching heart and choking voice, bade them adieu, with only a faint ray of comfort, in the hope that they would all meet again at no very distant day in California, where they could renew their friendships again, under more favorable conditions, than those by which they were then surrounded had proved themselves to possess.
It was hardly probable, that the poor woman spent the last night of her stay with that train in unbroken rest; she had heart the rumors and reports which had been told, of the attacks the Indians had made that season, upon lone wagons and small trains; and she would naturally be fearfull of the fate which might be awaiting her and her little children, after they were separated from the restraining influence which the large number of men in that train, had in keeping the Indians friendly and peaceable to them-"

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
57
Chapter 6
Mrs. Fogarty was ready with a few remarks which she willingly gave voice to.
"Sure! a woman livin' wid such a husband as he wor, wod have great made of humility an' a sign foreninst her two eyes, phwat wod be sayin'.
"If ye have a good timper-kape it;
If ye have a bad timper-dont lose it."
For sure! such a man wod be askin' his wife to sew a suspender button on his trousers, an' she wid her two hands in the dough, so he wod!."
But to return to my story.
"The next morning at day break, the Canadian with his family in the wagon drawn by three yoke of oxen, left the camp and his late friends and companions, and started alone as he had said he would the night before, he headed toward the west, and continued their journey down the north bank of the Humboldt river."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
58
"The train from which the Canadian had withdrawn, did not break camp until the sun was an hour or more old the next morning, then it continued its slow tortuous-two-miles-an-hour march.
The monotony of the march through loose sand, and across small alkali flats, where all were nearly blinded and quite choked by this fine alkali dust, which in that region seems to be able to permeate clothing, as well as fill the surrounding atmosphere with its noxious atoms-, was broken into by a stampede of the oxen of a wagon near the center of the train, who suddenly became possessed of the notion that they would like to explore the country lieing to the north of the road, and they started on a run in that direction, other teams near them seemed to become instantly affected with the same notion or mania, and they at once followed, without paying any regard to the beatings they received over their heads, from the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
59
whips in the hands of their drivers; soon half of the wagons in the train were moving at a rapid rate over the plain, drawn by half frienzied oxen, who would not turn or swerve from their course for either a man or a mountain, until compelled to end their mad race through sheer exhaustion, after the oxen had ran half a mile or more, the wagons with their loads which they had to draw through the deep sand, began to get heavier and heavier, and the speed of the run away oxen slower and slower, until they all came to a stand still of their own accord; soon their drivers had overtaken the panting run away teams, and they were started on the return track to the rest of the train, which had after much hard work and profanity, succeeded in keeping their oxen from joining in the mad race of the stampede; fortunately for the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
60
emigrants none of the stampede portion of the train received any injuries, with the exception of the necessary trouble of picking up the things which fell or were thrown from the wagons, by their frightened occupants, during the mad race-, the stampede caused no affliction to any except the oxen, whose sides were covered with perspiration, and whose tongues were lolling from their parched mouthes.
After a short rest the train got under motion again, and when the train stopped and camped for the night, the oxen appeared to have forgotten their escapade of that forenoon, and they had become as quiet and docile, as they were wont to be when grazing in their native pastures in some one of the states east of the Mississippi river. 
The relating of incidents connected with the stampede, caused much amusement for the emigrants, while lounging around

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
61
their Camp fires that evening, and they congratulated themselves that it had not resulted in serious injury to either man or beast.
Early explorers of the Western plains have informed us that Stampedes of Buffalo were of frequent occurance, and that they often resulted in the death of many of the weakly ones in the band, who were run over and trampled to death; but why! or for what reason our domestic animals the horse, mule, or ox, should catch the stampede fever or mania, when taken out onto the western plains, has never been intelligently explained, but the fact remains that they have been known to frequently do so, as many who crossed the plains in the '50s and '60s can attest.
The train had made a drive of about twenty miles, when they camped for the night, on the bottom land near the river, without having seen or heard from the Canadians during the day."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
62
"The following morning the train left camp about six oclock; after travelling five or six miles they came to the last nights camp of the Canadians, when they were horrified by finding the dead bodies of both the Canadian and his wife.
They had both been killed and scalped early that morning, as their present rigid condition would affirm, their oxen had also been killed, and their wagon set on fire, and it was now a heap of smouldering wood, beans, cooking utensils, and wagon irons; but they could not find any trace or sign of the two children.
As the train was a large one with a hundred or more men in its composition, they did not much fear an attack from the Indians.
So they immediately formed several scouting parties, for the purpose of searching the vicinity in the hope that they would find the two children yet alive."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
63
The search was continued for several miles in each direction from the camp, but it resulted in their not finding the children, or any clue which would help in ascertaining what had become of them.
The emigrants were sure that the Indians had not killed the children, when they did their Father and Mother, for if they had done so their bodies would be near by. 
Some of the emigrants were at the first of the opinion that the children had become frightened when the attack was first made, and they had stolen away without being seen by the Indians, and had hidden themselves under the bank of the river-which was near-, and the Indians had gone away without discovering them, then-after the Indians had gone away, the children had come out of their hiding place, and they had become frightened and bewildered upon finding their

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
64
parents both dead, and themselves all alone in that desolate waste, they would be very likely to wander away, they would now probably be found sitting in the shade of some of the large clumps of Sage bushes, not far from the camp, or else wandering aimlessly around.
But the exhaustive search proved the fallacy of that theory, and now the almost certainty that the children were still alive, and that they had been taken prisoners, and were then captives in one of the maraudering bands of the Pi-ute Indians, gave them a little hope-, hope! that in a short time they would be rescued and returned to civilization again, and eventually to their kindred and friends, for they were confident the Indians would not feel disposed to kill the children, after they had been to the trouble of taking them away with them, unless they did so

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
65
to keep them from being recaptued. 
The members of the train realized that they could not expect to rescue the children, without horses to follow the Indians, and they also realized that there was no use of their following them on foot with the expectation of overtaking them. 
The emigrants could only surmise how long a time had elapsed, since the Indians had left the place; it was probable that the Indians had made the attack soon after day break that morning, as at that hour in the morning, and about sun down at night, were the times the Indians usually chose for attacking trains in camp; because at those hours, the emigrants would be less liable to be keeping a strict guard, as their attention would then be taken up with the preparation of breakfasts, and in getting ready to continue their march, or in getting suppers and in making arrangements for their comfort during the night."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
66
"If the Indians had made their attack at day break that morning, they were probably through with their bloody work by the time the sun was up, and they had then quickly escaped-taking the childen with them- toward the foot hills of the Humboldt river Mountains, which lay some twenty miles or more to the north, where they were well acquainted with all of the many secret retreats which they contained, and where they could soon hide in canyon or gulch, and defy any party who might be in pursuit of them. 
Time was passing fast away, and the noon hour had come, and with it come the conviction that the Indians had had at the least seven hours start, and with their knowledge of the country, that was a sufficient time for them to get under cover and effectually hide themselves, in case they saw any pursuers following their trail."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
67
Chapter 7
"The emigrants were all armed, and they had a plenty of amunition; their fire arms comprised Rifles, Shotguns, and Dragoon Revolvers, all muzzle loaders, for breech loading guns and fixed amunition had not at that time come into general use; so that the question of either their strength or weakness, or any suggestion of fear, did not enter into their councils.
After a lengthy consultation the emigrants decided, that they could do no good by trying to follow the Indians, and that the best they could now do in the case, would be for them to report the facts of the massacre to the Commandant of Fort Churchill Nevada, upon the arrival of the train at that frontier Fort.
They had yet a sad duty to perform for the two poor mutilated bodies of their late companions; After the offering of a prayer, they with gentle hands and throbbing hearts, laid the two victims of mans stubborness

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
68
and Indian cruelty, side by side in the grave prepared for them, and quietly covered them from human sight, for all time to come, but this was not done without many imprecations being silently hurled against their murderers.
They rudely carved upon a board, this inscription and placed it at the head of the new made mound. 
Killed by Indians Aug 17, 1855.
In life they were husband and wife;
And death did not part them.
Soon the last wagon had moved on, and the last lingering look of pity had been cast toward the mound wherein the hapless couple lie, of whom there would soon be nothing but a rememberance left.
The emigrant train reached Fort Churchill in the due course of time, without having had any trouble with the Indians, during their long and tedious journey of six months through the country which they

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
69
claimed belonged to them, and for many years the Indians asserted their primary rights to that country, by attacking small parties of hunters or prospectors, and any emigrant train which they could expect to capture, either from ambush or by direct assault.
If it had not been for the tragical murder of the Canadian and his wife, and the incident of the stampede, their journey would have been without any excitement to break the monotony of a journey with an ox train. 
Upon the arrival of the emigrants at Fort Churchill, they reported the murder and capture of the children to the Commandant, but the soldiers did not succeed in rescuing the children.
The locality of the tragedy was more than three hundred miles from the Fort, and the time which had elapsed since the Massacre, would make it hardly probable, that the soldiers could find any trace of the Indians, or any clue as to the fate of the children."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
70
Mrs. Fogarty had remained silent for an unusually long time for her; She interupted me to say.
"Its the foine bold lads phwat thim soljers wor!, a lettin' the murtherin' Injins kape the two poor little childer, whedder they's wanted to be kaped or no! cud'nt they's have the dacency to foight wid the Indians until they's all got killt, an' thin they's nade'nt have to go an' live at the Soldiers Homes; an' if they's had it wod be a great blessing for all, so it wod!."
I did not see that her remarks required answering, so I continued my story.
"By those who had acquaintance with the tragedy, it was kept in memory by being occasionally talked of, and many of the emigrants related the incidents conected with it, to the new acquaintances and neighbors, they made in California.
An account of the Massacre was published in California Newspapers, and it was copied into newspapers which were published in the eastern

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
71
States; but without the finding of any of the relations or acquaintances of the murdered Canadians, as far as the general public had any knowledge.
Time passing on its endless course brought the year 1862, and its memorable events.
The prevous year our usually peaceful country, became involved in Civil War, with the North and South arrayed each against the other in deadly warfare; to wage war successfully, requires many soldiers; at that time the Army of our Country comprised only about ten thousand soldiers of all arms, including Cavalry, Artillery, and Infantry, and those soldiers were  stationed in several of the different States and Territories, where they were needed to garrison the Forts within their borders.
A large number of soldiers were required for immediate service, and a Volunteer army had to be at once raised."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
72
"The President therefore issued a proclimation, calling upon the several Northern States, for each to furnish its quota of enlisted men, for the defense of the Union.
During the War the State of California furnished about 16,000 enlisted men, as its quota.
