In the spring of 1862, a regiment of Infantry and five Troops of Cavalry were ordered from California to Salt Lake City Utah for the protection of the Overland Mail Stage line, from the maraudering bands of Indians, who frequently swooped down upon a Stage Staion, and after killing the station employes, would burn the buildings to the ground, and run off or kill all the horses and other stock, which they might find; many of the stages were ambushed in lonely places along the road between the stations, and such attacks often resulted in the wounding or killing of the driver or some of the passengers, before the red fiends could be beaten off."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
73
" With the Troops who left California for Salt Lake City, was a civilian teamster, who claimed that he was a native of Canada, and he also claimed that the Canadian who with his wife, was killed by the Pi-ute Indians in the summer of 1855, on the Humboldt river,- were his brother and sister-in-law.
He said his people had not received any news, by letter or otherwise from his brother or his wife. Since receiving the letters they mailed at Salt Lake City, for their friends at their old home in Canada, until the Spring of the year 1859.
He said that his brothers relations in Canada, had made many inquiries about him, but they had been unable to hear anything about him, or to locate him until the year 1859; he said that about two years after his brother started for California, his father had advertisements published in Newspapers at Boston, New York, Chicago, St. Louis, Sacramento, and San Francisco, making inquiries about his brother.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
74
and asking any one who knew any thing in regard to him, or his present place of residence, to notify the father in Canada, and he would pay them for their trouble, and he would also pay a generous amount of money, as a reward, for any reliable information which would assist him in finding his son.
The Advertisement remained unanswered for two years, then in the spring of 1859, his father had received a letter from California, which was written by the man, whom the Canadian had the quarrel with in 1855, in their camp at the Humboldt River.
The writer stated that, a few days before the date of his letter, he had read the advertisement in an old copy of the Sacramento Union, which had been printed in 1857, which he picked up one day in a deserted Miners Cabin, and put in his pocket thinking at the time he might possibly find something in the paper that

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
75
would be interesting to him to read; the following evening after he had finished his work for that day, he settled down to enjoy a rest and a smoke, then he remembered that he had found a newspaper that morning, he got it and sat down to read it, little thinking he would happen onto anything in its columns, which would carry his thoughts back to that tragedy of August 17th 1855, on the Humboldt river.
He wrote an account of the trouble, that the Canadian and he had, and told of the Massacre of the Canadian and his wife, and the capturing of their children by the Indians; he spoke of the buryal of the poor victims, also of the inscription which was carved on the head board.
It would appear as though none in the train knew the Canadians family name, and as there was nothing left of the wagon or its contents, except the irons and a few chared pieces of the wood work, when the emigrants arrived at the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
76
Camp, they were unable o find anything which would reveal their family name. 
It is probable that he had given his name when he first joined the train at Council Bluffs, but it would seem that the other members of the train, must have soon discarded his family name, and that it was forgotton by them; and they must have called him only by his nationality, so that he was to the other members of the train, only known as "the Canadian".
You will please excuse me Mrs Fogarty, for this digression! but I had to digress, in order to explain the reason the emigrants did not inscribe the name of the Canadians on the board they placed at the head of their grave; there are many parallel cases to this, for in the early days of the California gold fever excitement, many men died and were buried, without their daily companions knowing their true names, and their memories were perpetuated by the name by which they were known, being placed on a board at the head of their graves."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
77
Chapter 8
At this time Mrs Fogarty had a few remarks ready, which she kindly tossed in my direction.
"Sure! its the saft aisy way ye have of makin' the excuse, whininver yeze wits gets away from ye! an' Oi beze a thinkin' its the dale of money ye cud be makin', wid the tellin' of yeze stories to these folks phwat cant slape at all, at all! in the nights, becase they's wod be havin' phwat the Dochtors call insomnia or the loikes; for it wod be thimselves phwat wod go to slape quick enough aither day or nights, an' they's had to listen to yeze stories oncet, an' the nixt toime they's wod slape all the toime ye stayed in their houses, wid yeze nationalities an' yeze digressions, so they's wod!
And sure! aich of me foive fadders cud tell a betther story nor ye-."
I interupted her to say.
"Your five fathers! I do not understand

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
78
What you mean Mrs Fogarty! whenb you say- "my five fathers."
To which she quickly replied.
"Sure thin! an' did'nt Oi have thim? me first fadder phwat me mudder gives one, wor one, thin one two step fadders wor three, an' me two faders-in-law, wor two more, an' that wod be makin' me have the foive fadders, phwat wor all dead by this toime, lavin' me a poor orphan Widdy woman widout aither fadder or mudder to me name."
"You have established your claim to having had five fathers Mrs Fogarty! in a satisfactory manner, and now I will return again to the letter which the Miner wrote to the father of the Canadian."
The Miner offered the father his assistance in trying to find and rescue the two children, or some trace of them by which they could be informed, whether they were still living; he wrote that he was comparatively alone in the world, as he had no wife or family, nor any

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
79
one else depending upon him for their support; he a added that he had been successful as a Miner since his arrival in California.
He also wrote, that he felt as though he might have been an instrumental- but not an intentional- agent, in causing the death of his son at that time; he stated that he would be pleased to corrispond with the father, hoping that between them they would be able to devise a way by which they would gain some knowledge of the fate of the children; he offered to share his purse with the father, for the purpose of making an organized search for them, in the locality where they were captured.
Several letters passed between the Miner and Father of the Canadian, and as a result of this corrispondence, a younger brother of the Canadian went to California in the year 1861, and visited the Miner, remaining with him until the next spring, when they both engaged

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
80
to go with he California troops, who had been ordered to Salt Lake City-in the capacity of teamsters. The Canadian and Miner had come to the conclusion, that in case the children were yet alive, they would most likely be found still prisoners in some band of Indians whose home was in the vicinity of Salt Lake; they had fully agreed that they could do more toward finding the children, as civilians than they could do as soldiers; for the reason that if they were teamsters, upon the arrival of the troops at Salt Lake City, they would be discharged, and then they would be free to prosecute their search; but on the other hand, if they enlisted they would probably have to serve three years or more in the army, before they would be discharged, and again be their own masters, and be at liberty to begin their search for the children; then again as enlisted men, there was the possibility that they might be hundred of miles from Salt Lake or the vicinity of the Masscare, when they were

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
81
discharged, and besides these reasons, there was another which had at that time a good deal of weight with them, which was, that if they enlisted, all the time they stayed in the Army would be lost time as far as any benefit to them would be concerned, in fact it would be more of a detriment, as it would delay the search that much longer, and they felt more disposed to use the time in prosecuting the search for the children, than they did to employ it in undergoing hardships, privations, and a certainty of danger, for the sum of eleven dollars a month- and found-, in the Army, with the assurance that in case they lost any of their accoutrements, they would be sure to find the missing article on- the next pay roll-; for these reasons they decided to go to Salt Lake City with the Troops, as teamsters.
Right here Mrs Fogarty! I wish to call your attention to this act of unselfish generosity, on the part of the Miner."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
82
He gave up a lucrative occupation and his time, with the expectation of having to use more or less of his money, in the prosecution of a search for two children, who were not related to him, or whom he had never seen.
Now it could not hardly be, that he was doing all this, for mere self benefit, because it could not possibly be of any personal profit to him, to sacrifice business, time, and money, and also suffer hardships and privations, in the pursuit of an undertaking in which there was more or less danger, and also one which he had no assurance, would not end in complete failure or be positively disasterous.
Therefore it could have been only the nobility of his nature, which prompted him to do such a generous and wholly unselfish deed as this."
Mrs Fogarty had a few remarks to make on the subject, and she took this opportunity to express them.

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
83
"An' sure Oi am! it wod not be the loikes of yeze nature, to be doin' phwat ye beze lettin' the Miner done; for whin my bye Johnny broke his arm an' falled off the house where ye beze workin'; ye sinds him home an' the Docthor coomed an' set the arm agin, an' charged me tin dollars for doin' it, phwat Oi had to pay him; Sure now! Johnny broke that arm whin he wor climbin' round on some of the work ye beze doin' of, an' ye had the roight to be payin' the tin dollars phwat the Docthor wod be askin' me to pay, for sure it wor not his house phwat he falled off of, but it wor yeze. 
Sure Oi am! if a little gossoon loike that falls off me house, an' breaks his neck or arm, Oi wod pay for the fixin' of it loike a man, so Oi wod! an' not be askin' a poor widdy woman to do it, an' her wid one bye wid the broken arm, an' the odder bye not sinsin' enough to shew the pigs out of me gardin; for did'nt Oi sind Ned to the Drug Store one day wid a nickel, to git me foive cints

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
84
of washing soda; an' phwat wod he be askin' the Clerk for? but some- some-er of that stuff phwat tastes loike yeze phful wor aslape? an' begorra! phwat wod the man be givin' him but a glass of soda wather! So he did!."
"Well Mrs Fogarty I shall have to charge you fifteen dollars, for medical attendance on this occasion, and that ought to ballance accounts with all accruing interest; but to return to my story."
The Canadian told the Colonel- who was in command of the Troops- the reason why the Miner and he wished to go to Salt Lake City with his command, he also explained all he knew about the murder of his brother and his wife, and of the capture of their two children.
The Colonel at first told him, he thought he and the Miner had better enlist, for he was of the opinion that their chances for a protracted search- which might be necessary-, would be better if they were soldiers, that it would

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
85
be as civilians; but after they had explained to him in detail, their reasons for wishing to prosecute the search as civilians, the Colonel took a different view of the case, and after questioning them in regard to the extent of their finances, he told them he had become convinced that their plan was the proper one for them to pursue, and he would attend to having them both engaged for teamsters, for he considered them, both worthy of his assistance and protection. He told them they would probably find, they had many difficulties to overcome before they could rescue the children, whom they had no assurance were still living; he promised them that in case they succeeded in locating the children- or one of them- in any band of Indians who resided or roamed over the district over which he had command, he would send soldiers to assist them in the work of rescueing the children, even if it required the most of his command."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
86
Chapter 9.
"The Troops arrived at Salt Lake City in the last week of October 1862, and established a Camp about two and a half miles east of the City, on a plateau of the east range of the Wasach Mountains; the Camp was made a perminent one, and it is now known as Fort Douglas.
On the first day of Nov-, they having been discharged and paid-, the Canadian and the Miner had an interview with the Colonel, which resulted in their commencing the search for the captive children the next day.
About the 12th of Nov, the Canadian reported to the Colonel, that the Miner and he had learned for a certainty, that a white boy about twelve years old- which would be the age of his brothers boy if he was yet alive-, was held as a captive in a band of Pi-ute Indians, who had their village or winter quarters, about a hundred

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
87
and twenty five miles north of Salt Lake City, in the Bear River range of Mountains, a few miles from the boundary line of Utah and Idaho, in the Territory of Idaho.
The Canadian reported that Mormon settlers who lived in the vicinity of the border, had informed the Miner and he, that they frequently saw a half grown boy with the Indians, when they came to the settlements, whom they were positive was of white parentage, and they were also sure that he was being held a captive, none of the settlers had been able to talk with him, for the reason that the Indians guarded him closely when they were in the neighborhood of the settlements and out laying ranches, the Indians would not allow him to go near a house, nor would they let any of the settlers get near enough to him to have any conversation with him.
The Canadian brought several letters

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
88
from prominent Mormons who resided in the vicinity of the border-, which coroberated his report. 
The Colonel at once began active opperations for the purpose of recapturing that boy.
On the 15th of Nov, twenty Troopers under the command of a Captain, were ordered to proceed with a mule pack train loaded with ten days rations, and extra amunition, and scout in the vicinity of the Bear River range of Mountains, and if possible recapture the boy, which the band of Indians whose winter quarters were in that locality, were said to hold a captive.
The weather was dry, and the days were warm and pleasant, but the nights had begun to be chilly and cold; the party had no tents with them, but with two heavy woolen blankets each, and by two of the Troopers bunking togather, they could have two blankets under them and also two over them, they had also their large caped overcoats to spread over all, then with their

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
89
Saddles or saddle bags for pillows, and their Revolvers housed in one boot leg, with its top tucked into the leg of its mate, and their sabres and carbines lieing by their side, under the bed covers, the Troopers slept as soundly and arose in the morning, feeling as much rested and refreshed as they did in the "long ago", after a sleep on a feather bed, or on a spring matrass.
The Captain found abundance of proof, that the Indians camped on the Bear River, had a white boy prisoner in their village; but he could not succeed in finding either the Indians or their camp, nor could he find any citizen who knew or would tell- even if he did know-, where the Indian Camp was located; the Captain became satisfied that the Mormons and Indians, were on very friendly terms, and that the Mormons did not want the Indians molested by the soldiers, for the reason that they could frequently trade for horses and other stock,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
90
and also domestic articles, which the Indians had captured on their raids upon emigrant trains, and they got them for a small portion of their real value, therefore from a business point it was for their interest to protect the Indians when they could do so; as for the humane side of the question, the Mormons of those days did not appear to have many humane instincts, as the Mountain Meadow Massacre, and the scores of murders, perpetrated by the Mormon Church, by the hand of its willing tools, the 'Danites,' or 'Destroying Angles,'-upon Gentiles, and Mormons who had become unfriendly to the Church, and therefore obnoxious to it-, will bear testimony. 
After scouting through the country in the vicinity of the border, as long as he could- and yet have time in which to report at the camp at Salt Lake City, on the expiration of the ten days, the Captain reluctantly gave the search up, and without having seen an Indian he returned

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
91
to Camp; and made his report to the Colonel. 
After hearing the Captains report, the Colonel declared that if there were any Indians- as it was claimed- in the region of country through which the Bear River flowed, they could be found, and he proposed that they should be even if it took all the Troopers he had command of, a year to find them.
Consequently on the first day of Dec, another scouting party with pack mules, comprising two Captains, and forty Troopers, started from Camp with ten days rations, for a scout after those Bear River Indians.
The detachment met with a little better success, than the preceding scouting party did, as regards to seeing any Indians, for they captured three bucks- as male Indians are generally called in the far west-; but the Troopers could not induce them by either persuasion or threats, to tell where the Village of their band was located, or if there was a white boy prisoner in their band."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
92
"As a token of the regard the Troopers felt toward them, for their fidelity to their kindred and tribe, in refusing to betray them, the Troopers without any compassion, filled their bodies with bullets, after having first hung them by their necks to a Ferry boat rope, where they were left to be found by some of their friends, or to be eventually devoured by Coyotes.
That would seem to us, to be a barbarous and inhuman manner in which to treat those Indian prisoners. But my brother John said that many of those soldiers had had friends and relatives murdered, and their bodies mutilated by the Indians on the western plains.
He said, that only a few months previous the Troopers had had a fight with Indians, in which one Trooper was killed, his comrades buried him where he fell, and left him to his last sleep; two days later they found his body had been torn from the grave, scalped and hung by the feet on a tree,

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
93
where it was then dangling; those Troopers vowed vengence on all "Plains Indians", and the orders,- "take no prisoners"- from the War Department, aided them in furthering the work of compelling the Indians to put an end to their warfare against all whites upon the plains, and by so doing end the barbarous and inhuman treatment they had for years imposed upon the many white victims who had fallen into their hands, in their raids upon emigrant trains, and in their attacks upon other parties, and thereby making the safety of civilized human life on the western plains possible."
Mrs Fogarty had a few words to say on the subject of Indians, so availing herself of one of the privileges of her sex, she interupted me to tell her experience with them.
"Indade thin! an' dont Oi know the Indians beze all a murtherin' lot of blagguards? for did'nt they's commit one of thim atrocities

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
94
wisdme? Afther Oi had paid one dollar for a botthel of their midicine, for me liver phwat wor ailin',-to some of thim Kickempoos-, phwat beze goin' round wid the unclane clothes on thim, an' wid they's faces daubbed wid paint, an' the poor little po-pop-er-babies tied fast to a board on the backs of thim; the haythin! phwat cant be askin' for a bite of bread an' treacle, in a dacint Christian voice.
One day me bye Ned gits the botthel of midicine an' feeds it to me two pigs, an' dont you belave! it killt the two of thim! an' thim sax months ould, an' they's wor buties! be me faith! that wor a sad atrocity phwat thim Indians committed on me pigs the bastes! an' thim wid the foine healthy appertites for the corn male mush wid butthermilk, so it wor!."
I can see Mrs Fogarty that you have a good reason for thinking, those Indians are of no good use; but to return to my story."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
95
"At the expiration of ten days, without having seen any more Indians, the Scouting party reported at their Camp at Salt Lake City.
The report of the Senior Captain of the detachment, inclined the Colonel to be the more determined to find the Indian Camp, and rescue that boy.
Therefore, on the 15th of Dec, a Major in command of sixty Troopers, with three subordinate officers- a Captain, and two Lieutenants, also an Interpreter-, left the Camp for another scout after that Indian Camp on the Bear river; they had a pack train loaded with fifteen days rations with them.
The Major was an old Indian fighter, for he had been in each of the two last Seminole Indian wars. So that he was well acquainted with the cunning and strategy of the Indian nature, and he proved himself fully competent to command any expidition sent against them; the Canadian and Miner joined the command at one of the Northern Settlements, as they had each of the preceeding Scouting parties."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
96
Chapter 10.
"The weather still remained dry, the days were bright and pleasant but the nights had become very cold, the detachment had no tents with them, but had to sleep on the ground without shelter of any kind from the frost with which their blankets were each morning covered, but all of those Troopers were well and hearty, so they did not let the want of a roof over them, trouble their minds very long, for all of them were more anxious to find the Indian Camp and rescue that boy, than they were to sleep in rooms furnished with Mahogany furniture, and feather beds covered with silk coverlets, Army blankets and a barn or shed would have come just as acceptable to them at that time, as a palace and spring beds; but it is not at all likely that those soldiers would have refused the comforts of the later, provided they had had a chance to do so."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
97
Late in the afternoon of the eighth day since leaving their Camp at Salt Lake City, an Indian was seen to dodge behind a large stone or bowlder, half a mile or more to the right of the trail which the Troopers were following, and between them and the Bear river range of Mountains; the Major was immediately notified that an Indian had been seen.
He ordered the Troopers to continue to move forward in the same open order in which they were then marching, and to make no sign that they had seen the Indian, or that they were aware that an Indian was in miles of that place.
After following the trail they were on, until they had got out of sight of the big bowlder, behind which the Indian was seen to hide, the Major halted his command; he then ordered the Captain with twenty Troopers, to move forward on the trails, until he had reached a spur of the Mountain range-which was

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
98
pointed out to him-, upon arriving at that point, he was ordered to wheel to the right and carefully make his way along the base of the range, until he came opposite the big bowlder, where he was to halt and remain for further orders or until he was relieved; he was also ordered to capture any Indians he might see, if possible he was to capture them alive, but he must capture them either dead or alive.
The Captain soon moved forward with his detail, and in less than half an hour he had arrived at the point where he was ordered to change direction to the right, and his detail was soon moving along the base of the range.
As soon as the Captain had reached the base of the range and wheeled to the right, the Major countermarched the remainder of the detachment, and they soon arrived at the place where the first sight of the Indian was had; after halting and dismounting the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
99
Troopers, the Major ordered twenty of them to deploy as skirmishers.
Leaving one Lieutenant in command of the reserves or rear guard, the Major and the other Lieutenant, moved forward with the skirmishers, they were soon abreast of, and spread out on each flank of the big bowlder, when they were rewarded by the sight of three Indians in full flight a mile to the east of them; the Indians were making haste to reach the willows which grow in clumps upon the banks of a small brook, which had its source in the Bear River range of Mountains to the North.
The Indians had discovered that their retreat to the foot hills, was cut off by the Captains Squad near the base of the range, and now their only hope of escaping capture, was in their being able to secrete themselves , in some of the many clumps of Willow bushes along the brook, and then steal away in the darkness of the fast approaching night."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
100
Mrs Fogarty interupted me to remark.
"Sure Oi am! Oi wod rather have the bit of wood in me phfut, or the tathe ache whin Oi had to listen to yeze stories, for Oi be havin' a dale of comfort in hearin' yeze mellow voice croonin' the while; Sure! it beze that soothin' a body nade not be takin' the dirthy lodanum to quiet they's narves, an' will ye be done wid it sometime? Oi dont know?"
"Yes Mrs Fogarty." I replied. "I will try to end it-sometime-.." But to return to the story.
Pursuit was at once began after the three fleeing Indians; the Troopers were dismounted, but they were encumbered with their Carbines, Revolvers, amunition, and haversacks, but with the Major in the lead, they made fairly good time in reaching the creek, and then search and pursuit begun in downright earnest.
With no assurance that the Indians were not armed, the Troopers had to move cautiously and not unnecessarily expose themselves to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
101
a chance shot from the Indians.
It was near sundown when the Troopers reached the bank of the stream, and night would soon set in, as there was a clear sky, the stars would show brightly; so they might safely count on a little light, to dispell the intense darkness of a moonless night in that latitude, until about eight oclock when the full moon would rise, and aid them with its light in their search for the Indians.
The Troopers were very anxious to get another sight of the Indians, if they could only locate them once, they were sure they could soon hunt them down and capture them. Just as darkness begun to settle down to the ground, the three Indians were seen to cross an open space between two clumps of willow bushes.
Those of the Troopers who saw them, delared the Indians did not show any guns, and if they were armed at all, it was probably with revolvers and hunting knives; the chance

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
102
sight of the Indians caused the Troopers to be the more eager in the pursuit; trusting the report was true- that the Indians had no guns-, the Troopers did not have so much fear of being hit by a rifle bullet, as they had before they were last seen, they now had no fear for the result, for they knew that when it came to close quarters, they would have the advantage in strength of numbers. 
The object of the Major had been, from the first sight had of the Indians- to capture them alive. Therefore he gave orders that none of the Troopers should shoot them, except as a last resort, and then they were not to do so, until he gave the order. 
The search was long and wearysome, a sight would be had of an Indian for a moment, then he would melt away into the shades of the night, each sight offering fresh encouragement for further endeavor to capture them.
With the rising of the moon between eight and nine oclock, the Troopers found less

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
103
difficulty in moving around, and its light enabled them to distinguish objects, for some distance in each direction; a short time after the moon arose, the first one of the Indians was captured; contrary to expectation he had a rifle, but he did not offer to use it, for when he found himself surrounded and with no chance for escape, he quickly dropped his gun and held up his hands, then in a gutteral broken voice he said. "Me heep good Injin."Leaving the prisoner in the charge of two troopers, the others continued the search with renewed ardor.
The clumps of willows on both sides of the creek, for a long distance up and down its banks, were searched and researched until about eleven oclock that night, and then the last of the three Indians was captured, after several of the Troopers had forded that creek thirteen times; the Major and Lieutenant, and all of the Troopers had been

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
104
compelled to ford the creek several times during the search, so that the clothing of all of them was wet as high as their waist belts, and it was stiffened by the frost in a few minutes.
The last two Indians had each a loaded rifle, which they dropped when they surrendered, to hold up their hands and impart the very necessary information that- "Me heap good Injin".
The capture of the Indians has been accomplished without the firing of a gun, after a long chase of several hours; it is probable that if the Major had not given strict orders for the Troopers not to shoot them without his consent, the chase would have ended long before it did; for those Troopers would have made short work of capturing those Indians, had they been alowed to have shot them on sight, as the most of them were anxious to do; but they were restrained from doing so, by their respect for the orders they had received from the Major."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
105
" Their discipline had taught them that their first duty as Soldiers, was to obey all orders, and they knew full well that the violation of an order, ment condign punishment for the culpret, and that that would be especially true on the present occasion.
By the Troopers it was thought that the reason why the Indians did not make use of their guns, was because they feared if they did, they would be shot on sight; the Indians probably understood that it was their capture alive, and not their death which their pursuers were trying to accomplish, and their only hope of eluding the Troopers, was by keeping their presence in a locality unknown to them.
The Major and his victorious Troopers, with their three prisoners, returned as soon as possible to the reserves where their horses had been left; upon their arrival there the Major ordered "Recall" sounded for the Captain and his squad out near the base of the Mountains."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
106
Chapter 11
"The command mounted their horses and moved a mile or more to the South, and camped near a small Mormon Settlement; where it was soon joined by the Captain with his detachment.
Soon all in the Camp were quiet, the weary Troopers were lieing by twos on the frozen ground, and there appeared to be no one awake, except the few who were unfortunate enough to be on guard; there was but two guard posts or stations, one at the guards Camp fire where the Indians were being guarded, while they rested or slept, they had each been furnished with a blanket, which they had accepted in a stoical manner; the other guard post was at the picket rope, to which the horses and mules were tethered.
The next morning it was discovered that, the Troopers had made a very important capture the night before, for one of the prisoners was Bear Hunter, head Chief of the Bear River

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
107
band of the Pi-utes, another was Sam Pete, a sub chief of the same band, and the other was Little Neck, a trusted brave; as soon as breakfasts were disposed of, the Major with the help of the Interpreter- who could talk the Pi-ute language- had a 'talk' with the Indian prisoners; the Major questioned Bear Hunter in regard to the white boy, who was held a prisoner in his band. Bear Hunter stoutly denied that there was a white boy being held a prisoner in his Camp or in his band; the Major told him he was talking crooked, for he was sure that there was a white boy in his band, who had been kept a captive for several years, and he was there to rescue him, which he intended to do; and he should certainly do so, even if he had to attack and destroy the Indian Camp or Village, before he could accomplish his purpose.
Bear Hunter continued to deny the presence of any white boy in his band."

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
108
"After some further 'talk,' the Major told Bear Hunter, that he would release Little Neck, and he could send him to the Indian Village and get the boy and bring him to the Camp, and when the boy was given into his possession, he would release them all, and they would be at liberty to go to their village or any where else they might wish to, without fear of being harmed by him or by any of his soldiers; he also told Bear Hunter that in case Little Neck did not get back from the Indian Village by sundown that evening, he should have him and Sam Pete shot by his soldiers, after they had hung them on a tree.
The Indians confered togather in private for a few minutes, then Bear Hunter said that Little Neck should go to the Indian Village, but it was, "heap no good," for there was no white boy there for him to bring back with him.
Little Neck started for the Indian Village

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
109
about nine oclock that morning.
The Command remained in their Camp, and the Troopers passed away the time in growling, sleeping, and smoking, three very neessary acomplishments for a good soldier to possess.
During the day the Major had several lengthy conferences with Mormon Settlers, who visited him, but the troopers of course received no hint of the purpose of those visits, consequently there was much conjecture, whether the fact of their having the two Indians prisoners, had any thing to do with the visits of the settlers, but on that subject they were not officially enlightened, any more than they had been on many which would follow, as Commanding Officers as a general rule, only publish orders necessary for the good of the service, and not for the information of the rank and file.
About half an hour before sun down, Little Neck was seen approaching the Camp, but

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
110
he was all alone, for there was no boy with him; he was immediately conducted to the guards Camp fire, where he joined the other two Indians at supper; Bear Hunter greeted him with a "Ugh," and then seemed to forget his presence.
The Major, and Interpreter soon visited the Camp fire of the guards to have another 'talk'- with the Indians, but to all of their questions they could get but the one answer of,- "heap no white boy"!-from the Indians.
During the day one of the Majors Mormon visitors, had been induced to inform him where the Indian Village or Camp was situated, he also informed the Major, that only the day before he saw a boy who he was sure was a white one, in the company of two Indians going in the direction of the Indian Village, which was situated not further than fifteen miles distant from the present camp of the Troopers.
The Major had another "talk" with the

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
111
Indians, which he was overheard to say would be decisive, for after its conclusion, if it was without result, he should hang the three Indians, and at once send a courier to the Camp at Salt Lake City for re-enforcements, and upon their arrival he should move on the Indian Village and destroy it.
The Major told the Indians that they had been lying to him, because he now knew for a certainty that there was a white boy held captive in their band, and that boy must be brought to him the next morning, or he would hang them all, and then have his soldiers fill their bodies with bullets.
He also told them that he now knew where their Village was located, and that he had a Settler engaged, who would guide him and his soldiers to it, and if the boy was not in his possession the next morning, he would move on their Village, and destroy it and all the people whom he found there, just as soon as he could march there

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
112
after he had hanged them.
Bear Hunter at last weakened; when he became convinced that the Major did know where his Village was situated, and tht he would hang Sam Pete and himself, if the boy was not surrendered to him the next morning, he acknowleded that there was a white boy prisoner in his band.
He agreed to send Little Neck again to the Indian Village after the boy, and have him bring the boy back with him to the Camp, provided the Major would promise to release him and his companions, as soon as the boy was delivered to him. 
At this point, the negotiations were interupted by a Trooper's telling the Major that a Settler had just come into Camp, and he had asked to see the Major for a few minutes. 
The Major met the Settler and they conversed togather for a short time in private, as soon as their conference was ended, the Settler left the Camp, and the Major returned to

title: Theron Gaston memoir of 1861-1864 on the Western Frontier [vol. 1.1], 1903
transcription:
110
the guards Camp fire, and continued his 'talk' with the Indians.
The Major promised Bear Hunter, that he would release him and his companions, as soon as the boy was brought to him, but, at the time he warned him not to use any more subterfuge, because if he did and the boy was not brought to him before the sun was a hand high- about 8:30 AM- the next morning, he would hang him and Sam Pete, as he had told them he would; for he now knew that Little Neck did not go to the Indian Village that morning, as he had promised he should, because a Settler had just informed him that he had been up the canyon three or four miles from the Camp that day, cutting wood, and that Little Neck came to him about ten oclock that forenoon, and he had stayed there with him, until he quit work and started for his home, and they had come down the wood trails togather, until they

Address of the newly elected President, Roy Keister to the members of the Palette and Chisel Academy of Fine Arts

Fellow members
It seems strange to have such an honorable position after being in charge of the studio and usually one must work up to being President instead of down, as is my easen but there is one consolation. I will now be elgible for the Billard parlor.
My turn has arrived to take the chair for the coming year, and proper time to thank the members of the board and all the other members of the Club that have been so patient with my direction in the Studio For This Honored Position.
I assure you I feel my responsibility and will make every possible effort to keep the [[?]] Bell singing for another year
About three years ago Mr Hoffler (then President) ask me to be chairman  of the Studio committee up to that time, I didn't give the

2/
club very serious thought and every summer would forget thy [[?]] and start again in the fall - you will agree I was not very active in the work of the club, and three or four months away from the Club would throw my shooting arm out of it alignment, besides lose the comradship of all my fellow members !
Now,  the story is very different
I am very proud to hoast of my regularity, and do believe have always had a model on deck when the time came and if you have ever served on this committee, you certainly know your women when you retire from service.
We
 the Studio bunch never had any disagreeaments, just one grand bunch of fellows, and I want to thank all of you for the co-operation you gave me.


3/ We all make mistakes and I made plenty in choosing some of our models, but you didn't complain We just worked away - and here we are after three yearts together it has been a pleasure to me for I really enjoyed my responsibility and I consider those three years a treasure in my life.
There isn't much more to tell except that i feel from my own experience we should all be eager to get on the committee of service.
Its a great experience a constructive foundation of business and helpful in many ways that may give you a different [[?]]
This game of art.
Again I want to thank all of you for giving me the priviliege to be honored by this high rank as President and I assure you I will do my best !


P;S; - and after this fine bit of vocabularium the newly elected president invited the entire membership to our dining room where we had one on him - and so begins a new year 1937, full of spirit and hope and rekindled ambitions - John [[?]]

Report of the Outing Com.
for the Year 1917

The Camp was invaded by my very husky and able committee on march 10th. And it was put 9in ship shape order for the spring rush of our Camp friends.  They acted like a lot of hounds straining at the leash.  So that it was imperative to advance the date to May 26th instead of May 30th as in former years.  It was a joy to behold how they took up seems??? and with sagging jowls and, hanging tongues they bagged their quarry at Passadeloup's on the corner of Fox Lake.  Old Tome Moses Patron saint and father of our camp the best old scot that ever inhaled the Ozone of Bulls[??? - missing] or opened a Poker game was [missing] as jovial - jolly & frisky as ever regret to say we missed a great

The chairman and Committee extends a note of thanks for the way in which they unselfishly and ably upheld the tradition of our great organization and made it possible for us to survive a year of small attendance, which I attribute not to a lack of interest, but to general unsettled conditions ??? due to the present crisis.

THE PORTABLE HOUSE EPISODE

Tom Moses, a few years ago wa concerned in the building of a portable house for a traveling show. This statement bold and meager enough, nevertheless is the fatefull germ of much to do in this our hallowed Log Book, we ven-ture to say.
Thos aforsaid Thomas Moses after affiliating with the P.C.s decid-ed the one thing we needed for our camp, was this same vagrant P.H. and immediately started a still hunt for it. After an ineffectual foreign search it was found almost at his own door, giddily shouting with all the strength of blue, orange and yellow paint the beauties of a day in the Alps.
Tom at once wigwagged the owner who agreed to part with fifty feet of portable trouble for a doller per foot. Its was bought at once. Tom generously having it taken down and stored in his barn for the winter and hauled to the railroad in the Spring withou ex-pense to the Club.

It was the last of May, that after giving the P.H. a weeks start on a way freight, sixteen of the member boldly armed to the teeth with hammerr, saws

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 2], 1906-1915
transcription:
left for Fox Lake to do or die with said P.H. proved willing to provide both occupations.

On our arrival we found a box car full of dessicated house and an excited hamlet. The "Store" was very eager to learn the na-ture of the circus that threatened the town through the open door of the car. Disappointment hung heavy over the Store when we informed them it was simply a permanent crazy house for temporary artists con-temporary we ment to say.

The comittee at once found its hands full as no team was to be had and time fugiting as usual, also, they had a rival in the field. A florid and presipiring German was skipping back and forth on the villiage green (gravel) wailing for a "deem to ride his lunch by der laik". This was too deep for us, but we saw it spelled disaster for ours if he got the "deem" first, so we posted sentinals to waylay any-thing that wore wheels, while the frantic Ferman ran around in our circle sobbing about "das lunch" "der laik" and "dem deems". Adter we had secured the first hayrack that came along curiosity got the best of us and we looked in the car from which the German's gy-rations germinated. It was a gasoline launch.

We were now quite late and vegan feverishly loading on the heavy panels and lumber. Wat Williams and Kraft were on the wagon to adjust tje load the rest [[?]] shoving

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 2], 1906-1915
transcription:
it out. This uneven adjustment of the labor problem ended in disaster, as one end of a panel caught Kraft in the stomach, while the other knocked Wat. off the wagon. After every one in the car had told K. and W. what clumsy chumps they were the loading was completed and we proceeded to the camp site. 
We were met there by the othe contingent that had gone to Brophy's for the tent and camp outfit.

[picture]

By the time the tent was up we were ready for supper, which though prepared by a vast number of cooks was not spoiled to any great extant. 
Dishwashing 
Brophy's big white bulldog as usual appointed himself guardian of the camp and tho friendly to all in the daytime could see no earthly use of anybody coming into camp after dark. This embarassed the younger element that would a dancing go.

[picture]
We were lulled to sleep by weird strains of a wild Bohemian piano that has haunted Fox Lake for two sum-mers. All seasons long the bowels of the night have been pierced by its heartrending yibbering and writhing rythm.
As soon as the mud hen season opens, we in-tend to get that piano if it takes the whole [[?]]
Admiral Payne and Hinter Admiral Dau-man are at present working out a battle sketch [[?]] ultramarine and pajamas. It is thought the fight will be on the low C insead of the high.

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 2], 1906-1915
transcription:
The next day we were up not necessarily bright and early but up which is th main thing. The unwritten rule of the camp is, the first up gets breakfast so there is in-tense rival-ry among the cot warmers.
After a breakfast of bacon and childless eggs, everybody went at the P.H. with blood in his eye and valiant courage in his heart, but, alas; most of the crowd had little experience in building operations outside of birds-eye views of factories on labels and front elevations of fashion plates.
So round one over most of therm were found embracing a cot.

After the sides and roof fraines were up we dis-covered the roof would not go on because in following the undulating ground surface We had defied all the laws of squares and cubes. Here was a real problem, but by shoving one side south the other north, pushing out the east wall pulling in the west and raising it here and there, the roof finally dropped into place, thas is near enough to satisfy those who did the pushing. Very few were satisfied.
Arnold who was to stal all week said he would try to get along with it

At one thirty the Skidoo was sighted in the offing and shortly dropped anchor in Larson's backyard
where the hardy voyagers filed aboard.
After a strenous effort to climb a cedar
post backwards, the hysterical craft ambled
sideways for the open sea. Those on the
beach who couldn't go wept happily in each others
arms. While Larson who had arival boat,
made cheerfull forecasts as to our fate.  After ex-
ecuting some figure eights, grapewines and
Dutch rolls on the "outer edge" we began hitting
the low places, ignoring the high ones.
We were now going full blast sing-
ing and whopping lije Indians. The gaso-
line engine joined in the sport and threw oil
joyously over Wilimousky's laundried foreground.
Wili'sky was game however and  smiled hap-
pily between showers. After Fox we
passed through Nippersink and Pistakee lakes
down the Fox river past Johnsburg to Larsen's
hotel, where we stopped for spiritual consolation

On the way back the Skidoo broke her
spocket chain. At the time we were
near the centre of Pistakee Lake and
to the feminine at the mercy of the ferocious
elements. One young lady very much
wrought up loudly shrieked for "Charley".
The married men all started guiltily but quickly
regained their composure.  While the choir
struck up, "Nearer my God to thee", to reassure
the timid. Upon Irvine taking soundings and finding we were nearer the earth than
God the song was changed to "sailing [[?]]".
During the excitment Behr discovered
he was seated astride the engine and had
parboiled - at least he went up on the poopdeck
to cool off. After an hour delay we again started for the camp.
It was now nip and tuck to catch our train and the drawbridge-

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 2], 1906-1915
transcription:
still in front of us.
As was to be expected when we reached it the draw was out of business, the machinery and keeper having collapsed after we passed through on the way down.
There was nothing for it but to go back to the first landing and foot it, which we did with fortitude and an economical amout of congenial cus-sing amoung the men.
However all reached the train tired but happy.
That is all but Mauch who had a new rifle and two hundred rounds of cartidges but had fired only one shot owing to the sensitiveness of people who were entire strangers to Mauch.
Even he found consolation in saving a half acent on every shot he didn't shoot.

THE Thirteen outing 
AND THE VOYAGE OF THE "SKIDOO"
was started Sat. July 13 and closed Sunday with 13 Ladies, 13 Men and 13 children present, The 13 Ladies with 13 differant kinds of headaches, voted it the best ever and 13 males voices said "Do it again".
At 1 oclock Sat. they began to assemble at the [[?]] and St. P. station and were soon in pos-session of a chair car the road had put in the shuffle for a joke. This was an exciting and novel change from the old Wan-derlust sewerpipies with gimlet hole windows we were used to. It is thought the and [[?]] and St. P. is losing it's nerve.
Probably at 13 minutes past one there was a fierce commotion among the sardines at the gate and from out the seething mass emerged the struggling figure od the Out-ing hero, Fritz Curley Bertsch. And well [[?]]ight he struggle, for deftly cocealed in his [[?]]ight hand was the backbone of the Outing, [[?]] alledged portable organ, complete with

The orchestra having came the train went without any more foolishness. At Fox Lake we were met byr Irvine who presented Fred with a bicycle to transport the organ. 
Irvine and Engle biked over to Merkie's landing to charter the good ship "Skidoo". That "good ship" is a courteous conventionality. What we saw was an open faces machine shop married to a windmill.

Preamble
 With a view to raising the Standard of Music, and benefiting ourselves and the Community in which we are located, we the undersigned agree to form a Club and for its government do hereby adopt the following
 Constitution
Title
Article I The name and title of this organization shall be "The Chicago Commons Choral Club"
 Objects
Article II
The objects of this Club shall be
1st For the Musical and Social  advantages of the members. 2nd Raising the standard of Music in the Community through Recitals and Concerts
3rd Co-operating with the other Social Settlements in Musical Extension and director of entertainments
 Officers
Article III  The officers of this Club shall consist of a President, Vice President, a Secretary, Assistant Secretary, a Treasurer and a Librarian [[& conifer?]]

title: Chicago Commons Choral Club minutes, 1900-1905
transcription:
Election of Officers
Article IV Officers shall be elected by ballot at the first regular meeting of this Club in the month of November, and shall hold office for the year following.
Duties of Officers 
Article V The President shall preside at all business meetings of the Club. In his absence the Vice President shall take the chair. Sec. 2 The Secretary shall conduct the correspondences, keep the records of the Club and read at such times as shall be desired by the members, a report of the work done. Sec. 3. The Assistant Secretary shall take the place of the Secretary in his or her absence and assist him or her when requested. Sec. 4 The Treasurer shall keep the funds of the Club, making a semi-annual report of all money received, disbursed and the amount on hand. Sec. 5The Librarian shall keep in a care-ful manner, all music and records in the possession of the Club.

title: Chicago Commons Choral Club minutes, 1900-1905
transcription:
Committies
Article VI. There shall be appointed by the President after the first meeting after his election, the following committees, to consist of three members each, namely on Music and Socials. The Music committee to be a standing one and the Social committee to be appointed each month.

Conditions of Membership.
Article VII. Any lady or gentleman may become a member of this Club by a majority vote of the members present and the payment of twenty-five cents (25c) membership fee.
Sec. 2. It shall be the privilege of the members to elect by a majority vote any person whose presence may be advantageous to the Club, an honorary member who shall not be required to pay membership fee or dues. 

Collection of Dues
Article VIII. The monthly dues of the Club shall be twenty-five cents (25c) which the secretary shall collect in advance.

title: Chicago Commons Choral Club minutes, 1900-1905
transcription:
Time of Meetings
Article IX The regular meetings of this Club shall be held at eight o’clock on Thursday evening of each week, and at such other time as our Director may deem necessary for the preparing of music for concerts, etc.

Penalty for Violating Rules
Article X Any member who shall be absent four consecutive regular meetings without reasonable excuse or who neglects to pay dues, shall be deprived of membership until reinstated.

XI? Amendments 
Article XII By given written notice of change at any regular meeting, this Constitution may be altered or amended by a vote of two-thirds of the members present.

The singing exercises led by Miss Hofer occupied the time from about 8;15 PM. to about 9:30 P.M.

Miss Hofer then suggested that we have no further delay in rendering the Old Folks concert which as first projected by the chorus has since been shelved and that we set a time and place for rendering said concert.

The President Mr. C. Falconer was unexpectedly called away and our Vice President Miss Ida L. Rasmussen presided.

Minutes of meeting March 6th 1900

Singing exercises led by Miss Hofer occupied the time from 8:30 P.M. to about 9:30 P.M.

Meeting called to order by Vice Pres. Miss I.L. Rasmussen who presided in the absence of Pres. Mr. C. Falconer.

Mr. Silgander had made a verbal report as to his progress in securing a hall and said that we could secure Aurora Hall for that date for the sum of Fifteen ($15.00) Dollars or Seaudia Hall for the sum of Twenty-five ($25.00) Dollars.

The report was thoroughly discussed and the discussion culminated in a motion by Miss Hofer, which motion was duly seconded that we have a further talk with Mr. Silgander and that he be directed not to go ahead just yet about securing Aurora Hall as we had hopes of securing Seaudia Hall for the same price. On regular vote the motion was carried.

The secretary was then directed by the chair to notify committee on programme to be present on Tuesday Eve. March 13th 1900.

There being no further business the meeting adjourned on regular motion and vote.

The roll was then called and the minutes of the previous meeting were read and approved.

The secretary then reported that Scandia Hall could not be secured for less that Twenty-five ($25.00) Dollars.

These foregoing reports were thoroughly discussed and the discussion culminated in a motion which was duly seconded that the date of the concert be changed to April 6th 1900 and that Aurora Hall be engaged for that evening.  Our regular vote the motion was carried.

Mr. Siljander was then instructed by the chair to engage the hall for that date.
