title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
1
Narrative of the Expedetion of Major John Doughty with men to the Choktaw nation of Indians in the year 1790, + his desperate fight in the Tennessee River with (double his number of) strange Indians, whom he beat off with great loss; as contained in an authentic account trans-mitted from the Western Territory, immediately after the affair.
It is with sincere pleasure we inform the public that Major Doughty who was repor-ted to have been killed by the Indians on the river Tenassee, safely arrived at Fort Harmer on the Ohio, the 15th of April last. This valuable officer was charged with important public business to the Chick-esaw nation of Indians, while ascend-ing the Tenassee, on the 21st of March, he was met by a party of forty Indians in three canoes, having a white flag dis-played.— This party proved to be a banditti of Cherokees & Shawanese, with three Creeks.
Marjor Droughty was at the time in a barge with Ensign Sedam & fifteen non-commissioned officers & privates. The Indians appeared very friendly, & their Chief & several others even came on board the barge. There they received presents with the greatest apparent thankfulness, presents of corn & tobacco. When the business of giv- giving & receiving presents was finished,

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
the Indians endeavored by every means in their power to persuade Major Doughty to land & pass the night with them; promising to hunt huskies & buffaloes for him. But he being suspicious of their designs, evaded their entreaties. After having thus passed upwards of an hour, they shook him by the hand very heartily & left [[?]]: as was feared; the Major's men had scarcely taken their oars when they received from the Indians a severe fire, which was immediately returned; or as soon as oars could be exchanged for fire arms, & the boat put about. The barge now drifted with the stream, & an incessant fire was continued for four hours. During this time the Indians manifested an intention to board the barge, but the cool & well directed fire of the whites prevented the design. The Indians now became discouraged, having lost a great number of their company & retired to the land, leaving their equally distressed opponents to the th[[?]].
Notwithstanding this long & severe fight, Major Doughty had but five of his party killed, & six wounded. Being thus reduced, he was un-able to return up the Tenessee; he therefore descended that river & the Ohio into the L'Anca a la Graise, a Spanish post, about 45 miles below the mouth of the Ohio. Here he & his men received every attention their wretched condition re-quired from Mons. Foucher, Lieut. Commandant of that post. Three of the wounded, too badly hurt to be removed, were left here, & the Major, with the remander proceeded on their return homeward. On the Ohio they were met by Capt. Heart, who had been previously despatched by Maj. Doughty to the Chickasaw nation, & they proceeded together. And thus terminated the expedition.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
3

Copy of a Letter sent by Gen. Mc Gillivray,* Chief of the Creek nation of Indians to Edward Telfair, Governor of [South Carolina crossed out] Georgia, relative to the then existing difficulties between the Creeks & the [South Carolinians crossed out] Georgians.
Note. The following letter will show with what magnaminity an Indian chief could treat the insolent demeanor of those claiming all the advantages of civilization. It is true Gen. Mc Gillivray was brought up partly educated among the white people, but he was nevertheless an Indian; thought and acted as an Indian, and showed himself a far better [pattern?] of civilization than many of the elevated men of our country did then, or do at this day. Of this chief I have somewhat fully spoken in the Book of the Indians.
In order that the Governor may have a fair trial, or that a fair comparison may be instituted, we give, in the first place, the substance of his letter which elicited the answer which will follow.
"State House, Augusta, Jan. 8th, 1790. Sir the favorable representations I have had of your disposition to suppress violence & restore peace have induced me to open a correspondence with you; not with a design to enter into the merit or demerit of past transactions, farther than the restoration of property belonging to the people of this state. And also that every species of future depredation be withheld. Humanity will readily dictate the propriety of liberating and sending forward the citizens and other persons belonging to this state, now in the Creek nation."
Here it is observable, that, notwithstanding the tone is dictatorial, (to use the mildest term it will allow,) yet his excellency acknowledges that he is addressing the head of a nation, a term [sneezingly?] used by governors since his time, when speaking of those Indians--but upon this we have commented elsewhere, and will now proceed to the answer given by the chief. 
Little Tellassee, 30 Nov. 1790
Sir I received your letter of the 8th of January last, by Ash;

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
he being unable to return on account of the extraordinary floods, I send this to Gen. Pickens to forward.
In answer to yours I have to observe, that, as a peace was not concluded on between us at the Rocks Landing meeting, your demand for property taken by our warriors from off the disputed lands, cannot be admitted. We, also, have had our losses, by captures made by your people.
We are willing to conclude a peace with you, but you must not expect extraordinary concessions from us. In order to spare the farther effusion of human blood, & finally to terminate the war, I am willing to concede in some measure, if you are disposed to treat on the grounds of mutual concession.
It will save trouble & expense if the negotiations are managed in the nation. Any person from you can be assured of personal safety & friendly treatment in this country. 
I am, sir, your most obedient servant, Alex. McGillivray.
His Excellency Edward Telfair, Esq.
Note.-- In explanation of the above correspondence it may be necessary to observe, that President Washington immediately after sent Col. Willett as an agent of the government to invite the chiefs of the Creeks to visit New York, to hold a treaty for the settlement of difficulties. They complied with the request, & all matters of difference, were adjusted without delay. In our Book of the Indians will be found the circumstances at large, & therefore it is not requisite that they should be gone into here.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
Narrative of the  most extraordinary & barbarous proceeding of some white women, in falling upon a number of captive Indians at Marblehead, & cruelly beating them to death in the year 1677. Taken out of an old, & now almost illegible MS Deposition of Robert Rouled, an eyewitness of the transaction.
Introduction-
The following account was accidentally discovered by  me many years ago, among a large quantity of old papers. the chirography is so very bad, that with the badness of the ink & meanness of the paper, that I was at first, deterred from an attempt to decipher it. However, it sometimes happens that the very circumstance of obscurity serves only to sharpen more keenly the appetite of the antiquary. It was so in this case, & I did not find myself satisfied until I had made the transcripts, in different years: & by a comparison of these, & each with the original, I felt confident of its authenticity, & its antiquity there cannot be a shadow of a question. In endeavoring to make it intelligible I have been obliged to write it anew, as in the original it had so many abbreviated parts as to be completely obscure to all but those conversant in the chirography of those days, in such, peculiar kinds of document. The only notice of the event ever before published, is probably that in a note of Hutchinson, [[HW2. Mas.i 307.?]]
I Robert Roules of Marblehead, mariner, aged thirty years or thereabouts, belonging to the catch Williams Sarah of Salem, do upon oath say, that Joseph Bovey went out master of the said ketch upon a fishing voyage to the eastern coast. After we had caught, & being about half laden with fish, & riding at an anchor at port LaTour, near cape Sable, & on the easterly side thereof, on the 7th of this instant, July,  it being Saturday, purposing here to take in wood & water, & in two days to be again upon our fishing design, but on the Lord's day, being the 8th instant, in the dawning of the day, there came suddenly on board of us a canoe of Indians in number nine or ten, as near as I could judge, with their arms ready fixed, loaded & cocked. I first discovered them, & dropped down upon deck to save myself from their shots. They immediately fired upon us & their shots chiefly struck against the windlass

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription: & so did not hurt us. I then called to them, & said, what for you kill Englishmen? They answered me, If Englishmen shoot we kill - if not shoot, are no kill. They then ordered us to come up. By this time they had boarded us, & we were obliged to surrender without conditions. We then proceeded to bring me, the other four men with me, the master, capt. Booey being one. They stripped us, one after the other all our clothes, on by having me a greasy shirt & waistcoat, & drawers we used to fish in, our shoes & stockings being in the cabin. They then gave us liberty to sit upon deck, bound as we were all, till a boat two of the clock in the afternoon. After this they unbound us, & commanded us to sail our vessel towards Penobscot, which are endeavored to do; but the wind shortening, all were forced to tome to an anchor again & lay there still the second day of our capture. In the meantime, they told us they intended to kill all of us, & all the English being in number twenty six, including boys, except [[?]]. They had taken four other vessels besides ours. On the second day, they commanded with the other ketches to sail together for Penobscot. The Indians had dispersed [[?]] into all the ketches; there being seventy or eighty of them. As we sailed onward we espies a [bank?] & gave her [chale?] & soon took her, & found it Mr. Watts vessel. The Indians compelled us to hail him, & he answered us he was from Boston, bound on a fishing voyage. To present the murder of him & his men, as soon as we came up with him we told him he was taken, but he thinking it only a joke, laughed at us. The Indians now rode up & told Capt. Watts if he did not strike they are all dead men.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
All but four of the Indians then went on board him; divided & mixed the Englishmen in the different vessels with themselves; sending master Bovey with one man more of our company, on board another ketch; and left me as master of the ketch, --(they wholly disliking the said Bovey) with an old man, which I desired. And now being on board with Capt. Watts, the Indians having sent two of their number away, took two of Capt. Watts' men in their place, whereof one was William Buswell.
We had not been thus situated but a short time, when another sail was discovered, & we were commanded to give chase. We did so till it began to grew disky, & then the Indian Sagamore of our vessel ordered me, who being at the helm, to bear up; but I refused. Thereupon the Sagamore grew angry, & was about to fall upon me, which William Buswell observing, seized him by the throat, & a close scuffle ensued. Buswell however soon tripped up his heels, fell upon him, & kept him down with his knee upon his breast. Meantime, another of my companions in captivity, named Richard Downes, closing with a second Indian, succeeded in getting him down also; & in attempting to throw him overboard, his legs became entangled, which Buswell perceiving, left his man, & seizing upon him too, they quickly threw him into the sea. 
While this was going on the other Englishmen were enabled to confine the other Sagamore in the cook room, by shutting down the scuttle upon him. All hands then grasped another Indian and threw him overboard. It was a desperate attempt, but the victory was now certain. The two remaining Indians were Sagamores, one was an old man. The other was a young man. One was fast in the cook room, & the other was glad to surrender to save his life.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
We next proceeded to find the two Indians, I then made all the sail we could to the southward, & on the fifteenth day, a little before sundown, we came to our anchor in Marblehead.
News had reached this place that we were all killed, & many people flocked to the waterside to learn who we were & what other news they could, concerning the many vessels that had been taken by the Indians. They hailed us, & then some came on board; and when they saw the Indians, they demanded why we kept them alive, and why we had not killed them. We answered them, that we had lost everything, even to our clothes, & we thought if we brought them in alive we might get somewhat by them toward our losses. But this did not satisfy the people who were angry at the sight of the Indians, & now began to grow clamorous. We told them we should take them on shore & deliver them into the hands of the constable of the town, that they might be answerable to the court of Boston; so we carried them on the shore with their hands bound behind them.
Being on shore, the whole town flocked about them, beginning at first to insult them & soon after, the women surrounded them, drove us by force from them (we escaping at no little peril). & laid violent hands upon the captives, some stoning us in the meantime because we protect them, others seizing them by the hair, got full possession of them, nor was there any way left by which we could rescue them.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
Then with stones, billets of wood, & what else they might, they made an end of these Indians. We were kept at such  distance that we could not see them till they were dead, & then we found them with their heads off & gave of their flesh in a manner pulled from their bones. And such ws the humiliation these women made, that for my life I could not tell who these women were or the names of any of them . They cried out & said, if the Indians had been carried to Boston, that would have been the end of it, & they would have been set at liberty; but said that if there had been forty of the best Indians in the country, they would have killed them all, though they should be hanged for it. They suffered neither constable nor mandrake, nor any other per[[?]] to come [[?]] them, until they had finished their bloody purpose.
Taken a pen oath this 4th of July 1677.
Edward Rawson, Sec.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
Narrative of the captivity of Baron de Graffenried, Governor of the Palantinate in the North Carolina, & John Lawson, Esq., Surveyor General of that province. The fortune & death of the latter by the Tuscanora Indians, in the year of 1711, as communicated by the Baron himself, in a letter to Gove. Hyde of N. Carolina.
Introduction
IN the beginning of September, 1711, the people of North Carolina began to grow very distrustful that the Indians intended their mischief. Their fears soon proved to be too well founded. The Tuscanora undertook an attach on the plantations on the Roanoke river, & from there to that of the Pamblico; & the Indians living on that river (The Pamlicos from above it took its name), were to fall upon their immediate white neighbors. The [Cothechneys?}, who  dwelt in what is since Greene County, were to join the [Cores?], & with them to strike a blow upon the whites along the Neuse & Trent rivers. The [Mattasuneskets & Matchapangos?] were to go against the plantations in the vacinity of Bath. And says the judge Maston, "notwithstanding the many great numbers of individuals of different tribes, to [ashore?] was committed this secret enterprise if was not betrayed by any." The Tuscanoras had a large palisaded town, into which they sent their women & children preparing for their setting out on their expedition. "From there on the day preceding new moon, twelve hundred warriors secretly marched in [[?]] [[?]]." Spies had been sent forward, as had been practiced at Dover in the days of Major Waldron, who were admitted into the houses of the settlers, & at the signal of the warwhoop, they were instantly joined by others from the neighboring woods, & indiscriminate massacre

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
was immediately begun, which was continued with all its horrors for the fall space of three days. The first blow was as struck on the eleventh day of September, 1711, in the plunder, drunkedness, or exhaustion had disabled the perpetrators. One hundred & thirty persons fell in this terrible affair.
It was only a few days before this massacre begun that Baron de Graffenried (or as recently written Graafffenriedt) & John Lawson left Newbern, attended by a Negro, with the intention of ascending Neude river so expansive the lands on its banks. And we will now proceed to give this narrative of what befell them, in the language of Graffenried himself, according to our promise. 
I have many things to relate to you, but for want of time must delay them to a future day. At present I shall only inform you of the fate of Mr. Lawson the surveyor general.  We had both taken to my boat on the Neuse river, in order to discover what kind of land there was further on, & what distance anyone might go on the same. To what I had the more readily consented, as Mr. Lawson had assured me the country on this side was not inhabited. But when we arrived at [Corutra?], a village about 12 miles by water from the town of [Corane?], with an intention to farry there all the night, we met with two Indians, whom presently after a great number joined [Greene?] & me. I told Mr. Lawson I did not like the appearances, & that we [[?]] to proceed on, which we accordingly

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
did, but no sooner had we arrived at our boat, such a number of Indians pressed upon us, that it was impossible for us to keep them off. They took our arms, provisions, & all we had. There were upwards of sixty of them, all well armed, who compelled us to travel with them all night, & until we arrived at an Indian village, a considerable distance from the river, where we were delivered to the king, or chief of the village or town. He called a council, at which one of the Indians delivered a long speech with great  [[?]]; whereupon a question was put - where we should be bound, which was passed in the negative; & the reason given was because we had not yet been permitted to make our defense. The next morning we desired to know what they intended to do with us. Their answer was, that the Chief would have that evening a number of their Chiefs at an entertainment, who must also be present at  our examination, after which they would come to a decision.
Accordingly, in the evening, upwards of 200 were collected, from which numbered about 40 got together, who were considered as chiefs of the people. Before these we were examined very strictly concerning our intention, & why we had come hither. Our answer was that we were endeavoring to find out a shorter and better road to Virginia, because the other road from our settlement was a very bad & difficult one; & that, for that reason the Indians from there we could not conveniently trade with us. Whereupon the Indians complained very much of the

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
conduct of the English colonies in Carolina, & particularly named Mr. Lawson. Charging him with being too severe, & that he was the man who sold their land. They also said that Mr. Hancock had taken a gun from an Indian, & that Mr. Price also dealt too hard with their people. Nevertheless, they would consent to our being set at liberty, & that we should return home on the day following.
The next morning, however, we were again examined, & we returned the same answer; that one Col. Thom being present, whom Mr. Lawson reprimanded for sundry things which had happened, gave a very unfavorable turn to our affairs. After the council had broken up & the major part of the Indians had gone off, Mr. Lawson & myself were talking together on indifferent subjects, an Indian who understood a little English, informed the remaining Indians  that we had spoken very disrespectfully of them, which, however, was totally grounded. Whereupon, three or four of them fell on us in a furious manner, took us by the arms & forced us to sit down on the ground before the whole of them that were there collected. They instantly took off our wigs & threw them into the fire, we were at once condemned to death. Mr. Lawson was indeed sentenced to have his throat cut with his own razor, & I was to be put to death in another manner. 
On the day following we were taken to the great place of execution, where we were again tied & compelled to sit on the ground; being stripped of our [[?]]. Before us a large fire wood kindled, whilst some of them acted the part of con-

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
jurers, & others made a rind around us which they strewed with flowers. Behind us lay my innocent Negro, who was also bound, & in this miserable sitaution we remained that day and the subsequent night.
On the morning of the next day, at which we were to die, a large multitude was collected to see the execution. Behind us there were an armed party, who acted as a guard, & around us sat the chiefs in two rows. Behind them were the common people amounting to upwards of 300 in number, who were jumping & dancing like so many devils, & cutting a variety of [inferual?] & obscene capers. There were also present two executioners, of wild & terrible aspect, & two drummers. The council again deliberated in order to put and end to this dismal tragedy.
I recommended my soul to my savior, Jesus Christ, & my thoughts were wholly employed with death. At length, however, I recollected myself, and turning to the council of chiefs, asked them whether no mercy could be shown to the innocent & with what propriety they could put to death a king (for the Indians call a governor a king) & I was king of the Palatines. Thus God in his mercy heard my prayers and softened the hard hearts of the savages that they, after much talk from an honest Indian altered my sentence of death, and will appear from the treaty of peace.
I was a short time before Mr. Lawson's execution set at liberty, & afterwards conducted to the house of the Indian who had interested himself & spoken so much on my behalf. But my Negro also suffered. 
I remained in captivity until the sunday following, when I was brought on horseback to [[?]]; from thence I had to foot it as above related. I should be very glad to have some conversation with you on that subject, & to consider what measures ought to be taken

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
against those people; but that must be deferred for the present.
Note
This is the narrative ot the baron wrote if perhaps not intended by him for publication; if it had been so intended, he would doubtless have described the closing scene of Lawson & the Negro with more minuteness. Indeed the next & last sentence of his narrative indicated this conclusion. He says, "I shall however, write more fully to you on the subject." And in a letter to a friend in Germany, of 4 January 1712, he says he remained five weeks in captivity. It appeared that before he left the Indians he made a treaty with them, which is dated "October, 1711." It is very short and is as follows: "I. To show friendship towards each other.-II. In case of war between the English & the Indians, the Palentines do remain neutral.-III. No land to be taken by the baron or his people without consent of the Judicious.-IV. To be a cessation of arms for 14 days.-V. Hunting to be allowed in the open country.- VII. Trade to be conducted with justice to the Indians.-VIII. Signatures to be added, which shall be signed that no injury shall be done the Indians.
Signed with a [[?]] for the Neus Indians, & another for the Tasacoras.  & also that of Graffenried.
Note: - The war which was begun by the massacre which had been detailed in the introduction to the proceeding narrative terminated in a great destruction of the Indians. A considerable blow was struck by Col. Barnwell, who with about 600 whites & 366 Cherokee, Creek & Castaubee Indians came upon a body of the enemy in the upper part of what is since [[?]] County, where they had fortified themselves with a wooden breastwork, on the borders of the Neuse river, & about 18 miles west of Newburn. They met the whites without their fort, but were soon defeated, & destined to it. Accounts differ in the numbers of Indians killed in the first engagement, some stating them to be 50  & others 300, with 100 prisoners. Barnwell besieged their fort, but is said by some to have made a "shameful capitulation." But in the course of the war more than 1000 Tuscanoras were killed or taken.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
Sequel to the narrative of [Massy Herbeeson?]. That narrative (in the form of a deposition) as given in our previous volume, are one enabled now, from the detailed generosity of a gentlemen on the spot, to give the following minute particulars. He drew up this narrative on the 1st of June, & it was sent to Philadelphia & published there on the 13th, followng, 1712.
I was but a few days at home, when the Indians broke into the settlement by Reed's Station. It was garrisoned by [[?]]; but they had never scouted any, & had been frolicking, & were surprised in want of ammunition, & the officer was absent from the station at the time. However, the Indians fired only a few rounds on the blockhouse, with which they killed one man & wounded another. They then killed & took Harbison's family in sight of the station. The alarm was quickly spread, indeed they thereabout promoted the news of their coming, by burning some of the first houses they came to. This occasioned the inhabitants to fly before then with the greatest rapidity; & they, being about forty in number, took the country before them, keeping nearly the course of the Kiskeminestas, going in small parties of from five to seven, as far as had been observed. They do not seem so anxious to kill as to plunder & destroy; however, some at remarkable escape I have been made; for instance, two families belonging to Massers Teal & Miller, who were surrounded in a bottom, only two of them taken. Two men & a woman were surrounded, but are likely to live. One of their sons who escaped saved two of the families who were just entering the bottom. Their ardent desire to get horses seemed to divert their attention from shedding blood. They greedily seize every kind of plunder. After some of them had been so closely pushed in recrossing the Allegheny, as to leave some of the horses, hopes were entertained that they were gone off; where however they appeared at different places much further in the settlement.At one plantation, above the mouth of the [Loyalhanner?}, they went boldly to the stable and fields, taking out the horses, killing a stallion which proved unruly. That seems to be the true way of writing that name. It is so written in Mr. J. [?'s} narrative, troughout, & he wrote from the mouth of Mr. Harbison.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
& taking off the rest without disturbing the family, who were trembling within. Perhaps, they were afraid that some of them would fall in attempting the house. 
About the same time they killed a man with a load of dry meat going to the [[?}}, & took his horse & load. Two days ago one of them was wounded by a young man, who perceiving three of them waylaying his father & another family carrying off some grain, & to a place of safety. This was on the course towards Hannah's town.
By a letter from Col. Campbell I am just informed that a scout had pursued the party of Indians that appeared as high up as the mouth of Black-Leg creek down to the Alleghany, where though they saw them different times, the ground was so unfavorable, they could not get a shot at them; but had recovered ten horses. Another scout goes out there today. A scout is also out from the neighborhood where I live. Though there was sufficient matter for alarm & terror without telling he's to promote it, I believe more have fled on the account of false alarms mischieveously contrived, within this two or three days past then formerly.
Hannah's town is now the frontier & they have erected block houses at Greensburgh. North of [Loyalhanning?], Dennison's is frontier. You will see by the map, Westmoreland is now desolate till near the centre, & the rest much disturbed. At the first alarm, Col. Campbell called upon two battalions of militia to turn out a company each; but before the days of rendezvous, these two battalions were chiefly broken up. The [[?]] since ordered out two other battalions, & is advised to call for assistance from Fayette county.
The scarcity of arms among the people is a distressing circumstance; voluntary excursions are prevented, & the flight of many families promoted from that cause. The people were so confident that they would never see war again, & in such necessity for money to repair their desolate places when peace was obtained that they sold their guns to people going down the river.
I hear from Pittsburg that Mrs. Harbison escaped from the Indians, & has discovered some treacherous persons among us. I also understand that a private expedition is on foot, but I expect you will receive more perfect

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
accounts from Pittsburg than I am possessed of. My house, & many of the neighboring houses being crowded with families that have fled, & frequent consultations being necessary, I have not been far abroad since this distressing scene commenced; therefore my information is necessarily local.
All the public exertions against the hostile Indians having been hither to unfortunate, the distresses of the people have consequently increased instead of being removed; and the people themselves have appeared to lose heart, & not to be capable of those exertions which they made the last war. My endeavor to encourage them, I find has much less effect this year than it had in the [[?]]. Though the army is slowly raising, yet its permenancy gives ground to hope that this occasion is more critical than any that is to follow.
From the narrative of Mr. [Minter?] the following facts concerning Mrs. Harbeeson are gathered. He informed the reader that in his instrumentality in bringing the narrative of Mrs. Harbeeson before the publlc, he was not influenced  by the promise of reward, but she [[?]] at repeated solicitations of a poor widow, who in the final settlement of this western county, acted the noble part of a pioneer, & encountered those [[?]] privations, hardships & sufferings, which are related within". "Her captivity, the murder of her two children, the length of time she was in captivity, and thereabout miraculous escape from Indian barbarity, any facts well known to hundreds yet alive.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
Artful Revenge of a Tribe of Indians on a French Trader
The Mifsonunis, a people of Louisiana, were strangers to the Europeans, till about 50 years ago, a traveler, or hunter, coming into their country acquainted them with fire-arms, & used their muskets, powder & shot, by means of which their next hunt was very successful; & of course, furnished them with a great quantity of skins. Sometime after adventurer went thither with ammunition: but the savages, part of their stock being yet remaining, were not very eager to deal with him; so that retrieve this disappointment, he bethought himself of a pretty odd strategem. The savages being naturally curious, asked him in what manner gunpowder, which they call grain grew in France; & he made them believe that it was grown in the savannah, or fields, & reaps at certain times, like indigo & millet. The Mifsounis, overenjoyed of his information, which seemed pregnant with such [[?]]-
By some men that came lately from Capt. Mayrens ship at New York, we have an account of a remarkable exploit performed by one of our Northern Indians, when the Land Forest were before [Carthafence?}: The said Indian, hearing, with much importunity, declined of his commanding officer to fight the Spaniards in his own doing at [[?]] obtained Leowe, whom he separated himself, & went alone skulking among the bushes & shrubs for several days, & when he saw any of the scouts or spies of the enemy, then fire upon them & then retreat & hide; which  practice carried on 'till he had killed no less than 27 Spaniards: but at last being wounded by more a shifts to take to his health & return to his company: he for his bravery, went taken in pay on board one of the ships of men.
[?] Eng.wreck.Journal, 14 July, 1741.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
even lent him their common hut as a warehouse to some were his goods spread aboard, & notice given of the sale, then the Mifsonunis rushed in, & all [[?]] had been so credulous as to sow their powder, carried off a portion. The French man inveighed against such a procedure, with all the gestures of rage, & even made his complaint to the chief of the nation, who with a solemn account, [[?]], that gratification should be made, but that nothing could be done till the harvest of the powder; & that on the word of a sovereign, he would them order a general hunt, & every skin of beaver, deer, or other beast, should be delivered to him, as the first fruits of the important secret, for which they are indebted to his ingenious countrymen.
Boston Weekly News-le[?] 13 Dec. 1770.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
Weisers Special Embassy of 1745.
To The Five Nations.
Strenuous exertions were always made by both parties when a was expected soon to take place between the English + France, to secure the aid of the Indians bordering on them. Success was always in favor of the France, because they mixed more freely with the natives, + their settlements were in the midst of them; while the English settlements presented to them [before?] front, + that of vast extent. This front was constantly moving in land, + consequently crowding the Indians back, + nearly depriving them with all communication with the Sea, whence, before the English came, afforded them one great means of subsistence. It was vastly otherwise with those living far in land, with the French settlers in their midst, who never deprived them of their use of the great lakes, rivers + forests.
With these considerations in view it is not at all difficult to account for the ascendency of the [Gauls?] over the Indians far beyond any that the English settlers could claim. Hence when any event occurred which was likely to give the Indians cause to distrust the infalibility of their great ally, advantage of such event was at once seized upon by the English. One of these happened in the year 1745, which was the very important one, the taking of Louis [[?]]. So soon was this event known throughout the colonies, but an embassage was resolved upon. There were no competitors for the office, not [[?]] great importance. Conrad Weiser of Pennsylvaniastood out in as bold relief for such a mission, as did Washington

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
Washington afterwards as a leader of our [[?]].
What time Mr. Weiser set out on his embassy is not stated, + our account of it (probably communicated by Dr. Franklin) opens rather abruptly, + proceeds this:-
"Our Ambassador, Mr. Weiser, who went to the Court of the Five Nations, with a complaint of the robbing our traders in their territories by Peter Chartier under a French Commission, is returned; + tells me, their deputies immediately departed for Canada with orders to insist on Restitution, which he thinks they will do with more resolution, + the French more easily comply , after they have heard the news of the [Redestion?] of Louisbourg, which would probably [[?]] at Canada during their negotiations. He saysthat one of the Chiefs who is gone on that [[?]], asked him privately what was his opinion of the English attempts against that place, + whether he thought it possible they should succeed; + that he assured them the English would take it; adding, when you come to Montreal your father Onontio*(the governor) will tell you it is taken. No, said the Indian, if it is taken we never shall hear it from him. - But Weiser says, when their enemy returns it cannot be kept secret. - An Indian lately here among others to congratulate this government, said, the French used to tell them all the world could not take that place, but he believed his father, Onontio was now grown an old woman, + that his brethren the English were now grown up to be strong young men. - This you see, that one good consequence of the taking that place, will be the increase of the English + Diminution of the French reputation among the Indians.
Amer. Kagaz. ii, 372.
*Onnontio:- Lakoutan, original edition, i, 51.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
A notable instance of suffering Indians of many from the perfidy of the few.
In the year 1749, some of the [[?gewok]] Indians visited Miscapet, the chief town on the Sheepscot river, probably to exchange some of their wares for other articles. While here a quarrel arose before. These Indians & some white men, in which some of the latter killed one of the Indians. A treaty had recently been made by the Abenaquis & the white people, by which either party agreed that in case of difficulty, the party aggrieved was not to revenge the wrong, but it was to be adjusted in accordance with the aims of said treaty. The murder just mentioned was therefore a case for adjustment, & the government of Massachusetts (then [[?]] Maine) promptly proceeded to carry out its part of the agreement, by securing three men, the reputed, [[?]] [[?]] the real, murderers. They were to have been tried in a court in the county of York, but were rescued out of the hands of the officers by their ruffianly comrades. It appears, however, that in due time they were brought to trial, but the jury acquitted the principal, one Abbe. The government convinced that justice could not be obtained in that region, ordered the remainder of the accused to be tried in Middlesex; & in August [[?]], 13 Indians came to Boston to be present at the trial, that they might see for themselves & whether the while people could conform to the treaty. How the trial terminated does not appear; but it is clear

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
clear that there had been so much delay, that the Indians became satisfied that if there was ever to be any satisfaction for their murdered companion, they had got to take it in their own way.
It is said that the immediate friends of the murdered man could easily have been appeased by presents; but that the Aroosaguntacocks & Wawenocks belonging to the same tribe, living on the river St. Francis & under the immediate influence of the French Jesuits, determined to retaliate upon the white setters, & accordingly, (in September of 1750,) an army of 80 Indian warriors marched upon that region; & on about the 11th of September they attacked for Richmond, & on the 21st they took one prisoner at New Marblehead, now Windham, & stragling parties succeeded in carry away to the number of fourteen captives to Canada, after doing a vast amount of mischief in killing cattle, destroying crops & killing cattle. All of which was occasioned by the acts of a few villainous white men whose diabolical acts could not be punished owing to the obstruction of others, their aiders & abettors. Hence the retaliation upon a large number of innocent people, & an amount of suffering, which, could it have fallen upon those who were the occasion of it, would have counted little regret.
A circumstance happened during this invasion deserving of special notice. On the 20th of September the enemy appeared in the midst of the settlement at Georgetown, & beset a house

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
house within the hearing of a garrison on Parker's Island. The house seems to have been occupied by one man, or he happened to be alone in it when the attach was made. He defended his house as long as his could, but finally seeing the enemy were about to succeed in gaining an entrance, he leaped out of a back window near to the water, & seeing no other chance of escape but by swimming - with the Indians close upon him, he plunged in & swam for Arowsick Island. The enemy had the advantage of a canoe, & they pursued, soon expecting to be able to dispatch him in the river. But being an expert & nimble swimmer, & the desperaten[[?]] of his situation, instead of par[[?]]ing his exertions, inspered him with a courage which saved him. Turning suddenly upon his pursuers, seized & overturned the boat, thus putting his enemies on a level with himself; & while they were in a bewilderment by this sudden & unexpected plunge into the river, their intended victim reached the opposite shore & made good his escape; meantime the [immended?] Indians retuned to the little house belong to the poor man, gratified themselves by burning it to the ground.

title: Indian incidents, 1873-1875
transcription:
A hundred Indians burnt to death!
Such is the announcement in the papers of the 29th of October, 1869. How the fire occurred which caused this awful destruction of so many human beings, is not mentioned. It is mostly mentioned that the prairie was set on fire, but whether purposely or by accident is left to conjecture.
"A dispatch from Omaha, dated October 27th, [1869] says, that on the 22nd of September, a hand of the Sioux, under "Little Bear," was encamped on the south side of the Missouri river, above Fort Rice. They had encamped for the night, & had all gone to sleep. At about midnight the prairies contiguous to their lodges were set on fire, & before the alarm could be given or measures taken to save their lives, about one hundred were consumed. About seventy ponies were likewise burned."
Boston Morn. Journal, 29 Oct. 1869

LYONS (lettering is in a sketch of the cottage and its surroundings)

Let us have a Summer Cottage! was the closing cry of  the Winter Lesson 1898-99. The Cottage was secured at a moderate cost (at Lyons) along the Desplaines River The club ushered itself into the premises one Saturday eve. early in June, with a Summer night Festival and a grand Barbecue. The immediate surroundings of the cottage were illuminated with Japanese Lanterns, the delicious odor of Porterhouse Steak (broiled ad libitum over a bonfire) and favorite songs of the club filled the air from the cottage to the Desplaines River and back to the village of Lyons, far into the night. Lubrications of all kinds had not been forgotten. Thus the natives of Lyons made their first acquaintance of a crowd seen later in the season carrying back and forth canvasses from this its summer home. The cottage favored attraction, the absence of anything luxurious gave it a typical bohemian aspect. Its furniture consisted of nothing but paint stools, paint boxes, stretchers for canvasses, also a couple of stretchers whereupon one might rest with nothing to disturb the eye or mind; A few sketches tacked on the wall,  and a wonderful technique of brushwork on the ceiling, executed by a Lyons Artist when whitewashing the quarters for the club gave the place a charm of its own never to be forgotten. 1896

   When the Palette and chiselers began to straggle into the Polk Street depot one Saturday afternoon in the summer of '96, the depot copper told his mate that the grade of immigrants was improving, and he was glad to see it

   "Emigrants! --- what's the matter with you?" said the other man, pointing to C.A. Higgins, the assistant general passenger agent of the Santa Fe, who was shaking hands and cracking jokes with the new arrivals.

   "Well, -- they look like emigrants, anyhow, --" was the cop's retort pointing in his turn to Rawleys bundle of blankets and the new fangled combination of painting outfit and prairie schooner borne by March[?].  And even when Hunter showed up with only a light field equipment, consisting of a toothbrush and a small water color box, he refused to be convinced. To him they were still[?] immigrants.

    And such, in a certain way they are. Traveling from Chicago's flat and busy streets to Kelly's hostelry at Knappa -- and on, by various stages through woods and fields and studio[s] and dreams and disappointments and achievements to Paris or Parnassus -- or Pontiac -- who knows? 

   The conductor and passengers on the train were a trifle { } and relieved when "Knappa" was called, and the crowd began to gather up  their traps and steer for the platform. And Kelly had a trainload of sympathising hearts as he waited at the "depot'" with a wagon, and his little boy who wanted to see the "artists" arrive. Poor boy. It was his first experience with the breed and even now he is probably wondering what it all means.

   Without any unnecessary loss of time the table was filled and Mrs. Kelly had locked the doors

   The ones left outside stormed around for awhile, till the trees and sunset and fresh air worked their charm -- and then the wagon was unloaded and sketching traps came forth.

   In the course of this operation a few wise guys explored the clubhouse and began staking out their claims on the beds which Kelly had thoughtfully provided and soon everyone awoke to the necessity of a place to sleep. Finally all were located, and then a session was called on the old bridge spanning the canal. Pipes and cigars were lighted, and beer was discovered in sufficient quantities in the basement, and speedily transferred to the bridge. The moon came up and the gang sung the "Boarding House" -- and some of them didn't go to sleep till morning.

 -- Kelly's big gobbler was the first to awake. He cruised around the  clubhouse for awhile, then peeked through the window -- and recognizing an old friend, as he supposed, he hailed him with "Gobble vouble obble obble ouble -- Rowly!" But Rowly knew him not and would have returned to sleep if his friends had not asked home to rise and acknowledge his old pal. -- Then someone said "sunrise" and in an exceedingly short time the ambitious ones had hung themselves on fence posts and trees and were painting sunrises in their sleep.

   It was a hot day -- but they sketched through it. Part of the time it rained, -- but that never fazed them.  Those who were near the house simply flocked in and persuaded Miss Kelly to pose. Those who were near the bridge took refuge under it and painted rain -- and those who were near neither shelter -- painted away as if nothing had happened. Dave Hunter caught a turtle and brought it into the house where it was

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 1], 1895-1906
transcription:
1896

Executed with great pomp and ceremony.  Boehm burned all the skin off his shoulders by sitting in the sunlight with his undershirt hanging on a bush beside him. Others had more surprising adventures which they kept to themselves and all were ravenous when supper time was called. (There were no absent ones at lunch, Either) Then it rained some more -- and by and by Kelly dug up a lantern and the choir was dragged away from the piano where they had been singing "Maurine" [?] -- Everybody said goodbye to the Kelly's and the procession started through the mud to the station. There the California limited found them when it stopped on Mr. Higgins order -- and a little before midnight the Palette = and = Chiseler's filed out of the polk street depot and headed for their several homes.

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 1], 1895-1906
transcription:
DEVILS LAKE 
                     [red, green and blue watercolor illustration]

   Tradition tells that the trip to Devils Lake began one Friday evening about seven o'clock, when Sterba, Carr, Gandy, Irvine, Twing[?], Mazzanovich, Mulhaupt, Persson, Birren, Larson, Cresswell, Shiffen[or Shippen?], Swanson Jansse[?], Hutchinson, Hunter, Boehm and Loewenheim piled on a train at the Northwestern depot. Beyond the fact that the gang decorated themselves with oil colors and ingenuity, to represent indians hobos, scarecrow[s] and posters;  and in this guise scared the attendant and patrons of the lunch counter at Madison by flocking in with whoops and yells when the train stopped, -- no one seems to remember anything unusual till they found the hotel man waiting for them at midnight, at the station, at Devis Lake. Then their pipes went out and they went to sleep.  Saturday they all ate breakfast -- this is sure -- also dinner -- and supper. Some made sketch[s]    [long blank space]    rocks

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 1], 1895-1906
transcription:
1876

some carried bottles of beer along with their paint kits.  Some feared rattlesnakes and all made pictures.  And at night they told stories on the hotel lawn and presented the grand and comically pathetic opera "The Artists Model" in the dancing pavilion with the aid of the piano and a few corkscrews. And then  
   
   They all got up early Sunday morning. And again they sketched and ate and then at night they had more singing and some watermelons.  And Mazzanovich worked over the decoration of the hotel register till another fellow stole his girl. Rumor says it was Sterba but you can't prove it. Anyhow there were lanterns parading around entirely too promiscuously and everybody was glad when they marched in a body over the bridge a'la "carnival of Venice.  And more than a dozen fellows have promised to put a sketch of that same procession on th[?] page. Now you can [?] bet on which will d[?] -- Anyhow they all got up early next day an[d] were back in Chicag[o] by eleven a.m.

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 1], 1895-1906
transcription:
1896
                                           STARVED ROCK
   (Pencil illustration: figure with painting equipment, portrait)

   The trip to Starved Rock was done under the personal supervision of a guide, who fell in love with Maueh[?] at first sight, and refused to leave him for a minute. He not only told him all about the sights of the place but recited poetry to him of his own composition. The crowd left Chicago at 10:30 one Saturday morning in October -- '96 -- and got to Starved rock without mishap by 1:30 pm. Of course they had dinner the first thing. The day was bright and cheerful when the guide and Maueh started up the gulch, the rest of the party trailing along after them. -- Soon Maueh's eye lighted up as it took in the grand scenery and he stopped, opening his easel as he did so. -- "No -- no. Don't paint that. I will show you something a thousand times better. Come with me." Thus spoke the guide -- and Carl obediently shouldered his traps and moved on once more. They walked possibly a mile,

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 1], 1895-1906
transcription:
1896

passing several interesting subjects, then Maueh rebelled again, and settled himself to paint a delicious arrangement of trees and mountains that pleased him. But no -- the guide -- "Oh don't waste your time here. Come. I will show you something that will drive you crazy. Again Maueh yielded  --  another mile -- then he began to cuss. Then the guide recited poetry and Maueh remarked "donnerwetter" and a few observations in a similar vein. Then the guide said some more and Maueh burst forth. And the sky clouded up. And the lightning flashed and the rain came down -- and nobody knew, (but Maueh and the guide) what made it rain that day.

   But they all showed up at supper -- and the one solitary waiter told them while he was resting, between orders, the story of "starved rock" and "lovers leap" -- and Cresswell paid extra for another piece of pie.

   And then he went into the bowling alley and bowled up -- and the piano in the dancing room awoke and the musical members sang songs and the others had a mock trial. Nobody knew what the indictment was about but Bredtschneider was the

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 1], 1895-1906
transcription:
1896

prisoner and Magganovich defended him. Carr was prosecutor -- and Judge Mulhaupt sentenced the culprit to five years in the Washingtonian home. Then they all sang "Annie Laurie" and went to bed.

   On Sunday they worked hard and by 4 o'clock they were ready for the train. And at 8:30 they were all back in old Chicago, ready for work the next day.

IL JANITORE

(Pen & ink illustration of bold-lettered title, laurel leaves and a conductor at a podium)

   Grand Opera at 10.20.8:30. And their own opera too -- with music specially composed by their own special compositor[?] -- that is what the Palette and Chiselers dished up to a crowded house in the big lecture hall of the Atheneum building on the night of June 10th - 97. When we say that the cream of Chicagos artistic and literary circles composed the audience we tell the strict truth -- and it is a safe bet that no amateur performance given in Chicago, ever had a more cultured or select or appreciative audience.

   -- The special scenery was painted by L. Magganovich and E. H. Brotts[?] from thrilling pastel sketches by F. Holme[?] in the dead of night just before the performance. In fact at 6 o'clock of the day of the disturbance Brotts was still painting and when the spectators saw the scene shifters tacking the tremendous fire scene up at a quarter to nine they knew the show was really about to begin.

Other acts not rehearsed nor intended were introduced from time to time and the curtain made a few bad breaks on its own hooks. The opera, sung in a 24 foot ring was presented with the assistance of the following cast: 
   Mr. Tyler -   E. H. Brolls       Belle of the flat -  Swanson

   Il Janitor     C. Mauch           Giddy old Maid      Twing[?]

   In the great fire scene, while forming himself into a living picture Hunter collided with Nolf and a seltzer water bottle borne by the latter caromed on Hunters pale brow, producing an entirely new phrenological development together with that tired feeling. The messenger boy whom Mazzanovich rung for and then held prisoner while he wore his uniform in the Opera, came near losing his job through this performance. The fireman who foolishly loaned his helmet and overcoat to Nolf was run over by a truck next week and the only incident that promised a streak of good luck was spoiled by its incompleteness, when President Mulhaupt pretty nearly broke his neck while doing a funny fall with Henry Hutt. He was

title: Palette & Chisel Club scrapbook [vol. 1], 1895-1906
transcription:
1897
(Small illustrations of paint tubes at right and left of date)

too tough though and only fractured his collar bone. This gave him an excuse for laying on his back for 2 months while a beauteous young lady fanned him and the gang brought him flowers and the doctor figured out his bill. Of course Hutt didn't like the press notices but then, what could he expect?

    -- But the general impression among those who lived through the performance was that it was a success, and that its purpose - to get the artists and art lovers of the town on friendly and sociable terms with the club - had been achieved.

   At the close of the performance the members of the club met their guests in the club room and ice cream and cake was served. The walls were hung with pictures by members of the club. 

   -- And then they all went home.

Dear Mrs. Hecht.
Just a note to assure you that your opening night tickets have been taken care of - & a short report on "A Flag is Born" ala Chicago.

The opposition was taken by surprise & then took they weren't expecting the play quite so soon! Also they didn't know that we know how they planned to hurt us - that is thru Balaban & Kata - & that we got there first.  On my first

day in Chicago I got a contribution from one of the Balabans - & after being on record - they will have to either co-operate or do nothing.

Was determined to have $100 opening here as we did in N. York - & I'm terribly proud to be able to tell you the house is almost sold out.

Of course, everyone here loves Ben - I find that practically everyone I run into tells me stores about the good old Chicago days.  Dr. Preston Bradley told me quite a few last night - I asked one to send

My very best love to you & Ben - I can't thank you enough for your great work.

Love

Kay Norton

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
4/29/64
Dearest Rose:
You have been in my thoughts daily during the past few weeks but it is difficult to express in words one's true feelings. You, your dear daughter and all your dear ones have our deepest sympathy, as we well know what it is to experience the sudden loss of a dear one. While I had never had the pleasure of meeting your dear Ben he had written such a very friendly note to me about the Peony Painting that he made me feel that I had always known him. I was so flattered that he had taken time out to write this note as I realized what a very busy person he was. You as well as your dear Ben have brot much pleasure to many many people and it must be very consoling to you to know that you were so very helpful to your dear husband during his lifetime. W all are very proud of you, and sincerely hope and pray that you keep in good health and carry on your great work. Lydia is on a case and of course Olga is still in Florida. Sincerely trust your dear daughter keeps in good health & wish her continued success in her career. All good wishes & much love from each of us, as always
Bertha

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
Roma, Italia
August 25, 1967
Midnight
My Dear Rose,
I turn to you this evening, because for the very first time in 3 months I feel a bit blue, alone, ready to give up and come home--and so I need a good friend's words, advice and consolation. Perhaps I'll feel better tomorrow but at least for tonight I'll pretend that you're here with me and perhaps I'll arrive at some sound decision before the end of this letter. I received your cable in Calabria and waited until I arrived in Rome to send you my address-- Well, I really haven't got one to send you. Here's why-- my friend arrived from America and decided to spend a month in Naples with her relatives and then come to Rome around October. Because of my financial condition at present, I couldn't possibly afford the lovely duplex apartment for $140 per month -- so -- I came to Rome yesterday,

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
2

tired, weary and hungry and guess what--not a hotel room to be had other than 1st or 2nd class. So here I am paying $7.50 a day in a tiny, dingy room, surrounded by loads of noise (my "room" overlooks an alley and is right over the kitchen of the hotel restaurant) and after walking all over Rome today (walked for 9 continuous hours) was unable to come up with a single decent room with shower or bath for less than $16 a day. I was even willing to take a bathless room (bath is in the hallway) for $3 a day but oh, my, God ---- you should see what these rooms look like -- I'd be lucky to escape without contacting some sort of illness. To add to my discontent, I tried desperately to get in touch with both Haggiog & Guido (I figured if I started working & earning money, I could afford a better hotel) but

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
3

Guido isn't listed and the Haggiag address seems to belong to their studio which has since moved and they don't know where. The final straw came when I checked the convente, and even they are booked solid until October. So I sit here, staring at my remaining $100 in traveler's checks and wonder what to do next. Maybe I should come back to the States, work real hard & come to Rome next year (never, never, never again in Summer) -- but, then, I haven't heard from Len at all and I'm a bit worried because he had been severly ill several weeks ago (another friend wrote & told me) so I don't even have a job ready in the States! I know this sounds crazy, Rose, but it makes me feel good talking to you as though you were here because I'm sure you would say something that would make sense. Up to now, I've been defiant, determined and ok -- so happy.

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
4

And although I've been alone all this time, tonight for the first time, I'm beginning to feel it. My "independent" spirit is being threatened and I don't like it. I may very well head back fro Calabria and wait until mother sends me my ticket for my passage back home. Unless something unforeseen happens, I'm afraid this is it ---- for now! I still have hopes and I can always try to work something out from the States ---- at least, I've learned a great deal and I will know exactly how to handle the situation when I return. I'm so very sorry to send you such a depressing letter but it's been all so grand up to today -- I really haven't any cause to complain -- except that d--m it all, why should this city be any more expensive than New York -- someone should have told me! Ah, well -- at least I'm more than admired when I walk the streets here and certainly that doesn't always

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
5

happen in New York. Still, it's going to seem a bit strange for me to see New York again -- but I imagine that after being there 24 hours, I'll hate it again.
Well, Rose, I'm going to try to deliver your letter to Haggiag (if someone knows where VIa Mercadante is) (God bless these Italians--they never know more than they have to know) and then I'll head back to Calabria and back in the sun once more before returning. So if you have any kind words of advice (I'll even accept hard words from you) please send them to me at my uncle's address: 
Via G. De Nova 37
Reggio Calabria, Italia.
I've been so absorbed in my own little miseries, I haven't asked a thing about you. How are you and how have you been bearing the terrible heatwave? Anything new with Jenny? How is dear Harriette?

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
6

Please do write and let me have some news. I do so miss you -- most especially when I see something of real beauty (which is almost always here in Europe) and I automatically turn as though you were near me and want to say "isn't that gorgeous?" or "isn't she a beauty?" or something to that effect. What great "adventures" we'd have walking around this fabulous city -- and it is fabulous, Rose -- the kind of city one never wants to leave and always want to come back to (my, God, I've forgotten my English after all this time!)
I send you (along with my depression) much, much love and affection and am really looking forward to seeing you very soon. Please write when you can and if something

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
7

should happen to make me stay on in Rome, I'll write immediately & send my address. I'm at present at the Hotel Diana
Via Principe Amedeo 4
but I'm certainly checking out tomorrow (and I would do so even if I stay on). Just to insure my return to Rome, I throwing a few coins into the Fontana Di Trevis since it worked the last time I came to Rome.
Loads of love and let me know where Jenny is playing -- if she's anywhere near Calabria, I'll get to see her.
You "long distance" friend,
Lydia [Moses]
P.S. If you wouldn't mind, could you phone Len and express my concern over his illness and let me know how he's fairing? Many thanks.

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
Roma, Italia
Monday
August 28
Dear Rose,
What a difference a day (or 2) makes! After writing this letter to you, I took the bull by the horns, checked out of the hotel & found a lovely one right down the street. They didn't have a single ready for me so they put me into a lovely double for the price of a single. An additional bargain is that my window overlooks an open cinema and at night I see "free movies." To boot, I encountered (during one of my many hikes) a very nice, charming gentleman (he's probably around 40, or a bit older) who has volunteered his time to show me around Rome. I refused his first offer for dinner but upon getting to know him a little better (over a few cups of capucino) I've decided it's all quite "proper." He's really quite interesting, not at all the type I fall for -- he's nothing too much to look at, but very soft spoken, intelligent,

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
and thoughtful--I don't mean to imply that this is a romance, but at least I can spend a few enjoyable hours in the company of someone nice. So much for that! I finally traced Ever Haggiag (address:
Via Raimondi 8 - Tel: 864851
I called - he was out so I left a message & am waiting to hear from him. Robert is in (of all places) the U.S. As far as Guido Guidarini is concerned, he is not listed in the phone book, so I'll go directly to the address & try to find out what's happened. I'll come back with some report - never fear. You know what a good detective I am! So much for now --
My address is as above & hope to stay here until September 8 -- will try to accomplish everything in this time. My "depression" has disappeared (I told you that writing you would help) and I'm my old, defiant, "set the world on fire" self. Much love & do let me hear from you ----
Fondly,
Lydia

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979

October 4, 1967
Reggio Calabria

This came on 10th

My Darling Rose,
I started a letter to you when I was in Rome explaining my reasons for returning to the States, but decided it will keep until I see you. At the moment I am back in Calabria for a few days to say my goodbyes and then I'll return to Rome where I'll remain for another week before heading for Paris & home.
Yes, I finally received your letter at good old American Express (the only things they seem to "express" are their wisecracks) and oh, I'm so sorry to hear that Len is THAT type of individual. However, it's no different here and I'll explain why.  Haggiag (after that first wonderful meeting) never called me. I tried to reach him and left messages but no response. As for Signore Guidi, after speaking to his mother

transcription:
2

I know he's tied up with 5 films but I should think that the name "Hecht" merits at least a return call. But never mind Rose, I've still a lot faith left in people despite all of this and I'm going to call Haggiag again to get that info for you. 
I made another interesting contact however, and English writer by the name of Lawrence Wilkinson (he was a correspondent with General Patton in WWII, his son is an apprentice reporter for London Times so you can just about imagine what a lovely day I spent with them. He is currently

writing espionage novels and I found both he and his wife extremely helpful & interesting people They made up for the "bad guys." And best of all, they know just about everyone in the cinema world and I think they would be very helpful in the future.

Yes, Dear Rose, I'm exasperated with the Italian mode of "non-working."  It's all such a waste of time and I haven't too much time to waste now. So, I'll probably head for Rome Monday or Tuesday &

go directly to Cunard & try to settle this. If all else fails, I'll simply fly home and that's about the best idea I've had yet. However, I'll write again when my plans are more definite and give you any other news I may have re: Guidi or Haggiag. Woodmere, Long Island

[[In pencil: P]]

December 1, 1954
Dear Mr. Hecht:
The first fan letter I ever wrote was to F.D.R. when I was ten. This is my second, and I am now twenty-six. My father dictated the first one, explaining the value the great man's signature would have in years to come. Mary Le Hand answered my note and I was crushed.
This one I write of my own volition, not only for myself, but more for my husband who is probably your greatest unknown admirer.
We have read, reread and discussed just about everything you have written that we could find. Eddie has gone out of his way to see every picture you've ever scripted, and could probably, with a short rehearsal, take just about any part in "Twentieth Century," "The Front Page," et al. You have been dear to our hearts for many years. You've often mentioned your own fine qualities and abilities, so we can do little more

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
than agree with you wholeheartedly. 
But now to the point. During the past years, Eddie has countless times expressed the desire to meet you--just to spend perhaps ten minutes with you so that he could find out if you are really real, and so that he could have the great pleasure of telling you why such a  meeting is a great pleasure.
And further to the point, I would be most grateful to you if you could arrange for me to give him this very brief encounter as a Christmas gift this year.
I can also assure you of ten stimulating minutes of your own, because I think you may perhaps meet your image, though not yet fully grown (age 34).
I hope you will not think this ridiculous; that you will take it seriously, help me solve a gift problem, and most of all, make

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
Mrs. Edward M. Meyers
815 Jefferson Street
Woodmere, Long Island

an awfully clever young guy thrilled as hell.
If you say yes, name the date, time and place and we'll be there. If you say no, I'll finally be convinced that there is no Santa Claus.

Most sincerely,
Betty Meyers.

Marcus

January 23, 1962
Dear Mr. Hecht,
How can I thank you enough, not only for giving me your book, but for writing it.
I can't tell you how delighted I was when Lily brought me your book in the hospital. I started reading it, but I decided to wait until I stopped taking those damn pain pills, which made me more dopey than usual. 
Little did I know that afternoon when Lily and I visited you and you spoke of your

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
book coming out that Friday, what an impact it would have. Everyone is discussing it in quiet, shocked terms of awe. For once the loud Zionists have been quieted. Thank you --
Lily and I hope to spend the weekend with Helen in Nyack, and I'll drop over to thank you in person and tell you of our wedding plans (only so that you will keep the date open) --
My warmest regards to you, Mrs. Hecht, and Jenny --
Sincerely,
Jim Marcus

Dear Ben and Rose Hecht:
Blanch not, dear hearts, this fearsome screed portends (let's pray!) no such fanatic avalanche of verbiage as snowed you up from this frolic source last year. The annual report of the Hechtameron Society (Irish branch) shall be terse and jubilant. In brief, there is ceaseless dancing in the streets at the blithe resurrection of Twentieth Century, fandangoes in every faubourg at the discovery of Double Exposure (available here in the latest Ellery Queen anthology) and tarantellas in all town taverns at the thought that two new movies may contain shreds of the Master's dialogue... (The Marx Brothers' "Love Happy" and "Where The Sidewalk Ends" have only just been released in England, held up till now because of

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979
transcription:
the British Exhibitors' ban on you, the press here says—so this ban is apparently raised! The screen-play credit for "Sidewalk" is given to "Rex Connor," which is said to be a pseudonym of yours. Is this true?)
Those on this remote untropical isle who forever love you and your works would much like to have news of both. Ah, for a regular bulletin from headquarters instead of newspaper crumbs invariably a year out of date!
Peter Marron.
P.S. The Oxford Companion to American Literature—a monstrous reference book—is, surprisingly, quite good on you, but leaves me damnably panting to read The Scoundrel's namesake, Fantazius Mallare!

Dear Rose,
How difficult to put on paper (for someone like myself) what one feels inside. The past few weeks have not been quite so pleasant, as a free rolling, Irish peasant, like myself, is used to. Our conversation, via, telephone was such an uplift, to a soul so downcast. 
Its an odd thing, but I discovered in the past few weeks, that there are few people one can turn to, in a time of depression. 
To-day I did something I haven't done in years. While walking up Lankershim Blvd.,

title: Ben Hecht letters [07], 1914-1979

I spotted a church with open doors. I have no idea why, but I went in. The building was deserted, except for one very old man, polishing the floor. I sat in a pew at the rear and within a few minutes felt almost at ease, a feeling rare to me nowadays. After twenty minutes I exited, to cope with cross walks, cars, trucks and bill collectors. Somehow the World didn't hold so much terror for me. Within an hour I had received news of Ben's telegram, and hence our conversation. 
I'm sure I sound mushy now, but Rose, my conversation with you and Jenny, gave me such confidence and faith, that

Indeed I know it is somewhat late on my agenda--And  you must know it too--to be thinking about keeping the most important of my promises to Ben. I am now seventy-nine. Dear and favorite Editor Kogan: There was a sensational editorial in the N.Y. Times yesterday. William Safire (Nixon's mouthpiece if you remember--for who can follow "the times" or the new New York Times?) listed several lies that our "novelty" President had indulged himself in on the subject of Israel. He also warned President Carter wittily the the Mideast does not lend itself to quick study.
This is NOT the subject of my letter. But (I had already written two or three other pages, with leads further afield, almost all hesitant to begin) as you will understand when I name the subject:
Shakespeare. Also Ben's, and my, conviction after some 25 years [[in pencil: It became]] of making the Research our secret hobby, that Shakesp.  [[in margin: (I like to alternate the name, as if he were a character in one of his plays)]]was a Jew. This is not an attempt at that old banality of Jewish official leadership that this or that "prominent" artist, musician, financier, collector that everybody knows about was Jewish - in other words, an apology. Ben has done that too. How else embrace the hungry mob waiting two thousand  years for one word of praise amidst all the pain and pathos of the concerted attack of churches, literature and caricature against one word: "Jew." I'm thinking of the mob waiting outside the old Madison Square Garden in 1943 to see "We Will Never Die," and the equal number who did not go away after the arena was filled, but forced the marvellous "apology" to be performed again. 
And so with Moss Hart's lovely joke (I mean his staging) we heard the history of the Jews begin: "There was Moses!" And a tall Beauty, a girl, emerged, carrying a lighted candle. Aaron--another

My dear Ben,
Enclosed: 1) "The witch of Endor" (2/3 of the book and a synopsis of the remaining chapters)
2) "Yossel Rakover speaks to God" and 2 meditations on the story by two of Germany's leading contemporary writers. (That's the story which the late Thomas Mann hailed as "a shattering religious and human document.")
There is a story about the story "Yossel Rakover". I first published it in Yidish in an Argentine Jewish daily (In 1946). 8 years later, when I came on one of my visits to the USA, I found out that Yossel Rakover is being published and republished here (in Yidish) as an original document found in the Warsaw Ghetto. I have also learned that it was published as an original testament of a ghetto Jew in Germany and in France (The two meditations on the story by two German Autors were written when Y.R. was regarded still as a "document")
I found out soon how and who was responsible for presenting my story as a "document." but that is another story.
The translation of Y.R. into English (as well as the translations of the meditations) is mine, and, therefore, faulty.
