March 3, 1949
Gene Fowler
Dear Ben:
Have had three days in the Mojave Desert, a holiday which for me was a long one. Am at last out of the obstetrical stirrups, and am trying to rally a few business deals to keep Sheriff Biscailuz and his winking horse away from the premises.
I got to thinking about you, and found myself looking forward to your book. A Hecht book always is a special event in my life, and has nothing to do with my long admiration of the artist. Your virtuosity has been applauded these many years but I believe that the critics have overlooked one important thing in your successive works: that, slowly yet inexorably, there looms a fine and understanding heart, something that a great mind and a great talent kept in the shade because of intellectual stature. It is, and long has been,

title: Ben Hecht letters [04], 1914-1979
transcription:
2
my conviction, that you are just at the beginning of your career as a writer As you enter the "stretch" on your memoirs, I wish you as much peace of mind as Fate allows the artist. By some fiendish paradox, the backslapping comes at the wrong time. The lonely bastard sits at his writing-board with no encouraging word. After months of expensive pain, and when one has grown ill of seeing the mauled pages, the passengers of the Gravy Train clamber aboard with well-meant but ghastly flatteries. It is impolite to reply to them with a hoarse "Fuck you, Madams and Messieurs!"
My best regards to you and your household.
Gene

[1943?]

Dear Ben: 
Your letter was one of those things that would have saved the boys in the Alamo. I remember that you once said that an author gets to the point (isolated as he is in a hotel room) where he either is buoyed up or flattened out by the psychological interruption of a word. I am so glad that you at once "get" what I am trying to do.

I don't know whether or not Pat is really enthused over my strange, and, as you shrewdly put it, "untimely saga." If the book is what I hope it will be, I think that he eventually will clap hands over the fact that he has on his list one item that does not smell of hand grenades and leaking aortas on the field of battle.

I am wondering one of two things: is the book so bad that Pat can't bring himself to hurt the feelings of an old and doddering pal? And/or is Pat in some sort of spiritual or physical funk ("FUNK," not the other "FU")? I wish you would make a Sherlock Holmes-Havelock Ellis survey of my friend, and advise me as to his status.

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
2

He has been splendidly polite to me--always a bad literary sign--and I most certainly am trying not to let him down. In fact, I am sitting in a kind of sublime and industrious delirium, using my guts for a Morris chair, and my flickering heart for a footstool. I remind myself of Sir Walter Scott (without his talent of course) pushing his quill with fevered fingers, Carlyle with a bellyache, and Stevenson regurgitating his bronchial tubes. Don't worry. I am in there like Harry Greb. I shall complete the task, only, I'd like to find out if my publisher is in my corner, or has he been coffering his bets?

I sense that Pat is worried about the length. Well, you and I know that a work never is long. It may be dull, and thus earn the sobriquet of "long." 

If you see eye-to-eye with me as to the worth of the book, I wish you could convince Pat that length is not a handicap. He always used to have such a remarkable, pin-wheel enthusiasm over his authors. Has the fire gone

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
3)

out of his fuses? Is he, perhaps, caught in some pelvic trap? or am I kidding myself in believing that my present work is the best thing I have done? In the latter event, I shall be in one hell of a fix. I have thrown the dice on a great "fade." More than all else, I'd hate to think that I fell down on Jack. It's a kind of obsession with me, to give him a monument. Maybe I should have taken the hundred grand I've shoved aside, and spent it on a mausoleum. 

I am so glad that Rosie the Nonpareil is doing so well in the training camp. The main event will find her at top form, I am sure. Please tell her for me, an old fan, to take easy from now on, till the bell sounds. It is no disgrace to rest a bit.

I have made up a title that I like, and written a small verse from which it is taken. I shall not bother you with the verse. The title is: "THE STARLARK." 

With the best to all three (or four) of you.
Gene

P.S. The Baron is married now. Is in hock up to his navel. Has asthma, but keeps his spirit.

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979

[1949?]

Gene Fowler

Dear Ben:
Have just returned from San Francisco, where I stepped smack back to my foggy youth with the companionship of Tyrus Raymond Cobb, old Tom Sharkey, and numerous old timers of diamond and ring and of the press rooms of the land. There was a press club meeting which had all the grace notes of our hey day, together with the almost forgotten noises of reporters falling into spittoons, and the social attars of stale beer pools and oases of puke on battered chairs and tables. It was such a grand remnant of tradition, to be found only in the gallant town by the Golden Gate, and today I feel as if it had been an old man's reverie, and I look out on this dusty Hollywoodian terrain with a feeling of deep frustration and farting kismets. 

I have nothing to look forward to other than an appointment with Sam, tomorrow morning, when he will massage my bulbous prostate whilst speaking behind my back of Freud and the glandular deficiencies of Hitler. I feel as if I were entirely surrounded by Brooklyn.

While holding a journalistic-athletic salon at the St. Francis up north, I ran into a nice anecdote concerning Tom Sharkey. By the way, the old warrior volunteered a poem

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
2

when introduced at the Press Club--a grand, moth-eaten antique which stemmed from the rocking-horse-rhyme school of "The Kid's Last Fight." The fine old veteran of a hundred grisly, thumb-gouging, belly-ripping battles, attested in verse to the rewards which are always to be had "by fighting fair, lads." But the anecdote...

It seems that when old Tom was training for the first Jeffries fight, he frequented a saloon celebrated for its free lunch. He put such a dent in the lager buffet as to cause the proprietor some agony. Inasmuch as Tom was a noted figure among the fancy, and, to be sure, might one day be the champ, the oner of the saloon, not wishing to offend the great man, resorted to a ruse to discourage the sailor's Gargantuan tripes. He said to his bartender:

"Take away all this free lunch for a couple of days, Al. Then get some dog biscuit. And get the hardest God damned dog biscuit there is. If you can crack it with an axe, we don't want it. Get some real hard dog biscuit. Then let's see if this Sharkey son of a bitch can go on eating us out of house and home."

Th dog biscuit was laid out where the pickles, sausages, hams and other provender used to be. Sharkey arrived after the workout, saw the biscuits, sampled one, then proceeded to eat his way through the starchy concrete pile. The next day he did the same, presumably relishing every bite. This so dumbfounded the proprietor--whose trade was beginning to lessen among those who did not like dog biscuit--that he told the bartender:

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
3

"Al, it's no use, for God's sake! So clean up the crumbs, see, and put back the regular lunch, see. The son of a bitch Sharkey!"

On the third day Sharkey reappeared, looked at the assortment of meats and hams. Then, after searching the free lunch bar, called out rather sharply:
"Hey, you, where in hell's them tasties I been getting lately?"

Appreciated the news from the East. Remember me to Rose, and to the lads at "21."

[[McCarey?]] is not feeling so well. Confidentially, he is going to rest for a month or so. Meanwhile I am going to do a job, possibly "Kitty Foyle" and then come home to write a bit on my own.

I have survived the shock well enough. A sore back is about all that bothers me, although I also have a rib which hangs in space, like a bedslat after a pimp's visitation. 

With the best,
Gene

P.S. Have been stewed but once since I enjoyed that state at your house, and on this occasion ran into Leland, and insulted him for all of us. He says he feels quite hurt and claims I didn't know what I was doing at the time. 
G.

[[in pencil: Farbman]]

In times like this one feels more than ordinerily the responsibilities resting on shoulders of a newspaper correspondent stop The present conditions in Germany throw out in strong light the tragedy of a helpless and humiliated people who have fallen from the pedestal of arrogance and are now groping and crolling to find firm ground again stop It is particularly hard for a foreigner just arriving in Germany to penetrate deeply into the psychology of the people but this is especially so at a time when the political life of that people is, as in Germany today amorphous stop Judging from external evidence it would seem as if Germany had not undergone any revolutionary change stop The new regime has not yet superseded the old militarism in German life stop The writer is involuntarly reminded of his first impressions of Russia after the March revolution stop At that time the break between Tzarist and new Russia was complete and obvious even to the superficial observer stop The material wretchedness to which the the Russian people had been reduced by the war did not hinder the great spiritual revival stop All observers felt that whatever the faite of the revolution the old regime is gone for good stop It must be frankly admitted that the impressions I have so far received in Germany have fallen very short of those which still send a thrill through my hearth when I remember the early days of the Russian revolution

stop In recalling the words of Prince Max of Baden just before the armistice last october that Germany had lost the war but had gained a greater victory the victory over herself I have nevertheless forced to admit that this victory has to be won stop Germany used to be a wolf and would not believe that other nation were any different stop That was the substance of the German theory that might is right stop Then came a time when Germany showed signs of believing that there is something more than brute force and that there is such a thing as right and justice in the world stop The human conscious in fact began to awaken stop That was the German revolution and to let that belief develope to foster and encourage it was the obvious policy which interest as well as sympathy ought to have [[unclear]] to the Allies stop During the past six months there has been a continual collision between two Germanys stop The dark old Germany clinging to the rapatious instincts of the wolf laughing at and dispising Wilsons sense of justice and the new young Germany puting all its faith in a real reconcilliation of the peoples stop The Versaille peace terms have come like a tunderclap justifying the old Germany and paralysing the new stop The old Germany is now coming to its own again stop It is triumphantly throwing into the face of the idealists the frase we told you so--that is your

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
May 10, 1963

Dear Mrs. Hecht,
I guess it is quite wrong of me to leave New York without saying good bye to you--without thanking you for every one of the wonderful things you have done for me. But I think you would not have wanted to talk to me, do probably not want to read this letter. I cannot ignore this fighting thing that I do not understand. How does one play this kind of heart-break game? It must be too intellectual for me, maybe I am predominantly a country bumpkin, for I don't understand how I became such a repulsive person to you. Was it that I took too much from Jenny, from you? I did, I did and was wrong. I am sorry. Or is it something else? Is it Lionel Shepard that (I should say "who") caused your anger. Well, if it was him, I cannot be sorry. I did not want to fall in love with him, that was a sad piece of fate, but he is 5,000 miles away now, (and so is my heart) but young ladies of almost twenty are always told patronizingly that they will "get over it" and maybe the tellers are right. Anyway, now I feel like I'm a modern day Job, I have very little left, it has all been pulled, torn, shattered, Jenny, Lionel, New York, all has been taken from me, and I don't care how gauche it is, but I want

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
to know, as much as is possible, why? Why did I become so undeserving. Did I hurt Jenny, do you think? Oh, I never, ever meant to. Maybe I wanted to proselyte her sometimes, but I never meant to hurt her. In fact, I sometimes tried to save her from herself. That was, to me, a personal duty. And, when you, you Mrs. H, who can be a very best friend or most confusing foe (no, foe can't be a word to use, I wasn't fighting; I had nothing to fight) started hating  me I was so confused. Don't you see, it isn't the Plaza, or my story to Doubleday or any of the tangible things I valued half as highly as the, well, sort of warm understanding, rapport, I guess that we had. Maybe you will think this letter emotional, or ingratiating, but I'm trying to be clear and honest. Please don't be mad of my candor. Unlike Jenny, I don't believe things will return to what they were, I seem to have done something too dastardly for that, but I would like to know it, and if I am still so hate-able. And I want to say eighty-billion thank you-I'm sorrys at once and especially that I should have done something about the bathroom and, do do do love Jenny a lot and let her live and grow up with a little extra nod of, oh, encouragement from me. 

love
Carol

2 February 1977
Dear Rose,
Such pretty presents! Many thanks. I tried the lapus on Baby Rose (she likes to have pretty things put on her, especially necklaces, scarves and eyeglasses) and one of the beads broke off from the rest, so I'm having them restrung. It was such as tender and loving set of comments about my mother--I'm sure daddy's death is as wrenching for her as your Ben's was (and is) for you. She appears intent now on drinking herself to death (and who's to blame her?).
When I received an edited typescript yesterday from JAMA (they never send proofs), I thought o your gay funny story of going to all the eye doctors. I think JAMA prints silly things now. They are so establishment/doctor oriented--they've lost their inquisitiveness and panache (I'm sure they were different when you had dealings with them.) Now their English counterpart, Lancet, there's a fine charming old journal; all full of chatty letters from curious (and curious) physicians with a word or two to say to their colleagues. But I ramble. Did I say what a lovely doll's tutu?

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
I tried to think of which doll it would have been made for (too small for Gigi)--it could have been one of those Italian ones with the rooted hair and the porcelain face (remember them in that toy store in Laguna Beach?). I'm going to find mine next time I'm in LA and try on the tutu--I've put it away carefully; its seems like its sewn with memories, especially because of its dusky rose color. You know, I'm taking some ballet lessons now--they're so pretty and soothing See you in April.
Love
Carol [Fegte]
PS Don't you die!

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979

Dear Rose
We love your letters and read them over many times. Were you implying in the last one that you might possibly come visit us if we weren't moving? If so, you should plan it. title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
Jan. 21, 1975

Dear Rose,
Yes Anna's "Rose" is for you, as you have always been my fairy godmother. I thought I'd give her your name as a good charm. She's tough, tiny and lovely, and, even though she was born 3 months too soon, she fought her way out of all the parephenalia the doctors could think to trap her life in, and now she is quietly growing, day by day, until we will soon be able to bring her and her tenacity to the room waiting here for her (a room with, mind you, a blue ceiling with stars on it..., even if I am a copy cat.)

I hope your stomach is troubling you somewhat less. Mine, which was troubling me during my brief stay in NY, turned out to be baby Anna, after all--the only sort of stomache ache worth have.

Accept my daughter (or the middle of her), as a token of my love,

as ever,
Cassie

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
2/25/74

Dear Mrs. H,
You mustn't take my silence for anything more grand or meaningful than it is...I have been moving, setting up my tiny household (one roomful) and trying to cope with a new job. I spoke to my mother last week, and she said she'd had a good talk with you on the phone, and you'd wondered why I'd not called; well, actually, I had just received your letter that day in the forwarded mail, but most especially, I really despise the telephone, and only use it (1) at work and (2) in most dire circumstances. If you'd really like to speak to me on that abhorrent instrument, I have some numbers. In the daytime, I can be reached at 415+666-1241. After 5 I am (sometimes) at home at 415+566-8349.

You asked in your last letter (with the picture of how nice New York used to be), why I was coming up here. Well,

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
it's a bit sad and rather brave and intricate of me (or so my friends say), involving a lovely young architect who is in LA not feeling quite so peachy and rosy about me as I feel about him. (I didn't have the energy to take the insults waiting out on the porch for me). I s'pose at one point I get to be happy pretty soon, but not quite yet. About that crazy house I was in--it was cause of a man; it was 2 years ago now. I was quite desolate--he left me etc. The story, I blush to confess, is never any different or interesting, more interesting, even if you are different and interesting. More than "Dites Moi" do I remember "La Mer," and the whirr of the sea behind the whirr of the singer. You certainly gave us a most exquisite childtime. I have lately been thinking of a story you once told me (in Nyack) about you and Mr. H and some others spending a time in
./.

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
Dear Rose: 

I understand the "magic" you speak of in relation to Carol. Our meeting had it: unlikely, unexpected, but totally convincing. We went through a deja vu time--like entering a space in which we had always lived. Anna Rose, as a child of first-meeting magic, was with us 6 months after we first met (very fast and potent this magic) All the choices we have made in relation to her have been a manner of willing necessity. (and she is not so much a part of us as a spirit that has found access to this world through us.) We feel like we're right where we're supposed to be--brain-injured Anna and all. Days wear us out--doubt about the value of our existence don't. Perhaps I should tap this paper (in lieu of knocking on wood) at this point. I read somewhere that it is bad policy to let the world in on one's secrets--that one dissipates their energy that

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
way. I don't feel like that "world" applies to you. In some ways you are like a part of Carol that I haven't met. I hope that makes sense--the secret being safe because you shared it before I wrote it.

Thank you for your letter and your love to us.

Love,
Carol     [[in pencil: Fegte?]]

Dear Ben, (if I may),

By this time you will have received, from my secretary (Miss DiRienzo), all the pertinent information on our purchase of reprint rights to "The Sunset Kid." 

Is there anything more I can do? Please do not hesitate to let me know.

Dear Ben,
We have corrected our office records to show that Chambrun no longer represents you. I'm sorry we didn't know this before--it would have saved you some trouble. From now on we'll get in touch with you direct - often, I hope! (Did Brother Chambrun at least send you the money we paid him for you?)

About the story you'd like to write for EQMM: as you know, it's impossible to judge a theme before reading it. But perhaps the following will reassure you: I published anti-lynching stories long before the race issue became so "hot"; I published the first story about a Negro detective, with the character treated seriously, not à la Octavus Roy Cohen (I persuaded a young

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
2

Negro newspaperman to start the series); and I could list other examples, although in all honesty I must admit that so-called "controversial" themes have not appeared in EQMM as often in recent years as they used to. 

But even more important: I would be deeply interested in anything you would like to write for EQMM. At the risk of sounding gushy, I want you to know that I've been a tremendous admirer of your work for as long as I've been able to read; and we miss your stories in EQMM. (I had to get a special dispensation from the "Post" to reprint "The Sunset Kid.")

So I look forward to hearing from you. With best wishes to you and to your family for a healthy and happy new year -

Sincerely,
Fred Dannay 

29 Byron Lane
Larchmont, New York

9 November, 1970

Dear Mrs. Hecht,

When I returned to work this morning, the nicest thing that awaited me was your letter. 

How happy and relieved I was to have heard from you--It was so long since (17 September to be exact.)

You will never know how much you were on my mind, even on my honeymoon - I had such dreams about you, and so real. I even walked

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
II

by your building this morning - I said to myself "Dear God please let Mrs. Hecht be well and alright." 

Did the girl at the bank tell you that I was already away when Miss Thompson brought your letter? That's why I was unable to answer. 

I got married on the 17th of October, and returned to work this morning. 

Our honeymoon was beautiful. Sarah and I went to Jamaica, W.I. The weather was beautiful, as was everything else.

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979

So very happy to hear from you, and yo know that you are well. I'll be able to sleep

better now.

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
9 June, 1971

My Dear Mrs. Hecht,

I had to write to you because I saw you today and tried to catch up with you, but you just seemed to have disappeared. (Also it's an excuse to write you). 

As I was taken my usual after lunch walk, and walking up 67th Street from Central Park West, I saw you walking west. the light was against me, so I ran up 68th Street, across, and around to 67th & Broadway.--and I am a fast runner--But you were gone by the time I got there. I looked  up-down-across. I even went into the Post Office, but no sign of you--How disappointed I was, in not being able to say hello. But what really puzzles me is where did you disappear to?

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
II

I know that you are a fast walker, but you couldn't have walked that far away from me. You must tell me when we meet again. I was going to invite you for lunch or cocktails if I caught up with you. And there I was - so close to catching up to you.

Well even though I didn't catch up to you, you can't imagine how good it was to see you, even from the back. 

I am feeling better these days, as is Sarah. I've gained a few pounds. 

I was just reading some chapters in your Ben's A Child of the Century, and one particular chapter mentions your "Royal Tropicana." The name alone sounds delicious - if its not a secret recipe - maybe you can pass it on to Sarah.

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
III

Well Mrs. Hecht - you know I love writing to you [[and?]] you probably might even get angry at times - But I enjoy doing so (writing that is)

I bid you pleasant dreams and God watch over you always. Sarah sends her love to you.

As Always
Bob [ELLSON]

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979

My Dear Mrs. Hecht,

Have you ever thought of somebody so much, as I have all this week, that the person suddenly appears before you?

How good it was to see you today, even for that short minute or two. For when I see you, my day is complete. 

But I really feel so bad when you aren't yourself--How

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
II

I only wish there was some way to ease your heartache - I'd give part of me if I could make you happy again. 

I know and understand what you are going through - there are time when I am just sitting around, and saying how nice it would be if I could talk with my dear sweet friend, Mrs. Hecht.

And Mrs. Hecht, I want you to remember one important factor, and that is if you ever just feel like talking, or if an emergency ever

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:

pops up, don't ever hesitate to call me up either at work or home, no matter what time of day or night.

I look forward to hearing your Ben's anecdote about the wicked poet Baudelaire, and the true God.

I close now with many a prayer--

Do try and look after yourself, for there is still someone who cares very much about you.

Your Dear Friend,
Bob Ellson

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979

[In pencil:  Essen, Viola]

August 15, 1949

Greetings, Ben -

Many moons have passed-but I have often thought of you and yours-and wondered when our paths would intersect again-

My show closed three months ago - and - after winning the Donaldson Award - I am now sitting on the back of my lap - sweating it out - And - I mean literally - The temperature has been a pretty consistent 99° for what seems an unbearably long time - Christ! Isn’t there some one in Hollywood who can use a dame with dancing feet?

I’m in a bit of trouble with the government, Ben - Nothing serious - but - it seems my not ever having filed an income tax report has upset the big-shots and they want a complete report of wages earned and income tax withheld.

title: Ben Hecht letters [03], 1914-1979
transcription:
since 1943.  I have most of the data - but - I do not have a withholding statement on “Spectre” - It’s called Form W-2 - Is it possible, Ben, for you to get this important slip of paper for me from the Jenny Corp.?  I hate like hell bothering you about this - but - my goose’ll be cooked if I don’t come thru with the demanded information - I’m sorry and grateful for whatever inconvenience this request may cause you -

The latest on the in-human side is this - I’m estranged from my third marital “[underscored]encounter” and divorce proceedings will commence as soon as finances permit - Oh joy!

My little extention, Robin, is very well - as every other damned soul in New York - is suffering under this excruciating heat - As you’ve probably heard - we’re in the thick of a Polio epidemic - I’m desperately earnest when I say I’d give my right arm to get Robin to safety in California - Reconsidering - I don’t think I’d look so good playing a love scene with one arm - Seriously, Ben, if you should hear

title: Ben Hecht letters [02], 1914-1979
transcription:
[penciled notation] Eck, Nathan
P. [/penciled notation]

New York IX . 27. 1946

Dear Sir

Although I am not sure whether you will read this letter - since you'll notice at once that it it slon and written in a poor English - I think it is my duty to write it and send it to you.

I am one of the remnants of European Jewry who reached this country about a year ago.

Sir, you have put in the mouth of "David 'l" in "A flag is born" strong words of reproach against the Jews of the allied countries. As far as I know you are the first writer who dared so openly and in such an impressive manner to accuse them of the "sin of silence". Therefore I want to inform you of two facts which are characteristic instances of this "silence."

1) A couple of months ago I published three articles in 3 different Yiddish and Hebrew papers in New York demanding the appointment of a Jewish fact finding Commission whose task it would be to inquire into the behaviour and the reactions of the Jews of America, Great Britain etc. during the time the mass murdering of European Jewry was going on. This Commission should give the exact answer to the question:  What has been done or tried to be done by world Jewry in order to rescue at least a part of the victims?  If serious attempts have been made why didn't they succeed?

I did not make yet any proposal about how such

title: Ben Hecht letters [02], 1914-1979
transcription:
-2-

a Commission could be created, who should be its members and by whom they should be appointed. To my mind the practical steps to be taken are not difficult as they may appear in the first moment. But my first purpose was to initiate a public discussion of this matter.  We cannot afford to swallow silently the fact of the unique slaughter in world history and not even to endeavour some scrutiny of our souls " (Hesbon Hanefesh - in Hebrew).

We will never be able to perform any really great effort, a fighting or constructive one, if we will not have the courage and strength to investigate our own deeds and omissions, to repent and purify.  Neither will the world of gentiles take us seriously if we will continue to display such a weakness of character.

And last not least. It is high time to prove and to show, in an authoritative, impressive and irrefutable manner, to the whole world what was in fact the attitude of the allied governments in the 4 years of wholesale Jew slaughtering.  You can't demand directly an inquiry into their behaviour, but a Jewish fact finding Commission investigating the attitude of the Jews will implicitly unveil that of the "enlightened world" too.

After my 3 articles were published - purposely one after another in 3 different periodicals - there was - a "silence".  No word of approval or disapproval came from any writer, journalist, rabbi or politician.  The articles were widely noticed

title: Ben Hecht letters [02], 1914-1979
transcription:
3

and thoroughly read, I know it. But nobody dared to touch this "dangerous" topic. So weak, fearsome, dependant, rotten and spineless are, on the whole, the spiritual and political leaders of our generation.  I am deeply concerned that the non-Jewish world observes and understands this state of affairs and - draws its consequences.  The heroic performances of the Palestinian Jewry does not out weigh the weakness displayed by 10 millions of Jews the world over. -

Now the second fact:

2)  Among my innumerable experiences in Nazi occupied Europe there is one, which throws a flashlight upon the question mentioned above (attitude of Jews and non-Jews in the allied countries). It is like that single drop of water which indicates the content of the whole ocean.

In the year 1943, as I was still in Poland, 70% or more of the Jews there were already murdered.  The remaining Jews were expecting a miracle or - death.  One day, it was in March 1943, I received from Geneva a passport issued by the consul of Paraguay and a letter where he assured me that thanks to the efforts of my "relatives" I was granted the Paraguayan citizenship. At the same time many thousands of such passports (of Paraguay, Honduras etc.) were received in Poland. Most of the adressees

title: Ben Hecht letters [02], 1914-1979
transcription:
4

were no more alive.  2000 Jews managed to obtain passports and the Germans recognized those Jews as South American citizens, not destined to annihilation. They were transported to various camps as civil internees.  The bulk of them went to the famous Belsen, where a special section was established for "enemy civilians".  Some 250 Jews - and I was among them - were brought to a quite decent camp in Vittel, France.

In the beginning we were sure that world Jewry had found at last (late enough!) a way to rescue at least a couple of thousand of Jews whose names - for one reason or another - were known abroad.  was it so naïve to believe that world Jewry and our gentile friends had managed to obtain from various South American countries the citizenship for several thousands people doomed to death? We were only afraid the Germans might not recognize our new citizenship. But they did.

After a while it became clear that those passports were issued by the respective consuls without authorization of their governments. It was bad enough, but we were sure that the thing will be settled very soon.  who could doubt that our "friends"of the democratic countries will not legalize the passports ex post after failing to do it before hand?  And we waited.  Queer enough: the Germans waited too.  They intended to carry out some experiment with us, but after a couple

title: Ben Hecht letters [02], 1914-1979
transcription:
5

of months the Germans got tired and deported the Jewish passport-holders from Belsen to an annihilation camp in Poland.  no one of them is alive.

But we, the 250 passport holders of Vittel were luckier.  we were left untouched in Vittel for months and months. We had the right to communicate with our friends abroad.  We were sending alarming letters to America, England, Palestine - got answers! The Plight of the 250 Jews in Vittel was well known throughout the world... The Germans laughed and mocked at us:  "Where are your friends?"  They asked us.  (The "friends" meant by them were: Roosevelt, Baruch, Churchil etc...) "Why don't they send the piece of paper with the official recognition of your passports we are waiting for?"

The end was that the Germans deported us also to an annihilation camp in Poland. It was in Mai 1944, three weeks before D-Day. As our deportation train reached Paris I managed to escape. It was my 5th escape during the war. Four times I succeeded to rescue my wife and little daughter. This time I was not so lucky. I lost my wife. But taught not to complain, because I rescued my child; she is in Palestine. - The "piece of paper" we have waited for so anxiously came finally, as I heard the liberation, but it was after all of

title: Ben Hecht letters [02], 1914-1979
transcription:
6

our group - with the exception of some escapees - were dead. It came at the time, as the allied armies stood before Paris...

The deportation of our people from Vittel took place in a very dramatic manner.  There were suicides. 1500 Christian fellow internees witnessed the sad performance, many of them are probably now in this country.

Now, is not this episode like that drop of water which explains to you the whole ocean?
250 people were gathered in a well known place, supervised by the International Red Cross in Geneva and by 2 protecting consuls (the Spanish and the Surs); they bombarded the whole world with S.O.S. - letters; there was a clear and comparatively easy way to rescue them; their rescue wouldn't have constituted any technical difficulty because their number was small, neither any "dangerous" precedent since no more passport holders were alive; there was plenty of time, we spent more than a year in Vittel; the Germans were willing to let us live if the "peace of paper" had arrived. Nevertheless--

I tried to publish this story in the "Nation" and then in the "New Republic". I wrote it in Yiddish and it was translated. I was ready to publish it without a penny.  But they refused. It isn't because the story

Dear Sir, I will not express any definite request or proposal. I saw your "flag" and I heard your cry about the "silence".  I believe that if you will by chance read this letter till to the end, you'll certainly wish to react in some way and let me know about it.


Very truly yours

Dr. Nathan Eck

Thursl, Dec 30, 1943

Dear Ben Hecht,

I realize "you don't know me from Adam."  In fact as far as you know, I may be Adam. I'm writing this mass of scribblings in what might be a vain effort, but as an honest expression of a sincere and moving sentiment.

First let me introduce myself before my motives are impugned. I happen to be the commanding officer of a landing craft. We've taken part in 4 invasions in the Southwest Pacific. In our last engagement my little ship shot down 5 Jap planes with very minor damage to ourselves. I've been recommended for the Navy Cross for gallantry in action. Of what importance is this self-eulogy, you may ask.

Well, I've just completed your 1001 Afternoons in New York, which represented a composite of your journalistic meanderings for a given period.  You and I shore one heritage in common - being Jews. Our emotions and thoughts

title: Ben Hecht letters [02], 1914-1979
transcription:
3

can readily be relegated to the scrap heaps.
I ask for no favors from you as there's little materially I need.  I don't want you to misconstrue my "noble" intentions.

I was so impressed with the sincerity of your well-conceived thoughts which I profess to have you over frequently in my mind that I was prompted to annoy you with this thing.  My objective and here also includes elevating the average man's opinion of the well-meaning Jew. That's one dominant reason why I'm thankful that I've been able to convince a number of people that I'm one Jew who can face adversity and the intensity of many an enemy attack without begging for mercy. I take my Jewishness seriously when the need arises, even though I take no credit in being a race bearer.

Please answer this letter which reply will find another letter from me in the mails. 

Very much yours,

Ens. Andrew Edelstein

My dear Rose:

Congratulations. On the production of your play "LENTIL" - and such a good manager, Charles Lederer.  I hope it will be a hit-and it gives Jennie a good chance.  Work is the necessary thing for a young actor.  A Child of the Century is climbing up on the bestseller list.

I got my book back from Halligan, he wrote me Ben's inscription to him, flattering to me, I guess he'll pay more attention to me hereafter.

Love to Jenny, you and Ben, always.

I sincerely hope that you were not to angry with my efforts to get you to the station on time anyway we made it. When you receive this letter I shall be on my way to Italy, or perhaps be in Rome. My wife is very sweet in letting me go but she realizes that I hope to have my own car this year so that I may work for myself, so after three or four days at home I shall be off once again. I have changed the cheque you gave me and gave the money to my wife who wants to thank you and on behalf of my two daughters that through your generosity we were able to give them extra little things and save a few pounds they are really very grateful. And myself I can't find word's to escpress my feelings. On two occasions in my life a lump has come in my throat once when my little girl was ill and the other was at the railway station to see you off.  This was not for what you gave me I am saying this, but in the manner you cared for me.

Dear Ben.

I just a week or so ago received a copy of your book, "Child of a Century".   And with the aid of a dictionary I enjoyed it very much.  It really was most wonderfull reading, And if I , could of enjoyed it so much with the handicap of needing a dictionary to understand better certain words, and paragraphs of it, I can now well understand why it is a best seller.  And the reason for your reknown reputation.

As you have already probably recognized by being in my company, my complete lack of an education, you can - then understand my need for the dictionary.  This letter writing is also a comparativly new proposition with me, and I am also dependent on the dictionary for most of my spelling.  And at times I get to disgusted to even look for correct spelling of a word in the dictionary, as you will notice by my letter. 

All in all I want you to know that I enjoyed the book completely, even the part about me, Although I don't recall the exact incident about the five thousand, but you are probably correct about it, as I was in such a turmoil at  the time, and trying to get up some much needed cash at the time to defend myself with, really had me running around in a circle. You know our Government has a peculiar way of doing - business, first they tie you up, then they indict you, then -

your supposed to go hit your head against the wall for cash to defend yourself with. And go try to get cash at a time when your the hottest potatoe around, esspecially cash that had to be shown, as to the source to where it came from.  With all the heat that was around at the time with the element of people it was nescessary for me to go to for money, esspecially for money that I would have to show from who I got it from, you can well imagine the dilemma that I found myself in. But it was bad enough, I now find out that you didn't give it to me, but then you go tell the whole world about it. "I-AM-ONLY-KIDDING-BEN.

Now to get down to what I really started out to write you about. I understand that my brother Harry is going to meet with you. and racket element into the picture of his investigation of the F-H-A - You can take my word for it Ben, that until all of the stink started in the papers, and over the radio, I never even knew what the - letters F-H-A, stood for, or that any kind of an agency like - that existed. My Dear Ben,

I hope that this letter finds you Rose and Jennie in the very best of health and happiness. That book of yours - Gaily, gaily, not only brough much enjoyment to myself, but to every one else that I have let read it. The funniest thing about it, is that every time I allow some body there next with the book, they always say to me, how much time do they have or how many days can they take to read it. And then they never fail to return it the next day or so, with the comment that once they started into reading the book they couldn't let it go.  A couple of the guys told me that they stood up most of the night once they got into the book, and read by the glare of the light from the toilet, as the lights go out here at ten oclock.

"Boy", that guy who came up with that saying that truth is stranger than fiction, sure come up with a heck of a good saying, and Gaily, Gaily, sure proves the saying correct.

The more I think of it the harder I can kick myself in the rear end, for not staying with you and for not nudgging you more to get our book to an end.  I would of stayed out of here, and wouldn't of wound up a cripple for the rest of my life. But I guess thats the way the ball bounces, and what fate had in store for me.

In some of my letters to Champ Segal, I mentioned

They struck me so God darn funny thinking of what your kisser must of looked like during the happenings of the incidents you tell about in your book.  Its a wonder to me, that you haven't wrote more comedy in your days, as some of your storys as they were told in Gaily, Gaily, sure busted me and some others up pretty good.

how touched I was.

We had a little service in a room in the chapel here, about 380 people came.  The casket was covered with a blanket of vibrant green fern and below were little bunches of flowers, all in water; so that it looked like a bank with flowers growing beneath it.  The sprays and wreathes were around the walls. She would have hated any funeral atmosphere.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
Home.
June 6, 1869
Chicago U.S.A.
In the library.
Sunday. 
Europe is a dream, Miss Pelel's a myth, while hotels, bad eating, & sea sickness, are things of the past. I know that it won't last but a few months, nevertheless I am home, yes actually at home. Here I am in the old house, where I was born, & where I wish I could always live; it is the dearest place on earth to me & worth all London Paris & New York put together. Sister & Mother may talk & say what they like, still I shall persist in my opinion, that there is no place equal to Chicago & no place like home. It is very different coming home this time, to what our arrival has always been heretofor; very sad, & strange, but

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 2that is a subject I can not talk nor write about either. Our breakfast of pigeons, fried potatoes & corn-bread tasted deliciously, as did also my favorite dinner; roast-beef, asparagus, & strawberries. I was made happy this afternoon by a visit from Annie Tinkham -- mercy! wasn't I glad to see her? she has grown immensely & changed considerably; she is not pretty, but she is very nice looking & she has very pretty & lady-like manners. But dear me, she has grown so, and looks like a young lady. We talked and talked about everybody and everything; I brought her an amethyst ring like mine, with which she was most highly delighted. We inspected each other mutually and with curious eyes, she wears her hair straight down in curls, which I don't like.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 3Florence Arnold raced over to inquire how we were, and she has grown so that I thought it was Lou Phillips. This morning as I was looking out of the window, who should I see go by but Mrs. Dodge, accompanied by a tall and elegant young gent in light clothes, and a sky blue neck tie and to my utter amazement I recognized him as Johnny Dodge Esq. Nene says that he and Robby Dickey have been promenading the garden lately, and that both are extremely anxious for "Miss Julia's" arrival; the imps! Mrs. Dickey is very much interested, &hints about "the children" (Robby & I) having been brought up together; I should think so, when I have not seen her illustrious son for four years. Nene declares that Robby stays over till the 20th instead of going with his Mother on

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
Tuesday, entirely on my account; it seems he & Fay have been flirting pretty well. Nene has fixed the house beautifully, she has a new set of teeth and looks as handsome as possible. 
Thursday June 10th
Sister has been reading me a story she wrote when she was fourteen, it is too absurd. Fay Calhoun, Julia Rumsey Minnie Dunlap, Lulu Phillips, Lizzie Whitney, Minnie Whitney & Florence Arnold have all called. They have all grown tremendously. 
Sunday June 13
Hurrah! for Mrs. Higginson!!! she was down here on Wednesday & paid Mamma a visit. During the call Mother asked her, why when I was in so much trouble, she "my God-Mother had not written to me? Then it all came out! Mrs Hig declared that before we went away, Mamma had hinted (I was

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: then thirteen) that "it would be better if Dudley & I were not to see so much of each other," that it would not do, etc, etc. And Mrs. Hig like a motherly hen ruffled up her feathers & said that "of course" she could not write to me under such circumstances," etc. Mamma says she is so proud that she would rather have her son marry the poorest girl than "run after" a rich one! Mamma says she never thought or mentioned such a thing," she told Mrs Hig so, but Mrs Hig only persisted the more. She said that "it was very natural that Dudly should think a great deal of Julia, for he had always known her & heard her talked about at home, where they were all very fond her" etc etc. And Mamma told her that she had always thought her boys (she wisely called them boys) were some of the nicest in

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
town, and that they must continue to come here (that is Dudley) and that she should be very happy to see them. 
Continued June 18.
Nevertheless they must have talked to Dudley about it, for he has not been to see us at all. Annie Tinkham told him twice that I had arrived, and he only said "ah! indeed", evidently trying to play the indifferent. However the Friday after we arrived I took an evening walk, and on Dearborn Street who should I meet but Dudley and he was anything but indifferent then, he wheeled around directly and walked home with me. He is just exactly the same, I don't think he has changed a particle or grown a bit, in fact I don't think he is quite as good looking as he was. He has the sense to avoid both stovepipe hats and long tailed coats. He walked to the gate but would not come in (his Father was in the parlor) and it is fortunate he did

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: not, for Nene told me at the door that Johnny D was in the parlor. Sister told me not to go down and see him, but I finally convinced her that if I saw him that time, then the next time he called I could be "out". whereas if I did not, on his next visit I should be obliged to see him. So I brushed my hair and descended, image Johnny is now six feet high and a snip; however he really is not at all bad looking, his features are very delicate and his nose is especially good, when he has a moustache to cover his upper lip which advances to far, and if he gets tanned he will be very good looking if not handsome. I don't know what his natural abilities are, but anyway with such a horrid mother, he never can amount to much. He expects to go to Europe next Summer after graduating at the Law school

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: Sister acts as if I were eighteen she is so afraid of my seeing anyone. That she will never marry I am morally convinced, fifteen have already unclear in vain, and fifteen more would unclear with equal success. She is an old granny and rules this establishment with a rod of iron. Mamma is to be my guardian and when I am eighteen her office eases and I have entire control of my allowance for three years (or till I marry, if such an event should happen before I am twenty-one) and then of course I have my regular income. unclear and his Mamma sailed in the Ville de Paris on her return trip, it is perfectly splendid to have them out of the country, I should think that that perfect knight (grey haired and round shouldered) would begin to feel small; I wonder what he thinks about the "mesalliance" now. Sheffy in my opinion is stark mad, his actions are to say the

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: least eccentric. In a recent letter (Sister has refused him over and over and over again) he magnanimously proposes to settle his property on his daughters and devote his life to amusing and entertaining Sister, who he styles "an invalid" Sis nearly tore her hair she was so furious. In Paris he wrote Mamma that if we would only let him come and see us a little every day in Paris, he would never mention the word matrimony, and then he concludes the letter by saying that he can't write further for he has just cut off the top of his thumb. I have had a visit from Robby Dickey whom I do not fancy; (I have not seen him since he was here four years ago, and he behaved so at Mrs Howes) all the girls chime to the one everlasting tune Robby Dickey and I'm sick of it. He has very large features indeed, and a thick complexion, he is a very good boy I believe.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
II
This morning I received an invitation from Pumpkins to the h. at the Pt. If I was not in mourning I would give anything to go; I was told that he is now exceedingly fine-looking & has a most elegant figure. He does not graduate till next Summer, & if we go abroad, I may not see him for several, or perhaps a good many years; as it is I have not seen him since I was twelve. At any rate if he does not graduate pretty well, I'll have nothing to do with him, thats certain. I sent him this answer. 
following sentence contained within brackets "Miss J. Newberry returns her thanks to Mr____ with many regrets that she cannot accept his polite invitation to the h. at ____ this Summer." end brackets 
Mamma made me write it as formally as possible, Mamma is very wide awake & very much on the alert for such things, she is in fact much more quick sighted then Sister.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
June 30th
Wednesday
Yesterday the charming Mr Henderson Grant made his appearance, just from New York en route for Omaha. HE was most exquisitely put up. next word underlined They took him with next word underlined them to Telie D'Wolf's wedding yesterday at five P.M. The bride was pale as death & trembled excessively, the groom absurdly nervous & agitated, & the brides-maids seven in number (Mary Arnold, Telie's Cousin, Memie Rumsey, Mary Colts, Molly Clarkson, Mary Drummond, & Miss Rominson) all looked homely; they were the plainest brides-maids I ever saw. I thanked fortune I wasn't in Telie's place; her husband looked horribly old. Every-body was at the wedding; it was too funny to see the airs which the

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
girls put on as they cam in, & the affected way in which they sat down. Annie Beckwith in white musline & Grecian bend, & Annie Douglas looking as if she were forty. This afternoon Sister & I took Mr Grant up to Lincoln Park, we had a very jolly ride.
Saturday July 3, 1869
Lou Phillips came to see me the other evening, she looked pretty & intends going to Vassar College in the Fall, the Whitneys are going too. Fay is going to Farmington; there will be very few left at home of the girls next Winter. Mrs Hickey gave us our Sunday-school lesson at her house the day before she left. Fay in white alpaca & red trimmings, Mamie Sater? looking very pretty, Lou Phillips, Julia Rumsey with a chignon, Annie Kelly,

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: & Annie Beckwith all were there. Robby was of course the centre of attraction, but he disappointed me in not being especially sweet on Fay as I expected, which was strange when it was there last evening together before separating for some time; I mischevously gave him one of the tassels off the fringe of her dress for a keepsake, for which he doubtless was very grateful; (or ought to have been). He was next word underlined very snipish, & is about to enter Yale College, his mother of course thinks him perfection.   This afternoon I saw Amanda Shields driving out with a young gent. it seemed so funny to see one of the girls driving out like a young lady; she has grown quite pretty, indeed all the girls have improved, Fannie Sheldon among them.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: Mamma has decided to reject the Will and accept her dower; in accordance with a law (which though in existence for twenty years has never been used and had been entirely forgotten, and of which Papa was entirely ignorant,) she will probably have a life interest in one third of the real estate and uncontrolled possession of one third of the personal estate, which in our case amounts to over a million. The affair is to be refered to the supreme court in September. Sister does not like it at all, for she thinks it will not be doing as Papa would have wished for he did not know anything about the law, and if he had he would have made his will differently; his main idea and object was to keep the property so as it would go down undivided

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: to his grand children, and if Mama should choose to will away to somebody else the three or four hundred thousand dollars of which she will get possession, why then poor Papa's money for which he toiled so hard will be disposed of in a different way from that which he intended and it seems a sacrilige even to think of it. If Papa had only left us five hundred a year we would never have thought of saying a word, and when Mamma had ten thousand a year it does not seem as if she would have said or done anything. However she does not consider $10,000 sufficient for her support and so rejects the Will.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
16
Sunday
July 4, 1869.
There is nothing like constant occupation to keep people from feeling blase', the minute I cease doing something I feel disgusted with everything. What a curious thing life is anyway. We are born, then we live, then we die & are completely forgotten, it's true the evil that men do lives after them, & the good too I suppose. I don't know anything about my great-grand Mother & my great-grand children if I ever have any, will know equally little about me; it makes one feel what a mere atom one is in the Universe. Its a splendid thought for some men to be "immortalized"; a reputation that is only to last a few centuries doesn't amount to much, but to think of Napoleon for instance, or Shakespear who will be known as long as the

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
17
world exists, & to think of all the unborn millions who will know & admire them, & how in all the ages yet to come, their name & fame will be handed down from one generation to the other; while we poor ordinary mortals, in a few short years will be swallowed up in the great ocean of humanity which has lived, & died. A pleasant prospect truly; its fortunate that the grave is not the goal, & that dust thou art to dust returnest, was not spoken of the soul. If it was, there wouldn't be much good in living. I wonder if the knowledge that we acquire here will be useful to us in our future state? Certainly reading, writing, drawing, painting & playing on the piano won't do us any good, once there was a man who committed suicide because he was tired of buttoning & unbuttoning his clothes. I think it was quite natural, & rather a bright idea of his. - I can understand peoples taking poison, but I can't conceive anyone's being wretched enough to stick a knife into themselves. -

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
18 Sunday July 18th
Annie J. spent "the fourth" with me; we painted in the afternoon, & walked round with the girls in the evening. There were quite a number of fireworks, especially at the Niseous. Annie came over yesterday also stayed to tea & we had a splendid talk. We see each other nearly every day, & I have taken tea with her twice, since the Tinkhams moved into their new house. They have fixed & painted Uncle Mich's, & it looks very well indeed. The Tinkhams go East next week, it is too provoking; how however we expect to go to Richfield for the sulphur very soon, Sister is not at all well, & needs it very much. I am having a siege with my teeth, & I have to wear a horrid plate, but it is doing them good anyway.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
19
I have German three, & French twice a week; I hate German. The other night Annie Beckurth came after Annie & I with Hay, Lou & Minnie Whitney, to take a nocturnal ride on the Avenue. we went & it was very jolly. I had a long call from Dudley previous to his departure for the east. (he was going to Evanstone.) Pumpkins has studied so hard, that he has made himself sick, & is now with his Mother on leave of abscence. I had a dashing call from the Douglass's a few days since, in white dresses & black sashes. The other night all of us girls were on the Whitney's step. Annie, Beckwith, Douglas, & Tinkham, Lou. Nellie Parsons, Julia Rumsey, & Mary Hale, who is quite a young lady, & doesn't attend "childrens parties." Sisters & I drove to

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
20 Lincoln Park last Saturday, there was music, & it was very gay. We are going to add a new dining room, library, & bed room to the house, with a French roof, & a good deal more; I am so delighted.
Saturday July 24.
Annie Sister & I drove to the Park This afternoon, it was excessively hot, & everyone was there. I received a very nice letter from my Shadow, twenty pages long. I am to have a studio over my room in the new French roof, with a private staircase leading to it, & a sky-light; it will be delightful; & what would Mlle Gelet say to the enfant-gatee now. Every day I thank fortune my stay at Geneva is completed. We expect to get off in a week, & I am to go to Mip Haines this Winter, & so I shall not come back here till Christmas, & then the

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
21 
house will be done. Mr Builing was here fussing over the plan, for three hours tonight. Pumpkins is sick & with his Mother in leave of abcence; he studied too hard. Fannie Sheldon & the Sturger's called but I did not see them. - Uncle Nick sailed for Europe today.
Richfield Springs.
Thursday August 5 1869.
I have not written for an age, we have been so busy preparing to come here. Annie Tinkham left Chicago last week. The last evening about eight o'clock I went over to bid her good bye, & there of course were the Whitneys, Hay Calhoun, & Charlie Tinkham. We all sat out on the steps, & talked; then Charlie Tinkham went off, & Clarence Burleigh came. We all went in the Library, & then (botheration) came Pussy Jones & Louie McLagg. And they all stayed for ever, & Annie & I did not have a minutes' private conversation, & it was our last evening too.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 22. The house was in a dreadful way when we left, & nothing would have indured me to have stayed another week. The workmen had already torn down my piazza & Mothers' bed-room down stars, every carpet & all the books & furniture had been transfered to the bowling - alley, & billiard room. It was most dilapidated looking place when we drove off. Ernestine is to sleep in the dining room to her great horror, for she is in mortal fear of burglars, though Mr Burling has arranged with the police to have the place watched. The last night Mr Isham & Sammy Johnson called. Sammy & I took a moonlight stroll around the North side, Sammy was very confidential, not to say affectionate; he told me I knew more than half the grownup young ladies, which I thought was quite overpowering, for him. Mr Isham is our lawyer, & very nice every way, handsome too. We received them in a bare parlor, even the gas fixtures were gone, & we had to use candles.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription:
23. Sisters Birthday.
August 12.th 1869.
Richfield Springs.
This morning Mamma, Sister, Mr Dow & I drove to Cooperstown, where we remained all day & then drove home in the gloaming. We had a very good time; & had dinner at the Cooper House, & then we went to see Coopers grave, in a beautiful cemetary. Otsego lake is very lovely & only lacks the snow mountains to make it like a Swiss one._. We did not see the interesting Johnny Dodge but his Mamma was visible of course.
August 17, 1869.
Julia Douw is coming to spend a week with me. Mr Douw went to Albany on Saturday, carrying my invitation, & sent a telegraph to say he would return with Julia today. I am very to see if she has changed in the two years & a half that have elapsed since we were together in Florida. I wonder if she is pretty & as good & prim as ever. Yesterday Sister & I went fishing, & we caught ninety-four fish in all. Fifty four Shiners which we threw away.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 24) with quantities of sunfish & perch. Then we trolled, & caught two pickerel, that is Sister did, & I pulled one nearly into the boat, & then oh malheur it got away. We had a very good boatman who talked bad grammar pretty freely, - Coming back I headed the procession & walked into the hotel with this immense string of fish. Everybody stopped to exclaim & enquire where we had bought them. A lady & gentleman had sunburned themselves all day & had not caught a single fish. The first night I came here I was sitting alone in the parlor wishing I knew the nice looking girl at our table; when she came in the room, & sat down by her Mother. "There" said I, "she will stay there all the evening, & there is no chance of my knowing her for I would never dare to speak to her first." I had just settled it, when I saw the young-lady hop up, & come over to me. So we talked & were good friends directly.
