transcription: 231) told me that she is a martyr to neuralgia headaches of the most fearful kind, added to pains on her spine. - And yet she keeps up through it all though it has been going on for four years; besides which she had suffered fearfully from the trial of remedies which have done no good. She must be one of those wonderful people who can bear physical pain with a kind of Spartan firmness, & it is a faculty that I admire beyond anything else. Marie is very handsome, in a peculiar style. A classicaly shaped head, (always a great beauty,) around which her hair is arranged in a complicated but artistic manner. Large black eyes, & good but rather heavily moulded features; the outlines of her face, neck, arms, & bust are really splendid; & she looked more

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: (232 like an old picture of a French woman of the last century, than anything else. But it is alltogether rather a coarse "type", & she is too mature for a girl of seventeen. - Mrs Zborouska is a Southern woman by birth, with delicate features & black hair. A woman who can make herself immensely agreeable when she chooses, & yet who one feels is never quite sincere. A person such as you read of in novels, mysterious & irritating, & yet one that piques curiosity; but I am quite sure I never would trust her. Annie was the same as ever, if changed in anyway rather toned down & subdued. She has one of those characters which is entirely moulded by circumstances & the people she is thrown with - If she were to live with pious people she would be pious, & if she lived with fast people she would be fast.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: I cant understand such people they have no stamina whatever, + are as unfit to take care of themselves as so many babies. Minnie Clapp is just so; I could do anything with, or make anything of that girl that I choose. I went to the American church the first Sunday after we came, the service was half over when I heard a step in the aisle, + out of the corner of my eye, I saw the skeleton form of J. Hooker Hammersly, sink into a seat directly on a line with Sister. There he sat, singing psalms cheerily, as though the girl that had refused him were not within three feet of where he sat. So the world goes so the stream flows, + when the service was over we shooks hands as though nothing had ever happened. He blushed most tremendously when he spoke to Sister, + talked faster + louder than ever which was

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: the only sign of his embarrassment. Poor youth his Summer campaign has bee stale, flat, + unprofitable, how he must wish that he had never left his native land. Today we passed Stouty in a cab, grizzled + mounful as usual; + yesterday I saw Piquee doing the devoted, the pathetic, + the sentimental, in a salmon colored overcoat, to a young widow. It is not a little curious that four of Sister's + my departed lovers should be here at the same time, + successively promenade before our windows in the rue de la paix. We have so many romantic episodes, that I often prepare myself in the morning, for something that will surely turn up before night. I wonder if I shall ever settle down to quiet humdrum life in one place, + look back with regret on these days.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 235) October 11th.Yesterday morning Mamma & I drove to Pingat's, & ordered the last of my new series of gowns, after which we went up the rue de Rivoli. The street was crowded, & just at a crossing, within ten feet of us was Mr Little. He looked up & caught sight of me, looked down, & then I bowed & he took of his hat, I smiled & so did he in sprite of himself, & that is all the communication that has passed between us since he wrote that letter. I have seen him so constantly now for a whole year, that to see him is the most natural thing in the world, & not to speak to him the most unatural. Sister met Mrs Little the other day, they had quite a chat, & Sister says she was as amiable as ever. He must have mixed motives for staying away; & I am puzzled to know what he thinks about it himself.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: (236 Of course if he likes me well enough to wish to marry me, he must want to see me, & he can not be angry against me personally, for it was not I that talked to his Mother. I think he is to young in one way, & to unaccustomed to such things to understand why I acted as I did. When some other girl has first encouraged & then snubbed him, he will appreciate it. -October 13.I am perfectly bewildered with the rush of events, I dont know what to write or what to think. Half of Chicago is in ashes it is too awful to believe, to dreadful to think about. And the suspense is so fearful, the reports so vague & no one can get direct information. Mr McCagg & seven or eight other Chicago men are here, the fire began Sunday night, here it is Friday & we know nothing. I havn't a doubt the

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 237) stores on Kinzie street are gone, but I cant & wont imagine our house is burnt. But oh the misery of the people, & the destitution of the poor, the sick people & the little babies. And all the people who are just comfortably off, & have lost their all. The immediate destitution is bad enough but the wearing, saving, pinching years that will come to so many are worse. We may loose a very great deal, but Papa once said that if the entire city were to burn down, we should still have enough to live on. I am so thankful that he was saved the knowledge of this awful fire, & the destruction of the city he was so proud of, it would have embittered all the last days of his life. This state of suspense is perfectly dreadful: & I have begun to run down again, as fast as possible. My head is as heavy as lead, & I am so nervous & wretched that I dont know what to do.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: (238 Tuesday Oct 17.The fire began at twelfth street on Sunday night Oct . It swept the two magnificent avenues, & every building on the South side from twelveth street to the river. The Court House, with the original copy of Father's will & no one knows how many invaluable papers, legal documents, records, the beautiful Crosbie Opera house, a perfect bijoux of a theatre, all the banks, insurance offices, railway depots, churches, & block after block of stores, unequalled any where. And then oh misery, the fire, the red, angry, unrelenting fire, leapt across the river, & burnt & burnt, till Mr Mahlon Ogden's house was the only one left standing up to Lincoln Park. Yes the whole North Side is in ashes, literally in ashes, & every memory connected with my home is gone, every association, every link; never never to be again, irreparably & irrevocably gone. -

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 239) No one ever loved their home more than I did mine; I loved every angle in the house, every carpet, every table, every picture on the walls, every book in the library, the stairs, the basement, the garret. - When the house was rebuilt Papas' room was left untouched, & it was so exactly as it has always been, that his presence seemed to be there; it was sacred, & that is gone! And then by studio, my beautiful studio, & the private staircase & my room that I have looked forward to furnishing myself in pink & grey. Thursday October 19th.I shall go crazy if I write anymore about the fire; I have felt so bad that I have been in bed for several days & yesterday afternoon when Mamma & Sister came in, I was lying on the sofa, & feeling as bad as I have ever done since I was first taken sick. - My head felt as if it were filled with moulton lead, & it seemed to

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: (240me as if there was nothing left in the world to live for. I was so wretched that I could not determin how much of my wretchedness was caused by physical weakness, & how much by mental worry & distress. - There was to be a little dance at Annie Zborowska's in the evening to which I had been invited some time previously; we all know by experiance how much good a little excitement occasionally has done me, & so I decided to make a tremendous effort & go, as no matter what happened I could not feel much worse than I did already. - When "Auguste" had dressed my hair, & I was arrayed in a "Worth" gown, I could not help feeling more comfortable, & so away I went. It was a small affair, only a few girls, & about twenty men, but very jolly nevertheless. - Mrs Zborowska looked like a heathen godess, & the girls, particularly Annie, betrayed their seventeen years, by paying more attention

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 241 to their gentlemen guests, than to the ladies, when it was necessary to choose between them. - There was a Count Dornhoff introduced to me; I did not catch his name at first; & after a moment he laughed & said, "mais vous me prenez pour un Francais"! Je suis Allemand"! "Allemand mais pas Prussien? "Mais oui, Prussien de Berlin meme, je suis de la Legation." - I was so astonished that we both laughed, & laughed! It was so comical to find myself talking to an abhorred Prussian; I not only talked but danced half a dozen times with him, & he waltzed delightfully. - They got up an impromptu "Cotillon", & he led with Annie & kept asking me out all the time! My partner was a Monsieur Bixon, & genuine specimen of a Parisian exquiste; not my style of man at all, big; broadshouldered masculin, but a delicately made creature, with soft brown eyes, & brilliant white teeth under a moustache curled up at the ends. -

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: (242 He had that charming manner, which some men always have towards women, implying that for the moment you are the one person in the world in whom they are supremely interested, & a kind of chivalrous deference which is very taking. - But a regular Frenchman, false & fickle au fond, I am sure, & amusingly absurd. I told him it was my first cotillon, & so he took it for granted that I was a fresh fledged school-girl, though it puzzeled him all along as I could see, as my remarks did not savour particularly of the schoolroom. ----------------------------------------Not a thing was saved from our house not a thing; Mamma's picture, Sister's, my dear little brother Jimmy's, Jamie Clapps & my own painted when I was twelve years old, & which Papa was so proud of that he declared there was nothing in the world he would take for it; all were burned to ashes. - Then we have lost all our letters; those of my

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 243/ grand-father, great-grand-father & even further back, besides those of all my friends, & Sister has lost all of hers; but worse far far worse than all, I have not a morsel left of any of the letters Papa wrote to me; no not one; they were so precious that I did not dare to carry even a few around with me; I had them back to when I was a wee little girl six years old, & I used to write to him & he to me. I remember one, My dear Papa, There was an old man named Grundy, who wipped all his boys every Monday so all through the week, unable to speak, they only had rest on a Sunday. Your loving little July.Nice 1861 He took the most extraordinary pains during his long illness to write me the kindest & best letters that ever a Father wrote to his daughter & he kept mine as carefully as I did his; I had them all every one, & now? If I had put them in the safe it would have done no good either for it was burned with the Newberry block; the silver met the same fate in a bank on the South side, & some of it was very pretty.

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: (244. The tea pot from which Mama poured the tea, & the china service beautifully painted which we used on Christmas, the spoons we ate with, & the silver mugs we drank from all are gone. The library too with all Papa's favorite books, that beautiful library in which I expected to spend so many cozy evenings; all my drawings from the beginning & my first water-colors, my monogramme book, & oh misery all my journals that I have taken such pains to write & keep, a record all my ideas since I first began to have any! My twenty five dollies poor wretches each roasted in turn & all my inumerable presents & keepsakes, my beautiful pink bonbonniere with the rest! Mamma lost all her jewelry except her diamond earrings, her cachemere shawls, laces, dresses etc. Papa's letters to her; letters from Fenimore Cooper, President Van Buren, Washington Irving & Aaron Burr, (written to Grand Father Clapp,) & quantities of others besides. - But what is the use of trying to write about it, I have begun this over & over again & I never can go beyond the first few lines. -

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: 245/ [[image - house floor plan with rooms, etc noted] Back piazza, dining-room, green., Vestibule, Library, rack, Garden looking north on Erie St., Butler's pantry, stair case, hall 70 feet long, Middle room, buff, Blue parlor, bow window, Vestibule, Front parlor, pink, West on Rush St., front piazza, front steps. -]] plan of first story of our house. burned Oct 9. 1871. -

title: Julia Newberry diary, 1869-1871
transcription: \246 Who could have dreamed that when I drove away from the house on that beautiful June morning, 1870, that I saw it, & all my Chicago for the last time; if but one or two houses were burned, but they are all gone, all! It was such a glorious warm bright day, the trees were so green, the grass & the flowers; I had left it before so many times & yet I felt as badly as if it had been the first going away; They all laughed & told me not to waste any sentiment as I should be back in a year or two, & now, was my sentiment wasted? The house was so beautiful in itself, & it was home; & now I have no home anywhere; if I had always lived there it would not be so bad, but for years I have looked forward to going back there, & now I have nothing to look forward to. - Papa bought the land, Papa built the house, Papa planted the trees, Papa lived there, & now what is there left in the wide world of association with him? nothing, his picture his letters all are burnt away. Why is it so? The last seven months of his life are almost unknown to us, he died far away from us in mid ocean with no one to care for him when he needed it utterly, no one to learn his last wishes, no one to love him; & now with all that the few traces of him are swept away for ever.

title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940
transcription:
Helen Keller Jones
QUINCY, ILLINOIS
Mr. Sherwood Anderson
116 West 13th St..
New York City -
Dear Sir:-
The Round Table is the oldest literary club in Quincy.
For this year's study we have chosen a modern program.
We meet every Monday afternoon
One month we are to study the Modern Drama, one month Art, another Music, and in November we are to study the Modern Fiction writers - and my paper for the year comes in this month and is

title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940
transcription:
"Sherwood Anderson".
I find very little material on this subject in our library - only one of your books - "The Triump of the Egg".
I must have something more, so have come to you for help.
Am anxious to know if you have written an autobiography?
I read your "Tar" stories in the Woman's Home Companion. Have wondered if they are stories perhaps of your boy hood.
Would like so much to know some thing of your family life - am sure it would be of interest to our group of women - they will want more than a critics report.
May I ask where you get your inspiration for your stories - especially the title of your books? "The Triump of the Egg", puzzles me.
I would be most grateful for some suggestion as to where I may get some good material.
Thanking you in advance
I am sincerely
Helen Jones

title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940

On Native ground
PORT ARTHUR, TEXAS
Saturday Night
Mr. Anderson;
Since reading your grand novel "Kit Brandon", I have become extreme-ly interested in your life and your books. In my English classes we we-re told to select an American author and study their lives. I chose you because I thought your books and life would be very interesting!
Mr. Anderson, I wish you could write to me and tell me where I could locate some information on your life. I, myself am interested in creative writing and have written three short stories on which one receive a prize, the other received honorable mention. If you have a picture of yourself, you could send me I would really appreciate it.
Cordially
Mr. S. J. Guidry Jr.
945 Brazos Avenue
Port Arthur, Texas

Dec. 20, ’35

Dear Mr. Anderson —

It is doubtful if you will recall our meeting of a few weeks ago at the brief turmoil of Charles Stuben’s party for E. J. O’Brien. title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940

Solomon Juneau High School
6415 West Mount Vernon Avenue
Milwaukee, Wisconsin
November 2, 1938.
Mr. Sherwood Anderson
Trout Dale, Virginia
Dear Mr. Anderson:
I have read the story "Caught" which is taken from your book "A Story Teller's Story," and enjoyed it very much. Most of your stories written between 1916 and 1920 deal with America. The stories I am referring to are "Mid-American Chants" and "Winesburg Ohio." What caused you to change your type of writing? Where do you get your ideas? How did you get started in writing stories and poems? Did you ever do any newspaper work? I am interested

title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940
transcription:
in writing and would like to know if you thought working
on our school paper would aid me.
With National Book Week not far off, our English instructor thought it would be a good idea to write to some author of short-stories. Each pupil chose an author and I had the privilege of writing to you.
I would be very grateful to you if you did find time, and thought my letter worth answering. I can assure you it would make me very proud to know I had gained a little recognition from so famous an author.

title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940
transcription:
Both my English class and I will be patiently awaiting your answer.
Very truly yours
Patricia O'Brien

Mr. Sherwood Anderson

title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940
transcription:
11 Carroll Hall
Notre Dame, Ind.
November 20, 1939
Dear Sir:
I am a Junior here at the University of Notre Dame, and I am taking a course in the appreciation of the Short Story.  Our next assignment, due in approximately ten days, is one treating of a regionalistic author, an author who wrote about the territory from which we come.
I am a resident of Sidney, Ohio, which is about seventy miles west of Columbus and thus, I have selected your works as my subject. Your stories of northeastern Ohio fit in very well with the assignment.
Now I would like very much to include something a little different from the ordinary in my work which would add something to it. If you have had an interesting incident or two in your short story work, or what led you to write certain stories — childhood experiences, etc — anything like that, I will greatly appreciate. Something of this nature will appeal to any professor. I was pleased with every one of your stories I have read so far. That

title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940
transcription:
is one thing I have already gained from this present subject.
I know that you are very busy with your work. I am majoring in Journalism and someday, I hope to do newspaper work — and I want to thank you for taking the time to read this. Anything that you may send to me — no matter how small the item — will be greatly appreciated by me.
Thank you again for your trouble.
Sincerely yours,
John B. Aselage

title: Sherwood Anderson letters [02], 1920-1940
transcription:
Rural Retreat Va
Nov. 22, 1939
Mr. Sherwood Anderson
Marion
Virginia
Dear Mr. Anderson:—
My husband and I recently visited your country home Rip Shire. We were thoro-ly delighted with its natural beauty and the adaptation of the house to its surroundings.
We took some pictures and came back to read with new interest and insight your late articles in the "American" and "Reader's Digest".
We have been greatly interested in our own school library having worked to enlarge it and increase its circulation for some time. Especially are we interested in having worthwhile productions of the people of our own "Southwest" on its shelves. So I am writing to ask you what book or books of your own composition you think most worthwhile to place before American youth or on the shelves of a High School Library and should we secure one or more would you autograph them for us?
Thanking you
I am Very truly
(Mrs. Frank R) Virginia Umberger Brown

Young shot a buffelow on the bank but the river had been risen some and was falling we ware on a sand bank and did not know till we ware fast the seventh day after we landed here my Husband died the day following died his eldest sister we lay here two weaks after this before we got the boat off in which

transcription: time the river fell so that we though verry weak got the boat in to the river again, but by this time our provition was done all but one peck of flaxseed: which we parched, and beat to meal in a pot, and so made soope to save life. and accept, six dear skins, one bare skin, one buffellow skin, all in the hair: and one elk skin in the parchment; we had not anything to live on, for three weeks except when we saw anything on the shore that we could eat sutch as grass green[[?liveness]] berreys sunnylocust pods muskedines a fruit like to fox grass a wild kind of rough small peas and wild tongue grass which was the plentyest of any thing we could get and that was but seldom it this season so that what flesh I had left after two months sickness wore off faster than I ever view it to off one with sickness the fifth day that we lived the skins (which we burnend the hair off and then roasted it till we could grind it to powder betwen our teeth in the evening when we took up our lodging we had always to stop at night for fear of being hacked to peices on old logs and trees that lay in the river) the children all went up the bank to look for something to eat as was thair continuel practice thay all got up to the top but one of seven years old who came back to me who at that time was sitting in the boat with one of two years old in my lap and said he could not get up the bank I was then eating a peice of a roasted skin which I divideed with him he fretted I told him to go to bed and he should have some grass when the rest came down he did no and I did as I had promised but he continued uneasy

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription: and fretted all that nights the next morning he got out of bed to make his water and returned himself without help but mourned some for something to eat what we had ready was some of the elk skin cut into small peices and boiled over night but it was still exceeding tough this he strove to eat but thair was nothing that could quench his poor hart cutting to peices for the of the necesery supports of life (o that sutch things would teach us to make a wise improvement of gods free merceys) he continued striveing to eat until the sun was about an hour high and then he lost his Senses and lay quiet for about two hours and departed this life (my eldest Daughter) and his poor mother diged his grave in the sand on the bank and buried him then I returned into the boat expecting to see his sister ( a child about two years old) just departing also after I had been in some time I found some grains of coffe over a dozen them I parched and beat fine then boiled the powder in water and gave it to her to drink she revived immediately and was quit better all that day and the day following till after night and altho she was so near the gate of death she could stand alone and was sensible of sharp and cutting hunger the last day after night she would scream out as if some sharp thing stabbed her to the hart and continueed so untill about midnight then became silent with almost no motion except breathing till about sun rise and then she semed in an easy manner to leave this world which was a world of sore affliction and trouble to her the short time she had to live in it, my oldest daughter and myself burried her in the bank of the river the warm rays of the sun on the earth was verry helpful to us in diging her grave by drying

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription: the mud and causeing it to open almost wide anough to let her in between three and four feet deep. it may seem strange that thare was none to compassionate as so far as to doo the least peice of service to the dead bodeys of our departed relations but had to be cheifly and manely active in performing this business myself ny without any assistance except my oldest daughter thair was none in the boat with us of groan persons except myself and my brother's inlaw Jas. George the rest was all children and he was in sutch a way know not I dare not say what way that he would not so mutch as touch or come near the dead or the dying while it was possible to avoid it it is true he was unwell and weakly but withal he was able to go about and appearred to be the strongest person in the boat and although he was a good marksman and had been a tollerable good hunter yet sutch was his stupidity that he would not yuse the least endeavour to procure any thing that way nor would he let his own son go out to hunt and endeavred to dissuade my son from it all he could aledging it was not worth while not withstanding we frequently seen dears and bares on the shore as we past along. this brings me to the most dismal and deplorible part of my narative which as it in the publick and therefore cannot be canceled is as follows shortly after I had buried my youngest daugher already mentioned Jas. Young proposed to me that the children would be put in a lottery but himself and me should be left out for the safety of the rest if any should survive the danger of death which we ware in at that time for if we ware gibe thare would be none to take care of them. I told him that it was us that brought those inosent

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription:
Children to suffer and I thought if any was to die to save life that him or me was the propper objects of this dreadful [[?masseence?]] but I thought it was best to wait the divine disposel I then heared no more of this dreadful prosel for some days. one day as we past along we saw two bares on an island we landed to try if we could get them my son went out and his son went to the end of the boat to go but his father said so mutch against it that he drew back and not my son in a little returned without getting a chance the bares ware affrighted and ran off but before he returned Jas. Young said hunger was too hard to bare and thought it no sin to kill one to save the rest he then wrote down the names of the four youngest and the name of my sisterinlaws son which lived with him in tickets and put them in one hat and as many blanks save one on which he wrote death in annother then by his orders the tickets were drawn and given to me to read at the last out came his daughter mareys name and next came out death as soon as she heard that the lot fel on her she left the boat though scarce able to walk and she made her way along the shore she would cry out O! daddy will you kill me O! daddy will you kill me I sat Confounded and silent till now but could no longer forbair for I was persuaded that if he would stain our boat with the inosent blood of these dear creatures whose lives semed as dear to me as my own in a manner although his children that undoubtedly we would perrish and thare appeared nothing else to our short sight at that time I then intreated that he would spare her life till tomorrow
whoo

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription: knows but the lord will provide something for our relief I told him it was a trying time and it was us that brought them to this distressing circumstance as well as ourselves with this and the like persuasions I prevailed so far that he said thair is but little on her and that it was not worth while for all the time she would last just at this instant we heard two dogs bark a gun fire and some person speak to the dogs we called but none answered us then got afraid and put out on our way but the same day at evening the same person being an Indien who was out hunting with his wife and one child had killed a bare and when he had skinned it he put it into his canoe and followed us down the river and when he was come to us he gave us of the one quarter with the livers lights and hart and some dryed buffelow but the bare not being a year old and dryed meat we eat up at once and was not sufficiant for one meal we being fourteen in number the Indien however left us to hunt more the next day we over took him but he had not killed any thing save a cub not biger then a house cat which he gave us and we saw him no more we all lived on this three days then thare was a greater sense of hunger than thair was before the next morning after this small supply was done Jas. Young got up first and as he was siting by the fire the rest appearing to be asleep my eldest Daughter heard him say that  if it was not for dirtying the beadclothes that some of them should have the tommehock  this morning she told me what she heard as soon as I was a wake I heard it with-out

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription: Surprise but he who slumbers not nor sleeps had his watchful eye over us to see all that past and his gracious undeserved mercy was ever reddy to preserve both us and him from sutch horrid cruelteys. all hoo shall hear this greacious and wonderful deliverance remember to praise the lord for his gooness and for his works of wonder done unto the sons of men. the evening of the next day as we ware puting to land we aspied some Indians on the shore we thought was but death at any rate and so we made to them who gave us plenty of fresh bare meat and after night they came to us with more but then they took from us our clothes both bed and boddy clothes except what we had on two coverlets two blankets the bed I lay on and two sheets and a bed of Jas. Young and its covering thay also took some pewter knives and forks and every thing thay could find that sooted them and went off the next morning a little after the brake of day Capt. Barber met us who gave us one bushel of biscuit half a bushel of hommeny and two quarts of rice this was all he could spare for he said his georney was long but he told us thare was two famileys that was hunting on the river before us and if we would expeditious we would overtake them and thay would take us down for we had five hundred and fifty miles to the natchese and if we did not overtake them we would not get down and it was not in his power to spare us any more I then intreated that he would send

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription: one of his hans to help us or take us with him to Ohsark, which was eightteen miles up said river he he said he knew not how he could doo that for he was verry heavy but urged us to push on and we would soon overtake these famlyes we then left him but with heavy harts for by this time we knew to our sorrow what it was to be alone and it was fourteen days before we came up with families it was sixty leagues to the first settlement during this time we had plenty to eat but was many times like to be lost by the swiftness of the water which drove us on old logs and and trees that lay in the river and and through weakness was not able to avoid them at this time I was not able to turn my head on the pillow but as I did it with my hand through real weakness yet I could walk about when I was up we ware a surpriscing sight to all beholders and was thought by all that saw us that we could not possibly recover it was thirsday night which we thought to be the sabbeth that we came to these families the sabbeth following Jas. Young this cruel man as I cannot help calling him eat his dinner of bares meat and pumpkins stewed togather an hour as he became Speachless sensless and could not stir the the men laid him to bed whare he lay untill the wednesday morning following without motion except breathing and then departed one of the famlies took thir children in care and the other took me and mine I mite mention here that his youngest son a boy about five years old a few days after we received the supply from Capt. Barber occationed by the [[?water?]] comeing in about his head and was suffered to lay in it in this condition untill I chided his father for it and with deficulty

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription: I got him taken out but having no propper care taken of him he next day he died having been taken in to the care of these two families we all got down safe to the Natchese whare we lived eighteen months the people were verry kind to us thay let us want for nothing that was necessary for comforting and strengthning our frail bodeys we recovered contrary to all expectation though verry slow I was thare three months before the colour of blood appeared in my hands or feet nine months before the least sensible impression of either love or hatered was felt in my breast this was my doleful case but as my boddy recovered my sensibillaty returned also though verry slow so that when I came the length of reflexion to which I was alltogather lost though in body greatly recovered to think what I had brought the children to and what I was without any body to set agood example before these yonge ones knowing that example goes farther than I accept with the young and sometimes with the old too on conssideration of these things I often thought I could have left all society with mankind and mourned in the desert for my sins and the distressing situation thay ware in although thay thought them selves well enough but it pleased the lord to make me reflect that he requires nothing of us that is inconsistent with our duty as social creatures that he had left me some of the little ones to take care of with a charge to raise them for him and if I give up my self to sutch grief and trouble I would render my-self incapable of doing my duty these considerations often gave me some composure of mind with some hope that some time or other we would be deliverred from this place whare thare was nothing but a general correction of manners and brought to a gospel land but yet yet nothing appeared more improbible then this and even

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription: looked so like an impossibility for one so poor with a family too to get from this lace that when I made mention of it the people would laugh at my simplicity for having sutch a thought for thare was able farmers that could not get away and how was it possible for me that had nothing these things would sometime afflict me mutch but yet I thought that all things were possible with him who had done so much for unworthy me already and tharefore still entertained hopes of obtaining my wishes but however improbible it mite have appeared yet devine providence hoo doeth all things well brought about the mich desired event in a verry remarkable and unexpected manner, which is as follows in the month of Aprile in the year onethousand sevenhundred and eightytwo, having a strong desire of using some endeavour to bring about some means of releasment from this place I wrote a letter to my mother then liveing in the forks of Yough and was to have it at the landing early on a satturday morning to send it to her but through some embarisments I could not get from home untill tenn of the clock and therefore lost all hope of that oportunity but still I went to see if I could finde a chance of conveyance just as I came to the town that moment a boat landed from fort pitt I went along with the rest to hear the news as soon as I came to the place I found a friend an old acquaintance by the name of Thomas White he had heard of my destress and was making enquiry for me we ware soon made known to eatch other he asked me If I wanted back I told him it was my greatest desire he then went and consulted his pertners

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783
transcription: and came to me and said If the flower thay had would pay our passage and if could be thare the next day he would stay and doo what he could for us I immediately set of home but it was after night before I arrived thare the man of capt hous for was verry unwilling to let me go I beged that would take all I had but only let me and the children go he stood a long time but he who softens the hard hart made his to comply though on verry hard terms for I had to pay him forty six dollars and one fourth three months and three weekes boarding for my self and four children I alsa to the amount of fifty dollars which I could not sell or fetch a way the things I sold he stopt but would not take any thing. I had not time to dispute the time being so short and no time to wait I tharefore came away and left all when I came to ney Orleins which was some time in May thare ware no vessels at that place bound to Philedelphia save one and she was full so that I began to dispare of geting along but the merciful Lord opened the hart of the Capt. filled him with the bowels of tenderness and pitty so that he put two men on deck and gave us thair birth found us all necessary provision except some biscuit one bushel of rice and some shooger and all the reward he required for the whole passage was that my two eldest sons should wait on him in the cabbin which I could not deny in short I found him and the two mates contrary to my fears to bee as kind sivel and genteel as I could have wished we then preceaded to the Havanna whare we lay two weeks from thence we proceded on our way being often in danger of being taken by the English.

title: Anne Jamison memoir, 1783

transcription:
August 29, 1967
Sunday
Daily Report 
From the Desk of Lydia Amadeo
Roma
My Dear, Dear, Rose - 
It's a glorious day here in Roma - the sun is shining brightly and il Signore Hagging paid me a visit this A.M. Besides being devastatingly handsome, he was extremely charming, ready your letter & will try to get the info by next week.  After flashing my lovely "calling card" at him, we started some small conversation about opening up a branch office here in Rome for Len. He answered my questions and then proceeded to tell me that Robert (who is in New York at the moment but returning next week) is looking for an executive secretary & would I be interested.  I replied that I would be happy to meet with Robert to discuss it.  When I told him that Jenny had worked for them, he was both surprised & delighted - He asked how you were and

title: Ben Hecht letters [01], 1914-1979
transcription:
2
all in all spent a pleasant 1/2 hour together.  so you see Rose, not all of Ben's friends are wicked - at least, not his "real" friends.  I'm sure that the job offer came into his mind as he read your lovely letter introducing me.  So thank you so, Dear Rose because although we still have to discuss it, the offer was made because of his respect or you and this is indeed nice to know.
Am still going to track down Guido and will continue this missive as things happen. 
Sept. 5, 1967
My Dear Rose,
Oh, how fast & furiously things happen!  I received your cable and your much appreciated card (Pip & Flip) and may God really bless you for whatever money you may send me.  I cabled home for money but somehow Mother never received my telegram so it's a good thing I followed up my

title: Ben Hecht letters [01], 1914-1979
transcription:
3
cable with a letter and I now feel financially sound.  At least, I won't have to live like a pauper this week.  I won't spend a penny of your money unless I have to, but, oh Rose, how comforting it is to know that I have something - I can stand being frugal but it's frightening being broke.  Thank you so for your kindness and I will "watch my step" as you cabled.
Also, am having difficulty finding our friend Guido (by the way his name is Giuderino Guidi - called Federiz (Fellini's studio) & they told me he hasn't been there for some time.  He isn't listed in the phone book so I'll either go directly to his address or to Cinecitta where Fellini is now making a film & perhaps I'll find out where he is.  Many things have happened in this week that I'll tell you about when I see you (or if I stay here, I'll write a longer letter)

title: Ben Hecht letters [01], 1914-1979
transcription:
4
I met a man (don't get ideas, he's 45, married, etc.) who has become enraptured by my "charm" (he says) and who has turned out to be a real intellectual.  He has taken me out on the town, shown me Rome through the eyes of a Roman, is a magnificent guide who knows every little detail about every monument, street, fountain, etc. has taken me to Orvieto, a charming medieval town nearby; Lago de Bolseno - in fact, he's occupied my time most enjoyably - we discuss Shakespeare, Shaw, Contemporary Writers, Bach, Pop Art, Psychology, etc.  He is well versed and expresses definite opinions in all of the arts and the surprising thing is that he is a Physics & Math Professor (who are usually boring people). But he is an officer in the Italian Army (he still has his rank) was P.O.W. of the Germans, fought here in Italy as a Partisan - so you can just imagine how delighted I am with my new found Roman friend.

title: Ben Hecht letters [01], 1914-1979
transcription:
5
He thinks I am quite unusual - sends me beautiful flowers (just because I happened to have expressed my love for flowers) - and is also going to try to help me stay on in Rome. He has influential friends in the arts (Ballet, theatrical & symphony) but the lovely thing is this Rose - no strings attached - I don't have to "battle" with him and sense that he may be doing all of this for some ulterior motive because I made my position perfectly clear from the beginning - "friendship yes - but anything else then try the hundreds of other tourists in the city." He has accepted me as I am and this friendship has very deep meaning for me - my mind is being nourished every second I am with him - I know you understand the need for this - and to think that out of all the people in Rome, I came across an intellectual, by accident (or was it, indeed an accident?) All in all, I am so

title: Ben Hecht letters [01], 1914-1979
transcription:
6
delighted that I somehow feel everything is going to fall in place. I will keep you posted on everything and will let you know when I receive your money at dear, dear American Express (Ugh! what an outfit!) Please do let me know if Jenny will bey playing in Italy so that I can see her & I'll continue reporting to you as long as I am here.
Thank you for contacting Len, also & will be awaiting your report with baited breath.  I just love it so here, Rose, and dread to think of returning to New York only because of environment - here I feel really "at home" as though I belong among these people and all of this beauty.  In any event, you'll be hearing form me and thank you again for your concern &

1 
support (morally + financially) -
Much love to Hariette -
Regards to Len & Madame - 
Will write you again as things occur - 
Fondly,
Lydia
P.S. I promise to watch my step.
thanx

title: Ben Hecht letters [01], 1914-1979

January 9, 1970

My Dearest Rose - 
Because our Rome Pony Express functions like all Roman things, I rather doubt you received my last letter.  This is just a short note to let you know I received your thoughtful Chirstmas prezzy and thank you very much.  I just hope this letter gets through. Could you believe that a letter mailed from Rome and postmarked Dec. 12 was just received by me Jan. 7? And this is inter-city! Our mail is practically hopeless.  I'm just now receiving letters from N.Y. postmarked Dec. 10, 12 & 14.  Oh, well, who cares?  I love you - miss you - and please write when you can spare a moment.
Regards to Harriette - much love to you - Lydia [Amadeo]

March 17, 1941
Dear Ben Hecht,
I want too thank you for your splendid tribute to Sherwood. It was a masterpiece of understanding. What pity that he could not have seen it.
Embarking upon a new adventure would seem a perfect way for him to die, if only it weren't for the long trip home. They leave Panama the eighteenth and the burial will be at Marion, March 26. 
I almost subscribe to the belief that the spirit must restlessly flit about the Styx until the sacred rites have been performed.
Thank you again for the fine appreciation and its title.
Sincerely yours,
Cornelia Lane Anderson

Timothy Barnard's.
This gentleman lives on the right bank of Flint river 15 miles below Padjeeligan. He has 11 children by a [[?]]chee woman, and they are settled with & around him and have fine stocks of cattle in an excellent range. He has a valuable property but not productive; his farm is well fencend on both sides of the river, he has a peach orchard of fine fruit & some fine Nectarines, a garden well stored with vegetables & some grapevines presented to him by the Agent.

He is an assistant & interpreter & a man who has uniformly supported an honest character friendly to peace???? during the revolutionary war and to man.  He has 40 sheep some foals & stock of every description & keeps a very hospitable house.  He is not much acquainted with farming and receives light slowly on that subject as is the case with all the Indian country men without exception.

Goverment - 
The creeks never had till this year a national government & ever thing of a general tendency was left to the care & management of the public agents who heretofore used temporary expedients only & amongst the powerful & persuasive was the pressure of fear from without & presents.  The attempts in the course of the last & present year to establish a national council to meet annually to make general regulations for the welfare of the nation promises to succeed.  The law passed at the first meeting to punish thieves & mischief makers  has been carried into effect in a few instances

title: Andrew Pickens diary [2], 1802
transcription:
99
where the personal influence of the Agent for Indian affairs was greatly exerted.  On a trying occasion the chiefs were called upon to turn out the warriors & to punish the leaders of the bandittis who insulted the commissioners of Spain & the United States on the 17th Sept.  After this was repeatedly urged & the agent agreed to be responsible for all the consequences, the chiefs turned out the warriors & execute the law on the leader & a few of his associates in an exemplary manner.  While the transaction was fresh in the minds of the Indians, the Agent for Indian affairs convened the national council & made a report on the state of the nation to them, accompanied with his opinion of the plan indispensably necessary to carry the laws of the nation into effect.  The council after mature deliberation determined that the safety of the nation was at stake; that having a firm reliance on the justice of the President of the United States & friendly attention of his agent for Indian affairs they would adopt his plans.

Government of the Towns.
The towns seperately have a government and customs which they derive from a high source They have their public buildings as well for business as pleasure. Every town has a chief who presides over the whole, he is their Micco, called by the white people "King." The grades from him are regular & uniform throughout all the town In the description of the public buildings these grades will be explained -
The Publick Buildings
Choocothlucco/big house/the town house or public square consists of 4 square buildings of one story facing each other 40 by 10 feet 8 feet pitch, the entrance in at each corner. Each building is a wooden frame supported on posts set in the ground covered with slabs, open in front like a piazza, divided into 3 rooms, the back & ends clayed up to the plates. Each division is divided length ways into two seats the front 2 feet high extending back half way covered with reed mats or slabs then a rise of one foot & it extends back covered in like manner to the

The remaining pp. are the original and official account of the conferences between Genl Andrew Pickens Sr, Col. James Wilkinson and Col. Benj Hawkins (the commissioners of the Greeks) and the Chiefs in June 1802.
This [[?]] affords the earliest narrative known of the vuraus of GA., Tenn Tala, ante dating the date of publication of all the Eare Ridran Narratives and Boeder warfares - London 1809, Withers 1831, Goesaf 1826, Doddridge 1837, Bonne 1823, Smith 1799, Darnell 1812.

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
A sketch of the creek country in the years 1798 & 1799

The origin of the name creek is uncertain.  The tradition is that it was given by white people from the number of creeks & was [???] in the country. the Indian name is Muscogee.

The creeks came from the west. They have a tradition among them that there is in the fork of Red river, west of Mississippi two mounds of earth; that at this place the C[???}, C{???] of Chickasaws found themselves; that being distressed by wars with red-people the crossed the Missisippi directing their course eastwardly they cross to the falls of Tallapoosa{?} above  {?Lookauhatchi] settled below the falls of Chattahoche & spread down on the sea coast towards Charlestown. Here they first saw white people & from hence they have been compelled to retire back again to their former settlements  - 

+ g is always Land in creek - Muscogee a crrek, Muscogulgee the creeks - Chelokee a cherokee, chelocudgee the Cherokees.

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
The country lying between the Coosaw, Tallapoosa & Chattahoche about their falls is broken. The soil stiff with coarse gravel & in some places stone & the trees forest oak, white & black oaks, pine, hickory & chestnut, all of them small.  The whole well watered & the rivers & creeks have rocky beds clad in many places with m[??] greatly relished by cattle horses & deer & are margined with can or reed on narrow strips or cover with rich flats. On the coosall 60 miles above the junction with Tallapoosa there is Limestone & it is to be found in several places from thence up to [slow??] of its western branches.

The country above the falls of Amelgee & Flint rivers is less broken than the other rivers. These have their sources near each other on the left side of Chattohoche in the open flat land, the soil stiff, the trees forest of black oak, all small, the land is generally rich, well watered & lies well as a waving country for cultivation.  The growth of lumber oak, hickory & the short leaf pine, [???] line on the hill sides & in the hollows of a tall broad leaf rich grass on the richest land.  The whole a very desirable country.

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
Below the falls of these two rivers the land is broken & w[???]. The streams are, some of them, margined with Oakwoods & all of them with can or reed.  The upland of Ocmulgee pine forest. The swamp wide & rich with whole fine for stock. On its right bank below the old??? path there is some light pine barren with saw palmettos & wire grass.

Flint?? River?? has below its falls some rich swamp, for not more than twenty miles.  Its left bank is then poor with pine flats & ponds down water fifteen miles of its confluence with the Chattahochee.  These fifteen miles is waving with some good oak lands in small veins.  On its right bank there are several large creeks which rise out of the ridge dividing the waters of Flint & Chattahoochee; some of them margined with oakwoods & can & all the branches below the falls for seventy miles have reed, from thence down there is bay [galls??] of dwarf evergreens, cypress ponds with some live-oak.  Between these rivers there is some good ??? & black oak land strewed over with rock ore & the ridge dividing these waters has a vein of it extending itself in the direction of the ridge.  Within 25 miles of the confluence of the rivers the live oak

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
4
to be seen near all the ponds here are [limes??] [?] sinks the land here is good in being in the flats & on the margins of the rivers. The trees of every description small, the range a fine one for cattle.

That extensive body of lands between Flint Rover and Okefinscan[?], Alabamaha &the eastern boundary of the Creek claims is poor pine land with cypress ponds of bay galls.  The small streams are margined with dwarf evergreens.  The small streams are margined with dwarf evergreens.  The uplands have yellow pines with dwarf saw palmetto & wire grass.  The bluffs on the ??? are some part of them sandy pine barren; the remainder a compact, stiff, yellowish sand or clay with large swamps, the growth the loblolly bay [gums?] & small evergreen.  The whole of these swamps are bogs - in the rainy season which commences after midsummer, the ponds fill & then a great part of the country is covered with water; & in a dry season it is difficult to find water in any direction for many miles.

the lees [bees?] abound in the Okefinokaw & other swamps easterd of Flint river. The [???leberry] is to be found in the swamps & on the poorest of the land bordering on the Cypress ponds when the woods are not burned for a year or more.

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
the taller are on dwarf bushes grow large & in great abundance. The dwarf saw palmetto when the woods are not burned in like manner bear a cluster of berries on a single stem which are eaten by bear, deer, turkies & Indians. The berries are half an inch in diameter covered with black skin & have a hard seed; the are agreeable to taste, sweet accompanied with bitter & where full ripe the bush of the bees extract much honey from them.  The China briar is in the flat, rich, sandy margins of streams.  The Indians dig the roots pound them in a mortar & suspend them in a coarse cloth pour water on them and wash them.  The sediment which passes through with the water is left to subside; the water is then poured off & the sediment is baked into cakes or made into gruel sweetened with honey.  This briar is called Cooule & the bread made of it Coontetuca liga & is an important article of food among the hunters .  In the old beaver ponds in thick boggy places they have the bog potato (??uclauwau heaha) a small root used as food in years of scarcity.

the Okefinocau is the source of St. Mary's & little St. John's called by the Indians tau, wau, ne.  It is some

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
times called Ecunfinocau from Ecunnau earth & finocau quivering - the first is the most common among the crreks & it is from Ooha a choctaw word for water & finocau quivering this is a very extensive swamp & much of it is a bog; & so much so that a little m[???] will make the mud & water quiver to a great distance.  Hence the name is given.

Hoithlepoic Tushtunnugge Thlucco, an Indian who reside in it many years says that little St.John may be a???ded for in hte swamp that it is not practicable to go far up the St. Mary as it looses itself in the swamp. That there is one ridge on the West side of St. John & three on the East.  The growth pine live & white oak.  The solid good and the lakes abound in fish & alligators. On the ridge & in the swamps there were a great many bears, deer & [tygers???] He lived on the ridge west of St. Johns & was with his family very healthy.  Being unwilling to take part in the ware between the United States & Great Britain he moved there to be out of the way of it, was well pleased with his situation & should have continued to reside therein for the beasts of pray which destroyed his cattle & horses.  He could walk round the swamp in 5 days.

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
The land between the Chattahoche bordering on the southern boundary of the United States is better than that on the east side of the Fling River.  The Koenecuk rises between the Chattahoche & Alabama rivers & makes the bay Escambia at Pensacola.  Between Koenecuk & Cattahoche the land is broken or waving.  The ridge dividing their waters has high flats of light land well set with willows, leaved hickory & iron ore in places & all the streams have reed or can on their margins.

This country has the appearance of being a healthy one & a range fine for cattle, hogs & horses.  The pine flats have the wire grass & in some places the saw palmetto.  The soil of the waving land  is some of skiff & red, with stones on the ridges.  The fine land ??? generally & pretty good for corn.

Tallapoosa from its falls to its confluence with the Coosaw, about thirty miles, has some good flat lands.  The broken land terminates on its right bank and the good land spreads out on its left.  There are several fine creeks on this side which have their source in the ridge dividing these waters from Koenecuk. The land bordering on them is rich

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription: the timber large & cane abundant.  This good land extends to the Alabama & down it for 30 miles including the plains (Hequepulgee) There are 17 miles through going parallel to Alabama S.20.W.  They are waving hills & dale & appear divided into field.  In the fields, the grass is low no brush; the soil in places is a lead colour yellow underneath, within the abode of the ??? & very  stiffer (?) In the wooded parts the growth is generally post oak 7 very large without any under brush beautifully set in clumps.  Here the soil is a dark clay covered with long grass & weeds which indicate a rich soil.  One observation applies to all the fields, in the center the land is poorest, the grass the shortest & it rises gradually to the wooded margins where it is tall & the land apparently richer.  Four large creeks meander through the plains to Alabama.  They all have broad margins of stiff, level rich land well wooded & abounding with cane.  There is notwithstanding these creeks a scarcity of water in the dry season & all the creeks were dry in 1799 & not a spring of water to be found.

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
9
Alabama is margined with cane swamps & these in places by flats of good land or poor pine flats.  the swamp at the confluence of Towbig by & below the Mobile is low & subject to be overflowed every spring - above it is of great width intersected by lakes slashes[?] & crooked drains of much infected with musquetoes. The people who cultivate this swamp never attempt to fence it as the annual fr[??] in the spring rise from three to ten feet over it.  The land bordering on the swamp & for a mile back is a poor stiff clay the growth pine & underbrush, back of this broken line barren then cypress ponds & veins of reeds in the branches.  the range said to be a fine one for cattle.  The settlement of Taensau broders on the Mobile of Alabama 50 miles above its confluence with Tombig by the high broken grounds commence & extend for 60 or 70 miles upwards & abound in places with large fine tall cedar.

The land between Alabama & Koenecuk below the plains is broken or waving, the soil is stiff, very red in places & gravelly for 30 miles then stiff pine barren & Limestone a creek which enters

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
10
the Alabama has some good broken land with limestone, which gives name to the creek.  At its sources there is a fine body of land called the dogwoods.  The growth oak, chestnut, lind & dogwood.  This vein of land is nearly 20 miles in length & in breadth. The dog-woods are very thick set & some of them larger, ten inches diameter.  The whole finely watered.

Coosau has its source high up in the Cherokee country.  Elow wok & Oostenaulik are its main branches.  The land on the rivers is rich & abounds with limestone sixty miles above the confluence of Coosay with Talllapoosa there is a high waving limestone country settled by the Indians of Coosau, Augecooche, Mauche(?) & Eufawlauhatchen.  The settlements are generally on rich flats of oak, hickory, poplar, walnut & mulberry.  The springs are fine, cane on the creeks & reed on the branches.  The surrounding country broken & gravelly.  The land fit for culture is generally the margins of the creeks or the waiving slopes from the high broken land.

Throughout the whole of this country there is but little fruit of any kind; in some of

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
11

the rich flats there are fox-grapes & musquedines; the smaller cluster grapes of the hills are destroyed by fire & the persimmons, h?? of chestnut by the hatchet; a few blackberries in the old fields, red haws on the poor sand hills & strawberries thinly scattered; but not a gooseberry, raspberry or currant in the land.

The traveller in passing through a country as extensive & wild as this & so much in the ???? of nature expects to see game in abundance.  The whole of the Creek claims, the Simenoles inclusive, dover three hundred miles square; & if it is difficult for a good hunt in passing through it in any direction to offer enough for his support.

A description of the towns on Coosau & Tallapoosa generally called the Upper Creeks.

Telesee from Talafau a town & esee a ??? situated in the fork of Eufaubo on the left bank of the Tallapoosa opposite Lookaubatchean Eufaube has its source in the ridge dividing the

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
15
waters of Chattahoche from those of Tallapoosa & runs nearly w. to the junction with the river.  There it is sixty feet wide.  The land on it is poor for some miles up, then rich flats bordered with pine land, with reedy branches, a fine range for cattle & horses.

The Indians have mostly left the town & settled up the creek, or on its waters for 20 miles up.  The settlements are some of them well chosen & fenced with worn fences.  The land bordering on the streams of the right side of the creek is better than that of the left & here the settlements are mostly made.  12 miles up the creek from its mouth it forks.  The large fork of the left side has some rich, flat swamp, large white oak, poplar ash & white pine.  The trading path from Cussetuk to the upper Creeks crosses this fork twice.  Here it is called big swamp (opelsslucco).  The waving land to its source is stiff, post oak, pine & hard shelled hickory.

The Indians who have settled out on the branches & margins of the creek have several of the cattle hogs & horses & begin to be attentive to them.  The head warrior of the town Peter McQueen

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:

a half breed is a shug??? trader, has a valuable property with negroes & stock & begins to know their value.

These Indians were very friendly to the United 
States during the revolutionary war and their old chief Hoboissic Micco of the half way house improperly called the Talkse King / could not be prevailed on by any offers from the agents of Great Britain to take part with them. On the return of peace & the establishment of friendly arrangements between the Indians and the Citizens of the United States, this chief felt himself neglected by Mr. Seagrove, which he resenting he robed?  & ??? that gentleman, compelled him to leave his house hear Tookaubatche & fly into a swamp.  He has sence thenas from a spirit of contradiction formed a party in opposition to the will of the nation which has given muchtroubles & difficult to the chiefs of the land.  His principal assistants were the leaders of the bandetti who instilled the commissioners of Spain & the United States on the 17th Sept 1799 at the confluence of Flint & Chattahochi.  The example

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:

ry punishment inflicted upon them by the chiefs of the nation has effectually checked their mischief-making & silenced them.  And this chief has had a solemn warning from the national council to respect the laws of the nation or he should meet the punishment ordained by the Law.  He is one of the Great medal chiefs.

This spirit of party or opposition prevails not only here, but more or less in every town in the nation.  The plainest proposition for ameliorating their condition is immediately opposed, &  opposition continues as long as there is hope to obtain presents, the infallible mode heretofore in use to gain a point.

2nd Tookauhatche, the ancient name of their town is Ispocodee, the derivation uncertain, it is situated on the right bank of Tallapoosa opposite the junction of eufaube 2 1/2 miles below the falls of the river on a beautiful level.  The course of the river from the falls to the town is S. it then turns E 3/4 of  a mile & short round a point opposite Eufabe thence. W& W by S to its confluence with Coosau about 30 miles.

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
18
It is 100 yards wide opposite the town route to the S and here are two good fords during the summer.  One just below the point of a small island the other 100 yards still lower.

The falls after tumbling over a bed of rock for half a mile the water is forced into two channels, one 30 the other 15 feet wide.  They fall 50 feet in 50 yards.  The channel on the right side which is the widest falls nearly 20 feet in 10 feet.  The fish are here obstructed in their attempts to ascend the river. From appearances they might be easily taken in the season of their ascending the rivers; but no attempts have hitherto been made to do so. 

The rock is a light gray very much divided in square blocks of various sizes for building.  It requires very little labor to reduce it to forms for square walls.  Large masses of it are so nicely fitted & so regular as to imitate the wall of an ancient building where the stones had shaped through the hands of a mason.  The quantity of this description at the falls & in the hill sides adjoining is great, sufficient for building a large city.

title: Andrew Pickens diary [1], 1802
transcription:
19
The falls above spread out & the river widens to half a mile within that distance & continues that width for four miles.  within this scope are four islands which were formerly cultivated, but are now old fields margined with cane.  The bed of the river is here rocky, shoally & covered with moss.  It is frequented in summer by cattles, horses and deer & in the winter by swans geese & ducks.

On the right bank opposite the falls the land is broken stoney & gravely.  The hill sides fronting the river exhibit this quarry of building rock  The timber post oak, hickory & pine, all small.  From the hills the land spreads off level.  The narrow flat margin between the hills & the river convenient for a canal for mills on an extensive scale & to supply a large extent of flat land around the tow with water.  Below the falls a small distance there is a spring & branch & within 500 a small creek. Britheren
It gives me great pleasure to see so many of the Six Nations met together with your Allies, & I give you all a most hearty welcome to this place where our Fire Burns.
You have at this time a strong Proof of the Friendship which his Excell.y M.r Shirley, Gov.r of the Massachusetts Bay has for you by his coming in Person to this Interview, of which you will be fully assured for his Excell.ys own Mouth having Travelled by Land in such time of Danger under many Difficulties in the way, least you should wait too long here for him, if he had taken the easiest Way by Water. A string of Wampum
Britheren:
I Informed the King your father with what Zeal you Joined his Subjects here in the War against the French and their Allies in Canada where his Maj.y has sent me a Considerable Present to give you as a Token of being well pleased with your Conduct on that Occasion, And of the Confidence he still places in your fidelity & Zeal for his Service. A Small Belt

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(3)
Britheren:
I am very glad of this Opportunity to brighten & Strengthen that Covenant Chain, by which our Forefathers Linked us strongly together, & which has ever since continued firm & lasting to this Day, notwithstanding the many unwearied Attempts of our Malicious & cunning Enemys to break it; And I hope that neither the Rust of time nor their Policy  can prevent it's remaining strong & firm as long as the Sun & Moon shall Endure; our Mutual Strength & Security highly depends thereon, agreeable to the repeated Declaratoins of our Forefathers & while you remain strongly united with you Britheren the English (who have always been you steadfast friend.) you can have no reason to fear any thing the french dare to Attempt, unless they can Prevail upon you to trust to any of their Deceitful Promises, which I expect & insist upon you will not listen to. A Belt
Britheren:
I must Inform you of one thing, which I expect our Enemys the french may Endeavour to Accomplish as soon as you return home, because they have of late Attempted it, that it, to draw some considerable Men from among you to Canada on some Pretence or other, in hopes thereby, that the french Governour may have it in his Power to weaken, or break the Covenant Chain, which subsists between us, & to overset what I do now with Sincerity Declare to you, whereas he never speaks with truth but at all times deludes you with his smooth Tougue, & Artful Promises, which if you give Ear to will surely prove you Ruin, as your Forefathers by sorrowful Experience have often felt. Therefore I earnestly desire, & Conjure you by this Belt of Wampum, not to go that way, not listen to any Invitations from him or any of his Emissaries, nor give Credit to any wicked & false Stories, which he or they may raise among you. A Belt Britheren

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(4)
Britheren:
I have often told you not to suffer any french to resode among you and being Informed that many of them are from time to time Admitted to your Castles, & now remain there contrary to your promises to me, And as such people are sent among you to raise Jealousies & Differences between you & your Britheren without any foundation for it, I expect for the future that you will not suffer any French to Enter your Castles or [?] with you, & that if any do come for that purpose, I desire you will make them Prisoners, & send them to me, or else I will send for them, And I hope that none of you will oppose my Messages for that End. A large Belt
Britheren: 
As you have had my Art in your hands for some time past I must desire you will keep it & that you will hold yourselves in readiness to use it Jointly with us whenever you are called upon, as the Enemy are committing Murders Daily upon you & your Britheren on their own Land & as our Forefathers always said & agreed, that whatever happened to us should be sensibly felt by the other being as one Body & one Mind; I expect that you will remember & keep up to that agreement accordingly, & upon this Occasion I must Advise you to keep your Young Men at home & not let them go to War against the Flatheads, who are in strict friendship with your Britheren  the English. A large Belt.
Britheren:
I have sent a Number of french prisoners to Canada in order to [?] such of our Britheren as have had the Misfortune to fall into their hands according to my promise to you by Coll.l Johnson at Onondaga, & in this as well as on other Occasions, I have taken the same care for their [?] which I have done for his Maj.s other Subjects: His Excell.y the Gov.r of the Massachusetts Bay (to shew his regard likewise for you) has brought fourteen french prisoners to this place, that in Case the prisoners w.ch have

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(5)
have sent to Canada be not sufficient to redeem all your people from Captivity these may be Exchanged for them. A Belt.
Britheren:
You have since you came to this place given a New & Strong Proof of your Love to your Britheren, & Fidelity to the King your father by so chear fully & speedily sending out a Number of your Warriours with our Troops in Quest of the Enemy, who a few Days since surprized & killed many of our Britheren at Schenectady, And altho' those who earnestly pursued the Enemy had not the good fortune to Meet with them, you may assure yourselves that this Instance of your Affection & readiness to Join in our Cause shall always be remembered by me, & made known to the King your Father - A Belt.

Brother Corlaer Warachjago & Ychowanne
We heartily thank you for your great Esteem & regard for us that you have acquainted our Father His Maj.y King George (who we acknowledge to be our Common Father & Protector) that we have assisted our Britheren the English in this war against the French. We return thanks to His Maj.y for his Bounty & Goodness in sending us a present to be Delivered unto us by you. We promise that we shall not be wanting in our Duty, We thank you for acquainting & reminding us of the Antient Covenant Claim which has so long Subsisted Inviolable between us & our Ancestors, The Terms & Conditions you know better than we because you have them in writing, & we only by Oral Tradition. As you have renewed the same, we do solemnly in like Manner Confirm & renew the same with you, that we may hold fast together hand in hand 'till Death parts us. You tell us that the French continually are Artifices with us, Endeavoring thereby to break that Covenant which Subsists between us, this we cannot Deny, but do freely acknowledge it, but we faithfully promise not to hearken or give Credit to the french for the future but adhere firmly to

(7)
you our Britheren, & hope the Britheren will do all in like manner on their parts to us as long as the World Endures. Gave a Belt.
Brother Corlaer Warghjago & Ychowanne.
You told us that you suspected that after we returned home the french will invite & send for some of our Men to go to Canada in order to Delude & Draw some of them off from their Duty to our Common father or Endeavour to Overset or prevent, what we have now promised & Engaged to perform. We know it to be true as you observe that the french are Deceitful & Endeavour to Draw some of us over to them; We believe you speak sincerely from the Bottom of your heart, but the french speak Artfully & Deceitfully; We do Expect they will come among us as to try to Delude us craftily; but, we all the Six Nations are Determined not to give Credit nor hearken to what they may tell us, & not one of us shall go to Canada on any pretence according as you desire from us, We do not speak this only from our Lips, but Sincerely from the Bottom of our hearts. Gave a Belt
Brother Corlaer Warghjago & Ychowanne.
We the Six Nations know by Experience that the french of Canada are Deceitful & not to be trusted, that they will Endeavour to Draw som of us off from our Duty & fidelity to his Majesty, but they shall not be able to accomplish it. We promise not to suffer Jean Cour, the French Interprator, nor any frech for the future to reside or Dwell among us. We promise that if he or any other from Canada shall come among us we will either send them to your Excell.y or Deliver them up to any Messenger your Excell.y may send for them, or drive them out of our Country. Jean Cour had been given up already by the Sennekes, you may be assured that what we now promise to your Excell.y we shall faithfully perform as your Excell.y has desired from us. Gave a Belt. Brother

Brother Corlaer Warghjago & Ychowanne.
You told us we had your Hatchet a long while & Desired us to keep it in readiness for the french are Deceitful & not to be trusted. We may Expect Daily that they will Attack us or you as we have lost some people by their parties, We promise to keep our Warriours at home that we may be always ready, & not surprised by them, you desired us to keep our Young Men at home and not send them our against the Flatheads who we hear are friends to our Britheren the English; this we promise likewise to do as you desire you desired us two years ago that we should keep our Young Men at home that the war Kettle was hung over the fire by you since we received & have had teh Hatchet in our hands, some of us have made use of the same and others stayed at home expecting to be called upon, for this reason our Young Men have not been able to go on their hunting at any Distance from home as usual, which has impoverished us very much & tho' we are considerably sufferers by this war, we shall nevertheless keep our Warriours at home as you desire to be ready at your first Call. Gave a Belt.
Brother Corlaer Warghjago & Ychowanne.
When Coll.l W.m Johnson was at Onondago the last Spring he promised to use his Endeavour to get our people who are prisoners in Goal at Canada which promise we see you have Endeavoured to accomplish by sending a Number of french prisoners to Canada to redeem them, for which we are heartily thankful to you, & that you promise to take the same Care of our prisoners as you will of your own people who may have the Misfortune to fall into the Enemy's hands And we are much obliged to Gov.r Shirley that he has been pleased to bring a Number of french Prisoners to redeem ours for which we are very thankful to you.
Brother Corlaer Warghjago & Ychowanne. Gave a Belt

I am well pleased with the Sentiments which you tell me you have of the french. That they are not to be trusted, & that since they have received so many prisoners already, they ought at least to have restored some of your prisoners before any more be Delivered. And that None of you will go to Canada to Treat with the Gov.r of Canada, but that you will trust to me to have all your prisoners restored. The pretence which the Gov.r of Canada makes for his not restoring the Indian prisoners as I Demanded of him, is that some of the five Nations who have been in Canada disown that the five Nations had taken up the Hatchet against the french, & under that pretence would not treat your Men as prisoners of War; But I am resolved to tell him that he shall receive no more of his prisoners 'till he delivers yours, after which I shall set at Large all the french prisoners who are not desirous to stay.

You may assure yourselves that I shall take the same care of you as of any other of his Maj.'s Subjects, & that you may Depend on my favour for the Confidence you place in me, & that I will restore no prisoners to the french in Canada yours be restored, or that I have suff.t Security that they shall be restored.
