are necessary in this province, than in other parts of his Maj.y's Dominions Distant from Canada. If any among the french in Canada should not be well disposed towards us they may even in case of a peace privately set the Indians to do Mischief. And I think therefore that the Troops in the pay of this province & remaining in the County of Albany ought to be continued some time longer 'till the Inclinations of the french in Canada, & of their Indians be known, & we have reason to think that the inhabitants on the Frontiers are in safety, we have the more reason to be on our Guard since I cannot agree to the Terms Offered for a Mutual Release of prisoners on the part of the Gov.r of Canada by the Officer sent by him to me, consistent with that regard which I have for the Secutity & safe return of his Maj.'s Subjects of this Province, who have the Misfortune to be prisoners in Canada.
I have given Orders that some persons be sent from Albany to propose more equitable Terms to the Governour of Canada for the mutual restoring of prisoners than those which have been proposed to me on his part. And you may be assured that nothing shall be wanting on my part to procure a safe & speedy return of all the British Subjects prisoners in Canada that is in my power to do.
Gentlemen of the Gen.l Assembly:
As this is the Session in which you propose to provide for the [?] of the Current Year, I think it proper to observe to you that in the time of [?] Hunter, Burnet, Montgomerie & Cosby, the Establishm.t for the paym of the Gov.r's Secretary's Judges & other Officers Sallarys were made at the Entrance of each of those Gentlemen of his Administration for the Term of five Years, by an Act, entitled, an Act for the Support of His Maj.'s Governm.t within this province: But that upon my coming to the Administration in the Year 1743, instead of making the usual Establishm.t for the paym.t of those Asllarys the Assembly passed an Act, Entitled, An Act for the payment of

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(27)
the Sallaries, Services & Contingencies therein mentioned, until the 1:st of September 1744 & have continued this Method of granting the Saleries, for supporting the Gov.r & other Officers of the Government, from Year to Year ever since.
The Inclination Gentlemen, with w.ch I came to the Administration of his Maj.'s Governm.t in this Province, to do eveery thing for the ease & satisfaction of the people, consistent with my Duty to the King, as his Governour, & the Confidence I placed in the Advice then given me, that the Method proposed by that Act, for making provision for the payment of Salaries to the sev.l Officers of His Maj.'s Governm.t would not be Attended with any Inconveniencies; at first Induced me to give my assent to the Act: And the Rupture with France w.ch ensued before the time of Year came round again for providing for the payment of Salaries, and which has continued 'till the late Ratification of the preliminary Articles for a gen.l pacification at Aux-la-Chapelle, has prevented me from refusing my assent to the Acts passed in the three Subsequent Years for the same purpose, being unwilling to Move any point which might Interfere with the Assembly's Attention to other Important Affairs of His Majesty's Service, & the Gen.l Interest of this & his other Colonies in North America, depending before them during the Course of the War.
But now that the Conclusion of the War, & the Experience I have had of the Tendency of these New Acts in many points to weaken His Maj.'s Government in this province, have made it my Indispensable Duty to take the first Opportunity of putting a Stop to these Innovations; I must acquaint you that I do not think myself at Liberty to give my Assent to the like Acts for the future; & therefore I earnestly recommend it to you to make the same provision for the payment of Salaries that former Assemblies did during the Administration of my four immediate predecessors Chief Governours of this province & I hope the same spirit of Loyalty to His Maj.'s Government which

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(28)
which Animated those Assemblys, will Induce you likewise to comply with what I propose.
Gentlemen:
I am not seeking any personal advantage for myself or the other Officers of His Majesty's Governm.t by an Augmentation of any Sallary what I now recommend to you, And if you think it more agreeable to the Rights of the people, that the Sums to be paid fore every Officers Salary shall be Expressed in the Act, instead of having it Entrusted with the Gov.r & Council as was the usual Method before, I shall not oppose it in the least. You must be sensible, Gentlemen, that I am not offering to you any Innovation in the Method of providing for the Support of His Maj.'s Governm.t Established by former Assemblies; but only Endeavouring to put an End to those lately Introduced, & to put his Maj.'s Governm.t in this respect on the same  foot it stood upon in the time of my predecessors, Chief Gov.'s of this province, immediately before I came to the Administration; which I [?] to be my Duty to do, & necessary for his Maj.'s Service that it should be done.
It would be too [?] for me to enter into a particular Detail of the Inconvenience which would Attend the New Method of providing for the support of His Maj.'s Governm.t but shall observe only some of the principal Objections I have to it. viz.t That Establishm.t for my own Salary & Allowances, & the other Salaries & Services [?] provided for in former Acts of Assembly are now made from Year to Year instead of the Term of five Years; That many new Grants & Matters of a different Nature are intermixet in these Acts And Tacked to the Grants for own support & of the other Salaries & paym.ts which were usually Joyned with that; And that these Acts are passed the last of the sev.l Sessions; And the the Grants made to the Chief Justice & other Justices of the Supreme Court & so other Officers, are made to them personally by Name, not to the Officers for time

Coll.l Johnson Informs me that he has not been paid a Debt of 2138 due to him by this province, & which was Allowed & Ordered to by paid him by an Act passed last Sessions, Entitled, An Act to make provision for sev.l Services for thee Defence & Security of the Frontiers, & other purposes therein mentioned; And that the reason given by the Treasurer, why he did not pay that Sum is, that the Fund out of which this mony is to be paid is Surcharged £1600. We His Maj.'s most Dutiful & loyal Subjects, the Gen.l Assembly of the Colony of New York, thank your Exell.y for your Congratulations on the near [?] of a Gen.l peace, which we think his Maj.'s loyal Subjects of this Colony have the greatest reason to rejoice at, as it gives them hopes of a speedy Deliverance from the Ravages & Barbaritys of their foreign Declared Enemies, and the Defeat & Mortification of those that have been latent & Domestick: but as your Excellency tells us, the prospect of a Gen.l peace is near (and in the interim there is a Cessation of Hostilities) we are humbly of Opinion when we reflect on the Grievous & heavy Burthen of Taxes this Colony has to sustain for many Years to come by means of the late War, it is a Duty Incumbent on us, to be cautious of Adding unnecessarily to this Weight, which the Continuance of Forces in the pay of the Colony could greatly Increase: and we humbly conceive his Maj.'s three Independent Companies now posted in Albany consisting, or which ought to Consist of about One hundred Men each, will be suff.t in the present Situation of Affairs for the protection of the Northern Frontiers; and therefore agreeable to the practice in our Mother Country, this Colony may now very properly be relieved from the Expence of further Maintenance of Supernumerary Forces in their pay.
The Number of regular Forces usually posted at Oswego in time of peace has always been judged by your Excellen.y's predecessors; & the other Branches of the Legislature suff.t to Garrison that Fortress, And we will make provision for that Number accordingly.
We flatter ourselves that when your Excell.y shall pursue the Advice of sending some persons of higher Rank & Repute than those who have already been employed to Negotiate with the Gov.r of Canada, touching the Release of his Maj.'s Subjects of this Colony, late Captives in the War; instead of having a contemptible Reception, & their Errand become fruitless, such will not only be treated with the regard due to their Character, but their Negotiations will also more probably have

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(31)
have their proper Weight & Effect; and we shall then heartily Congratulate your Excell.y on the Success & chearfully provide for all reasonable Expence that may Attend the Service.
It was, Sir, a long & thorough Experience of the many Inconveniences of which the Settlement of a five years support was productive in the time of your Excell.y's predecessors, The Governours in Chief you have been pleased to mention indured the Gen.l Assembly's Resolution to Depart from it in the time of Lieut. Gov.r Clarke's Administration, & from the good Effects that have resulted from an Annual Support with regard to the Governour's Sallary & making the Grants to the Chief Justice & the other Justices of the Supreme Court, personally & by Name; we think we have the greatest reason to continue the same Method, & the rather, as we are fully persuaded, that had the Grants been made to the Justices for the time being your Excell.y (under the unhappy Influence you now are) would have filled the Office of third Justice of that Court with some unworthy person in the room of a Gentleman of Experience & Learning in the Law, whom you removed from that Station without any Colour of Misconduct, at least as we ever heard of under the Sole Influence of a person of so mean & Despicable a Character (as the Gen.l Assembly has sev.l times heretofore occasionally Signifyed to you) that 'tis astonishing to us that your Excell.y should persist in Submitting your Conduct to his Sole Council & Guidance. Your Excell.y was well apprized of the Sentim.ts of the Gen.l Assembly you first called upon those heads; And as you could have no Just reason to impute this Method of providing for the Officers of his Maj.'s Governm.t, to the least failure in them either in point of Duty or Loyalty to his Most Gracious Majesty, to whom, & his illustrious house the Gen.l Assembly & their Constituents are most sincerely Attached notwithstanding any futile Insinuations that have of late been Drop't to the contrary; and we cannot but think you was well Advised at that time; And your Excell.y did for very ample & suff.t reasons, & good & valuable Considerations as we have understood, accede to those Terms both

both for your Excell.y's benefit & the ease & Satisfoction of the publick: And we are much concerned & surprised that your Exell.y is now of a Different Sentiment & do not think yourself at Liberty to give your Assent to the like Act for the future; because from recent Experience, we are fully convinced that Method is most wholesome & Sautary; & are confirmed in the Opinion, That the faithful representatives of the people can never depart from it.
As to all other particulars you Exell.y has been pleased to recommend to us we Assure you, Sir, they shall also have their due weight in the Course of our proceedings: And as you are pleased to assure us that you shall do every thing in your power, which may contribute to the safety & prosperity of this Colony so your Excell.y may be persuaded, that nothing shall be wanting on our parts, that may or requisite to promote those desirable Ends.

Gentlemen:
[Left margin info truncated and indecipherable]
"Two of your Members brough me a Copy of an Address w.ch you propose to make to me, with a Message, to know when I would receive it: There is a Decency to be observed in all Addresses from your house to your Gov.r who in this Case, represents the King, from whom he receives his Authority: But in the paper brought to me you have had not regard to Decency; and therefore I think it no way proper for me to receive such an Address, however, that the Business now before you may be at no stand on this Account, I now send this answer to every thing in that paper, which I think can be of any use to you to know.
"You know that I can have no private Interest in desiring you to continue the Forces in the pay of this Colony, and now posted on the Frontiers: My only View in it is the safety of the Inhabitants there: Tho' the prospect of peace may seem near, yet we have no Account of it's being finally concluded: and I believe no Instance can be given, that any Nation Disbanded their Forces before a peace was concluded.
"We may even have reason to fear from the well known Temper of the Indians that we are not safe from their Hostilities, notwithstanding of the Cessation of Arms now subsisting between the powers at War: I think it my Duty to take care of

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749

(34)
"of the people committed to my Charge, on all Events, and in the manner I proposed; but This I cannot do, without your Assistance.
"It was not easy to find proper persons to send with the prisoners which were sent to be Exchanged in Canada: It was in time of war, when the Skulking Indian parties were abroad; and I am Informed that the persons which I then sent were in great Danger from a party of french Indians, that fell in with them. I have reason to think that M:r Williams, the person I Entrusted, behaved properly; since the Governour of Canada Declared he was well pleased with his behaviour; and that on that Account he had Released sev.l prisoners more than he had intended: and the prisoners now in Canada have certifyed to me, That they are satisfyed that Captain Williams has done the utmost of his Endeavours to procure the Release of those whom in Conscience though stood most in need of it.
"I have since desired the Gentlemen of the Council to Name such persons as they thought would be most proper to go back with the french Gentlemen who came hither for the Exchange of Prisoners, in order to procure a Gen.l Release of all the Inhabitants of this province; and not one of them Named any person, but said that they could not think of any person of Distinction that would be willing to go tho' at this time the Cessation of Arms takes place; and they were to go in Company with the french Officers, who returned to Canada. The Season of the Year do not admit of Delay, least the unfortunate people, who are now prisoners in Canada should be put under the hardships of remaining in prison during the Winter in that severe Climate; and as all of them are Inhabitants of the County of Albany I thought proper persons were most likely to be found there: And my Intention was that such persons should be sent as would have the Relief of their unfortunate Britheren most at heart: But now I am afraid that my Endeavours for the Relief of these objects of Compassion may be obstructed by the Doubts w.ch may be Entertained of your paying the necessary Expence on such an Occasion. (39)
"publishing that paper under the Name of an Address, in your Votes, & afterw.ds in a publik News paper published by the printer of your Votes, you seem to place the dernier Resort in all Disputes between your Gov.r & you, in the populace. How His Maj.y may take this; or how a parliam.t of Great Britain may take you claiming not only the privileges of parliam.t, but privileges far beyond what any house of Commons ever Claimed; deserves your most Serious Consideration. You seem herein to forget your Dependancy. I therefore think that I cannot at this time more Effectually shew the concern I have for the people of this province than by giving you time cooly to consult with your Constituents on the Consequences you proceedings may have; and that you may do this at a time when you are freed from that Influence which now to Evidently prevails among you.
"In most of the Bills prepared for my Assent, you continue so visibly to assume to yourselves the Executive powers of Governm.t, that nothing could excuse my giving my Assent to them, but the necessity of the Service for which you grant the mony; without which, those Services could not be performed: And as I have reason to think that you persist in your Obstinacy, in assuming almost the whole powers of Government; it becomes necessary for me to put an End to the present Session.

Gentlemen of the Council & Gen.l Assembly.
"I congratulate you upon the Establishm.t of peace by which this Province is freed from the Calamities of War, to which the Frontiers of it were Exposed from a Barbarous & cruel Enemy. I am not now to incite you to the prosecution of War, which when most Successful is Attended with Effects no ways desirable but to the Arts of peace for the future Security & prosperity of the people of this Province: & I assure you Gentlemen that I will chearfully Join with you in every thing which shall be necessary for the Legislature to do for this purpose.
"But Gentlemen of the Assembly, it can be of little Service to make Laws if they with whom the Executive powers of Governm.t are intrusted be disabled from putting them in Execution; and therefore I must ( previously to eveer thing which may be proper to be recommended to you at this time) Demand that you grant His Maj.y a Revenue for the Support of His Governm.t in this Province in a manner conformable to the Directions of His Maj.'s Commission to me by the Authority of which you Sit and Act, & of the Instructions which I have received for that purpose, and to make provision for the paym.t of the Debts Justly due for Services done, & for teh Contingent Services of the Ensuing Year, in manner likewise conformable to the Directions of His Maj.'s Commission & Instructions to me. In making this Demand I ask nothing New, or that any New Taxes or Impositions be laid on his Maj.'s Subjects in this province or what is not perfectly consonant to the English Constitution & conformable to the practice of parliam.t. There are Laws of this Province now in force granting to His Majesty funds for the support of His Governm.t; there is mony in the Treasury for this purpose: and yet tho' the monys arising from these Funds are granted to His Maj.y, he cannot, as these Laws now stand, make use of one farthing of it for the purposes for which it was granted. This is such an inconsistency in itself, so contrary to our happy Constitution, & so prejudicial to his Maj.'s Service that it mus be remedied: And therefore I must Demand of you, Gentlemen of the Assembly, to give me an Answer in direct & positive Terms previous to your going on any other Business, whether you will grant his Maj.y a Revenue for support of His Governm.t conformable

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(54)
conformable to His Commission & Instructions to me, the Copys of which I now deliver to you; and may you in giving your Answer make Manifest your Duty to your King, Your Love to the English Constitution, & your sincere regard to the welfare of the people you represent.
"Gentlemen of the Council & Gen.l Assembly -
As soon as I shall have received the Assembly's Answer, I shall lay before you what I think further necessary for his Maj.'s Service.
"I am sensible that the approaching Harvest may make this time of your Meeting inconvenient to some of you, but I could not think it proper to meet you 'till I knew the Sentim'ts of His Maj.'s Ministers in respect to the Assembly's refusing to Grant the Support of Governm.t in the Manner I asked it to last Fall. And now the pressing hardships that many of the people of this province are under from their not being paid large Sums of mony of a long time Justly due to them, but more especialy the sufferings of the prisoners still detained in Canada, and for whose relief I cannot do what may be proper 'till you provide the Expence which must Attend this Service, makes your meeting at this time necessary; And I hope these sufferings & hardships so many of your fellow Subjects are under will be of more weight with you than any Inconvenience some or you may be under by your being taken from Attending the harvest in the Country" G: Clinton Fort George in the City of New York 28 June 1749

May it please your Excell.y
We His Maj.'s most Dutiful & loyal Subjects, the Gen.l Assembly of the Colony of New York return your Excell.y our thanks for your Congratulations upon the Re Establishm.t of peace; & most sincerely & heartily wish that this & His Maj.y's  other Colonies on this Continent, may be entirely freed from those Calamaties to which they have been exposed during the War, & that your Excell.y may be more successful in cultivating among us the Arts of Peace as well for the future Security, as present prosperity of the people of this Colony.
We must acknowledge, Sir, with all Mankind, that it can be of no Service or rather that it would be in vain to make Laws if they with whom the Executive powers of Governm.t  are intrusted, be disabled from putting them in Execution, but we are not sensible that we have been accessary to any such Disability in this Governm.t; the Gen.l Assembly having always (as we humbly conceive) manifested their Duty to the Crown in making ample & honourable provision for the support of this His Maj.'s Governm.t tho' they may sometime have differed with Governours, as to the Modes & forms in the Method of doing & yet have had a proper regard to the Royal Intention, in the Commission & Instructions to Governours, by taking care that the mony given by them, should be duly applyed to the respective uses for which they gave it.
We hope your Excell.y will Excuse us if in our Considerations on the Extracts of His Maj.'s Instructions we happen to differ in Sentim.ts on the Constitution, tho' your Excell.y has not Indulged us with Communicating yours, we presume you Excell.y has not Just now received them (tho' it sho.d seem the Speech Insinuates as much) but that the have been standing Instructions to all your Excell.y's predecessors (some alterations in the Stile only of your Excell.y's Cppy excepted) & tho' there be no Royal Injunction apparent in them for the practice so much explanded for many

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(57)
many Years past, for the Mischief of which the Grant of a five Years support was productive, & of which your Excell.y seemed at first to be made sensible upon ample Considerations, yet we find Governours upon more mature Deliberation would willingly engross the Sweets of that Method to themselves, of which the people neither ever had or ever can expect any benefit.
We must beg leave to observe to your Excell.y that the Gen.l Assembly do not perceive any essential Difference with respect to His Maj.'s Services & the Royal Intention concerning the support of the Governm.t of this Colony, whether the Governour & other Officers of the Governm.t have their Salaries provided Annualy or for the Term of five Years, which last your Excell.y Demanded by your Speech on the fourteenth of October last, & the same Claim as we take it, your Excell.y now renews by your reference to it.
It must be obvious to every one that the time of our present Meeting is most inconvenient to much the greater part of the Members for the very reason mentioned by your Excell.y & tho' we shall at all times chearfully postpone our private Interest to the Attendance on the publick Exigency, yet we are constrained to Declare that from the Experience we have had of the unhappy Influence which has for some time past & does still direct your Excell.y's Administration we have but little hopes of Indulgence from your Excell.y at any time, however consistent it may be with the publick welfare -
And as your Excell.y is pleased to tell us you could not think it proper to meet us 'till you knew the Setim.ts of His Maj.'s Ministers in respect to our refusing to grant the support of Governm.t in the Manner you asked it last Fall, so as we are not further Enlightened in the Matter at this time, we cannot but continue in the same opinion we then were. -
That ever Just Demands there may be due for Services done the Publick besides the ordinary occurrencys, that they have remained so long unpaid, cannot with Justice be ascribed to any Default in the Gen.l Assembly, who have ever been careful to provide

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(58)
provide for such & did pass a Bill wherein provision was made, as may be seen in the printed Journal of our proceedings, & therefore their remaining still undischarged is solely to be imputed to the unseasonable prorogation of the Gen.l Assembly on the Twelfth of November last whereby that Bill with sev.l others was Defeated. 
We sincerely Lament the hardships which some of our poor Britheren, prisoners in Canada have & still do suffer, by their long confinem.t there, & are fully persuaded they might long since have been released had proper Measures been taken by those whose Province it is: And here we be leave to remind your Excelly of the Assurances we gave you on that head in our Address of the 19.th of October last, that we would chearfully provide for all reasonable Expence Attending such Service,
We must conclude upon the whole with Declaring to your Excell.y that we can give no other or better Answer to the present Speech than we did toward the conclusion of our Address, in Answer to your Excell.y's Speech of the fourteenth of October last, which was (among other things) in substance that we were confirmed in our Opinion that the faithful Representatives of the people could never recede from the Method of an Annual support

City of New York} ss Thomas Cumming of the said City being of the people commonly called Quakers, being of full age & duly Affirmed did Declare & Affirm for truth that on Fryday afternoon about the hour of five he this Affirm.t together with one John Wollaston, a Gentleman lately Arrived from  London called at the house of Andrew Ramsey a Tavern keeper in this City to Inquire for a Gentleman with whom they intended some real Business whose Name this Affirm.t did not then know (but he since learnt was one Hopkins from Virginia) and as his Name was not known at that time to this Affirm.t or to the said Wollaston (to the knowledge or belief of this Affirm.t) they Enquired for the Names of the persons in company with Oliver DeLancey having heard he had been in his Company, & were Informed that David Johnson was one whereupon they bid the Drawer call him to them at the Door & thereupon M.r Johnson came to the Door & Informed them that Hopkins was gone, & they upon being Informed so proposed to go from the House, that M.r Johnson Endeavored to persuade them to go into the Company which they Declined & he finding he could not persuade them took hold of each of them by one hand, & w.th one of them in one of his hands & the other in his other hand, he in a friendly manner pulled them into the Room where the Company was, which was a few paces distant from the place in the Entry where he first took hold of them.
That this affirmant & Woolaston were Seated & saw in that Company, Oliver DeLancey, the said David Johnson, Philip Vanhorne & one other person unknown to this Affirmant, whom he afterwards found to be one William Rickets a Gentl.n of a great Estate who lived in New Jersey-
That he this Affirm.t readily perceived they were all a little inebriated with Liquor & does not particularly recollect any thing that passed for about or near Ten or Twelve Minutes about which time Doctor Alex.r Colhoun Entered the Room, and that at this Affirm.t's  first View of him he saw that he was very much disordered with Drink, & with many Staggerings & other Simptoms of a Drunken Man

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:

Man Seated himself in Company, & this Affirm.t cannot with any certainty say whether Oliver De Lancey or Doctor Colhoun or which other of the Company began first to Quarrel for all were Speaking, & in a seeming Confusion Except the said Woolaston & this Affirm.t, & saithe that the first thing w,ch Excited in him a close & concerned Attention, was Oliver De Lancey's Delivering himself in a very warm manner in Expressions to the Amount, & in Substance, & as near as this Affirmant can remember in these words following, to wit, By God I say the Governour is an Arrant Villain, Scoundrel & Rascal, I  call him so & so are all & every Man who takes his part, Villains, Scoundrels & Rascals that Doctor Colhoun, who could scarce speak intelligibly, thereupon told the said Oliver that he ought to behave with good Manners, Oliver replyed, Damn you Sir, what are you to teach me Manners; this is the Second time you have told me to speak & behave myself with good Manners this afternoon, Sir, added Oliver, I say the Gov.r & every Man who keeps him Company are Villains, Scoundrels & Rascals & Sir, I beg you will go & tell the Gov.r I call him so, & further Added that if he could any way Bribe him the Doctor or any other person to Inform the Gov.r what he said he would Bribe him or them to Deliver the Message, & this Affim.t  remembers nothing more distinctly than that the Doctor said, well Sir, very well Sir, what the Divil have we to do with these things here why sho.d we disturb the Company with this Talk? there is another time Sir for that, & Oliver seemed satisfyed to be Silent, but in a few Minutes Exclaimed as above again against the Gov.r, the Mayor & all their Adherents in the above mentioned Expressions, & told Doctor Colhoun on his rising from his Chair & Endeavoring to leave the Company, that he might go away & be Damned for that if he (the Doctor) or any other person whatever could not bear to hear the Gov.r, Mayor & their friends called Villians, Scoundrels & Rascals, he nor they should not Enter any time into any Company where he should be, for that in all Company & to all people at all times he would call them so, that the Doctor went out of Company & David Johnson (who had either gone out before or with or soon after the Doctor, but which he the Affirm.t cannot remember) very soon & in a few Minutes came into the Room without the

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:

the Doctor & beckoned or called to Oliver who instantly went out, but Johnson sat himself down in the Room, & soon after Oliver DeLancey came into the Room holding the Doctor by the hand & both placed themselves as before & Oliver then asked Johnson whether he Oliver had given any Toast in Comp.y which had given offence to the Doctor, & David Johnson thereupon Denyed that he had told Doctor Colhoun so: Oliver DeLancey Asserted that the Doctor had Charged him with it at the Door, & the Doctor said they Misunderstood him & remembers he could make no Sense or meaning of what the Doctor said -
That a great Wrangle & Noise Ensued, but what the Doctor said to Oliver DeLancey or he to the Doctor the Affirmant could not hear, nor can he Declare, only that Oliver DeLancey soon after Quitted the Room & house & the Doctor Endeavoured to follow, & one of the Comp.y privately, & without the Doctor's knowledge, took his Sword out of his Scabbard & kept it concealed from him for some time, but the Doctor perceiving his Sword was gone, Searched for it & had it returned to him, that in a few Minutes after Oliver DeLancey had left the Room, a Negro Man came to the house & called for D.r Colhoun, & said he was sent by M.r DeLancey to desire Doctor Colhoun to come to M.r DeLancey's house directly; That this Affirm.t & the rest of the Company once more Endeavoured to prevent on the Doctor not to leave them, but after a while they all desisted, perceiving his obstinate Resolution of going, & he the Doctor then left the Room & house of Ramsay & soon after he was gone this Affirm.t went to M.r DeLancey's house with David Johnson to prevent any Mischief which he apprehended might Ensue & got there before him & found M.r DeLancey with a Cane or Stick in his hand at or near the Gate at the Street Door of his house in the Broadway, who asked them where the Doctor was & said he was affraid he could not come, but in a very short time the Doctor came & opened the Gate Door at the Inside & appeared to them to have Entered at the back Door of M.r DeLancey's house, & in a Laughing humour said ha! "In answer to your Address of the 5.th Day of this Month, I can (with pleasure) reflect upon my own Conduct since the unhappy Differences began between you & me after

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(68)
after every prorogation, I spoke to you at the opening of every New Session as if no Difference had preceeded; how far otherwise you have done is too remarkable; for what purpose it is done I shall leave your own Consciencys & others to Judge: but I cannot pass over that continued Endeavour to calumniate my Administration, for what other purpose have you taken upon yourselves to assert that you are fully persuaded the the prisoners in Canada might long since have been Released by those whose province it is: Let me ask you Gentlemen, had you any Evidence of this before you? I know it is impossible you could; and all the world must think you have but little regard to truth; when in a single half hour your Address was read Twice over & agreed to by your house, tho' the greatest Number of you must have known nothing of the Subject Matter of it, as nothing of it appeared in your house before that time.
"When ever the Matter shall come before proper Judges, it will appear that as to the Releasing of Prisoners, I have acted truly for the benefit of the Community.
"The Gov.r of Canada's Design it to withdraw the Indians from us to make them lose all Confidence in us, & with this View all his Negotiations for the Exchange of prisoners were transacted, and it is now further made Evident by the partys of Indians from Canada that have made Incursion on the Frontiers of the Northern Colonies, & by his sending large partys to the Westward, with a View (at least) to Destroy the English Commerce with the Indian Nations on the Banks of the great Lakes.
"The Mohawks have Delivered up all their prisoners into the hands of Coll.l Johnson & have refused to send Deputys to Canada, tho' again & again invited there by the Gov.r with a promise of having all the Prisoners Delivered up to them: They trust to me solely that I shall procure the Release of their Prisoners by Virtue of the Treaty of peace.
"At the conclusion of every War before this the five Nations sent Deputys  to Canada: there they made peace seperately for themselves, & Entered into Engagem.ts with

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(69)
with the French. How prejudicial this was to the British Interest, & what Advantages I have now gained is too obvious to need any Remarks.
"But, Gentlemen, unless I be Enabled to prosecute the Measures I have taken all these Advantages will be lost; and if the Indians find that words not protect them, they must leave us & turn to the french, & with such Resentment that we shall never be able to recover them.
"I could find no Man in this place would undertake any part of this Expence which attended my Endeavurs to have our prisoners Released on the Credit of your Resolves:  I have been obliged to carry on the whole of this Affair on my own private Credit, & by mony out of my own pocket; & it is no wonder that your Credit Should be so small, when it is considered  that on the 27.th of June 1748, you Addressed me to send Twenty five prisoners to Canada, to be Exchanged; & assured me that you would make good all such Expence as may necessarily Attend this Service. I did accordingly send a Flag of Truce with Twenty five french prisoners. The persons I sent went in Evident Danger of their Lives from the Enemys Sculking Indian partys: They performed the Service they were sent on faithfully. Last Sessions I recommended to you the providing for this Expence. Accounts of it were laid before you, & yet you would make no provision for it. 
"Pray, Gentlemen, consider what it is that has raised this Present m.t ag.t me can any Man say that I have Invaded either his Liberty or property or Endeavoured to hurt his Reputation; I have not only Advanced large Sums but I have resigned my whole Fortune for His Maj.'s Service & the benefit of this Country Consider on the other hand the Conduct of those who are in opposition to my Administration; the behaviour of their Fools to your fellow Subjects in the Streets in the Taverns & in their houses; & how by that opposition the publick good & Service has been in every Instance obstructed & publick Calumny propagated And then Gentlemen, you & all the world may Judge who is under the most unhappy Influence -
"I must complain of your Endeavouring to lead the people of this Province into mistakes, as the Demand I made of you. There is not in my Demand nor

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(70)
"nor in the Instructions which accompanyed it the least mention either of a Yearly Support of for five Years, nor is there in that Demand any Referrence to what was asked in the preceeding Session. The Demand & Instructions principally related to the Method of Issuing the Publick monys; & as to this his Maj.'s Intention both in his Commission to me & his Instructions, cannot be mistaken. I know well the present Sentim.ts of His Maj..'s Ministers, as to this; & you might have at least Guessed at them, by the Bill lately brought into parliament &  published in this place, for enforcing the Kings Instructions.
"It is an Essential part of the English Constitution that the power of granting of the mony & the Issuing of it be in different Branches of the Constitution as the best Method to prevent misapplications; for if those who grant the mony had likewise the power of distributing it among their friends & Relations under any pretences of publick Service there can be nine to call them to an Account for Misapplication, whereas when one Branch Grants & another Issues, it is natural to think that on any suspicion of misapplication the Grantees will Demand an Account, & satisfaction if any such misapplication do appear; the truth of this fully appears by Experience in this Province, where I am confident it may be made appear, if strict Examination were to be made into it.
"It is the constant practice in parliam.t to make no provision for any Service w.ch is not previously recommended by the King: you have given mony to private persons not only for Services w.ch were not recommended to you to be provided for, but for Services of which I to this Day remain Ignorant; and by incuring of these Grants in the same Bill wherein you provided for the Support of Governm.t, or other necessary Services, you put me under the necessity of giving assent to them, or of leaving the Governm.t without support -
"This is so Dangerous an Invasion of His Maj.'s prerogative & so Injurious to the people of this Province, that you may assure yourselves it will not be suffered to continue.

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(71)
"In the Bill which you prepared last Session for the contingent Services of this Governm.t, there is a Clause Impowering Cornelius Van Horne & Paul Richard, Two Members of your house to retain in their own hand Seven hundred & Two pounds (part of Nine hundred & Thirty four pounds of the publick mony in their hands) for the carrying of French prisoners to the French Islands, of bringing back English prisoners in Exchange: The paym.t of this Service was not recommended by me as no application had been made to me for such Recommendation: the usual proofs of the performance of this Service, by the french Gov.r's Letters, & [?] of prisoners or of the Numbers of prisoners Exchanged were not made to me: and you cannot be  Ignorant of the Gen.l Suspicions which prevail in this Place as to the performance of that Service. It does not appear by your Minutes' that you had any proofs of this Service before you 7 as there is no mention of it anywhere in your Minutes, I could not nor could any person not of your house know that this Service was under your Consideration, 'till your Clause appeared in the Bill for the paym.t of it, whereas it appears from your Minutes that all the Services, which I had recommended had been sev.ly Examined into, & proofs made of the Services in your house.
"Coll.l Johnson had advanced large Sums of mony upon the Credit of your Resolves, & as that Gentleman had otherwise conspicuously Distinguished himself in the publick Service of this province, I very earnestly recommended the paym.t of the Debts Justly due to him; his Accounts & the proofs were laid before your house: it does not appear by your Minutes that any objection was made to the truth of these Accounts; & I am confident no well grounded Objection can be made: You had in a former Session Directed paym.t of part of these Debts, out of a Fund w.ch was Exhausted; and now in the last Session you provided for the payment of but part of them, & entirely neglected to make provision for the payment of the greater part.
"Care was taken that your Members should not suffer by my refusing this Bill as more mony was in their hands than they asked; but it was far otherwise as to Coll.l Johnson

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [4], 1745-1749
transcription:
(72)
"Johnson from whom the mony Justly due to him, has been a long time detained. 
"You know best for what purpose you call the Copys of the Instructions which I sent you, Extracts only; when they contain the whoe of those Instructions without Addition or Abbreviation, as is cerifyed by the proper Officer; & why you say that I would Insinuate, that I Just now received those Instructions when the Day of their Date was likewise cerifyed to you; this does not Discover any great Attention in you to what is before you; but rather some Influence over you, that does not tend much to the honour of your house, or of those who make use of this Influence.
"But, Gentlemen, whatever opinion some people may give you, yet the Intention of His Maj.y appears to plain with regard to the Issuing of publick mony that I cannot be mistaken; and I can assure you that he never will recede from those Instructions; & therefore I must again Demand of you to grant His Maj.y a Revenue for the support of his Governm.t & to make provision for the paym.t of the Debts due, & future contingencys in such manner as the mony may Issue conformable to His Maj.'s Commission & Instructions which you have before you. & I must require a categorical Answer to this, for I cannot give my Assent to any mony Bill which shall not be conformable to these Instructions: As to other Modes & forms (as you are pleased to Express them) if there be any such in the Bill to which I may think it improper for me to give my Assent; yet if you will Add a Clause to any such Bill, whereby it shall be restrained from taking Effect or of being in force 'till His Maj.'s pleasure shall be known, & the Council give their consent I will give my Assent to it.
"Now, Gentlemen, I have done all that is in my power to put an End to those unhappy Differences, which have subsisted so long to the prejudice of the people you represent. I hope no only the sufferings of many of your fellow Subjects will weigh more with you that any private Influence whatsoever, but that you will likewise gratefully consider the great Libertys you are Indulged with by the full Enjoym.t of the English Constitution of Governm.t & how unwise

The Romans did not allow the same priviledges to their Colonies which the other Citizens Enjoyed, & you know in what manner the Republick of Holland Governs her Colonies, Endeavour then to shew your great thankfulness for the great priviledges you Enjoy. I have likewise Induced them to be Assiduous in Drawing in their Allies & Dependants into the same good Disposition with themselves, & who consist of Numerous Nations, & who can be of the greater Service in Distressing the Enemy: But I can no longer nor will no longer continue this Charge on the Crown. The preserving the Fidelity of the Indians can in the Expence occasioned thereby bear but a small proportion to the Charge of Recovering & hitherto preserving their Affections & fidelity, & of keeping them always in readiness and parties in Action; and therefore I cannot doubt of your Contributing on your parts to so small a proportion as is necessary at this time for the safety & Security of the people you Represent, & who I am well assured will chearfully bear any Taxes or Imposition that is so Evidently Expedient for their own safety and when it is considered what a Load of Taxes & Impositions the people of Great Britain chearfully bear, for the preservation of the Liberties of Europe; it cannot be Expected that they will bear with patience the Refusal of their Colonies to take upon themselves that Expence which is necessary for their own safety; especially when what may be saved from Superfluities, will be more than suff.t for all the means proposed for this purpose.
The Securing the Garrison at Oswego on all Events, is a Matter of the greatest Consequence, for preserving the Fidelity of the Indians, & deserves your serious Consideration in order to give the necessary supplys for that purpose: And unless you likewise secure the Indians by Building Forts on at least in every Nation, they must be wavering in their Resolutions; since if this be neglected they may Expect that we have no regard to their safety, but only to Employ them for our own benefit.
At the same time I shall with great pleasure think of & concur in every method, to make this necessary Expence as easy as possible to all, but especially to those who are least able to bear it, I mean the Labouring & Industrious

Tho' I think it absolutely requisite for you at this time to take the whole Charge of the Indians, as well as securing the Frontiers, upon yourselves; I shall use my best Endeavours by such Application as I shall think most Effectual, to persuade the Colonies to the Southward as far as Virginia to contribute a reasonable proportion towards the Encouragement & support of

As to your taking upon you at this time the whole necessary Expence of the Indians, I must Inform you that at my last Treaty with the Six united Nations, the Governm.ts of Virginia, & of the Massachusetts Bay, sent considerable presents to the Indians; the Massachusetts Bay have since that sent presents to the value at least of £1000. New York Currency, & Connecticut about £300. value in the same mony; this Governm.t gave no Presents at that Treaty; nor have they at any time since been at any Expence on Account of the Indians & therefore you have now the more reason to Advance what is absolutely necessary for your own safety, for some time, 'till the Neighboring Colonies be brought to contribute their Just proportion of that Expence. -
There is nothing in my power w.ch I will not chearfully do for the Welfare of the province, & safety of the people his Majesty has committed to my care: I have given as strong proofs of this as any Gov.r ever did before me. I shall likewise use my Endeavours that whatever you may give for these Ends shall be as frugally Managed as possible; and that all satisfaction be given you for that purpose either by Accounts or otherwise so far as can be Desired. -
You will see by teh Agreem.t herewith sent you, that the Approbation of the sev.l Governm.ts mus be transmitted to the others as soon as possible: The Season of teh Year makes it necessary to provide immediately for the Cloathing of the Forces at Albany if they are to be continued there at your Expence. -

As the Mutinous spirit which for some time has appeared among the New Levies now posted in the County of Albany seemed to me to be of the most Dangerous Consequences to His Majesty's Service & the safety of this province; And tho' I was far from being satisfyed that it was proper for me to comply with their Demand of their whole pay, I was willing as much as may be to comply with your Advice so far as I thought consistent with my Duty to his Maj.y in the care of those his people that he has Committed to my Charge as Gov.r of this province, & consistent with the Duty that every Man owes to himself & his family; I thought I might be Justifyed on both these respects by having the opinion of the Assembly with yours to pay the whole & your Indemnification as to what risques I must run in my private Fortune by taking that Step, The Assembly's answer to my Message I now lay before you, & as it appears to me in the manner in which that answer is given that they have been so far from having that Tenderness for me & the people they represent, w.ch I might have Expected, that they have not been able to keep within the Rules of usual Decency towards a person that they honour with the Title of the Kings representative. - And upon this pressing Occasion I shall lay before you the reasons which in my Judgem.t makes it not proper to comply with your Advice. It appears from the Duke of Newcastle's Letter that Gen.l S.t Clair or some other person would receive his Maj.'s Orders for the payment of the Troops, but I have received no such Orders, no one of teh Gov.rs of any of the Colonys which Levied Forces have paid any of the Troops Levied in their respective Colonys & I have no other Orders than what the other Gov.rs have; As to the Forces raised in Virginia tho' they have received pay that mony was from the Treasury of that Country & was an Inducem.t for me to expect the like from this Colony. It is probable his Majesty hath before this time taken some Method for the paym.t of these Troops, & if I sho.d now Draw Bills on the Pay Office this might be inconsistent with the Method his Maj.y has already taken, for Example Spanish mony may be already Ordered for this purpose as less Chargeable than by Bills of Exchange; But besides these Gen.l Considerations you know that it was agreed in Council not to be prudent to pay the Men their whole pay, but only {?] [?] of the Arearages thereby to prevent their Desertion. It was likewise thought to be against all Rules of good Policy to pay Men while they remained in their Mutinous Disposition, as it is truly rewarding them for a Crime of the highest & most Dangerous Nature, while they remain in this Disposition what Security can be given that the Complying with their present Demand will satisfy them, If they find that by threatening to Desert & to plunder their Country for their pay is a certain means to obtain it, may not
