not this Encourage them to make further Demands, even such as none at present think of [?] their Threatening be the only reason (as it is the only reason that I know for your [?] your Opinion that it was not prudent to pay the whole pay) this reason must be as [?] for any other Demand they shall please to make, & must have the same Force since that Argum.t can be well resisted now as at any time hereafter, when ever the Force come to be paid their whole pay; An Account must be made for every single Man from the Day of his inlistm.t, abatem.ts must be made for Cloathing & other Incidents, w.ch are paid for by Act of Parliament out of the Mens pay, & the Exchange must be settled, Now [?] Men think fit to find fault with any Article (however Just according to the Established R[?] of the Army that Article may be) the have no more to do but to threaten to Desert plunder & their Demands must be complyed with. They may even think it unreasonable their paym.t should be so long Delayed as shall be necessary to settle the Acco:t & they may Summerly resolve what shall be the pay, for if Force & Threatening are the Sure Argum.t to persuade us I cannot see but that it is as good an Argum.t for Forty Shill.s a Month as for Twenty, This reasoning seems to be too well founded on the Nature of Man who have Discovered the power of their own Force to doubt of their making use of it. [?]  this is Confirmed by Captain Honeyman's Information taken before you, wherein he Asser[?]  that if the other Troops Deserted the Jersey Troops would go off with them notwithstanding that they have received their whole pay, & it is hardly to be supposed that their [?] in this Case would prevent their Joining with the others likewise in the Plunder I am likewise Informed that the Numbers of Desertions in the Jersey Forces has not been [?] since that time they received their whole pay, Ad all the Officers agree that M.r Schuyler paying the Jersey Forces their whole pay is the reason why the others will not be contented with less, so that there is an Evident proof that the satisfying one Demand made with threatning naturally makes place for another Demand to be made with the same Argum.t, & which in all Cases where it is not resisted must have the same force . .  If it should so happen that the Mutinous Disposition sho.d continue after they have received their whole pay, or the Men Desert with their pockets full, may I not expect to be asked how I came to pay the Men in this Manner without any Order & against all the Rules of Discipline, & may not this be a good reason to refuse the paym.t of my Bills, & I & my Family must be in that case left to the Discretion of those who in more than one Instance have shewn what affection they have for me. [? faded]
Now Gentlemen I have given you my reasons for my op[? faded] you consider them & to shew me wherein they are Defective, & what Arg[? faded] contrary opinion & that this be done in writing that I may have an opportunity of [? faded] considering the Argum.ts on both sides in order to form a proper & final Resolution there[?] w.ch purpose I shall now leave you to consider this Matter by yourselves without Adding any more but that this Consideration will not Admit Delay, since the 15.th of this Month is the time to w.ch the Mutineers have fixed the putting their Threats in Execution. -

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(3)
Resolved Nemine Contradicente. -
That his Excellency's Declaring, that he will receive nothing from this house at this time, but what relates to his Message of the 6.th Instant, is irregular & unprecedented & manifestly tends to the Rights, Liberties & priviledges of this house, & of the people they represent. -
Resolved Nemine Contradicente. -
That whoever Advised his Excell.y to send this Message has attempted to undermine & Infringe the Rights & priviledges of this house; to Violate the Liberties of the people; to Subvert the Constitution of this Colony, & is an Enemy to the Inhabitants thereof.
                                     -------------------------------
About half an hour past 11 as I was in my parlour with Coll.l Johnson, Coll.l Phillips Lot & Beckman, & Maj.s Cruger & Thomas came at once upon me without any previous Notice, & notwithstanding my Message of Yesterday, M.r Clarkson pulled a paper out of his Bosom, & without and Ceremony was going to read it, I immediately stopped him & asked what it was, & what he was going to do, he then told me it was their Remonstrance that he was going to read, & asked where the Speaker was, his answer was that such things were frequently done by a Committee of the house in England; I told him I did not beleive any such thing, & that it was never done here without first asking if I would receive it or not, & said I made no doubt but that they had been considering the affair some time, & therefore I should take time to consider of it, especially as they came to me in so rude & obrupt a Manner. M.r Clarkson then offered to leave it with me without reading of it, which I refused. notwithstanding which they printed it in their Votes & publick papers, & Dispersed it all over this & the Neighbouring provinces
                                     -------------------------------
[Left margin info truncated and indecipherable]
This afternoon I gave my Answer to the Indians, & made them presents of £60. from the province. -
                                     -------------------------------
[Left margin info truncated and indecipherable]
Gentlemen: I have the pleasure to perceive from the 1:st of your Resolves to the 8:th Instant communicated to me by Order of your house, that the Scheme concerted by the Commiss.rs of this Colony, with those of Massachusetts Bay & Connecticut has rec,d so ready an Approbation since it Differs in nothing material from the Plan which I told

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(4)
told you in my Speech of teh 17.th of October, last Year, I had concerted with M.r Shirley & M.r Warren at that time, but that then the Scheme which I had concerted was put in Execution principally at the Charge of the Crown, whereas it must be [?] at the Charge of these Colonies; and that the Execution of mine did not Depend on so many uncertainties as this must do.-
Before the Meeting of these Commiss.rs I had likewise the pleasure to see the plan which I had concerted for the Security of the Frontiers, before I left Albany last Year, & which was Communicated to the Council of this Province, was [?] lately approved of by the Council that it was unanimously made an Instruction to the Commiss.rs of this Province, to Endeavour by all means to have one or mor Forts built at the Carrying place at the Joint Charge of these Colonies for the Security of the Frontiers, which is the very same thing I intended to have done last Year at the Charge of the Crown, when the Execution of it was so far retarded by [?] Commiss.rs withholding the provisions & other Disappointm.ts that it became Impracticable in that Season, & the continuance of the same Clogs upon the provisions, by your Acts, has rendered it impracticable at any time since. -
I am at a Loss to conceive what can be meant by the following words in your 4:th Resolve, viz.t "That the Committee is persuaded that his Maj.'s Orders to his Excellency with respect to Indian Presents are still Subsisting." If you mean I have not fully Executed his Maj.'s Orders, but that something still remains to be done; or that his Maj.y has not Determined his Orders, I must ask you who persuaded you to think so? what Evidence you have now before your house to persuade you, that either I have not fully Executed his Maj.'s Orders, or that he had not Determined them? Was ever his Maj.'s pleasure Communicated to any Assembly of this Province otherwise than by the Governour? Can it be immaginded that any Gov.r in his Senses would Avowedly & publickly Declare any thing to be his pleasure, that really was not so? or in the most Solemn Manner, refuse to do [?] thing which his Maj.y had Ordered him to do? But to proceed: no Man need be at any Loss to perceive the View & purpose of the following words of this Resolve. viz.t - "That tho' by sev.l Informations it appears, that his Excellency has the Summer last past made large Drafts on the Crown on the head of Indian Affairs, & no Disposition thereof for that purpose has yet been heard of." 
Now, Gentlemen, I will Venture to say, that notwithstanding of your [?] this

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(5)
this in such strong Terms, you know not, that one Word of it is truth, for tho' it may be true, that I have made large Drafts on the Crown, Yet this could not appear to you as a House by any Information; because you in that Capacity had no Information of it; for which I appeal to your own Minutes, tho' some of you may know something of it as Merchants yet the far greatest Number of you know nothing of it but by Blind faith in their Leaders. How can it be said that no Disposition of any Mony I have received on these Draughts has been heard of? this is as bold a falshood as ever came from any Body of Men. You assert that no person has heard of such Disposition; it is impossible for you to know this, otherwise than by full prove before you that none of that mony was Disposed of or that it still remains in my hands; And of this you have not the least appearance of Evidence, while you thus Endeavour to throw so gross a Slaunder on you Gov.r's Character. on the contrary I may ask whether there be any person of the least Note or Curiosity in this County, who has not heard of sev.l parties of Indians sent out at sev.l times against Canada last Summer, & since, & of no less than 600 Men Marching at one time? and that very considerable Numbers of Indians have been from time to time Cloathed & Armed & constantly found with provisions; & that sev.l persons both whites & Indians have been sent among the Distant Nations, with presents to Engage them in our Interest, & to bring their fighting Men to us; and Messages have been continually passing back & forwward on these & such like occasions.
Let me ask you whether this Province has paid one farthing of any Expence upon these Occasions? for you must know it: And if this Province did not, who must pay all this great Expence, if I did not? Nay, tell me who was capable of doing it without making large Drafts for it? -
It is well known how Difficult it was, before the Treaty I had last Year at Albany, to get a Dozen or a Score of Indians, to go out to Scout, & what a Charge these small Numbers cost; and now Coll.l Johnson Engages to bring a Thousand or more together, upon any reasonable notice.
It appears from M.r Johnson's Examination taken before a Committee of Council, and Communicated by me to you, at the time my Message was sent, that the far greatest Numbers of the Sachems were in the french Interest; that they had received Belts from the Gov.r of Canada; that since I Employed that Gentleman in Consequence of the promises they had made me, they had given up these Belts & were Entered heartily into the

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(6)
the War against Canada; and that mny Numerous Indian Nations living at so great Distance from us, whose Names are but lately known to us are now Courting our Friendship & ready to Declare against the french: Can any Man in his Senses immagine, that all these things could be done without a large Expence of mony? But Gentlemen, as to whatever Sums I received by these Draughts, I am in no Sense accountable to you; since none of it was given by you; neither are you Judges of the Disposition of it; nor if any Accounts of the Disposition were laid before you, can you give a Discharge or Acquittance for a single penny of it; & therefore you have not anything to do with it. -
The making peace & war, Treating with foreign Nations, & all the Executive part of Governm.t, are indisputed parts of the Kings prerogative; & at last before you conclude your Resolves, you discover for what purpose this Vile Slander is thrown up your Gov.r, with no less View, than to wrest his Maj.'s Authority out of the hands of his Governour, & to place it in the hands of the Men, with whom you propose to Deposite the mony; for since nothing ca be done without Mony; then the Gov.r cannot do any thing with the Indians, but at the pleasure of these Men with whom the Mony is Deposited, & by that means you, or rather a Faction among you, [?] the Governours of both Governour & Indians. -
Your fifth Resolve shews how little you consider the Danger of the Garrison at Oswego, at this time, & the Difficulties that may Attend the sending any Relief or any provisions thither. -
Your Zeal for Encouraging the Indians in prosecuting the war against Canada, I am sorry to see in what Manner if appears by your Sixth Resolve: when the Indians of the Six Nations Declared war against the french last year at Albany. they made it a Condition, that while their young Men were out fighting our Battles for us, the old Men, women & Children sho.d be taken care of by us, & protected; and for that purpose, desired to have one or two places Fortifyed at our Expence, in each Nation. This, in itself, appeared so reasonable, that I believe no Man in his Senses can think it ought to have been refused, and if I had refused it, & thereupon the Indians had Declined Joining us in the war, you would not have failed to have blamed me. What regard you have to the honour of this Governm.t & Justice to the Indians, appears from this Resolve; when to shew your thankfulness to the Indians, who have Exposed their Lives, & are ready again to Expose their Lives in Defense

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(7)
Defense of the people of this Province; and when they desire assistance from us, for the safety of their old Men, Women & Children: you, Gentlemen, in Effect say, we will take no more care of you that those will who live many hundred Miles from you, & never received any immediate Defence from you, & if they will not we will not.-
Pray, Gentlemen, from whence do you Expect certain & undoubted Advice, that the Forces at Albany are to be Discharged from his Majesty's Pay? Did you or any Assembly receive any Orders or Advice directly from his Maj.y or his Ministers, or otherwise than from the Governour of this Province? The Forces at Albany are under my Command only, & you never will know any thing of his Maj.y's pleasure about these Forces but from me, or from my Successor. This Resolve seems a very forced Introduction of a very modest Claim of the Command of the Army under the Title of Regulations: But, Gentlemen, I can tell you that, while you are this in vain mispending the time in making regulations of his Maj.y's Forces, which ought to be Employed in making provision for the safety of the Inhabitants of this Province; you will soon have none of these Forces at Albany to make any regulation about them, if you do not accept of them under such Regulations as His Majesty thinks proper; & this you can only know from me; and you must accept of them on the footing I proposed, or not accept of them at all. His Maj.y will not part with the least Branch of his Prerogative relating to Military Affairs; nor dare I, nor will I give up the least Branch of it on any Consideration, however desirous you may be to share in it, or to have the whole Command. -
And, to put this your Claim of the Command of the Army out of Dispute, you send your Orders next to me, relating to the Fort at Saraghtoga; & this you do at a time when some of you at least know, that tho' I heartily Inclined to do all that you now desire of me, it is at this time Impracticable. -
The Design of these Resolves will too Evidently appear, to all Considerate Men, to be no other than by raising a most unreasonable Clamour against me; or, what was not in my power to prevent, to throw an unjust Odium on my Administration when at the same time what may have happened is principally occasioned by the unreasonable opposition you have made to all reasonable Measures which were concerted to prevent it. -
You have not by the Constitution of the Governm.t any share in the Execution of Military Orders; you are not from the Nature of things capable of Judging of these Matters

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(8)
Matters, because you cannot pretend to [?] that knowledge or skill that is necessary for this Service; neither can you have suff:t Information to know what is [?] on the sev.l Events which may arise every Day in Military 
Affairs. -
I formerly told you that the Frontiers of this Province could not be secured by Fort, so as in any manner to prevent the Incursions of the Enemy; and in I have the unanimous consent of all who are capable of Judging, & who have Information to Judge; and what has happened to that Fort I forewarned you in my former Messages, was likely to happen, unless you gave me proper assistance to preserve it which you have not done: It has occasioned a heavy Expence [?] Crown in the Reliefs that became too frequently necessary; nothing has Caused so Disasatisfaction among the Soldiers, as their being sent to that Garrison, & more have been lost by it's Disadvantageous Situation, than by any other Cause in the Commencem.t of the war: It was at first placed there by Commiss.rs recommended to me by the Council as the properest persons to be Entrusted, who as has been [?] Discovered, had not the publick benefit in View, but to preserve some Quantitys of Wheat their own property, & then growing. -
No reason can be assigned for continuing a Garrison in that place, but as a step towards Canada, in case the Expedition had gone on this Summer, & because some of the warlike Stores for that Expedition were Lodged there, & that the [?] an Advanced post might give Discouragem.t to the Indians our friends, but who it could not be longer maintained without hazarding a total Dissolution of the [?] at Albany, & the Loss of the Cannon & Stores Lodged there, it became absolutely necessary to withdraw the Cannon & Stores, & to prevent the Enemy taking Advantage by those Misfortunes, & which were in a great Measure occasioned your behaviour in opposition of the Measures I had taken & Represented you as necessary for securing that Post. I must leave it to his Maj.'s Ministers to Judge, whether I have not done every thing Incumbent on me, or in my power on this Occasion, & to Judge whether you have done your Duty for his Maj.'s Service & the safety of the people whom you Represent.
Finding by the Minute of your proceedings since the last prorogation, that you were going upon Numerous Matters, & Bills, some of them of small Weight and Consequence

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(9)
Consequence at this time, when I think the Province to be in the greatest Danger, & when I thought all things ought to be postponed to the Consideration of the Subject Matter of the Message I sent you the first Day of your Meeting, for Securing the Frontiers & the Lives & Estates of the Inhabitants  of this Province; I sent the Message the 8.th of this Month to incite you to proceed on the Subject Matter of the first Message without Delay; & for that purpose I told you that I would receive nothing from you on any other Subject, 'till I should know your Resolutions as to the Securing the Frontiers, & the safety of the Province; after which you may have time enough to consider any thing else which you may think proper. -
The next Day after you received this Message, you Ordered the Door to be Locked & the Key to be laid on the Table: For what purpose was this Farce Acted on this Occasion? was there any appearance of any person without Doors attempting to break in upon you or did any of your own Members seem willing to run away? I am well assured that was not the Case. Was it then to assume a power to shut me out, that I might not have access to you by Message, or otherwise? if so, the doing of it is a high insult on his Maj.'s Authority, & a withdrawing of your Allegiance for that time. -
But, Gentlemen, wherein by this Message did I encroach upon your undoubted Rights & priviledges? I told you what I would do, or not do myself: that is, I would receive nothing from you 'till I knew your Resolutions for securing the province: I imposed nothing on you by that Message. Have not I Liberty to Act as well as you? And may I not complain of any Encroachm.t upon my Liberty & Authority as well as any other Subject or Officer of the King?
Consider, Gentlemen, by what Authority you sit & Act as the Gen.l Assembly of this Province; I know of none but by the Authority of the Kings Commission & Instructions to me which are alterable at hi Majesty's pleasure. you seem to place it upon the same Foundation with the house of Commons of Great Britain; & if I mistake not, you, by the Resolves of the 9.th of this Month, Assume all the priviledges & Rights of the house of Commons of Great Britain: If so, you Assume a Right to be a Branch of the Legislature of the Kingdom, & deny your Dependance & Subjection on the Crown & Parliament. If you have not the Rights of the house of Commons of Great Britain; then the giver of that Authority by which you Act has

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(10)
has, or can put, Bounds & Limitations upon your Rights & Priviledges, & alter them at pleasure; & has a power to restrain you when you Endeavour to Transgress them. And I must now tell you that I have his Maj.'s Express Command, not to suffer you bring some Matters into your house, or to debate upon them; and for that reason Custom has been long Established of the Clerk of your house, to shew every Day to Gov.r the Minutes of the proceedings of your house; and it is an undutifull behavior to keep any Secret from me, that is under your Consideration.-
In short, Gentlemen, I must likewise tell you, that every Branch of the Legislature of this Province, & all of them together, may be criminal in the Eye of the Law and there is a power able to punish you, and that will punish you if you provoke that power to do it by your misbehaviour; otherwise you must think yourselves independant of the Crown of Great Britain. But before I conclude on the head thee Extraordinary Resolves, I cannot but take Notice of that unhappy [?] taken up by you Members of the present Assembly, of ordering me to be served from time to time with Copys of your Resolutions; this is a Method no way Warranted any practice in parliam.t (whose practice you think ought to be the Rule of your Conduct) it is highly disrespectfull to that Authority which his Maj.y has placed in me, & is an Assuming, in some Sense an Authority over me, & a Direction to my Conduct; For what purpose else can this be done? Since without this, by practice Established ever since a Gen.l Assembly sat in this Province the proceedings thereof, are Duly Communicated to the Gov.r, and in pursuance of His Maj.'s Commands all your proceedings ought to be communicated that the Governour put a stop to them, when they become disorderly or undutyfull to his Majesty, or perhaps Criminal. -
This leads me to consider a most indecent behaviour of some of the Members of your house, who in a Quarter of an hour after I was served with a Copy of your said Resolves of the 9:th Instant, came into an Appartm.t of my house, where was then Busy, and without the least previous Notice, one of them offered to [?] a large bundle of papers, which he said was a Remonstrance from your house Does every private Man in this Country think his own house his Castle, & must your Gov.r; when in his private Apartment, be this intruded upon? would any private Man

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(11)
Man bear such behaviour in a Stranger, and must your Gov.r bear it with patience? I think therefore, from such behaviour, without any other, I had too much reason to refuse to receive it, or to suffer it to be left with me: And from some past Representations which have been openly made by your house, I never will hereafter receive any thing from your house in publick, the contents of which is not previously Communicated to me in private; that I may Judge whether it be necessary for his Majesty's Service & publick good, to give Access to me for that purpose. -
Gentlemen, I must likewise on this occasion observe to you that at the opening of the present Session you did not as usual, acquaint me with your being a house in order to receive from me what I should think necessary for your Consideration at this tim; and as I believe that you cannot give any Instance where this has been omitted by any Gen.l Assembly of this Province, before this time, I must think that this omission was with design: before I had any opportunity of speaking or sending any Message to you, you Entered upon sev.l Resolves (Viz.t) -
You Resolve to take the State of the Province & of the Frontiers into your Consideration but without doing this, or receiving any Information of the State of the Province, or of the Frontiers being laid before you.-
That the late & frequent Adjournm.ts & prorogations I had made of the Assembly have occasioned Interruptions in providing for the Defence & Security of the Frontiers. Now, Gentlemen, is not this an Encroachm.t upon the Kings Authority in my hands. & a taking upon yourselves a superiority over & controlling power of that Authority, without acquainting me with any reasons you had for taking the State of the Province into your Consideration. -
In the same Breath you resolve to make a Remonstrance upon the State & Condition of the Colony; and without resolving what shall be the Subject Matter of that Remonstrance, you Order a Committee to draw it up: The Committee in a very little time bring in their Remonstrance into the house, and it will beyond Contradiction appear, from the Minutes of the proceedings of your house, the time when you met, & the time when the Committee brought it to my house, that there was scarcely time to read it hastily over; & that it was impossible for the house to form any rational Judgm.t on what your Committee had done. Is this acting like rational

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(12)
Rational Men? Is this following precedents of the Parliam.t of Great Britain w.ch you pretend so much to immitate? No I'll Defy any Man to give any precedent of this Nature, unless it was in that house of Commons, that had resolved to take [?] the King's Life, & to overturn the Established Governm.t Nay Ill Defy any Man to shew that the Council or Gen.l Assembly of any Nation ever Acted in this Manner by where a faction had resolved to usurp the whole Authority & power over the Nation. -
I had reasons why I would not then take Notice of those Insolent Representatives as would have become me; But now that those reasons are removed, & on this Occasion, when I have reason to believe the like Insolence was intended, I must tell you that you therein not only forgot all kind of Decency or respect, to the Authority which his Maj.y has been pleased to Intrust me with over this Province (not to mention the regard which every Man of any tolerable Manners must think due to the Family where I had my Birth) but you thereby Endeavour to make me lose all Esteem among the people, & to render it as far as is in your power impracticable to do that Service which is required of me, in opposing the Enemy I further say, that without any regard to truth, yoou therein boldly asserted sev.l things, which from the Minutes of your proceedings can be proved that you knew to be falso; and in order to Excuse yourselves with the people, for Denying the necessary Supplys for carrying on the War against the Enemy, & for Defence of this Province; you Endeavour to Infuse in the MInds of the people; that I [?] to publick mony to my private use. But what little pretence you had for that Imprudent Assertion may appear to Strangers as well as to those better acquainted with the Affairs of this Governm.t when it is made known to them, that all the publikk mony of this Province, that came in any Manner into my hands in past Years, since my Arrival in this place, to be Disposed of by me for his Maj.'s Service or for the Service of this province did not in the whole, amount to little more than Eighteen hundred pounds this Currency for the use of the five Nations of Indians & other Indians tributary to them, when I met them at Albany; & who were more numerous there, than on such usual Occasions of Meeting them
NOW let any Man but consider what the Province could suffer by the most sinister

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(13)
Sinister Managem.t on these Occasions, when the Indians were Maintained out of that mony all the time they were at Albany; publick presents were given to all the Nations then there, & private presents, as is well known, were likewise made out of it to the Sachems of every Nation; and a considerable one to the Senekas, for their Claim to Oswego, which had been promised to them by my predecessors, but never performed; and the Indians were out of the same mony, transported in waggons from Schenectady Sixteen Miles to Albany, & from Albany back again to Schenectady,  with Provisions for their Journey: Now suppose what you please to have been saved by the most Sinister Means, Nay, suppose that all the mony which came into my hands, had been converted to my private use; could this Justify your proceedings, which by the Commiss.rs witholding the Provisions for the Forces, and your Justifying them in so doing, & refusing the other necessary Supplys, you did as much as your power prevent my doing that Service, which I concerted, Determined & was about to have done for annoyance of the Enemy & protection of the people of this Province? I say, supposing what you insinuated had been true, this never could have Justifyed you in your past & present Conduct; But, I assert your Insinuations are false; & which I shall make appear, whenever that Point shall properly come in Question. -
Had teh saving of the Country's mony been truly your Design, you would have in the first place privately acquainted me with any  Information you had on that head; & if I could not have satisfyed you, you might have applyed in some Manner to the King for Redress; which would have shewn at the same time the regard you had for his Authority, in the Character of his Governour. But to put it our of Question that the saving of mony to the people you Represent, was no part of your View; I need only observe, that since I had the Administration of this Governm.t, above Sixty Thousand pounds has been put into the hands of Commiss.rs Named by you, And none of them have been, to my knowledge, called to Account by you to this Day: is it because all Men in this Province, excepting your Gov.r, are incapable of turning any part of the publick mony to their private use? or because all of them were either of your own Number, or near Relations to some of you, or in special friendship with the Leading Men among you -
But the Spirit of those Representations  becomes still more Evident by the Malice

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(14)
Malice which appear in them, against those who in any manner Endeavoured to support [?] in my Administration; when you took upon you to Judge of their hearts, without Assigning on single Act to support the heavy Calumnies you Endeavoured you Endeavoured to throw upon them; and that in a manner that every Man who has the least Sense of honour, would be ashamed of in private Life, but much more unbecoming the Characters of the Representatives of a people who have any Sense of moral honesty: But this will be so far from doing an Injury to such persons Characters if you Establish their good Character, when after you shew so great an Inclination to Discover faults & Blemishes, you have not been able to point out one. -
I must before I leave this Subject take Notice of your refusing to supply the Independ.t  Companys of the Kings Troops with Provisions, who are posted at Albany in your Defence. It is well known that these Troops cannot at this tim subsist there on their Pay, as they have no means of supporting themselves otherwise when from Duty; or if they could support themselves, is it reasonable is it reasonable to think they could be satisfyed to serve for pay alone, when the New Levies in their sight have as good Pay & Provisions besides: This your refusal can have no other Tendency but that of the Dissolution of these Troops: and for whatever reason you may desire this it is my Duty to prevent it; and therefore if these Troops be not there furnished with provisions by you, I must withdraw them all into some other parts of the Province, where they can Subsist.
Now, Gentlemen, reflect from whence this so long continued unbecoming Conduct to your King & Country can arise. It seems to me that it can arise from no other but one or more of the following Motives. -
A firm principal of Disloyalty, that you would Endeavour by all Means in your power to deliver up the Country to the Kings Enemies. -
Or in favour of that shamefull Neutrality, which it is generally beleived [?] in this province have Endeavoured to Establish between this Province & Canada at this time, such as was Established in the war in Queen Ann's Reign, by which the french in Canada gained great Advantages over the Neighboring Colonies to the prejudice of the Common Interest of the Nation. -
A Design to overturn the present Constitution of the Governm.t by thus throwing the Administration into Confusion; Or Lastly

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(15)
Lastly to satisfy the Pride & private Malice & Rancour of a few Men at the hazard  of the Lives & Estates of your Constituents.  That such there are in this Country is no Secret, nor what share they have in your private Consultations. -
Gentlemen.
I have again & again when you had fallen into unreasonable heats and passions, so as to break out into Indecent Expressions, & undutifull behaviour, Adjourned or prorogued your house, that you might have time to cool; & to give you what Example I could, in preventing the Renewal of any past Differences: you cannot find one Instance wherein at the opening of any Session, I seemed to have any remembrance of any Differences which had appeared in the preceding Sessions; your behaviour has been quite otherwise; you omitted no opportunity to renew Differences, & often to lug them in head & shoulders, this among many other things will Evidently shew, whether you or I have had the safety of the people of this Province most at heart, in this time of Danger. And now, Gentlemen, when you have reason to expect a proper Resentm.t from me, I will Disappoint you once more. all these Aspersions you have Endeavoured to throw on me, cannot hurt my Character with those whose Esteem I value; & you are not capable of making a proper Reparation for the Injuries you have Attempted to do. -
And therefore I shall again recommend to you to make the necessary Supplys for the Security of the Frontiers & for preserving the fidelity of the Indians, & their Encouragem.t in prosecuting the War against the French; as I did by my Message at the opening of this Session; & that you Dispatch this Affair without Delay, by not intermixing any other Business than can be as well done afterwards as now, 'till all that is necessary be compleated by these Bills being passed your house; because no Man can tell what Inconveniences may arise, or what Mischiefs may happen every Day to the Inhabitants on the Frontiers. -
I am well assured that the Gov.r of Canada has too good Information of what passes in this Province; these open & publick Differences among ourselves may Encourage him to make Attempts, which otherwise he never would have thought of - And

The house (according to Order) resolved itself into a Committee of the whole house upon his Excellency's Message of the 19.th Instant: After some time spent therein, M.r Speaker resumed the Chair, & M.r Nicol reported the Opinion of the Committe thereon, which he Read in his place, & afterwards Delivered in at the Table, where the same was again read, & is as follows - Viz.t -
The Committee having maturely considered that part of his Excell.y's Message relating to the furnishing such Sums of mony or Credit as may be wanted to pay the Forces Levied in this Colony on the Expedition against Canada, untill provided for by parliament; are under the Deepest concern, that the present deplorable Condition of this Colony obliges them to give their Opinions, that this Colony having been put to a vast & almost insupportable Expence ever since the Commencem.t of the French War, for the Defence of it's Frontiers (continually Exposed to the Incursion of the Enemy) which has been greatly increased by the Charges Attending the Levying & supplying with provisions the Sixteen Companys of One hundred Men each, raised in this Colony on the Expedition intended against Canada, an Expence greatly beyond it's Just proportion; it's Northern Settlem.ts being also many of them over run & Destroyed, & Numbers of it's Inhabitants Murdered or carryed into Captivity, is altogether unable to bear the great & heavy Additional Expence now proposed; and therefore the Committee most humbly hope, that his most Gracious Majesty, whose glorious Character it is always to consult the Ease & happyness of his people, will not be Displeased, that this his loyal, tho' now almost ruined Colony (in regard of it's at present Distressed Scituation of Affairs) is, tho with the greatest regret, obliged to Decline Advancing such Sums of mony or Credit, as may be wanted to pay the Forces Levied in this Colony on the Expedition intended against Canada; it's publick Treasury being entirely Exhausted, & it's funds already Anticipated by it's many great and pressing Occasions. -
Resolved That the house doth agree with the Committee in their said Opinion. -

Gentlemen./. In the Minutes of the proceedings of your house on Saturday last,  communicated to me as usual, by the Clerk, I find the following Resolves; 
"The Committee having maturely considered his Excell.y's Message of the 24.th Instant are extreamly surprized, that his Excell.y should now recommend it the house to make provision for large Detachments of the Militia, for the Defence (as it is said) of the Frontiers &c.a -
Did not I by my Message of the 19..th of last Month (to which you likewise refer in the same Resolve) recommend to you by his Maj.'s Orders to Advance or give Credit for such Sums of mony as shall be necessary for the Pay of the Forces Levied in this Province on the Expedition against Canada! & did not I propose to you to retain, for the Defence of this province, so many of those Forces as you should be willing to pay on the same Terms or Rates on w.ch they Entered into his Maj.'s Service? have you complyed with any of the Terms of that Message? Have you not refused to give the King Credit for such Sums as may be necessary to pay those Forces 'till provision be made by parliament? have you not by your Speaker Communicated to me the Terms on which you are willing to pay Eight Companys of the New Levies - Viz.t by reducing the pay of Captains to Eight Shill.s pDay, & the Subalterns to 4.s pDay current

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:

Current mony of this Province; which is reducing their pay to less than one half of the British Establishment; such pay as no Man, who deserves to be Entrusted will accept, being less than what Tradesmen & Daily Labourers Earn in their Occupations in this Province in peace & quietness, without any risque to their persons? Will any Man undertake, or can any Man give reasonable hopes, that Eight Companys can be retained otherwise than by paying what is due to the Officers & Men & continuing them on the same footing on which they were inlisted? I formerly told you, & I now repeat, that I have no hopes of retaining them otherwise than in the manner I proposed. If then the new Levies cannot by retained, must not the Frontiers be Expoosed to the Enemy, by these Forces leaving the Frontiers? & may not the Inhabitants of this Province be Exposed to great Disorders, if the New Levies return in Discontent, & without any Cloaths or provisions, from the places where they are now posted, & March in Arms through the Country, provoked by your Contempt of their Services? Is it not my Duty to do all in my power to prevent the Mischiefs which I foresee on Events not only possible but likely to happen? -
Is there any Method remaining in my power, under this State of Affairs, to prevent these Mischiefs but by the Militia of this Province? & ought not the Militia of this Province to be in readiness, & suitably provided for the March on all Events in time of War, & when the province may be suddenly Attacked by a powerful & cruel Enemy? I confess that the Method of Detachments must prove very greivous to most, if not to all those to whom the Lot shall fall but perhaps this does not weigh so much with you, & others, who know themselves to be priviledged against such hardships; otherwise you would with more Compassion, think of relieving your Neighbors from such hardships, that you would very unwillingly lay on yourselves. I must do all in my power to protect the Lives & Estates of the People under my care, from a Cruel & merciless Enemy; but I cannot do it either in the most effectual Manner or in

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749

(24)
in the Manner least greivious to the Inhabitants, without your Assistance The people, I am assured, are willing to lend their purses for this Service, and their own Ease, if you would allow them to open them: why do you then Counter to the Desires of your Constituents? the time is pressing;  it Admits no Delay; we know not what Advantage the Enemy may Suddenly and unexpectedly take of the present State of Affairs in this province, and which I am afraid they have too good Information. -
It is a Matter of surprize indeed, that the Representatives of a people be doing all in their power, to render their Gov.rs Endeavours ineffectual, the preservation of the people; which your Resolves certainly have a Tendency to do: for what other purpose can this Surprise in you be pub[?] but to occasion Disobedience in the Militia to my Orders? And for what other purpose are the Reflections of unsteady Councils, continually Varying &c.a, out at this time? certainly Councils must Vary as the Events on which [?] are founded, do: you only have given Occasion to any Variation in [?] Councils at this time; but I shall still keep steady, in using my Endeavours with you, to furnish me with the means necessary to preserve the people Committed to my Charge in safety, as much as possible on all Events; I must therefore Exhort you to throw off this Surprize, & Enable me to Defend this Province, & the people in it, in the Manner I recommended to you in my former Messages, & which I am persuaded, must be both the most Effectual & the least grievous to the Inhabitants, of any Method which I heard proposed - G: Clinton

Gentlemen./. You will see by the Papers which I now lay before you that the Forces raised on the intended Expedition against Canada are immediately to be Discharged. -
By this you must perceive that the Frontiers of this Province will be Deprived of the Defence w.ch they now have, I foresaw & Informed the Assembly that this was likely to be the Case, & desired their Assistance to retain a suff.t Number of them for the Defence of this Province - I have done what is in my power by ordering Detachm.ts of the Militia to be in readiness to March for the support of Albany, & Defence of the Frontiers on all Events.-
The Assembly having refused to Advance any mony, or to give Credit for the pay of the Forces Levied in this Province, tho' I have reason to hope the other Colonies will comply with his Maj.'s Demands on them for the Forces raised in those Colonies; And as I am Informed the Assembly propose that the Frontiers be Defended by making New Levies of Volunteers w.ch may be impracticable & certainly cannot be done without a Considerable Loss of time & great Expence I must ask you Advice what is further to be done for the Security of the Frontiers of this province, for the pay of the Troops raised in it, & who are now to be Disbanded by Virtue of this Discharge, & to prevent any Disorders or Inconveniences w.ch may happen upon the Disbanding of these Troops, since it may not be in the power of the Officers to Disarm them & they may be discontented & become Disorderly if they do not receive pay before they are Disbanded. -

And further as his Excellency has been pleased to Inform them that the Assembly have refused to furnish such Sums of mony or Credit as may be wanted to pay the Forces Levied in this Colony for the Expedition against Canada until [?] provided for by parliam.t-
The  Council are humbly of Opinion, that his Excell.y [?] Order application to be made to the Merchants agreeable to the Extract of M.r Shirley & M.r Knowles's Letter of the 29 Ultimo, w.ch his Excell.y was pleased to Communicate to the Council Yesterday, And to Order that a Draft of such a Bill of Exchange as his Excell.y should think proper to Draw for the Monys to be borrowed of the Merchants, be laid before them at the same time.-

Whereas I conceive it highly necessary for his Maj.'s Service, the safety of the province, & Defence of the Frontiers, that a Competent Number of Militia well Armed & Accoutred, should be constant readiness to March upon any Sudden emergency against the Enemy.-
You are hereby required & Commanded in his Maj.'s Name to send the Adjutant or some other proper person as soon as possible to the respective Captains of the Regim.t under your Command, with Orders to each Captain, or in the absence of any Captain to the next Commanding Officer, immediately to call together the Company under his Command, & that while they are under Arms, every Tenth Man shall be pitched upon by Lott to be in readiness to March in four Days after he shall be pitched upon, & from that time to hold himself in readiness fully Equiped with good & suff.t Arms & Ammunition to March at an hours warning.
And that there may be no room for complaint in pitching upon the Men for this Service, the Captain or Commanding Officer of each Company is to Cause a Number of papers equal to the Number of Men in the Company under his Command, on every Tenth paper of which the word (Go) shall be wrote & the other remain blank, all which being put into a Box or hat, each Man shall draw one paper, & they who shall draw a paper with the word (Go) written on it, shall be Ordered to prepare to March as afores.d. If any Man shall be Absent when such Allotm.t is made, the Captain shall Order some other person to draw a Lott for him. -
You are likewise to Order the first Captain, the first or Eldest Lieu.t & Eldest Ensign in your Regim.t to make ready to March with & Command the said Men from the first Detachm.t of the Regiment. If

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(32)
If the Number of Men Ordered to March as afores.d, exceed the Number of Seventy you are to Order one Captain, two Lieu.ts & one Ensign to Command them; If Fifty under Seventy, One Captain, one Lieu.t & one Ensign, if Thirty & under Fifty, one Lieu.t & one Ensign, if Thirty & above Twenty, one Lieu.t, If above fifteen & under Twenty, One Ensign.-
When the Officers & Men so Allotted to March, shall at any time March out of the Country or go upon actual Service, the same Number of Men in each Company respectively shall by Lot be ordered to make ready agreeable to the above Directions & hold themselves in readiness as afores.d, & a like Number of Officers next in Rank, as to Seniority are to be in readiness to Command such Second Detachm.t & such like Allotments are to be made in each Company 'till all the Officers & Men in each Company of your Regim.t shall have taken their turn of Service. -
You are with all possible Dispatch to me return to me, by some safe Conveyance, what shall be done in pursuance of these Orders, & for that purpose every Captain or Commanding Officer of each Company is to make return to you what he shall have done agreeable thereto. -
You are likewise with all convenient speed to send to me an Exact Account of the Number of each Company in the Regim.t under your Command, together with a Roll of the Officers in which their Names are to be placed according to their Rank in Seniority, & also to which Companies the Subalterns belong. -
You are also to give me as full an Acco.t as possible of the State of the Regim.t under your Command, as to Arms, Ammunition or any other thing, of which it may be proper for me to be Informed for the good of his Maj.'s Service & the Security of the Province, & that you constantly make to me Monthly returns thereof And for so doing &c.a - 26.th Octo.r 1747.

May it please your Excellency. -
The great & imminent Danger, to which we apprehend the Northern Frontiers of this Colony will be Exposed the Approaching Winter, without a suff.t Force for their Security, & to repel any Attempts which the Enemy may make on that Quarter; the impossibility of Maintaining any such Force there, without provisions for their Subsistence, And the Apprehensions we are under, that the Severity of the Weather (which from the Advanced Season of the Year we may Daily expect) will render it altogether Impracticable to send any provisions to Albany for that purpose; constrain us, Sir, to make this Application to your Excellency, that the Bill which we have passed for purchasing a Supply of provisions for the Subsistence of such Forces as shall be posted on the Northern Frontiers, & which has already Eight Days since had the concurrence of the Council, may also without further Delay receive your Excellency's Assent; this Bill being no other in Matter & form, than two other Bills which your Excellency has heretofore Assented to, for the like purposes: The present great & pressing Exigency, we humbly hope will plead our Excuse to your Excellency for this Application; And the great Concern & Compassion w.ch your Excell.y professes to have for the people whom our most Gracious Sovereign has Committed to your Care, persuade us, that your Excell.y will not refuse this our humble, reasonable & necessary request   By Order of the Gen.l Assembly

"people of this Province at this time of imminent Danger may Excuse me once more in giving my Assent to the Bill mentioned in this Address; And therefore I resolve to give my Assent to it accordingly; But, at the same time, I must recommend to you to take care, that no Clauses be inserted in the Bill now before your house, for the pay of the Forces to be raised in this province, for the Defence thereof, to which any Just exceptions may be taken as Derogatory to his Majesty's prerogative; & that likewise Clauses may be Added to it, not only to prevent any Misapplication of the mony destined for the pay of those Forces, but likewise for Effectually preventing any Embezelm.t of the provisions, than is done by the Bill to which you desire my Assent; since I have reason to think, that this has not been sufficiently Guarded against by the former Bills, to which this is Similar. The provisions may be sent up to Albany without Delay. 
"By a Representative which I have lately received from the Officers of the three Independant Companys of Fusileers posted at Albany for the Defence of this province; I am Informed a total Dissolution of them is to be feared, it they be not found with provisions, or removed from thence; & therefore I must again recommend this to your Consideration." now lying before him for his Assent, But that one of them, whereby Bills of Credit to the amount of £28,000. are proposed to be Emitted was contrary to a par[?] One of His Maj.'s Instructions to him, whereby he is Directed not to give his Assent to or pass any Act for striking or Issuing Bills of Credit, without a Clause incerted therein, Declaring that the same shall not take Effect untill approved & Confirmed by his Majesty. -

His Excell..y's Speech
to the Assembly]
Your Resolves of the 12?th Instant, & your Order to the printer thereon published in your Minutes, together with your other proceedings makes it necessary to speak to you at this time in different Terms than I wished to have done. 
I must recommend to your Serious Consideration, when cool & free from the Influence of your Leaders, whether (if I had by my Order to the printer of the Gazette, infringed on your privileges) it would not have better become you to

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(37)
to have in some Manner applyed to me on that head: But this Method I suppose did not please; because thereby you could not so Evidently Assume an Authority over me, & to annul & Contradict the Orders of your Gov.r. This may be taken by those who have a Right to Inquire into your Conduct, as a Direct Assuming the Supreme in the Executive part of Governm.t, & which they may think Destructive of your Dependency on the Crown of Great Britain, & of which the people of great Britain may become Jealous.-
Consider likewise that paper published under the Name of a Remonstrance of your house, & your former Representations: They contain sev.l things which you knew to be false, as appears from the proceedings of your house; in others you manifestly Contradict yourselves; from things Notoriously known, it must appear, that what you Assert in other parts of them, is impossible to be true; no where had you any Evidence of the truth of the Facts which you Assert; you were guided by no principal of Action, but that of a blind faith in your Leaders. This must appear to any one who shall consider the Minutes of your proceedings, the time & Circumstances Attending them: all these things I say will appear to any person Attentively considering your Endeavours to throw the Vilest Aspersions on your Gov.r's Conduct. -
Can Falsehood, Slander & Malice, be supported by any other Methods than those which you have taken? would any Man who has the least sence of honour take those Methods to support truth, or to seek redress from any real Grievance, which are only proper to support Falsehood & Mmalice, & propagate Slander? For what purpose are those publications made, when those to whom they are made have no means of Inquiring into the truth of  them, & can give no legal redress to any Injury, if it were real? Can any thing be more pernicious to Society? -
Besides these things observable in gen.l throughout your proceedings, the Method you took to present that Remonstrance (as it is called) could only be with Design, to shew your Contempt of his Majesty's Authority in the Character of his Gov.r

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(38)
Governour of this Province: By that Method you Assume so far an Authority over your Gov.r, that you think it Incumbent on him to know, & to pay a regard your Committees, & to papers signed only by the Clerk of your house. Consider petition usually made by your Speaker when presented to the Gov.r for his approbation; your Speaker only desires access to the Gov.r's  person for himself & when necessary for the publick Service. Take the whole of your proceedings together, & the Spirit of your Actions to plainly appears. -
I must leave it to my Superiours to Judge, whether that printed paper called a Remonstrance of your house, has not Evidently all the Character of a false, Scandalous, & Malicious Libel against your Governour: I must leave to them to Judge, whether I acted as became the Gov.r of this Province, in forcing the printer to Reprint it in his News paper, as I was Informed the Speaker of your house had privately Ordered him to do, after it had been printed in the Votes of your house: I must likewise leave it to my Superiors, to Judge whether I could pass over such a publication in Silence; whether with any regard to my Character, I could take Notice of it in any other Manner which could give less Offence, than what I did; & whether you have Acted like honest Men & Loyal Subjects, in Ordering a Libel against your Gov.r to be reprinted Ten Copys of it to be given to each of your Members, in order to have it Disp[?] all over the Country as is actually done.-
As to the popular Outcry you Endeavour to raise, of the Liberty of the press, I shall only say, that certainly this Liberty as well as any other be abused, to the Injury of others: If any Injury is done, a proper remedy ought to be applyed; and such a Remedy can never be thought a Restraint of any Just Liberty: I am persuaded that no considerate Man can [?] that I offered any Obstruction to the Liberty of the Press, by forbidding the printer to publish that one paper at his peril: if no peril in doing of it: neither Author nor publishers of it can suffer by that Order. the proper Judges may in time shew whether I did a Service or Disservice to any by such Warning.-
You know with what Earnestness I recommended to you, to provide for the necessary Expence of preserving the fidelity & friendship of the Six United

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(39)
United Indian Nations, & other Indians, our friends Engaged in War with the Enemy; & tho' it be now so long since that was laid before you, you have not made the Least Provision for this Service, which none can doubt of being the greatest Importance for the preservation not only of this, but of all the British Colonies in North America: such a neglect can no otherwise be accounted for, but that by the Alteration which may be Expected in the Disposition of the Indians, from the Contempt which (they may apprehend) you have of their past Services, & from other Disappointments they have met with; you may have it in your power to give some Colour to the Vile Falsehoods & Calumnies you have published: in hopes of doing this, all the Mischiefs which may happen, are of no Consideration with you. 
It is also necessary to lay open another Design, which too Evidently appears thro' all your proceedings, & which it's probable you principally had in View. viz.t An Intention to Assume the Superiority in the Administration: For which purpose you throw out all the Aspersions on your Gov.r's Conduct that Malice can Invent, that thereby you might Disable him in retaining him in that Authority over the people of this province, which the King has Entrusted him with. For what other purpose have you Attempted to put in the most Odious Light the Endeavours I took for the safety of this province in this time of Danger? And which I must leave to my Superiors to Judge, whether they were not the most prudent that could be taken under the present Circumstances. -
The reason why it became necessary to keep Secret the Orders for Discharging the Forces raised in America on the Expedition intended against Canada, 'till the time they were to be put in Execution, are now obvious viz.t least the Defence of the Frontiers should be deserted before preparation could be otherwise made for the Defence of them. I gave you however timely Notice of what was to happen, that you might make the provision requisite for that Servic: At the same time I told you in what Manner any Number of the Forces then posted on the Frontiers might be retained with the greatest certainty. You refused to make provision in the Manner I proposed: you took a Different & much more uncertain Method; and after you had fixed on one Method, you Changed

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(40) 
Changed it to another equally uncertain in it's Success; and which on a fair Calculation must put the province to above four thousand pounds more Expence than the Method I proposed. It is well known how Dilatory you have been in your proceedings while the safety of the province required the greatest Dispatch in your Resolutions.
When I perceived the province to be thus Exposed to imminent Danger I took the only Course remaining in my power for the Defence thereof, either in case that the Frontiers should be Attacked by a greater Force than the Number of Men you proposed to pay, could resist.-
As the Dangers of the Enemy might happen suddenly (& when least Expected) it became necessary to put the Militia without Delay, into such a Disposition, that they may be always in readiness on every Emergency: for w.ch purpose I gave Orders, that Detachm.ts may be made of them upon the first Appearance of Danger, that may require more force than may at any time happen to be on or near the Frontiers. I never heard it Asserted that the Orders w.ch I then gave were either illegal or partial; that they either favoured on Man, or were oppressive to another, or that they were unnecessary. -
For what purpose I say then were your Resolves published? which Evidently tended to Create disobedience; & did accordingly produce disobedience to those Orders, which I am confident will appear prudent & necessary for the safety of this Province, to all Judicious & Impartial Men. Could this be done for any other End (,'/ you did not design to give up the province to the Enemy) than to usurp the Command of the Militia (& which was never disputed) must be fruitless & Ineffecual, unless he please to take that Authority from you, & under such Limitations as you shall please to set to it? It is too well known that base Insinuations were industriously spread among the people at that time, in order to carry the Spirit of Disobedience & the passions of Ignorant people to the most Dagerous heights, And how Industrious some of our Members were in propagating the most Mischievous Sentiments for that purpose: as I then publickly Declared that I had no Intention

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(41)
Intention to put the people of this province to any unnecessary trouble, so, since that time, I have done all in my power to prevent it, by my Endeavours to retain as great a Number of the Forces now at Albany, as can be done on the Encouragem.t which you had promised. I hope no bad Event may too Evidently Demonstrate the necessity of the precaution I Endeavoured to take, in having the Militia in readiness for prevention of it.-
Your refusing the King Credit for paym.t of what is due to the Forces Levied in this Province, on the Expedition against Canada, 'till such time as provision shall be made in parliament for that Service, too openly shews what little regard you either have to the Kings pleasure, so reasonably signifyed to you, or his Service; & likewise what little regard you have to those who have been willing to Expose their Lives in the Service of their Country, & have on sev.l Occasions Exposed their Lives in the Defence of this Province. This Contempt of such Signal Services & neglect of Men, who are now in the greatest Distress, arising from their Zeal for their King & Country's Service, must for the future Discourage the like Zeal in all others; & on many Accounts must be Detrimental to the people of this Province.
It is now well known, that if you had complyed with my offers of retaining the Forces posted at Albany, in the pay of this Province, on the Terms I proposed; a suff.t Number of Disciplined Men, Commanded by Gentlemen, could then have been retained; & it is now likewise so Evident, that a suff.t Number of Men cannot at this time be obtained in this Province, by the Method you have taken that the Council has found it necessary to Advise me, to apply to the Neighboring Colonies for Men: untill a suff.t Number can be procured, the Frontiers must remain Exposed to the Enemy; & it must remain uncertain for some time whether a suff.t Number can be procured. Thus from an Obstinacy & some other Temper of Mind, to which it is Difficult to give a proper Name; you are willing to Expose the Lives & Estates of the people you represent, to all the Cruelties & Ravages of a Merciless Enemy, rather than to Comply with any Demand of your Governour, however reasonable or necessary it be, for the Welfare of your Country.-
You

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(42)
You will further Discover your Desire of Assuming the Supreme Authority over all Military Force in this Province, by your Conduct towards the Independent Companys of Fusileers now posted at Albany, for the Defence of this Province & which have been kept in it above Fifty Years at the Charge of the Crown for it's Defence. No Man can say that the private Men can Subsist themselves there on their Pay at this time; or that they can at this time find any other Means for their Subsistance: Nor can any Man think that they can remain contented, to see others who do the same Duty with them, receive double the pay & provisions; while the Country w.ch they protect refuses provisions to them. Does not this plainly tend to a Dissolution of these Companys? And for what reason can this be desired by you at this time, when Men are so much wanted for the Defence of the Frontiers, unless it be that you cannot bear any Military force in this Province, not immediately dependent on you? And for this purpose you are willing to lose these Troops likewise, tho' necessary for the protection of the province. -
But the Bills you have framed for the Defence of the Frontiers, & to which I now give my Assent, for this reason only,  that you have put it out of my power otherwise to save this province from the most imminent Danger: These Bills I say put your Design out of Question. For what purpose do you put the provisions for the Forces at Albany, the pay of them, & the Ammunition Gunpowder & Ball destined for their use into the hands of persons of your own Nomination without Advising or Consulting with your Gov.r in the appointm.t of persons to so great a Trust? But to put it in the power of those persons to controu[?] any Order which your Gov.r shall give.-
The pretence which you Endeavour to Infuse into the heads of the people cannot have the least appearance of foudation, after the Declaration I made to you, that I would give my Assent to any Clauses proper to prevent any kind of Embezlement, or converting of either the Mony or provisions to any other use, than designed by the granting of them. It is well know that Method

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(43)
Method you formerly took, & still continue to take is as open to frauds as any other. It must be surprizing to have it supposed, that Frauds cannot be prevented otherwise than by a Breach or Alteration of the Established Constitution; for this can only be supposed by those who do not understand, or [?] Avowed Enemys to it.-
You have done all in your power to make my Endeavours for the safety of this province, clash & become inconsistent with my Duty to the King, by making the only Means you put in my power for the safety of the people contradictory to his Maj.'s Express Commands; & which you know to be such, & Derogatory to his Authority over you; while you obstinately persist in the same Method: But as I have a Gracious Master, I hope my Zeal for the safety of so many of his loyal Subjects as would otherwise be in Danger, will Excuse me with him, by giving my Assent to these Bills, under the present Circumstances of the province, which Admit of no Delay in preventing the Dangers all are in, but more especially many innocent people on or near the Frontiers.-
What ever vain immaginations your Leaders, or a faction among you may Entertain, I am confident his Maj.y has Numbers suff.t of loyal Subjects in this province, to prevent the ill Effects of the most daring Attempt on his Authority, & which all Men of Sense know, that no Act of this Governm.t can in any Light Deprive him of, or lessen his prerogative in any Circumstance; however vain you may be of your powers; but that every thing Attempted by you to that purpose, must be foolish, as well as Arrogant: Every Act to that Effect is of itself void.-
Many other Instances can be given, of your grasping at power, both Civil & Military, by your Assuming to yourselves the Nomination to offices, & the Sole rewarding of all Services, as in every mony Bill you oass; to which you will allow of no Amendment by the Council in any part of the Bill, how foreign soever to the granting part; neither do you previously Advise or Consult with your Gov.r, either in the Nomination to Offices, or in the rewarding of Services -
Take the whole of your proceedings together, there must appear no only a want of Candour, but open Malice likewise; & as by your repeated publications,  they are become generally a part in Conversation of all people in the Neighboring Colonies

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(44)
Colonies; this Conduct in you the representatives of the people of this province, can give no favourable Sentiments of the probity of the people you represent.-
Your continued grasping at power, with an Evident Tendency to the weakning of the Dependency of this Province on great Britain, accompanied with such Notorious & publick Disrespect to the Character of your Gov.r, & Contempt of the King's Authority Entrusted with him cannot be longer hid from your Superiours, but must come under their Observation, & is of most Dangerous Example to your Neighbours.-
As I know that great Numbers of the Inhabitants of this province Disapprove of the present Conduct of you their Representatives, I cannot at this time do more for the benefit of all, than by putting it in their power to Declare their Sentim.ts, that they may, if they please, vindicate their Loyalty to their prince & Love of the Country on which they Depend, & which protects them. -
Therefore I think it for the Reputation & Interest of this Province, well as for his Maj.'s Service, that the Gen.l Assembly of this Province be Dissolved accordingly. - G: Clinton

The carrying this Agreem.t into Execution tends so Evidently to the Benefit & Security of all the British Colonies in North America; that I think it needless to use any Argum.ts with you, to contribute every thing Incumbent on you to carry it on; & however Chargeable it may be at this time yet when it is considered that a great part of the Annual & heavy Expence, which this Province must bear for the Defence of the Frontiers only, may thereby be saved for the future, I persuade myself the people of this Province will chearfully submit to any Expence w.ch shall be necessary for such beneficial Consequences.-
The Advantages w.ch all the Colonys, but more especially this, may receive [?] from the Friendship & hearty Assistance of the Six united Indian Nations, & the Mischiefs which may come from a contrary Disposition, & their Acting in favour of our Enemys are Notorious: Therefore it will deserve our most serious Attention to Consider, how far their Disposition at this time may be affected, by the Diappointm.ts they have met with from the intended Expedition against Canada being laid aside; from the Disbanding the Forces w.ch were at Albany: & by the Influence w.ch the french Emissaries may gain thereby over them, by Infusing into their Minds, our want of strength or Courage. The humble Address of his Maj's Council of the Province of New York
May it please you Excellency-
We his Maj.'s most Dutiful & loyal Subjects the Members of his Maj's Council for the Province of New York, return your Excellency our thanks for your Speech, & for the readiness you Express therein, to concur in any Measures w.ch shall be proposed to you for his Maj.'s Service, & the Interest of the province.-
We are fully sensible of the Advantage w.ch all the British Colonies on this Continent, as well as this in particular, may receive from the friendship & hearty Assistance of the Six united Indian Nations, & the Mischiefs w.ch a contrary Disposition may produce; and as these as your Excellency observes, are Notorious, it is therefore Evidently the Interest of all the Colonies, to Join together in concerting such prudent Measures, as may most Effectually secure the friendship & Dependence of the Indians & thereby prevent the Evil Effects w.ch would unavoidably follow from the french Emissaries gaining any Influence over them.-
We agree with your Excell.y that peace & unity are always desirable, & we Assure your Excell.y we shall Endeavour to Cultivate them: And your Excell.y may Depend that our known Loyalty to his most sacred Maj.'s person & Governm.t & the regard we have for this Country will always excite us to promote every [?] that has a Tendency to his Maj.'s Service & the Welfare of the Country we live in.

May it please your Excellency./. 
In Obedience to your Excellency's Order in Council the 24:th Instant, referring to our Consideration an Extract of a Letter from His Grace the Duke of Newcastle to his Excellency Gov.r Shirley, Dated the 3.d Day of October last we beg leave to Report our Opinion thereupon as follows -
The Committee observing by the Extract of the said Letter that His Grace is Directed by his Maj.y to recommend it in the strongest Manner to your Excell.y & Gov.r Shirley to Employ your Utmost Dilligence & Attention to Cultivate the friendship of the Six Nations of Indians, & to keep them steadily Attached to the King's Interest & to take care that the necessary Measures may be taken, as well for their protection & Defence against any Attempt that may be made upon them by the French in Revenge for their having Acted against them, as for preserving their Friendship & keeping them strictly Allied to his Majesty, & for that End that such presents be made to them on his Maj.'s part as have been usual, & shall be Judged necessary by your Excellency & Gov.r Shirley: are humbly of Opinion in order to promote these his Maj.'s most Gracious Intentions -
1.st - - - - That some person or persons of Credit & Influence over the Indians be sent into their Country as soon as may be & intrusted to use their utmost Endeavours to Dissuade them from going to Canada, w.ch the Committee think the more necessary at this time, as they have been Informed the Gov.r of that Country hath given them an Invitation to go thither this Ensuing Spring, & to render their Endeavours more Effectual, That they be furnished with proper presents to Distribute among the Indians, as they shall find Occasion & that they be also Directed to Assure the Six Nations that a Conference will be held with them some time the next Summer, at which they will receive further & more Valuable presents.-
2.dly - - - - That for the protection & Defence of the Six Nations against any Attempt that may be made upon them by the French, & also for securing their old Men, Women & Children, when their young Men go out against the Enemy. The Forts already begun to be Erected in some parts of their Countrys be forthwith finished & others Built in proper places, & that the persons to be sent among the Indians as above be Directed to Consult & agree with the sev.l Nations on the most Convenient places for that purpose, And that they be likewise Instructed to use their utmost Endeavours to

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749

to prevail on them to settle themselves as near these Forts as may be, w.ch will tend much to their safety.-
----The Committee conceiving from the Extract of the s.d Letter, that the Destroying the French Settlem.t at Crown point is approved of by his Majesty, Are humbly of Opinion that a Copy thereof be sent to each of the Governours of the Colonies not already Engaged to Assist therein, in order to induce them to Act in Conjunction with the other Colonies in this intended Enterprize & to furnish their proportion of Men & necessary Stores.
----That your Excell.y & Gov.r Shirley do make Application to Adm.l Knowles or the Commanding Officer of His Maj.'s Ship of War, that may then happen to be Stationed at Louisbourgh, to Employ some of the Kings Ships to proceed upon the River S.t Lawrence, in order to Occasion a Diversion, & thereby oblige the Enemy to Divide their Strength while the Attack is carrying on against the French Fort at Crown point.-
----The Committee are further humbly of Opinion, that if your Excell.y & Gov.r Shirley should think proper to Join in Maintaining a Garrison at Crown point, at the Charge of the Crown, in case the proposed Expedition should go on & succeed, It might not only prevail upon the Assembly of the Massachusetts Bay to reconsider the Alteration they have made to the Agreem.t Entered into at New York of the 28:th of September last, but also be an Inducem.t to the sev.l other Colonies to Engage the more readily in this Undertaking.-
----If the Expedition should be proceeded on, the Committee are humbly of Opinion & do desire your Excell.y would be pleased as soon as may be, to Order an Acco.t to be taken of the Battoes, Cannon & Warlike Stores & Implem.ts in this Province provided at his Maj.'s Expence, That the sev.l Governm.ts Engaging therein may provide & furnish their respective proportions of what may be wanting for that Service.-
Lastly ----The Committee are humbly of Opinion that proper Measures may be timely concerted for carrying on the Expedition, & to remove any Difficulties that might otherwise happen & also to prevent any Delay; That the Commiss.rs of Massachusetts Bay, New York & Connecticut do meet as soon as may be at New York or some other convenient place, & that pressing Instances be used to the other Governm.ts
