M:r Chief Justice read & presented, to his Excellency, the Committees Report on the sev.l Letters & papers laid before the Council Yesterday by his Excell.y's Directions which Report, on the Question being put was agreed to, & approved of & is as follows -
May it please your Excell.y./. The Committee have considered the Letter from Gov.r Shirley to your Excell.y which (your Excell.y being indisposed) you Directed to be laid before them and as that part of Gov.r Shirley's Letter which relates to an Enterprize against Crown point, appears to them to require immediate Dispatch, the Committee beg leave to report their Opinion on that head as follows.-
The Committee conceive that an Expedition under taken ag.t the French at this time, when they are Employing all their Arts to withdraw the Six Indian Nations from their Dependance on his Majesty, cannot fail of having a very great Effect in retaining them in his Maj.'s Interest.
And as the Committee think the Engageing the sev.l other Governments to Join in such an Enterprize may in some Measure Depend on the readiness shewn on the part of this Province, They are humbly of Opinion that your Excell.y do send a Message to the Gen.l Assembly on this head, & the more easily to Induce them to Declare themselves chearfully on this point the Committee are of Opinion it may be proper for your Excell.y to signify to them that by his Maj.'s Orders signifyed by his Grace the Duke of Newcastle your Excell.y & Gov.r Shirley are Directed to Employ your Utmost Dilligence & Attention to Cultivate the friendship of the Six Nations of Indians, & to keep them strictly Attached to the King's Interest And that by the Measures already taken, & others to be taken in Consiquence of these Orders

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(62)
Orders, the provinces Joining in this Undertaking will be Eased of a large Article of the Expence, w.ch must necessarily Attend an Enterprize of this kind, & the Committee further conceive, that your Excellency's acquainting the Gen.l Assembly, That in Case of Success your Excellency & Gov.r Shirley will Join in keeping any Forts that may be taken from the Enemy at the Expence of the Crown will have great weight with them: These Considerations & his Maj.'s Declared pleasure in the Case, The Committee think suff.t to prevail on the Gen.l Assembly of this Province to shew their Readiness on this Occasion, And when pressed on the Neighboring Governm.ts, will be powerfull Inducem.ts to Engage them to Join in a Measure calculated so much for his Maj.'s Service, & the Visible Interest of all the Northern Colonies -
The Committee observe, with pleasure, in a paragraph of Gov.r Shirley's Letter that he is intirely of Opinion that the Forts should be finished for the protection of the Indians as proposed by your Excellency, And that the Engaging Coll.l Johnson to go among the Six Nations with an Indian Interpreter to prevent their going to Canada in the Spring, & to prepare 'em for their Joining us in the Enterprize against Crown point, & his making them the presents proposed by your Excell.y & compleating the Forts begun, are Measures Extreamly well concerted for retaining the Indians in his Maj.'s Interest; And that 'till the Enterprize against Crown point is ripe for Execution the Indians with a suitable Number of Christians Joined with them, should be kept constantly Employed in Acts of Hostility ag.t the Enemy, for which the Indians should have a proper allowance by way of pay or present, or in some other Method, of which your Excell.y is the best Judge: Upon Consideration of which, the Committee are humbly of Opinion, that Coll.l Johnson should be Engaged & sent on this Service without Delay, & that the Employing the Indians in the Manner proposed by Gov.r Shirley will be a great Encouragem.t to them, & fix them more steadily in his Maj.'s Interest: And as Coll.l Johnson by his Letter laid before the Committee by your Excell.y's Order conceives the going into the Indian Country without a strong Guard may be Dangerous, the Committee are of Opinion that some few white Men, with a party of Indians will be the properest Guard

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(63)
Guard he can take with him; And that while Coll.l Johnson is on this Service, it would be Expedient to begin a Fort in the Onondaga Country -
And as Coll.l Johnson has Represented to your Excellency the Necessity of having always in readiness a Number of Men for any Sudden Emergency, the Committee are humbly of Opinion that Orders be sent by your Excell.y to the Commanding Officer of the fourteen Companys to keep such a Number of them as he should Judge necessary in readiness for that purpose.-
The Committee are also humbly of Opinion that a Meeting between your Excellency & Gov.r Shirley for concerting proper Measures for carrying into Execution his Maj.'s Commands in relation to the Six Nations of Indians & on Interview with them will greatly Conduce to his Maj.'s Service.-
By Order of the Committee Council Chamber, City of New York, 29:th March 1748 Ja.s De Lancey, Chairman

"I need not repeat to you how great Importance to all the British Colonies in North America to Join together in concerting Measures for Annoying the Common Enemy & that a Vigorous Exertion of our united Strength cannot but afford us well grounded hopes of Success in any Enterprize against them; and as a readiness shewn on the part of this Governm.t, may be an Inducem.t to the Other Colonies to Engage; I Do therefore (with the Advice of his Maj.'s Council) recommend it to you to set the Example; & as I have received Information that the French are Employing all their Arts to withdraw the Six Nations from their Dependance on his Maj.y, it is become necessary to undertake some Expedition against them at this time as the most Effectual Measure to retain the Indians in his Maj.'s Interest.
"That you may the more Chear fully Declare yourselves on this head, I must observe to you, that his Maj.y has signifyed his Approbation of such an Undertaking. I must likewise observe to you, that by the Measures already taken by me in Conjunction with Governour

His Excell.y Communicated to the Board the following papers to wit. An Extract of a Letter from Coll.l Johnson to his Excellency of the 14.th Instant touching his Interview with the Six Nations of Indians at Onondaga & Advising that the Six Nations are much in want of provisions, of which they had Desired him to acquaint his Excell.y, And that he is of Opinion that any presents made to the Indians will be to no purpose, unless a Law be passed to prohibit the Buying of Arms, Ammunition & Cloathing of the Indians of the Six Nations or their Allies.-
A Letter from Coll.l John Stoddard to M.r Lydius of the 2.d Instant Inclosing a Letter from M.r Williams to M.r Lydius of the 4.th Instant, Advising that the English prisoners at Canada desired one Blake (who was Arrived at Hatfield & had been a prisoner among the French) to send Intelligence that the french & Indians were preparing for an Expedition against Coll.l Johnson, & the Settlem.ts on the Mowhawks River.-
And a Copy of Coll.l Johnson's Journal containing an Account of what passed between him & the Six Nations of Indians at his late Interview with them at Onondaga, w.ch was read & ordered to be Entered in the Minutes, & is as follows Viz.t -
April the 24:th 1748-
At my first Entering Onondaga, I  was received by all the Sachims & Warriours who stood in order with rested Arms, & fired a Volley, after which my party returned the Compliment, then I was Conducted by some of the principal Sachims to my Quarters, w.ch was a large Indian house cleaned out with New Matts laid in the Cabbins to lie in; They had another large house clean for to Lodge the Indians whom I had with me, & two houses more for my party, all in very pretty, Neat Order. Every

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(69)
Every Castle I passed through did the same hoisted English Colours, such as they had every where, & beat their Drums realy beyond Expectation.-
In about an hour after I arrived they called all the Sachims of every Nation together, & then sent for me to the Meeting, w.ch was a very full one.-
Ganughvadeagah an Onondaga Sachim spoke.-
[?]ther. We the five Nations now Assembled here all bid you hearty welcome to our fire or Meeting place, & are thankful the Lord, who is above, has spared your Life to come among us at this Bloody time. Gave three hands of Wampum.-
[?]other. You sent a Belt of Wampum through all the Nations some time ago, desiring us all to stay at home, & not one offer to Stir or go to Canada upon any Account whatsoever untill we heard further from you, or should see you - Now, Brother, we the five Nations here together must tell you, we think it very hard, being kept from hunting now almost two years (except a Trifle about home) & that all for nothing, as we can see no Sign of your doing any thing with your Army as well Expected; What shall we do now to live being in a miserable poor Condition, & if we have a trifle to lay out, Goods are so dear at Oswego, that we can have nothing without paying three times as much as we used to do, so that we are to be pittyed; Notwithstanding all these Difficulties we have at your desire staid home. Gave a Belt of Wampum
[?]other. You some time after sent another Message, desiring us all to Meet you here at Onondaga, & that you would be soon with us, we have accordingly agreed to your Desire, & are here now Assembled this long time, expecting of you, in a hungry Condition, having nothing here to Eat, & are far from home.-
Delivers more Wampum
[?other Being quite out of patience & hungred, waiting your coming, we at length resolved to break up, & go home, when we received another Message from you that you were then at Ganaghsharagey Castle within a Days Journey of this place, & desired we might by  no means break up 'ere you come, but desired we should buy what Hogs

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(70)
Hogs, Corn &c.a, we could, which we have done, & are all here ready to hear your News & return you thanks, for considering & supplying our wants. So we finish for this Day: Returns another Belt of Wampum -
My Answer to the a foregoing-
Britheren of the five Nations, I return you all my most hearty thanks for your kind welcome & Assure you, I am very glad to see you all well here, at the old Meeting place of our Forefathers whose steps I have now Traced here in order to keep the Road clean and open, according to the old agreem.t made when we first Joined in Brothership, which I hope you all remember -
Britheren I must now tell you, I am come here by your Brother the Governour's Orders to speak to you, & tell you his News; But as I am a little fatigued after my Journey cannot speak to you this Day, wherefore desire to meet you all here Tomorrow Morning when I shall tell you my Message as also your Brother's News, so hope you may be Easy in your Minds & content yourselves so long, And I will this Night provide a Feast for you Sachims, & another for the Warriours & Dancers who I hope will be merry, which is my greatest pleasure to make & see them so.-
Finished for this Day: Wampum given by me.
April the 25-1748. My Speech -
Britheren of the five Nations, I have made what Dispatch I could to meet you here, but the Danger of Travelling these Roads now is so great, that I did not think ii safe to come without a Guard, which together with the Battoes with Presents Stores &c.a has Delayed me longer that I expected I am sorry for it upon your Account, but now I will make Amends, by making what Dispatch I can.-
Bretheren of the five Nations - I will begin upon a thing of a long standing, our first Brothers [?] My reason for it is, I think there are sev.l among us who seem to forget it; It may seem strange to you how I a foreigner should know this; But I tell you I found out some of the old Writings of our Forefathers, w.ch was thought to have been lost And in this old Valuable Record I find that our first Friendship Commenced at the Arrival of the first great Cannoe or Vessel at Albany at w.ch you were much Surpised

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(71)
Surprised, but finding what it contained pleased you so much being things for your purpose as our people convinced you of by shewing you the use of them, that you all resolved to take the greatest Care of that Vessel that nothing should hurt her, whereupon it was agreed to Tye her fast with a great Rope to one of the largest Nut Trees on the Bank of the River; But on further Consideration on a fuller Meeting it was thought safest fearing the Wind should blow down that Tree, to make a long Rope & Tye her fast at Onondaga, w.ch was accordingly done, & the Rope put under your feet That if any thing hurt or touched said Vessel, by the Shaking of the Rope you might know it, & then agreed to rise all as one, & see what the Matter was, & whoever hurt the Vessel was to suffer, After this was agreed on & done, you made an Offer to the Governour to Enter into a Bond of friendship with him & his people, w.ch he was so pleased at, that he told you he would find a strong Silver Chain, w.ch would never break, Slip or Rust, to bind you & him forever in Brothership together, And that your Warriours & ours, should be as one heart, one head, one Blood &c.a, & that what happened to the one, happened to the other after this firm agreem.t was made Our Forefathers finding it was good, & foreseeing the many Advantages both sides would reap by it, Ordered that if ever that Silver Chain should turn the least rusty, offer to Slip or Break, that it should be immediately brightened up again, & not let it slip or break upon any Account, for then you & we were both Dead. Britheren these were the Words of our wise Forefathers, w.ch some among you know very well to be so - Now Britheren understanding or hearing that the french our & your Common Enemy were Endeavouring to Blindfold you & get you to Slip your hands out of that Chain, w.ch, as our forefathers said, would certainly be our Distruction I now, out of a Tender regard for your safety & welfare as well as ours, Conjure you not to listen any more to the Deceitful french, who aim at nothing more than to Destroy you all if in their power; but stick fast to the old Agreem.t which you will find the best. A large Belt of Wampum-
[?]theren of the five Nations, in the next place I must tell you, I am sent here by Order of your Brother the Governour, as also the Gov.r of Boston to stop your going to Canada they

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(72)
they having heard (to their great concern) that you were Determined soon to go that way again, w.ch is quite contrary to your Engagem.ts, & contrary to the Custom of all Nations in the World in time of War. Britheren you take wrong the first Message I sent you with a Belt of Wampum by immagining I meant to stop up all your Roads, for I only Meant that Road leading to Canada; you may remember your Brother the Governour & I ever since the War desired & pressed you all to use your Interest every other way, where you had or could make any; Now I must tell you & assure you, that he & I are of the same Mind still, & desire you by this Belt of Wampum to use your Interest every where you can, but by no means whatsoever offer to go to Canada.
Britheren - I am to assure you, that if you stay home from Canada, that your Brother, the Gov.r of York &c.a, will Endeavour as soon as possible to get back your flesh & Blood from Canada, which you say is the only thing induces you to go; This they would have tryed before now for, but that you went down last year, when they immagined you might get them, but finding that would not do, I desire you now by this Belt of Wampum not to Trye any more, but leave it intirely to your Brother &c.a, who will use their Endeavours, & are most likely to succeed - a Belt
Britheren of the five Nations, you all came to me last Spring, with sev.l Belts of Wampum desiring Liberty to go to Canada, & take the last Tryal to fetch your flesh & Blood (the Caghnawagees) from there, w.ch was agreed to at your Earnest request, & promise of returning back again in a Month, but instead of that you staid there the whole Summer & did not bring one of your flesh & Blood along with you w.ch makes me think that that was not your Business there, only to talk with our Enemy the Gov.r of Canada, which is quite wrong. You at the same time {?] Earnestly that I would keep all the Warriours of the five Nations at home (altho' then ready to go) untill you returned, w.ch I expecting would be about a Month agreed to, fearing, as you told me, that their going to War while you were there would Overset what you went about, & might be the Occasion of all your Deaths in Case they had Committed any Hostilities in the french Country while you

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(73)
you were there; Now Britheren, I am sorry I have reason to tell you, That I think, your going to Canada last year, has been the Occasion of our loseing sev.l of our people, whose Scalps I don't doubt you have seen brought in there in Triumph while our hands were Tyed here by you, w.ch was a hard Case, & should you now talk or think of going that way again, what must the Consequence be, nothing surer than Death & an Everlasting Scandal for ever; Wherefore, Bretheren, I most Earnestly desire you all, by this Belt of Wampum, not to listen any more to the Deceitful French, who have ever been your Enemy, nor offer to look that way now. a Belt.
Britheren of the five Nations, I desire you to open yourselves, & Mind what I say to you, as I have in the beginning reminded you of the old Agreem.t made by our Noble Forefathers which was, that we were, & should ever remain, as one flesh, one Blood, one heart, one head &c.a, & that what happened to the one, happened to the other. Now Bretheren you see we have got the Frenchman's Ax sticking fast in our heads Day after Day, & the five Nations also, some of the most principal you see were Murdered the other Day in their own fields by the french & Cachnawagees; you the five Nations have not hurt the Caghnawagee as yet tho' in your power often to do it, so that it appears plainly by their useing the five Nations in such a barbarous unprecedented Manner, that they Aim at nothing else, but to Quarrel with & Destroy you, which has ever been their view, as you all by sorrowful Experience have formerly seen & felt when they used to Destroy your Castles, & sacrificed such Numbers of your brave predecessors, that there lies large heaps of their Bones ever since scattered over the whole Country. That alone any Man would think was sufficient to Stir up Everlasting Resentment in you against such a Set of Barbarous people, if there remained the least Spark of that great Spirit in you, which your brave Ancestors were Noted through the World for.-
Wherefore, Britheren, as you may plainly see they mean to Sacrifice you as well as us if they could; I now desire you, if there remains the least Spark of that Noble Spirit in you, which your brave Ancestors were Noted to have through

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(74)
through the World, that you may now follow your Brother's desire, & use the Ax ag.t them which you have so long in your hands. A very large Belt.
Britheren of the five Nations, I have one thing to desire of you, w.ch as Brothers I expect you will be sincere & tell me your going to Canada last year, & desire of going there now, makes me think you cannot be sincere or hearty in your Brother's Cause, for it is impossible to be true to both, wherefore I desire you to drop the one intirely & stand by your own Britheren, otherwise I insist upon your Declaring your Sentim.ts that I may when I return give an Account of it to your Brother, & likewise to your father the King - A Belt.
Britheren of the five Nations, as I have desired, & expect you will Mind your Brother the Governour's News, This is to assure you if you do, that the King your father has sent Orders to the Governour to take Care of your Castles & Familys while your Men are out at War, And has Ordered me to look out proper places to Erect Forts for your safety, w.ch I have done since I came up here, & will immediately set about Building them, provided you all agree to it & come together, I have also one thing further to tell you Britheren, That the King your father has sent you a parcel of Goods for the use of your Families, as a token of his Love to all those who are hearty in his Cause & Mind this News; I expect you will soon see & receive 'em from your Brother the Governour at Albany, where I desire you may be all ready to come & meet him, when called upon. A Belt.
April 26:th 1748. -
The five Nations Answer.-
Brother we are very thankful to you for reminding us of the old Agreem.t made by our Forefathers, & are overjoyed to hear that you have found it out, & hope you will take care not to let it be lost again, for we are sensible that keepiing up in them Rules laid down to us thereby, is the only way to Enable us & you to withstand our Enemys & preserve our Lives, wherefore you may Depend upon it, that all the Arts or cunning ways of the french, w.ch it's true they use a great deal of, shall never get us to drop our friendship to you our Britheren - A large Belt.

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(75)
[Left margin: [?]ther]
As you have now stopped the Road to Canada, & desire us by no means whatsoever to go that way, we the five Nations now Assembled here cannot help telling you, that we think it very hard & cruel to be hindered from fetching our own Flesh & Blood from thence who lie Rotting & Dying in Irons, when we are offered them only to go for them. Had you got them from thence as you have your own people, we should not think of going to Canada as friends but in another Manner, however upon your promise of Redeeming them soon, we all agree to your desire, & promise you we will not go to Canada nor look that way, before you make a Tryal for the Redemption of our people, & as you say you have so many french prisoners, you may Easily do it if you have a Love for us. There is nothing in the world would give us all a greater pleasure than to have our people from thence, wherefore beg Earnestly Brother you will make hast, & we assure you by this Belt of Wampum that we shall not go to Canada. A Belt.
[Left margin: [?]ther]
What you say is right about our going down to you last Spring for Liberty to go to Canada to take the last Tryal for our flesh & Blood the Caghnawagees, we assure you when we went away, we had no other View & Thought to return again immediately but as we were at Montreal, the News of the five Nations killing & taking sev.l french Just came there, w.ch we did not Expect, upon that we were all Ordered to Quebec where they were going to put us all in Goal, however they did not, but kept us there as prisoners 92 Days, & so came away at last with only two of our prisoners who were in Irons, the Gov.r telling us that if we come or sent this Spring, for the rest he would let them go, provided the five Nations committed no hostilities in that time, If they did the least harm he assured us that he would then immediately put all the prisoners to Death, Now, Brother, as to your hands being Tyed by us it is true we begged of you that the Warriours of the five Nations might not go a fighting to Canada untill we returned, but only to Scour about the Woods near home, which we thought best, not immagining at the same time that there would be so much mischief done as there was, expecting when we got there to prevail w.th the Caghnawagees to be Easy at least if we could not get them along with us which we

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(76)
We find we could not being too much under the Directions of the French, Now Brother as we have told you the Affair, we hope you will not blame us as you have done but be assured that our Resolution is to live & Dye by you.- A Belt.
Brother, We listen to you with open Ears & Mind what you say, you may Depend upon it& we hope that you will not make a Doubt of it, that our firm Resolution is to keep up in every step to the Rules laid by our Forefathers, And as we have your Ax so long in hand we Assure you, that we have been ever since we first took it up always ready to make use of it in Conjunction with you, & will ever continue so A Belt.
Brother. As you desired us to open our Minds & tell you our Resolution, we now tell you in Answer to that, our firm Resolution is to stand by you as Brothers forever, & to make use of the Ax we have in our hands, whenever it is thought requisite, But, Brother, we were in hopes to have used it before now to some purpose, as you told us two years ago that you were ready to March with your Army against Canada, but instead of an Army you only sent out small parties, sev.l of whom were by that means cut to pieces. Had you gone on with your Army & Ships as you told us you would, & assisted us properly to get over the foreign Indians to our Interest who offered their Service; then we should have been able with the loss of a few Men to have drove the french & his Allies into the great Lakes & Drown them. But as you have not done that w.ch we are sorry for, We tell you now Brother that according to your Desire, we used what Interest we could that way & have gained a considerable Number of the foreign Indians, who were ready to Join you & us; But as there is no Sign of an Army now, Nor the Encouragem.t given to them which they Expected, we cannot pretend now to say what they will do. A Belt.
Brother - As you now take a view of some of our Castles, & told us the Gov.r, our Brother, Ordered you to fortify them provided we all agreed to it, & came together, We return him & you many thanks for your Care of us & shall as soon as possible Move & come together, & then we will acquaint you of it, & Expect you will then fulfill your promise

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749
transcription:
(77)
promise; We also return you many thanks for the present brought us now, w.ch saved us a great deal of Trouble of going down so far & fetching them, which would fall hard upon several of our old people; We also assure you we will be ready to go & Meet your Brother the Governour when he calls us - A Belt.
[?]theren of the Five Nations, I now return you all my hearty thanks for your ready & agreeable Compliance to all my Desires, w.ch I hope will tend much to your Advantage as well as ours, for by such a good Agreem.t between us, we shall better be able to preserve our Lives & Destroy our Enemys, Britheren, if what you now promise me this Day comes from the Bothom of your hearts, as I expect it does, than I shall return to your Brother the Governour with a chearful heart & tell him you are still sincere & true to your Engagem.t, & I dare Assure you all that you will ever find him so to you in every respect - A Belt.
The Council humbly Advised his Excell.y to write the Gov.r of Quebec acquainting him that he is willing to Exchange some french prisoners now here for those of the Six Nations of Indians who are now prisoners in Canada, & to Inclose that part of the Treaty of Utrecht by which it appears they are acknowledged to by Subject to the Crown of England, And to signify to the Governour, that if he should refuse to Exchange the said Indian Prisoners, he will detain a like Number of french prisoners, untill the said Indians are Released or Exchanged.-
Ordered, That the further Consideration of the papers before mentioned be referred to the Gentlemen of the Council or any three of them, & that they make Report thereon with all convenient speed.-
The Council Advised his Excell.y to send a Copy of Coll.l Johnsons Journal to Gov.r Shirley: Also to Adjourn the Gen.l Assembly of this Province to Monday the 6.th of June next, & to Order Circular Letters to be wrote to the Members to give their Attendance.-

"In My Speech of the 12:th of Feb.y last, I recommended to you, to make provision for sev.l Services that had Incurred, or were necessary to be done at the publick Expence; but as the Season of the Year did not then permit you to provide for them, I shall Order the particulars thereof to be again laid before you; & recommend them to your Consideration, not doubting but they will have their due Weight in your Diliberations -

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749

(82)
"had with them, which I have Ordered to be laid before you, with an Extract from his Letter) that there is the greatest Danger of a Total Defection of those Tribes to the French Interest, unless we can give them proof of the sincerity of our Professions by speedily & resolutely Joining with them in prosecuting some Enterprize against the Enemy. Therefore I hope you will readily unite w.th the Governments of Massachusetts Bay & Connecticut, in Executing the Agreem.t Entered into with them, as the Advancem.t of the Kings Service, the safety of the province, & the well being of the Inhabitants greatly depend thereon: And you may be assured of all the Assistance in my power in Conjunction with Gov.r Shirley, to Encourage the Indians to do their parts for the Reduction of Crown point, or to carry on some other Acts of hostility against the Enemy; And I refer you to a Message of the Gen.l Court of Massachusetts Bay to Gov.r Shirley on this Occasion, a Copy of which I have Ordered to be laid before you.-
"I have Invited the Six Nations of Indians & their Allies to meet me at Albany the beginning of next Month, in order to partake of the presents His Maj.y has been most graciously pleased to send them. But I am Informed it will tend to little purpose to give those presents, unless an Act is passed before that time, forbidding all persons whatsoever, to buy or Exchange any Arms, Ammunition, Cloathing &c.a from any Indian of the Six Nations or their Allies; or to sell them any Rum or other Spirituous Liquors under certain penalties without a License from me, or the Comm.r in Chief for the time being: And I recommend it to you to prepare an Act for that purpose before I go.-

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [3], 1745-1749

"wanting for the Security of the City, I must recommend it to you, to take the same into your Serious Consideration, & provide amply for the Works he has Advised me to be done, agreeable to his Report herewith Delivered to you.-
I have Ordered to be laid before you Copys of two Letters with some Affidavits which I received from the President & Council of the Province of Pensilvania representing the Danger our Trade is Exposed to from sev.l Privateers Infesting our Coasts; And as the protection of Trad is of the Utmost Consequence to the province, I cannot doubt of your falling upon some Expedient for the preservation of it from the Attempts of the Enemy.-
"I have Ordered an Extract of a Letter from the Gov.r of Canada to Gov.r Shirley, to be laid before you, wherein he complains of there being no Cartel, or Rules Settled for the Exchange of prisoners between the Government of Canada & this Government And you may see from that Extract what may be the Consequence, in case something is not done for that End. I must therefore recommend to you to provide for the necessary Expence, which must Attend the Maintenance & Exchange of prisoners, & redeeming from Captivity, such of the Inhabitants of this Province & Indians belonging to the Six Nations, as have had the Misfortune to fall into the hands of the Enemy in Canada: but especially for the Redemption of those who are in the Custody of the french Indians, & which must be Attended with greater Expence than what usually Attends the Exchange or Ransom of prisoners in other Cases, as they are a barbarous Enemy. I must also recommend to you to provide for the usual rewards given by this Province for Scalps & prisoners taken from the Enemy -
"On the 18:th of February last I appointed W:m Johnson Esq.r Coll.l of the Levies raised for his Maj.'s Service in Defence of this Province & Annoyance of the Enemy and being satisfyed that this Gentleman has taken particular pains in Regulating the Disposition of those Troops, to the best Advantage for the Defence and

Crown Point must be taken by Breach, & at this Season of the year how is it possible to be repaired, as it is impossible for any Masons or other Artificers (necessary for that purpose) to be able to do any work towards it, & if it was possible or probable to put into the same State as it was before the whole Garrison is not capable of containing more than 300 Men & the Forces absolutely necessary to take it mus be without any proportion to that number, much more superior, & consequently must oblige all above that number of 300 to return, & is it not easily immagined that the french upon advise of all of them that the Fort could not contain, being gone from it would not immediately send a Superiour Number of Forces to those in Crown Point & retake it almost without Opposition, which would Dis-hearten the Troops very much, as well as the Indians, & be the means of loseing them more than any one thing that could happen -

Is there one Instance of such a Number of Men raised to remain with pay or provisions, & within 100 miles of their own homes quiet & contented or can it be immagined that these poor wretches almost starved with hunger& Cold, & Entirely Naked except a Coat & Blanket can in these Cold Nights sleep upon the Grouind, it must, nay inevitably it will be the Cause of a very great Desertion, which we must use all possible means to prevent for such a thing should happen, it must be of the most fatal Consequence not only to our own forces but to the fidelity of the Indians.

The Commiss:n of Indian Affairs at Albany have thought necessary to send us here to Represent to your Excellency & Council the Miserable Condition to which the City & County of Albany is reduced by the Inhumane & unnatural War in which we are Involved with french & Indians, & humbly to offer what in our opinion we judge necessary most speedily to be done for the Defence of the s. City & County in Ordere whereto, as we think it necessary to Report the particulars of the Murders Committed upon sev.l of our Inhabitants, Information whereof having been sent to your Excellency from time to time we will therefore proceed to give some Accouint in what Condition we have left the County.
All the Inhabitants to the Northward of the City of Albany are removed from their Plantations, which are left Intirely open to the Enemy, Even to the Gates of the said City; The people between Col.o Renslaier's Mills & theCity being retired since the frequent Murders committed so near them, on the East Side of hudson's River Kinderhook is now the Frontier of our County, Except a few people who are withdrawn into some fortifyed houses, And at Kinderhook [?] the Inhabitants are likewise flocked together into small fortifications built by themselves, & cannot stir out of them without being in Eminent Danger of being Murdered by strong parties of Indians, & all the Inhabitants on the Mohawk's River are likewise gathered together in small Parties with their families & it is the same in the lower parts of our County, so that the whole County except Albany & Schenechtady is now at the Mercy of the Enemy. By this Account it will plainly appear how very little we are able to do for our own Defence, If it be considered that the people of Albany are continually obliged to Mount Guard equal at least with the regular Troops posted there & besides that obliged to range the woods upon every alarm without any allowance from the Country for their Services, which it is not possible for them to hold out, the greater part being poor people, who cannot subsist their families for any time without following their usual Employm.ts, and as to the people who live in the other parts of the County as in the Mohawk's River, Kinderhook, Coxlackie, Kattskill & almost the whole Country who are retired into the small Fortifications, They cannot withstand the Enemy or
assist

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(102)
Assist the City of Albany, They having enough to do to keep their Families from being Murdered, & cannot with any reason be Commanded from their Families & leave them Defenceless, & what other Method they can take to Secure their Families than they're by gathering together in small Parties we know not, They cannot bring all their Families to Albany & Schinechtady, which places cannot contain them, & if they could, how shall they be Maintained, the planters for the most part are poor as soon as they leave their Settlem.ts; by this Acco.t of the Circumstances of the County of Albany, it appears that the City of Albany sho.d it be Attacked by the Enemy which is very probable cannot depend upon any, or at least a very small Assist from the County, and the fatal Consequence the Distribution of Albany would be to their & the Neighboring Governm.t is not easily conceived, but by those who are acquanted with the Terrible Effects of an Indian War & wo.d then be soon Experienced by those who live to the Southward of us, when the french would set almost all the Indians upon the Continent against the sev.l English Governmts, they having a Communication between Canada & the River Mississippi, & almost all the Indians upon that [?] are Devoted to them already, & the remainder would follow the Example immediately & our own Six Nations among the rest-
In former wars the preservation of the City & County of Albany was looked upon as of very great Consequence to the Country in Gen.l, as may be seen by the Acts of Assembly made at that time to raise Men and Mony for the Defence of the Frontier. And it was thought reasonable that the s.d City & County of Albany sho.d be Excused from Taxes, but now it is left without the assistance of one Man except the King's Forces your Excellency sent up, & is Taxed at least it's full proportion as in times of peace We humbly represent to your Excellency that we conceive it necessary for the preservation of the City of Albany & the Township of Schinechtady, & to prevent the Enemy Incursions further Southward, that 150 Men at least out of the sev..l Countys be as soon as possible sent up to Albany to Reinforce that City, & there to remain for the Defence thereof, Except when it shall be judged necessary to send them out upon Parties in case of necessity -
2d - - - - That 100 Men out of the sev.l Countys be sent to the Town of Schinechtady for the Defencs of that place & to go out upon Parties when Ordered & 50, of the Inhabitants with proper Officers & 25 Indians be taken into pay to Range the woods from thence 
3.dly - - - -  That 100 Men belonging to the County of Albany be taken into Pay with proper Officers to range the woods from the City of Albany & 25 Indians be likewise into pay to join them
4:thly - - That at least 150 Men be posted at Saraghtoga with 50 Indians, 50,
w.c

transcription:

which Men with proper Officers to be out of Albany County, & that as many of them be obliged to Range the woods from time to time as they shall be ordered, And it shall be necessary that Barracks be built in the Fort there for their Reception & all necessaries provided -
5 - - - - That 50 Men & Officers be taken into pay to Range the woods to the Northward of Conafshorie & Burnets field as they shall be ordered.
6 - - - - That 50 Men & Officers be taken into pay to Range the woods to the Northward of Kinderhook Between Hudson's  River & New England-
These Articles we humbly conceive to be necessary to be put in Execution with all speed to stop the Career of the Enemy & their further Incursion into this province tho' we are of opinion that a strong Fort at the Carrying place with a strong Garrison wo.d tend more to the Security of the County than at any other place whatsoever; But we are of the opinion that it would be Difficult to get a Fort built there at this time.-
We are Informed that the Gen.l Assembly have raised a Sum of mony for Block houses to be Built upon the Frontier, w.ch Resolutions have been so long making That the principal End of that Scheme cannot be thereby obtained, the upper Settlers being all removed, & the french send Indians ag.t us in stronger Parties than in former Wars, w.ch wo.d render Block houses Garrisoned with 20 or 25 Men Quite useless, as not being able to make head against Parties of 50 or 60 Indians, who might keep them beseiged in the Block houses, for which reasons we think it will be more for the Interest of the Province that, that scheme be given up & the mony & Men Designed for that purpose, be applyed toward what we have above mentioned.
We likewise think proper to acquaint you Excellency That the Commiss.n of Indian Affairs have not been able to get one penny of the mony allowed for the Outscouts except £ 300. for the first year of the loan, & all the Indians who go upon the Outscout expect to get immediate payment upon theirReturn, which is impossible for three or four people to continue Advanceing, & without mony nothing can be had & every thing is wanted, neither can the Allowance to the Comm.n of Indian Affairs be got from the Treasurer. We hope your Excellency will give such Orders and Directions herein as will occasion a speedy Relief
The Comm.n for Indian Affairs should, at this time in an especial manner, be Enabled by presents to prevail upon the Six Nations to Engage in the War against the French, which is of the utmost Consequence at this time-

We have received you Excellency's Letter of the 27:th of October, with the Extracts from Gov.r Bladen's Letters. His Rule, That the Forces of that "Colony are now out of his care & the care of that Government respecting their provision "& other necessaries, & that those things must be supplyed by the Gen.l, or some-"Body, he does not know who," is very singular & extraordinary: If we can make a Judgem.t by his Maj.s Orders contained in the Duke of Newcastle's Letter to Governour Shirley, which we received the latter End of May last (which we suppose to be the same in substance with the Circular Letters to the other Governors) we must conclude, That saving the Pay, Clothing & Arms, which his Majesty has undertook to Defray, all the other Charges are to be borne by the respective Governments- And it seems more extraordinary that those large Southern Governm.ts, who furnish so small a proportion of Men, should make any Difficulty as to these matters. As to the Motion of taking the Provisions out of the pay of the Officers and Soldiers, we can say nothing on that point 'till we know something further of his Majesty's pleasure on the Matte, which we Daily expect by His Majesty's Ship the Mermaid; but in the mean time we apprehend it to be absolutely necessary that the sev.l Governm.ts sho.d supply their own Troops, otherwise the Service will inevitably fall to the Ground; for if the Troops cannot be substituted, we can expect nothing but that they will Divert, as to the present pay of the Troops,  it plainly lies upon the sev.l Governm.ts to draw for their own Troops; and as Mr. Shirley has no Warrant for any but his own, if he supposes the other Governm.ts have

May it please your Excellency - Your Excellency having been pleased to take Notice in Council this Day, that the Committee of the Council had by their Report made to your Excellency on the 19th of January last Expressed themselves in Gen.l Terms That an attempt upon Crown Point in the Winter Season is liable to many Difficulties

transcription:
(3) 
Difficulties & is an hazardous undertaking & therefore Desired that the Council would be more Explicit on that head, and referred to a Committee to draw up their Sentiments thereupon at large, which they have accordingly done & beg leave to to Report them as followeth -
For Frederick at Crown Point is reported to be a very strong Fort, not to be carried without the use of Artillery; And is at least 100 Miles Distance from Saraghtoga, which is about 36 Miles from Albany; The way to it, as proposed is by the Wood Creek, which is in Summer a small Run of water with low Lands on each side, covered with Trees & thick underwood & Brush; which makes it almost impracticable to pass near the side of it.
The Question is whether it be advisable to send a large body of the New Levies to attempt now in the Winter Season the Reduction of it. That it is not, the following particular reasons are humbly offered-
1.st As His Majesty has been pleased to set on foot an Expedition against Canada and in order to facilitate the Reduction of it, hath thought proper to Cause a Levy to be made in the Northern Colonies of as many Men as the time would permit part of which are to be Employed against the Southern parts of Canada, whilst the other in Conjunction with the forces from Great Britain, are designed to Attack Quebec; that so the french being alarmed in two Quarters, at the same time, their Councils may be Distracted, & their forces Divided, by which they will necessarily be much weakened, Now what Authority there is from His Majesty, to warrant the Employing the New Levies in a manner Different from that which was understood to be his Maj.s first Intention, we are yet to learn.
2.dly If the New Levies should March in this Winter Season & attempt Fort [?] Frederick, the carrying the Artillery with them (and they cannot succeed without it) must retard their Marching, by which means the french will have Intelligence of it, & able to March to it's Relief from Montreal, and be there as soon as our Forces; and as Quebec & the lower forts of Canada, are altogether Secured by the Winter Season, against any Attack from Sea, The french my March against us with the strength of Canada: And sho.d our Troops meet with a Disappointment

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(4)
Disappointment, or a Repulse, it may Defeat the Plan laid at home for the Reduction of Canada (should it be his Maj.s pleasure to have it carryed into Execution the Ensuing Spring) as it is Expected the British Forces are to be joined by a considerable Body of Americans -
3.dly - - - -  The season is now so far advanced, That should the Forces March with all possible Expedition, they will not probably be at Crown Point 'till the End of February or the beginning of March:  And as the Winter usually breaks up early in March, should a thaw happen in their March thither, or while they are there, they must unavoidably lose the Artillery, most of their Ammunition & provisions, & be obliged to March thro' thick woods & Swamps almost impassible at any time, but in case of a Thaw up to their Knees in Water, or else perish in the way -
4.thly - - - - If our Army should be Defeated at Crown Point, it will be such a Blow as these Provinces cannot easily recover,  besides that in it's Consequence it may lose us the Six Nations, & other Indians, & thereby hazard the greater parts of these provinces -
For these reasons, the bareness of Clothing of the Levies, & shortness of time to Engage the Indians, and as a Fortnight's more time is escaped since our last Report was made to your Excellency, and we hear of no further account from M.r Shirley, or any thing about the Resolutions of the Governm.t of Connecticut upon this head; the Council are of the Opinion that the attempt upon Crown Point this Winter Season is become less practicable -

[Left margin: 7 Feb 1746 Lre from Gov.r Shirley to his Excell.y]
Since my last Letter to your Excellency by the Post, affairs have taken a New Turn in this Governm.t, with regard to the Expedition ag.t Crown Point, by means of the Advices I received yesterday from your own Government. Mr. Lydius is arrived here, and Informs me that the Troops of the Southern Colonies now posted upon Hudson's River are in good health & Spirits, and expect to March this winter to Crown Point, who has likewise shewed me a Letter he received from Col.o Johnson Just before he left Albany by which I perceive your Excellency had give Orders, the 24.th of last month

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(7) 
to Col.o Johnson to send to the sev.l Tribes of Indians to be in readiness for this Service, And that he had already Engaged the Indians of the two Near Castles, who were now ready for Marching & impatient of Delay, and had sent Messengers to all the other Nations to prepare for Joining our Forces upon Hudson's River, & doubted not of Assembling a suff.t Number of them to proceed with the English Army: This aspect of affairs & the continuance of the hard frosty Season, induces this Governm.t to Judge it both practicable & necessary to push on the Expedition with all possible Dilligence & Resolution; And our gen.l Assembly are of these Sentim.ts (almost to a Man) as your Excellency will find by the Inclosed Copy of their Message sent to me yesterday Evening agreeable to which I shall give immediate Orders to your Officers to March their respective Companies, as soon as possible, without waiting for a Gen.l Randezvous. And I desire your Excellency would appoint as short a Day as the Distance of the place will allow for the Indians of the Six Nations to appear upon the Hudson's River well furnished for this Service, I would propose it for your Excellency's Consideration that the Troops of the Southern Colonies sho.d March without Delay to the carrying places & build wooden Forts there, for securing our Stores & for the Shelter & Comfort of the Troops, & their Defense in case of any Emergency, and I hope your Excellency will not forget to send a good number of field pieces with Shot for the Defense of those Forts, and annoyance of the Enemy, and that whatever Deficiency there may be in the Stores of War, particularly in Gun Powder; got ready at Albany, you will be pleased to supply without regard to it's being more than the proportion of your Governm.t: For I will be answerable to you, that this Governm.t will not hesitate in the least to pay their full proportion of all Articles whatever, necessary or proper for the Service; And it is almost Impracticable for us now to Transport heavy Stores so far as we must do, if we send them from hence to Albany: It seems to me that the powder requisite for the Six Battering Cannon Bomb Shells, Field pieces, & small Arms for 4000 Men (which we may well hope to have, including the Indians of the Six Nations without depending upon

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(8)
upon the Connecticut Troops) will amount to 300 Barrels at least, and that we sho.d have ready in our Magazines, 350 or 400 Barrels: I would also desire your Excellency forthwith to send your Orders to Albany, & the County of Kingston for Impressing Carriages &c.a for Stores of any kind, if that sho.d be found necessary; And I hope & Doubt not but that your Excellency will persevere in the same Zeal & spirit for his Maj.s Service at this critical Conjuncture, which has carryed you hitherto thro' all your Difficulties, & not suffer the Important piece of Service, which you have done his Majesty & the Colonies, in reclaiming & [?] the Indians of the Six Nations in the English Interest, when they were wavering, be lost at last by not proceeding in the present Enterprize with utmost Vigour: And instead of our forever establishing those Nations in our Interest, & lessening the attachm.t of the french Indians to our Enemy [?] we have now an opportunity of doing, forever lose the Six Nations over to the french, & heighten the Spirit of the french Indians against us, which will most probably be the consequence if we remain inactive this Winter, & beget a [?] & Diffidence of us in our Indian Allies, after our promises to 'em of acting forthwith against the french - This would indeed be an irrecoverable Blow to us, and I think, tho' sev.l more reasons might be urged for our proceeding against Crown Point now, that this, even of itself, is a suff.t Motive to Induce us to it. Nothing shall be wanting on my part, nor (I dare say) of this Government in this Affair; And I persuade myself of success in it if we are active & unanimous. I purpose in Order to Encourage our forces to March upon their Duty with the more chearful regard to Advance twelve pounds old Tenor to each Man, in part of his pay, I shall raise here by Drawing Bills on the Governm.t at home, as I have Hinted to your Excellency in my former Letters: I shall once more [?] the Governm.t of Connecticut with such Argum.ts as I hope & beleive will prevail upon them to send their forces after us, for I shan't Delay the March of our Troops one Moment for their Answer; Since, tho' they don't join us, I hope

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(9)
I hope we shall be strong enough by the help of God to obtain success in this Important Enterprise - I must repeat that your Excellency having in so many Instances Manifested how much your heart is in this affair, I doubt not bu you will now put your last hand to it, by perfecting you preparations for it & giving such Orders about it, as will have the best Tendency to render it successfull. I shall be glad to see Col.o Roberts here if he comes.
I am [?]
W: Shirley

On the 25th of last Month by the return of my Express from New York, I had your Excellency's Letter Dated Six Days before in answer to me concerning the proposed attempt for the reduction of Crown Point this Winter inclosing a Copy of the Advice of his Maj.s Council for the province under your Governm..t upon it, Dated the 17.th of Jan.y, wherein they Declare their Opinion "That it is Advisable for your Excellency to Join in the Attempt, under the provisoes mentioned in their Report." And your Excellency assures me in your Letter of all the Assistance you can give agreeable to the Opinion of the Gentlemen of the Council; And Inform me that you had sent for Col.o Roberts down from Albany purely to meet Brig.r Waldo (that we might [?] upon Matters (who you proposed should set our for Boston in two or three days with your Instructions which might prevent losing time - On the 2.d Instant, I received the Resolve of the Governm.t of Connecticut, w.ch was not to Join in proceeding in the Attempt against Crown Point this Winter, yet leaving a Discretionary power with their Committee of War to act in case &c.a as is mentioned in the Resolve, a Copy of which I Inclosed to your Excellency by the Post with a few Lines to Inform you, that I supposed that would put an End to the late Scheme for the Reduction of Crown Point, as it had in reality done with me 'till the 6th Instant when M.r [?] arrived here from Albany with an account that the Troops of the Southern Colonies, consisting of Twenty Nine Companies, in which he computed there might now be about 2400 Effective Men were in good health and Spirits & [?]

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(11) 
me a Letter from M.r Johnson, Dated at Mount Johnson, 26 Jan.y last, wherein he informs M.r Lydius that "two Days before he had received a Letter from your Excellency telling him the forwardness of the New England Troops, & desiring he would prepare as many Indians Warriors as possible to assist the forces of the Colonies in the Reduction of Crown Point, which he heartily wished to see,  and should not make the least doubt of it, were all the Colonies Active in it; That he had then sent sev.l of his Officers among the upper Nations to prepare them, but had laid on no certain time fearing a Disappointm.t, That he had the Day before assembled the two next "Castles, & did assure M.r Lydius that nothing could give him more pleasure than to see the willingness they shewed to join us whenever required; the sooner they said the better, for they were almost in Dispair, or out of patience at waiting so long, that he made no doubt of bringing as many into the field as would be sufficient for that Enterprize, and he only wished our forces (meaning those of the Southern Colonies) were all as ready & willing" - - -  upon reading this account of the Disposition of the Indians of the Six Nations & receiving Mr. Lydius's assurances that there were at least 2400 Effective Men among the Troops at Albany, and in the Neighbourhood of it, which with 1500 of the Levies of this Province computed to be now in it, I ever Judged (as I still do) a suff.t Number with the Assistance of the Six Nations to Attack Crown Point, or even 3,000 with their Assistance,  and finding that your Excellency had proceeded to give M.r Johnson Orders to prepare the Indians to Join in the Attempt before you knew what wo.d be the Determination of the Governm.t of Connecticut, so that it seemed to be from your Excellency's Letter of the 19th of Jan.y, And your taking these steps with the Indians, might a great measure depend upon your Joining with me in this Enterprize (even without the Connecticut Levies) for Executing which I thought a very fair opportunity presented itself, the Severity of the Season having likewise then a favourable aspect for us; And that besides there might be a considerable risque of the Indians cooling in their present Attachm.t to us upon being Disappointed

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(12)
Disapoointed of their Expectations of our Entring upon Action this Winter, and being pressed by the Council & Assembly of this Province (to whom I communicated the accounts I had received from M.r Lydius, & M.r Johnson's Letter) to prosecute the attempt against Crown Point this Winter, I determined to to it with your Excellency's assistance, and gave Orders to the Officers of the Massachusets Levies to March 'em forthwith, some to Saraghtoga, & others to Albany in order to Join the Troops of your Governm.t & the other Southern Colonies upon Hudson's River of all which I apprised you Excellency by Express w.ch I suppose, you may have received before this time. On the 12th instant in the Evening Mr. Bayard delivered me you Excellency's Letter of the 4th Instant, inclosing a Second Advice of the Gentlemen of the Council Dated 2.d of February Instant; wherein "They Declare themselves of opinion to your Excellency, that it is not Advisable to make the Attempt against Crown Point this Winter." which, as the Gentlemen did not then know, what would be the Resolve of the Governm.t of Connecticut, concerning Joining the forces raised in their Colony with us in the Attempt, must be understood to be their Opinion, even tho' that Governm.t should Join with us in it.  Your Excell.tly will easily conceive that the Gentlemen of your Council resuming the Consideration of this Matter, & the sudden alteration of their & your Sentim.ts upon it, after you had transmitted to me their former opinion & your own assurances of Joining with me in the Attempt upon both which it was reasonable to immagine I should Depend & Govern myself in my Measures, must be a surprise upon me, as I found myself proceeding in this Enterprise without a prospect of being assisted, either with the Southern Troops, or any of the Six Nations, or Cannons: all which Depended upon your Excellency Joining in it: This has made me Determine without hesitation to lay aside all thoughts of the attempt this Winter, & to Countermand the Orders I had given for Marching the Troops raised within this Province to Albany & Saraghtoga, which I now apprise your Excellency of that no mistake may happen upon your having received my last Express.

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(13)
As to the reasons offered by the Gentlemen of the council to your Excellency in support of their last opinion, I find they say thus in their first reason, "Now what Authority there is from His Maj.s to Warrant the Employing the New Levies in a Different Manner from that, which was understood to be His Maj.s first Intention we are yet to learn." upon which I would observe to your Excellency, that it is plain from the Duke of Newcastle's Letter to me, which Communicated the plan of the Expedition as first concerted at home, That it was his Majesty's Intention that that plan should be subject to such Alterations as General St. Clair, Adm.l Warren & myself should think proper, His Grace's Expression is, "Doubtless it wouild be left to us three to act therein as we sho.d think proper" evidently Declaring His Maj.s Intention & grounding it upon the reasonableness of having the Gen.l Plan of Operations (tho' first proposed at home) to be finally settled by some persons upon the spot, who may be supposed to have better opportunitys of knowing what may be the most practicable Scheme for Executing his Majesty's pleasure in that Case, than can be had at so great a Distance from it as England is:  And tho' I don't think that Clause in the Duke's Letter Vests M.r Warren & myself with an Authority to Order the Levies to be Employed in the Reduction of Crown Point, in the Manner we recommended it to your Excellency, & the other Governm.ts concerned, yet I am persuaded since it has happened that the New England Troops could not be employed this year by Sea against Quebec, as was intended by his Majesty, And it was M.r Warren's & my opinion that the Employm.t of them in Conjunction with the Troops of the Southern Colonies this year for the Reduction of Crown Point, wo.d not only be for his Majesty's Service in Gen.l by wresting a most Dangerous Fort to the Security & Welfare of his Northern Colonies out of the Enemy's hands, but greatly facilitate the Reduction of Canada, which was the End of raising these Troops, it will Justify us in recommending it, and if the several Governments

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(14)
Governments had concurred with us, and Employed their respective Levies in this Service such Concurrence with our Recommendation, would have warranted the Employing of [?] But be that as it will, I think the objection sho.d have been made when M.r Warren & I first recommended this Enterprize to your Excellency's Consideration; It would then have saved us all no small trouble & this province the Expence of transporting Provisions
& Ordinance Stores to Hudson's River, besides other considerable Charges, and should have employed 500 more of the Massachusetts Levies than I have done for Driving the Enemy out of Nova Scotia, tho' I have no other Warrant for my Employment of them in this manner than the good of his Maj.s Service & the welfare of the Colonies (that under my own Governm.t in particular) which  I shall always think upon any pressing Emergency, where I cannot have an opportunity of receiving his Maj.s Directions in time for the Service, a suff.t Warrant for my proceedings, so far as they shall be conducted with prudence: And I must own, after the Gentlemen of the Council, that attended your Excellency to Albany, had themselves formed the plan for carrying the attempt against Crown Point into Execution, Determined the Number of Troops necessary to be employed in it, made an Estimate of the Stores requisite to be provided for it, & settled the Quota of Men & proportion of Expences for the sev.l Colonies proposed to be concerned in it, & your Excellency had sent me a Copy of it under their hands, for the Concurrence of this Government, And 
at the same time pressed M.r Warren & myself to Name a Commander in Chief of the forces to be employed in this Enterprize, with the privity of your Council at Albany, as I apprehend, which we accordingly did: And Gentlemen of the Council had from time to time in other Instances given your Excellency their Advice upon the particular steps to be taken for carrying this Enterprize on, never making the least Question of the Warrantableness of employing the Kings Troops in it; And therefore by common

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(15)
Common intendment Admitting such Employm.t of them to be warrantable, I must own I say after proceeding thus far, I did not expect that they would now object to the warrantableness of the attempt itself with respect to the Forces to be employed in it -
In the second reason, the Gentlemen of the Council think it probable that our Troops may be opposed in their attack upon Crown Point by the whole strength of Canada, And sho.d they meet with a Disappointment or Repulse it may Defeat the Plan Laid, at home for the Reduction of Canada; upon which I wo.d observe, that Admitting the Canadians can draw their whole strength from Quebec as well as from Montreal so suddenly for the support of their Fort at Crown Point as is supposed, which it seems to me it would be very Difficult for 'em to do, and that they would Endeavor to do it, which I think is still more Questionable, as very probably they expect the Expedition against them from England to go on in the Spring, & know it is in our power to Encounter them at Crown Point with a much superiour force from the Colonies; and their Defeat there might in it's Consequences be the Loss of Canada to 'em; Yet I thing the Body of Levies proposed to be employed in the attack against Crown Point, tho' they sho.d find a superiour force there to receive them, would be able with the help of their Artillery to make good their Ground 'till they could be reinforced from the Colonies, & if the Enemy sho.d continue to draw fresh forces from Canada 'till they had Mustered up their whole strength for the Defence of Fort St. Frederick, yet since the three Colonies of New York, Connecticut & Massachusetts Bay alone have at least five times the Number of fighting Men in 'em that all Canada contains, they might & should in such Case forthwith assemble a suff.t force to overpower the Enemy, And I think if Matters were to be brought to an Issue at Fort Frederick it would be a Method of Deciding the Point between us & the french, that we sho.d be fond of. And sho.d our Troops in such case be so unfortunate

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(16)
unfortunate as to meet with a Repulse or Disappointment, that it would be a bad accident, yet if might not Defeat the Plan laid at home for the Reduction of Canada, if that should be attempted from England this year, but on the other hand even the advantage gained by the Enemy might in such cases prove fatal to them by greatly weakening 'em for the Defence of Canada; whereas the American Forces might be Recruited in time to Join the British Troops in their Attack upon Quebec, & to penetrate into the South parts of Canada from Albany as was proposed last year: But I think a Repulse or Disappointment of our Troops in this Attempt ought not to be supposed since it seems in our power from the superiour Number in the Colonies to carry this Fort against any force that can be suddenly drawn from Canada to Defend it; which should be resolved upon being done let it require what time or Numbers it will to Exert it, and sho.d we not be able to compass it by spring, & a. British armament sho.d be sent then ag.t Quebec; That would necessarily draw such part of the Enemy's force from Crown Point, as would make the Conquest easy to us, & be a great point gained towards the Reduction of Canada itself; But if no armament should be sent from England against Quebec in the Spring the reason will hold still stronger for wresting Crown Point now from the Enemy, since the Colonies may possibly never have so fair an opportunity of attempting the Reduction of it as they have had this Winter.
The third reason seems to me the strongest: should a thaw happen when the forces were upon their March to Crown Point, or the Artillery Stores were drawing thither; which may possibly happen; the Enterprize must be at an End, & the Cannon, Ordinance Store & provisions in Danger of being lost.
The fourth reason is "If the Army should be Defeated at Crown it will be such a Blow ;as these provinces cannot easily recover, beside that

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(17)
that in it's Consequences it may lose us the Six Nations, & other Indians, & thereby hazard the greatest part of these provinces - If that is the Case, the Colonies seem to be in an unhappy situation: They have sat still & looked on whilst the French were Erecting Fort St. Frederick plainly within the limits of the English Territories, & now with 250,000 fighting Men upon the continent they are afraid to make an attempt to remove this Encroachment, or Dispossess the Enemy of it, least if they should fail in it, the French with 15,000 Men by the help of the Indians should Destroy the greatest part of the English Provinces - what is to be Determined in this Case; shall we suffer the Enemy to remain unmolested within our Borders, & Fort St. Frederick to stand the Trophy of their Vigilance & our Subjection, for the Downfall of our Colonies; or will Spring be a better opportunity of Dispossessing the french of this Destructive Encroachm.t, when by the Arrival of a British Armament before Quebec their Councills will be Distracted, & their forces Divided",  But put the Case that the late intended Expedition against Canada sho.d not proceed, and thereupon Orders sho.d be sent in the Spring for Disbanding the American Levies: will the sev.l Governm.ts keep these Levies in their own pay 'till Crown Point can be reduced or will they desire his Maj.y to do it: If they sho.d, May it not probably be asked, why he kept these Troops Idle in his pay all the Winter & neglected to Employ 'em then in this Service; And will it be a satisfactory answer for them to tell his Majesty that they were of Opinion they had no Authority from him to Employ them for this Service in any other Manner than according to his Majesty's first Intentions, as Declared in the Plan laid at home for the Reduction of Canada; tho' in the Duke of Newcastle's Letter, which Communicates the Plan, it is expressly Declared to be part of His Majesty's Intention, that the Plan should be subjected to such alteration as three persons therein Named sho.d think most for his Service, two of which had recommended it

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(18)
it to them to employ those Levies in the Reduction of Crown Point this Winter as what would best promote his Service in the intended Expedition against Canada if it sho.d be his pleasure to prosecute that in the Spring or will it be a better answer to say, that the Winter was not a proper time to Attempt the Reduction of Crown Point in, because, "As Quebec & the lower part of Canada are altogether Secured by the Winter Season against any attacks from Sea the french might March against us with all the strength of Canada," and consequently that unless we are supported in that attempt by His Maj.y with an Armament before Quebec at the same time in order to Distract the french Councils & Divide their Forces it will be unsafe for the Colonies wer to make the Attempt, least in Case of a Defeat it sho.d hazard the greatest part of them" - How different is the Spirit & Conduct of the french; They with a handful of Men, in comparison with our Number upon the Continent burn Canso, Attack His Maj.s Garrison at Annapolis Royal, Cut off the Village of Saraghtoga, & one of our Forts in this province & District & harrass our Frontier Settlem.ts in all parts at the same time without the least Dread of hazarding any part of Canada (which lies more Scattered & Exposed than our own Settlem.ts) by our vastly superior forces - I once thought this was bad policy in the French, & was in hopes the cutting off Saraghtoga in the Inhumane manner they did, by their Indians ( which is doing it themselves) & their Insults upon the City of Albany would have roused a Spirit in us to their Distruction: But it seems to have had a Different Effect, & I find the french are not mistaken in their Politick
I think the Conduct of the French of Canada has been ever such as leaves us no room to flatter ourselves that they will suffer a quiet Partition of Power between them & us upon this Continent, and who are likely at any rate to be the Masters of it in the End, I will leave to your Excellency to Judge.
As to the Danger of our loseing the Indians of the Six Nations by unsuccessful Attempt against Crown Point, I always understood that the [?] Argument

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(19)
Argument used for our proceeding upon that Enterprise immediately was by Entering them as soon as possible upon Action, & involving 'em so deeply in Hostilities ag.t the french, as to make a Reconciliation between them & the french Impracticable during the War, to fix them unalterably in their attachm.t to the English & Secure their Assistance for His Maj.y  in the Reduction of Canada the next Spring against the artifices of the Enemy to draw 'em over to their side; I am sure this was the principal Motive which Induced me to Engage in this attempt; and my chief concern now is, least by our having drop't it we sho.d beget in the Indians a Contempt of us, & give the Enemy an opening to Instill Jealousies into them, which it seems to me from the acco.t given in M.r Johnsons Letter of their impatience & uneasiness at our Delay there may be some Danger of. And I should be extreamly glad if your Excellency would think of my proper Method for keeping 'em Employed in Action against the french, in which I will most readily Join, if that is necessary; And I here Inclose your Excellency a vote of the Assembly of this Province, which has a Tendency towards it that your Excellency; may make use of it with your own Assembly if you shall think proper.
Thus, Sir, I have with the greater freedom given your Excellency my thoughts upon the Report of the Gentlemen of the Council & the reasons offered by 'em in support of it, which tho' they are the strongest that can be given for our not proceeding against Crown Point this Winter, & come from Gentlemen for whose Judgm.t I have a particular regard & Deference; yet I acknowledge I have apprehensions something different from theirs upon this point; and as the Reduction of the French Fort at Crown Point, and the Establishing of the Indians of the Six Nations, in our Interest, are Matters of so great Importance to all the English Colonies in Gen.l, that they deserve the most thorough Consideration

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(20)
Consideration &close Attention, I have Endeavored to be as Explicit in my Sentiments upon 'em to your Excellency as may be, taking it to be the best method for coming to a Right understanding of each other, & by that means to an Union of Councils, which is necessary to our Acting with unanimity & vigour in the Common Cause, as I hope we shall always do.
Your Excellency proposes to me in your last Letter the Building of a Fort large enough to contain 500 Men near the great Carrying places but the Gentlemen of your Council express themselves in their first Report as if they thought that was impracticable at this Season of the year, and are silent about it in the Second, however I recommend it to the Council & Assembly of this province to Join in the Erecting one as you propose, it being necessary for me to do that because the Grant for providing Material &ca must come from them but they Decline doing it being something Chagrined (I believe) at their Disappointm.t from your last Dispatches; However I should think the Expence of that must be inconsiderable, and you have a suff.t Number of Men posted much nearer the Carrying place than ours to Employ in it, without any assistance.
I don't wonder at your Excellency's being Indisposed, the great fatigue you have gone thro' may account for that, but I hope there will be some End of it, tho' I cannot say there is a very near prospect of one. 
By my last Letters from home I have reason to Expect the Arrival of an Express from the Government every Day, after receiving which I shall be better able to give your Excellency an Answer concerning the french Captain at Rochelle.
I am with the greatest respect
Sir
Your Excellency's most obd.t
hble Serv.t
W Shirley

His Excellency communicated to the Board a Letter to him from Gov.r Shirley of the 14th Instant Signifying that he had laid aside the Design of carrying the Expedition against Crown Point into Execution at this time, which was read.

I have Delayed calling you together 'till this time, in hopes of receiving his Maj.s Commands and thereby to have been enabled to speak more Explicitly to you, with respect to the Expedition against Canada than I can at present.
But the Season of the year is already so far Advanced, that it is become necessary to make preparations without Delay for posting & Employing the Forces in such manner as they may be most useful, & for the Security of our Frontier, & the Execution of any Enterprize that shall be thought proper for annoyance of the Enemy.
I sent Col.o Roberts to Boston to concert Measures with Gov.r Shirley for this purpose; which is done accordingly. 
I have likewize retained the Mohawk Indians from hunting that they may

transcription:
(23)
may be ready on any Occasion for Service; and have used my best Endeavours among the other five Nations to preserve them in the good Disportion in which they were after my last Treaty with them at Albany, & to have them in readiness upon every Occasion in which they can be of Service.
Parties of Indians with some of the Inhabitants of this province are gone & going out, with Design to Intercept any of the Enemy that may be abroad near our Frontiers, & to range the woods in all places where they Expect to meet with any of the Enemy.
Gentlemen of the Gen.l Assembly
You know thqt provision is only made for Victualling the Troops Levied in this province to the 1st of May; I must currently recommend to you the making of a further provision for this purpose.
I have, with great Expence & Charge to the Crown, & without any Charge or Burthen on the Inhabitants of this province, Secured the friendship of the Six Nations of Indians, & of the Nations Dependent on them. I have likewise at the same Expence & Charge, received hopes of Joining some other of the more Western Nations of Indians, in the War against the french, & who were formerly in the french Interest.
I think it may tend much to his Maj.s Service, the Security of all the English Colonies in North America, but more particularly to the Security of this province, & the Success of any Enterprize that may hereafter be undertaken against the Common Enemy, that this good Disposition among all the Indian Nations in Amity with us, be confirmed & Established by all the means in our power: For this purpose I propose to go as early as possible to Albany; and I hope you will think it Incumbent on you to contribute as largely as the Circumstances of the province will permit towards the Expence that must necessarily attend this Service.
Among other things which are concerted with Gov.r Shirley, two Forts are to be

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
