(24)
be Built at the Carrying place towards Crown Point, for Security of the Magazine & Stores, & of our Frontiers & Forces, on sev.l Emergencies that may arise & a Body of Men from the sev.l Colonies are, as soon as the Season will permit, to be Encamped there, for the more Secure & Effectual Carrying on of these Works, & other Services, And as no Directions are Arrived from His Maj.y or his Ministers; for Defraying the Expence of any part of the Expedition against Canada; it is proposed that the immediate Expence of these Services be at the Charge of the sev.l Colonies who have Levied Forces for the Expedition against Canada according to the Rates & Quotas w.ch were agreed upon by the Gentlemen of the Council of this province who Attended me at Albany, & the Commiss.rs of the Governm.t of the Massachusetts Bay, & presented to me at Albany as a reasonable proposal to be laid before the Legislatures of the sev.l Colonies, for their respective approbation.
Gov.r Shirley assures me that he will promote this Service as much as it is in his power to do: As this tends more immediately to the Security & safety of the people of this province, I expect that you will set a good Example to the other Colonies, by your cheerful Contribution towards the Expence of it; And this I must desire you to do as speedily as possible, for I cannot so much as desire the Concurrence of the other Governm.ts 'till I am assured of yours. I shall order the proposal for the Rates & Quotas, as it was Delivered to me at Albany to be laid before you Gentlemen of the Council & Assembly. 
I shall offer no other Business to your Consideration at this time, because the Nature of the Service to which I desire your assistance requires thee greatest Dispatch; & besides the Meeting of the Indians, which seem to me requisite to be without Delay; the present State of the New Levies, & other Services, require my presence at Albany as soon as may be.
This therefore must be a short Session, but you will meet again as soon

usual, & if it were in my power I would not lose one Moment in Employing the New Levies in forwarding the purposes for which they were raised & his Majesty be in no manner Disappointed in any Expectations he may have of our being in readiness to Act in the Enterprize for which the Levies were intended & of our having done every thing that can be expected to be done without his special Order For that reason I think it may be proper to March some part at least of the Troops of New England as well as those in this Province as soon as possible to the Carrying place above Saraghtoga between Hudson's River & Wood Creek & there to Erect two Forts, one at each end of the Carrying place sufficient to protect Magazines & Stores from any sudden Surprize as was proposed by Col.o Roberts at Boston, & to which your Excell.y by your Letter of the 10th of last Month agreed: And that the Magazines & Stores be Transported thither as soon as may be, that we may be enabled to put in Execution whatever Orders we may receive with all the Dispatch that may be Expected from us. 
I have the doing of this the more at heart, because I think it at the same time the most effectual Method we can take for Security of our Frontiers & preventing the Incursions of the Enemy upon the Inhabitants: But the great Difficulty which remains with me is the pay of the Troops & of the Charges which must necessarily Attend their March;  For I am of Opinion that it may be hazardous even to propose their Marching 'till they have at least some part of the pay due to them, for in case they sho.d refuse to March without it, Disobedience or Mutiny may be introduced, of which it may not be easy either to foresee or prevent the bad Consequences.
It seems to me likewise necessary that whatever be done with respect to the pay of any of the New Levies of any of the Colonies it be equally done to all, & that the Rates of Exchange be fixed in such Manner that no one have reason to think he is better or worse than another.  These seem to

to me Matters of such Consequence that they are absolutely necessary to be fixed & ascertained before any particular Orders given for putting the Forces in Action, And therefore I must desire your Excellency's Sentim.ts & Advice in these particulars, as on what else you may think proper on this Occasion, that we Act uniformly & in concurrence with each other.
As it seems reasonable that Connecticut Join with us in Erecting the Forts at the Carrying place & in Marching their forces thither, I think it proper for me to write to the Gov.r of that Colony to know his Sentim.ts And as you know (I suppose) that the forces of Connecticut are under my Commission being appointed Captain Gen.l of Connecticut as well as of New York, I must desire your Advice & opinion as to the pay of the Levies & Commissions to the Officers in that Colony; at what Rate of Exchange is to be in their mony in case that they shall insist on having any part of their pay, what method is to be taken for paying them & for giving their Commissions for so far as I am Informed the Officers have received no kind of Commission more than their Gov.r's Warrant to Inlist Men. 
Now to Enable your Excellency to give your Sentim.ts on the sev.l points which I desire, & upon others which you may think requisite on this or any future occasion, I must Inform you that from what I can observe The Assembly of this Province will Endeavor to avoid a kind of Expence that they can with any Colour or pretense throw up the Crown, and that some of great Influence are desirous, if they can bring this Province into a kind of Neutrality as it was in Queen Ann's War. It was, I believe, with this view that the Gov.r of Canada sent the Message to the Six Nations after my treaty with them, wherein he told them that he took pity of the people of Albany, & would after that turn the Indians against their inveterate Enemys of New England. The Reason given for this was, that this kind of Service is so expensive in wearing of Shoes & other apparel, while they are obliged to March Thirty or forty Miles a Day, on the Track or pursuit of the Enemys Sculking Parties, as it may happen, thro' Brush & thick Swamps, thro' water & over Rocks & Hills; that the Expence of apparel would at least amount to that Sum. the new Levies cannot be sent under any Command but of their own Officers; and no proposal is made for Defraying the Extraordinary Expence of the Officers, nor for their Encouragem.t under such fatigueing Service.
But, Gentlemen, as these Resolves are introduced with an assertion that "the New Levies had remained hitherto unemployed," & are so much of a piece with some other things that have come from you; I find myself under a necessity of laying before you, a view of my past Conduct, with respect to the Care of the Frontiers, since the time that any of the New Levies Marched to Albany, & my own going thither.
The securing the fidelity of the Six United Indian Nations, seemed to every Man to be of the greatest Consequence to the safety of all the British Northern Colonies, & to the Success of the Expedition intended against Canada, with what Difficulty & with Charge to the Crown this was done, is well known, and that it was of the highest Importance to the safety of this Province, it was done without any Charge to the people of it.
At the same time the care of providing every thing necessary for the Marching of the forces, viz.t, Arms, Ammunition, Clothing, Tents, Battors, & all the untensils necessary for a Camp & a March fell upon me: All this was done at the Expencce of the Crown, without any Charge to this Province, and with great Advantage to the private interest of many in it. This unavoidably took up a great part of the Summer; and though at that time I was thus Engages in a Multiplicity of Business & had my Cares & thoughts Diversifyed by a Variety of unexpected incidents & Disappointm.ts & during the time of an Extraordinary Sickness (which I had my share of) & Mortality at Albany; I did not neglect the Care of the Frontiers: I sent Parties of Indians as far as Crown Point & Sacrament Lake for Intelligence, & to Intercept the Enemy's Partys: I sent out the Captains Langdon & Tebout severally, with Parties of the New Levies, for the same purpose; I sent likewise Captain Staats

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(33)
Staats, with a Party of Chosen Men of the New Levies at Albany, such as he thought the fittest for the Occasion, the Range the Woods with a number of Indians that were joined with them; likewise at the Expence of the Crown.
It is needless to tell you by what means any Enterprize against Canada last year became Impracticable, otherwise than by sending Parties of Indians to harrass them, which was done with Success. Immediately after the thoughts of any kind of Expedition against Canada were laid aside for that Season I gave Orders for posting the New Levies in such manner as by the best Information I could obtain might tend most for the Security of the Frontiers & at the same time forward any Enterprize for annoyance of the Enemy that should be thought proper, as the Season of the year would permit. For this purpose I gave Orders to Fortify a Camp capable of containing 500 Men at least, at or near the Carrying place. This I thought might serve two good purposes - 1st - As all the Enemy's parties make their Incursions in our Frontiers by this Pass it would be Difficult for them to Pass without being Discovered either in their going or returning; And that probably they must be intercepted by such a Number of Men posted there.  Next it would afterwards serve as a Security for the Magazines & Stores, for the Forces that shall at any time be Employed by Land against Canada: And it is agreed by all whom I have heard speak on the Subject, that this was the fittest place for both these purposes. The forces did March for this End, but by the unexpected Interruption in the Provisions for the Men, who were to cover the Works while they were Erecting & to Defend the place after it was Erected, & other Difficulties thrown in the way; this work (tho' in my opinion absolutely necessary) was laid aside and the Officers who had the Command were by the Cold Weather, which came on, forced to take up with the old Ford at Saraghtoga, only enlarging it & making new Defences to it; tho' by all the Information which I had of that place

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(34)
Place, it is the most Disadvantagiously Situated that any thing of the kind can be as it cannot serve for any of the purposes which I had in View by the fortifyed Camp at the Carrying place; & is so overlooked by Hills, covered with woods that the Enemy's Sulking Parties can discover every Motion in the Fort by the lowness of the Ground, & the Watry Swamps round it it has always been unhealthy, & has brought on a continued Sickness in every Garrison that has been placed in it: The Event has on too many Occasions proved the truth of these things.
In pursuance of my Orders, one Company of the New Levies was posted at the Mohawk Castle for their Security, another Company betwict that and Schenectada, two Companies at Schenectada, one on each side the River; Three Companies at Ganestigayane; four Companys at the half Moon, two Companys at Schalehook, & three Companys besides Detachm.ts from the others at Saraghtoga; so that there were Garrisons of the New Levies, in a Line from East to West cross the Northern Frontiers of this Province in every place where a Number of Men could be placed with safety in the Winter Season. The rest of the Forces were kept in & round the City of Albany, on both sides of the River, for the Defence of that Important place for your safety and at all places by which the Enemy can approach to it.
I was sensible that some other places ought to have been Secured by Erecting small Forts on them; and I proposed to have done it, but as you absolutely refused to contribute to any other Expence besides furnishing provisions for the New Levies, I could not put the Crown to an Expence, the Charge of which you did not think necessary for your safety.
I kept the Mohawk Indians (as I told you in my speech) from going out to hunt; & I sent likewise among the other five Nations to keep them in readiness to Join us, one party of Indians are gone out, some other parties were sometime since preparing to go. By these means I hope to force the French to keep some of their Partys at home to Defend themselves by

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(35)
by which they have so cruelly treated the Inhabitants on our Frontier; And this is done without any Expence to this province.
I sent Col.o Roberts to His Excell.y Gov.r Shirley to consult & concert Measures with him on what may be proper to be done, 'till such time as more particular Directions should come from His Majesty. It gave me some pleasure to find that what I had projected for Building a Fort at the Carrying place was thought so necessary for the End for which I intended it that some of the Neighboring Colonies appeared willing to Contribute a share towards the Expence, no one doubting that as the Security of this Province is more immediately concerned you would readily set a good Example to the others; It was for that reason agreed, that I should in the first place propose it to you: in doing this, I avoided every thing that I thought could give any handle to renew the Differences that had appeared last Fall; what return I have to all this care of the people of the Province, I shall leave to you their representatives to Judge, & to consider what the Neighboring Colonies must think on this Occasion.
Your Declining every Expense that seems necessary for the Security of the British Colonies in North America & the well being of this Province at this time and the Disrespectful Behaviour to me (such as was never shown to any Gov.r in Chief before me at this place) must give such conceptions to Strangers, or to those unacquainted with the true State of Affairs, that I am laid under a necessity, from the common  justice which every Man owes to himself, to speak out some things, which otherwise I should have thought prudent to conceal, but more especially, because any Disrespect shewn to me in my Station, must in the Common Acceptation of the World, be taken as a Disrespect to the Fountain, from whence I have the honour to Derive my Authority over this Province.
Gentlemen
You cannot be Ignorant that many in this Province & also the Neighboring Colonies are persuaded that the principal Traders & the Richest men

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(36) 
Men in Albany, do not wish well to the Success of any Expedition against Canada and this from a view which a few Men of Considerable Estates, & Influence by their Family Relations, have to their private Advantage gained by a Trade with Canada, & is always most Advantagious in time of War with france and which for common good, I have Effectually stopped: I must therefore tell you, that I am suspicious that all the Difficulties I met with in my treating with the Indians, & Engaging them heartily in this War arose chiefly from this Source; for if these Men could have prevented the Indians Joining in the War, & could have prevailed on them to Declare for a Neutrality they hoped to lay me under a necessity of falling into the same measures for the same purpose, all the Difficulties that could be contrived without an open Declaration of their Intentions, were laid in the way of every preparation [?] became necessary for the Success of any Enterprize against Canada. This scheme there is some reason to believe, was in concert with the Gov.r of Canada, from a Message which he sent to the Six Nations at the time of my last Treaty with them; wherein he tells them, that he took pity of their Britheren at Albany, and would form that time turn his Indians from that place on the most inveterate Enemys of New England. It is no wonder that the poor people of the County of Albany exposed to a Merciless Enemy should with some pleasure Entertain any Scheme by which they sho'd hope to be freed from such Cruelties, tho' they be loyal Subjects, & abhor the Beneficial part of it by Trade with the Enemy: But I hope you have too much Sense of your Duty & perception of the Mischievous Consequences of such a Scheme in any manner (now I have laid it open before you) to contribute towards the Success of it: surely you will with Abhorrence receive the thoughts [?] any Design to enable the Common Enemy of the British Nation and Protestant Religion, to over power our Bretheren, a part of our own Nation, from a hope of private Gain or Temporary Quiet to a few amongst us: when, if the Enemy should Succeed any way by your needs your posterity must be forever Sufferers- You

You may likewise remember (as I am told) that before the last Negro Plot and during the present War, Information was given of sev.l Popish Emisaries sent about in the Colonies to sow Seeds of Dissention, and to blow up every spark of Discontent; it has been the constant practice of that treacherous Religion to Act so: and as they have too frequent opportunitys, & too open a Door for such Vile Practices in the British Colonies, there is too much reason to suppose that they will not, and have not, omitted such a fair prospect of making us the Instrum.t of our own Ruin: They send Men well skilled in all the Weaknesses of humane Nature; They know how to work the sev.l Tempers of Men to their purposes; Men of Violent Passions, or of desperate fortunes, or of wrong heads, have always been the Tools of these cunning Emisaries; and when such happen to come by any means popular, they have too often proved the most Dangerous Instrum.t to the Distribution of the Religion & Liberty of their own Country, without knowing that they are used as such; as is Evident from sev.l Instances in teh History of your Mother Country, & of other Nations, you may hereafter woefully blame yourselves for your fatal Security, if you imagine that no such thing can happen at this time in North America, consider only what has happened since the Commencem.t of the present War with France; how the Enemys of the Liberty of Makind, had the Artifice to raise a most Dangerous, as well as unnatural Rebellion in Scotland, and by the like Artifices, have brought Confusion, & Dangerous Revolutions, into sev.l Courts in Europe: nothing has been so Effectual for these purposes, as raising Jealousies among the people, of their Rulers & Governours, by false Reports & Insinuations, which the low Rank of Mankind are too apt to receive; and though they Discover that they have been Deluded with a thousand false Reports, they swallow the next of this kind with greediness.
You may learn from the Publick News Papers, what great Armam.ts the Enemy is making by Sea, that it is suspected that some part of it is designed

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(38)
Designed against North America; let me Conjure you then, Gentlemen, to take care of yourselves: can it be immagined, that now, when your Mother Country is at such prodigious Expence, both in Men & mony to support the War that you will omit any thing in your power, for your own safety, & annoyance of the Common Enemy.
Gentlemen.
After doing what I think at this time incumbent on me, I return to the Subject on which I began. With what truth can it be said that the New Levies have remained hitherto unemployed, and for what purposes are Insinuations thus publickly made, of my Neglect of my Duty.
I assure you there is nothing in my power, that I shall not heartfully do, for the Security of the Frontiers & to preserve the Inhabitants from the Incursions of a cruel & barbarous Enemy; but then it Depends on you to Enable me to do it to the purpose, by contributing to the Expence which must necessarily Attend it.
Notwithstanding the opposition which have been made to the Measures which I thought necessary for his Maj.s Service, I shall have the satisfaction to know that I have (to the utmost of my power) Exerted myself for the welfare of this Province, & with these thoughts I remain easy.
After I shall know your Resolution of taking Care of yourselves at this time, when I apprehend the Province may be in Danger, I shall return an Answer to your Message of the 23d Instant.
G. Clinton

We have an Account from Albany that the Party of Indians which was sent 
[Left margin info is truncated and indecipherable]
out by Coll.l Johnson, under the Command of L.t Walter Butler Jun.r this Spring ag.t the French was returned with Success. They set out from the Mohawk Castle the 3.d of April & went to Crown Point where they lay two Days upon a Hill from whence they had a good View of the Fort, in which time they Discovered nothing except two large Canoes full of Men that they saw go from the Fort toward Albany, & by the Shouting of the Men in those Canoes made as they left the Fort it was concluded that they were going out to Scalp.  The third Day the party came down from the Hill, & Divided into two parties, one of which consisted of thirteen Men, came upon the Tract of sev.l persons going towards the Garrison. They pursued them 'till they got withing half a mile of the Fort, when they Discovered a Party of the Garrison resting on a fallen Tree, & were employed in beating & dressing some Touchwood which they had found in the woods where they had been upon the Catroll & our thirteen Indians took this opportunity of

transcription:
(44)
of approaching under a Bank, & by the Advantage of the Bank they got very near the french without being observed, & found that the Enemy consisted of 27 Soldiers & three Indians. Our Indians fired upon them & killed three whereupon the Enemy flew to their Arms & returned the fire briskly but without any Execution, our Indians having loaded again, gave them a Second Volley, killed one Man more & wounded three upon which the Enemy gave way, but one of their Officers brought them back to their Ground again, & then they fought smartly, & the Chief our Indians was wounded through the Breast & one arm, & another Slightly on the Knee; upon this it is said our Indians in rage fought more like Devils than Men, and observing one of the French Indians presenting his Piece, one of our Indians ran up within Ten Yards of him & Discharged his piece loaded with Swan Shot into his Breast, upon which he fell down Dead. The other two french Indians on this run for it. This Discouraged the french so much that they all likewise fled towards the Fort, except their two Officers & a Serjeant, who continued fighting bravely 'till they all three fell. Part of our Indians in the mean while pursued those that fled 'till they came withing Musket Shot of the Fort, & say they saw Nine wounded Men carryed into the Garrison by the others - They then returned to the place of Action, but observing a Party from the Garrison coming upon them, they had only time to take Six Scalps - Our Indians were closely pursued for two Days 'till they got into a Lake from whence a River Issues that runs towards the Mohawk Country.
One of the French Officers was a Young Man, Dressed in Blue - trimmed with a broad Gold Lace: This Gentleman, the Indians say, fought with much Courage, & being Dangerously wounded called out in the Indian Language for Quarters; but they perceiving his wounds were Mortal put him out of Pain - By all accounts of this Action it is looked on as the Gallentest thing done by Indians since the commencem.t of the War

You will find by the Inclosed Copys of papers the State of the New Levies in this Province, intended for the Expedition against Canada, My greatest concern is for the Garrison at Saraghtoga, where there are Six pieces of Cannon of Eighteen pound Ball, four Brass field pieces, a large Quantity of Ball & Powder, which I ordered to that place in the Winter Season to be ready on any Enterprize that should be thought proper to be undertaken against the Enemy by Land, as the Cannon & Amunition would be carryed with the greatest Ease & safety in that Season of the year, and might be of use likewise in case any Enterprize against Crown Point should be undertaken before Spring, as was proposed by the Governm.t of the Massachusetts Bay.
The New Levies in this Province absolutely refuse to March to support that Garrison notwithstanding all the Endeavors of the Officers to that purpose; And indeed in their present Disposition & Considering that most of them consist of Servants merely out of their time, who it is to be feared are transported Felons, I suspect they are not at this time to be entrusted with a Garrison of such Importance: I must therefore earnestly intreat you to send sufficient Detachm.ts of the forces of your Governm.t with all speed to the Relief & support of that Garrison, & that the Officers who shall Command any Detachments for that purpose, send some person into the Garrison at Saraghtoga before the Party approach near it to acquaint the Commanding Officer there that they were sent at my request for their relief & support - I am of opinion it may likewise be proper to March a Considerable Numbere of the Troops of your Government to your Frontiers near

His Excellency then observed to the Board, that if the Jersey Forces were paid all their pay the Forces of this & the other provinces would insist on the same & what his Excellency had, with the Advice of the Council Determined to allow them would be to no purpose.

The Council further Advised his Excellency to write to Coll.l Schuyler & acquaint him with the purport of his Excellency's Letter to M.r Hamilton & that as the Jersey Levies are now within this Governm.t, his Excellency intends to pay them in the same Manner as the other New raised Levies now posted on the Frontiers of this Province, & Directing him hot to pay the Jersey Levies the whole or any part of the pay due to them.
And the Council also Advised his Excellency to acquaint Coll.l Marshall by the Express now going to Albany, that he is getting the mony ready in order to pay the New Levies, & will send it up as soon as possible or come thither himself.

Gentlemen:
You cannot avoid seeing the Importance of the Papers which are now Ordered to be laid before you; the safety of the people you represent is immediately concerned: it is needless therefore on this Occasion to use any Argum.ts with you to provide for their safety: you'll see the opinion of His Majesty

Majesty's Council thereon. I am ready to do every thing that can in reason be Expected of me in pursuance of the Advice which I have received -
I have already Engaged my private fortune for his Maj.s Service in this Province further than I think I was under any Obligation to do; And I think every Man in the Province is obliged as much as I am to contribute out of his private fortune for the safety of the people of it -
The Nine thousand pounds which I have already received on my Bills shall all of it be applyed to the paym.t of the New Levies -
If you will not advance so much mony as shall be further necessary on this Occasion, I am ready to Draw Bills for any Sum, & at any rate of Exchange w.ch shall be thought necessary & proper -
But at the same time I must tell you that I insist on it that my Family may be Indemnifyed from whatever may happen on what I have done, or shall do by advice of His Maj.s Council in the paym.t of Forces Levied on the Expedition intended against Canada, & posted in the County of Albany; and I assure you I will to the utmost of my power Sollicit the Paym.ts of such Bills.-
If the safety of the people of this Province, in their Lives & Estates does not Deserve your taking this upon yourselves, I am not in the least apprehensive of Incurring any Blame on whatever shall happen: it remains then with you to provide against the Evils which are threatned & which cannot be prevented without your speedy & sufficient assistance, in the manner at least that I am contented to take it. -
Though I be under a necessity of laying these Paypers before you, yet the Contents of them ought by no means to be made publick. -

The House according to Order resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House upon his Excellency's Message of teh 2.d Instant, & the sev.l papers therewith Delivered: after sometime spent therein, M.r Speaker resumed the Chair, & M.r Clarkson reported the opinion of the Committee thereon; which he read in this place, & afterwards delivered in at the Table, where the same was again read & is as follows - viz.t
The Committee having intirely Considered his Excellency's Message to the House of the 2.d Instant, & the sev.l papers therewith Delivered, touching the paym.t of the Forces Levied on the Expedition against Canada, & posted to the County of Albany, & having on this Occasion had recourse to his Grace, the Duke of NewCastles Letter of the 9th of April 1746 - to his Excellency & by him Communicated to the house, touching the raising the said Forces; & in  one paragraph thereof find these words, "You will assure all those that shall Engage in this Service as well Officers as Soldiers, that they will immediately Enter into his Maj.s pay; the Officers from the time they shall Engage in his Maj.s Service, & the Soldiers for the respective Days on which they shall Inlist" The Committee are therefore unanimously of opinion that his most Gracious Majesty did not intend that the people of this Colony should contribute or Advance any monys towards the pay of the said Forces; the part of Expence Assigned to this Colony by his Majesty, as appears by the said Letter, being the supplying Provisions for the Subsistence of the forces raised in it w.ch has been chearfully complyed with; tho' by the large Number of Men raised & their long continuance in the Service that Expence has been very great. That the care of the pay for the said Forces seems to be his Excellency's province who may (by Drawing Bills of Exchange whose Credit is nowhere Questioned) procure monys sufficient for that purpose: And that his Excellency's insisting that the house should Indemnify him & his Family with respect to what he has done or may do in Drawing Bills for the paym.t of the said Forces implies such a Distrust of his Majesty as ought by no means to be suggested. And

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(57)
And the Committee are further humbly of Opinion that when his Excellency shall have seriously reflected on the Duty he Owes to his Majesty as his Representative here he will not so far forget himself as upon Private Considerations of his own Family to refuse drawing Bills for such a Sum as seems at this time necessary (from the papers laid before the house) to prevent the total Disertion of the New Levies; more especially as the Committee apprehend (from the Minutes of the Council of the 31.ar od May last laid before the House) that his Maj.s Council did Advise his Excellency to Draw for the whole pay of the said New Levies at Albany.-
The Committee also conceive that the Diffidence of his Excellency to Draw Bills for the pay of the said Levies on the pressing Occasion is altogether unreasonable & without Grounds, as he has the most Solemn Assurances in his Grace the Duke of Newcastle's Letter, that the Soldiers shall immediately Enter into his Majesty's pay, from the respective Days on which they shall inlist.
And upon the whole the Committee are clearly of Opinion That if the safety of the people of this Colony in their Lives & Estates should be Endangered by the Forces not being paid, his Excellency only will be to blame, & as it is altogether in his power to provide against the Evils which are threatened; And which may be so easily prevented by his Excellency's Discharging the Duty which he Owes to his Majesty. Vide my answer to the Council upon this Report Fo:99 at the end of this Book.

the Expence, which it may be thought reasonable for the sev.l Governm.ts to bear without rendring any Attempt for this Year Impracticable.
The whole of the Extraordinary Expence, exclusive of Provisions for the Soldiers & Indians for carrying the Plan of Operations to Effect is computed at fourteen thousand Pounds -
The Safety of the people of this Province is so immediately concerned in the Success of the Enterprizes proposed & in their being set on foot speedily & prosecuted without Delay, that I must earnestly recommend to you, to take such a share of that Expence on yourselves, that the Massachusets Bay & Connecticut may not hesitate, but be Encouraged chearfully to take the rem.r upon themselves -
I am persuaded that your Constituents are fully convinced of the Necessity of something to be Undertaken at this time, that any Zeal shewn for so necessary a work, by taking upon ourselves more that what is a Just proportion may be thought proper on any other occasion, where there is time to Adjust Matters will be agreeable to them: For unless the Forces now at Albany, be put on some Action this Season, it may not be in our power to Employ them in the Spring of the year, or afterwards.-
The Six United Nations of Indians are all hearty in our Interest; I have the strongest assurances of their most vigorous assistance; & I have likewise hopes of the Assistance of sev.l other Indian Nations, some of which were formerly in the strictest friendship with the french; but if we remain longer inactive - we shall certainly lose all Esteem & Interest among them, & give the french Advantages with them, which you may grievously repent.
I shall lay nothing else at this time before you that you may immediately Deliberate & Resolve on what share of teh Expence you will think proper to take, & to make provision for it accordingly that I may at the same time I Communicate the Plan Concerted here, import your Resolutions to support

To His Excellency the Hon.ble Geo: Clinton Esq.r Captain Gen.l & Gov.r in Chief of the Province of New York & Teritories thereon Depending in America, Vice Adm.l of the same & Vice Adm.l of the Red Squadron of His Maj.s Fleet.
The humble Address of His Maj.s Council of the said Province. - We His Majesty's most Dutiful & Loyal Subjects the Members of His Maj.s Council for the Province of New York beg leave to lay before your Excellency the present Dangerous State we apprehend the City of Albany to be in. -
Your Excellency cannot but be sensible that the preservation of the County of Albany & of the great part of this Province, The fidelity of the Indian Nations, & we may add in it's Consequences the Security of great part of the Neighboring Provinces, does chiefly depend upon the preservation of that City, we were therefore deeply Afflicted with the late Accounts received from thence, That the New Levies which had been posted to the Northward of the City of Albany had been all withdrawn for thence (Except one Company of about 70 or so Men left at the Mill a short Miles Distance from Albany) & Encamped at Green Bush below the City & on the opposite side of the River, greatly allarmed at this

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(72)
this Report & being Informed that M.r Collins Town Major of Albany & M.r Cayler late Mayor of that City, were in this Town, we sent for & Examined them upon their Oaths, & they confirmed the truth of this Report; As this step appeared to us to be of Dangerous Consequence to His Maj.s Service & is Evidently to hazard the Loss of the City of Albany, we thought we could not Discharge the Duty we Owe to his Majesty & to our Country, if on this Occasion we should be any longer silent. We are therefore constrained by the Dangers we apprehend ourselves Exposed to, to have Recourse to your Excellency, & to lay before you some Facts, such as either consist with our own knowledge, or we received upon the Oaths of teh Gentlemen we Examined. The City of Albany is situated on the West Side of Hudson's River; the Town of Schenectady is also on the same side of that River at about Sixteen Miles Distance, the Fort at Saraghtoga is at about 36 Miles Distance to the N.ward of Albany, Green Bush where the Levies are Encamped is on the East side of Hudson's River at about [?] Miles Distance below Albany where the River is about a third part of a Mile Wide & not fordable being of Depth sufficient for large Vessels: upon these facts we must observe to your Excellency that the Levies Encamped at Green Bush cannot March to the Assistance of Albany or Schenectady or the Relief of Saraghtoga Fort, without first Crossing the River below Albany And sho.d the Enemy make any Attempt upon Albany or Schenectady we leave it to your Excell.y's own Reflection to consider what Delays & Confusion would Attend the passage of Troops not very Orderly & many of them [?] half Disciplined; & how for such an unnecessary Delay would hazard the [?] of such places sho.d they be suddenly Attacked; And since the Levies are Encamped on the East side of Hudson's River (Except that handful at the Mills) there are no Inhabitants to the Norhward, all that part of the Country being except the Fort at Saraghtoga, what is there to hinder or Molest the french their Indians from coming with the greatest Confidence & Security near [?] of Albany and watching an opportunity to surprise it. It was with great concern

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [2], 1745-1749
transcription:
(73)
concern & grief that we heard of the Distressed & Deplorable Circumstances of the City of Albany. The whole Number of Men able to bear Arms, even including the Greyheads of Seventy & upwards, does not exceed three hundred; They are obliged to do Duty on the Guard every fourth Night sometimes oftner without Distinction of Age or persons; so that even the Judge of the Court of Common Pleas for the County, a very Antient Man, is obliged to take his turn; And yet notwithstanding this great fatigue upon the Inhabitants they have had no Assistance or Ease from the New Levies -
We beg leave to acquaint your Excellency that we are Justly apprehensive that these Difficulties & Discouragem.ts may Induce such of them as can Support themselves else where, to leave the City & thereby render it weaker & more exposed to Danger & Ruin,
Sir
At this Distance from his most Sacred Majesty we cannot lay before him for immediate Relief, the Deplorable Circumstances of our Country, from whose paternal Care of all his faithful Subjects (and such with truth we may call ourselves from our known Loyalty to his Majesty & Affection to his illustrious house) we could not fail of Assistance: At this Distance therefore, we apply to your Excellency, & we flatter ourselves that upon the few Considerations which we have laid before you & the Reflections which your own Judgem.t may Suggest to you, your Exellency will be pleased to give your Orders for posting such a Number of the New Levies (untill his Majesty shall Dispose of them otherwise) to be Northward of the City of Albany in such places as your Excellency shall think most convenient for its protection & Security; and to keep the Enemy at a greater Distance, And we pray the God of heaven to touch your Excell.y's heart with Compassion to the Distressed Inhabitants of the City of Albany That by posting some of the Levies in that City the Inhabitants may be partly eased of the heavy Duty they Undergo, & be induced to continue in the City for it's Strength & Defence, and we are humbly of Opinion that those Companys of Levies which were raised in & about the City would be most proper for that purpose

Your Excellency was pleased on Saturday last to Deliver some particulars in writing to the Council, for their Consideration, which were referred to a Committee of the whole Council, or any five of them;  The Committee met the same Evening, & not having had Copys, were of opinion they should be made out next Morning & Delivered to the Members, that they might consider of those Matters contained therein, against their next Meeting: which was appointed the Night following; when the Committee again met, but as most of the Committee did not receive their Copys 'till the Meeting, they had not had a suff.t time for Consideration; but however, the Committee entered into the Matters referred to them

Upon this answer we humbly beg leave to observe to your Excellency how widely you have mistaken the Intention of the Committee, into whose thoughts it never Entered to call your Excellency to Account; we know your Excellency is accountable to his Majesty, and, as our Duty is, to His Majesty we leave it. But surely, Sir, if the Council, or the Committee of the whole Council conceive that there is any Obscurity in what your Excellency Delivers, or that you are able to furnish them with further help to Inform their Judgm.ts, upon things referred to them;  it is proper for them to apply to your Excellency; And the Application, as the Committee conceives, can in no sense be Misconstrued, or misrepresented as a Calling your Excellency to an Account; and to clear ourselves for any Misrepresentation of that kind, We take the Liberty to let your Excellency know the reason on which we proceeded. -
Your Excellency says "You likewise must observe to the Council, that you cannot any longer find provisions for the Forces at Albany, either of the Independant Companys, nor the New Levies; nor continue the Expence the Crown has been put to, for Securing the fidelity of the Indians, or for sending our Partys of them, either as OutScouts or to annoy the Enemy."
As your Excellency has for a considerable time past found provisions for some of the New Levies at Albany, not raised in this Province, & put the Crown to a great Expence for Securing teh Fidelity of the Indians; it was Natural for the Committee to desire to be Informed by your Excellency whether

Upon the whole the Committee are humbly of Opinion as to the first point, That as M.r Shirley & M.r Knowles are to meet together to Advise to the Disposition of the Forces levied on the Expedition against Canada would be advisable for your Excellency to write to them in the most pressing Terms representing the Danger that would attend the Removal of all the Levies from this Province, and we make no doubt but that upon a full Representation, it will plainly appear to them, to be so evidently for his Majesty's Service, to continue, at least the Levies raised in this Province that we cannot doubt, from those Gentlemens Capacity I Knowledge, they will be of Opinion to continue them in this Province, and dispose of them in such manner as is of most Advantage to his Majesty's Service. 
As to the Second & third Points, your Excellency may observe the Committee cannot come to an Opinion without further Light.
As to the fourth, your Excellency says, "You expect that great Numbers of the Distant Indians are now with Coll.l Johnson, their meeting with a Disappointment in their Expectations at this time may be of the most fatal Consequence."-
Tbe Committee beg leave to observe, that as your Excellency must have Expected those Indians to be now with Coll.l Johnson, They cannot but [?] your Excellency had before made suitable provision for that Event, and [?] therefore they cannot meet with a Disappointment of their Expectations.

"You well know in what Temper & Disposition the Six united Nations of Indians were before by treaty with them last year; The Commiss.r for Indian Affairs gave repeated Advice of their unwillingness to enter into the War against the french, many of them had actually gone over to Assist the French, and the fidelity of all of them became suspected: the Success of my treaty with them was so unexpected, that it is also well known, with what Reluctance any Account of it was received; and that all Manner of doubts were Encouraged & propagated 'till the Effects of their Incursions on the Enemy appeared in this City: after this the Numbers of those gained heartily to the British Interest were with great Assiduity every where represented to be very small; while at the same time the Number of the Disaffected were as industriously magnifyed, 'till the great Numbers of Indians who have Joined Coll.l Johnson with the greatest Alacrity in this Enterprize, at this time against a Body of the Enemy discovered by his Parties in Lake Sacrament, from whence the Enemy send out great Parties to Murder cruelly the Inhabitants of this Province; And it has Evidently Discovered the falsity of all these Reports and given you an opportunity to reflect for what purposes these Reports have been so Industiously propagated to the prejudice of the British Interests.
The Crown has been at a very great Expence in recovering the Affection of the Indians; the people of Great Britain are now at a greater Expence of Treasure in Defending the Libertys of Europe than ever they were at any time since they were a Nation; the King then must Expect, that you will at

at the Expence necessary for the safety of the people you Represent, in preserving the Affection of the Indians, which otherwise must be lost.
My concern therefore for the Welfare & safety of the people whom our most Gracious Sovereign has Committed to my Care, makes me again insist that you provide for the necessary Services that I recommend to you in my Message, for two Months at least; after which we have reason to hope, the Neighboring Colonies will Join in the Mutual Defence of the Frontiers & concert proper Measures for the Effectual Annoyance of the Enemy: If you continue to refuse this, consider that you may thereby Expose yourselves to the Displeasure of your King, & perhaps to the Resentm.t of your Mother Country; at least you will take upon yourself the blame of all Misfortunes that may happen thereby to the people of this Province: nothing in my power shall be wanting for the Defence & Security, or for the Annoyance of the Enemy; but if you deny me the necessary supplys, all my Endeavours must become ineffectual & fruitless; I must wash my hands, & leave at your Doors the Blood of the innocent people that may be shed by a cruel & merciless Enemy.
Unless the Affection & fidelity of the Indians be Effectually Secured, it will be impracticable to preserve the Garrison at Saraghtoga; and therefore I cannot resolve on a Relief of that Garrison, 'till you have given a proper answer to this.

(63)

"Gentlemen, I must on this Occasion tell you, that the provisions for the Army are so necessary a part of all warlike Enterprizes, that any Defect or Obstruction in the Daily supply of them, may Defeat the best concerted Measures, And that if the Provisions for the Army are not Subject to the Orders of the Genl., of Commanding Officer it is in the power of those persons who have the Directions of furnishing provisions, to Defeat any Enterprize. I must therefore recommend it to you, to amend the former Act in such Manner, that the Service for which these Provisions are designed may not suffer, but be rather promoted + made easy; And for this purpose, that you will provide for Transporting the Provisions along with the forces. And as I have Ordered part of the four Independent Companys of regular Troops to go with the other Forces Levyed in this Province, I must desire that you will put them as to provisions, on the same footing with the other Forces.
"As the Officer Commanding the Forces of this Province has Informed me, that 1380 Men have appeared at the place of Randezvous; that the Commissioners for paying the additional Bounty of 40. + a Blanket to such as shall appear there, have only received 2400 pounds for that purpose; And that this Deficiency may Occasion Disertions + Disorders among the soldiers; I must recommend it to you, for the making up this Deficiency; And that you will likewise furnish Blankets for such of the Regular Troops as shall be Employed in the same Service with the Forces Levyed for the Expedition against Canada"

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(64)
To His Excellency the Honble: George Clinton Esq. Captain Genl. + Gov. in Chief of the Colony of New York + the Territories thereon Depending in America, Vice Adml. of the same, + Vice Adml. of the Red Squadron of His Majesty's Fleet-
[[To:?]], 20, 4 Nov. 1746 Minutes of Assembly - Representation of the Genl. Assembly. }
The humble Representation of the Genl. Assembly of thes. Colony
May it please your Excellency..
We his Majesty's most Dutiful + loyal Subjects the Genl. Assembly of this Colony, beg leave to lay before you the following Representation, in answer to your Excellency's Speech, Delivered to us by our Speaker on the 17th: + your Message on the 23d. of October last.
We are entirely unacquainted with the bad Disposition of the Six Nations of Indians, + who have been the occasion of it; what was recommended to us the last year with regard to fixing the Six Nations in the British Interest, we have complyed with by giving a Sum of mony to [[defray?]] the Expence of your Excellency's Voyage to Albany, and an Additional Sum of £600. beyond the usual Allowance for purchasing proper Goods to make presents to them. In what manner that Service has been performed, your Excellency, + those you have thought proper to Employ, can certainly best Determine.
We are pleased to hear that the Six Nations, with the Neighbouring Indians have solemnly Joined with us in the war against Canada: And it will greatly Increase our pleasure, when we see their Actions Correspond with their Engagements, It will be then the Inhabitants of Canada will feel in their own Country, the Effects of your Excellency's last Meeting with them
Your Excellency is pleased to tell us that the Diffidences + Disorders "that have appeared among the Six Nations could not have happened without some neglect or Misconduct in the Managemt. of Indian Affairs": And as your Excellency has been pleased to recommend to our Consideration the Conduct of those Affairs, we shall very readily enter into a strict [[Examination?]]

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(65)
Examination of them; and we beg your Excellency will be pleased to put it in our power, by Ordering to be laid before us, when we shall call for them, all Letters + Papers that have been passed between your Excellency + the Commiss. for Indian Affairs; or between your Excellency + any other persons concerning Indian Affairs, since your Excellency's Arrival to this Government: And when we find who have been the Cause of this Misconduct in their affairs, we shall use our utmost Endeavors to remedy so great an Evil: untill this be done, it may not perhaps be advisable to allow a larger Sum than usual for the Managemt. of Indian Affairs, least it be liable to the same Misconduct.
The Orders which your Excellency has left behind you at Albany for forming a Winter Camp, we apprehend may be attended with a great many Inconveniencys; the Severity of the Cold in that Northern Climate, with the Deep snows that usually fall in that Season, will render it almost impossible for the Troops to Defend themselves from the Inclemency of the Weather: Hence a great Number must either Dye or Desert; + thereby, as we conceive, the Expedition against Canada by Land (should his Maj. think proper to have it carryed on the Ensuing year) will be either retarded or entirely defeated; as nothing can be a greater Inducemt. to Desertion, than Exposing the Troops in a Winter Camp.
We are truly sensible at what great Expence our Mother COuntry supports the present war against the Enemys of the Libertys of Europe, + of the Protestant Religions; and how much this Expence have been increased by the late unnatural Rebellion in Scotland: But, thank God, this unnatural Rebellion is suppressed, by the success of his Majesty's Arms, under the unparallel'd Conduct of the Glorious Duke of Cumberland.
We are sensible of the great Expence the Crown is at on this Expedition, + the Advantages we shall reap by the success of it; and however popular the

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(66)
the Term of parsimony or saving may have become, it has never been mentio[[ned?]] in our house on this occasion. But we can with truth + Decency say, tha[[t?]] we have chearfully done even more than his Maj. recommended or expected from us. We declare ourselves at a Loss to know the meaning of your Excellency's recommendation, "that whatever Expence we shall judge necessary to be made the least Burthensome possible, especially to those who are least able to bear it," as not being conscious to ourselves of having ever acted otherwise.
We are equally surprised, as well as concerned, that your Excellency should Entertain an opinion, that there is not a perfect Harmony subsisting between the sevl. Branches of the Legislature; we know full well the Inconveniencys of intestine troubles at all times, more especially when we are Exposed to a powerfull, cruel + Deceitfull Enemy: And we think ourselves capable of Guarding against the private Views of Artfull + Designing Men; and should be sorry to find, that any such should prevail on your Excellency to break that Harmony, so necessary for the preservation of us all: And if any persons have taken upon them to Advise your Excellency, to entertain a Distrust of the sevl. Branches of the Legislature; at this critical Juncture; we may Venture to Affirm, they are not friends to their Country; but have some sinister Ends in View.
We Join with your Excellency in observing that every Branch of the Legislature ought to keep strictly to our happy Constitution: We cannot Charge ourselves (+ we believe none else can) with any Endeavors to Encroach upon the powers + priviledges entrusted with the others.
Your Excellency has observed, that the weakness of humane Nature is such, that Mankind is seldom free from real Causes of Mistrust; hence Differences have happened more than once in this Government; but they who lived in those times + know the secret Springs of Action, allow their Differences to have arisen more from the bad advice given to the Gov. for their Political Conduct, than from any Imprudent or wanton Stretch of

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(67)
of power in the people: But these Transactions have been long buried in oblivion, + never should be revived, but as Land marks to direct us to shun the like Evils.
We come now to your Excellency's Message. 'Tis difficult to conceive how your Excellency could Expect the Commiss. to deliver the provisions otherwise than at Albany, since no allowance has been made for the Carriage or Transportation thereof to any other place. To set in a clear light a Matter wherein we differ with your Excellency, we beg leave to repeat the following words of the Message. "When you resolved to find Provisions for the Forces raised in this Province for the Expedition; it was thought you was at the same time, resolved to bear all the Charges incident thereto, of which the Carriage of the Provisions with the Army was part." A Review of our proceedings what passed between your Excellency + us, + the Resolutions we came to with respect to the Carriage of the Provisions along with the Army, + other incidental Charges, will surely discover our Intentions. Our first Resolutions were founded on your Excellency's laying before us an Extract of his Grace the Duke of New Castle's Letter, signifying to your Excellency his Majesty's pleasure, to recommend it to the Council + Assembly, to provide a sufficient Quantity of Provisions for the Subsistance of the Troops that should be raised here for the Service of the Expedition. Your Excellency will remember, that the very Day that Extract was laid before us, we voted the Victualling all such Men as should be raised: And a few Days after, to forward the Levies, we Voted the Bounty of £6. Even so great a Bounty had not the sudden Effect we wished. We then resolved the Additional Bounty of 40. + a Blanket.
The Importance of the Expedition, + the Exigency of the times, have unavoidably brought us thus far: The Circumstances of the Colony (of which we are the most competent Judges) will not suffer us, consistent with the trust reposed in us, to take one step further. Your Excellency may know how far this war, the Securing of our Frontiers, + the present Expedition have Involved

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(68)
Involved us + our Posterity. As to the Justness + Expediency of our Measu[[res?]] we may Appeal to your Excellency. If the Sums given for a Bounty to the Levied, had been Voted for the Carriage of the Provisions with the Army or for any other Charges incident to the Service, what an inconsiderable Number of Men would have been raised in this Colony, + to Transport the Provisions to Albany, the place of Randezvous appointed by His Majesty there to be Delivered to the respective Captains, all which will appear by the Journal of our proceedings, + the Act passed in Consequence thereof.
To shew your Excellency that nothing shall be wanting on our parts, we immediately Voted the Additional Bounty to the 180 Men, as recommend[[ed?]] by your Excellency: Hence your Excellency may perceive the readiness + chearfulness with which we have Engaged, + will hear our parts in this Expedition; and we conclude, with assuring your Excellency that we shall always endeavor to make your Administration easy, as far as is consistent with the Duty we owe to his Majesty, + that regard for the prosperity of this Colony, which our Constituents, in Justice to themselves expect from us.
David Jones - Speaker

Gentlemen-
"In answer to your Representation of the 5th. Instant, I shall Inform you that they Apprehensions which were generally entertained through this Province, + in some of the Neighbouring Colonies, but more especially by the Inhabitants of the County of Albany, of the bad Disposition the Six Nations were in, + that it was occasioned by the ill usage which they received from persons who traded + had other Dealings with them, I thought so notoriously known, that it needed no more particular pointing our, then what I have done; when it is so notoriously known, that most of those usually Employed in the Conduct of Indian Affairs are Traders + Dealers with the Indians. This I thought may deserve your serious Consideration at this time, when the good or bad Disposition of the Indian may be of the greatest Consequence to the safety of this Province; and when all the Advantages which I have obtained, by regaining their affections, at a great Expence to the Crown, without any Charge to this Province, may be again lost by a like ill usage. I shall give you all the Assistance I can in any Enquirys you shall think proper to make for this purpose; And I shall give Orders to the Secretary for Indian Affairs, to lay before you Copys of all Letters + Papers that have passed between me + the Commiss. for Indian affairs, whenever you shall please to call for them
"If you had used like Caution in forming an Opinion of the Disposition of the Forces under my Command, by the Orders which I left behind me [[at?]] Albany

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(71)
"Albany, which you have done in Judging of the Conduct of the Commiss. for Indian Affairs, in desiring to be Informed of the Nature of that Winter Camp, + of the Views + purposed I had in giving such Orders, perhaps your Sentimts. would have been different from what they now are; but I am sorry to observe to you on this occasion, that the Publication of your Dissatisfaction in the Manner you have done, may [[countenance?]] disrespect to the most necessary Orders I can give, the Consequences whereof are too obvious to need Explanation.
"I thought is proper to Express my tenderness for the people of this province, when it was necessary to Demands an extraordinary supply from them: The King has frequently Declared the like Tenderness on the like Occasion: and I am persuaded it cannot displease you, that I Endeavor in my Station to immitate his Love + Tenderness for his people.
"I am sorry that any Expressions which I have used, in recommending a good Agreemt. among us, in this time of Danger, have given offence; but as I find it has, I must leave it to my Superiours to Judge, from your own Representation, + your ordering it to be printed, without waiting for or Allowing any reasonable time to give you an Answer for your satisfaction, whether that Recommendation was unseasonable-
"It always has been, + shall be my Endeavour, to preserve a good Agreemt. among us; I am not conscious of the least stop that has been taken on my part towards raising partys or Divisions among you. An on the contrary, my Resolution is fixed, that in all Cases wherein I may differ from you in opinion to rest my Judgement (when the publick good will permit Delay) 'till such time as I can lay the Matters in dispute, before the King + his Ministers, + receive their Direction thereon.
"Now, Gentlemen, I think this an occasion on which I may be allowed to tell you, that within this Six Months past, I have gone through more Difficulties, I have had less assistance, + I have done more for this Province, than I believe any Governour of New York before me. I feel in my own Breast my Zeal for my Country's Service; and therefore I can with pleasure lay

15th: Nov 1748.... The Speaker came with sevl. other Members to me with a Private Message about the Provisions, + said he hoped I would give Assurances that there shod. be no want or abuse of the Provisions, this private Message was read to me by the Speaker, and I asked him for that paper, or a Copy of it, that I might not forget the Subject Matter of it, which he refused. Gentlemen/
"I find myself under a necessity, from your Resolves of the 8th: Instant communicated to me by order of the house to make my observations thereon, in Vindication of the Measures I took at Albany last Summer, in obedience to His Majesty's Commands for the good of his Service, + the better Security of this Province; and in order to clear from Aspersion the Characters of the Gentlemen of His Majesty's Council, who assisted me in the Genl. Conduct of affairs, during my stay at that place.
"I agreed with Mr. Shirley + Mr. Warren (the only two persons in America who had power to concert) on a Plan for the operations in the Expedition against Canada, whereof the greatest part remain yet to be Executed; and for that reason I thought it inconsitent with my Duty to make them publick; but this occasion obliges me to tell you, that the forces of this + the Neighbouring Colonies, whose Randezvous was at Albany were thereby to March from thence.
"This being premised, I conceived it would greatly tend to the advantage of the Service, to Join with them so many of the four Independent Companys as could be spared from the Garrisons-
"The new Levied Companys of this Province amounted at first to 1600 Men, besides Commission Officers, whom you have Engaged to furnish with the Provisions, during the Expedition; but so great a Diminution having happened by Disertions + Death, as the remainder did not exceed 1400 Men, including Officers; I concluded it would be agreeable to you, to supply in part that Defect, by Joining to them 200 Men of the Independent Companys, without putting the Province to any other Charge that that of Provisions during this Service-
"When I granted my Orders for Issuing Provisions to these Men, there being an Absolute necessity of supplying them in like manner with the new Levies, I sent Major Clarke to the Commiss., with assurances to them, that if you would not allow provisions to these Troops, I would either pay or replace the same, as none could be got at that time in the City of Albany, to enable them to March-

The House taking into their serious Consideration His Excellency's Massage of the 24th: Instant, delivered as an answer to the Resolutions of the House of the 8th: Instant, unanimously came to the following Resolutions, [[Viz.?]]
Resolved
That the answer returned by his Excellency to the Resolutions of this house of the 8th: Instant, is in no respect satisfactory; And that this house cannot, in faithfulness to the people they Represent, Pass any Bill for a further allowance for Provisions for the forces raised on the Expedition against Canada, whilst the Notorious abuses committed in such as have been already provided, are openly avowed + Encouraged.

At a council held at the Council Chamber in the city of New York the 24th Day of November 1745.
Present: His Excellency the Honble. George Clinton Mr. Kennedy Mr. Hownmanden Mr. Ch: Justice Mr. Cortlandt Mr. Moore.
His Excellency communicated to the Board a letter to him from the Commissioner of Indian Affairs dated the 21st: [[Instant?]], advising that a party of French and Indians had destroyed the settlement of Saratoga on the frontier of this province, burnt the homes, killed and scalped some of the inhabitants, and taken the rest prisoners.
Also the examination of Richard a New England Indian who made his escape from the enemy informing their proceedings against Saratoga.
Also Jacob Rutson's account from the manor of Livingston touching the course the enemy have taken.
And a letter from Lieutenant Butler devising a supply of powder for the defense of Fort Hunter.

At a council at the Council Chamber in the City of New York the 27 Day of November 1745
Present: His Excellency the Honble. George Clinton Mr. Kennedy Mr. Howmanden Mr. Ch: Justice Mr. Courtlandt Mr. Moore.
His Excellency having sent for two persons lately come to this City from Albany. The [[Fish Kills?]] about 90 miles from Albany and they attending accordingly, were called into report, that the enemy had taken a settlement called Woodstock and cut off about 150 or 200 of the militia that went to attach them. They further say that they heard the enemy consisted of French and Indians about 1500 or 2000.
His Excellency desired the opinion of the council what they would advise [[?]] to do with respect to the Six Nations of Indians and if he should now give them orders to go to war against the enemy.
Whereupon the council advised his Excellency to send for all the warriors of the Six Nations to come to Albany and then acquaint them by the Commissioner of Indians.

The humble representation of His Maj. Council of [[?]] Province may it please your Excellency-
The Council having lately had under their consideration a Bill brought up to them from the house of Representatives, entitled, "An Act for emitting Bills of Credit to the value of Ten thousand pounds for the uses therein mentioned, and for raising + collecting the sum of Then thousand pounds for sinking + cancelling the said Bills; many difficulties + objections arose thereupon; and in order to remove them, the council on the 21st instant sent a message to the house of Representatives; to desire a Conference with them upon the subject matter of the said Bill, whereto, the house returned for answer, that the said Bill being a mony Bill, the House could not consent to any Conferences wth the Council upon the subject Matter of the said Bill.
This being the case. the Council found themselves under a necessity of rejecting the Bill, and have unanimously rejected it accordingly, for the following, among many other reasons.

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
1: The Council observed a principal defect in this Bill; the mony proposed to be levyed by it was not granted to His Majesty, or to be issued by warrants in Council as it ought to have been, + has been usually done.
2: The Council observes in Genl., that sundry matters were contained in this Bill, that have no necessary or proper connection with a Bill for raising + levying mony, to which the Council had exceptions, some whereof they propose to point out to your Excellency hereafter; [[not?]] but that the council conceive they have an equal right with the House of Representatives, to exercise their judgemt. upon mony Bills, even when abstracted from all foreign matter; an the Council conceive they had most cogent reasons for the exercise of that right upon this Bill, for
3. The inequality of the quotas rated by this Bill, are notoriously apparent, and the Council would willingly have been informed upon what grounds + reasons, + by what measure; that house had so apportioned them, that the Council might the better have been enabled to judge of the equity + justice of them; for as no reasons were assigned by the Bill for their manifest disproportion, 'till the Council were better informed, they could not but look upon them as unequal + partial; the Council have been at the pains to look into the [[Jaications?]] of former times, so far back as the year 1699, and it appears from the printed [[arts?]], and by an extract from the Treasurer's [[accompts?]] (which we beg leave to lay before your Excellency herewith) that from that year to this time, the City + County of New York was rated at sometimes about a fifth, sometimes about a fourth, but never so much as one third of the whole tax; two instances excepted, first upon the particular occasion of raising a small sum for solliciting the [[?]] Act; which, as the Council have been credibly informed, was looked upon by the House at that time to be a more immediate advantage to the inhabitants of that city: + secondly, when a tax was imposed for levying mony in the year 1744. The house was [[induced?]], as the Council then understood, to raise the proportion of the said city, as great part of the mony was to be employed in fortifying that city, + expended there; for which reason the Council did not then object to that Bill, which [[rate?]] however, even with these considerations, did not appear altogether satisfactory, but as no such, or any other reasons. appeared upon the present Bill.

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
Bill wherein the City + County of New York were rated at seven sixteenths + a half of the whole tax, the Council could not in justice agree to it. The Council are fully perswaded that no one can be of opinion that the real + personal estates of the inhabitants of the City + County of New York, to amount to near one third of the value of the real + personal estates of the whole provinces; and yet even upon the supposition that New York was to be rates at one third, it's quota as proposed by this Bill beyond one third, would exceed the entire quotes or Queens, Suffolk, + Richmond Countys, together by upwards of thirty pounds; and yet Queens County has been rated a fifth, [[never?]] less than a tenth, excepting in those two years of 1729 + 1744; - Suffolk County has been rated near a fifth, never under a fifteenth but in those two years, and by this Bill less than a nineteenth: Richmond County has been rated [[as?]] a fifteenth, never under a twenty fifth, excepting in those two years, + in 1699, and is now rated under one thirty eighth.
As to Albany the Council observe, that although upwards of eight of the the thousand pounds proposed to be raised by this Bill, was to be applyed for the defense + security of that City and County, + expended there; that the County is large + extensive, containing a wealthy City + a large thriving Town with the whole benefit of the Fur Trade, yet as it is a Frontier, has already felt (and is exposed to) the insults + attack of the enemy, therefore the Council are of the opinion, all due consideration ought to be had of it's advantage with regard to a taxation.
The Council are of the opinion that when any parts of the Province are [[unusually?]] rated, the reasons for enlarging or diminishing such rate ought to be set forth in the Bill, that the Council may judge of the reasonableness of them.
The Council have not entered minutely into the consideration of the respective quotas rated by this Bill upon the sev. other Countys, but the allotment for New York did, in their opinion, far exceed the bounds of equity.
The Council cannot but be of the Opinion, that the House having denyed a Conference upon this Bill was highly unreasonable if they though they were capable of [[giv?]] satisfaction

satisfaction to these particulars; without which the house might well imagine the fate of this Bill must necessarily be determined by a rejection.
However the Council beg leave to observe to your Excellency that could the house have satisfyed the Council concerning these matters; as the Bill was framed 'twas impossible it could have had its intended effect, nor could the mony have been [[?]] for
4thly.... The oaths framed by the Bill to have been [[coministred?]] to the persons proposed to be intrusted with the numbering + signing the Buills for the Ten thousand pounds paper currency to be emitted, were penned in such manner, that no [[?]] person could take them, or if taken would it have been practicable to comply with the terms of them, so the mony could not have been issued, and consequently the [[main?]] end of the Bill must have been frustrated, had it even proceeded so far as to have been exacted into a Law.
The Clause inflicting a penalty on persons altering or counterfeiting any of the paper money out of the Colony is to the Council unintelligible; the indictment to be by any Grand Jury in the Colony, + yet the [[petty?]] Jury  to come from the body of the City + County of New York, nor do the Council understand what is meant by foreign issues as expressed in the Bill.
5thly... The Council further observes to your Excellency that by this Bill the house took upon themselves not only to nominate the persons to receive + apply the mony proposed to be issued, but others to appoint the places where the Block houses should be built upon the frontier in Albany, and both (as the Council understand) without your Excellency's approbation, which the Council look upon as interfering with the executive part of the Government; and were it any [[wile?]] necessary that such persons should be harmed in the Bill, and had the house your Excellency's consent so to do, yet the Council apprehend they had good reason to expect to house would also have advised with them therin; but if (as the house would have it) it is to be a Rule that mony Bills must not be conferred upon, nor amended by the Council, then it will follow that whatever defects + inconsistencys the Council discover in such a Bill, or whatever foreign matter the house thinks proper to tack to it, which would be justly lyable to exception (even if contained in

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749

in a seperate Bill) because it is by them called a mony Bill, all must be submitted to by the Council, or it must share the same fate with the resent Bill, + the publik service be [[defcated?]]
These, sir are but a small number of the many exceptions to which the Council conceived this Bill was lyable, to particularize them all, would be taking up too much of your Excellency's time, + mispending their own; however, they flatter themselves that such as they have pointed out will be sufficient to show that they had good reasons to reject such a Bill

May it please your Excellency.
In pursuance of your Excellency's order in Council of the 5th. Instant, we have duly weighed + Considered the sev. Letters + minutes of the Commiss. of Indian Affairs, + other papers to us thereby referred, + humbly Report our Opinion thereupon as followeth, 1st: As the Council conceive the want of some other [[?]] Forts + Garrisons within the Countrys of the Six Nations, who live scattered + Dispersed at a great Distance from each other, whereby, in case of the war, they lay naked + exposed to the Incursions, Ravages + Crueltys of the Enemy, + cannot have [[that?]] protection + assistance from the English, which is necessary for their Security + Defense, which they if they could have, 'tis most probable 100d. Dissipate their terrible terrible Apprehensions + Dread of the french + their Indians: This seems to the Committee to be a Principal reason of the Present Resolution of the Six Nations, not to enter into the war with us against the Common Enemy, + whatever other [[specious?]] Pretences they have assigned for their Conduct in this particular, the Committee cannot but judge this Defect as a Main Cause of it: Therefore the Committee are of Opinion that 'tis advisable for your Excellency

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
Excellency to write Circular Letters to all the Neighbouring Governmts., inclosing to each a Copy of the minutes of the Commiss. of the 25th. feb. containing the Resolution of the Six Nations, and the reasons they have assigned for their Conduct upon this [[occasion?]] as signified by the Interpreter, in answer to your Excellency's message, requiring them to enter into the war with us against the french + Indians in Alliance with them, and to suggest the sev. Gov. upon the aforegoing Reasoning, how highly it [[imports?]] the sev. Colonies upon the Continent respectively to unite with us in Endeavoring effectually to preserve the Six Nations + the other Indians in Alliance with us + them in their Fidelity to His Majesty + Dependance on the British Interest; and in pursuing all such measures as are most likely to prevail with them to perform their Engagemts. to us, ratifying by sev. Treaties all Albany, or at all Events to prevent this Revolt, which, if we fail in these Attempts, seems next to be apprehended + that the means which seem most likely to be available to one, or the other, or both these purposes, is for the respective Colonies to contribute their proportion of the Expence of Building such proper Forts within the Countrys of the Six Nations. + Maintaining such Garrisons in them, as may be judged effectual for their Protection, Security + Defence against any attacks which the Common Enemy may attempt to make upon them, For such an Union the Committee are fully persuaded must be judged most equitable + just, + that it cannot be thought reasonable that the whole Expense of Measures so absolutely necessary to the Security Defense + Preservation of all the Colonies, as well as the honour + service of His Majesty in these parts, shod. be borne at the Sole Charge of one single Province, when all are so nearly concerned in the Consequences of them, + more especially considering the heavy Burthen this Colony has constantly borne even in time of Peace, in the preserving the Six Nations hitherto in the British Interest.
2dly... The Committee are humbly of the Opinion that 'tis necessary the sev. Letters + Minutes of the Commiss. and the Petition of the Inhabitants of [[?]] to them referred should be laid before the Assembly, and at the same time that your Excellency acquaint them, that you have wrote such Circular Letters to the Purpose before mentioned, + when you shall have received answers thereto their Contents shall be communicated to the House, + such Measures proposed to

That the Assembly should be pressingly urged to take effectual Care that the Commiss. of Indian Affairs be immediately supplyed with ready mony to Discharge all Demands upon Account of the services already performed for the Government + that they may have always [[suff.?]] in their hands to answer the like for the time to come.
