Gentlemen..
"The Circumstances of the Province are such, that I think myself obliged, for the better security of it, to recommend to you, to make Provision with the utmost Dispatch, for Erecting Sic Block houses upon the Northern Frontiers; + for the Maintenance + punctual payment of the Militia to be Garrisoned in them; as likewise for Twenty five men; to Garrison two Block houses already Built at the Charge of the Inhabitants of [[Schaatacook?]], pursuant to the request of their Petition herewith laid before you.
"You may observe by the Letters + Papers from the Commiss. of Indian Affairs (which I have also ordered to be laid before you) that the Six Nations of Indians have refused entering into the War: Therefore it it behoves us, to fall upon such means as will most effectually Engage them therein, + prevent their going over to the Enemy; to which End it is absolutely necessary, that such Measure be immediately Entered into with the neighbouring Governments, as will save this Province of the great Expense we mus be at in keeping the Indians firm in the British Interest, whereupon

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749

"Whereupon the Security of most of the Colonies upon the Continent Depend; and I conceive there can be no greater Expedient to answer the Purpose than an Union of Councils of the sev. Governmts., whoa are equally concerned with this Province in the Common Danger we are now Exposed to: and I can assure you that sev. of the Governments have already Convinced me of their Inclinations to promote our mutual safety, + only wait for the appointmt. of the Commiss. from this Province to [[concert?]] proper measures-
"The Commiss. of Indian Affairs greatly complain that the Publick Service cannot be carryed on, for want of mony to Discharge all Demands on that Account; and I am confident you will agree with me in Opinion, that there shod. at least be a sufficiency in the hands of the Colony Treasurer, to answer the wants of the Governmt. in times of war: I am the more concerned to Press this upon you, as the funds which have been given prove Deficient.
"The Season of the year draws near for sending Provisions to [[Oswage?]]: I have ordered the Contractors to supply that Garrison as usual, for which I expect you'll make Provision.
"I received a Letter last Post from Adml. Warren + Genl. [[Pepperell?]], jointly informing me, That it is absolutely necessary for His Majesty's Service, as well as the honour + Interest of the Colonies, that [[Levies?]] of Men be raised by them respectively, + sent to Louisbourgh early in the Spring, in support of that Garrison, until a suff. Number of Troops arrives from Europe for it's Defences: I have not been been wanting to Represent to you, the necessity there is of sending a Quota of Men from this Province thither, as the preservation thereof is of the utmost Consequence to His Majesty's Colonies upon this Continent: Therefore I hope no time will be lost in contributing what lays in your power for securing so considerable an acquisition.
Gentlemen..
"My Desire to make the people safe + easy in their settlemt., occasioned me to allow you but a short Recess; I now promise myself a happy conclusion of this Session, by your providing speedily for the Protection against [[any?]] attempts of the enemy; who cannot be more Industrious to contrive it's ruin, [[?]] I shall be carefull of preserving it in the Quiet Possession of His Maj. Subjects

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(23)
"it to you in the most earnest manner, to make ample Provision, and that with the greatest Dispatch you possibly can, to enable me Effectually to answer his Majs. Expectations, from his loyal Subjects of this Province; that we may Signalize ourselves in the part his Majs. expects we shod. bear in this intended Service. it is with the greatest pleasure I have now Reviewed your Resolve of the 25th. of February last, in answer to Mr. Shirley's Letter of the 13th. of January preceeding, wherein you have expressed yourselves with a becoming warmth + heartiness, That if His most Gracious Majesty should think fit to undertake the Expedition therein mentioned, this Colony would chearfully contribute anything in it's power, for the Vigorous Prosecution of such an Enterprise; which leaves no room for doubt, as you have now the Opportunity Offered, that you will Act with Spirit + resolution becoming the Importance of the present Occasion."
Gentlemen of the Council..
"I am perfectly assured also, that you will co-operate with the Genl. Assembly with your usual Ardour for His Majs. honour + Services; and that nothing will be wanting on your parts, for the advancemt. of this Common Cause."
Gentlemen of the Council + Genl. Assembly.
"I am perfectly satisfyed, That is is needless for me to recommend the Cultivation an Union + Harmony amongst you, upon a Subject so agreeable to all your Inclinations: His Majs. Paternal Care of his remotest Subjects, has been always remarkable during the whole Series of his Auspicious Reign, but more eminently conspicuous upon this Important Occasion; and His Majesty having been pleased to take into his Royal Consideration the Dangers these Colonies have constantly been exposed to, from the Incroachmts. + Insults of the Subjects of the french King; has been graciously Disposed to set on foot an Expedition, the Success whereof will free you + your Posterity from that Danger, + the heavy Expence Attending it: This Instance of His Royal Goodness + tenderness towards you, cannot, and I am persuaded, will not, fail of meeting with all due Returns of Duty, Loyalty + Gratitude-"
G: Clinton

This Resolve marked with a hand is Scandalously false for the whole house then seemed to come into the providing of every thing, + it is my opinion they would have done it, had it not been for some of the Council, as I was [[with?]] them often after the House was up, when Major [[Vanhom?]] agreed about the [[Oznabrigs?]] for the Tents, + Capt. Richards to undertake the Battows; and I only waited to see what they would do before I wrote to Brigad. Gooch; + [[when?]] they agreed not to provide these things; on the 12th. in their Minutes they made a [[N3:?]] to have this Resolve Entered the 6th.; and the 14th. they sent Coll. Morris + Coll. Philips to desire it might be put in the 6th.; wch. I refused, + told them it was flinging that Reflection on me, because if they had made that Resolve the 6th., I could have wrote directly to Mr. Gooch. but it was their fault, I did not write, + insisted it should not be put into the Minute 'till the 14th.; Coll. [[To:?]] 19, 4 July 1746 Message from His Excellency to the Gen. Assembly
Gentlemen..
"During your late short Recess, in pursuance of Representations from the Commiss. of Indian Affairs at Albany, + the Coll. of the Regimt. there I found it Expedient, + was advised by his Majs. Council, to Commissionate proper Officers, to raise a Company of Volunteers out of the Militia posted at Albany, to Range + Scour the woods, the prevent the Enemy, + their Savage[[s?]] penetrating into the County upon the Frontiers, + from Committing the like horrid Murders + Barbaritys for the future, which they have of late perpetuated; and a Company of One hundred Men has been accordingly [[?]] and (as I am Informed from the same hands) have been of great Service; [[?]]

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(25)
"as the latter has acquainted me by Letter since his Return to Albany, that that Company refuses to continue in that service, without an additional pay is provided for them; which indeed I promised to recommend to you to do; but it has thro' hurry of Business been thus long omitted; and I hope you will take care that their pay shall be adequal to the Service.
"I have here lately received answers from Mr. Gooch, Mr. Thomas, + Mr. Law, upon the Subject Matter I have heretofore acquainted you, I wrote to sevl. Governours of the Colonies upon, namely concerning their bearing respectively a proportion of the Expense which will attend the Engaging the Indians to take part in the war; and what I aimed at principally, was touching the Article of Provisions, with which the warriors of those Nations that go upon the Expedition must necessarily be furnished. I shall Order Copys of the Paragraphs of these Letters relating to this Matter, to be laid before you; whereby you will find, at least as to the two latter, that their respective Governmts. refuse to bear any Share of that Burthen; + as to the former (as I conceive) it may be intended to relate to nothing more than a Present he intends to make them; it will remain then for your Consideration + care at this time: For a failure in so material a Point, may be Attended with very bay Consequences.
"As this is the Opinion of those Governmts., with regard to their bearing a proportion of the Expence of furnishing with Provisions such Indians as Engage in the Expedition; I apprehend from thence, that they will not Engage to bear a Proportion of the Expence of Provisions for such of the Thing's Troops as I shall judge requisite to send out of the Province upon this Service; And as the Shortness of the time will not admit of my waiting to know the Sentiments of the sev. Governmts. upon this Article; I must therefore again recommend it to your care + Consideration; although for want of His Majesty's particular Instructions I cannot as yet resolve upon the Number.
"I think it proper likewise, that Provision should be made for transporting the Warlike Stores, Six Pieces of Cannon, + the provisions designed for the [[?]] + Subsistance of the Troops raised in this Province, along with the Army"
G. Clinton

His Excellency communicated to the Board a Letter from Lieut. Christie, dated at Annapolis the 22 ? June last, complaining of the ill condition of the Fort there, of the want of many necessary of the Garrison, also of the expense he is at in treating the Indians of which there is no allowance.

The Council advised his Excellency to lay the said Letter before the Assembly.

His Excellency acquainted the Board that he had waited on the principal merchants in the City to know what he could further meet with for Bills of Exchange, which his Excellency might draw on the proper offices for providing Arms, Clothing, & other Necessaries for the Men to be raised in the province to go on the expedition; that he had not been able to get more than 500 sterlings; that conceiving himself unable to procure so great a sum of money as will be necessary for that purpose otherwise, he had therefore prepared a Message to the General Assembly recommending to them to advance the money which may be requisite for making the necessary preparations in the province for transporting the men & military to be sent from hence and for Arms, Ammunition, Clothing, and that for so much of the money as they shall think it is not expedient for the province to bear the charge, his Excellency will give his Bills for repayment on the respective Offices belonging to the Crown as relates to the several Materials to be furnished on this Occasion.

Which Message his Excellency laid before the Board, and the same was read & approved of.

Informations of the present Inclinations of the Indians, particularly those of the Six Nations, + the Difficulties the Interpreter + those Gentlemen accompanying him meets with in persuading them to come to Albany to meet the Governour are of the Opinion that his Excellency shod. send up Tim. Maggin, who we are Informed has very great Interest with the [[Oneydo's?]], from which Nation the Interpreter has received no satisfactory answer, + an absolute Refusal from the Caijugas, upon which Nation + the Tuscororas, we were Informed the Oneydo Nation have very great Influence, + give him such Instructions as his Excellency may think properest to induce them to Join us in the present Expedition against Canada, particularly to Inform them that his Excellency Gov. Shirley has sent Commiss. from Boston to meet + [[treat?]] wth. them here, + that they will be obliged to return soon to Boston, to assist in forwarding the Army + Fleet that are to set out with all Expedition in order to go up St. Lawrence River to Attack Quebeck, for which purpose many Ships are already Arrived at Cape Breton, + the whole Fleet expected every Day, + some thousands of Land Forces ready at Louisbourgh, + sev. Thousands in New England ready to Embark, And that many Soldiers are Arrived at Albany, + some thousands more expected speedily from Virginia, Maryland Pensylvania + New Jersey, which will be a force so much superiour to any in Canada, that the Indians need to be under no Apprehensions of their Familys being in any Danger of any Attack from an Enemy in their Absence

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(43)
your Excellency has recd. from Gov. Shirley + Adml. Warren by their Letters of the 13th: + 19th: Instant
We are humbly of opinion that it is absolutely necessary to Attempt the Reduction of the French Fort at Crown Point by the Joint Forces of all the Colonies now raised for the Expedition against Canada, + that this be done without Delay + with all the Dispatch that the present Circumstances of affairs will Admit [[of?]], for the following reasons-
As your Excellency has by an unwearied application + Influence gained the Six Nations to Join with us in the most Solemn + hearty Manner in the war against the french of Canada, + their Indian Allies, + to promise not only to Join their whole force to ours, but the force of all the Indian Nations over whom they have any Influence, + who are very Numerous, we are of Opinion that the best use is to be made of so happy an Event of your Negotiation with the Six Nations is Entering them immediately upon Action against the french + their Indians-
As your Excellency in Order to Engage the Six Nations in the war was Obliged to Communicate to them the Design of attacking Canada by Sea + Land, if every part of that Expedition be now laid aside, the Six Nations will Apprehend that they have been deceived, + in Consequence of such Opinion the English Colonies may lose intirely the friendship + Esteem not only of the Six Nations, but of all the Indian Nations in North America, + the French thereby gain so great an Influence over them as may enable them to put their grand design in Execution of setting all the Indian Nations in North America upon us + harasing the Frontiers of the English Colonies on all Sides from Annopolis Royal to Georgia, by which means the English Colonies would be so far from being in a Condition, as they are now, of making any Attempt upon Canada, that their whole force must be employed, + would not be sufficient to Defend their Settlemts. from the Incursions of the Indians on all Sides-
By the best Information we can obtain in this Town, we do not think there can be above 12,000 Men in Canada including their Indians + Regular

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(44)
Regular Troops, + therefore we are of Opinion the Forces now Levyed in the sev. Colonies will be sufficient to reduce the French Fort at Crown Point if care be taken at the same time to harass their Settlemts. everywhere by incursions of the Indians, which we think it will not be Difficult for your Excellency to Effect in the present Disposition of the Indians + the City of Quebec at the same time be kept in continual Apprehensions by Appearance of as great Number of Shipping in the River of St. Lawrence as can be spared from Louisbourgh, while the Forces may be supposed to be before Crown Point-
We are informed that a single Forty Gun Ship will be sufft. to Plunder + Destroy all the french Settlemts. below Quebec-
We are likewise of Opinion that, whether the Attempt on Crown Point be made or not, all the forced now Levied must be kept on foot Cloathed + supported with Provisions, + placed on the Frontiers towards Canada so that the Reduction of Crown Point can occasion a very small Additional Expence to what is now become absolutely necessary without making such Attempt.
We even doubt whether it will Occasion a greater Expence than will become necessary otherwise for the Defence of the sevl. Colonies by Building of Forts [[?]]
That if Crown Point be reduced this Fall, as we hope it may, then next Spring we think Montreal may with much more Ease be Attempted + carryed by Land Forces to be sent agt. it by two different Roads ([[viz?]]) by Chambly + Oswego down [[Cadarachiu?]] + St. Lawrence River, + that in the Winter Season small Vessels may be built for Transporting the Troops + Artillery to the Chambly, + that these Vessels being made large enough to carry small Cannon will cover the Men while they are Landing near Chambly as the Season of the year is so far Advanced, that there is not time left to Consult the sevl. Governmts., we humbly Advise your Excellency to Encamp the Forces now at this place, + to order them to march with all the Expedition may be towards the Carrying place [[there?]]

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(45)
that under their Cover the Roads may be repaired, + new Roads where necessary made + Blockhouses or Forts be built whereover it shall be thought necessary or convenient for securing the Transportation of all necessarys for the Army + this place + to prevent the Incursions of the Enemy; That a Party of Indians with a sufficient Number of Christians be sent to harass the Settlemts. of Canada at as many different + Distant places as possible to keep the Inhabitants every where in Alarm, + to prevent their sending [[?]] to Crown Point.
We very gratefully thank your Excellency for your Communicating to us your design of leaving the Nomination to Goo. Shirley + Adml. Warren of the person to Command the Army in Chief on the Expedition against Crown Point, as it shews you Excellency's Disposition to remove every Difficulty which you apprehend may obstruct this Enterprise + that you will consent to any form of a Commission or Commissions, which they shall think necessary or proper for that purpose
As the Officers + Soldiers now raised are supposed to be in the King's Pay, it becomes highly necessary, that Gov. Shirley + Adml. Warren think of some Method, by which they may receive their pay from time to time without Delay, + that the Rate of their Pay according to the sev. Currencys of mony in which they shall be paid be Determined, otherwise we apprehend that mutinies + other Disorders may arise in the Army-
The immediate Reduction of the french Fort at Crown Point appears to us to be of such Consequence to the safety of all his Majs. Colonies in North America, that we can make no doubt of the sevl Governmts. readily agreeing to bear their respective Shares of the necessary Expence for that purpose, we have in Conjunction with the Commiss. from the Massachusts Bay made an Estimate of the extraordinary [[Charge?]] which we think may arise, + of what we + they immagine may be a reasonable Quota for each
We are very sensible how little it would have become us to have advised

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(46)

We are humbly of Opinion that your Excellency is to pursue such measures as may tend to the greatest Security of the Province + of the Frontiers thereof + at the same time may be of use in carrying on + promoting any Expedition agt. the french in Canada next spring, if the same shall be though then Expedient
For which purpose (being Informed that the present Fort at Saraghtoga by reason of it's Situation + otherwise is not Tenable nor large enough to contain a sufficient Number of Men) we are humbly of Opinion that a Fort be Built on the most proper Situation at or near the Carrying place above Saraghtoga + capable of containing at least five hundred Men, and that a Communication between this Fort + Albany be secured by small Forts or Block houses to be placed at such Distances as shall be thought necessary for that purpose
That a Fort be Built at or near [[Barnet's?]] field capable of containing Two hundred Men for the Security of the Frontiers on that side + facilitating the Relief of Oswego in case of any Attack, And that small Forts or Blockhouses be Built on the Mohawk's River for Securing the Communication Between [[Schenectady?]] + [[Burnetsfield?]], + Between [[Schenectady?]] + half Moon. That

We are likewise of Opinion that [[600?]] pair of Snow Shoes be prepared [[?]] two pair of Makasins or Indian Shoes for each soldier that shall be in Garrison during the Winter in any of the above Forts + Block houses-

[[?]] 1746 [[? Excellency's]] [[?]] to the [[?]] Report [[?]] Notice [[?]] minutes
Gentlemen,
As by your Report to be on my Reference of the 21st: Instant, I suspect that you take amiss that I have not before this time Communicated to you the Transactions in Council at Albany. I now [[tell?]] you I designed to have done it, soon after by return from that place; but as I at the same time expected that you Gentlemen, who resided in this place during my absence from it, would have reported to be what you had done in the Matters which I had committed to your care in my absence, I was desirous that your regard to his Majesty's Governour of this province might appear in a decent Order on the Minutes of Council. Now Gentlemen I must tell you that I am of opinion from a parity of reason between the Council of State in Great Britain + in this Province, that as the Council of State never Assumes that Name, but when the King or Regency is present, and at all other times I believe are called a Committee, it was a Mistake in you to Stile yourselves the Council. I have the more reason to observe to you on this, because before I left this place, I desired that as many of you as could, would go with me to Albany, by reason of the Matters of great Consequence, that at that time must come under Consideration [[there?]], but

title: New York colony council meeting minutes [1], 1745-1749
transcription:
(54)
but all of you declined it, except the Gentlemen that did Attend me. I was then under a necessity of Acting with those Gentlemen, + I must refer it to your reflection whether two Councils of State can Subsist in this Province at the same time, and what may be the Consequence if the Major Number of the Council should at any time refuse to Attend the Governour, and set themselves up as a distinct Council.
As his Maj's: Authority in this Province is in a great measure committed to me, I think it my Duty to support it. If in what I have now said, you think me under a mistake, you will do me the greatest pleasure by Informing me better, and you shall find me now + at all times ready to Correct my Errors, and so I hope you will in any case you discover that you have slip't, for I suppose we all agree, that as on Man is, so any Number are Subject to Error. Nothing I desire more than that there may be a perfect understanding + Harmony among us, and that you may be convinced what regard I have to your advice; I now deliver to the Clerk of the Council in your presence the Minutes of the Council at Albany, to be deposited in the Secretary's Office for your perusal-

[[?]] 1746... I Delivered to the Chief Justice a rough Draft of a Speech (I intended to make to the Genl. Assembly) for his perusal, + desired that he would shew it to Mr. Murray + Horsmanden, + if he or they had any objections to alter it + return it, for as I did not pretend to be so particular in every point myself (especially as I was then very much Indisposed) I asked his Assistance + theirs, as they were all three of His Maj: Council, + as such it was their Duty to assist me with the best advice they could, for the good of his Maj: Service + the Welfare of this Province, The Chief Justice read it + said he only Objected to that part relating to the Indian Affairs, but on my telling him, that I thought there was very great mismanagemt. among the Commiss. for Indian Affairs he was in my Opinion, but told me as the Commission was only in my power, he thought it was giving up too much to the Assembly, who might make a handle of it - I answered him, I was ready on my part to do any thing that Business might go on as it ought without any Delay: he put the Draft of my intended Speech into his pocket, to make what Observations he, Mr. Murray + Mr. Horsmanden should think proper.
[[?]]...... The Chief Justice returned me the Draft + said he had no manner of Objection to it, but advised me, as I was then very ill, to send to the Speaker, + desire he would read it to the house
[[?]].... I sent for the Speaker (being still very much out of Order) + gave him the Speech to read, + on asking him how he liked it he told me he approved much of it, + said it was a very good one, as did the chief Justice. I desired the Speaker (as it was impossible for me to go out of my house, or if I did, I was not able to read it myself) that he would make my Apology to the House, + read it for me; notwithstanding wch. the house made the following Resolves-

a sudden Indisposition, he was thereby rendered unable to do it, and therefore desired the Speaker to lay it before the House in his Name, which being [[done?]] + the House conceiving that Matter of Delivery to be irregular, took the [[same?]] into their Consideration, + were unanimously of opinion, that it was unprecedented, + contrary to the usual Course of Parliamentary proceeding but in Consideration of His Excellency's Indisposition, and that the Dispatch of Business at this Extraordinary Conjuncture, might not be retarded, consented to accept + receive it.

[[To:?]] 5 17 Oct. 1746 His Excellency's Speech to the Council + Genl. Assembly
Gentlemen of the Council + the Genl. Assembly-
"In Obedience to His Maj. Command I went in July last to Albany, in order to Engage the Italian Nations to Join with us in the Expedition against Canada. You are not Ignorant of the bad Dispositions the Six Nations have been in for some time past; and the french of Canada have been Indefatigable in using all the Artifices in their power to turn that Disposition to their Advantage; It is not then to be wondred at, that I met with many Difficulties in that affair; but this I hope will now Increase your pleasure, when I can Assure you, that the Six Nations + the Neighbouring Indians, have, in the most solemn Manner, Joined with us in the War against Canada. Had the Fleet from Great Britain Arrived [[at?]] the time it was expected, the good Effects of the Treaties I had with these Indians, would have been much more manifest than what can now appear, when from unexpected incidents publickly known, we ourselves have not been able to pursue any steady Measures; And the Mortality of the City of Albany having been communicated to the Indian Camp (it being impracticable to keep the Indians from the Town, or the Inhabitants from them

"When I left this place, I was in hopes of being freed from the principal Care of the Forces intended to proceed by Land against Canada, by the Arrival of Mr. Gooch, whom His Majesty had appointed to Command them, and who was then every Day expected; but that Gentleman having absolutely Declined the Service, I was oblidged to take that care upon myself
"After we had been so long Disappointed in our Expectation of the Arrival of the Fleet, and that any Attempts by Sea Seemed Impracticable; I concerted Measures with Mr. Shirley + Mr. Warren, to employ the Land Forces to the best advantage, for the Security of the Frontiers + annoyance of the Enemy; but these Measures were Disconcerted by the Accounts received of a fleet of ships being on the Coast of Nova Scotia, which was suspected to be the [[Brest?]] Squadron: It then became necessary for me to make such Dispositions of the forces at Albany as I thought would best serve for the Security of this Province, and at the same time facilitate any Enterprize against the Enemy that may at any time hereafter be thought advisable; And I have before I left Albany given Orders accordingly: the Danger all the English Colonies in North America are exposed to, by the Arrival of a Squadron of the Enemy's Ships, with a considerable Land force, as it is said, on

"A larger Sum than is usually given for the Managemt. of the Indian Affairs, is at this time necessary; and as by the [[Order?]] which I have left behind me at Albany, a Winter Camp is to be formed, + sevl. small Forts + Block houses to be built for preserving the Communications with the Army, + Security of the Frontiers, a considerable Expence [[must?]] thereby be Occasioned, Estimates of which, so far as I can procure them, shall be laid before you: your own safety is immediately concerned in the Execution thereof; + as this Province must sensibly feel the Effects of any Misfortune that may happen; [[I will?]] likewise gain the greatest Advantages from the Success of any Enterprizes against Canada; I make [[no?]] doubt but that you will chearfully contribute all that is in your power in furnishing the means requisite in this Occasion: you must be sensible at what great Expence your Mother Country supports the present war against the Enemys of the Liberties of Europe, + of the Protestant Religion + how much this Expence has been increased by a most unnatural Rebellion, which is now happily suppressed; and therefore how Justly the King must Expect of you a liberal Contribution to the utmost of your power when you consider the great Sums which the Crown expends on this Expedition of which you'll reap the choicest fruits; any Parsimony or saving (however popular this Term may have become) cannot at this time be mentioned in your House witch Prudence or Decency: And I must recommend it to you that whatever Expence you shall judge necessary, may be made the least Burthensome possible, especially to those who are least able to bear it."

"It is always to be wished that a perfect harmony may Subsist between

transcription:
(59)
Between the sevl. Branches of the Legislature, which never was more necessary than now, as we are exposed to a powerfull, cruel + Deceitful Enemy. Differences often arise from immaginary Evils, and the weakness of humane Nature is such, that Makind are seldom free from real Causes of Mistrust: But these likewise are often agravated by the private Views of Artfull + designing Men. What I shall propose to you on this Occasion is, only to observe to you, that every Branch of the Legislature ought to keep strictly to our happy Constitution, without any one Endeavoring to encroach upon the powers or priviledges intrusted with [[y.?]] others. When unhappy Differences have arisen, in our Mother Country, from an Imprudent or wanton Stretch of Power in any one of the parts of Governmt:, a Cure has been often Attempted by throwing an over Measure of that Power into some other part, by which the Ballance between the several parts of Government has been destroyed, the Cure become worse than the Disease, whereby Confusion + Calamity has ensued, 'till the Ballance was again restored. I am told that something of the like Nature has more than once happened in this Government; let us then Guard against such Mischiefs; And let us resolve to shew by our Actions, as well as by words, that we understand + love the English Constitution, and thereby convince each other of the sincerity of our Intentions for the good of our Country; and then I make no doubt all of us shall Enjoy the pleasure which necessarily arise from the good Effects of such a Resolution-
G: Clinton

His Excellency The Governour made his Speech to the Assembly touching the Expedition in the words following

Gentm [[Gentlemen]] of the Council and General Assembly

It has been signifyed to me by a Letter from his Grace the Duke of New Castle of the 9th of April last (which I have received by [exchange] from Governour Sherley an Extract whereof I shall order to be laid before you that his Majesty has been pleased to Order an Expedition against the French Settlements in Canada and I am Commanded (as the other Governours of his Majesty's Colonies are) forthwith to make the Necessary Depositions for raising as many Men within my Government as the [[Shortness]]  of the time will permit to be employed in Concert with his Majesty's Regular Forces on this important Service

It is his Majesty's intention That the Troops to be raised in North America should consist of Cmpanys of one hundred Men each and that those which should be raised in the Several Provinces of New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia be formed into one Corps, to be commanded by Wm [[William]] Gooch Lieutenant Governour of Virginia whom the King has been Pleased on this Occasion to promote to the Rank of Brigadier General.

The Happy consequences which will redound to his Majesty's Colonies on this Continent, the Advantage of the Common Cause of the

British Interest in General from the [[?]] of such an Enterprize [[?] be thought of weight Sufficient to inspire every Loyal Breast and true lover of his Country with available Zeal and Resolution for contributing the utmost in their power towards the Accomplishment of the present undertaking.

Gentlemen of the General Assembly

In Consequence of what I have now mentioned I must recommend it to you in the most earnest manner to make ample provision and th[[an]] with the greatest dispatch you possibly can to enable me effectually to answer his Majesty's Expectations from his Loyal Subjects of this Province that [[wee]] may Signilize ourselves in the part his Majesty expects [[wee]] should bear in this [[unlended]] service, it is with the greatest Pleasure I have now received your Resolve of the 25th February last in answer to Wm [[William]] Sherley Letter of the 13th January preceedings, wherein you have expressed yourselves with a becoming Warmth [[and heartings]]

That if his most Gracious Majesty should think fit to undertake the Expedition therein mentioned. This Colony would Chearfully cont[[?]] any thing in its Power for the Vigorous Prosecution of such an Enterprize which leaves no Room for Doubt as you have now the Opportunity Offered, that You will Act with a [[Specill]] an[[?]] resolution becoming the importance of the Present Occasion

Gentlemen of the Council

I am perfectly Assured also that You Cooperate with [[y.]] General Assembly, with Your [[?ual]] Ardour for his Majesty's Honour

& Serivce; and that nothing will be waning on your parts for the Advancement of this Common Cause

Gen [[Gentlemen]] of the Council & General Assembly

I am perfectly satisfyed that it is needless for me to recommend the cultivating an Union and Harmony amongst you upon a Subject so agreeable to all your inclinations, his Majesty's paternal care of his remotest Subjects has been always remarkable during the whole Service of his Auspicious Reign but more eminently conspicious upon this important occasion and his Majesty having been pleased to take into his Royal consideration the Dangers these Colonies have constantly been exposed to from the Encrochments & insults of the Subjects of the French King: has been graciously disposed to set on Foot an Expedition the Success whereof will free you and your Posterity from that Danger, and the heavy [[?]] attending it. This Instance of his Royal Goodness & tenderness towards You cannot, & I am persuaded, will not, fail of meeting with all due return of Duty, Loyalty & Gratitude.

G. Clinton

18th A Message from his Excellency to y General Assembly

Gentlemen. 

As I look upon it to be a matter of great concern to the present Expedition. That the Six Nations of Indians and others in alliance with & Dependant upon them should be engaged with us in the War. I have with that View ordered the Commissioner of Indian Affairs immediatly to send up a Message to them

invite them to meet me at Albany on the Twentieth of next Month; And in order to bring this Design to Effect I am Commanded by his Majesty, to make them such Presdents as I think may be of use for that Purpose, and I think it's proper likewise that the Colony should make them some additional present at the same time. If you are of that Opinion you will timely make Provision accordingly. And that my endeavours may be rendered yet more effectual. I have wrote to the Several Govern to the Westward and to the Governours of the Massachusets Bay and Connecticut recommending it to them to endeavour that their respective Governour do [[?]] their proportion of the Exchange which will attend the engaging the Indians in the War. That the joint influence of these Colonys might be Exerted for the Accomplishment of an event which would greatly facilitate the present undertaking & gives us still further Assurance of the Success of it: and in the Interim, tend much to the Security of our Northern Frontiers.

That the Indians may be induced to join heartily with us. I think you should also provide for proper Encouragment for them; & the Sooner it is known what they are to be allowed for Bounty and Subsistance the Better.

As I have had no directions from his Majesty to provide [[?]] Tents or other Particulars for the intended expedition ([[?]] Arms & Clothing) and as the forces cannot proceed without things Necessary. I desire to be speedily informed whether you will make Provisions for them as well for the use of the Troops to be raised within this Province, as for such of his Majesties regular Troops posted here as I may think proper to order to March and occasion my require.

July 4th. A Message from his Excellency to the General Assembly

Gen. [[Gentlemen]]

I have very latly receiv'd  Answers from Mr. Gooch, Mr. Thomas, and Mr. Law upon the subject matter I have heretofore acquainted you I wrote to the Several Govenours of these Colonies upon namely concerning their bearing respectively a proportion of the Expence which will attend the engaging the Indians to take part in the War and what I aimed at principally, was touching the Article of Provisions with which the warriors of those Nations that go upon the Expedition must Necessarily be Furnished. I shall order Copies of the Paragraphs of these Letters relating to this matter, to be laid before you: where by you will find at least as to the two latter. That their Respective Governments refuse to bear any share of that Burthen, and as to the former (as I conceive) it may be intended to relate to nothing more than a present he intend[[e]] to make them: for a failure in so material a point, may be attended with very bad Consquences.

[[?]] this is the opinion of those Governments with  regard to their bearing a proportion of y.[[?]] Expence of furnishing with Provisions such Indians as engage in the Expedition. I apprehend from thence that they will not engage to bear a proportion of the Expence of Provisions for such of the things Troops as I shall judge requisite to send out of the Province upon this Service and as the shortness of the time will not admit of my waiting to know the Sentiments of the Several Governments upon this Article: I must therefore again recommend it to your care and

title: New York colony documents, 1746-1751
transcription:
and and consideration; although for want of his Majesty's particular Instructions I cannot as yet resolve upon the Number

I think it proper likewise that Provision should be ma[[de]] for Transporting the warlike stores, Six pieces of Cannon and the provisions designe'd for the use and Substance  of the Troops rais[[ed]] within this Province along with the Army. 

G. Clinton

July 8th. A Message from His Excellency to the General Assembly 

Gentlemen

Since your Resolves of the 20th of last Month were communicated to me, wherein, among other things, you declare Your Opinion, that his Majesty does not Expect this Colony should be at the expence of the providing Batoes Tents, or any other Necessary requisite for the Expedition besides the Particulars you had resolved to provide for in the said Resolves; I am informed that the Neighbouring Governments have resolved to Advance all the Money (on the Faith of his Grace the Duke of Newcastle's Letter in Confidence the Crown will Repay it) that shall be wanting for Transporting the Troops they respectively raise and for every contingency that may enable them to Act [[?]] such Vigour as may be Expected from them, and as I am persuaded that this province in return (in return for the many Specil Favou[[rs]] received from the Crown) will not at this time, suffer themselves to be out done, by any of the Neighbouring Governments in such

title: New York colony documents, 1746-1751
transcription:
such measures as will tend to facilitate and promote the present expedition on the Success whereof the safety & prosperity of this Province is more immediately than any other concerned. I must  recommend it to you Gentlemen to Advance the Money which may be requisite for making the Necessary Preparations in this Province for transporting the Men & Artillery to be sent from hence and for Arms, Ammunition, Tents & Cloathing; and for so much of the Money, as you shall think it is not it is not expected that this province is to bear the Charge. I shall give my Bill for repayment on the respective Offices belonging to the Crown, [[?clate]] to the Several Matterials to be furnished on this Occasion, and I am in hopes you will the more Chearfully follow the Example of your Neighbours, because thereby one Third or one Quarter of the Charge which otherwise must fall on the Crown, may be saved; it being a Common observation. That Merchants take Advantage of great & unusual Demands, to lower the Exchange unreasonably and from them only Money can be Obtained, unless you Assist me in the manner proposed. 

I make no doubt of your Chearfully contributing every thing in your Power, to ease the Crown of the Charge of this Expedition at a time when your Mother Country bears the heaviest Burthens of a most Expensive War occasioned by the unnatural troubles in Great Britain & threatened invasion from abroad.

I have delayed sending this Message, in hopes of receiving more particular Directions in this Affair than as yet I have but now the time for the Necessary Preparations does not Admit of further delay. 

G. Clinton

The subject which I propose to preserve for your entertainment is historical in character; and claims your attention from the importance which attaches to all such inquiries. History is philosophy speaking to us by example. This is privilege, says one.
Some things "long observed by time" but once forming a part of the stirring life and kinship of the very lands which we now inhabit we shall pass in review before you. One particular object is to present in a connected form all that can now be ascertained of that Tribe of Indians who inhabited this portion of our state. You will please therefore to imagin all the beautiful [[?]] to be in a wilderness state, our villages and farms as having no existence and the gloom of the primeval forest unbroken and the wild red man chasing the deer through them, or by some rude contrivance indeavouring to [[ensnare?]] the [[?]] tribes in their brooks and rivers.

"It is the privilege of Hist to impart the experience of age without its infirmities: to bring to bring back things long obscured by time, or sinking into oblivion; and enable us to form some reasonable conjectures of what may happen to posterity"
There are several interesting inquiries intimately connected with my subject which I shall be obliged either wholly to omit, or touch in such a cursory manner as to be almost equivalent to not having noticed them at all! Such is the question. Whence came the Aborigines which Europeans found in possession of the soil in every part of this western continent when they discovered it? To what nation do they belong? How did they find their way here? At what period of the world come? We can now only remark that they unquestionable had an Asiatic origin and this several of their traditions point to the north west as that part of this continent from which they came, to occupy their several places and in which they were found, at the commencement of the seventeenth century when the Europeans took permanent possession [[?]]
This is specially true of the Lene-Lenape or Delaware tribe, which, with a few exceptions, embraced all the different minor tribes or families, which inhabited New Jersey; amounting, according to some authorities to near forty; and which acknowledged them as their "Grandfathers" or parent stock. They relate that many centuries ago, their ancestors dwell far away in the western wilds; but emigrating eastwardly they arrived at length at the Namaesi-sipu (Mississippi, where they met the Mengwe; who had also come from a distant country and had first approached the river somewhat nearer its source! On the eastern shore of this mighty river, they found a powerful, numerous, and as their spies told them, robust, tall and almost gigantic people known as the Alligewi from whom the Aleghany mountains and river derive their name. Their towns were defended by regular fortifications

The Lenape requested permission to establish themselves in this vicinity, but were refused: but they obtained permission to pass the river, in order to establish themselves in the Country farther toward the East. But while in the act of crossing they were attacked by the Alligewi who destroyed many of those who had made the Eastern Shore, and threatened a like fate to those which remained, should they attemp to pass over. [[Fired?]] by this treachery the Lenape eagerly accepted a proposition from their neighbours the Mengwe,  to unite with them for the conquest of the country. A war of great duration was thus commenced, which was prosecuted with great loss on both sides, and eventuated in the expulsion of the Alligewi; who fled from their ancient seat by way of the Missippi never to return, and spread out afterwards in the Southwestern and Southern tribes. The vacant country was apportioned between the conquorers: the Mengwi choosing that portion in the neighbourhood of the great lakes, and the Lenape dwelling the lands south.
After some years thus the hunters of the Lenapi crossed the Aleghany Mountains and discovered the great rivers Susquehannah and Delewar! Continuing to travel toward the east, they explored the [[Sheyichby?]] country (New Jersey); and finally reached the Hudson, to which they gave the name of Mahicannittuck, the river of the Mohicans! When they returned to their nation they described to them the country which they had visited as abounding in game, fruits, fish and [[fosol?]], and possessing a mild and genial climate, destitute of inhabitants. Now with that portion of the wild nation, whose emigration we have thus traced, which was embraced within the State of New Jersy, our immediate interest lies: But if I should endeavour to combine within the limits of one discourse, all the notices which may be collected from the history of our State, relating to them, the view would necessarily be so general as to be both unprofitable and uninteresting. They acted a conspicuous part in most of the tragedies which marked the first intercourse of the European and the Aboriginal races on the shores of this part of the western continent. The Indians which Hudsons men saw in Monmouth were the Navesinks. But on the 11th when John Coleman and his four companions passed throught the Narrows into the upper bay and through the the hills as far as Newark they met upon its waters Bay five canoes, containing 26 of these Indians, and in the conflict which ensued Coleman lost his life and one or the other men was wounded. The individuals of the Raritan tribe then, were the first to shed the blood of the strangers! What was the provocation will now never be known- Who were the first aggressors is forever hid from our knowledge by the veil of oblivion- The result is only told us in Hudsons Journal. The life of John Coleman was the sacrifice of the first [[heat?]] of strength between two races which had never before looked each other in the face, but which were destined to inflict mutual injuries, the one upon the other, until the stronger prevailed, and the weaker passed away, like a shadow, leaving only a few names and scanty remeniscences, to [[?]] that they had ever been here as the original proprietors of our pleasant homesteads.

From the time of the conflict between Hudsons men and the death of Coleman, until 1634- a period of twenty five years, no special difficulties seem to have arisen between the Raritans and their neighbours the Dutch on Manhattan Island. There must have been almost daily intercourse between them, for the purposes of traffic in beaver and other furs, for it is to be remembered, that the principal danger of all the establishments of the Dutch West Indian Company in New Netherland was, to profit by the trade. In 1626 The Raritan Indians had sold the whole of Egh-qua-ous or Staten Island to the Director General and Council. This was in the time of Peter Minuet the first Governor, and the purchase arose out of a desire on the part of the Dutch to give greater security to their possessions: at the same time a block house surrounded with cedar palisades "called fort Amsterdam was erected on the south end of Manhattan Island. Fear seems to have originated those measures for defence on the part of the Dutch. In a letter to a friend in England dated 30 May 1683 giving an account of East Jersey- he remarks- we have one thing more particular [[?]], which the others want also which is vast Oyster banks, which is constant [[?]] victuals during the winter to English as well as Indians: of these there are many all along our waters from the sea as high as against New York, whence they come to fetch them and again before concluding his letter- speaking of Amboy- round about the point are oysters of two kinds, small as English; and others two or three muthfulls, exceeding good for washing and stewing; the people say our oysters are good and in season all summer: The first of the 3rd month i.e. May- I eat of them at Amboy very good." As evidence of the [[?]] which these primitive Jerseymen the Indians were accustomed to enjoy, there are yet to be seen heaps of Oyster shells in different places near Amboy indicating not only the large number consumed but the foracity with which the delicacy was devoured! Prof Mather in his Geology of New York also mentions that at Browns point on Staten Island there is a bank of shells about two feet thick which appear to be recent shells, deposited there, not by nature but by the Aborigenes of the country. The [[?]] of which are- they are all edible species- the opposite valves of bivalve shells are scarcely ever found together- and the localities of these [[?]] banks are such, as would naturally be selected for camping grounds and villages, by such people as derive a large share of their food from the [[?]] waters!
N And fear being added to jealousy made them exceedingly dissatisfied with the conduct of the Authorities of New Amsterdam who had absolutely forbidden any of their leaders to sell fire arms to any of the Indians.

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
Eberhart
11-10-40
New Canaan
1506
Woodsedge
New Canaan
Connecticut
Dear Fanny:
I’m still nuts! Cannot get anything serviceable, or at least definite out of Alan but he doesn’t know himself. It is a mad house he says: thousands of men: gangs of 200-500 regimes in one gang; 160 miles of roads to be built; hospital to be built for 2000 beds. It’s a cantonment: some distance west of Jacksonville; Camp Blanding— near Starke (little tiny town) and 25 miles from Green Cove Springs

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription: where Alan has to stay— as cannot get other accommodations. Which is a good word in view of circumstances; only thing he could get nearer was a cot in half of boarding home! He bought a car (picked up one — nothing much I gathered) and drives. Says it is all Boom Town stuff. Roads lined with shacks, tents, old cars — “scum” says Alan. $7 a day without meals at little Green Cove Springs hotel! 5X Regis prices. I don’t have much notion how long he’ll be there but imagine for some time. So if

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
…or in any case I imagine… I shall trek down there: 
I don’t know yet (except by looking at map which doesn’t take into account the roads and driving time) how far it is from Daytona. Same thought struck me about the house; if he can get there, why don’t I take for the season. I note asking him definitely about driving time to Daytona but haven’t yet heard. May 'phone. Have 'phoned only once so far. He is 45 minutes from St. Augustine— but I think St. Augustine might be a little on the chilly side. He says there are some nice-looking houses near Green Cove on

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
the St. John river; but often all the sea is Florida’s main attraction; says he has to get up around 6 to leave: gets back 5:30-ish. So far. It all sounds hectic and he’ll know more after awhile. 
Only thing for me now seemed to be to stay on here and work on present afairs; then see how things go there. Helen (former secretary) was coming to Boston for a visit and was coming down here so I asked her if she’d come here first & stay a month on salary. She did and is here now. It was very nice for me; staying alone would have been even grimmer than Alan being away which is grim enough. Have to amend that which doesn’t

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
3.
say what I mean: I hate Alan’s being away but it would have been still worse alone. You know. Well, anyway, Helen has been very helpful: had a lot of work to keep her fairly busy; aside from a silent and bitter feud between her and Lee about a dirty tennis ball, all is well in the house. Or was at last accounts! I have either John or Lee drive for me: election night forgot I had tickets for Louisiana Purchase (Alan had got — then we had to cancel date): gave 2 away and Helen & I went to town (had Lee take us and Grace go along to see mob at Times Square). The political jokes fell a little flat as it was all too true about the

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
Democrats staying in. Not at all a hilarious crowd! Carnage trade mainly supports theatre and all were feeling pretty sober by that time as electoral votes were stacking up. — Otherwise have been nowhere: want to get as much work done as possible so I can go south. Will let you know more soon as I can discover. 
Name of medicine is SYNTROPAN: I think it has to be by doctor’s pre-scription and anyway you’d better ask him first: you might be allergic to it. Doc gave me; and I started an attack the week Alan left and took it and didn’t have one. Be sure to ask before you try it, though. Tell Dick I understood about Christmas present & thanks. Was in doubt as didn’t know what anybody could really do with it but it had your name on it. Am okay, don’t worry about me. Love,
Mignon.
Have not said much of election: Cannot do feelings justice.

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
Eberhart
3-29-42
400 EAST 57TH STREET
NEW YORK
Fanny dear:
In town again today - dunno how this is going to go. But have discovered I really have reduced living expenses incredibly. Doesn't seem possible. So far no repercussions from Mama: will try your argument too - although one thing about Mama is she isn't afraid of things like that - or at least wouldn't

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
be unless caught in a bombing when any of us would be. Somehow I don't feel that we are likely to get it: hope not. 
But what I meant to write about is Easter. I love your present to me - you always do too much though. It is perfectly darling and it was so like you to put a surprise inside it. I will carry it constantly; very much like to have tiny bottles of smelling salts in my bag. Thank you - I'm always thanking you. Was surprised to hear you received lambs: what I sent was a hat full of soap rabbits looking very surprised and soap eggs - good soap, too, I hope. But the boy was right and am pleased you liked it. Funny how we sent same things. I like mine from you best!
Have kept my eyes open for a striped suit at Saks but no go: saw one last fall at Abercrombie's but in funny colors

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
and very heavy: didn't like or think you would. Will keep on watching. Be sure to let me know plans; am so hopeful and just about dying to see you.
Chatham is doubtful: connecting doors (can hear through them) may bring on noisy neighbors. Small suite $11 a day and service good. Believe though St. Regis is preferable. Unless 14 E 60th: you told me about that and I looked and it seemed nice. Old-fashioned and comfortable. Felt I would like it. Wish now I had 2 bedrooms: would so love you to stay here. Seems awful not to. Will try to get even though.
Love as ever, 
Mignon

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
Eberhart
8-27-42
MIGNON EBERHART
Dearest Fanny:
Well, I'm sitting under the apple tree, but with nobody else but me. Unfortunately! After darn near 20 years of good masculine company, there've been times during the war to date, when if a man (any man, by golly!) walked unguardedly past the gate I'd have felt like dragging him in. You've no idea (and I hope you never do have) how much one

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
miss: A. - The masculine viewpoint. B. A voice and heavy footsteps and a man at the other side of the table at night. C. A hundred little things like a hat on the mantel, the sound of a car coming up the driveway - all that. This is not a complaint: I made a vow about that (I'm going to raise hell and yell like everything about it after the war, though.) It is merely a reflection.
Came back from a visit to Washington exhausted. Was never as tired in my life. It was wonderful to find you letter

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription: night one! The child is gone, a nice kid; back to Wellesley Friday. She was a help in the way of company & made wonderful fudge! Which I can now eat as I've lost about 20 pounds. She idolizes Maurice Hindus! Will get over it as she gets older: at the moment it is funny - she & Lonnie mixed over it. (He is old family friend.) Imagine he is on his way home now. So far as I'm concerned he could stay there. Oh, I don't mean that: he just is so very Russian! Guess I told you. Shall avoid as too Russian for me! - Am

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
about to look over the winter clothes situation so as to have things packed away while maid still here. How right you were about that Rosemary, my God. This is a volume: don't make a chore of answering. You sound abysmally tired. Be careful about resting in Washington. Crowds terrible and climate enervating. Look out for horrible air-cooling systems: always take a wrap. Now mind me, about that. Best to Dick always and to you from both.
Much, much love, 
Mignon.

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
here: uncanny again too, in a way because I wanted it as much. Have never been so unsettled even in a lifetime of a more or less alarums-and-excursions nature.
Alan thinks he's going to be in Washington fairly permanently: that does not mean all the time but pretty permanent. Unless he is sent somewhere else at a moment's notice. May be sent abroad: might have a little sea experience but doubtful. I hope not. We see each other often of course but not often enough. I'm closing the house

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
the 1st. That's in a few days now: shall have Tom here to see to things as it is more expensive to undo damage than to pay Tom and heat & food for him. My apartment lease expires soon, thank Heaven. It is a grim, cold, unhappy little place: have never wanted to stay in it and have done it as little as possible. Cannot write there: too dejected - also too noisy.
Would like to go to Washington but there are so many problems about that that I'm trying to get everything straight and settled in my mind. I wouldn't mind doing

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
mignon eberhart
2.
all the navy things required of me as gracefully and tactfully as I can. I am not sure how successful I would be but I have never yet let Alan down when he wanted me to do anything and wont begin now. It would not be easy: am not sick but am not particularly well - mainly am tired and think the long economic strain I've had is catching up with me: have worked pretty hard for a long time. You know about this. (Don't read this to Dick. Bless you. for understanding.) - We can't live on his navy pay. The

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription: war will be over: and we will have to eat. So I can't deliberately throw away the market I've built up. I would have little chance of resuming it: people forget - times change and I might be sick or something. I could not sell my house without taking a great loss: nobody wants a country house & no gas & no fuel oil. Property values have gone in a tailspin. I have to pay my taxes. I have to think of Alan's people and of Alan and of myself: I could live on little enough but it's like getting

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
a bear by the tail. I have write about as much to keep my markets. And I find myself incredibly tired. So a serial and Washington in conjunction is something to plan very carefully. - 
Another problem is living. Washington is horribly crowded: everything absurdly high priced. Alan pays $120 a month for one room. I found a tiny house (many inconveniences) for $300 a month. Without heat - telephone, servants. Moving to Washington as an economic measure would be like jumping out of the frying pan. - I don't like the alternatives either: living alone and going down there week-ends.

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription: But I do have financial responsibility. Can tell you all this. Couldn't tell Janet for she knows nothing of bread-winning and thinks that Alan helps (does: I mean through money) me and I'd rather she kept on thinking so. It is a queer situation. I saw some of the navy people: had some to dinner: heard their talk. There is much more of the traditional, hard and fast navy ceremony and custom than I thought would be possible in time of war. I would have to put that first or hurt Alan. I would have to conform in every way — and write if or when I could. And I've got to keep my job and it's not an easy one. — Well;

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
MIGNON EBERHART
3.
having written all this down to you, I feel better. As the quakers say: a door will open. I think I'll get it straightened out. — Sometime though Fanny, when we are old and sitting together over our cake and tea, I want to talk to you as I can't now and still be fair to everybody. Can only now do the best I can do now: and hope it is the best. This is nothing to worry you, dear; believe me; nothing new. I can't say any more. Except bless you for being you.
Am practically certain there'll

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
be a letter from you tomorrow or next day! Never fails. Hope it won't this time. Let me know your plans and if I can make it will dash to Washington again. Would you believe it I'm still rewriting that grisly novelette! It is exactly like castor oil to me now — taking it, I mean.
Hair has been drying. Gas situation obliged me to learn to do my own hair. Also nails. Hair goes up okay — but nails are difficult especially

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
Eberhart
9-23-42
Fanny, Fanny dear;
I had your letter and you'll never know how much I wanted to pour out the heart to you. But I couldn't hurt you; I couldn't talk even to you about the thing between Alan and me; and I'm a bad dissembler — I couldn't write and not tell you, you've known, though, for a long time that something was wrong. I wasn't myself and you knew it. I knew that when Alan read me your note to him, over the 'phone tonight.. He said I must tell you. If you can, please give Dick as little as possible of this. It is so important to a man's self-respect that I can't bear to tell another man, even, though Alan says I must tell you. And it's going to hurt you Fanny and I can't bear that either but I have to make

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
you know that I love you just as always; more so because friends grow with every minute.
Well, I've got to say it. I'll be as brief and clinical as I can be. You see Alan and I never should have married; but we didn't know it until we were married. We both had ideas of marriage; so we were determined to make a success of our marriage. Alan was content; I don't think happy with the sex part, but content; I was a convenience to him and went through a certain amount of hell before I learned the self-control I did learn. Also I found as many substitutes as I could find. Hobbies, work, all that. And you know of all the people in the world how genuinely we love each other and how much sympathy we share, — Well, eventually it caught up with me and I got a nervous crash,

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
2.
I've done everything I've been told to do. Alan has gone to doctors and doctors. It is not anything that modern science or surgery can help. I reached the end of nervous endurance. The whole fact — bald and clinical — is that I cannot live in marriage with a young attractive male and a man I love and not have what should be a normal part of a woman's life, any longer.
I'm trying to build myself up. I've been in a nervous slump for months; lately it's been acute. I have a nurse — am in bed now but get up during the day and the doctor makes me go out — walk, see people, go to movies. I haven't been able to get my mind on work + I've got to do that.

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
I stopped to read this and I've tried to soften it and I've unconsciously tried from old reticent habit not to tell all! I can see that. But it's so hard, Fanny. It's a terribly hard thing to write about. I love him and have always wanted to protect him, as he does me. Can you manage do you think not to let Dick know the whole thing? It's Alan's pride I'm thinking of. Somehow telling you is allright but another man knowing — even Dick — is, oh you know.
I want you to know that I've got a doctor! I'm building up nervous depletion. I tried to hide it from you because it would pain you so much, and the situation would so worry you. I don't know what is going to happen. We are both doing our best to work

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
3.
it out. We see each other and write and phone. It's crazy but if there was another woman or if we wanted to divorce or hated each other it would be so much easier. My only hope is getting myself in hand, again but I've used up the self-control. I'll get some of it back. And I didn't take to drinking and I didn't take to drugs. It was lucky about the work really. We had a lot of happiness, a funny kind of happiness but real. Only the core and center of marriage wasn't there. But now it's the nerves that have given up. Blood pressure is low (90 over 70) but mainly nerves, which held out for 1+ years. Except for those headaches and upset stomach. —
I've had a lot of sleeping pills —

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
— am afraid this is not the way I'd like to write it. Fanny, please don't — oh, you'll hate it so. Knowing it. But Alan said it was worse for me not to tell you.
Now then: I'll be better. Physically, this was due for a long time. I can brace up and see people and seem almost like myself. I'm in very close touch with Alan. This helps enormously.
This is a burden to put on a friend. Fanny dear Fanny. Don't try to say anything about it. It would be wonderful for you to say you had this and like me and like Alan and tell me about yourself, what you are doing. Oh, Fanny I've often thought how happy your marriage must be. You look so complete; and contented. — Well. Don't think of this any more than you can help.
My love and Alan's
Mignon.

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
Eberhart
11-19-42
MIGNON
Alan goes on training ship soon: don't know when. Or details.
Dear dear Fanny:
I am furious about the situation at the paper: it's so outrageously unfair after all you've done for them. And they are out of their minds not to have the sense to realize it: somebody who knows something there ought to talk to publishers here. They do not, obviously, have any knowledge of how they like you and how much they value you and how they feel about the Sunday supplement. The lack of advertising is the answer: they are fools not to see it. They were fools and obviously did not know what they were

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
doing when they took over your idea, that you'd planned, developed, done all the hard spadework for, and then gave it to somebody who had not done all that (that alone was very bad business judgement). Let alone the fact that you've built up your name in literature as you have and it means as much as it does. You are really tops. Don't forget that for an instant for it is true.
They will come to you to beg you to take it over and fix things up: eventually they'll see that only you can. When they do, I hope to god you drive a hard bargain! They aren't trying to get you so tired

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
MIGNON EBERHART
2.
and disgusted that you leave: probably really they are seeing more clearly every day what a mistake they made in not begging you to do the supplement in the first place. My feeling is for you to wait — hard though it is: be thankful physically if you don't have the hellish grind of the Christmas supplement, and let them stew in their own juice and find out how little the Sunday editor knows about books. My feeling is all this may be a blessing in disguise — too damn well disguised at the moment but eventually will show the

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
paper something of your true worth to them. You have worked so hard that you've not press-agented yourself. I've always thought that was the way to do: but am beginning to see that press-agenting seems to help a lot of people get by: so maybe the real ones agent to consider it! — It --- whole situation makes me so god damn mad I can hardly write without boiling over. It's so dumb of them: and so preposterously unfair to the best Book Editor and critic I know about. But hang on for a while, Fanny. (Poor comfort. But I think I'm right. — Loved your letter as always: I mean hearing from you. Wish we could both go to Dr. Bennett. House question not yet settled. Take better care of yourself.
Love as always
Mignon
P.S. Sent one of Christmas things: only small gadget but note: only don't open. From B[[?]]ts. Didn't have card. —
Eberhart

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
Eberhart
12-22-42
Fanny dear:
There are two Jensen packages: main present is in one of them. If it doesn't get there before Christmas I'll personally kill Jensens. They promised and sent it air mail, registered. The Soles + B[[?]]ts are small things: and didn't get something for Duncy but will try to make up later. Bless his little black — well, no, I was about to say heart! Wagging tail, anyway. — I am not too

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
satisfied with my shopping either: I earnestly and honestly want you to exchange; or tell me and I will, and no nonsense about it! Nothing seemed right: and we ain't get used to shoddy materials.
Reminds me I took another look for the black knitted suit while I was at Woodsedge, packing. Scoured the house for it in fact: had already looked where it was supposed to be + not found it. I'm afraid that so-and-so Rosemary got it too: did I tell you — yes. I did. But I will look some more: could wring her neck and shall repeat to insurance but it wont accomplish the [[?]]als.

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
2.
She was wacky, besides.
Here the situation domestique is unbelievable Tom is very sick: if only he doesn't get pneumonia: have got him in some flamed pajamas of mine and Alan's bed. (Intended to get a room here for him — I mean within bus distance as house too small to live in, but hadn't had time or gasoline to accomplish it yet). No nurses available: have a colored girl who lumbers around + cannot make a bed passably, cook or wash dishes clean. Resorted to bribery at Employment agency: dirty pool, but there it is. Seems to be the custom, here! Everybody — grocery, etc. here blithely promise and as blithely

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
fail to deliver. Washington is many strange ways seems to be a Southern city, overwhelmed, and tradesmen, telephone girls and the like vaguely (or not too vaguely) resenting the whole thing. Tom smashed a fender: rather somebody else did but Tom was fired. (Naturally, paid it myself) but couldn't mend his feeling of injustice. — Have been writing out menus: if only I had your gift of taste in meals. Mine are so dull. Have tried to think up some of yours, like steamed lettuce. Have to order groceries 24 hours ahead and Saturday a roast (for dinner) arrived at 7:00 P.M. + no veg.
Read a book called The Navy Wife

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
3.
and nearly went back to Connecticut. My God — Well, I'll do my best.
So far have not succeeded in getting what New Canaan politely calls a Refuse Service. Consequently cartons + such still at back gate, brightly visible from my own and neighbors windows. This is really a triplex-garden-apartment, in New Yorkese. You can hear everything through the side-walls. But it does have bathrooms and gas heat, and was a lucky find.
Am desperately behind in work; and still low on blood-pressure. Haven't figured taxes and can't yet: they, Woodsedge taxes and upkeep: this house — what fun. I must get to work:

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
with or without blood pressure.
Alan is gone for a couple of days. Hope to get a decent cook + get Tom better by the time he gets back. Poor old Tom: will take tons of soda myself. Also must get a laundry —
If Alan goes to sea, really and for long I would love to stay with you, if I could be not a bother. There's no place in the world I'd rather stay and I can't tell you what it means to have you say that. So far as I'm concerned you are the best in the world, ever and always. — This badly expresses what I feel. For a writer I'm ridiculously inarticulate about things that move me deeply.
All our love for Christmas Eve and always.
Mignon.
Eberhart —

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
MRS. POPE DODGE
Dear Fanny,
It was a joy to see and hear you on color TV last night, with Bob Cromie. You looked so lovely in that blue gown and your interview just sparkled. Wonderful to know you look and feel so well. Can't wait to get your book.
Had an evening in Palm Beach with Doris and her husband. My daughter, Virginia, married

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
a magazine publisher a year ago - Oliver Johnson - they live here and were in Convention at the 'Breakers' in late April. Bob + Natalie were there at the time on their cruiser Johnsons live in Princeton - 13 miles for me
I was persuaded to sell my house in Coral Gables and buy one here in "Leisure World" so I would be near Ginny and her family. Am far from settled. Have met some very congenial people. We shall see. I expect to winter in Florida. Bob + Betty are fine saw them last August -
Do keep well and keep writing
Love, Gena

9813 Rosensteel ave
Silver Spring, Md.
From Harpers'
Dear Fanny
Long time to when I got your letter of June 15 about magazine editors. I got an unread return of my article on Austria. I've not sent it to any one since. With an American perspective on Austria now I'll let it smoulder until something threatens between Austria & Moscow - - which seems a long way off.
Had some eye trouble after landing from Europe in May. Sole metal slivers got into cornea - - and, oh well, had no reading in my life for quite a bit. However am in good shape again. Health seems to run along well - - and knee trouble 95% all right.
My wife, as an Austrian, brought in a Volkswagen on the 1 year basis by international agreement. I have enjoyed showing her the Skyline Drive - - indeed from mountains to Tidewater in Virginia. Also Maine [[?]], N.H. and Vermont. I look back with pleasure on the winding Vermont reads to the time you took a day off to travel with me & my Chautauqua ingenues. They still wind through woodlands as they did then, (The roads, I mean)
