title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
It seems strange to think that it was a quarter of a century ago that I came to Chicago as a cub reporter from Iowa, wrote a book review, and was given a desk as a literary critic. Those days, curiously enough, were not unlike the present times — indeed, in retrospect, they seemed like a rehearsal or a small scale of the vaster drama of today. Then American had suffered from what seemed at the time to be a huge and disastrous panic. Middle West was in chronic revolt against Wall Street. The structure of existing society was being widely criticised. And the reading public was beginning to think about economic and social questions. That, I suppose, was why young critics who knew something about social and economic matters were allowed to occupy the literary pulpits and preach sense to their elders. At least that was what we did, at every opportunity — with some new book as our text, we interpreted the realities of America to a generation a little bewildered by them and rather anxious for guidance. Naturally we preferred realistic novels, and did our best to help create a taste for them in the reading public.
Christmas was a time when we could tell people what to buy. In the Friday Literary Review we published

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
a list of fifty "recommended books"; and I can remember my gratification in learning from McCh[?]]'s that people came in with those lists and ordered from them — one good customer, I was told, buying all fifty! But, though we tried hard to help sell the books of which we approved, we felt no obligation to pay any special attention to "best-sellers." We were teachers, we were discoverers, we were creators of a new public taste — a taste which in fact was to become fashionable among what we were beginning to call intelligentsia. But wise as we were, we did not dream that our world would so soon be pushed off into the abyss of universal war; we preached, so far as I remember, no Christmas literary sermons or general disarmament — that would have seemed too Utopian. We were feminists, discoverers of new movements in poetry, drama, art, all of which lighted brilliantly and delightfully the path along the edge of the precipice into which we were presently tumbled.
And now — after the romantic illusion of post-war prosperity, so frightfully collapsed — the reading public is again taking a disturbed interest in social and economic questions. I have no doubt that, as before, a better American literature will come out of it — if there are any talented young people left alive in America to write it or any of their elders left with leisure to read it. ¶ These Christmas reflections

title: Fanny Butcher letters [2], 1930-1946
transcription:
would have seemed to me unduly pessimistic a quarter of a century ago, when I was twenty-one. But I note that literary criticism is again taking up the task of educating the public in social-economic matters, and I am glad of it. Literature is a fascinating by-product of the world's struggle for freedom and security; and I should think that the Christmas hope in the mind of every literary critic today would be for Peace, without which we can have neither freedom nor security.
Floyd Dell

BERNARD DEVOTO
LINCOLN, MASSACHUSETTS
Dear Fanny:
Someone has sent me a clipping of your Bread Loaf story and I'm tearful + confused. I know how to handle myself when the hammers are unsheathed, the sleeves rolled up, + the rough going reached, but there have been so few kind words in my literary life that they tend to trip me up + I'm all left-handed + left-footed.
Anyway, thanks a hell of a lot, even if I do think you must be cuckoo, for who am I but that Western loud-mouth standing on his hind feet + making a bit of gas about writing that the customers better not take very seriously. But wasn't B L a lot of fun? This was much the best year ever, what with you + Margaret + Ann Allen + Fr[[?]]s + Josephine and much better liquor supplies. I figure we ought to do again with just that set-up. Only you can't ever sit out in front. Hell, you wouldn't be comfortable there anyway, and think of a cellophane hat — no, my dear, the customers are much more dignified. And I'm glad as hell you're getting behind Josephine's book. What a charming child she is. I had a note from

Nov. 15, 1984 
Dear Mrs. Bokum,
This is just a brief note to tell you again how much I appreciate the opportunity of working for you. It was a challenging experience for me as I always wanted to do nursing. But to do it well, I now realize I need some training and much more practice. Thank you for the times you were very patient with my blunders. 
If our Governing Board deems it advisable at my age, I hope to sign up for a course in Home Nursing. My present certificate of "Care to the Sick and the Elderly" does not include personal care, or cooking, both of which I'd like to do

title: Fanny Butcher letters [1], 1930-1946
transcription:
much better. 
Joliet Junior College here is giving a course in Nurses Assistance beginning January 29. If the concerned authorities approve it, I'd like to take it. If I pass the exams in theory and practice, I would become certified......
I stopped writing this note momentarily to read the article about you in The Encounter-"A Famous Journalist interviewed on p.10-11. Has anyone sent you the article? If not, I'll bring my copy of our college paper. 
I'll see you Friday as usual around 4:00 o'clock P.M. 
I did speak to Sister Ambrose as you asked me to. She said she could get no one to take my place except, perhaps Sister Agnes Marie, who as yet has the time and is willing under certain conditions- if you want her. Otherwise, there is no one else available on this end. Good luck and God bless you. 
Love, Sister M. Cherubim

Number Five Bank Street
New Year's Day
Dear Fanny Butcher:
I've delayed writing to you because of certain anxieties here, and now I must tell you that all your nice plans are off. I will not be able to stop in Chicago at all. I am taking my mother on to the Mayo Clinic at Rochester for a serious operation. She had one done this last April, and a return looks discouraging. We have had a perfectly wonderful month, however, and in this world I suppose we have to take the good seasons with a light heart and meet the dark ones with calmness. Anyhow, a Happy new year to you, dear Fanny and my love.
Yours Willa Cather

Dear Fanny Butcher:
I said legend, didn't I, not folk-lore? There's such a difference. Folk-lore is unarticulated - detached. But legend is a sort of interpretation of life by Faith. It was that background of order and discipline that gave the lives of those missionaries proportion and measure and accent, like a work of art.
Yes, of course you may use anything I said, provided that

title: Fanny Butcher letters [1], 1930-1946

I'm so sorry your tired and used up - I'm a wreck myself, trying to get rested enough to start for Arizona. Of course I'll let you know when I go through Chicago. Rush your Archbishop for autograph along to me here - you can have it bound afterward. I'm not likely to have an address for some months. Awful way to live!

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894

Lan. Pa. Oct. 9, 1889
James C. Pillilng;
Please accept my sincere thanks for your "Sioux Bibliography" and I would be under many thanks to you if you would place my name on the list for the subsequent volumes as they are issued in order that I may keep a full set. In the annual reports of the Smithsonian Institution for 1863-4 are translations by [[Roer?]] of a work on the California Peninsula Indians which contain language lists, etc. The original book was by a Jesuit-Father Baegert-and was printed in 1774. I have not noticed this work in any of your bibliogaphies which I possess.
Please accept the enclosed slip which is from my own pen. I have a Shawanese list of words in manuscript in my own possession, which was compiled by Judge Yeates about-1778, published in "Notes & Queries; No. CCXXXII." These

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
Notes & Queries are edited by Dr. Egla, State Librarian of Pennsylvania and are published in the Harrisburg Telegraph and subsequently are issued in book form by Dr. Egle. title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894

Elizabeth N. J. Aug 13. 1887
My dear Mr. Pilling: 
I was taken down with a bilious fever the week you were here, and though after a couple of days I managed to come up to the scratch again, it floored me a second time the next week, and I was regularly laid up.
I am getting up again, but the Doctor urges me to go off for a time. My own opinion, however, is that doctors do not know much. Those of these learned gentlemen once decided in consultation that I was dead. as that was fifty years ago, I have been a pretty lively corpse for half a centure. 
Many thanks for many things

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
so many, in fact, that I hardly know where to begin. First for the two essays of Maj. Powell which I read with interest, and for which I wish to thank him as well as yourself.
Secondly for the Chippewa Testament. Trumbull ought to give us a paper on the various Ojibwa Bible translations, and their discrepancies. There must be fun there for some one.
As if it were not enough to send these, you follow up with a box of New Mexican pottery. This finds high appreciation, I assure you. The ladies do not see the asthetic value of Indian books, but when any thing is odd quaint and barbaric, it is hugely admired in these days of bric-a brac.
While I can enjoy Major

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
Powells's disquisitions or spend an hour comparing Bible versions, they can show their friends Pueblo pottery and talk about it.
A suggestion of mine that they should study Gatschet's German work on the Pueblo language, was, I am sorry to say, indignantly [[discounted?]]. This is a frivolou world. 
With best regards
Your old [[friend?]] John Gilmary Shea
Mr. Pilling

St. Joseph's Mission
Lewiston, Idaho, June 10, 1892
Dear Sir:
Please find inclosed the translation of the Nez-perce specimen, which was sent to me for deciphering.
The mere translation of it would have been a very easy work, but the english spelling adopted to express the indian sounds, besides being quite senseless, was somewhat troublesome.
How to pronounce the english vowels no one can guess, except in the english language, therefore I was compelled to stick to the import of the consonants, and for the rest to do as in reading of some of the oriental languages.
Now having nearly completed the work of the Nez-perce Dictionary, which is written in english and not in latin, as the grammar, I beg to ask, whether there is any probablility to have it printed by your Institution, and on what conditions.
Moreover, I have been contemplating the translation of the Nez-perce Grammar from the latin into the english language, and, of course, not for my own sake. Would your Institution care for it, and on what terms?

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
Lewiston, Idaho
Aug. 18, 1892
Mr. J. C. Pilling.
Having compiled the Nez-perce dictionary for the help of our young missionaries, I addressed myself to the Smithsonian not for the sake of publicity, but in hopes of multiplying copies of it in a speedy way. The printing of it by your Bureau, as it appears from your answer, depends on circumstances. 
Now you will allow me, Sir, to express my mind. Expecting to be recalled to Europe before long, I do not wish to leave behind me the mss., which might be of interest to philologists somewhere else.
I inclose therefore two pages of the dictionary for inspection at your convenience. These two pages are

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
sufficient to give an idea of the entire work, which consists of 370 pages.
In a future time, if your Bureau will decide on printing it, before my going to Europe, or making any other arrangement, I shall have no objection to send the mss.
With regard to the rules in force for government printing I say, that I am not much concerned with accidental changes, which do not require any further work on my part; I only remark, that I am not disposed to do again my work, if not in accord with your rules.
Now supposing that your Bereau should be satisfied with the work, I wish to know beforehamd, on what terms the mss. will be accepted, and how many copies given me.
Thanking you very much for the interest manifested in my behalf,

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894

I remain, Sir,
Your humble servant
A. Morvillo S. J.
N.B.

All vowels as in the latin or german language.

Ch as in the german language or as the letter x in the greek.

Muscogee, June 15th, 1891.
J. C. Pilling Ch'f Clk,
Bureau of Ethnology,
Smithsonian Institution
Washington. D. C.
Dear Friend, I have just had the pleasure of putting up two copies of the new edition of the Creek New Testament which contains, of revised and newly printed books, the Three Gospels after Matthew, Acts, Romans, Galatians, Ephesians, Titus, James and the three epistles of John.
Mark needed less revision than the rest because translated by myself

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
entirely, with the advantage of having previously done much other Testament translating.
On the revision of Luke, I had different helpers, but Rev. T. W. Perryman ws my chief helper in the final revision.
I could not now recall the names of all the natives, from whom I gained more or less help in the revisions of John's Gospel, as it was years from the time I began correcting it, (as opportunity offered,) until the second edition was needed, during which time I referred questions that arose to those to whom I might have access, but the final and thorough review of the whole was made with Rev. T. W. Perryman's help, who had given me assist-

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
ance on the most of the books of the Testament for their first edition.
On the second edition of Acts I likewise had the help of many, but, on the final review, my chief helpers were Rev. T. W. Perryman, Hon. D. M. Hodge, Hon. Taylor Chissoe, and Mrs. F. B. Severs, all of them former pupils.
On the Second edition of Romans, and on the three epistles of John, also, Mrs. Severs was my helper.
On Galatians, Ephesians, Titus and James, Judge James Scott was my helper, he, also, a former pupil.
I cannot tell you how glad and thankful I am to have been spared to accomplish the revision of all my earlier work on the Testament, as, having become

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
more familiar with the idiom of the Creek, I was able to see that, in the first translation, in my case to be literal, my translation has in many instances been less clear to the Creek reader than it had been my intention to make it.
Should I be spared to see new editions of the remaining books needed, I will gladly revise each one, although there is not such need of it in any of these books, as there was in those the revised editions of which now appears. 
You will find in the copy of the Testament in which I have put your name the date of the revised edition of each book, and I thought you would put the same into the Smithsonian copy in such shape as you like best. 
I believe I will enclose a leaf of John's Gospel as it was sent to the printers, as it will give you  better idea of the work put upon it.
As ever, your friend,
A. E. W. Robertson

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
March 8th '92
Dear Mr. Pilling,
I am as busy as ever, thought I do not know when the work of the last eight months -Genesis-will appear in print. It still needs much careful work with native help.
Will you be so kind as with your pen and penknife to rectify the title page of the last edition of the Creek Testament, as I am doing with those I have. I insert, "Revised Edition", and change the year to 1891.
Then in the translation of the words "Translated

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
from the Original Creek," please scratch out-the two words "Mv of" and insert above between "enhoteceskv" and "cohoyvte", es, which takes the place of ofv, and in "tohtvlecicvhotel" scratch out "cv" and change t to c in "hotet", making "tohtvlecihocet" and so greatly oblige me. Both the type setter and myself made mistakes in that word, which I overlooked in the edition of '87. The vtes etc. in such [[cut off word]] indicate that of which the writer or speaker has not personal knowledge, in their specific character, and I overlooked the fact, and the type setter made an entirely unknown word of it. 
I think I have written to you of my conviction that the question where to use the terminal n and t contains the key to the language, (or rather its answer does.) I found striking proof of this the other day in reading in Hebrews 12:5 (Creek Testament). I found "Mv Pucaset vnokecan estemerricet" etc, where it should be vnokecat. With the general idea that

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
the terminating n belongs to the object, I had made the mistake, and the interpreters had not noticed the force of the English carefully enough to correct. With the n we make "The Lord chastens the one who loves Him," instead of, "chastens whom He loves," a very important difference, you see, although both are true.
It was my work on Genesis that first showed me what enabled me to detect the mistake, and I wonder that I should have worked in this language all these years without getting hold of this feature. Early in my work I began the plan of cutting out verses containing this relative participle, (as I call it because it includes in itself the force of the relative pronoun,) and placing them in parallel columns as to the terminal n and t, but I had too much other missionary work on hand to continue work in that way. I find at last the principle that if the participle expressing the object expresses the action of the subject of the sentence, as in this case, the terminal letter mujst be t, otherwise n. This looks very simple, but the trouble is that this form in [[?]] expresses the nominative so constantly, that you

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
fail to notice that it is ever used in the objective. At any rate I have to confess any failure, and I fancied myself pretty good at digging out the grammar of the language. But it is in this case, as so often in other things, as soon as discovered, it seems wonderfully simple.
So now will you be so kind as to turn to Heb. 12:6 in that Testament and substitute t for n in the word "vnokecan."
Also in Luke 6:20 20, 21, 22, in the word "herakes" please turn the a into v making hervkes as that v shows the person in the plural number.
Am I presuming in asking so much of you. I think not, as I am so sure, that, like myself, you want a thing correctly given, even thought very few might ever know the difference. 
I thought I could take time for very few words, but my desire to make sure of having the mistakes corrected, has driven me on.
I trust yourself and family are well and prospering in the highest sense.
As ever sincerly your friend, A. E. W. Robertson
My love to your wife please.

Yours of the 9th received in my last I omitted to mention that from the year 1846 to 1855 I was under the auspices of the American Missionary Association without salary.

The hymns on the [[slip?]] sent were my own translation mostly published in 1878 at Omena. Two other editions, one in 1879 & one in 1883 composed of some of my own translating & some selections as from earlier translations. About 50 pages.

In 1879 I published one with the following title. Gospel Hymns and Sacred Songs, translated into the [[Ojibway?]] language by the Rev. [[William?]] Wahlher, French Boy, Language Anglais-- Published by Rev. A. Barnard Omena, Mich. 1879 It contained 186 pages. 

[[JWP?]] has one with nearly same title, same date, but 24 pp, & apparently complete. 4076

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894

I found enclosed a red slip containing a copy of the first Hymn of the book published in 1863;
In 1878 at Omena it commenced the second time to get out an elementary Ojibway Grammar a copy of which it enclose. I abandoned the project for want of means to continue, also want of [[?]] type to make it easy of [[acquiring?]] to learners. 
I find among my papers some manuscripts of grammar. In about 1850 or/57 I was applied to by a man from Washington by the name of Foster [[?]] a synopsis of the language which he wished to publish in a work on Indian customs language [[?]]. I filled a number of fools cap sheets giving a brief summery of the language or a translation of 500 words the [[?]]. He promised to send me a copy of his book but I never heard of it again. 
Respectfully [[yr?]]
A Barnard

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894

Mr. J. C. Pilling
Washington D C.
My dear Sir:
Yours of the [[4th?]] received. You may keep the Hymn Book & whatever you may please to send me of your publications will be gratefully received & appreciated.
I have 2 copies of the Ojibway New Testament, the work of  the late Rev. Sherman Hall, assisted by his interpreter Rev Henry Blatchford. It was published by the Am. Bible Society. --If you have no such copy & would like one I will sent it to you.
If my life is spared & I can get time to devote to it I shall try to put in manuscript something
Ayer N A ms 727

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
in the shape of an Ojibway Grammar which would greatly assist those who wish to learn that language.
I would willingly spend all the rest of my days in that work if Providence should open the way: but cannot do much without assistance from some source. No benevolent society seems to have funds to spend in that line of work.
It is to be regretted that a language so complete & regular in its grammatical [[construction?]] so extensively spoken should not receive more attention from those who wish to enlighten the Indians.
I am truly yours

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
Benzonia Mich Jan. 30. /90

J. C. Pilling
Washington D C.
Dear Sir,
Enclosed please find receipt signed. Many thanks for the books. I shall take great pleasure in reading them.
I send by same mail the Ojibway Testament. It is a revised edition from one published in 1845 = or 6. which was very imperfect.-- Even this one contains grammatical errors in almost every chapter But no doubt the translator did his best, so we must not criticise his work to severely. 
It is a great pity the whole Bible could not be correctly translated

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
into that language. But I see no prospect of its being done as so few persons ever attain a sufficiently correct knowledge of it to translate it as it should be. To depend upon even the best interpreters will not insure a sufficiently correct translation as their knowledge of the English is very limited, & they have no correct idea of the grammatical construction of their own language.
I learn from my friend in Dacota that he has donated that little [[?]] book to you. Am glad of it but did not like to request it of him as he so earnestly sought to [[profess?]] it.
Very truly yous [[?]]
A Barnard

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
Enclosed please find Receipt signed--What little I have done seems so insignificant compared with those in the Bulletins that I do not think it worthwhile to trouble you with a biographic account. will merely say--Born June 2 1817 in Peru, Bennington Co. Vt.--united with Cong. Ch. at 13.--moved to Ohio at 17 educated at Oberlin. Entered mission field 1843. First at Red Lake Minnesota--at Cass Lake 1846--at St. Joseph (now Wolhalla) Pembina [[Co.?]] at Dacota in 1893 where lie the remains of her who shared my labors--In 1854 the wife of my fellow laborer late Rev D. B. Spencer was murdered by the Sioux in the Spring of 1855. I was compelled to abandon the work there & take refuge in R. R. Settlement--(now Manitoba). Spent some two or more years with the Inds about Lake Winnepeg [[?]] under the Bishop of Rupert's Land--in 1863 removed to this place since have labored 5 years among the Inds about Grand Traverse Bay under auspices of the Presb. Home Miss Soc--Resigned in consequence of a partial deafness, which unfitted me for effectual work--am now a retired member of Grand Rapids Presbytery.
From 1846 to 1855 was under the auspices of the American Missionary Association.
Respectfully yours [[?]]
Alonso Barnard

[[Transcriber's note: R. R. Settlement refers to Red River Colony in Winnepeg?]]

I have the pleasure of announcing you that I am about to leave for a trip to France and Metz, my native country I shall leave from Halifax on the 28' inst. Vinita I. T. March 6th 1890
Hon James C. Pilling
Dear Sir--
I am indebted to you for certain books, [[reposted?]] from the Smithsonian Institute. While I have not time to give them that close examination I would like to, it is gratifying to have them for reference.
In the introduction to "The Problem of the Ohio Mounds" page 8 "Fourth". "that the C. were the [[Tallequi?]]."
I had long wondered how the name of the Cherokee Capital originated. It is not modern--Does not correspond with Cherokee words, or like most names have a definite meaning--It was imported here from Tennessee. The Tellico Plains, and Block House are the same--It was said to be a town or settlement of the Cherokees rather noted--said to be a kind of City of Refuge in the olden time (Ta li qua.) This, and Tallequi must have a common original--
I have inended sending you a copy of my little "Cherokee Pictorial Book," but neglected it. Will

TESTAMENTS LONDON.
BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY,
146, Queen Vicoria Street,
LONDON, E.C.
May 26th 1892
Dear Mr. Pilling
I have been an unconscionable time in replying to your kind note of March [[10 or 16?]], but the delay was really unavoidable.
You ask about the Tuki[[?]]. What I meant was that I thought you had the gospels back & I promised you the Epistles [[tr.?]] to complete the New Test. translated by Archdeacon Robert McDonald & edited by Archdeacon Reeve, (now Bishop of Mackenzie River, by the way.)
I find to my dismay, that the sheets were sent to the binders in a hurry, & when the N. T's. were made up & bound, the books

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
were dispatched to the mission field without keeping back even a copy for the library. I have since  recovered one from an exhibition set, somewhat scratched by nails in packing, but as there is no other to be had, I hope you will excuse its outward condition
I send with it two copies of the Tukudh Pentateuch, as printed. More portions will doubtless follow, but these are all now ready
Slave. Alas for your theology! The same excuse (I don't like the word!) must be given in this case. [[?]] as we have no need to keep permanent stock of the out-of-the-way languages in London, when these orders are completed & our small wants attended to, the bulk are sent off at once. The Slave Gospels vol. is nine years old, too.
[[?]]? the  Algonquian bibliography, returned the receipt. For this please

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
accept my best thanks. I shall shortly now, no doubt, have the pleasure of acknowledging receipt of the office copies, of which I hold the advices.
The pictures pleased me exceedingly. My wife was much interested in the two Indian chiefs -- I think I was more taken with the scenery of the four smaller pictures.
Since I wrote you my mother has died. I have been somewhat in arrears with my work through a short absence with a severe cold. I also delayed a while, hoping to resurrect another copy of the Tukudh N.T. and the Slave Gospels.
Now that the Survey volumes have com in (for which I return

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894

receipts by this post, for 3 copies of Vol. VI. Some of Vol. II, pts 1 & 2) I must not put this off any longer. Their arrival reminds me that kind friends are more thoughtful of others than I have been. I hope the safe arrival of these two or three book I send will show you that we are not altogether unmindful of you, though I must admit my long silence goes against me.
I trust you & your family are will, & thinking Mrs. Nelling might like to possess one of the little pamphlets bearing the facsimile of the Queen's writing, I have enclosed one. We are projecting a new edn. -- I will not forget to send you two but they can't be ready yet awhile
Yours very sincerely,

L. J. C. et M.I.
New Westminster, B. C.
the 2ond July 1872
Dear Sir
Your favor of the 20th June is received.
I am very much pleased to see that you take such interest in our Chinook. By this mail I send you a few copies of the vocabulary made by Rev. Father Lejeune. Should you need a certain numbers of said copies, you have only to send a word to Father Lejeune. He will be happy to satisfy your wishes.

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
It gives me a great pleasure to hear that the Revd. Father St Onge is helping Father Lejeune in the Chinook, by issuing free to him weekly copies on Religious Instructions in stenographic Chinook. I know Father St
Onge, he has succeeded to me in the Yakima Mission, amongst the Indians of Washington State, and he speaks the real and beautiful Chinook of Mgr Blanchet and Mgr Demers, the two first Missionaries on this Pacific coast.
Though I speak Chinook, I have no manuscript of any kind in that language. For any think you wish to have in that language, you will find it at Father Lejeune's.
I have the honor to be,
Dear Sir;
your humble Servant.
Paul Durieu
Bishop

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
Mission de la Nativité
Lac Athabaska
28 May 1894
My Dear Sir.
Your very kind letter dated 28 October 1893 came to hand on the 7th of March 1894 and now is my first chance of answering you. You may judge by this that we are shut out of the civilized world for all practical purposes. that is why the R[[superscript]]d Fathers I mentioned to you in my letter have escaped so far your searching eyes. Another reason of their being unknown is that they have had none of their work printed and of course their names did not come to the notice of the public. Besides, M[[superscript]]r l'abbé Petitot who has been for a long time working with us had published such a large quantity of informations about the Indians of the far North and their languages that we thought

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription: he had done enough for the whole of us as regards missionary contribution to the learned world. You have I think all our printed books and the other works I mentioned in my letter are manuscripts. As to the identity of the Fathers I named to you, viz Father Lecomte & Father Lecorre they are not at all to be taken for the Abbé Lacombe or the Abbé Legoff, both of whom I know personally-Only I am very sorry to say Father Lecomte is no more. He died in September 1892 at the age of forty. He was so skilful in the Slavy language that if you had heard him talk with some Indian without seeing them, you could not have distinguished the French priest from the Red man- Father Lecorre is still working amongst us and is Superior of our Mission at Providence on the bank of the MacKenzie River where we have a large establishment including a convent

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
of Sisters of Charity with a school and orphanage and an average of 40 children of the different tribes of the country. 
As to the informations you require about our method of publication, how, when & where our printing press was introduced, I will be as concise as possible-Having become sick when in Mackenzie River I was ordered to France by Bishop [[Faraud or Sarand?]], then our Vicar Apostolic, who charged me with the publication of part of his work: the history of the old and the new Testament in Montagnais. He had the types cast, I bought a Stanhope Printing Press of moderate size on account of the difficulties of freighting heavy things in the Northern country. I learned to set the types and the other operations of printing at Paris during my convalescence in 1895-96, in publishing at that time. [[Nioltsi be diklise yaze?]]- this work done I packed my printing press, types [[?]] and started in April 1896 to come back to Mackenzie River.

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
but I was ordered to stop at Lac La Biche Mission. The printing press remains with me. I put it up and according to the hours of leisure I could spare in the middle of other missionary work I published the books I sent you and some others of which I kept no specimen. In 1883 I was sent to Peace River amongst the Beaver Indians and the Chekenes. During three years I visites all the tribes along Peace Riverways to the Rocky Mountains. Thence I went back to Lac La Biche printed some new books and came in 1888 to Athabaska Lake where I brought my printing press. Here I have just finished a new edition of our book of prayer in the Cree language, of which I will send you a copy as soon as we have bound our books. I remain, my Dear Sir, yous truly
+Emil Grouard B. of Ibora O. M. I.

May 7th 94
J. c. Pilling Esq
Dear Sir
As mail communication between the Islands & the mainland is very difficult & last year we received our letters twice only namely in June & November, therefore I have been prevented from answering your letters before. I now send you two copies of the St. Matthew's Gospel, & six more copies of the two little cards.
As the S. [[PCK?]] have not yet sent the Old Testement stories in book form, I now send you the proof sheets & will send the books as soon as they arrive.
The Grammar & Dictionary are still in the hands of Dr. Dawson at Ottawa for whom they will

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
be printed by the Royal Society of Canada. As soon as I receive my copies will forward you three of each.
The Haida Creation & [[Dieties?]] is printed by the Royal Anthropological Society of Great Britain & Ireland, before whom I delivered my lecture & they doubtless would be glad to send you three copies if you were to write to them. I have given all mine away, but send you one copy that was printed by a dealer in curios at Victoria.
As regards No. 4.5 & 6 I left the whole of the MSS with the C. M. S. for publication & and have not yet heard from them whether they are being printed or not, but if you should care to print them will send you the M.S.S of the

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:

As soon as I have time will send you a short account of myself etc.
I am
Yours Truly
C Harrison

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
St. Mary's Church, Winnipeg, Man.
Jan. 3d - 1890
James C. Pilling, Esq.
Sir,
I am in receipt of your letter of Dec. 17, which was wrongly addressed to Ft "Kappel" 9 (sic), qu'Appelle. I was there, formerly, but left it, nearly four years ago.
However, your letter reached me here.
I am, indeed, the very man who had the book: Niina Masinaigou - you refer to, printed in Montreal in 1886. In the same time I had another small book, a catechism printed in the same language, Algonquin. And, also, another one in the Maskegon language, printed in the

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
syllabic caracters.
I have not one single copy of any of these books, but I think I could procure them, if you are very anxious to have them.
For several years until last summer, I was with another tribe of Indians, called Sauteux. Unfortunately, we have no books written in that language, owing to the want of means. We use the Otchipwe books, which, though a little different, are generally understood.
Those two languages, Sauteux and Otchipwe, as well as the Cree and Maskegon, are, I believe, derivations of the great

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
Algonquin language.
I have here some Cree & Otcipwe books, Dictionary, Grammar and prayer books; but I suppose you have them also.
I did not receive the set of Ethnological Bulletins mentioned in your [[articles?]]. I heard a good deal about the Smithsonian Institution, but never could afford to go and see it. 
Some 25 years ago, whilst travelling among the Indians on the shores of Hudson Bay, I gathered specimens (Beatles) for a gentleman

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
interested in that grand Institution. So that I am sure there are specimens there which I handled. 
Anything I could still do for you, I'd gladly do it
I remain
Sir,
Yours truly
L. Lebret
O. M. I

title: James Constantine Pilling letters, 1881-1894
transcription:
V. D. Sir.
We had some new chapels blessed lately: the Book "Benediction of a Church" was made for the purpose and is only the responses taken from the Roman Ritual with a few verses in Shushwap.
The little [[parts?]] "After Communion" & "Ntlakupmoh etc." were composed & printed by me before I thought of introducing shorthand to the natives. I made besides a beginning of catechism & prayer book in Tompson language to which belong the two above. My book got to page 75 or so when I left it & took the shorthand; which contains now the same things & many more. 
I am now essaying a new autographic press from Paris. Success is coming but very slowly. 
Yours Very truly,
J M R LeJeune O.M.I
Oct. 25, 1893

[headed paper of Allen School]
[La Moille, Ill.,] May - 12, 1893.
My Dear Pupils: -
During the evening of June 7, '92  my heart was filled pride as each of you did so well his or her part and many times since as I have heard of your success or noted it I have felt proud of you and glad to think of the pleasant relations which existed between us as teacher and pupils. I rec'd the Class letter on the morning of May 3d, & as I read it I felt very proud of you as a class but with the feeling came many others not so pleasant, among whem the tho't of the great responsabilities before each of you and the fear, yea even the positive knowledge that I had failed in many ways to help prepare you for them. But with thankfulness I remembered that the most of you were consecrated to the work of the Heavenly Master & the firm belief that all would be I felt again like asking Him to take you into His keeping & make each and every one of us more faithful & worthy. For the many kind expressions in your letters concerning myself I am very grateful. Pummie suggests a vote of thanks to me & while I thank her

title: Dean family letters [5], 1779-1883
transcription:
June 19 1888

Dear Friends, Mary and Albert are all sympathize with you as we have felt the same thing your little one has passed away. Still how sweet to think they are at rest after so mutch sufering perhaps not in Boddy so mutch but in Mind being deprived of so mutch that he could injoyed had he been well these many years; now we can think of him with the loved ones that have  left us and gone before. What a pleasent thought; he has escaped the ills of life that Menny Young men have to pass through. a Kind Father has taken him

title: Dean family letters [5], 1779-1883
transcription:
home; we started to go on to the funeral the storms overtook us we were so long detained that we came back got home not fare from Two, it rained very hard where we were; if we all keep [[well?]] think shall be over before long.

All well at present.

When your can we would like to have you come and make us a nice visit.

With mutch love,

title: Dean family letters [5], 1779-1883
transcription:
East Woodstock

April 15th 1867

My Dear Cousin Mary,

When I received your letter I cannot express to you my feelings, as I in some degree realized the great afflictions you had been called to pass through. I well remember what you said to me one day when you were looking forward to the time when you should return to spend the vacation with your friends. You said Oh Abbie What a dear good Mother I have got. Yes Dear Mary you did have a dear good Mother and what a comfort it must be to you that you were able to be with her through most of her sickness and listen to her sweet council and to do what you could to make her last days comfortable. In one of her last letters she spoke of what a great

title: Dean family letters [5], 1779-1883
transcription:
comfort it was to have your face to look upon every day and spoke of how kind every one was to her. I very much want to hear how you are all getting along. You have still a dear Father and sister left you for a comfort. I trust you all will be spared to be a great blessing to each other. I think I realize the loss of my friends more as I grow older. I feel the loss of my mothers advice and council. But we know that God orders all things for our best good. 

I have not been to home much for the last two months. I was to your Uncle Leonard's and kept house while your Aunt Luisa went to Boston and Lowell. She went to see Anna. She found her quite well and happy. I am now with Aunt Mary Chandler. She has had very sore hand and has not been able to do her work. She is better and I think I shall not have to stay much longer. She wishes to be remembered

title: Dean family letters [5], 1779-1883
transcription:
to you and Anna. I suppose you have heard that our minister has left us we have not got any one to preach for us yet, but hope we shall get someone for a year at least but do not expect to find one that will fill Mr. Pratt's place in every respect. I saw Marzam Paine the other day she spoke of the pleasant visit she had to your house, although it made her feel sad to see your Mother failing so failing so rapidly. She enjoyed her visit out west very much indeed. 

I think Pamelia Mason's health is not as good as it was a year ago. She seems to be loosing flesh and does not seem so strong. I do not know how she will get through the spring she has not been out much this winter perhaps the warm weather may agree with her. Your Aunt P said she had writen to you so I suppose she wrote you the particulars about their family. Oh Mary how much I would

title: Dean family letters [5], 1779-1883
transcription: like to see you and have a good long talk with you. I hope you will write often and let me know how you are getting along you must take good care of yourself and not work too hard. I should be very glad to have Anna write to me I think she promised to when she was out here. I should like to see her very  much. I am intending to write to our Aunt Hannah soon. I was very glad she could be with you at the time of your Mother's death I think she must feel very lonely. I am very glad she has so pleasant a home. I hope soon to hear from you all and I will try and be more punctual about answering your letters and be asured you are not forgotten by your, cousin Abbie

title: Dean family letters [4], 1779-1883
transcription:
a good supply is about the color of mine. and her eyes blue. Not grey. blue, and she bids fair to show by the hue of her skin that she belongs to the European race. I went to meeting last Sabbath and took her. She remained during the exercises without making any disturbance. She with two other children, was baptized. The call her Mary Charlotte.
I wish you had been here to have gone with us to a wedding we attended this (Thursday) afternoon. There were over 30 present. The house contains only one room besides a small bed-room and pantry. The cooking stove was moved "out-doors" and after the ceremony - while they were setting the table for supper - the ladies were invited to occupy the chamber. lighter by removing one of the lap-boards. The entertainment consisted of chickens. pies. cake. preserves &c. &c. - What Yankee would think of making such a wedding with such accomodations
It is an Ohio family, But we had a very pleasant time. I dont know as any one took their knives and forks and spoons along with them. for doubt[[?]] those things went beforehand.
Mr. Gru married a couple before breakfast the morning of the 4th of JUly. He was invited to be at the place at sun-rise. It is about 4 miles from here.
I believe we have not given you an account of a hail storm we had here in the afternoon of the 12th of June. Our house has three windows in front. containing each 12 panes of glass and they were all broken but two, and some in other windows making in all near 50 panes broken. Our [[?]] [[?]] the same fate. some experiencing more damage. others less. these having most north windows. losing most glass. Some wheat fields were nearly or quite destroyed. and fruit was much injured. In Pe[[?]] it

361 Washington St.
Boston Jun4 14/88

Dear Mary - Your letter received this morning - I long to start at-once for Illinois - or be ready to when I hear from you again - Not that I could do Dean(??) any good - but if it would be any comfort

title: Dean family letters [3], 1779-1883
transcription:
to you - it would be a great satisfaction to me.  I hope he will not suffer long.

If he is better and conscious when you get this give him a kiss and tell him his aunty would like to see him.  My vacation time as??? put at July 23rd two weeks - and I had expected to spend it

title: Dean family letters [3], 1779-1883
transcription:
with Aunt Pauelia - as the summer months here have been divided up between the different clicks. I presume I could go this month - and it seems to me now as if if I must go.

Affectionately -
