title: Dean family letters [2], 1779-1883
transcription:
this past summer in Cambride Port, which will cost, together with the land, about fifteen thousand dollars, I expect Charles will moove out here and take my post when it is done, It will be a very fine house when done. I sent you a paper, The Courier, and ordered it for one year, whether it is still sent or not I dont know, (I will call and see, and still have it sent. What do you think of the Mexican war? I think it an abomination. and a curse will follow the party that draged us into it. I learned thro Ezra that Mr Reynolds had some root for us. he may keep it till I come up. as we do not want it at present. Remember me to all our friends who may enquire after us. Before I come up, I hope that little back-house will be up.
My best regards to all the house hold.
Affectionately your brother
Ezra Dean

title: Dean family letters [2], 1779-1883
transcription:
Cambridge Port May 20 1848
Dear Sister,
I write to let you know that we are all very well, and that I shall, if nothing happens, come and see you in the course of June
Charles has another son, which makes to daughters and two sons, so that the name is not likely to run out at present.
Tell Mr Reynolds that we want he should send the root which he has on hand as soon as he can, for it is wanted immediately, by the cars, and direct to "Geo. A Williams Cambridge Port, care of Maynard & Noyes, Merchants Row Boston" written on the outside on a piece of posteboard tacked on strong. Being in rather a hurry and not having much, that is material to write, I shall close by hoping you are very well. give my love to all Mr Reynolds family.
Your affectionate Brother
Ezra Dean

title: Dean family letters [2], 1779-1883
transcription:
Miss Lucy Dean
North Killingly
Con.

title: Dean family letters [2], 1779-1883
transcription:
Cambridge port July 22 1849
Dear Sister
I arived home the day I left Killingly, and found all our friends well, but my cold hang on untill a few days since, but am now very well, I have sent you the ear-trumpet which I promised, which I think will be a great service to you, if it should not answer I can exchange it for another, if you can have a chance to return it soon, but I think it will answer as well as any, it cost $ 1.50. I think very cheap. You must put the tube to your ear, or in your ear and hold it up, and let those talking to you speak right into the bole, and I think you can hear from it very well. I hope you are geting better, for I think you will, and yet enjoy prity good health for one of your age, but try and get along without taking much physic,
Charles says he should like to see you and talk about the Deans, he is geting up a history of the Deans, and going back as far as the name can be found in old England, and will have it published, which will make quite a book, when I come up again if the book is published, I will bring it up. He finds in England some noblemen and som Bishops and some Generals - and some Admirals, so I think we shall be able to make out a prity good name.
Leonard will attend to your affairs, and you must let him do as he wants to, as I have no dout he will do every thing right. I think you ought to be willing to hear every thing done to make you comfortable and those that take care of you you must have a back house built and have your house repaired to make it warm before cold weather. and whatever else Leonard thinks necessary

title: Dean family letters [2], 1779-1883
transcription:
I am very glad you have somebody to take good care of you, and Mrs Reynolds must be satisfied for her trouble and you must let Leonard say what he thinks she ought to have, we all want you to have every thing that is necessary to make you comfortable, if you spend all your money while you live to do it. I dont think I can find a place that will suit William Henry, businiss is now dull and nobody seems to want, to give a boy his board and clothing
Regards to Mr and Mrs Reynolds, and remember me to all the neighbours, Doct G[[?rsvenor]]or in particular, and Mrs Copp.
Your loving brother Ezra Dean

title: Dean family letters [2], 1779-1883
transcription:
From Brother Ezra Dean
Miss Lucy Dean
Killingly
Con

title: Dean family letters [2], 1779-1883
transcription:
East Woodstock June 24. 1856
Dear Sister
Yours of the 26th of May comes to hand in due time & I have been thinking of writing you for Several days but have hardly been able to do so (at least for some 8 or 10 days) having been sick for the last four weeks with a slow fever and diarrhea. I have been able to sit up & walk about most of the time. I am improving a little but am flat as dishwater, no strength and very little appetite except what is made by stimulants. I am getting about as thin a little legs (you remember him of course). I believe I wrote you that my health was not as good as last winter, but I did not mind much about, it except to do a little something for my throat &c. About four weeks since I had an attack of Cholera Morbus & have been lying abed & [[mopessing?]] about ever since
Pamelia Mason is in very poor health this summer. We sometimes fear almost that she will go into consumtion [consumption] though she is much better now than she was four weeks ago. She & I ride about some - on short-drives. She is very poor in flesh & I am ditto I have lost 25 lbs since last winter

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
20/4 91/14 22/18 23/31 23/26 25/27 26/27
Macomb Ills. Feb. 7th 1885
Dear Ezra D. Richardson,
Was very glad to get your letter some weeks since and have been very busy, or would have replied sooner. I supposed you do not go to school this cold weather, but are studying under the tuition of your mother. Do you not think she is a splendid teacher, and could you not go away beyond the girls, who have teachers, who have not graduated at mt Holyoke Sem.? I think you might, if you try hard. We have had a good deal of snow, and sleighs have run merrily, and to-night it

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription: seems as if we might have more snow soon. Have you had any sleigh-rides, or does not your father take you, when he goes to see sick people? Some of these cold days, I think he must be glad not to have people get sick very much. You have nice papers to read I presume. I have been reading some numbers of the South's Companion recently, and I was very much interested in them. You take that, do you not? There are lots of nice things to read, but do you not know, that the best book, in the world, for you and every one else to read, is the Bible. Do you study your Sabbath School Lesson a good deal? I have been studying mine, at times, all the week and tomorrow. When my young ladies come to the class, I hope I shall know enough about the

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription: why the Jews treated Paul, because they supposed he did and said, what he had not the right of saying or doing, to say some things, which they have not thought of about accusing others of doing wrong when we do not know of a certainty, that they have so now Dean, do you ever say Edna or Anna have done things, which you are not certain they have done, and did you know, that is telling a falsehood? Do you not think those Jews acted very badly to want to beat Paul, and that was just what Paul had wanted to have done to Stephen twenty six years before. Do you suppose he thought about how he took care of the clothes of those, who

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
stoned Stephen? I hope you study these lessons every week and think about them too. Now Dean you are eleven years old and did you ever think you are old enough to be a very good boy and help every body around you, in some way? Some boys never think of any thing, but having their own way, and making others do just as they want them to. You do not do so, do you? I do not like men, women or boys and girls who feel and act so, do you? The teacher, who boards here has one such boy, and she does not like him and I do not wonder at all. Much love to all the family. I send the letter your mother sent to me in this envelope. 
Please give it to her.  Yours affectionately
H. A. Bailey

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
East Woodstock Conn. July 24th.
Dear Mary,
Anna is here, and has read your last to us, and we can all realize, how lonely your home is, now that one has gone from it, who was always there, and while, for years, you could not foresee what must be the ultimate result, yet (as it always is) when the end came, it took you by surprise. I have thought of you very often, but have been at Leonord's till Saturday night last, for two or three weeks, and have been so busy, that letters could not be written by me, to any one. I can not write what [[underlined]] I have been doing but will tell you, when I see you
[[left-hand side]] Anna will write in a day or two
[[upside down top of page]]
P.S. All send love. Please write me whether Albert can accommodate me. H.A.B.

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription: I do not think, I shall go home now, until Sept., as I want to do a little more at Leonard's and shall be here, now, till past the middle of Aug. Found the house needed repairs both inside and out, and I have had to use strength and money to put things in decent order. William has not sent me my Spr. allowance, and I suppose will not, until I get home, and, of course, having to spend so much, runs one short of money. Could Albert send me fifty dollars or so, to be replaced, when I get home? To secure him, I will send him a note of his own, to hold, until the money is send back with, perhaps an addition, as the Oct.

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription: allowance will come  very soon after I get home. I do not care for the money from Albert until Sept. as I expect some, from Margaret, for rent, to-day or tomorrow. I am very well and think with all the hard work, I have gained steadily in strength. Went to the Park on the Fourth and to the reception at Mr. Bowen's the evening previous, and had a very enjoyable time. Your Aunt Pamela is about as usual. She wished you were here, to visit with Anna and the rest of us. When are you going to Waterloo? I think a change will do you good. Anna seemed well and very cheerful. Your Uncle Leonard is fully as well as usual, I guess.

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Love to All

or was on Saturday night when I left there. He met Anna at Quinebaug, and brought her to his house, and then we both came here. We hope to make Anna enjoy her vacation. After her return to Boston, Mrs. Dean and Mrs. Carpenter will go to the sea-shore, for a week or more, and I will [[underlines]] keep the house for the cats, if they wish, [[underline ends]] and then stay at Leonard's a week or two longer, and then I think, I will go home. Will stop a day or two in Boston, with Anna, then go on and stop at Sycamore to see the Cemetery and will stay a few days with you and get home in Sept., I guess
Yours affcly H. A. Bailey

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
10
East Woodstock Conn. June 24th
Dear Mary,
Yours containing the intelligence of Dean's death, came to Pamelia last Monday, and she, at the time, being in the midst of her painting and papering, sent the letter to me, at Leonard's, thinking I would write you immediately, but it lay in the office there so I did not receive it until yesterday. Thus much, for our seeming neglect. We sympathize with you, in your affliction as we always have in his trouble, but that the poor little suffering body is at rest makes us feel

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription: that we can, easily, say from the heart Thy will be done. I feel as I did, of Ezra and of Louisa, there was nothing but suffering in store and it was a mercy to them, when it was ended. I have thought of you often and wondered how your strength held out with the demands upon it, but now, when the care is removed, do you not feel as if you could not go another step? Still there are other cares, to occupy time and strength. I hope you will not find that you are all worn out. Now there is time to think of yourself. It does seem sad, that of the few friends you have, all were too far away to come

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription: to you at the time of your affliction, but I know there are friends not allied by ties of blood, who could be there to help and to sympathize. I have been at Leonard's most of the time, since early May, and come back here, this A. M. to abide until after Fourth of July, and then I do not know, whether I shall stay two or three weeks there again, or start home. Leonard and Pamelia have both urged me to stay a little longer, now, that it is a pleasant season to go about, I am vain enough to think I have done something to improve his home, and he said, yesterday he never expected his

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
home or clothes to be fixed up again, as they now are If I stay there longer, I shall do more still. If Anna could have her vacation in time, I would like to wait, until she comes here and could visit with her, better than I can in her business hours. I will write her soon. I am well and growing fleshy. All send love to you and much sympathy.
Love to all
Yours affectionately
H.A. Bailey

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Sabbath Day March 27 1864
My dear Niece, (Mary Jane
Last evening I re'd a letter from you of March 11 and one from Rev Phinehas Bond who lives & preaches the Gospel
in Jay, where my dear Sister [[Fuller?]] lived and died--& he is a faithfull labourer, lost 1 of his 3 army Sons by sickness some time since & wants me to see to grave stones for him.
On Mond last I entered by 91st year, in as comfortable health as I dare ask for, & as poor as any of my friends could wish from a Misfortune at the close of my business likely by mismanagement of them when too old to do business myself. But I have long hoped I had a "treasure in Heaven" of which none can ever deprive me, and that is my condition, 50 years since my conversion

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
I believe I have but 6 of my Nieces living and they are well stricken in years probabably all over 60 years--in 1847 I had 12 in all Decr 15--but you are one grade later.
I am not certain that I have over 4 or 5! Some doubt on my mind & so I have had you & those of your grad for pleasant correspondents this far Mary B Homer of your Grade is one of those left Bri.  A well trained Physician in Holyoke Seminary MD to her name of Uncle Williams grade, a pleasant correspondent & you can take my place as I am going Home!
340 or 246 not certain, one part of the time You that are well educated ought to keep good our good line Tell her if you please that I wanted you to take & fill up my place as I was expecting to go home a long Sarah & Bond a School teacher in Jay Maine is another pleasant friend of mine & correspondent daughter of Rev Phinehas Bond in Jay Maine

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Dont forget My friends but write them & help to keep up the chain at least so far as I have done up to 90 years. -- I am now looking out for a letter from my Son Elias & hope not to learn that he has lost his Wife, as I have some reason to hear --His good mute Son doing well at the Hartford Seminary & I have rec 5 or 6 letters from him Man 100, Conn & Maine 50 each when I heard the number, and a first rate Institution as to be Manager & Instructor [[?]] has made good improvment & will doubtless make a [[?]] [[?]]  man
He has a fine family growing up & doing first rate in Education with all as fast as they are ready for good efficient School teachers 
I shall aim to tell you of my Son & Wife "If the Lord will" if I get his letter soon to relieve your mind 
My Love to your Mother & family Uncle

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Tell them all I am going up to see that Long and Beloved Sister of mine when'er the Summons comes to me saying "Your work below is done and you must come up & see a Host of departed friends"-- No man here so old as I am by about 13 months the next in our Village almos 7 years younger! One Woman 93 in June next & in good health I believe.
Oh the solemn thot of having lived 5 years with no relative here to call in Socially & spend an hour with me since I have done with my business & Society. Not one of the most prominent complaints of aged men so common to be felt!
Competent to every known duty! 
[[I kept?]] in about home some weeks to avoid all th cold winds as one an able Physician cautioned me to do - and live on nourishing food
Such now is what 90 years will do
I remain very Aff your
friend & relative E Bond
Dont forget my love to all friends

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Hallowell Wed March 21 1849
My Dear Niece, 
As I descend the rate of years you are no doubt meditating occasionally when the time when you are to hear that the last has fallen! On the 14th Inst I entered upon my 76th year, and yet I am enabled to write tolerably strait & plain for one of my age for so it is generally acknowledged, & here I stand as a monument of spared mercy far along on the 27th year beyond all of a large family except your dear Mother who has been gone home almost 5 years & 10 months, and I am still left to make my way alone in one sense, but Oh! how unexpected has been the ways of Providence to us all at such a dispensation, but so it is among us and I am almost as much surprised at your age & your Brothers as at my own, to think how you & he have followed so hard after me, and he but about 8 years short of my age.  11 days short of that! Where is he and how is his health and family? I think he lives in Dartmouth Mass--is it not so? --let me know all when you answer this letter if you please, as I wish to hear.
I recd a Paper which gave me the acct of the death of my last Brothers Widow very suddenly at Brimfield aged 79. I wrote her a letter & sent a paper printed here in wh it was inserted. But I learn nothing further. Four Brothers & their Widows all gone & left me alone! What a situation I stand in! but one more arrow to fly all all gone forever from this vale of tears! and what a gloomy thot with out they all had a [[?]] of grace in th heart

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
But to those prepared what a Glorious thot!
It has been a consoling thot to me that atho gone I could think of so many in our time who were pious I will perchance and all others we can leave in the hand of God, knowing that He will do no injustice, no not the least. You have had your trials and afflictions and I have had mine and we have been spared to survive them all as dealt out to us as Infinite wisdom has seen most for our good perhaps-- tho we cannot see the why or wherefore--
His ways are equal but not ours--& He might say to us as to one of old, "What I do thou knowest not now, but thou shall know hereafter" -- It was hard work for me to give all up & become a boarder after more than 40 years of housekeeping, but I have seen the hand of God in it many a time I can asure you & very impressively.
With my declining years I have found a burden rolled off from my mind and myself relieved very sensibly, and have been able to go & come with confidence that your Aunt was in good hands. After a pleasant year of boarding in a pious good family--On the 12 day of last May your Aunt went to Augusta to spend some time in the families of 2 of her connections, one of whom was an only tho a half Sister as we call them, as all the family here have been dead some years--dying at various times.
I went to my Son William's at the same time where I still remain, tho I go up & thence 2 or 3 days there continually. She has the Influenza badly but is now better.
I have spent about 6 or 7 days at Gardener since about the last of Jan. where my Son Franklin & Son were at work William's oldest Son Wm Mason also, his Cousin's name from Spencer

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
You will almost think of me like what is called "A Bird of passage" while about doing wh my 75th year, tho not common for my age, I keep along comfortably and oversee all money matters in my business and Wm takes care of the sales. I am doing a carefull prudent business but we are neither of us very modern, but I have now kept along 45 years in this village and outlived about 16 that selling concerns, and even now no one but myself keeps a full neat assortment but myself alone at 75! Wm entered his 51st year last month & is in comfortable health but far behind father in energy & activity after all. But all are like themselves, & I can move quick even now wherever [[creation?]] calls for it. Walked with Augusta and down again one week with a small exception of one short ride--about 2 miles where yr Aunt boards--with a Widow who has 2 little Sons--a very likely woman whose Husband run to ruin in about 6 months & died in Chicago - Wisconsin! and there lies far away from all friends! She is about   years old I believe a fine active woman and greatly esteemed and beloved in a general thing.
I expect yr Aunt will move her place a few rods to her half Sisters in all next month, but I know of no further move for me--permanently except to "The hour appointed for all the living"--and I feel the great necessity of being ready, with all my work done, & I only ask that I may be as well prepared as your dear Mother was.
That calm peaceful countenance seems so familiar even at this day of my life that I love to dwell upon the [[?]] and hope to meet her on Mt. Zion above! 
Oh! the Blissful thot! that I may hope to meet many friends there

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Wed March 20, While my letter has been delayed another from Cous Elias has reached me this day and very welcome, dates from Aug 22 untill Oct 6 Inclusive--as full of business as he can be and can see no relief from any quarter--so far as none seen--all is going on well & improving  for the good of his people there and a Blessing seems to nest on all his endeavors in doing good.
His health remained very good--and his move promising.
Mond Apr 2 Our [[?]] boat left for Boston for the season. [[?]] broke thro on the night of March 20, and I went wh to see yr Aunt next morn and found her but hourly improving--no chance to get out, but much depends on dry & favourable weather for her to move round.
I shall be pleased to hear from you and your Children & all friends and wish to be kindly remembered to Mrs Mason and family.
Oh! how I should find things changed were to be permitted to visit you again! But that you are well aware is all uncertain as my days are so near the close and altho in good health, I may fall to unexpectedly to you, no security against it.
Let your Children have a large share in my affections & their families     Your very aff friend & relative 
E Bond
When you write your Brother will you remember me very kindly to him & family. I intend writing when I hear from him thro your [[?]], wh I hope will be soon as I really wish to hear from you all once more. No word from Mrs Homer
Mr Elias Bond
from E. Bond uncle Woodstock
Mrs. Lucretia M Dean
Woodstock
Care of Mr. Leonard Dean

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Hallowell Tues Oct 15 1850

Dear Niece,

              Last evening I had the pleasure of receiving & reading your kind letter of the 10 Inst and thank you for the information it contains respecting my relatives and friends, tho I regret that your Brother enjoys so little health & has become so much broken down and feel surprised to read in the great Family Record that he is now more than [[underlined]] 60 1/2 years of age! not quite 8 years younger than myself! and with far less health it would seem I had forgotten that your daughter out west married a Clergyman, but I rejoice for her that she has such a man for her Companion in life. You see in (in regard to Grand Children than [[underlined]] myself - Wm has 2, Wm Mason who will be 20 Dec 1 --and Edward Emerson 17 last July. My son Franklin has one only child, a Son Wm Spencer who will be 21 [[underlined]] early in [[underlined]] April next --works in the Boston [[underlined]]City Printing Office in State Street No. 10, a promising young man. Hos father has [[underlined]] no family no settled home Your Cous Elias has a daughter, Ellen Mariner for her Mother, who is 9 years old. Born Sept 29.

The next a Son "George Shepard", named for our former Pastor, in whose Class he graduated in the Theo Sem at Bangor Sept 1840. "Elias Cornelius" whom you know so well as an agt for the ABC in whose service he died on his [[underlined]] hist journey in [[underlined]] [[ ?]] I think - & his name united mine with it. Those 2 Sons were both Born May 21 on the anniversary of the Parents landing on heathen shores while the annual Missy meeting was holding in 1841. They stood on the shore to bid them [[underlined]] welcome

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Born [[underlined]] just 2 years apart--perhaps 1844 & 45 so I think "Thomas Spencer" Born Feb 20 1849, so you will see they have [[underlined]] one majority at [[underlined]]Kohala, Island of Hawaii Sandwich Islands, & all healthy Children.

I am not without my fears in regard to the health of his Wife, who has more energy than constitution and I wait patiently to hear again, as she was not well June 10 his last date, and he was not without some [[underlined]] fear as to the state of her health, & no woman but th natives for many miles around them, so that you will see at once the critical situation he would be left in were she to fail, but I hope [[underlined]] not for she has been a [[underlined]] real Missy Wife to him and is an [[underlined]] excellent Mother  I hope I may hear before I send this, as our letters come thro the San Francisco Post Office latterly to us 

I have not room to give you his chequerd history but it has been very trying as well as deeply interesting, and I am glad you [[are?]] any out of his misfortune and the movement to rebuild his Chh. To be [[underlined]] 90 feet by 50--of one high story and all of [[underlined]] Stone, hoping to withstand the tremendous gales which prostrated his other noble house all in one common amt
Dec 21 1849 as you may have seen. Very [[underlined]] earnest appeals have been made in his behalf in some Religious papers as you may have seen. Over $200 had been entrusted By the accounts  we have seen in [[underlined]] our Christian Mirror in various plans by several Societies individuals & a [[underlined]] Christian sympathy His unfortunate situation went after having toiled 6 or 8 months on the other & expended 5 or $600 from his own means by hard pinching in his own means of living while it was building. But [[underlined]] after all, I rejoice that his faith in the precious promises of God is unwavering, tho at times so much shaken especially when he saw the Name of God all in ruins and not one place as to a building where they could assemble.

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
He says "We [[underlined]]will keep on trying untill the Day Star again were upon Zion" in our midst" Tho a darker day I never saw". Again he says "Justice & Judgment, I will know are the habitations of the Almighty's Throne, but Oh, the thick clouds & darkness which are now round about it! Yet however much my own heart may may despond, an [[underlined]] appearance of their full hope must be kept up, before our people. Should the [[underlined]] "Kumu" (missionary) be suspected of faint heartedness [[underlined]] not another stroke [[underlined]] would be struck in our work". Such is his situation all depends (under God) on his [[underlined]] cheerfully going a head.
During the sweeping sickness of Oct 48 to the close of 49,  400 of his people died, while but 80 were Born! Jan, Feb, & March but 100 deaths & but 40 Births, which shows how they are wasting away as a people as a Nation. About 1400 Chh members in good standing by the last amt I have seen reported of his Church.

I have been this particular as I concluded you would all feel a lively interest in such an [[?arduous??]] work as he has been engaged from June 26 1841 to this time. Who can wonder at the Christian sympathy felt for him under such circumstances, when he is so well known and his untiring diligence has not been out of sight, more of wh I could tell you did it become me [[underlined]] as a Father to speak or write of it, but I leave it here and just remark that unless Providentially called away from his present place of labour, he expects never to leave it, but to labour thro his days in that field.

The attachment is mutual & happy between him and his Chh, and they have [[underlined]] blead hard for him never to leave them. And when I think of the great change among them since he commenced the building the other Name of God I am fairly astonished. A large well clad audience in the place of [[underlined]] dirt & rags before him and sitting down in the [[underlined]] dirt without any floor!! Oh the change that God has wrought thro him as His instrument.

At the last anniversary of his Schools between 14 & 1500

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
all [[?]]--all well clad, some [[underlined]]richly so & nearly all tastfully so, and each of the 20 Schools had its own [[underlined]] Banner, took a circuit of about one mile & then all returned to the feast" where they had full enjoyment.

Now let us all for one moment that he arrived at his station over a mountain & among the clouds June 26 1841, & then descended to his new home where he arrived about 1/2 part of PM, in Co with Rev. Mr. [[?]], who spent 2 or 3 Sabbs. & preached & got him introduced so as to concurse a little by [[underlined]] signs only. Did not know [[underlined]] 6 words of the language when he entered there, and yet in [[underlined]] 3 months he could lead all his [[underlined]] meetings during the week, but not teach of course. 749 were added to the Chh in one year of the great Revival 300 of whom as the [[underlined]] first fruits of his labours [[underlined]]January first & 277 at the next quarterly Communion, blessed work!

God has indeed armed & blest his labours in His service and I feel the most [[underlined]] unshaken confidence the He will "Never leave him nor forsake him" but will sustain him [[underlined]] even unto the end in all his arduous labours

Think, Oh think what a self denying life a faithfull Missionary must live situated as he is, shut out from all truely civilised Society with any refinement.

We had an excellent young man ordained on Wed last. One who was Ordained  on Dec 6 1848 died Oct 29 1849 of Typhoid fever 20 years old, & a [[underlined]] choice man.

I am pleased to learn that you have one so worthy connected with your family-- a [[underlined]] rich blessing--and to learn that all your Children are doing so well in this "Vale of Tears". The Lord ever richly Bless them all as members of His Chh on Earth and prepare us all for a reunion beyond the [[?settings?]] of Jordan. 

I was laid by with Influenza about 2 weeks But am now comfortable again. 76 & 7 months [[underlined]] yesterday

My kindest & best wishes to all yr Children & friends Mrs Mason & daughter particularly, blessings upon you all

Your ever aff friend & relative E Bond

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
My dear Niece               Hallowell April 26 1824

Rev. Mr. Gillet our worthy Pastor being about to commence a Journey to your State to see his friends, and to pass through your Town where he has a Sister-(The widow Johnson) I could not well let the opportunity pass wholly unimproved as to writing.

I have lately written your good Mother, and am daily expecting an answer by private conveyance, & hope to hear that the friends there are well & happy

I was glad to hear that you had got into the [[underlined]] Ark of [[underlined]] safety, & embraced the Gospel of our Lord & Saviour

We have a Unitarian Society (small) and they have money, & are building a Meeting House, and have a [[underlined]] smooth pleasant preacher of Morality. But the [[underlined]] Truth will stand unmoved amidst all the changes & errors of this world, & shine [[underlined]] brighter & brighter untill [[underlined]] perfect day. We have a Congregational-a Baptist & a Methodist Society here, and these have united in a plan of good for nearly 15 Months, by a [[underlined]] Union Prayer Meeting which is held every other Tuesday Evening, and has been attended with a Blessing, as the LORD has evidently began a good work among all 3 of these Societies, which is deep, silent & solemn of late, and humbly hope that 50 persons are more or less awakened. 

In Winthrop, 6 miles from me, your Cousin Phinehas Bond has been preaching about 4 months to general acceptance, and a week ago yesterday, he was Baptized there, and 11 have been Baptized here. Baptists & Methodists by immersion of late, and the good work is going on in many places in our vicinity & State, and I know of nothing equally important to Souls destined to exist forever in Sorrow or joy inconceivable. 

Your Mother and myself being all that remains of our family, it gives occation for many solemn reflections as we believe that we also are far on the downhill of life, and bound ere long to our Eternal home, but I hope in at least some good measure prepared, tho so undeserving of it

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
We all need the comforts and consolations of Religion to
to support us under the trials, sorrows, disappointments
and afflictions of this life--but above all to prepare us for
the final Judgment, and the Glories of Heaven hereafter.

My family are as well as usual, & your Aunt Bond & her son aged about 6 years have been with us 4 months.

O! how numerous the changes & the deaths among our connections for about two years past. But such is this life. Nothing permanent but the Religion of Christ.

Remember us to all your family, tell them all to [[underlined]] seek Religion & become permanently happy for Time & Eternity.

If time admits [[underlined]] now, on on Mr. Gillits return, write us an answer to these few lines, & let us know how you are and your friends so far as you know. With many good wishes Mrs L Dean     

                                  Your affectionate Uncle E Bond

NB I am glad to learn from the Missionary Herald that your Town is somewhat engaged in the great concerns of the Christian world at this day, & it becomes us all to be up & doing while life & opportunity lasts. We collect annually about $10 in our Family Mission Box which we have now kept in our family for about 3 Years.


                        Mrs. Lucretia Dean

                                             Hillingly

Rev. E Gillet                                    Con.

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Hallowell Aug.t 2 1820
My dear Niece, I am sensible that this letter will be a very unexpected one to you - tho I hope not the less welcome - however unimportant in its contents - I feel desirous to embrace this very favourable opportunity of writing by a friend of mine about to travel that way, & I hope near your plan of residence. As you probably correspond with your Mother I presume you hear from us occasionally as to our family concerns and may therefore have learnt that in Oct 1818 we had a Son wounded on his head by a mischivous School Boy - by which means he became derang'd - & remind so with some intervals of reason for many months - from the first he kept but little food down - & for about a year eat but one regular meal each 24 hours & that he retained but a few minutes - for about 4 months he had been wasting away untill he became a mere skeleton - but owing to the derangment walkd about untill almost the last - was not confind to his bed a whole day and on the 4th of July rode about a mile the[[?]] had not rode for months. On Friday July 7 at half past nine Oclock he passd the great change which awaits us all - and died in the exercise of his reason without a struggle or a groan - & to him death seemed to have lost all its terrors - and his countenance was pleasant as the clear setting Sun and at the last he seemed to forget all his pains & sufferings which had been great & of long continuance. We calld him Joseph Davis and he was born Sept 27 1806 - and was a most affectionate as well as a beloved Child from his very early years. Altho he was young he was not unmindfull of the necessity of a seasonable preparation for the great change which he was evidently sensible for months awaited him - and we had many consoling evidences that he was (in his intervals of reason) endeavouring to prepare for the day of his death - & he lived a

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
bout two months longer than he or his friends expected - and people who saw him were astonished to see his life so protracted - & he so wasted away - he had ever been an attentive studious Child & made good improvement & perhaps we hoped too much in him - in such cases how often are all our anticipations of future satisfaction cut off in a moment least expected - which ought ever to teach us "To set our affections on things Above & not on things on on the Earth"  that we may be ever ready to say - "Not my will O Lord but thine be done". And then we view the lifeless remains of our dear Friends we can then say - "the Lord gave & the Lord hath taken away, and blessed be the name of the Lord". Seeing that life & all its enjoyments are so transitory how all important that we improve our present opportunity in a seasonable preparation for another and a better world - lest we should have to say at the last when it is too late "The harvest is past - the Summer is ended & I am not saved" - "Now is the accepted time and Now is the day of Salvation" and we are called upon in the most solemn manner by the word of GOD and also by His providences to improve the day of life that we may not be found unprepared at the last. Without vital Religion we can find nothing to support us amidst the cares the trials & afflictions of life _ in sickness and death nothing else will bear us up
I hope you have found this Pearl of great price - this "One thing Needfull" to smooth your way through this state of trial and probation. If you have you enjoy "that peace of mind which this world never gave and has not the power to take away" that Peace of mind which nothing destroys

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
I hope I have been a traveller in this path for seven years . and I can assure you that it is a most pleasant one - I had tried to make Morality answer as all sufficient but happily for me as well as your Aunt we were undeceived. Morality is indispensably necessary - but will never answer as a substitute for Religion - that Religion of the Heart which will smooth the rugged path of Life and make our way to Heaven safe and sure. It is a never failing source of comfort on a sick bed gives light joy & animation in death and uninterupted Bliss through the endless ages of a boundless Eternity.
For a few months past we have had a very unusual attention to Religion among us - for about three months we have had in our three Societies about 20 Religious meetings weekly - 13 have been added to our Church & 14 now stand propounded and 6 have joind the Baptist Church. The Methodist Society take them upon 6 month trial in their Class - and I do not know how many will eventually j[[oin?]] thi[[?]] Church - your Cousin George Bond who lives near me joind with us in June as did a number more of young people and most of them who are now propounded are young people - and appear to have been renewed by Divine Grace - so far as we are capable of judging from the best evidence we can get - the change is sensibly striking among many of our youth as well as others - and we hope that there will yet be a good addiction made to the Church of Christ before the end of the Revival and many are now seriously

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
concernd respecting those all important considerations that without a change from nature to Grace they can never be happy truly happy in time or Eternity. Let us then endeavour to improve our short space of life in such a manner as will give us peace in Death & a welcome to all the joys of the Paradise of GOD when life is done
we have a Son about 14 months old in a feeble way - the rest of our friends in our quarter are at least comfortable.
Accept for yourself & family our united love and best wishes for your happiness temporal and Eternal. Your Affectionate uncle
E Bond
Mrs L Dean

Mrs Lucretia Dean
Killingly
Conn

title: Dean family letters [1], 1779-1883
transcription:
Watertown November 15th 1802
Dear Friend
The first letter from an absent friend is sureley the most agreeable thing to amuse one in nature, you wrote you enjoyed health and happiness, such revived in me those pleasing remembrances which not only enlivned but expand the heart, the agreeable acquaintance I have had with you entices me to write to you hopping thereby to gain a correspondence with you in writing which if you believe me I am verry desireous of, I want verry much to see a letter from you and hope you will not omit the first opportunity I flatter my self with the pleasure of seeing you soon but I shall not unless you will take the trouble to come to see us
I must acquiese myself in being separated from the girl that I so much vallue and esteem, it has ben pretty sickly around here & there has several  small children died of the dysenterry in this town

[[?]]itty Bond

the clock has struck nine but I cannot delay writing any longer as so good an opportunity is presented for sending it. but I trust I am writing to one who is considerate enough to excuse an incorrect re[[?]] as I have 
no time for composition; we have all been in good health since grandman left Water....except Mr. F[[?]] he has ben  failing ever since and gets no help from any one, he has ben to one Mrs. Shaw in Boston which advertise in the newspaper for curing consumptions she cured one girl in Boston which was reduced to almost nothing, and since he found no relief from her he has ben very much discouraged and say he never expects to be any better, and it is though in general he never will see March out.

by her [[heart's?]] breaking inwardly the Doctor told her if she would undergo the operation of being cut open there was a chance for her life, but she said she had got to be old and thought it of no use as she would not live always if she did, thus we see the young and old cut off with some without a minuets warning, and others, with a long any lingering sickness; behold a young man in the prime of his life labouring under the distressing sickness which he bears with fortitude and patience and trusting in the mercy of him who made him that he shall recover but alas! no relief is found and he dispairs and sinks away.

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
Extract of a letter from the Secretary of War to Gov Blount—dated Department of War Mar. 23—95—
"These observations will furnish the answer to a third question—whether the Cherokees shall stop, & if not otherwise to be prevented, destroy any Creeks passing this their country on their way to the frontiers of the United States? Certainly not, if the United States are thereby to be involved in an open war with the Creeks; & such appears to be the tendency of the act of the Stallion and his party in killing the son of a beloved man of the Creeks & of your advice and direction thereon addressed to the Cherokee chief James Davidson, as this chief in his message delivered by Ecooe" at Tellico Blockhouse on the first of February declared his intention not to deliver up the Stallion to the Creeks, it was not necessary for you in your answer pointedly to avow the propriety of his determination and by your advice in any measure to commit the United States—
In your letter of the 20 Jan.y to General Robertson you considered the safety of the Chickasaws to depend, for a time, on the ignorance in which the Creeks would remain of the killing of five of their nation by the former: Yet on the 3d of february in your answer to James Davidson you mention the fact, and the celebration of it by the Scalp Dance at Nashville, and you desire Davidson to have your letter shown to Mr Dinsmore and read at the general meeting of the Cherokees
Ayer N. A. ms. 926

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
Cherokees at Ellijay, where Davidson, in his speech by Ecooe had told you a number of Creek Chiefs were to be present.
Why you should decisively pronounce a War inevitable between the Chickasaw & Creek Nations, as the consequence of the killing of the five Creeks as above mentioned, I cannot discern. That the Creeks should seek revenge would accord with Indian usages: but, a general War between the two Nations cannot be a necessary consequence, unless by a repetition of hostilities the Chickasaws choose to bring it on. In the case of the Creek killed by the Cherokees, your communications show that satisfaction was to be demanded by the Creek Chiefs, and if given by the delivery of the Stallion, the matter would end there; if the Stallion should not be given up, and the Creek Chiefs could not be persuaded to acquiesce in the reasons suggested by Davidson for the killing of the Creek, the death would probably be retaliated on some other Cherokee, and here also the matter would end. In this case, you do not intimate any expectations of a War, as necessary to follow between the Cherokees & Creeks; & yet you consider it so "precisely in point with that of the Chickasaws killing the five Creeks," that the Instructions from the Executive in one case will be your guide in the other.
The act of the Chickasaws in killing the five Creeks, you judged of such importance, and involving such consequences, as to render it your duty to forward the information thereof by express, yet in your letter of the 29 Jany. to the Bloody Fellow, John Watts and the other Chiefs & Warriors of the Cherokee Nation, after mentioning

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
mentioning the killing of the five Creeks by the Chickasaws, you add- "These are the proofs the Chickasaws give of their love for the people of the United States." Was not this saying - You Cherokee Chiefs and Warriors go & do likewise. -
In your letter of December 4th to General Robertson you express your opinion that Congress will order an army in the course of the ensuing Spring or Summer sufficient to humble if not destroy the Creek Nation, but the General has acted very unadvisedly in expressing & repeating the same opinion to the Chickasaws. They would take hold of the opinion which presented a prospect so gratifying to them as Warriors & the inveterate enemies of the Creeks but forget the caution with which it was accompanied. This opinion thus often uttered in the ears of the Chickasaws (possibly enforced by other like indirect encouragement) may have led them to commit an act which you have pronounced would certainly involve them into a War with the Creeks, in which if the Chickasaws should not be supported, you feared we should loose their friendship, & General Robertson supposes they would become our Enemies.-
Upon the whole Sir I cannot refrain from saying that the complexion of some of the transactions in the Southwestern Territory appears unfavourable to the Public Interests. It is plain that the United States are determined if possible to avoid a direct or indirect War with the Creeks. Congress alone are competent to decide upon an offensive War, and Congress have

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription: have not thought yet to authorize it. The acts of individuals and especially of public officers apparently tending to such an event ought not then to be silently overlooked.—

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
War Office August 28, 1795.
Sir
I delivered to Col. Hays a few hasty lines acknowledging the receipt of your letter of June 15th & a preceding one dated May 10th 1795; intending to answer more at large when I could find time. My object is to exhibit some facts and observations which may vindicate the General Government from reproaches which appear to me the offspring of prejudice and misinformation.
You assume it as a fact, that the Chickasaws' taking up arms and joining our troops against the Northern Indians rendered them obnoxious to the Creeks and has produced the present war between those two nations. Sir, I can discover nothing to give even a colour to such a conclusion. It is now four years since Piamingo with a few Chickasaw warriors joined General St Clair. It is as long since the Creeks have been murdering and committing depredations on Cumberland. It is three years since the Conference at Nashville when Genl. Pickens uttered the sentiment to which you refer - "We will always look upon it that your enemies are our enemies, and ours yours."
Now, Sir, if the trifling aid given to Genl. St Clair in 1791, was cause of war against the Chickasaws, why did the Creeks so long forbear to strike them? Are Indians so slow to take revenge

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
revenge, that for four years they can restrain their resentments? It is true some few Chickasaws have since been with General Wayne: but we hear of no Creek War against the Chickasaws until Major Wm. Colbert & his party killed five Creeks. This act Governor Blount pronounced would produce a Creek war: but perhaps it might not have taken place, had not the Chickasaws repeated their blow, and killed some time afterward, ten more Creeks. You think Governor Blount perfectly acquainted with Indian Affairs: I do not doubt it. You see above to what he ascribes the Creek war against the Chickasaws. I believe he never dreamed that the Creeks would commence this war because some small band of Chickasaws joined our forces against the remote northern tribes.
You think the Government of the U. States violate their treaty and promise because they do not aid the Chickasaws in their war with the Creeks. The "promise" refers to Genl. Pickens's speech above cited. Now let me ask, If the Chickasaws were to feel the blow which struck the United States, how has it happened that during two years and a half they did not feel the blows by which the Creeks destroyed the people and property of Mero District according

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
According to your construction of General Pickens's words, they ought to have been in arms against the Creeks from the day the Conference at Nashville was concluded. Thus, Sir, as they forbore doing this for near two years and a half, I may well conclude they did not think themselves bound to do it. In truth, it appears to have been, as my memory serves me, only a declaration on one side: the Chickasaws did not make a corresponding declaration on their part. But if the declaration had been reciprocal, I should then say, that on the part of the United States it was without authority. General Pickens was and is highly respected: but he was not empowered to enter into an alliance offensive & defensive with the Chickasaws: and such would, upon your construction, be the effect of his declaration.
The design of the Conference at Nashville was expressed in a letter from Genl. Knox to Governor Blount, March 31, 1792, in these words: "The President approves of the calling the Chickasaws & Choctaws to Nashville the fifth of June, for the purpose of conciliating & attaching them cordially to the interest of the United States." It had indeed been contemplated to invite a band of their warriors to join our army northwest of

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
of the Ohio, but the Conference not taking place til August, & our army not being likely to act offensively I do not observe one word said on this subject. Towards the close of the conference, Govr. Blount remarking to those Indians that they were the nearest neighbours of the Cumberland people, makes this request -- "I beg you to give them the earliest information of any hostile design you may know to be formed against them." Let me ask here, if Governor Blount had imagined Genl. Pickens's speech had imposed obligation of mutual aid in arms, that he would have contented himself with begging information? No,  he would have demanded that their warriors should in arms oppose such hostilities. But the Chickasaws did not even promise they would give the required information.
You suppose the United States are bound by treaty to aid the Chickasaws. Here, as in most other facts assumed, you are under a mistake. I will cite treaties, and draw the consequences.
At Hopewell in Jany. 1786, the Chickasaws acknowledged their tribes and towns "to be under the protection of the United States of America, and of no other sovereign whosoever."
At New York in Augt. 1790, the Creek Chiefs acknowledged all parts of the Creek nation within the limits of the United States, "to be under the protection of

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
of the United States of America, and of no other sovereign whosoever."
At the treaty of Holston, in July 1791, the Cherokees acknowledged their nation "to be under the protection of the United States of America, and of no other sovereign whosoever."
In like manner the Choctaws, at the treaty of Hopewell in January 1786, acknowledged their land withing the boundaries of the United States and their towns & tribes thereon, "to be under the protection of the United States of America, and of no other sovereign whosoever."
Here, Sir, you see that the four southern nations of Indians have, in precisely the same terms, put themselves under the protection of the United States. Two of them are now at war with each other. And from the terms of the treaties each has an equal right to demand protection. Suppose both should demand it: and suppose military aid given to both: it need not be observed that in such case we should not protect but destroy. This proves that the furnishing military aid was not the kind of protection intended in the treaties; and the words "of no other sovereign whomsoever" explains the design of our commissioners: these tribes or nations of Indians were not to put themselves & their country under the protection of any nation which

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
which, like ourselves, claimed a territorial title where Indians were the proprietors of the soil Accordingly the protection of the United States was confined to those parts of the Choctaw and Creek nations which were within the limits of the United States, leaving the parts of their countries southward of our south line to the Spaniards.
Thus we are not bound either by promise or treaty to join our warriors to the Chickasaws in making war against the Creeks.
With respect to the applications to the President to call out the militia or to allow them to turn out against the Creeks, the justification of his denial is extremely easy. Such a step must infallibly cause a general war between the United States and the Creek nation: and as the President has no authority to declare war, he certainly will sanction no measure that must necessarily produce it.
The General Government is not chargeable, as you intimate, or as your expressions imply, with a disregard to justice & sincerity towards the Indians; nor so absurd as to imagine them not entitled to the benefit of those virtues as well as civilized nations. But I have known people who by these practices & declarations do not deem Indians entitled to the common rights of humanity: but these people have

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
have lived very remote from the seat of government. It is because such people murder & plunder Indians whe[[&]]ever they can do it with present safety, that when a peace with an Indian tribe has been made, government find it so difficult to preserve it.
It is not the General Government that has done or countenanced any measures to lead the Chickasaws into their present difficulties; of course it cannot be charged with "deceiving and deserting them." I cannot account for the two attacks before mentioned of the Chickasaws upon the Creeks, by which fifteen of the latter were slain, but by supposing the Chickasaws to have been encouraged to do it by some people in the southwestern territory. I have before remarked that the Chickasaws lay still near two years and a half after the conference at Nashville, before they felt one of the blows which the Creeks had given the Cumberland inhabitants, whence it is clear that the Chickasaws did not think themselves under any obligation to take up arms in our defense. On this subject I had occasion to write Governor Blount in March last. An extract from my letter is inclosed. In that extract my opinion is too clearly manifested, not o be discerned. The Governor acknowledged the receipt of, and proposed to answer that letter: he has not yet done it. You have pronounced his

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
his [[?]]logium; while you reproach the Congress and the Executive Government of the Union. My animadversions are founded on the Governor's own communications; and in the present circumstances I feel no obligation to conceal them. When men in the highest offices in the territory, and men specially charged with the interests of the Indians, have so plainly encouraged the Chickasaws and Cherokees to strike the Creeks, am I not to suppose that some private individuals have been equally forward? With the Chickasaws the encouragements were effectual: the Cherokees were more cautious.
The inveteracy with which the Creeks committed depredations on Cumberland satisfied me that they had some latent claim to the land. I enquired of Mr. Seagrove, and his answer justifies my suspicion. The Creeks said their claims on those lands had never been extinguished. However, in a conference between Mr. Seagrove & a great number of their Chiefs last June at Savannah, the matter was discussed, and the Chiefs formally relinquished all their claims to the Cumberland lands, and engaged to live in peace & leave that settlement & all others of the United States unmolested. Since that time I believe the southwestern territory

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
territory has been quiet, and during eight or ten months past I do not recollect a single report of mischief done by the Creeks on the frontier of Georgia.
It is extremely unfortunate that Government can do no public act regarding the Chickasaws that is exempt from misrepresentation. How the proceedings at Nashville three years ago have been wrested I have already explained. When Opoiamingo was in Philadelphia last year, he described to the President the boundaries of the Chickasaw country, & desired protection. The President adopting Opoiamingo's own description signed a paper or parchment importing such a protection: but only against our own citizens: for immediately after declaring the Chickasaw country under the protection of the United States, the President adds: "And all persons, citizens of the United States, are hereby warned not to commit any injury, trespass or molestation whatever, on the persons, lands,  &c. of the said Indians." It has also been pretended, & I suppose the Chickasaws have been made to believe, that the President had

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
had guaranteed to the them their country as they themselves had described it. But no man of understanding, with fair views, could suppose and suggest that the President meant to decide the boundaries between the lands of different Indian nations; at least on the mere representation of only one of the parties.
At the same time the President gave commissions to a number of the Chickasaw Chiefs, and now it is said Major Wm. Colbert thought himself authorized by that commission to kill the Creeks. Yet the Commissions explicitly declare their object to be for the operations "against the hostile tribes northwest of the Ohio."
Have all these misrepresentations of the words and plain meaning of Government spring from accident, or from ignorance? or must we trace them to some other source?
Here, Sir, I will pause. It would take me more time than I can command to remark on all the passages in your letter which might be noticed. I have said enough to vindicate the government of the Union for its determinations in respect to the war between the Chickasaws and Creeks. If you are

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
are convinced, it will be in your power to remove or silence the complaints of others. You are an officer of government, and manifest a concern for its honour: you will then assist in its vindication from groundless aspersions. Aiming only to do good by displaying truths of some importance, I speak with freedom; regardless of personal consequences.
I am respectfully
Sir,
your obt. servant
Timothy Pickering

War Office March 23, 1795
Sir,
Your letters of January 10th and 22 were duly received. The completing of the building you call a Barrack for the purposes mentioned, will be desirable. But my experience in public teams which you think should be provided convinces me that they would only be a bill of Cost without adequate advantages; and now that the public goods would be transported  cheaper and at least as safe in private as in public teams. There may be the same check upon the fidelity of the waggoners as the private traders have; I mean by invoices and receipts.
You say the public arms want repairs. Is there no armourer to be obtained on the spot? Are tools and materials wanting? If you will give particular information in this matter, what is necessary shall be done. 
It will doubtless be useful to furnish you with the old invoices of Goods sent to Knoxville that they may be accounted for. They shall be collected and forwarded.
If the quantity of Cloathing which you mention as lying at W. Richardson's at Jonesboro be considerable, it would be well for you to go and examine it yourself: or if this be impracticable, to send some one to do it on whom you can depend; and if worth transporting to have it transported before it finally perishes-

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
War Office May 11, 1795.
Sir
I received your letter of March 23rd on the 21st of April. Having written fully on the subject of hostilities between the Chickasaws & Creeks, in my correspondence with Governor Blount, and anticipated your enquiries, it was not necessary again to answer them. I have no doubt that, as you intimate, those hostilities have been participated on the part of the Chickasaws by men who sought neither their true interests nor the interests of the United States. Governor Blount has been informed, that the United States cannot support the Chickasaws and I think satisfactory reasons have been given him for refusing it.
Money to pay the expenses m[[&]]ed the last year in the Southwestern territory, was forwarded by Mr. King of Knoxville, who left this soon after the departure of Major Evans.
I have not to inform you, the goods to

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription: to the amount of about three thousand dollars will go off this week (perhaps tomorrow) for Pittsburg, whench they will go with little delay down the Ohio and upon the Cumberland to Nashville, for supplying the Chickasaws, according to a voluntary promise made to their Chiefs who were last year in Philadelphia. To whom should they be delivered at Nashville, as the public storekeeper. The Secretary of the Treasury has formerly written to you about the storing and [[?]] Indian supplies in Knoxville. As far as circumstances will admit the likemode should be pursued at Nashville. But [[&]] whether the quantity of supplies will render it worth while to have a special storekeeper

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
storekeeper, who shall issue on the order of the superintendant, General Robertson? You will have teh means of knowing character there, will be able to determine. The superintendant for the Six Nations receives and issues himself all the supplies to the Indians. We have a perfect confidence in his integrity. The like supply to the amount of 3000 dollars is annually to be furnished for the Chickasaws.
I shall write you again on this subject; in the mean time you will think how the business may most properly be conducted; and consider this letter as confidential.
I am, Sir
with much esteem
your obt. servt.
T. Pickering
Colo. Henley

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
War Office May 29 1795.
Sir,
Five hundred dollars are now sent to Captain Richard, to begin the recruiting of his company. Should he be successful, & need further supplies before remittances can conveniently be made from hence, you will furnish him with the requisite sums. The recruiting service demands encouragement. You will have money to spare from other funds.
The accountant will advise you of the monies transmitted by your express, & of the various purposes to which they are to be applied.
I am, Sir,
your obt. servant
Timothy Pickering
Colo. David Henley

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
War Office July 22, 1795.
Sir,
I received your letter of the 4th of June by Captain Chisholm. In the course of my conversation with the Chickasaws and Choctaws, of which they have a copy, I have mentioned my opinion of the leading cause which induced them to kill the Creeks, who probably ere this time have retaliated the injuries done them. With sufficient plainness I last March manifested to Governor Blount my opinion on his own & General Robertson's management of Indian affairs. The Governor promised an answer to my pointed animadversions: but hitherto he has contented himself with the general profession of his having constantly endeavoured to promote the public welfare. I have no doubt of great abuses existing in the conduct of affairs in the Southwestern Territory: but the ceasing of the Creek depredations I hope will put an end to most of them. I wish however that you may not slacken your attention to discover and communicate them. Endeavour also to obtain facts and proofs of surveys of Indian lands -- if any are made.
Serjeant Brent I think has been formerly recommended: but no ensigns have been appointed of late, except four under special circumstances from the militia army. Captain

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
Captain Chisholm will receive two thousand five hundred dollars, to support the Indians now returning to Knoxville, and to pay for the transportation of their goods seven or eight waggon loads from Richmond to that place. For these expenditure he is to account with you, and any balance remaining, after charging his pay, at three dollars a day for himself & horse (exclusive of expenses) is to be paid to you.
I expect to forward herewith invoices of the goods now furnished to the Chickasaws & Choctaws but if I do not obtain them seasonably, I will send them by post.
I am, Sir,
with great regard
your obt. servt.
Timothy Pickering
Colo. David Henley

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
War Office July 23, 1795.
Sir,
I have heretofore informed you of the goods sent by the way of Pittsburg, in care of Anthony Foster of Mero District, for the annual allowance due to the Chickasaws. Unfortunately one of the waggons, tho' it started hence in good season, did not reach Pittsburg until Mr. Foster had sailed with the goods there arrived. What he received will appear by the copy of the invoice with his his receipt [[?]], now inclosed. Another paper will show what articles remain behind, about which directions will be given to have them transported to Nashville or Fort Massac. But seeing their arrival might be precarious, and the Chickasaws who were here desired a further supply, an additional small assortment has been provided, amounting, with the good and presents to individuals, to upwards of fifteen hundred dollars. The annuity to which they are entitled is three thousand dollars.
The President has also been pleased to make a handsome present to the Choctaws of the Five Upper Towns, amounting to about five thousand dollars, exclusive of the presents for particular Chiefs designated by the deputation, and which would make the whole value of the Choctaw presents rise to at least six thousand dollars.
Among other things, a set of tools for a blacksmith

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
blacksmith and gunsmith has been furnished for the Chickasaws, with some materials: but iron must be furnished to them by you at Knoxville. I have also promised that you should give a set of plough irons to James Kemp and another set to James Colbert the interpreter here with Kemp.
The Chickasaws were very solicitous to be furnished with a negro blacksmith: but it did not seem to me very likely that a good one, whose fidelity could be depended on, would be found. I therefore promised to request you to engage a faithful man at Knoxville to go for some months to the Chickasaw nation, to perfect in those costs (of the blacksmith & gunsmith for the ordinary purposes of the Indians) some man who Kemp said already knew how to handle such tools. This I must desire you to do, either now, or as soon as one can be found & the season and circumstances would render the measure most useful.
I am, Sir,
with great regard
your obt. servt.
Timothy Pickering
P.Sl By the Invoice receipted for by A. Foster will appear what goods he will have to deliver to your agent at Nashville.
Col. Henley

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
War Office Augt. 31 1795.
Sir,
I have just time to inclose you copies of the President's Talk & mine to Major William Colbert, and a copy of my letter to David Campbell, Esq. You may make such use of the whole as you think proper, to vindicate the United States from the virulent complaints of some people in your quarter.
I am yr. friend Genl.
Timothy Pickering
P.S. The copies of the two Talks are only sent to Gov. Blount
Colo. Henley

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
War Office Augt. 26, 1795.
Sir,
I received your letter by Colo. Hays. I have not time to enter into any detail. As soon as I can I will write you again. I have declined settling with Colo. Hays for his pay as muster master. He was very liberally paid before. I was much governed by his own information of the quantity & extent of his services. Since then they must, I conceive, have been greatly lessened. And as I know not what they are, I have referred him to you. There is no establishment for such service. It must therefore be regulated by the value of the service performed.
I found Major Colbert singularly difficult to please: perhaps because the President could not gratify his wishes in making open war against the Creeks. Besides cloathing him & his companions, I have agreed to furnish their families with cloathing, in like

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
like manner as Opoiamingo and his companions were gratified for their families: but as the Major & friends had no means of transporting the cloathing for their families, I agreed to have them supplied at Nashville. I have written Governor Blount on the subject; and you will execute his order.
The Governor will doubtless show you my letter to him about furnishing the Chickasaws with some provisions to save them from distress. Here also your agency will be necessary.
To grant his request and to soothe him under his great disappointment, I have given Major Colbert four hundred dollars to buy and elegant stallion: but he seemed to consider this sum as hardly sufficient. As I said before, it was not easy to please him.
In great haste your
friend & humble servant
Timothy Pickering
Col. Henley

title: Timothy Pickering letters, 1795-1798
transcription:
War Office Nov. 9, 1795
Sir
A quantity of goods has been provided for opening a trade with the Southern Indians. To the amount of 15,000 dollars, prime cost, will be sent to Knoxville; accompanied by a person who is to be the factor for the U. States in the sales & returns. I hope you will not have set out on your proposed journey to Philadelphia when this arrives: and in that case that you will remain at Knoxville until the factor & goods arrive, to make the necessary provision for commencing the business, and giving your advice to the factor. Your letter of the 26 Sept. has been received.
With the goods for trade, will be forwarded the Annuity in goods for the Cherokees

In what shape?

It told me I should raise the siege of Orleans, and that Robert de Baudricourt would give me people to conduct me. Twice he refused me, but the third time he received me, and sped me on my way, appointing me a knight, an esquire and four servants for ocmpany. He made them swear to take me safely; and when I left him, he said 'Go! and let what will come of it, come!'

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Hoopeston, Ills. Nov. 15, 1894.
Dear Miss Ruthrauff :-
We came home to no end of funerals (not my own family) - a home full of people (just got rid of the last) - and I have not yet sifted my bushel of mail. Part of it will have to wait until this manuscript is done. I work constantly. The first week my neighbors came in [[shoals?]] - they are so good to me. Now I am comparatively

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
undisturbed - except by distant cranks, one of whom had just written from Massachusetts that if he had the money he would come to visit me. "Had seen my picture in a book," and proposed on the strength of it! I never heard of the creature before. What queer human beings there are.
It is just about the hour you and I always went to your room for our talk. I shall go up with Hazel and sit on the side of her bed. We always make love, the baby and I. She is so well now.
I want to hear from you - and to see you. I put your [[great?] lovely picture on the piano. Hope you have been very well since I came away.

transcription:

We had a good voyage; really very warm the first three days. Only one day of rough weather. We went north of the banks. Reached quarantine Friday night, were befogged next morning in the bay, and didn't land until 11 o'clock. All this is stale news perhaps.
I wonder what that pension is like, in November weather. Is the house warm? And is dear Mademoiselle La Belle there? And does Madame Bellot continue to make the table lively? I feel that I did not [[?]] thank her for her kindness to me, and the many services she did for me at the very last. And Mademoiselle Lillie - I should like to

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
see her. But perhaps all the people I knew are gone.
I am getting down to work with satisfaction. It is comfortable to be shut in down here when one doesn't want to be interrupted.
You have probably had a thousand adventures since I came away. Relate them to me. There were lots of nice people in the Touraine, among them two really beautiful blonde women. But I didn't find anybody that I really would care for afterwards. - Do you know, I think your mountainous New York women crossed: her name was May - a strawberry face, white hair, and perfect dresses.
[[Goodnight?]], with love, always,
Mary H. Catherwood.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898

I am so sorry to hear about the operation Miss Mather is to undergo, and hope she is well through it by this time, and very comfortable. Please give her my very kindest regards and Hazel's love for herself and her brother. Her cheerful face is before me. It is such a blessed thing she has you to comfort her.
"Jeanne" is on the home stretch. I have refused invitations, been into the city but once (and all sorts of interesting people are coming and going, I hear. Miss Hosmer was there:) - and I have worked as never before in my life, from morning till midnight. Sometimes I think I shall perish of it, but I love it as my life, and look

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
forward to mournful loneliness when it is done. One night I fainted and tumbled out of my chair. Mr. Catherwood was fortunately near, but had never seen me faint before, and was frightened. He got me up to bed, and gave me a horrid dose of hot brandy and water. Since then when deadly exhaustion comes on I lie down and rest a bit.
We have piercing cold weather, ice and snow: zero weather. There has been much sleighing. I take vigorous walks every day to keep my health, and enjoy the cold. But a furnace heated home evenly warm all over is a comfort when one comes back from the cold plunge.
We are horrified over the sinking of the Elbe. Has

2
not the North German Lloyd been called the safest line of all? - and it has now furnished the most horrid shipwreck on record. I shall never feel quite safe on water again. The iron compartments used to be my abiding trust; but is seems they smash like pasteboard. I hope none of your friends were on that vessel. So far, I see no names I recognize.
You must tell me how your dear little singer, Miss Dodd, gets on. As for the old Baronne, I hope she will live to be a hundred, so we can come back to Madame Bellot's when next we cross. Give my warm regards to Madame and her family, and to Mademoiselle Lilli, and dear Mademoiselle La Belle, and Madam de Russi - all of them. Sometimes - if I

transcription:
were not so busy, I should be desperately homesick for Paris. How is it in the winter? It does seem that one could be very happy there - only I should want you for neighbor, and I should want to have letters to all the interesting people.
Did you ever meet Madame Juliet Adam? I wish you would tell me about her if you meet her: and the salon life - the literary life of Paris if you see much of it. My opinion is that you will see something of everything that is interesting, and in American slang, "Keep up with the procession."
Hazel is pretty busy with her school and music practice. I still read to her nearly an hour after she is in bed, and am under her thumb in every way: but she is such a truth-speaking fearless open

souled darling: I wouldn't have her different if she is tyrannical.
No special American news that I know of. I only glance at the papers in the evening.
Your picture stands on the piano where I can see it many times a day.
Do write me when you can.
With much love,
Mary H. Catherwood.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
