April [[20?]]
Dear Miss Ruthrauff:
Your letter was greatly enjoyed, but it found me in my last struggles with "Jeanne." I am now out of the strain, though I expect to have to go to New York to knock it into the heads of these men that I will have it begin in November. I can do more with them in half an hour's talk than in a dozen letters. Mr. Gilder told me the story moved him greatly.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Oh, how hard I have worked! Have great big gray hairs. Was in Memphis Tenn. from Monday until Thursday, meeting lots of very proud charming southern women at their own request. One woman sent me a bushel of flowers. Oh, how beautiful the roses and magnolias are there now!
Wish I could see you - very much. Poor Miss Mather! I hope she is better. What you told me astonished me. I could not have dreamed it. But how few people we know by mere superficial acquaintance. Everyone has his burden, but it does seem a pity that poor girl should have to bear such unkindness with her affliction.
Hazel rides like the wind on her new bicycle. She is growing remarkably.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
When I am in New York I shall wish you were there, for then I know I should see you.
At a function in Chicago next Tuesday eveing I am to "say something. Picture me trying to say something! Would rather sit down and have a cup of tea and hear more stories about Miss Hosmer or some other interesting person.
This is merely a note to let you know I am alive. Will write later. Meantime, write me. Regards to Madame Bellot and all the dear pension folks, I am so glad you have my own corner for me. Remember it is mine. I shall be very jealous of it and will not move out for anybody.
With dear love yours, Mary H. Catherwood.

Dear Miss Ruthrauff: -
Your letter just reached me, and I have at once written the note of introduction. Mr. Krehbiel is a hard worker, exceedingly busy, and as much in demand as a government official. I hope you can catch him with a little leisure. But you will know exactly

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898

I am so sorry you have trouble, and hope it will come out in sunshine. It is like you to interest [[Grundy?]] in this young pianist. I will certainly try to hear him in Chicago. Mr. Krehbiel can almost make or unmake him in New York. But Mr. Krehbiel is sincere as daylight. He will deal fairly. Your friend need have no fears concerning honest conscientious work.
I am correcting proofs for "Days of Jeanne d'Arc" in

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
the Century, also for little book with Houghton Mifflin's, going in with my Mackinac series for Harper, and up to my eyes in other things. It is the hardest worked winter I ever had. One week I went into the city, shut myself up at hotel with hired typewriter, and worked literally day and night finishing an important piece of work. Two thirds of the propositions made me I am obliged to reject. There is really nothing else so glorious on this earth as achievement. If I can do all I want to before I die - c'est assez. Did I tell you a lovely lunch was made for Sol Smith Russell and me (!) in January?
With love as always yours M. H. C.

Mackinac Island, Mich. 31 Aug. 1896.
Dear Miss Ruthrauff:
In my migration your last letter and address were lost. But I am going to chance it as I remember it: though you may be anywhere else this summer.
We came to the island the 9th of July, and shall go home next Sunday - the 6th of September. The summer has been almost the hottest ever known in the United States. But here in the sweet blue straits it is always cool - always heavenly. I have had to work, but enjoyed the social season, too. An island dinner at a swell cottage with great national officials and clear bright women, is something to remember.
How I should love to see you. I hope sometime we shall pass a long season together. The country winter is

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
again before me. I hope I shan't be kept in as I was last winter: shall be able to be more in Chicago. A great deal of work is before me. But Mr. Catherwood is much better.
Do give me news of yourself. You are always doing something interesting. I expect to hear of adventures when I hear from you.
Hazel is a tall child nearly twelve now. She revels in this island. And as there are children here from every part of the country she has playmates enough. A little steamer, a sail boat, and an ice boat here, are all named the "White Islander" for my story which you may remember.
My "Jeanne d'Arc" will be published this year.
You will hear about the presidential contest. We were in Chicago when Mr. Bryan was nominated, and he gave Hazel one of his badges. He is a relative of our intimate friends. But we are not silver democrats.
Don't forget me. With love
Your friend,
Mary H. Catherwood.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Hoopeston, Ills.
3 December, 1896.
Dear Miss Ruthrauff:-
I have certainly thought of you every day and dreamed of your unanswered letter by night, since receiving it. I was so glad you are in this country, but loath to attempt writing you until I had plenty of time. My dear, I shall

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
never have plenty of time. The work is piled ahead of me as never before, and I shall soon have proofs to read for two books. "Jeanne" is coming out in the Century soon - may be spring any month.
I want to say this - am in Chicago every other week this winter, Mr. Catherwood's health being so much better, and Hazel needing less attention as she grows older. If you come to Chicago you must also run down here to see me. The one servant menage - and that a raw young Swede -

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
may horrify you. But if I can stand it nine months in the year you ought to stand it while you can stay. We have poor service here. 
I have not been to any social affair lately. Have to sent regrets for Saturday for something at the Palmers'. I am working with all steam on, and keeping directly to the main track.
Write me when you can.
With love always, 
Mary H. Catherwood.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
20 May, 1897.
Dear Miss Ruthrauff: -
How sweet you are, to think of me when I am so driven with work that I stand almost helpless in the snowstorm of the mails! And how good your praise is!
I expect to spend the summer either at the Old Mission on Mackinac Island, or on the Atlantic coast, perhaps at Little Boar's Head, New Hampshire

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
(within two hours of Boston) - to be near libraries, in the latter case. I have to work, and if I make a contract for another book - the fifth on hand - must be within easy reach of historical authorities. Hazel always goes with me. Mr. Catherwood, after his two or three weeks' fishing at Brevoort Lake and in the Straits, comes back to his office work. Men always squirm if they are out of their office chairs a month at a time. 
At Little Boar's Head the two of us can have board for from $16 to $20 per week. It would be cheaper, of course, for a single person. I do wish

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
I could see you this summer. Have you any good place in view? I prefer being where refined people are but I cannot go in for a fashionable place. The Old Mission in Mackinac - O my Mackinac! I love it as the White Islander did! - is a happy go lucky old den, not half kept. But I love every timber in it: and the people who keep it [[?]] and bow down to every whim I express. I have been there four summers. 
Write, and let us plan for a meet if possible.
With love always. M. H. C.
Board at the Old Mission is $14 per week for one person.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Answered July 10th
Mackinac Island, Mich., June 28, 1897.
Dear Miss Ruthrauff: -
I had to pick up the family and [[reach?]] here from the heat, which was enormous. Shall be here all summer, except may have to be a week in New York on business. But won't if can arrange otherwise. I have so much work. Shipped my type-writing machine here, and shall turn out steadily.
If I come east, want so much to see you somewhere, if only for a run between stations on the train! Shall probably come and go over Michigan Central R. R.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
Write me when you can.
With much love always,
Mary H. Catherwood
It was nice of Mr. Collyer, and [[lovely?]] of Miss Ruthrauff to tell me!
Do tell me about Mr. Krehbiel. I don't understand.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Mackinac Island, Mich. July 13 1897.
Dear Miss Ruthrauff: -
I am sorry you are feeling the heat, but since you have been in that little town you have written me oftener, and I cannot help being glad you are where you remember me more.
But I do like the picture, and was so glad to have it. It is on the mantel in my room. You are certainly very handsome, and it is a great pleasure to me to see your kind brown eyes watching me. Thank you very much for sending it. I had such a dreadful time packing in the heat, the day before we

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
left home, that I forgot to put in photographs and many little things which I always bring to adorn my room.
We have been deliciously comfortable here, all through the dreadful heat reported south of us. I am now glad I did not go to Boar's Head. The tropic heat of our American summers kills me. This is the only place where I am sure of being cool. O how I love this shaggy island! The soldiers are now back at the fort, and the swell yachts are coming.
Mr. Catherwood is at Brevoort Lake fishing with a chum, and will return home on Friday.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
I have everything in train for a hard summer's work. A gentleman whom I have never seem - a literary man of New York City - is coming on the Great lake steamer Northwest, tomorrow - (via Buffalo) - to collaborate with me for two weeks. I dread this, as I know nothing about him except the commendations of other people, and that he is a gentleman. This fact reassures me, however, and I hope we shall do well together.
Hazel is very happy, is grown tall, and really pretty. She has a remarkably good figure.
I wish you were here. Whenever I come east I must see you. With much love yours -  M. H. C.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Mackinac Island, Mich., Aug. 23, 1897.
Dear Miss Ruthrauff: -
Your letter just at hand. I wish I could make a date in New York. But there is no urgent errand just now in business matters, and I am full-handed with matters at this side of the country.
We expect to start home about Sept. 1, stopping at Petoskey and Cross Village. Hazel is to be got ready for boarding-school by Sept. 22, and I do not know at this date whether our homestead is sold or not. I am all torn to pieces, Mr. Catherwood had his price offered him. He wrote me to wire him if

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
I objected. We have long foreseen we must make a change, and now Hazel is going to Chicago to school it seemed best for me to go with her; either take a flat or board. But to give up the home seems too terrible. When you have owned your homestead so many years it is like tearing the heart out. I did not wire. But am beginning to have nervous chills.
I don't know how it will turn out. Either way, it will be hard. I have so much work contracted it seems impossible to run a house. We shall have to be settled next month somehow.
With much love,
M. H. C.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Ottawa April 5th [187-]
Dear Madam,
I have read very carefully the pages of MSS which you have been so kind to intrust to me for perusal. Certainly, they are promising, & I cannot see in them any reason for the fears which seem to embarrass you. This fragment is the very reverse of a "failure" I am glad you see the advisability of generalising as much as possible. Some

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
years ago I followed my own advice in writing tales of Canadian life, & think I succeeded.
I shall read your book with much pleasure, & hope my friends will do the same. I shall see that my bookseller here has plenty of copies for sale.
In the meantime finish the work courageously, & let it float on the current in full confidence that it will be borne on safely & reach that destination which we all aim at - the harbour of success
Yours sincerely,
Jno. Geo. Bourinot
[Sir John George Bourinot (1836-1902)]

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Dear Mrs. Catherwood: It is so pleasant to have met you. I hope, and I am sure, that we shall always be famous friends. If you have not read all the little books I have published, please let me send you those which you have not. And as a guarantee of good faith I am forwarding to you by this mail two or three of your charming stories which I want you to autograph for me, please. I regard your Tonty as one of the most poetical tales I have ever read. The passage telling of the appearance of La Salle's ghost and the pathetic words uttered by the fleeting spirit are particularly fine. But it is too hot to tell even complimentary truths. Let me reserve to another time a recital of the many pretty things I have in store for you. I am, dear madam, yours most cordially,
Eugene Field.
Record office, Chicago, July 14, 1893.
I agree with you that the Congress was dreadfully stupid! There were too few westerners in the [[?]]ed-up.

Chicago, July the 24th 1893
Dear Mrs. Catherwood: With a gleam of reason - for I do have lucid spells - comes the humiliating recollection that I did not inclose stamps for the return of the books which I sent to you last week. I now hasten to make amends for that characteristic oversight on my part. Moreover, for the purpose of letting you know that I know wat a shameless demand I have made upon your availability and your time, I inclose a bit that appears in my column today. Dear madam, with the eloquent remark of the immortal Plato to the effect that 
[quotes a four-word phrase, possibly in Greek]
I am always yours most regardfully and sincerely, Eugene Field.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Dear Mrs. Catherwood: Thank you very much for the reply to Garland. It will evoke a roar from him, I am sure. I wish we could stir up Miss French into taking her pen in hand. I hate fighting, myself, but I like to see other people at it. I am sending you large paper copies of books of mine that are getting scarce. One I have autographed pretty freely and otherwise marred. These books are you due - I owe them to you for your courtesy in writing in the volumes I sent to Whoopstown. I am still your debtor for letting you fight that anti Christ, Hamlin Garland, single handed and alone, when, as all know, I am the champion Greco-Roman gladiator in this neck of the woods. When you come to Chicago again, please lunch with Mrs. Field and me at the club. With every cordial regard, dear madam, I am yours sincerely.
Eugene Field.
Chicago, July 31, 1893.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Dear Mrs. Catherwood: I thank you for your very cordial letter. Your visit to Mackinac will do you good. I have never been there, but I associate the place with nude half-breeds, and coon-skins, and tremendous expanses of clear water and clear sky: temperature away below zero. I am a survival of the reptilian age, my blood is cold and thin, and I am very shivery. I pine for the tropics. I want to live upon a red star when my life ends on this planet. It is pleasant to know that you like the books. Have you my Little Book of Profitable Tales? I am sorry that Garland made me appear so slangy in the August number of the McClure magazine. That is hardly fair: but I cannot expostulate, for Garland meant to do me a good turn. When I read that alleged interview, I recalled the immoral words of La Salle to his beloved protege. "Tonty," said he - I quote the free translation made by a linguistical neighbor for me: "Tonty, there is no fool like a - fool!"
We shall have that luncheon yet - you, Mrs. Field and I. And as for being good friends, sakes alive!
"If you love me as I love you,
No knife shall cut our love in two"!
Always cordially yours,
Eugene Field.
Chicago, August 14, 1893.

transcription:
Dear Mrs. Catherwood: Suppose you come to the Union League club on Wednesday and lunch quite informally with Mrs. Field. One o'clock would seem to be the best hour. I shall try to be there but for ten days past I have been down with bronchitis and it's a question whether I shall be able to frisk around very much this week. Are you really at a Dormitory? It must be very dreadful; the very sound of the name fills me with dread unspeakable.
Cordially yours,
Eugene Field.
Buena Park, Oct. 15th, 1893.
Tomorrow Mrs. Field and I will have been married twenty years.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Dear Mrs. Catherwood: I have been flat on my back with pneumonia ever since the party at Mrs. Conley's. Today I sat up for four minutes and cried to be put back to bed again. I had no idea I could get so weak. That bed quilt did me a heap of good. I had it spread over a screen at the foot of my bed for 24 hours and it made the whole room bright. I thank you ever so much for the beautiful gift. And little Hazel D. - I am delighted with her portraits and shall send her mine as soon as I get well and handsome again. No more platform business for me this season. As soon as I am able to travel, I am to go south for five months. Presumably, I shall go to California. I have written to brother Cable, canceling my eastern engagements with him and I have called off all my dates in the west. I shall send you my new book of tales in a week or two.
Cordially yours,
Eugene Field.
Buena Park, Ill., Nov. 12, 1893.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
Greenfield, Ind. Sept. 16 '79.
Dear Friends:
Seems like ages since I wrote you a letter - but its ages I've been engrossed with a thousand things that prevented. Everything about me is tangled - tangled - tangled. I'm all right myself, but my younger brother has been scandallously drunk for a square week, and I've been following him about the country for four days. He's anchored at last, thank God! - with a black eye varigated with green, cherry-color, and purple shades, and a face on him like a spoiled sponge. My other brother is growing well, I think, but is yet quite feeble and oftentimes discouraged over his slow recovery. The old promises for my brilliant future are still promising - they never let up on that, and I'm still believing as of old that I'm goin' to make it - Though just now I'm

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
considerably muddled with a complication of prospects. Of course I don't want to go on a newspaper if the lecture business will pan out, but would like to reserve even that in case the lecture shouldn't pan out as I am hoping. Its big work I'm doing now just staying straight, but you can bet your bottom dollar I'll do that though all things else go to pieces. - but I've sworn I wont dwell on the infernal topic so the dead must bury it right here and now!
By the ending of this week I hope to have ready for presentation the lecture - then somebody's got to suffer, and they shant dodge it. The probabillities are that should I read at Indianapolis it will be at the new Park Theater, which I understand will be the place, but its a venture, you know - fifty dollars for hall - to say nothing of advertising, Tra-la-la-la, etc.

My attention has just been called to a "personel" in the Journal, stating that a complimentary benefit will be [[?]]ed the Riley at Grand Opera House in the near future And now this letter must be put aside for business - The cold chills and hot flushes are sweeping over me as I write. It seems a great undertaking to me [[?]] - "Where shall we land?" I just take time to quote this poem for the [[Mittern?]], by Hester A. Benedict. There are some delectable touches in it

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [2], 1874-1898
transcription:
FOR MY SAKE.
Muttern mine, across the mountains, if you sleep or if you wake, Turn your face this way, I pray you, just a moment, for my sake; For the winds are going westward, led by spirits sweet and fair, And I've given them my kisses for the silver of your hair.
I have told them what to whisper in your ear and to your heart, Of the much my life has leaned to since we journeyed far apart; Of the storm and of the sunshine, beating here and blinding there; Of the roses and the rain; of the passion and the prayer.
But I think if I could find you by the lifting of my hand, All the burden I am bearing you would better understand; And it may be you could tell me, as none other tells me true, Why to-night my arms are empty - why my life is empty too.
So I'm calling, calling to you! And the night is calm and still; Can't you hear me crying, Muttern; hear and heed it if you will! I'm tired of this farce of life - the social mask I wear - Of the purple of the velvet that can cover only care.
And I want your arms to hold me as they held me long ago, Ere my head and heart were handled by the fingers of the snow; Want to lie and watch the sunrise, with the lilies of my face Changed to roses in the heaven of my long-lost resting place.
Ah, my life would lean to laughter from such recompense divine, For its mockery of manna - for its mockery of wine! But I cannot find your bosom, and you cannot hear my call; And another day is dawning in the old way: that is all.
Hester A. Benedict
How I hope those influential friends of mine in the city are awakened to the true sense of their obligations(?) to your long-suffering, but still hopeful
- [[Graygrole?]]
