transcription:
Newburgh, NY.
Monday_ Sept [1874?]
Dear Folks,
Please write to me. I have not had any letters yet: either home letters or forwarded letters. I do hope you are all well! How is the baby? Bless his little rosy face! I would love to see him & all of you. I hope you are having a good time. I love you all and think lots about you. Though I am having a splendid time. My [[Tenoroon?]] is lovely. I think she is the handsomest woman I ever saw, & so little and girlish! We took lunch at a restaurant this evening, then went out rowing on the river: - taking the swells of steamers and the ferry boats. No use trying to tell you how heavenly it is! And the pinky light in the mountains, and the red lamps slanting across the water, & boats, ships, schooners,

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
steamers &c! We haven't gone to the city yet. I ain't ready. Not my clothes! I don't think much about them - but am going to alter story before  I go. She wanted me to take "Old Gargoyle" out & send it to Atlantic Monthly, & not keep it in long story, so maybe I will. I'm writing with a quill now, as you observe. It is so much easier & plainer, and a change from steel & gold pens.
Went to church twice yesterday. She plays the organ and I love to hear her play it. Not rattlety-bang like some of those organists. But you say I'm partial! The church is very handsome, dark - with Gothic arches &c.
I thought of Auntie Hat rowing in the river this evening. Oh, I wish, dear you could come and see the Hudson and these mountains!
I wrote you on Saturday and hope you got it. Be sure to write: I am so anxious to hear from you all. How are Aunt Sade's?
They don't want me to come back, &

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Oh! I hate the thoughts of teaching. It looks as if I could make money enough writing - but I don't know. Everything is so cheap here. If weren't in debt would send you no end of things! Never mind!
Do you go riding yet, Aunt Nelly? And who has been there lately? O, I love you all, and you mustn't forget me - not [[Kirt?]] nor any of you forget me! Have you named the baby? - This town is the prettiest place I ever was in. It is all up & down nice forest trees, streets paved & boats & ships always passing by its feet. I'd love to live here forever, while I live on earth, that is!
Auntie, have you heard from Sister? I think of her so much; yet I don't know how to write to her. I could tell you a thousand things but must stop now. 
Mr. Catherwood, you mustn't forget what I told you, if you all got into scrapes, I'll come!
- Your loyal and affectionate "Jack." 
P.S. I'm going to send Aunt Harrie "Locke" with "Bilkinson" in it. Please keep it for me.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Newburgh N.Y. 
Sept. 22nd 1874
Dear Aunt Harriet:
I have written to you, to Aunt Nellie, to Mr. C. & sent a book to Aunt Nellie & a Magazine to you! and I receive no acknowledgement, no word nor message of any kind - not even a printed circular to say you were well. 
I waited anxiously for a reply from Mr. C. concerning the school for if it could not be satisfactorily arranged, I intended

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
starting back soon to keep my promise with regard to it. But, of course, now I have given up all thought of coming into a family that can't give me a good word in a month: and even couldn't enclose a card in the one letter forwarded, when time was taken to open it! I don't understand it at all, but I don't meant to fret anymore. Have no business at hands yet, but keep writing. It is not all gaiety & fun as you may imagine.
But I wish you would do this one thing for me. I want to make a collection of certain 10 sketches & have no copies of "Perkins" and "[[Bangs?]]

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
In my old trunk among the Magazines you will find two "Locke's Monthlys" - with these two sketches - "Sorrows of H. J. Perkins" & "Man Who Hadn't Time."
If you will put up with them the last Locke I sent you with "Bilkinson" in it, you will greatly oblige me. Please do this at once if at all.
Hope you are well. No use to ask how the baby is, nor its name, nor anything I want to know! -
Address Box 909-
Truly and grievedly - 
Mary

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Newburgh, N.Y., Oct. 7th 1874
Dear Aunt Harrie:
Your letter just rec'd. It is not necessary to say I was astonished - I was delighted! It is was a dear, nice letter, and showed me so much of what was going on there at "home!" - So Lillie is really going to Hoopeston, after all? I am glad. Charge her not to forget to write to me. I don't think it will hurt her to write to that bean of hers. A girl must have a lover, and if she is frank and childlike as Lillie is naturally, the lover will be a good friend.
Tell my boys - bless them! - and [[Tutie?]], to surely write to Cousin Mary. I love them all so!
It was nice of you not to fly up at my indignat, grieved letter.
Did Aunt Nellie tell you my "Woman In Armor" is going to be published in a serial in "Hearth & Home?" Wish you'd get up a club for the paper then, & be sure and let publisher know you want the paper on account of that story!!
I began another little book yesterday but don't tell anybody! - Haven't had much encouragement in

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
short sketches since came here. I'm wanting to get into active, editorial work - and so is [[Tenoroon?]]. She is very sweet and beautiful. I love her dearly. 
She has a friend - correspondent of N.Y. Herald - in N.Y. City, who is trying to get work for us in papers or Mags then. He put a long advertisement in the Herald today. Indeed we've got to get into business soon, for editors don't pay promptly for what they do use, and our resources are running low! I'd love to go to the City tho' the Hudson & this place are so exquisite. If can spare the stamp am going to send you a little pamphlet about the Hudson River. My new book - story is going to be partly located in the River I'd like to send you Drake's "Culprit Fay" - (remember the biographical sketch of him in September Harper?) - for it is descriptive of C[[?]]ect, the mountain in sight of me as I write.
I sent a cheque of $22 to Mr. Catherwood last week - Oct. 1st. My $15 cheque hasn't arrived - nor Locke's. Be sure always to put Box 909 on letters & papers - otherwise I may not get them - will write at once if any changes - either of base or prospects, takes place. I am not making money - & you know, I must do that. Bless the baby: I dreamed of him last night. Do call him Karl. Please write soon. Love to all. Tell [[Kirt?]] I haven't forgotten the dog.
Your affectionate - Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription: P. S. Hi! good for corn! I wish I'd put my whole two hundred into it - don't I! - will send the rest of my money for the $40 soon as possible - Going to include a note to Mr. C. on corn matters.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Newburgh - N. Y.
Friday, April 23rd 1875.
Dear Aunt Harrie:
Your letter enclosing Rob Karl's picture, received yesterday. He is a dear boy - he was much admired when I handed him around. I think he has grown to be a stylish looking baby. Thank Aunt Nellie for the photo, many times, and not the less for putting "Benjamin to Joseph"  in it. That touched me.
I feel in great trouble. I wrote to Mr. Catherwood this morning. Now, I tell you this pulling up and moving every few months is just killing me. And I've been interrupted at my writing (lately) during the day, and forced to write at night. And publishers don't pay, and my new story is retarded by my feeling so distressed.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Aunt Harrie, I have made up my mind this afternoon (if 'tis Friday) I an't going to be pulled around the world any longer, nor tied to other women's caprices. [[Tenoroon?]] is a woman - not a saint. She's very sweet & charming, but pretty soon she may marry, and then after growing to her long enough to feel her my family, I'll be out with a wrench! You know how that is. This pulling up to start for Cincinnati has taught me a great deal.
I have a new plan in my head. Since you told me you don't want to marry, and don't mean to, I want you to think this over, and answer quick. If I go to Cincinnati I don't think I shall stay - I want my own home somewhere. I want to take a cheap flat or a [[?]] [[rent?]] or even 3 or 4 pleasant rooms in New York; and let's you & I keep house together. We could do it cheap if

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
we just learn the ropes; live within our incomes, and be perfectly independent. After I am out of that wicked debt, I shall sail. - And, Auntie, I have a dear Boy down Connecticut. I haven't seen him yet - except his picture- and he's younger than I and I mustn't like him too well. But he's howling to see me - and he is a dear fellow - I think his first name is "Edwin Ruthven." He says he loves me best. I don't believe him but I want to see him - and I don't want to go away from New York.
Aunt Harrie, say you will try to come and make a home with me in the big city. The Cary sisters got on. I have a good hold on the public - I can certainly get on, and you could teach me to economize. Think of it, and write at once. Please do. And we'll plan for it. 
Love to al,
Your Mary
P.S. Don't forsake me!

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
[1875?]
Cincinnati - O -
Sunday evening -
At Kepplers - 4th St.
Dear Aunt Harrie: I suppose you received my letter and did your usual amount of meditating without replying. So I'll "have at you again!" We arrived here, on Friday evening after a very weary journey, I half sea-sick all the way: we came by the Pennsylvania Central - as rough a route as I ever passed over: but the sleeping-berths always make me vomit anyway! The Great Jubilee is just over here, but the city is still decorated with flags. I am still tired, and we have been unsuccessfully hunting boarding for a day or so. I tell you I am sick of jamming round - "too much is plenty," you know - and I want this week as I never wanted in my life, my own - own home. I don't want to be hauled around and stared at, you remember the suggestion I made you in my other letter. Don't you think you would like to take to take Tute and come, by and by, with me and set up household gods in New York City?

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
you see I couldn't do it alone - you being a widow would give the right "tone" to the establishment!! You could financier, too, which I can't, I can make the money. We'd begin very modestly. - By the way, Mr. O'Laughlin - one of my Editors - says I mustn't come to the city to live - I shall have my "society courted" &c and so be interrupted at my work. He thinks I have a "very original genius" and it is "quite within my power to make a wide and brilliant reputation!!" But we'd have Thursday receptions - and keep such folks as wanted to "call" &c out the rest of the week. I would write hard & gloriously. Now I am so kept from work and worried that I shall probably [[lose?]] that money Uncle promised because I had to find money for extra expenses and postpone finishing my novel. It seems very hard, but I won't grumble. I'll

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
do my best and will maybe accomplish it! However I know I could do more & better work in a home of my own & I might as well have that home in a literary center. You would like New York: it isn't as expensive as Cincinnati. I know very few persons there, but the city is easily learned. You and Tute would find endless amusement while I scribbled. If my "Woman, In Armor" sells well, I can afford it soon: but if it doesn't I shall have to write the harder and wait longer. Say, Auntie, wouldn't you like it you could have Tute - and she could go to the great Public Schools - Aunt Sade would let her go with you - wouldn't she? - You never found me a very bad child - did you? I think we could manage.
I don't mean to get married, but I want my home, - Oh, by the way, my Boy I told you of - came up from Danbury to see me at the Stevens House in New York, Guess I will enclose his picture and make him send me another. Don't show it except to

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
4
Rob Karl & mamma, I didn't look at him much when I saw him - I was so worried. He is ugly - but smart as a steel-trap. He runs the News & [[bosses?]] the office when Bailey is absent. I will cut off a corner of one of his letters to let you see what a loving-hearted little rat he is. He thinks I'm engaged to him - but I ain't, I won't be tied - and he's younger than I - but I do like his love & his letters. He writes me every day - and sometimes twice a day, and tells me every time he speaks to another girl.
He has given me the name of "Mary-Gold," I'm not fond of the flower, but I do like the name!!!! He's going to send me Aldrich's poems pretty soon. I remember when I saw him I though he was just a country boy (or young man - he loves to be called "Boy") but he was nicely dressed & carried himself in good style. He is just awful in love: if I didn't like him I'd think it was wicked, But I do like him - and will be

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
5
more to him than the common girls in Danbury - though I can never - of course - marry him. Probably he'll get over it soon: & perhaps if I have him around me every day he'd be a nuisance. But he does get up the nicest letters I ever say! Keep all this within the triangle formed by
Aunt [[Nim?]]
Aunt Hat
Rob Karl
[sketch of a triangle with names at each angle]
I needn't have gotten into that scrape about money if it hadn't been for getting up & dusting. Oh, if somebody would financier for me! I have a regular salary of $25 per month - besides my serial income when that is running - and 'miscellaneous" catches. Locke will pay me $40 or $45 soon in 3 installments for short continued story I sent them. Oh, I could make money, I tell you - in my own home!

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
[[Tenoroon?]] is sitting near me writing home. She begins work tomorrow in "Golden Hours" for Hitchcock & Walden, I can't begin work till we get settled: will have to spend time hunting board. This is a very expensive place.
Love to all of you. Write me here very soon. Better address in care of Grand Hotel. We went there first but had to come here - no room - the Jubilee crowd. Get your pencil and scribble me a word. I give you a good long to meditate for I can't leave here probably before the summer is over - and, I want at least to know if you think you would like to try home life in Babel.
Kisses for Rob Karl, & all, I am tired: I haven't written a pretty letter, but I send love in it. Your affectionate
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
125 John St. Cincinnati.
Saturday. Oct 2nd[1875]
Dear Aunt Harrie: -
(Excuse this paper - I am rather "out of pocket" just now.) I wish we could have a good long talk. How is Robbie? I am so troubled about him. - I have often wondered what you thought about my New York plan. I was so nice. But alas! I can't go now. Butterick's can only pay me forty $ per month now for awhile. But I know if things go successfully I shall have chief oer there by and by. My "Toadstools" are a nice success. - We have taken 2 rooms in a pleasant house on John St.: parlor & bedroom. Both large and pleasantly furnished. Think we can live on about $6 pr. wk. each. Board at Hunt's restaurant. We pay $25 pr. month rent; enything is due for us: don't build fires or anything. It saves time. Locality splendid - just off Fourth St. I think I can work splendidly here this winter - and I shall have to! - Do you know - don't tell! - I've been sitting an hour and wondering how on earth I'm going to hit - a cloak! - before cold weather comes for sure!! I went without last winter, and it would be too cruel to freeze again!! I have just Butterick's for sure now. The miscellaneous cheques are too slow to count on.
Uncle asked me to "wait" - or "loan that sum to him till times were brighter." Do you know it seems sometimes - such as the present for instance, when I do want my cloak so bad - as if I was always working hard

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
and earning money - and never getting it!! - There's no use thinking about it, however - don't think I'm grumbling or discouraged! I ain't! I'm like a lark! jolly and cheerful and rushing all the time! Wrote two stories tis week - but shan't get the money till December: - I don't care a speck for money so I get enything I owed paid - it's only when the pinch comes that I think about it this way! And Auntie, Mr. Kerr did not sign over my Insurance Policy to me. I asked him twice. And now he has softening of the brain, and is probably unable to attend to anything. I am so sorry for him. But I think it would only have been the thing if he had signed it over when he sent my receipt in full to me. I had to pay the dues all the same. - Oh, dear! I get tired of such things! As Osborne says, Men are lazy and selfish - always excepting Mr. C. who, Aunt Nellie, and you, have been my best friends.
I believe I will put in a leaf out of Eddie's last letter. Poor little fellow! He's out of position yet. You must return it, as I shall have to keep his letters intact for fear we have a tear-up, and return epistles &c &c. Besides, that will insure your writing!!!! He has awful hard luck. And I am as good to him as I can be, to keep him cheerful.
I work just as hard as I can all the time. Keep my "Toadstools" always 3 wks. ahead of publication, and have generally 3 stories in my head at once - (ahem! with a [[basement?]] of consideration on finances!!)
There! I feel "g[[?]der" as if I had set down on the floor by you and told you what troubled me! I'll e'en scratch away now, on "Toadstools."

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
But first: I want to go and see [[Mosby?]] soon. I dream about him. I can't get any letters from there, and if seems as if he were growing a man - stranger to me! - I'll certainly go this Fall or Christmas. Getting out of money tangles was all that kept me from going before. How are Aunt Sade & Mr. [[??]]zet and my youngsters? Does Tute see herself in "Toadstools?"
Do write & tell me all. If I do have a little house of my own you have got to come & live with me.
- Oh, say, Aunt Harrie! would you mind packing my picture - have I more than that little cross - I forget, and sending it to me? Wrap the frame lots, so it won't get scratched. [[?]]ges at this and the route. We are "keeping house," you know & want our [[traps?]] I wonder if I have any books there? - I am making Christmas presents of evenings, when we girls get together. (Girl! This old lady is nearing her 28th - do you realize it!!! yet that little blessed Boy calls me "Baby Goldie!!")
Oh, you darling Aunt Hat! If I get "forehanded" this winter, you shall come and make me a little visit. Wouldn't you?? And you shall have a good time!
Don't forget the picture, please. I could talk to you folks all day if there wasn't work calling me!
With lots of love - arm-loads of it -
Mary.
P.S. Maybe the little cross had better be packed between their boards or pasteboard. I will thank you so much if you can send it. Maybe will have to sent for my old trunk next time I move!

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Monday Jan. 31st 1876.
Dear Aunt Harrie: -
Your good little note was rec'd. I was so glad to hear about the baby, and wish I could see you all - so much. I would have had something pretty to send the girl, but she must wait a little. I have made up my mind what to make for her, and as soon as I have time & some spare change, she shall have it.
I am glad Aunt Nellie is getting along nicely. I think the Lord must love her or He wouldn't take so much pains to give her a nice family. He must love you too, or the children wouldn't be so fond of you as they are.
I just got your note on Saturday. You see I am answering soon.
Now about the loan you so kindly offer, Aunt Harrie, I think more of your

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription: letter and of the good, comforting love in it than I can tell. I shall always remember and appreciate it; but I do not feel as if I could take the loan. I keep working away, and times may look up brighter. I wear old clothes, and get my boots patched, and put on everything to look as well as I can. I have met my half of the rent promptly, and with skilful managing have got along so far. With all its ups and downs, it's better than teaching, and you'll see me come out all right if I live. But I tell you there'll be a revolution among authors before long. Publishers have skinned them about long enough. No, dearie, I don't want to borrow any more, but I kiss may times the hand that offers. I suppose HC thinks I'm dreadfully slow with that other, but I'm doing the best I can. All kinds of literary work is at a standstill now. Wm F. Gill & Co of Boston (Gail Hamilton's last publisher) has failed. The Overland Monthly & Oliver Optics Mag. are dead. Publishers are issuing no books except what

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
went into press at the holidays. But I suppose you know all these things.
T. De Witt Dalmage lectured here not long since. I had lots of tickets offered to me, but declined going. - The weather is lovely, but I am writing in a little dark den of a room. Guess we shall look for lighter rooms soon. Cincinnati is in a hollow. People in Mt. Auburn want us to come up there. Did you know the name Hartwell is well known here. One of the suburbs is named Hartwell, and named for a rich old fellow. They never ask me how to spell my name. Everybody knows it.
Did you get Rocky's letter I sent? I am so glad over it, that it lightens any troubles of my own! I trust she has done very well. If I were able I would give her a piano when she goes to housekeeping. But it sounds silly to tell what I would do!
Tell the boys & the rest I am going to write them soon. The box has not come nor have I been once notified. They lied to you about it. Which Company

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
was it, United States or American?
I have not heard from Mosby or from Hebron at all. As soon as I get my debts off I am going to see him.
[[Tenoroon?]] is well & sends love. I want to see you all.
I have a little cold, but am very well. Oh, if you could see the poor in this city it would make your heart ache. God was good to send such a mild winter, tho'. I have given away all the old duds I had.
Love to all of you. Excuse this scratch. I do not feel brilliant today. My head stays feverish so much I don't know what to do with it. Packing it with wet stockings gets very monotonous. I thank you again & again for your kindness, Aunt Harrie. I just love all of you.
Marie.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
wear two in my hat. I will write to them & tell them all about the Mardi Gras here tomorrow. Kiss both the babies for me. Love to all & everyone.
Please write. I miss it when you don't.
With great, great love,
Marie.
125 John St. Cincinnati
Feb. 28th 1876.
Dear Aunt Harrie:
I want to have a good long talk with you. None of you write to me, and I am lonesome for letters. Weren't you glad Rocky got married to a man who seems able to do well by her? I have not heard from her lately, nor from Hebron at al.
Are you all well? What you going to call the baby? I have thought a great deal about it. I wish you would call it "Nellie" after its mother. How is Karlie? I suppose Aunt Hat won't let his nose get out of joint.
If I were them I would sit down on the floor, lay my head against your knee, and say, "Auntie Hat, I've been having it tough. Working hard and not quite meeting a fellow's expenses, is uphill business, to say nothing of what she owes besides." This is all business talk and you mustn't read it out loud.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription: About a month ago a man came along and wanted me to edit a subscription book for him. He was going to have his publishing done by Hitchcock & Walden so I thought it was all right, and promised. He promised to pay $500, in installments and to send the first materials for his book in a week. That is the last I saw of him. He got prospectuses printed with my name conspicuous, and went to Cleveland, and hasn't paid his bills. He owes me nothing, but if he is a cheat and is going around with my name on his prospectus, he is doing me incalculable injury. However, I hope he isn't. Shutes, the Household man, is down in Texas, flourishing, I believe, while I am trying to pay for my bread & butter from day today. I get my rent paid, and my washing, and struggle bravely with the restaurant bill which is as low as we can make it. But I don't get a new  [[Luddeen?]] from month to month. A couple of weeks ago when Helen's beau was here from New York, we were all invited up to Mt. Auburn to Mrs. Whetstone's to tea. Mrs. Whetstone is nice. I like her. She takes a great fancy to us. She is rich, keeps a carriage

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription: lives in good style &c. Helen had just got her new seal brown silk that her father gave her, made up, and it is very stylish. I haven't anything new - not even a bit of lace. But thinks I, "Come, now, John Osborne's daughter can go well dressed and do him credit; Marcus Hartwell's daughter is just as good; and if he died young, before he was able to lay up money and give his children advantages and good clothes, that wasn't his fault; so Marcus Hartwell's daughter will do him all the credit she can, anyway." And I hauled out my old black silk. The skirt and overskirt look very well, but the waist is simply horrid. I took my white shawl & cut it up, and made a waist over white lawn. Hadn't a cent for buttons or even thread, and wouldn't borrow. So managed. Trimmed it with black velvet which I had, covered buttons with velvet, and put in my black silk sleeves. And it made a real stylish combination of black and soft yellow white, that suit did, and I looked as well as anybody. I think a good deal about doing my father credit, and I expect the thought that maybe he has great hopes for me, keeps me from doing many rash things in this position.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
I shall have a pretty good story in Christian Union next week or week after. I guess Helen will get married to her Karl about June, I hope she will.
Aunt Harrie, you offered me $90, but I could not take it. I think about it so much and how kind you were. Now I feel impressed to ask you to do this for me: I think there may be a little opening in New York, but I have had such luck lately that it isn't best to count any eggs. But if things should turn out as I hope in a month or so, could you have $40 or $50 at hand, so it I should be pressed to the wall for the cash, I could count on it? I don't think I shall want it, but I want to plan, you see. I shan't go to New York, unless I can at once take a good paying position. - On second thought, I guess you need not do it, Auntie. I can't bear the thought of getting in any deeper. I must manage some other way. [[Tenoroon?]] thinks I do wonderfully, considering all drawbacks and the unaccountable misfortunes that do really tag me. But I am of a disposition to be comfortable, rather than heroic, and I confess to you freely, that this long strain is not good for anyone.
Tell my boys & girls I thank them again for the wings, which everybody admires. I
[letter concludes top of page 1]

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Wednesday evening 3rd May [1876]
Dear Aunt Harrie:
I wrote a little note on the typewriter immediately on receipt of that cheque, but could not say all I wanted - it seemed like thinking out loud. I think you are dear and good. I was so surprised when I saw it was fifty, but said to myself - "That is just like Aunt Hat!" You do not know how you have helped me - not by the loan, simply; but it was like a hand reached out when everything was against me. You folks there are my folks. If I didn't have you I should certainly be desolate. Things are all in chaos yet. I do not know just which way to turn, but shall try to act for the best. The Meth. Conference is holding in Baltimore; Miss Osborne may lose her position; but there are 10 chances to one that she will keep it; she wants to keep it, marry or no marry. Locke's Monthly is going to be suspended.
Rocky is going (in course of time) to have a baby - so she thinks. Bless her! I wish you would all write to her. Kiss Karl and Nora-bird (I call her that) all over for me. Give my love to all. 
Your Marie.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Achilles Martin
Abstract and Real Estate Office [letterhead]
Danville, Ill. Tuesday A. M. 1877
Dear Folks: -
I congratulate you! Girls are not exactly to my taste, but make the best of her, make the best of her! Am glad she brought such a pleasant change in the weather. I have had a lovely time. Bob called last evening & pretty nearly put me in love with him. He looks awful nice & eyes me just about the way he always did when he was about to propose. He doesn't know there is any "mortgage" on me, and his relations make really more of me than ever! Ahem!
I am down in Mr. Martin's office for my mail. He gets it & takes my letters out with his. Annie Hoff is feebler than she was, and very despondent. Poor girl. "Hoppity-flop" is to be published & illustrated in the Boston "Cottage Hearth" for January. The editor is mad because he didn't get a sight of that letter the book keeper sent back to me. He is going to send me a copy of his Mag. for a year. I told Mr. Martin what was in the wind, & instead of lecturing and looking solemn, he took me by the arm & shook me and

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
cried out "Confound it. I wanted you myself!" 
Keep me posted about Miss Catherwood's progress. Love to all. If you see any of the girls (Club) give them my love. Love to Aunt Anna & all. Mrs. Hooper was inquiring particularly about her health. Write me a note soon. Alice's baby is awful sweet. They call her Marian Harman.
With love -
Marie.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Oakford, Howard Co. Ind.
8 Jan. 1878
A. H. Dooley: -
My Dear Sir: -
Your postal card rc'd. Also your Argo, which I like, and hope you will continue to send me. Glad you approve of my work. I always like to make friends among journalists. As to "data of my writings," I hardly know how to comply with your request. I have a juvenile serial now running in the Boston "Wide Awake": and shall have an illustrated article on the Mardi Gras in the March "St. Nicholas." I have done work for a great many of the eastern publications, and I am glad to say, have received very pleasant complimentary letters from great literary people. Am an Ohioan, born not far from Columbus; my last home was in Cincinnati: in fact I prefer that city to the east. Have been obliged to do so much work and to do it so

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
rapidly, that all my time has gone to magazine and newspaper writing. I furnished two serials for "Hearth & Home" before if was merged into the "Daily Graphic." The last three years have been occupied with juvenile writing, but do not intend by any means, to make a specialty of it.
Thank you for your pleasant appreciation.
Very sincerely yours,
Mary Hartwell Catherwood

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Mary Harwell Catherwood
A. H. Dooley
Box 193
Columbus, Ohio.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Oakford, Howard Co. Ind.
29 Nov. 1878
My dear Aunt H: -
Enclosed please find $ 6. After turning over that fifty dollars last winter, there remained a surplus of several dollars which I owed you. I think it was five and some cents. To make sure at any rate I enclose six dollars: with thanks.
I never have rec'd that promised letter from you. How did you spend Thanksgiving? Ive had a lovely little turkey with oyster dressing, celery cranberries, vegetables, cake and coffee. We invited the Bennetts, but they had a previous engagement so we ate our first Thanksgiving dinner alone, read "Scribner" for December, and Tennyson, in the evening. We get regularly now (and shall get all next year) "Scribner's Monthly," "Harper's Monthly," "Atlantic," "Blackwood" and the "Edinburg Review," besides a half a dozen papers including the "Independent," and we don't pay money for any of them. Were going to bind the volumes

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
of magazines: but Steele wants to send his sister [[Lid?]] one of them regularly after we get through reading it, so I guess he will send her "Scribner." It was a regular Thanksgiving Day here: snowy and cold. I think I shall go to Indianapolis next week. You never said whether you liked your cloak and dress. Mary Jane has not sent my camel's hair yet. We have our sideboard for the dining room. It is just as handsome as it can be: black walnut inlaid with French walnut, the silver drawer lined with blue velvet. The house doesn't look as it did when Uncle A. was here. The dining room is the prettiest one. Tell him the hall and stairway are matted, and we have our sofa and a dozen other things I don't think we had when he was here. The other day - in the city - I just happened to look at some linen sheeting - just lovely: and I am going to have half a dozen pairs of new linen sheets out of next week's cheque. They will last a lifetime. It always pays to buy the best. Seems as if Providence has prospered Steele and me, and sent us wedding presents (straight from the celestial store-house and not roundabout by any friend's hand!) - every day since we got married. The only crook in our lot is that was [[abbor?]] this place, but time will

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
bring us out of it nicely.
I would love to see you all: - especially Rob: and when I say him especially I do not mean that I do not want to see the rest badly, but only that I want to see him very much indeed! Steele has promised his mother we will run out to see her in the holy days. But when I said we would make a loop to Hoopeston he declared he could not spare the time. He will only stay over Sunday at Taylorville. In February I wish you & Rob would run in and see us. I can only room a pair of you at a time.
Now, please write me a letter Aunt Hat [[Put?]] down your dry ink horn, or take a stub of a lead pencil and give us a word. I rec'd a note from Mr. Wilson, and he enumerated some guests he expected the following Sunday to dinner: he wound up with "and Hattie," as a climax.
By the way, would you like Butterick's Monthly? I get it, and make no use of it, farther than to run through the fashions.
Give my love to all the friends: tell Aunt N. I am getting some fine imported engravings, after the old masters. Expect them from N. Y. City this week. She would enjoy them so much. What are you doing for Christmas? (By the way, Annie Hoff writes me that Kate Mann & Alice Calhoun - whom I visited in Danville - both expected new arrivals the last of November. My gracious!)
With love - Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
St. Charles Block -
Indianapolis, Ind.
31 Dec. 1879.
My Dear Mr. Dooley: -
Kindest and fullest wishes for your further success and happiness in the New Year.
I send you a little poem in acknowledgment of the pleasure your paper has given me. Yours sincerely -
Mary H. Catherwood

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Mary Hartwell
A Yellow Rose
I drink your breath with a most cruel passion,
Gold rose, my yellow rose:
O I could crush you ages in this fashion,
Then sink below your kiss, my sweet, through ages of repose!
All other roses may have bloom and sweetness,
Gold rose, my yellow rose:
But only in yourself I find completeness --
This tingling rare perfume, my sweeet -- the sun's heart when it glows.
Give me -- give out your life with full surrender,
Gold rose, my yellow rose:
Infuse my flesh with all your fragrant splendor,
Then let us die in ecstacies a poet only knows!

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Saturday July 19 [1890]

Dear Steele: -
Am sending this letter to Taylorville in the hopes that you will get it out of the office there before Judgment Day! Had letters from Hazel and you both this morning. Will write Lucy Wallace. Hope you will have a good time at Em's, as I know you will. Give my love to all of them. I would live to be there. But is is so cool and sweet here. The woods are so lovely; the water is so delicious. I

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
never enjoyed them more.
Mrs. Parkinson has made a study for me in the circular room-like clump of birches and pines south of the cottage. A rustic table and chair remain there for me.  I use pebbles for paper weights I got good work done at the first chapter yesterday. It is the divinest place for writing you ever saw. If I don't get two chapters done at least, while I am here, I ought to be dropped off the dock. The first chapter is always the hardest, except the last.
It is so clean, so clean here, after the city! The air is so pure, the woods are so fragrant!
You will manage the crop sales all right, I am sure. We ought to be thankful for such crop prospects, when

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
awhile ago it looked as if we should have no income at all! If we manage with economy this summer, and pay off a big piece of the debt in August, the [[lambie's?]] prospects of sufficient inheritance to keep her out of the poor-house, ought to be good: - if her own extravagance can be curbed. Explain things to her. She is sensible. Don't let her pull your leg too hard. But at the same time, this is your occasion to get the best kind of a hold on your daughter.
There is a gentle rain here today. The family send regards. The "Irish wash-lady" is just as dear as she can be. I think I enjoy it here almost better than ever before! All care is dropped. I have only to get on with my work. Hazel and you and looking after each other. And don't forget to look after Norue.
With love - Mary

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Hoopeston, Ills.
Sept. 29, 1890.
My Dear Mr. McClure: -
When I get through the stress of my "Lady" I will as soon as possible have a short story ready for you.
Sincerely yours -
Mary Hartwell Catherwood.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
[Spring 1891]
Thursday afternoon.
O Aunt Hat! Steele's telegram has just come! It is as I was afraid it would be: you refuse to go further in the matter. I felt that I must urge you up to this point; but now I can't say anything more, but it breaks my heart. You shall not lose a cent. We will pay it back whether we ever collect anything off McCulloch or not.
When that letter came from Reed this morning, it was the

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
worst blow that I had had. To think that fellow put you off the boat when your berths were unsold and you had already paid for them. 
I shall follow him up and disgorge him if it takes my last cent. I have documents all together to meet him with. 
I feel as if I were a thousand years older. 
Hazel is getting on well. Fever almost gone. She is weak, and is yet kept on milk and beef juice: but good as an angel. Waked me only once last night, at 3 o'clock.
O, Aunt Hat! I feel as if I could never face you again, after having brought such annoyance and

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
chagrin upon you. If you could go on - but I wont urge you a word more. If we had five in the Boston party it would never have happened.
Forgive me for ever having urged you to this journey. I was so anxious to have you enjoy. You shall make the trip yet, if we both live, and have me for escort; and I hope I am neither a thief nor a lunatic.
Mame cannot yet give you up, though I told her when Reed's letter came that I knew that would so prejudice you that you would not move again.
We will attend to your trunk. Love to all. Think hard for me that I may get ahead of that man.
Your distressed niece, Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Before trip of '91.
Written to her Aunt Mrs. Harriet De Vault who did go, after all. Miss Mary Emma Catherwood neice, was 4th in party, a it at 18
H. C. C.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
[July, 1891]
3rd day out. In Gulf Stream.
Friday A. M.
Dear Steele: -
I wish you could see what the sea is doing for Hazel. She was carried on board. The first day I got her on deck and kept her there in steamer chair all day. She ate well from the first, being squeamish only once when I waked her suddenly for lunch. The second morning she got up, helped dress herself and had her hair curled. This morning she carried her own wraps and knitting wools up to the deck.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
She walks everywhere, but sits still a good deal, crocheting. She is making you a wonderful mat of 12 colors. Am afraid I have not been careful enough of her eating. Have kept her to the Waukesha water, but she fairly howls for oatmeal, buttered toast &c, and seems to thrive on it. I can't keep her to liquid food any longer. She sleeps like a log all night and seems stronger every day.
Aunt Hat has been very seasick. Mame a little so, so that she takes her meals on deck instead of in the dining room. I had one qualmy time at the first evening dinner, but got over it in a half hour, and have been all right ever since, so I could wait on the others. The deck stewards are very attentive, though,

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
and bring their meals for me. Hazel & I go down to the dining-room every meal.
We are all saturated with the delicious salt air. It was rolling heavily last night. This morning lots of white caps, but comparatively calm. Our stateroom very hot last night. It rolled so yesterday the portholes were screwed up tight. I am enjoying every minute of this voyage, and I think it is filling Hazel with health. There is a swing riffed under our awning on deck, and she swings herself in it. She wrote you a long letter today. The child looks still a little pale, but quite like herself.
We sat on deck without wraps this morning, the air is soft and warm. The Gulf Stream makes that. The first night & day out were very cool. We can taste the salt air on our finger nails. Am going to give Hazel & have myself a salt bath tonight. With love always,
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Sunday 1 P.M. July 11 1891
Dear Steele: -
Last night we were blown before a gale which followed us all night, and is not settled down yet. The vessel rolled so that the decks seemed to stand up like walls. We stayed out until we could not get along the deck alone. Some men helped me. People were rolling around in heaps. I got Hazel and Aunt Hat in the drawing-room, and then started to look for Mame

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription: who was around with some young people. But the floor tipped and dashed me against some furniture until I was glad to grab a seat and hold on. When we went below a steward carried Hazel. Mame had got to our stateroom, drenched with spray. My trunk slid down the floor and all our things tumbled all night long. It was glorious. Hazel made no fuss at all. Everybody says she is the best child they ever saw. She is so sweet and obedient. She enjoys everything, and sits soaking the salt air with silent delight, saying once in awhile that the sea likes her; it has cured her. Her appetite is hard to restrain,

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
though she fires up at once about anything I do not want her to eat. She runs all around now, is full of play, mews and sings. I never think of her as a sick child: and this is only our 5th day on the water! Her favorite joke is that Aunt Hattie carried her on the steamer and she will have to carry Aunt Hattie off!
Mame is a good sailor, enjoys everything, was jolly in the rolling about last night. But I never saw anyone more seasick than Aunt. She can hardly sit up. Neither claret nor champagne help her for any length of time. Every huge heave of the ship

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
sickens her. I don't think she will get over it now until we land. She was on the way to get well before this gale, but it fixed her. She has scarcely eaten anything since we sailed. But I think it will do her a world of good. Her skin is clearing, and the whites of her eyes, as I never saw them do before.
I found after writing you my first letter on board that we couldn't mail anything until we reach Queenstown on the coast of Ireland. So I will mail the

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
batch all together. Never did I enjoy anything as I enjoy this voyage. It is like a salvation to Hazel. She sits in her steamer chair wrapped in all the rugs until ate in the evening, sleeping or crocheting, or watching the waves. Then we often get up and walk the decks, and she can walk as long and as well as I can.
We had two really hot days in the Gulf Stream; but had left it when this gale began. It is cool and delightful now.
Some of the passengers were frightened last night, but there was really no danger. Aunt Hat

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
got pitched against the piano, and bumped her cheek. I hope you can read this. The boat is rolling greatly. Love to all. Take care of yourself. We are having a grand time. I don't believe months on land would have so straightened Hazel out. She dressed herself this morning: and can hardly wait from one meal to another, the sea air so strengthens and increases digestion. With love always,
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Tuesday A. M.
We land at Queenstown some time today. The weather was awful [[rough?]] Sunday afternoon. We were all a little sick except Hazel, who waited on us, the darling. She runs along the deck now.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Ayr Scotland.
July 16, 1891.
Dear Steele: -
We came in here today with the party, and have had a grand day. Visited Burns' birthplace, and old Kirk Alloway where the witches danced. It is the most delightful wierd place I ever saw. Hazel found [[mon?]] by the old wall, & carried it off. She enjoys everything.
I have been in Tam O'Shanter Inn. This morning before leaving Glasgow we visited the Cathedral which was built in the 12th century

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
century.
This country is lovely as a dream. We start toward Shakespeare's county tomorrow. Will be in London on Wednesday where I hope to hear from you. I hope you are well, dear.
Hazel is doing nicely.
With love always,
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
him after dinner, and talked everything out plainly without the least anger.
He and his wife both declared before Mary that our stateroom was bought and occupied (in the Chester) by a Mrs. Lizzie Marston of Cambridge. The steamship company probably sold them, & Gaze's agent did not know about it.
We shall probably go on with his party tomorrow. Where the money went for stateroom bought by Mrs. Marston went, he says he does not know; but thinks it will all be straightened out. I talked simple straight facts, and think it was best.
Hazel is well, and happy as a linnet. I take great care of her. She sings and meows, and knits, and takes a nap every day & I let her with fear and trembling have some fruit today. Strawberries here big as a baby's fist. The finest fruit of all kinds I ever saw.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
The scenery is simply sublime. The mountainous hills covered with mist.
I must hurry to bed. Take care of yourself. Aunt is well. Mame is almost wild with enjoyment. She doesn't look like the same girl.
With love -
Mary

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
London, Wednesday Jul. 22, 1891.
Hotel Metropole.
London.
Dear Steele: -
We came to London from Oxford this afternoon. It has been a wonderful week. I wrote you on Sunday at Leamington. From there we went on Monday to Warwick Castle and the ruins of Kenilworth. I am bringing some photographs which will give you a little idea of them. They are both in their way magnificent. From there we went to Stratford-on-Avon, where Shakespeare

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
was born and is buried. I saw the very old slab and inscription under which he lies. Am bringing you a view of that. Then we went on to Oxford, the old University town where there are 23 colleges, some grand pictures and stained glass. One of the most interesting towns in the world. All these journeys were short, and Hazel has enjoyed them. She eats like a bear, and has got back her flesh. I still have her drink 5 glasses of milk a day. She eats breakfast, then lunch, then I buy her oat cakes or rolls to munch in afternoon, and in the evening she eats straight through an eight or ten course table d'hote dinner.
I probably did a foolish thing today:

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
I found a quaint old ring with nine perfect pearls in it, and had it cut down for her, paying $4 for it. It is a beautiful thing, one she will value when she is a young lady: for I did not have it cut to fit her tight now, but very loosely. She is enormously proud of it. She is getting strong on her feet, but is not as springy as she was: I take great care of her. She does enjoy everything so much.
She has taken a great fancy to Mr. McCulloch, and he is very kind to her. We smile a little at it. Though Mary says she now believes he will do his best and intends all right. I have not yet turned the balance of the money over to him but will do it tomorrow. He seems to try to save us money, though we pay our own omnibus and street car fares and lunches. It is so funny to hear some of the women growl and try to borrow money of each other. One missed going in to see the tomb of Lord Leicester because she had not twopence. I offered her sixpence, but she was mad then, and would not go in at all.
We hope to find letters at Gaze's tomorrow. It was too late to get them when we arrived here tonight.
I hope you are well. Hazel had fits of being homesick for you, and prays long and loud for you every night and never ceases wishing that you had come with us. I do wish it so much myself. It is great experience, seeing all these stores of Old World treasures. And it is so much better for families to travel together than to go piecemeal. With much love always,
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
London, 24 July 1891
Hotel Metropole.
Dear Steele: -
We are having fun with Mr. McCulloch yet. When I went to turn over the money to him he said he wanted $275 more from me, $275 more from Aunt Hat, and $125. each more from Mary & Hazel.
I told him plainly he would not get it, and buttoned all

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
the money up in my dress again. He hasn't seen the color of our cash at all. We went to Gaze's to arrange a tour for ourselves. Gaze said he was the responsible man about our outward passage.
We may get our money back before we leave London. In the evening Mr. McCulloch sent me a note and we all had another conference. He wants us to go in with the party, figured things up and made it appear if Gaze returns our money and we turn over to him what Aunt & I held

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription: back the $157 in the pool, we could make our trip all right. He said our leaving the party would make him lose $150. It struck me that his losing it might be our saving it. Still, I would rather make the trip with him (if we keep him muzzled) than by ourselves. The slippery old thing means no harm, but he really has not much sense. If we get our outward passage refunded and do go on with him, I intend to have a written agreement with him.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
He and most of the party went to Windsor today, and stood around hours; and finally found out the palace would not be opened. That's the way he "conducts." We four started out by ourselves, spent part the day in St. Paul's Cathedral, took omnibus to South Kensington Museum, stayed the afternoon amid wonders untellable, and came home by the underground R. R. in about 10 minutes. We had

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription: a delightful day: saw Temple Bar, a glimpse of Newgate, the Strand, Regent St. &c &c. Yesterday we went by ourselves to Westminster Abbey; and in the evening to Madame Tussaud's Wax work. Hazel was so delighted with the wax work. She has just had her bath and gone to sleep, after a day which tired us all but her. She eats so much, and enjoys all the sights with ceaseless interest. Yesterday we received your first letter since leaving home. The tears ran down her face because there were none directed to her. She said she had written you so

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
many. But when I read the letter aloud to her, and she found it was nearly all about Hazel or to Hazel, she stood and laughed and shouted. I had to read it 3 times to her.
I am glad you are comfortable. We were afraid we were going to be kept in Europe a week longer than the date set for coming home. Our return berths were sold before we got here. But of course they have to send us back as our passage is paid, and it is likely we can get some berths after all on the steamer the party came home on. That will have to be settled before we leave London.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
I hope I shall hear again from you tomorrow. I have sent back letters every two or three days, and you must be getting them regularly.
I sent that Ms. to Scribner's in haste: and my impression is that I told them I would call at their office on my return; but I think I also gave them my Hoopeston address.
I have bought you a lovely

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
cigar holder - the handsomest I ever saw, and hope I can get it through without duty. May have to ask someone to smoke it once. It cost $4.00. I got it in Oxford. I got Marcus a pipe, too, a pretty one, but not so expensive. It will certainly have to be smoked.
With all our annoyances about the muddle with McCulloch, the trip has been grand ever so far. If you were along, and we were free from any party, it would be life and no mistake.
Hazel seems now in normal condition, and regular as a clock. I do not yet allow her to eat

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
fruit freely: give her very little, but lots of milk and bread and butter. She is getting freckles on her nose and has some color.
It is 10.30; I must go upstairs. This is an elegant hotel. McCul. takes us to good hotels whatever his shortcomings. We are going to see Henry Irving & Ellen Terry tomorrow evening. One of the girls of the party who is not going volunteered to stay with Hazel, and Hazel is willing. Love to all. Tell Rob that Aunt Hat climbed to the top of St. Paul's dome today.
With love, Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Hotel Metropole, London.
Thursday 4 P. M, July 29, 1891.
Dear Steele: -
We are in a box now. Clark has arrived from New York. We waited long this morning while men came and went, and finally got at Gaze & him. They [[utterly?]] repudiate any responsibility about those outward berths, wont pay a cent, say they don't know who sold them and McCulloch is to blame. If any settlement with anybody is made it will not be until we reach New York again.
We straightaway [[swapped?]] out an independent tour and intend to cut loose from McCulloch tomorrow morning.
You wanted me to buy a nice dress

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
or two. I have bought two lovely ones, and now almost wish I hadn't, for we shall need the money. A silk velvet - dark wine brown, and a black lace. The velvet is made V shaped neck, no sleeves but long gloves. It is the grandest gown I ever had. The black Chantilly lace is long sleeved. It cost only $4 ore than that Chicago dressmaker charged me for making one dress, and it is on a silk foundation, beautifully made. The two cost me $108. I ought not to have bought both, though I will not regret it when I get them home. But am afraid (now that we are disappointed of this refunded money) that I shall run short.
We have not settled with McCulloch yet. I will tell you the result before closing this letter. He had a charge of about $50 against Hazel and me last Wednesday - a week ago.
We shall make the plunge alone to Paris tomorrow. We get tourist

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
tickets and hotel coupons, and the trip by Paris, Switzerland, the Rhine and Antwerp, is estimated at $97, our money. I can get half fare for Hazel as far as Paris. After that, may have to pay full fare for her at all hotels and on all roads. She is well, and really fitting plump, and enjoys everything.
[next paragraph has an "X" drawn through it]
Please send me the moment you get this, $50. When we get round to Antwerp we may not have enough for hotel and sleeping berth home from New York City. As to getting that steamer money in New York, I don't expect anything more of these sleek knaves. Among them they intend to let us hold the bag. Send it in foreign exchange if possible: and send it to me Care of
Messrs. Von der Beck & Marsily,
Red Star Line,
Kammenstrasse,
Antwerp.
[below "X"d out paragraph:]
I cancel this. You will see why as you read on.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
4
I may not need it at all, and we may be in straits if I don't get it. It takes 26 days for a letter to reach you and bring a reply, so there is no time to lose.
I have had only two letters from you. Our berths back are not certain yet. We may have to come a week sooner or a week later than Aug. 29. We may have to separate, two going on one steamer, two on another. We are at the mercy, you see, of Gaze & Son; though Mr. Gaze declares he is doing all he can to arrange for us. 
With love, Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
5
Thursday morning.
Mr. McCulloch was so mad at me last night that he trembled. He said we had been doing an underhanded thing to map out a separate trip. I asked him what folks could do when they hadn't as much money as he demanded. And as he had known all the time what we were doing at Gaze's how was it sneaking?
It ended by our all going to bed without any settlement.
This morning we settled. It all came to this: - we had to go on - following the tour we [[?]]ked for ourselves which leaves out a few things only - and pay him. Or we leave to try to go home - and pay him. We can't get a steamer now. Gaze is in Antwerp today, trying

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
6
to get our berths for the 29 Aug. If he gets them there would be complications again. And I intend to get what I pay for. We shall go on around the Swiss tour. But I had to cable to you for $75 more. The truth is, as you know, I have had to hold the bag for Mame and Aunt. Of the pool money left ($157, which I turned over to him this morning) nearly all is really mine. But I took only my half (that is, Hazel's and mine). If I had taken it all Mame and Aunt would be unable to go on. Mame has had to cable for some money, too. Besides, I have paid lots of small expenses for Aunt. She is so close and so scared at the expense, and so sorry she came (as I knew she would be,

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
7
though you all blamed me for telegraphing her before she started) that I have loaded up with everything I could, and not told her. Consequently, I who brought the most money, am the one who cannot make the trip without sending for more. In the long run it will pay me. But never again will I set foot to any journey with anybody but Hazel, you and myself. I expected such a good rest. And the complication has been a torment. Don't think, though, that I am not enjoying the trip in spite of all; for I am. Nothing shall spoil it for me. I may come home from New York with a pile; and I may come home with next to nothing. Anyhow, Hazel shall not want anything she needs while she is over here.
She looks so well, and is so proud

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
8
of getting her strength.
I got receipt from McCulloch this morning for all money turned over to him. I paid him altogether 60 £, and Aunt gave him her balance less her share of the pool. We have to pay our own cab hire, our own lunches (and how Hazel does eat! You know I don't care for any lunch.) - and all the little expenses which he pretended were covered in his estimate. But he hasn't got all that he says I owe him yet. I make it hard as pulling teeth.
I waked early this morning and thought and figured a long time before I would decide to cable for that $75 more. Then I made up my mind I would not be charged full director's fees ($100) and everything else in proportion, without getting something for my money. We have led him a dance, so far.
With love - Hazel sends kisses -
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Hotel Burgundy
8, rue Duphot, 8
Paris
Aug. 5, 1891.
Dear Steele:
Your 4th letter just rec'd this evening. I am glad everything is going so well with you.
Hazel is sitting beside me writing a letter to you. We have passed the day in the Louvre, looking at pictures and statuary. I was so tired I felt half dead; but I think she is the least tired of the party. Tomorrow we go to Versailles. Saturday we start to Switzerland. As I told you in last letter, we sail from Antwerp on the 22nd of this month - about 18 days from this. When I got that $100 you cabled me I thought I would have money to bring home, besides buying everything I wanted. But McCulloch brought in a bill promptly for the big, end of it. It made my hotel bill in London about $40 instead of $30 as

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
he said it would be. His figures look all right. But we have to pay for everything ourselves; cabs, lunches, entrance fees to everywhere. Of course I have to pay double. My fare and meals are paid to Antwerp. Hazel's are not. I have them all to pay, and I have about $70. It frightens me. I am not buying a thing in Paris for fear I shall run short. After sending home once for money this seems an awful thing. But I shall manage the best I can and try to do everything to the best advantage. If I had not bought dresses, or even if I had my own money back, I should have abundance.
Mary has had no answer to her cablegram yet. She is very stoical. But if she doesn't get it I believe it will make her sick.
The 2 McCullochs seem to deny themselves nothing. They have wine when it is an extra, operas, cabs & so on. It does disgust me so to think we are paying for carting such imposters around. He

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
does not seem to know anything. HIs almost invariable answer to all questions is, "I don't know." Instead of his showing me things which "money would not buy admission to," he had shown me almost nothing. I have [[?]]ed for myself, and paid enormously for his scanty society. I am registered in a [[?]] under his name, without my name, so nobody came to see me. It has been a misfortune that I ever changed from that Frazer party. I hear of it constantly, and the Frazer woman seems to be a splendid conductor.
Hazel selected her doll, and is delighted with it. I will have to send it on with my dresses to Antwerp. We saw some magnificent pictures today: several Murillos which Hazel doted on; and the Venus of Milo, and many fine Coreggios, Rembrandts, Titians, &c. The whole many miles of gallery are wonderful.
We will come here together sometime, and not hurry. Then we can enjoy things. I want to travel by ourselves - you and Hazel and I: no outsiders. I have spent almost enough to have brought us all this time; and it vexes me so, when I think you might be here, finding out things and helping me so; and I have this old nightmare of a money-sucker to carry around instead.
I am sorry you did not hear from us before the 22nd of July. I sent off a big letter at Queenstown, the day before we landed. You must have received it soon after mailing this 4th letter of yours. I have written many letters since, sending them at intervals of three or four days.
I do wish you were here this evening.
With much love,
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
crossing. I ask for the $10 as a precaution against having nothing for sleeping car & meals when I land.
I wish you were here, and we had plenty of money and no care. We could enjoy things so. I will never undertake another long journey unless you are along to see to things, and I will never try to lug anybody else around with me again.
With love - I am very tired and must be up early - We went to the Luxembourg today and saw beautiful modern paintings.
With much love,
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Hotel des Boulangeres.
Berne, Switzerland.
Monday, Aug. 11, 1891.
Dear Steele:
We left Geneva this morning and arrived at this quaint old town at 4.30, this afternoon, after stopping long enough for lunch at Lausanne. We are now by ourselves. Mr. McCulloch has written out our itinerary, and written ahead to all the hotels. He has done the best in his power, I think, and I believe we shall get on all right.
Hazel is in bed, sending her dear love to papa. She is getting so boisterous I often feel impatient with her, but you would rejoice to see her plump cheeks and good color.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
I took her the first thing to the bear pit. Everything in Berne is bears. There is a clock tower, on which automatic bears march around every time the clock strikes. Then there is a very old fountain, so old that no one can give any account of its origin or meaning, yet it looks fresh in color. There are bears around the pedestal, and on top the pedestal is a figure called the Kindlifresser or child-eater. It is a man with his pockets stuffed with babies, and babies hung on his back, while he is devouring one. Hazel thought it was very funny. Then we went through the arcades - the covered sidewalks where the shops are. There is to be a fête here shortly, and the city is gaily decorating itself, and that is pretty to see. But Hazel was most delighted with the live bears in the bear pit. They act so comically. I got her a two-penny bunch of carrots, and

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
she tossed them into the bears' mouths one by one. They would sit up and beg like dogs, and would rock themselves, holding their feet in their hands. I could hardly get her away from them.
She is not a bit sore from her mountain climbing, sleeps well, and eats like a hopper; she is never full longer than a few minutes at a time.
Put the description part of this letter away for me so I wont have to write it in my notes.
We have had no letters since leaving Paris. I do hope we shall find some at Antwerp if not before.
With love always,
Mary.
We go to Interlaken tomorrow, then on to Lucerne.
At Lausanne we began to have very light down-sacks like little feather beds for coverlets. They have them here. And stone floors upstairs, or big patterned hard wood floors; and long brass door handles. Europe is delightful. The weather just suits me: so cool.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Geneva, Switzerland.
August 11, 1891.
Dear Steele: -
Only 10 more days in Europe. For here we turn and start for Antwerp, stopping along the way, going down the Rhine, &c. Here we leave the McCulloch party. He has written down our itinerary, and really humped himself a little to arrange for us. We came down Lake Geneva by boat from Lausanne, and it was the heavenliest ride.
Sunday afternoon we (most of us) started, led by him, to climb Mt. Saliere. He thought Hazel ought not to try it. But she was wild to: so I started with her, intending to turn back if she tired too much.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
It was a zig-zag climb of more than four thousand feet up the face of the mountain, narrow, but not dangerous, protected by trees and bushes along the edge. Hazel went up like a cat. I made her sit down and rest every few minutes. At the top she was not even flushed, when the others sat panting, red as boiled lobsters. Aunt Hat and two others came last, a long way behind. It did up Aunt, but she is none the worse for it, and thinks she would not feel it had it not been for the long walk afterward.
We got refreshments at a little auberge, and crossed the plateau, to see the sun set on Mt. Blanc. Mt. Blanc is lovely and snow crowned. The view of vast spreading mountains was grand.
We went down the mountain on the other side by a plain road, to take the train back to Geneva. Hazel & I lagged, because I had promised if she wouldn't gather moss & ferns and load them on

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
me going up, she might gather all she wanted going down.
At last she said she was tired, and that scared me directly. I made Aunt and Mary go on with the others while I stopped at a turn-off road to parley with a donkey man. He put Hazel in the saddle, but the donkey balked, and she was afraid of it. So I got her down, and thought I would wait for a cart, at the risk of losing the train. But a lady came out of her summer cottage, and told me if I took that turn off road if was only a few minutes to the R. R. station. So I put all the moss &c in my umbrella, put arm around Hazel, and we went easily on down to the station. None of the party were there. But I got my tickets. The train was due in 15 minutes. None of them came. I inquired, and found they would have to take that train from that station or go home au pied (on foot.) Hazel and I took

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
4
the train, and I still thought when I got to hotel that they must have reached it before me. But they hadn't. I was eating dinner (Hazel & I) - it was after 8 o'clock, and three of the party came in. They had got separated from the rest. Then I was afraid the others had stopped to hunt for us. but they hadn't. They had walked with the "director" clear around the foot of the mountain to the terminus of the street railway. Mary says she knows it was 16 miles. Of course it wasn't. Aunt was, so used up she could not eat anything. Everybody is sore today except Hazel & I. We weren't tired a bit. They say now that Hazel is the toughest child they ever saw. She stood that tramp better than anyone in the party. And how she does eat! Her lunches are crumbling my little pile awfully.
I have not had any letter since leaving Paris. Only 4 letters from you, in all.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
5
Hope to hear from you before leaving Geneva, as this is the last chance until Antwerp.
Hazel laments for you every time she particularly enjoys anything. She wishes papa were here, and she would stay always in Europe.
With love,
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
Lucerne, Switzerland.
Aug. 14, 1891
Dear Steele: -
We arrived here yesterday from Interlaken (where we saw the Jungfrau peak, and Hazel reveled in moss and mountains) and went straight to Gaze's office to get our tickets stamped for remainder of journey. We each of us got two letters. Aunt Hat at last received one from Aunt Nellie and me from Lute.
There were your 6th and the one you sent the draft in. Where the 5th has meandered I don't know, I was so astonished when I opened that letter & found the draft for 20 pounds. For you all understand by this time that Mame did not (or thought she did not hear from

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
2
her expenses are paid through to Antwerp, except the cabs and lunches. I shall get it cashed and hand it over to her today. She says she will only use $50, and I must carry the other $50 in my chamois bag in my bosom for her. But I doubt if that extra $50 ever sees the American shore.
I have greatly enjoyed this trip through the Swiss lakes and mountains. Yesterday as the train was crossing the mountains, you could see from there to five or eight waterfalls at once. The scenery is grand beyond anything; - even the Saguenay.
Lucerne is a queer old city, one of the Switzerland capitals, fronts on a lake, has little streets and wide open spaces.
As I told you before, we expect to sail on Aug. 22, from Antwerp, on the steamer Friesland. Our steamer tickets had not arrived when we left the McCulloch party. I spoke very impressively about it to Mr McCulloch, and he said he

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
3
would telegraph - he would do anything - he would certainly get them to us in time.
I do confess that I hate to leave Europe. If you had been along, and we had been alone with Hazel, and had been spared all this bother, it would be the happiest time of my life. The old civilization suits me, the old cities, the vivid vegetation which is never dry; the ease of getting around. In France, I had no trouble at all in rail travel. They threw the doors open at stations, and called six or ten minutes waits, and I hustled Hazel right out to one of the little "cabinets."
She is plump, and in better health than ever before. She wails to see you, and is now glad she is going home, but she has enjoyed it.
Mame says tell you that you are the best man in the world, and she is going to write & thank you.
This may be my last letter, as later ones would probably reach you about the time I do. With love,
Mary.

title: Mary Hartwell Catherwood letters [1], 1874-1898
transcription:
her cablegram. The cabled draft came to Mrs. Mary Catherwood, and was from Chicago. She said her uncle never sent anything from Chicago. We both though it was mine. I meant to let her have $25 of it, but as you know, McCulloch brought in a bill for $60 directly. If I had had to wait until now for my draft it might have been as well. For I should not have paid the bills he brought, and run myself short for the home journey. I should have left him in debt, and let somebody else do a little bag-holding. As it is, I think I shall have plenty to get home on. Hazel is not costing as much as I feared she would, and I have about $45 yet.
Mame rejoiced exceedingly over this hundred dollars. She actually did not need it, but wanted more money to buy presents with. She had $10, and
