To their Excellencies the Lords Justice,

May it please Your Excellencies

We have lately receiv’d a Letter from Mr Thomas Wier dated at Sta Lucia, the 20th June last, a Copy of which is hereunto annex’d wherein he informs us, that he had been at Martinique two Days before, where the French were then fitting out Twenty Sloops, who were to sail with Six Men of War, lately arriv’d there from France for St Vincents, One of the Islands under the Government of Barbadoes in Order to endeavour to get off the Negroes there, which are in Number about 4000. And in Case they shou’d have Success in this Attempt they intended to go with the said Negroes to attack St Domingo on Hispaniola. That the French were likewise going to make a Settlement at St Lucia which is also one of the Islands under the Government of Barbadoes, were sending all manner of Tradesmen & Materials for building a fort there, and that one Monsieur Martin, who is appointed Governor of that Isl[[?]] was daily expected with two large Ships full of families to settle there. The said Mr. Wier being since arriv’d here, We have discours’d with him and he has confirm’d to Us, what he wrote in his Letter and added that before he left

Mark

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [1], 1717-1722
transcription:
sign'd and seal'd by the said Commissioners for preventing Hostilities or violent proceedings between the respective Subjects of both Crowns in those parts until the 1/11[[?]] January then ensuing and from thence forward until further Orders. And by the said Letter, Col. Stede is requir'd to give an exact Account of the Boundaries & Limits of the Government of Barbadoes. But We do not find any Copy of the foresaid Instrument nor any Account of the proceedings of the said Commissioners.
In prosecution however of the foresaid Directions to Col. Stede, We find that he appointed Commissioners to make Inquiry into the King's Title to the Islands of Sta Lucia, St Vincents & Dominica which Commissioners accordingly made a Report, Dated 23 Septemr 1688 and he transmitted the same to the Lords of the Committee for Trade & plantations.
And as it appears to us by the several papers beforemention'd that His Majesty's Title to the Island of Sta Lucia is fully demonstrated anticedent to any pretence made by the French; We humbly crave leave to take notice of the great Importance the preservation of the said Island may be to this Kingdom.
Because the Wood and Timber that grows upon it, and which has been constantly fetch'd from thence to Barbadoes, is of absolute
Ne[[?]]

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [1], 1717-1722
transcription:

but they paid no attention to him. A bold warrior now demanded of Brown the key to a large chest, which contained his most valuable stores, which he refused to give, telling the Indians that Mrs. Brown had it. 
The Indian now demanded it of Mrs. Brown, but she boldly refused to give it up.
The Indian then split the top of the chest open with his tomahawk and his example was immediately followed by the other Indians, who broke open and rifled every box and 
package on the boat. While this was going on, an Indian rudley took hold of Joseph Brown, a lad fifteen years old, and the old man seized the Indian and forsed him to let the boy go.
An instant after, the Indian seized a sword which was lying on the boat, and while

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
old man Browns back was turned to him, struck him on the back of the neck, almost severing his head from his body. 
Brown turned in the agony of death and seized the Indian, and in the struggle was thrown overboard into the river, when he sank to rise no more.
The boat was now turned into the mouth of a little creek, in the town of Nickajack, and the whole party taken on shore, in the midst of several hundred warriors, women and children.
In the meantime, Vaun continued to tel the sons of Brown that all this was a violation of the treaty of Hopewell, and that Breath, who was the chief of Nickajack and Running Water, who was expected there that night, would punish the marauders,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
restore their goods, and send them on their voyage. 
But at this verry moment, several leading warriors of the upper towns had seized upon Browns negroes  as lawful spoil, and dispatched them in canoes to their several homes.
Whatever may have been Vauns true motives, his interfearence on this occasion had the effect to peace the whole party at the mercy of the Indians, without a path of resistance.
If he acted in good faith, he was samefully  deceived by his followers; but if he onley used his address to disarm the voyagers, that they might the more easily fall victims to savage ferocity, his conduct exhibits the climax of perfidy. 
A party of Creek braves, who now engaged with the men of Nickajack and Running Water in this outrage,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
having seized upon their share of the plunder, and having taken posession of Mrs. Brown and her son George, ten years old, and three small daughters, immediatley began their march to their own nation. While the Cherokees were deliberating upon the fate of the prisoners and a division of the spoils, they adroitley withdrew from the counsil, on the plea that this all belonged to the head men of Nickajack.
Thus, in one short hour, deprived of husband, son, friends, liberty, and all, this devoted woman, with her five small children, began her sad journey on foot, along the rugged flinty trails that lead to the Creek towns on the Tallapoosa river.
At the time of this outrage, there was living at or near Nickajack, a French trader named Thomas Tunbridge,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
who was married to a white woman, who had been taken prisoner near mobile when an infant, and raised by the Indians.
After she was grown, she was exchanged, but refused to leave the Indians, distrusting her ability to adapt her habits to a civilised life.
She had been married to an Indian brave, by whom she had a son, now twenty two years old, who was one of the boldest warriors of the Cherokee towns. He had already killed six white men in his forays to the Cumberland settlements.
Having all the versatility of his mother's race, as well as the ferosity and courage of his fathers, he was fast rising into distinction as a warrior, and bade fair to reach the first honors of his nation. His praises for dairing and chivalry were in the mouths of all.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
His mother was now growing old, and having no young children, her son desired to present to her some bright-eyed boy as a slave; for, acording to the savage code of the times, each captive became a slave to his captor.
This woman's  son, whos name was Kiachatalee, was one of the leaders of the marauding party who seized upon Brown's boat, and from the first new the fate of the party.
Before the boat landed, he tried to induce Joseph, a boy then fifteen years old, but quite small, to get into his canoe, with the intention of withdrawing him from the general massacre that was soon to take place, but the boy would not go with him.
When the boat landed, Kiachatalee took Joseph to his step-father, Tunbridge,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
who in good English told the boy that he lived a mile out of the town, and invited him to go and spend the night with him.
This the boy did after asking the consent of his older brothers.
Tunbridge seized the boy by the hand and hurried him away. They had scarsley gon out of the town before they herd the rifles of the savage braves, who were murdering his brothers and friends.
What were the felings of this poor boy at this moment? His father slain by an Indian brave; his brothers, and friends withering in their blood, amidst the yells of savage [[?]]; and his mother, and brothers, and sisters borne off, he new not whither, by a band of lawless Creek marauders! To add to his agony at such a moment,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
an aged Indian woman, with her hair disheveled, and her round, fat face discoloured with excitement, followed them to the trader's house, calling upon Tunbridge to produce the white man, exclaiming, with a fiendish air of triumph,
"All the rest are kiled, and he must die also"!
The trader calmly replied to her, He's onley a little boy. It's a shame to kil children. "He shal not be kiled"
The old hag was excited, and vowed that the boy should be kiled. She said, "he was two large to allow him to live. In two or three years he would be a man; he would learn the countrey, its towns and its rivers; would make his escape, and come back with an Armey of white men to destroy us all".
She said her son, Cutty-a-toy,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
was a brave chief, and that he would be there in a few minutes to kill the boy. 
In a few minutes, Cutty-a-toy, followed by many armed warriors, rushed upon the traders house, and demanded the white boy.
The chief said the boy was too large that he would be soon grown, would take his escape, and bring back an armey to destroy their town.
The trader stood, with cool courage, in the door of his lodge, refused to surrender the prisoner, saying it was not right to kill children, and so warning the angrey chief that the boy was the prisoner of Kiachatalee, his son, and, if he was injured or slain, Kiachatalee would be avenged for it. 
As Kiachatalee was onley a young warriour, and Cutty-a-toy a chief and a

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
grey-beard, this threat of revenge greatley insensed him.
In an instant he raised his tomahawk, and, with the air of a man who intends a deed of murder, demanded of the trader, "And are you the friend of the Virginian?"
Answering the look rather than the words, the trader stepped out of his door, and said to the bloody brave, "Take him."
Cutty-a-toy then rushed into the trader's lodge, seized the  boy by the throat and was about to brain him with his tomahawk, when the wife of Tunbridge interposed, in a tone of suplication which at once succeeded . "Will the brave chieftain kill the boy in my house? Let not the boy's blood stain my floors." 
The appeal of the woman reached the savage's beast heart. He droped his weapon, and slowley draged

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
the boy out of the lodge into the midst of a crowde of savages, who waved their knives and hatchets in the poor boy's face, in order to enjoy his terror. 
In the path which led from the house, the boy fell upon his knees while the savages were tearing off his clothes, and asked the trader to request the savages to give him one half hour to pray.
The trader roughley replied, boy it is not worth while; they will kill you" As they boy stood in momentary expection of his fate, the traders wife again interposed, and begged the savage chief not to kill the boy in her yard, or in the path along which she had to carry water, but to take him out into the mountains, their the birds and wolves might eat up his flesh, where she could

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
not see his blood!
The appeal of the woman was again herd, and, giving the boy his pantaloons, they held a short talk, and agreed to take the boy down to the Running Water, saying to the traders wife, "We will not spill this boys blood near your house; but we will take him to Running Water, where we will have a  knocking him in the head."
Having gon about three hundred yards, they halted and formed a circle around the boy, and with their tomahawk seemed to be on the point of kiling him. 
The boy again fell upon his knees, and, with his face upturned towards heaven, and his hands firmley clasped on his breast, remained in prair, expecting at each moment the fatal blow.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
in that dreadful moment the boy thought of Stephens, to whos vision the heavens were opened at the moment on his death, and was happy.
As the savage braves stood around him, young Brown saw their stern brows of revenge suddenly relax, and a smile of sympathy and pity succed.
They called the trader, told him to take the  boy, that they would not kill him; and Cutty-a-toy said he loved the boy, and would come back in three weeks and make friends with him.
It was afterwards asertained  that Cutty-a-toy had taken some of Browns negroes, and claimed them as his prisoners, and that his fear lest Kichatalee might retaliate by kiling his negro prisoners, was the thought which suddenly turned Cutty-a-toy to

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
mercy and pity.
So thought his own followers; for when he said he loved the boy, and would not kill him, his savage followers replied: "No, no he does not love the boy; it's the boy's negro he loves."
When Cutt-a-toy's mother saw that the boy's life would not be taken, she seemd displeased; went up to the boy and cut off his scalp-lock, and kickid him so rudely in the side as almost to kill him, "I've got the Virginians scalp".
The Tuskegee chief, Cutt-a-toy led his party away, leaving the boy in the hands of the trader and his wife.
In two or three days, the boy was taken into Nickajack, and kind old chief, Breath, who greatley regreted what had taken place in his absence, took Joseph by the hand,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
consisting of a pair of dearskin moccasins. 
In this condition he was pronounced an Indian, with the execption of a slit in each ear, which the kindness of the chief defered making untill cold weather, the trader's wife took him to see his two sisters, Jane, aged ten, and Polly, aged five years, who had just ben brought back to Nickajack; a party of Cherokees having persued the Creek braves, and recaptured from them thes two small girls, after they had ben taken some distance towards the Creek towns.
From his sister Jane, Joseph learned the destination of the party who had carried off his mother, his brother George, and his sister

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
Elizabeth.
These children were now in the same town adopted into different families, and it was a source of consolation to them to be allowed to see each other occasionally.
In the various toils which were imposed upon these captive children, such as carrying water and wood, pounding hominy, and working corn in the field, and on the part of the boy, in looking after the stock, nearley a year passed off, without many insident worthy of note.
Hostile parties of savages came and went, and tales of barbarous deeds done by them on the distant frontiers were often told in the hearing of these children, but none of them brought deliverance for them.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
Yet in but few instanses did the savage neighbours of these captive children trat them unkindley. 
Three or four times the boy's life was in dainger from lawles braves, whos blood thirsty natures panted for the blood of the white man.
The good old chief Breath, hearing of these things, caused young Brown to be armed, and declared that it should be lawful for him to slay any Indian who should miss treat him.
In a few months Joseph was allowed a rifle and a horse, and permitted to go into the woods to hunt.
He might often have availed himself of the kindness of his savage friend, and made his escape to the frontiers,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
but he loved his little sisters, and his love for them restrained his desire for freedom, lest his escape might add to the rigors of their slavery, or perhaps for ever prevent their deliverance. 
In the mean time, an open [[?]] had been going on between the Indians and the people of Cumberland in East Tennessee.
Two thousand warriors, principally Cherokees, of [[?]] four of five hundred were horsemen dressed as white men, made [[?]] into East Tennessee, [[?]] every thing before them.
During this invasion, the Indians, sending forward their mounted men, dressed as white men, were enabled to surprise many, and thus to make havoc which they could not have done otherwise.
This [[?]] of the Indians was caused, they alleged, by murder of Tassel, there chief, when he gave under a white flag to General Sevier, to hold a talk.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
In this foray, the Indians took fort Gillespie, murdered the garrison, and carried off Mrs. Glass, the sister of Captain Gillespie. 
The whole country was aroused. General Joseph Martin and General John Sevier headed a large army, marched into the Indian nation, burnt up towns, and carried off their women and children. 
Amongst other prisoners taken this time, was the daughter of Turkey, chief of the Cherokees. 
In the spring of 1789, an exchange of prisoners was agreed upon, at a talk held with General Sevier.
It was agreed that the Cherokees should make an absolute surrender of all the white prisoners within their borders, and runners were sent to each of the head 
[[?]], to send their captives to the Little [[?]] for an exchange. 
When those runners came to Nickajack, young Brown was on a trading trip down the river with his Indian brother Kaichatlee, all did not return until Mrs. Glass

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
and all the other prisoners had gone to Running Water, where the chief was awaiting their arrival. 
When young Brown got home, he was sent with one of his sisters to Running Water, in order to be sent up to the treaty grounds to be exchanged.
His little sister would not leave her Indian Mother, who had ever treated her kindly, but wept and clung to her neck, declaring that it would break her Indian mother's heart if she left her.
This tender feeling was a tribute to Navajo kindness, but young Brown finally took his sister in his arms and carried her some distance, before he could reconcile her to go with him.
His eldest sister belonged to a trader that said he had bought her with his money, and would not let her go.
Young Brown had to leave her and, being wholly unable to redeem her.
At Running Water, young Brown heard Turkey, the head chief, stating to

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
chiefs around him the terms of the treaty he had made; and in doing so, his followers upbraided him for agreeing to give so many prisoners without any ransom.
To this the chief  replied that Little John (meaning Governor Sevier) would have it so; that he was a very [[?]] man-a dog; but he had my daughter a prisoner, and he knew I would have to agree to any terms, to get her back."
The next morning, when the Indian chief was about to start his prisoners forward, young Brown refused to go, and was taken to the chief to give his reasons. 
He then stated that one of his sisters was left in Nickajack, and that he never would consent to be set at liberty without his sister.
The savage chief immediately sent for the girl, and after some delay, Col. Bench, chief of the mounted regiment of Indians, went himself and brought the girl to Running Water. Thus, about the first of May 1789 young Brown and his two sisters were once

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
restored to liberty. Being reduced to [[?]] these now orphan children were sent into South Carolina, to sojourn with some relations and their elder brother, who was in Cumberland, could go often there, or until their mother would be released from her captivity amongst the Creeks.*
During the Creek war of 1812, Joseph Brow a Colonel, met a French trader who lived at Nickajack, who told him he had his father's library, taken from his boat on the 9th of May, 1788, which he had bought from the Indians, and generously offered to restore it to him at cost.
Although the books were valuable, Col. Brown never succeeded in obtaining them, they are now in all probability in some Cherokee Library in the West.
In order to keep up the thread of our narative , we must now return to the 9th of May, 1788, to continue the narrative of Mrs. Brown's captivity. 
Having seen her husband fall by hands of savages, she was hurried

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
away by her captors, and took the road southward, just as she heard the yells and rifles of the cruel savages who also ordered her sons and their companions. What must have been the feelings of horror and agony of this poor woman, herself a prisoner in the hands of she knew not whom, and borne she knew not where!
To add to the horror of her situation, she then saw two of her sweet little daughters torn from her side by a party of Cherokees, and borne back, she knew not whither, nor for what end!
[[?]] forward on foot for many days and nights, she continued to bear up under bodily fatigues and mental anguish in which she was tortured, her feet blistered and swolen, and driven before pack-horses, along a flinty path, 
every moment expecting death if she failed, and every moment expecting to fail! 
She [[?]] accomplishes many day's trail, and finally reaches one of the upper Creek towns

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
the Tallapoosa, far down in the wilderness, prisoner and slave of a savage brave.
Arrived at the town of her captor, she [[?]] she is a slave, doomed to bear [[?]] and water, and to pound hominy, to do all the servile offices of her savage mistress.
To add to her distress, her son, nine years old, and her daughter seven, are taken to different towns, and is left indeed alone in her sorrow.
At the period of Mrs. Brown's captivity, Alexander McGillevray, a half blood Creek of Scotch descent, was the [[?]] chief of the Muscogee Indians, he actually assumed the high-some title of Commander-in-chief of Upper and Lower Creeks and the Seminoles; being the military as well the civil governor of all the Indians in Florida, Alabama, and lower Georgia. 
He was a man of letters, of keen sagacity, forest-born and forest-bred, combining the shrewdness of the savages with learning of the civilized man.

transcription:
Historical  Tradition's of Tennessee.
The captivity of Jane Brown and her family until the year 1700, the teritory of North Carolina and Tennessee and an indefinite region extending south-west and north-west, in the language of the Royal British Charters, to the South Seas was known as "our Counties of Albermarle, in Carolina." 
Even as late as 1750, the country lying west of the Apalachian mountains was wholey unknown to the people of the Carolinas and Virginia.
When, a few years later, the British army under Braddock crossed the mountains from Maryland and Pennsylvania, and marched to Fort Du Quesne, now Pittsburg, that march was described by the writers of the times as an advance into the deep recesses and fastnesses of

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
savage wilderness. At that time the French owned all the Canada's, the valley of the Ohio and all its tributaries, and claimed the rest of the continent to the confines of Mexico westward from the Ohio and Missippi rivers.
The old French maps of that period, and the journals and letters of the French trader and hunters, together with the Tradition's of the Indians, affords the only reliable information in relation to the then condition of the country now composing Kentucky and Tennessee.
In the French maps of these times, the Kentucky, Holston, Tennessee and Ohio are laid down.
The Kentucky is called Catuway, the Holston is called the Cherokee; and little Tennessee is called Tanasees. The river, after the junction of the Holston and the Tennessee, is called Ho-go-hegee, and the only Indian town marked on its banks is at the mouth of Bear Creek,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
near the north-west corner of Alabama. There were forts (which were little more than trading-posts) at several points on the Ohio and Missippi; Fort Du Quesne, where Pittsburg now stands and one at the mouth of the Kenhawa river; an other at the mouth of the Kentucky,
and Fort Vincennes, near the mouth of the Oubach, or Wabsh; Fort Massac, half way between the mouth of  the Ohio and Tennessee, on the Illinois side, and an other on the Tennessee, twelve miles above its mouth. 
They also had a fort where Memphis now stands, called Prud'homme; another at the mouth of the Arkansas, called Ackeusa; another near Natchez, and one at the junction of the Coosa and Tallapoosa, called Halabamas. 
South of these last forts, the Spaniards had possession in Florida, Louisiana, and Texas. 
A great part of Kentucky, Tennessee,and Western Virginia, was represented on these maps as wholey uninhabited. Certain it is that, not more than a dozen years

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
afterwards, when the pioneers of Tennessee and Kentucky first explored that region, they found the banks of the Holston, Watagua,Cumberland, and Kentucky, with their tributaries, wholey uninhabited.
It was all our vast wilderness, into which hunting-parties of Indians from its distant borders entered and roamed in pursuite of game, but in which they made no permanent lodgement.
Numerous warlike nations lived south, west, and north of this wilderness, but it was a "dark and bloody ground", in which they loved not to dwell. And hither it was that the lion-harted pioneers of the Cumberland and Watauga came, with ax and rifle to subdue at once the savage and the wilderness.
In 1758 Colonel Bird, of the British army established Fort  Chissel, in Wyth county, Va, to protect the frontiers of Virginia, and  advansing into what is now Sullivan county Tenn, built a fort near Long

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
Island, on the Holston  or Watauga.  There was not then a single white man living in the borders of Tennessee.
The year before, Governor Dobbs, of North Carolina, had at the request of the Cherokee Indians, built Fort Lowdon and the Indians agreed to make grants of land to all artisans who would settle among them. 
Fort Lowdon was on Little Tennessee, near the mouth of Tellico river, in the center of the Cherokee nation, and about one hundred miles south of the fort at Long Island.
Between these forts were the first settlements, which struggled for several years againss the fearful ravages of Indian was before the beginning of the Revolution.
During that period, that region became the refuge of many patriots, who were driven by the British invasion from Carolinas.
From the years 1780 to 1790, many of the best families of the Carolinas, Georgia, and Virginia, sought houses beyond

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
the mountains.Many of them, patriotic republicans, who had sacrafised everything for their countrey in the struggle for independence, and hoped to have found, in the secluded vales and the thick forests of the west, that peace and quiet which they had not found amidst the din of  civil and foreign war, soon experienced all the horrors a savage, marauding, guerilla war-fare, which swept away their property,  and deprived them of their wives and children, either by a barbarous death, or a not less agonizing slavers captives, draged into the wild recesses of the Indian borders.
Many fearful tales of these bloody scenes,which would illustrate the early history of Tennessee, are only known to a few, as familey  traditions, and, even amongst the descendants of the sufferers, are only remembered as stories of the nursery, and not chapters in the great historic record of the past.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
It is not always in the most distinguished achievements that mans virtues or vices, may be best discerrned; but
often an action of small note, or short saying, or a jest, shal distinquish a person's real character more than the greatest sieges or the most important battles."* And so it is, in some sort, with history of a people or a nation.
The experiences, the sufferings, and conduct of a single individual of community, may better illustrate the condition, progress, or character of  the people, than whole chapters devoted to the details of a campaign.
In this point of view, the traditional recollections which are detailed in the following sketch of the family of James Brown connected, as they were, so intimatley with some of the most important political events of that period, cannot fail to throw new light upon the pioneer history of the countrey, and inspire our
*Plutarch's Alexander.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
[[?]]nets with renewed gratitude to those [[?]]udy, but wise men and women, who built up so goodley a state, amidst so many troubles, in the dark and bloody valleys of the  Chauvanon, Tanasees and ho- go-iegee.
The subject of this sketch was born in Pensylvania about the year 1740. Her father was a pioneer in the settlement of North Carolina.
Her family was one of the most respectable as well as the most worthy in the county of Guilford, where they resided during the Revolutionary War.
Two of her brothers, Colonel and Major Gillispie, were distinguished for their gallantry and devotion to the caus of liberty, and were honored as brave officers.
Herself and most of her familey were members of the Rev. David Caldwell's church at Guilford, and ardently espoused both his political and religious principles.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
About the year 1761 or 1762, Miss Gillespie became the wife of James Brown, a native of Ireland, whose familey settled in Guilford some years before. 
In the beginning of the Revolution, Mrs. Brown had a large familey of small children, but she freeley gave up her husband when his countrey demanded his servises. 
During the masterley retreat of Gen. Greene, in the winter of 1781, on Dan and Deep rivers, Mr. Brown was the pilot and guide of Colonels Lee and Washington, and by his intimate knowledge of the countrey, its by-paths and fords, contributed not a little to the successful counter-marches of the American armey, by which they were enabled to allude and brake the spirit of the armey of Lord Cornwallis. 
When the American assumed the offencive, and, from a retreating, suddenly became a pursuing armey, Brown pressed eagerley into the fight

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
with the bold troopers of Lee and Washington. 
Being in moderate circumstances, and pressed by the cairs of a large and increasing familey, Brown's ardent temperament was not satisfied with the prospect of a ploding  life of toil in Guilford.
For his revolutionary services he had received from the state of North Carolina land warrants, which entitled him to locate large quantities of lands in the wilderness beyond the mountains. 
His neighbores had honored him as the sheriff of the county, and as a  justice of the county court, and he was rapidley rising in the estimation of his countrey men, for his patriotism, integrity, and many other virtues of a good citizen.
But he readiley saw the advantages which he might secure to

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
his rising familey by striking out into the deep forests, and securing for them the choisest houses in the Tennessee and Cumberland valleys.
He could command onley a trifle in money for his land scrip, but, by exposing himself to a few years of hardship and danger, he could secure independent estates for his numerous children.
With him, to be convinsed was to act: his decision and his actions went together.
Tearing himself from the bosom of his familey, and all the  endearments of a happy home circle, he set out on his journey to explore the valley of the Cumberland.
The whole of Tennessee was then a wilderness, exept  smal  spots on the Holston and Watauga, on the East, and a small spot around Nashville and Bledsoe's Lick, on the west of Cumberland Mountains.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
Taking with him his two eldest sons, William and John, and a few tried friends, he explored the Cumberland valley.
He secured lands on the Cumberland river below Nashville, at the place now known as Hyde's Ferry. 
He also explored the wilderness south, as far as Duck river, and located a large body of land south of Duck river, was Columbia.
The whole Countrey was then almost untrod by foot of the white man. It was the hunting ground of the Chickasaws, Creeks, and Cherokees, and was full of deer, elk, bars, and buffaloes.
The rich uplands, as well as the alluvial bottoms of the rivers, were covered with cane-brakes which were almost impervious to man. Whoever penetrated these regions, did so with knife and hatchet to cut away the cane,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
and with rifle to oppose the savage beast, and savage men who swarmed through its deep fastnesses.
But Brown's hart was a bold one, and his hopes for the futures anamated him to perserverance.
Having located by actual survey several fine tracts of land, he determined to return to Guilford, and remove his family to their new home in the west. 
Leaving William as a deputy surveyer under Colonel Polk and John to open and cultivate a small field, and build some cabins at the mouth of White's Creek, he returned to North Carolina.
In the winter of 1787-8, Brown and his family, having disposed of his property, found themselves on the banks of the French Broad, in what is now Hawkins county, Tennessee, awaiting the opening of spring,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
before beginning their journey across the mountains to the Cumberland valley.
In 1785, the treaty of Hopwell had now concluded with the Cherokees, guaranteeing  reciprocal friendship between that nations and the Americans. 
At the time Brown arived on the banks of the French Broad, there was apparent acquiescence in the terms of this treaty, and the Cherokee and the white man seemed, for a time, to have smoked the pipe of peace, and buried the tomahawk forever.
There were two routes to the Cumberland valley at this time: The one way by land, the other by water. The land route was a long and tedious one, through Cumberland Gap, across the head-waters of the Cumberland, Green, and Barren rivers, in Kentucky,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
to Bledsoe's Lick, or Nashville the other route was easier of accomplishment, and more desirable; because, being by the desent of the river, it admitted of the transportation  of the goods and aged persons.
Brown, on his recent visit to Cumberland, had had of Colonel Donelson's voyage down the Tennessee up the Ohio and Cumberland, to Nashville, and one or two other parties who had succeded in making the same voyage.
As he had women and small children, and packages of valuable goods which he was taking to the West, he resolved to hazard the decent of the Tenness river.
He was not ignorant of the fact that there were many populous Indian towns on the Tennessee river, of both the Cherokee and Chickasaw nations, and that marauding parties of Creeks and

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
Shawnees were often on its shores and towns. He new the danger of the voyage, on account of the hostile Indians who might be encountered on its water or its shores; and he also new its numerous shoals, rapids, and eddies, rendered its navigation perilous of such frail open boats as could be constructed.
But he confided in the honest disposition of the Cherokees to conform to the treaty of Hopewell, and felt that the marauding Creeks and Shawnees would prove less dangerous on the water than on the circuitous land route to the Cumberland.
Having been habitualy exposed to danger for many years, it is probable that he rather sought the most perilously dangerous route, feeling a sort of manley desire to meet and over come it.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
having built a boat, after the stile of comon flat boat, moddled as much as posible after the stile of Noah's ark (except that it was open at the top,) he prepared to adventure the fearful voyage.
About the first of May, 1788, having taken onboard a large amount of goods suitable for traffic among the Indians and pioneers in Cumberland, his party embarked upon the bosom of French Broad.
The party was a small and weak one, considering the daingers it had to encounter, and the valuable cargo it had to defend.
It consisted of Brown, two grown sons, three hired men and a negro man, in all, seven grown men; Mrs. Brown, three small sons and four small daughters; one aged woman the mother of one of the hired men,

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
and two or three negro women, the property of Brown.
To make up for the weakness of his party, Brown had mounted a small cannon upon the prow of his boat, and  no doubt relied as much for his security upon the known terror which such guns inspired in the breasts of the savages, as  upon any damage which he expected to inflict upon them with it.
Thus appointed and thus equipped, this happy familey began its eventful dicent of the French Broad and Tennessee.
All was gladness, all was sunshine. The land of their fathers, of their loved friends, and pastor, was behind them; beneath their oars flashed the bright water of a lovely stream, whos winding chanel would soon bear them to the enchanted valley of the fairy Cumberland.

title: Jane Brown and family 1788 captivity narrative, 1851
transcription:
As they passed rapidley along the curent which was to bear them to their new home, the father sat in the midst of his little children; hopefully describing their new home in the deep forests of the West.
They then descended  the French Broad to the Tennessee, and went on merriley down its waters 
Chickumauga, a considerable town of Cherokee Indians, situated not far from the present site of Chattanooga. Hear the Indians appeared friendley; the principal chief went on board the boat, and made inquiry for various articles of goods, proposed to trade, and finaly took his leave, with many professions of kindness.
Our voyagers continued their decent, rejoysing in the happy omen which the friendship of the Chickmauaga chieftain opened for their future.

A man by the name of John Vaun, well known half-breed, who spoke good English, was the leader of the party, but he was unknown to Brown. Vaun spoke to Brown, and said his party came in friendship; that, as an evidence of that, they had raised a white flag; that they came as friends to trade with him. For our Redeemer's sake"-
{L.H.S.-}

title: Antoinette Putnam Metcalf commonplace book, 1886-1898
transcription:
Extract-
"Since trifles make the sum of human things,
And half our misery from our foibles springs,
Since life's best joys consist in peace and ease,
And though but few can serve, yet all may please,
Oh let the ungentle spirit learn from these,
'A small unkindness is a great offence';
The mild forbearance of a brother's fault,
The angry word suppressed, the taunting thought;
Subduing and subdued, the petty strife
Which clouds the color of domestic life,
The sober comfort, all the peace who springs
From the large aggregate of little things,-
On these small cares of daughter, wife, or friend,
The almost sacred joys of home depend."
{Hannah Moore}

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription: Excelsior Diary

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  TUES. JAN. 11, 1898  Ther. 

Sehr trübes, häßliches
Regenwetter. Ich früh  
mit Arthur in die Stadt 
gegangen. Bei ihm und
Eddi auf der office. 

Zum lunch Eddi bei
uns gewesen. 

Nachmittag Mama 
und ich zuhause. Klavier
gespielt, geschrieben. 
Viele Briefe aus Europa 
erhalten. Herr Jürgens 
geschäftlich bei Mama. 

Abends zuhause gesessen,
gelesen. Früh zu Bett. 

Arthur bestimmt mit Tosetti abgeschlossen. 
O


Wea.  WEDNESDAY 12  Ther.

Trübes, regnerisches, windiges
Wetter. Vormittag 
zuhause geblieben. Eddi 
nach dem lunch gekommen. 
Nachmittag Mama 
und ich in den Columbia
Damenklub zum Kaffee 
gegangen. Sehr gut amüsirt.
Emma Eitel, Lily 
und Nelly Stern, Ida Kochs 
Paula Andersen, Rapps, Frl.
Böttcher, Frau Bluthardt, 
Frau Prüssing etc. etc. 

Nachher zu Arthur auf 
die office: Günzel dort
Arthur nicht zum Abendessen,
erst um 10 Uhr nach Haus gekommen.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  THUR. JAN. 13, 1898  Ther. 

Trübes, warmes Wetter.   
Sehr früh aufgestanden. 
Ich Vormittag in die 
Stadt gegangen, auf 
Eddies Office, Eddie mit 
mir zum lunch nach Hause. 

Nachmittag Dr. Bluthardt 
bei uns gewesen. 

Zum Abendessen Eddi, 
Toni und Herr Brucker 
bei uns. Abends Herr 
Brucker mit Mama und 
Eddi große geschäftliche 
Unterredung gehabt. 
Arges Schneegestöber. 
O.


Wea.  FRIDAY  14  Ther. 

Trübe, aber nicht kalt.
Ich Vormittag in die 
Stadt gegangen, Einkäufe 
gemacht. 

Mama mit argen 
Kopfschmerzen den ganzen 
Tag zuhause geblieben. 
Gegen Abend 
besser. 

Nachmittag viel 
Haus und Küchenarbeit 
gethan. 

Abends wir drei:
Mama Arthur und ich 
gemüthlich zusammen 
gesessen, gelesen, geplaudert. 
O

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  SAT. JAN. 15, 1898.  Ther. 

Patsch- und Regenwetter,.
Vormittag Mama und 
ich in die Stadt gegangen.
Eddi zum lunch 
bei uns. Nachmittag 
gewirtschaftet. Ich Kopfweh 
gehabt.

Abends Eddi, Toni, 
Arthur und ich zusammen 
bei uns ein Diner
gegeben. Gäste: Brands,
Nelly Stern, Günzel, 
Eitels, Webers. Zwölf Personen 
bei Tisch; bis halb 
eins geblieben. Sieben
Gänge. Alle Schwips gehabt. 


Wea.  SUNDAY 16  Ther. 

Schönes, sonniges, kaltes
Wetter. Schnee. 
Morgens bis elf geschlafen. 
Arthur Katzenjammer 
gehabt. 

Den ganzen Tag 
Arthur, Mama und ich 
allein zusammen 
zuhause. Gelesen, 
musicirt. 

Nachmittag Arthur 
und ich einen Spaziergang 
gemacht. 

(Um diese Zeit 
Eddi's erste sh[?]ts 
fertig geworden).

Früh zu Bette.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  MON. JAN. 17, 1898  Ther. 

Schönes klares Wetter. 
Vormittag Hausarbeit 
gethan. Briefe aus Pesth.

Nachmittag Mama und 
ich in der Stadt, bei 
Arthur gewesen. Dann 
zu Ryckoffs zum Kaffee. 
Ich vorher einen Augenblick 
bei Toni. Malchen Kochs 
dort. Frau Leeb getroffen.
Bei Ryckoffs Frau Bauer 
und Klärchen gewesen. 

Sehr nett. Klärchen wunderhübsch. - 
Arthur abends nicht 
ganz wohl. Ich mit ihm langen
Spaziergang auf Westseite gemacht.


Wea.  TUESDAY 18  Ther. 

Wunderschönes, klares
Wetter. Ich früh mit 
Arthur in die Stadt gegangen,  
Einkäufe gemacht. 
Frl. Gustchen zum Nähen
bei uns. Eddi zum lunch 
zu uns gekommen. Mama
Nachmittag in der Stadt.
Abends in Gallauer's Halle 
Klub-Zusammenkunft unter 
meiner Oberleitung. Erst
Kartenspiel mit Preisen, dann 
lunch, musikalisches Programm 
(Sänger Camman, 
Günzel, Miss Blocki) und zuletzt
Tanz. Erst um 1/2 2 Uhr 
aus. Wir um 3 zu Bett gekommen. 
O

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  WED. JAN. 19, 1898  Ther.

Schmutziges Thauwetter.
Vormittag Hausarbeit
gethan. Frl. Gustchen 
bei uns. Nachmittag 
Mama und ich zu Fuß 
in die Stadt gegangen, 
Einkäufe gemacht.

Dann ich zu Emma 
Eitel zur italienischen 
Stunde <strikethrough>bei</strikethrough> mit Frau Mels
Mattie Arnold Clothilde
Schmidt dort.

Abends zuhause. 
Mama arge Migräne 
gehabt. Ich Arthur vorgelesen.
Briefe aus Pesth erhalten. 


Wea.  THURSDAY 20  Ther. 

Trübes, schmutziges Thauwetter.
Mama besser.
Frau Scheuermann und
Frl. Gustchen zum Nähen
bei uns. 

Ich Vormittag ein 
wenig spazieren gegangen, 
dann den
ganzen Tag zuhause, 
genäht. Kaffeekränzchen 
bei Frau Heffert, aber 
Mama nicht hingegangen.

Abends Alle 3 gemüthlich  
in unserm Zimmer 
gesessen, vorgelesen. Ich 
mit Arthur ernste Unterhaltung 
gehabt. 
O

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  FRI. JAN. 21, 1898  Ther. 

Trockenes, trübes, warmes
Wetter. Ich früh 
mit Arthur zu Fuß in die 
Stadt. Bei Eddi und Herrn
Pietsch. Frl. Gustchen bei uns.
Mama nicht wohl. Eddi 
zum lunch bei uns. 

Nachmittag Mama
und ich einen Spaziergang 
gemacht. - Ich mein Haar 
gewaschen. 

Abends wir drei
gemüthlich in unserm Zimmer 
gesessen, vorgelesen.
Barnell Günther uns besucht 
auf ein Stündchen. -  Ich gebadet. 
O.


Wea.  SATURDAY 22  Ther.

Schneegestöber. Ich früh
mit Arthur zu Fuß in die 
Stadt, zu Fuß zurück. Frl.
Gustchen bei uns.

Ich Nachmittag zu
Toni zum Kränzchen. 
Stella, Laura Kranz, 
Frida Gugler, Janet Klocke 
dort. Sehr gemüthlich. 
Abends Mama, Arthur 
und ich zum Abendessen 
bei Leebs. Prachtvoller 
Apfelstrudel. Frau Krause,
Frau [Camwert?], Leebs. Sehr 
spät geblieben, geplaudert. 
Im Wagen nach Hause. 
Fürchterlicher Schneesturm.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  SUN. JAN. 23, 1898  Ther. 

Sonnenschein. Alles
fußhoch mit Schnee bedeckt.
Prachtvoller Anblick. 
Vormittag und 
zum Essen wir drei
allein. Nachmittag 
Hans Mannhardt uns 
besucht, drei Stunden
geblieben. Eddi und 
Toni zum Abendessen 
gekommen. Eddi stark
erkältet. Arthur uns 
Veilchen gebracht. Abends 
Arthur und ich mit Eddi und 
Toni zu Fuß nach der Stadt,
und zurück. Früh zu Bett. 
O. 


Wea.  MONDAY 24  Ther. 

Schönes, kaltes Wetter.
Früh Hausarbeit gethan.
Dann Mama und ich 
zusammen in die Stadt 
gegangen. Einkäufe 
gemacht. Bei Schlesinger 
und Marger im Café
lunch gegessen. Nachmittag 
zuhause geblieben,
genäht.

Tosetti mit der fire 
insurance fertig geworden.

Abends Arthur, Mama
und ich gemüthlich 
zusammen gesessen, gelesen. 
Früh zu Bett.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  TUES. JAN. 25, 1898.  Ther.

Fürchterlicher Schneesturm 
den ganzen Tag. Fußhoher 
Schnee. Entsetzliches Schneegestöber. 
Den ganzen Tag 
zuhause geblieben, gearbeitet. 
Arthur schon um 
vier von der office gekommen. 
Große Toilette gemacht. 
Mein Brautkleid. Mit Mama 
und Arthur auf dem German 
American Charity Ball 
im Auditorium gewesen.
Eddi, Toni, Bruckers, Leebs, 
Irma Stein, Emil Eitel mit 
uns bei Tisch. Mit Lotz, Lee, Eitel
getanzt. Um 4 Uhr nach Haus. 


Wea.  WEDNESDAY 26  Ther. 

Sehr schönes, sonniges, 
kaltes Wetter. Lange geschlafen.
Ich schrecklichen
Katzenjammer gehabt.
Zuhause geblieben, Nachmittag
geschlagen. Unser 
Empfangstag, aber Niemand 
gekommen. 

Abends Mama, Arthur 
und ich in die Germania 
gegangen auf Janina Zeggels 
Einladung. Dort Theateraufführung
des Thespis-Klub
unter Frau Hüfners 
Leitung: W. Mathäi, Aug. 
Kochs, Spielmann, Frl. Riel.
Sehr gut. Alle Bekannten dort.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  THUR. JAN. 27, 1989  Ther. 

Wunderschönes, sonniges 
Wetter. Lange geschlafen. 
Ich mit Walther 
zu Fuß in die Stadt.
Bei Jürgens und Pietsch. 
Mama Kopfweh gehabt. 
Frau Leeb's Geburtstag. 
Nachmittag zuhause.

Abends Arthur und
ich nach der Germania 
gefahren zu Emma Eitel's
Schlittenparthie. Zu spät
gekommen, wieder 
nach Haus gefahren. 
Unterwegs im Bismark 
eingekehrt.
O.


Wea.  FRIDAY 28  Ther.

Wunderschönes, warmes
Wetter. Morgens Mama 
und ich mit Herrn Pietsch 
und Jürgens in der
Staats-Zeitung Geschäfts-Conferenz 
gehabt. 

Lunch bei Schlesinger 
und Marger Café. Auf 
Eddi's office gewesen.
Zu Fuß nach Hause. 

Mama sehr aufgeregt 
wegen ihrer Vermögensverhältnisse.

Abends wir drei 
gemüthlich in unserm Zimmer 
gesessen; gelesen. Arthur und 
ich "blues" gehabt. 
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  SAT. JAN. 29, 1898  Ther. 

Wunderschönes, kaltes
Wetter. Vormittag 
zuhause geblieben, Briefe 
geschrieben. 

Nachmittag Mama 
und ich zu Fuß in die 
Stadt gegangen. Ich 
zu Mattie Arnold zur 
italienischen Stunde, aber 
Frau Dr. Mels nicht dort. 
Clothilde Schmidt, Maria Eitel
auch zum Kaffee dort. 

Abends Günzel bei
uns bis nach 12 Uhr wegen
Theater-Aufführung.
Mädchen auf dem Maskenball.  
O.


Wea.  SUNDAY 30  Ther. 

Sehr schönes Wetter. Leichter 
Schneefall. O. Morgens 
sehr lange geschlafen; ich gebadet. -
Zu Mittag wir 
drei allein. Nachmittag 
Arthur und ich langen Spaziergang
gemacht. Zum
Kaffee, Eddi und Toni
Günzel, Emma & Emil Eitel
bei uns. Zum Abendessen 
geblieben, alle. - 

Abends wir drei 
mit Eddi und Toni ins
Deutsche Theater gegangen. 
"Hans Huckebein" von Schönthan 
und Kadelburg. Nachher 
im Bismark. -

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  MON. JAN. 31, 1898  Ther. 

Wunderschönes, kaltes,
Wetter. Ich früh mit
Arthur zu Fuß in die
Stadt, zu Fuß zurück.
Hausarbeit, Briefe geschrieben.
Mama wegen
ihres Vermögens sehr
aufgeregt. Ich ihr den
Kopf (wirklich) gewaschen. 
Frau Madlener uns 
besucht. Ein Stündchen 
geblieben. 

Abends Arthur, Mama
und ich gemüthlich zusammen im
Vorderzimmer gesessen: Englisch 
gelesen und geschrieben.  
O.


Wea.  TUES. FEB. 1  Ther. 

Sehr kalt, aber schönes, 
klares Wetter. Mama nicht 
wohl. Ich Vormittag zu
Hause geblieben, Hausarbeit 
gethan. Junge Frau 
Kölling gestorben.

Nachmittag ich 
zu Fuß in die Stadt, 
zu Fuß zurück. Schöner
Spaziergang. 

Mit Mama gemüthlich 
Kaffee getrunken. 

Abends Arthur nicht 
wohl, schlimme Augen 
gehabt. Trüber Abend.
Früh zu Bett.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  WED. FEB. 2, 1898  Ther. 

Sehr schönes, aber kaltes,
windiges Wetter; Schnee.
Arthur krank. Ich früh mit
ihm in die Stadt gefahren, 
ihn gleich wieder mit nach 
Hause gebracht. Günzel 
gesprochen. - Arthur und
Mama nicht wohl. Den
ganzen Tag zu Hause. 

Ich Nachmittag in die 
Stadt gegangen, sonst aber 
zuhause geblieben und
Arthur gepflegt. Abends 
gemüthlich in unserm
Zimmer gesessen, gelesen.
Arthur Fieber gehabt. 


Wea.  THURSDAY 3  Ther. 

Sehr kaltes, aber schönes 
Wetter. Arthur krank
zuhause geblieben, auch 
Mama nicht wohl. Ich
Vormittags Beide gepflegt. 

Nachmittag zu Toni
gefahren, sie abgeholt, 
zusammen zur großen reception 
bei Stella Leicht; 
alles großartig. 

Dann zum Kaffee 
zu Frau Leeb, zu Ehren 
Irma Steins. 13 Damen 
dort. Alles mit Rosa 
und Veilchen. Gut unterhalten. - 
Abends Günzel 
bei uns, Arthur besser. 
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  FRI. FEB. 4, 1898  Ther. 

+++

Trübes, kaltes Wetter. 
Arthur wieder in's
Geschäft gegangen. Mama
nicht wohl zuhause. 
VormittagHandarbeit 
gemacht. Nachmittag zu
Clothilde Schmidt zur ital. 
Stunde. Frau Dr. Mels, Emma 
Eitel, Mattie Arnold dort.  

Ich bei Eddi und Toni 
zum Abendessen. Arthur mich
dort abgeholt, zu Frau
Madleners Empfangstag gegangen.
Junge Leichts, Eitels, Frl.
[Velger?] und [Hedler?] dort. - Nachher 
noch bei Bruckers. Leebs, Champagner.
Um 22 Uhr zu Hause. 

+++


Wea.  SATURDAY 5  Ther. 

Trübes Thauwetter. 
Mama schrecklich krank 
mit Migräne. Den
ganzen Tag im Bett. 
Ich sie gepflegt, auch 
den ganzen Tag zu
Hause; nicht wohl. 

Herr [Platky?] aus
New York uns besucht,
aber wir uns verleugnen 
lassen. 

Arthur schon Nachmittag 
nach Hause gekommen. 
Mama viel
besser. Abends gemüthlich 
zusammen gelesen.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  SUN. FEB. 6, 1898  Ther. 

Schönes Wetter. Spät
aufgestanden. Zu Mittag   
wir drei allein. 

Nachmittag Arthur und 
ich zu Emma Eitel (theilweis 
zu Fuß). Dort unser Theaterstück
geprobt: Günzel, Zeisler
Emma Ryckoff, Eddi, Toni, Eitel. 
Zum Abendbrot bei Eitels
geblieben: Nellie Stern, M. Frank,
A. Woltersdorf dazu. Abends 
Alle ins Deutsche Theater: <underlined>"Dr.
Claus"</underlined> gesehen. Drei Logen gehabt,
zu Ehren von Irma Stein 
und Nellie Stern. Nachher im <underlined>Bismark</underlined>
großer Commers. 24 Personen. Um
1/2 3 Uhr zuhause. 


Wea.  MONDAY 7  Ther.

Sehr schönes Wetter, aber 
furchtbarer Schmutz. Vormittag 
Hausarbeit gethan. 
Ich nicht ganz wohl. 

Mama und ich Nachmittag 
in die Stadt gefahren 
(bei Frau Schüttler 
vorgesprochen), Einkäufe 
gemacht. Dann ich zu Stella
Leicht ins Lesekränzchen. 
Toni, Jamie Blocki, Laura 
Kranz, Paula Andersen,
Frida Gugler dort. Zum
Abendessen zuhause. 

Abends gemüthlich in
unserm Zimmer gelesen.  
Früh zu Bett.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  TUES. FEB. 8, 1898  Ther. 

Warmes Wetter und 
entsetzlicher Schmutz. Vormittag 
zuhause gearbeitet. 
Nachmittag Mama und 
ich in der Stadt, Besorgungen 
gemacht. Herrn Jürgens 
getroffen. Bertha 14 Jahre 
bei uns. 

Abends Mama, Arthur 
und ich in die Germania 
zum Club-meeting gefahren. 
Kegeln, dann oben
Essen, Valentine-Vertheilung 
Tanz. Von Emma Eitel arrangiert.
Ueber 30 Personen.
Um 1/2 2 Uhr nach Haus gekommen. 


Wea.   WEDNESDAY 9   Ther. 

Trübes, nebliges und entsetzlich
schmutziges Wetter. 
Vormittag zuhause gearbeitet. 

Mittags der alte
Graf Contin uns besucht. 
Dann Mama und ich 
Visiten im Coupé gemacht.
Bei Pietsch's (Frau Pietsch 
nicht zuhause) bei Frau Floto 
(blos Mama), bei Frau Brüning 
und Ireen (Kaffee getrunken. 
Dann bei Frau Petersen und
Ida Kochs und bei der alten
Frau Rehm. - Schrecklicher
Nebel. Abends gemüthlich 
mit Arthur zuhause.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  THUR. FEB. 10, 1898  Ther. 

Sehr warmes, trübes 
Frühjahrswetter. Ich früh um
10 Uhr Emma Eitel bei Emil in 
der Stadt getroffen. Zu Arthur 
hinauf, dort Brand gesehen.
Dann mit Emma zu Mandels,
dort Mama getroffen und wir
dann in's Bismark. Dort 
mit Arthur, Emil Eitel, Willi
Hüfner, Weber zu Mittag gegessen.
Nachher zusammen 
Besorgungen gemacht. 

Abends gemüthlich wir
drei zuhause geblieben. 
Mama nicht wohl, gelesen,
genäht. Ich gebadet.
O.


Wea.   FRIDAY 11  Ther.

Trübes, schmutziges Wetter. 
Vormittag zuhause gearbeitet. 
Nachmittag Mama Kaffeegesellschaft
gehabt. Alles in 
Gelb dekorirt, sehr schön. 
Frau Leeb, Frl. Böttcher, Frau 
Conrat, Frau Eberlein, Frau Zeggel
und Janina, Frau Bauer und 
Klärchen, Frau Ryckoff und 
Emma, Frau Brucker und Toni. 

Zum Abendbrot Eddi,
Toni und <underlined>Willi</underlined> bei uns.
Spät geblieben, sehr lustig 
zusammen. Beim Kaffee 
selbstgemachte Tischkarten (mit 
baby-ribbon) und Lichtmanschetten 
(tissue-paper).
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.   SAT. FEB. 12, 1898   Ther. 

Trübes, warmes, schmutziges
Wetter. Mama und ich 
früh mit Arthur in die Stadt,
Besorgungen gemacht. Bei
Eddi und Arthur auf der office. 

Nachmittag zu Arnolds 
gefahren, Mama und ich,
zu Mattie's Geburtstag. 
Emma und Maria Eitel, 
Clothilde Schmidt auch da. 
Zum Kaffee geblieben. 

Abends Mama, Arthur 
und ich zusammen gemüthlich 
zuhause. Ich schlecht
gefühlt: nervöses Zittern gehabt.
Früh zu Bett. Schlecht geschlafen.  


Wea.  SUNDAY 13   Ther. 

Wunderschönes, trockenes
Wetter. Arthur Vormittag 
auf die office. Mama 
und ich Spaziergang westlich
gemacht. Zum Mittagessen
Günzel, Eddi und 
Toni bei uns. Nachmittag 
Emma und Emil Eitel, Herr
Zeisler, Emma Ryckoff, Willi 
Hüfner dazu gekommen. 
Probe für Theaterstück 
gehalten - Alle zum Abendbrot 
und abends bei uns 
geblieben. Musicirt, lustig
gewesen. Arthur und ich zu Fuß 
mit ihnen bis an die Brücke und 
zurück gegangen. Ich nicht wohl.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  MON. FEB. 14, 1898   Ther. 

Mama mit Kopfschmerzen 
aufgewacht, den ganzen 
Tag krank in ihrem
Zimmer. St. Valentine's 
Tag. Ich eine reizende, gemalte 
Karte von Arthur 
bekommen. Auch nicht 
ganz wohl. Früh mit
Arthur zu Fuß in die
Stadt gegangen, zu Fuß 
zurück. Einige Stunden 
lang heftiger Schneefall. Ich 
zuhause geblieben, genäht,
gelesen, geschrieben. Abends 
gemüthlich in unserm Zimmer  
gesessen. Früh zu Bett. 
O.


Wea.   TUESDAY 15   Ther. 

Trübes, kaltes Wetter.
Schnee. Mama recht schlecht 
gefühlt. Ich auch nicht
wohl: <underlined> nervös aufgewacht.</underlined>

Nachmittag in die Stadt 
gefahren,  Einkäufe gemacht,
mit vielen Paketen nach
Haus gekommen. Dr. Bluthardt 
inzwischen bei Mama 
gewesen, sehr strenge 
Diät verordnet. 

Abends wir drei zu 
Hause geblieben, vorgelesen,
genäht. Ich immer etwas 
nervös und aufgeregt. 
Spät eingeschlafen; noch 
lange mit Arthur unterhalten.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  WED. FEB. 16, 1898   Ther.  

Trübes, kaltes Wetter. 
Vormittag sehr viel gearbeitet. 
Mama in der 
Stadt. Ich Mittags einen 
"lunch" für meine 
"graduating-class" gehabt. 
Toni, Luise Woltersdorf, 
Fannie Skinner, Ida Wright, 
Mattie Simpson und  ihre 
Cousine aus Pittsburg dabei
gewesen. 5 Gänge, sehr 
gut. Alle bis nach 4 Uhr  
geblieben. Eddie und Toni 
zum Abendessen bei uns.
Maskenkostüme geschneidert.
Ich arges nervöses Zittern gehabt.


Wea.  THURSDAY 17   Ther. 

Trübes, kaltes Wetter.
Unsere Ida krank, Bertha 
geschäftlich bei Herrn Pietsch. 
Vormittag zuhause mit
Mama Maskenkostüme geschneidert. 
Ich sehr nervös, 
aufgeregt, zittrig. 

Nachmittag Regenguß,
abscheulicher Schmutz. Ich in
die Stadt gefahren, Einkäufe 
gemacht, bei Arthur gewesen 
auf der office, bei Eddi und 
Emil Eitel. Mit Arthur zu 
Fuß nach Haus. Ein wenig
ruhiger und wohler
gefühlt. Abends gemüthlich 
zuhause gelesen, etc. -
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  FRI. FEB. 18, 1898   Ther.

Trübes, kaltes Wetter. 
Morgens Frau Scheuermann 
zum Nähen gekommen und 
Toni gegen Mittag. Maskenanzüge 
genäht. Toni
zum lunch, nachmittags 
und zum Abendessen bei uns.
Ich während des Tags wohl
und ruhig, abends wieder 
etwas nervös.

Gleich nach Abendessen 
Toni und ich ins Bismark gefahren,
dort Arthur, Eddi, Willi 
und Eitels getroffen. Schon um 1/2 9
Uhr nach Hause. Arthur und ich 
zu Fuß. Arthur krank, Magenschmerz.


Wea.  SATURDAY 19   Ther.

Arthur die ganze Nacht krank
gewesen, fiebrisch. Vormittag 
zu Hause und im Bett geblieben. 
Regen und Schmutzwetter. Ich 
morgens in die Stadt zu Günzel 
und Eddi. Herz Nachmittag auf 
die office; recht schlecht gefühlt.
Ich später auch nicht wohl, nervös,
aufgeregt. - Abends Mama, Arthur
und ich auf Germania Maskenball.
Bei Eddi und Toni umgekleidet.  
Mönchsgruppe gehabt: Willi, Kochs, vier 
Eitels, Rasters und wir zwei. Alle
gleich, als Männer, viele angeführt. 
Nachher umgekleidet, getanzt,
gekneipt. Alle Bekannten dort.
Erst um <underlined>5 Uhr</underlined> früh nach Haus gekommen.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.   SUN. FEB. 20, 1898  Ther.

Trübe, Schnee, Schmutz, Eis. 
Ich bis <underlined>2 Uhr</underlined> Nachmittag 
geschlafen. Furchtbaren
Katzenjammer gehabt,
Kopfweh, Uebelkeit. Mama
und Arthur beide wohl. Arthur 
Nachmittag zu Brands gegangen;
Brand krank. 

Ich gegen Abend wohler,
ein Stündchen spazieren
gegangen. Nach dem Abendessen 
wieder krank; nervösen
Anfall gehabt. Zittern,  
Schwindel, über 100 Pulsschläge
Später wohler; sehr früh zu Bett.
Arthur sehr lieb zu mir.


Wea.  MONDAY 21  Ther.

Schreckliches Schneegestöber den
ganzen Tag. Wind und Kälte. 
Ich Vormittag sehr schlecht gefühlt;
nervös, schwindlig u. s. w. 
Nachmittag zu Arthur auf die 
office, mit ihm bei Henriçi
Kaffee getrunken. Dann zu
Frl. Böttcher, dort mit ihr und 
Emma Eitel Berathung gehalten. 
Später zu Bruckers zum Abendessen. 
Arthur und Frida Gugler 
dort. Ich schlecht gefühlt, später
besser. Nachher zu Toni und 
Ed zur Theaterprobe. Günzel, 
Zeisler, Emma Ryckoff, Eitels,
Ralph, Tutzi dort. Erst um 1/2 1
Uhr nach Haus gekommen. 
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  TUES. FEB. 22, 1898  Ther.

Abscheuliches Schmutzwetter;
nicht kalt. Washington's
Birthday und Fastnachten.
Vormittag zu hause; ich recht 
schlecht gefühlt, nervös. Nachmittag 
Kränzchen & italienische 
Stunde. Ich zu Beiden <underlined>nicht</underlined>
gegangen, aber nachmittag
zu Arthur auf die office.
Mit ihm bei Henrici Kaffee 
getrunken, Herrn Rapp getroffen. 
Nachher wieder auf
Arthur's Office: [Murner?] dort.
Während meiner Abwesenheit Dr.
Bluthardt bei uns. Abends Ed und 
Toni bei uns Fastnacht gefeiert. 


Wea.  WEDNESDAY 23  Ther.

Schneewetter, kalt und schmutzig. 
Ich Vormittag bis elf 
Uhr im Bett geblieben. Den
ganzen Tag krank gefühlt.
Nachmittag Lily Brand und
Frau Schlesinger uns besucht,
gerade als wir im Begriff 
waren wegzugehen. Die Beiden
mit uns auf die Nordseite gefahren.
Mama und ich bei 
Zeppels zum Kaffee. Frl. Böttcher,
Frau Leeb, von [Ammons?],
Toni dort. Gut unterhalten, 
aber ich nicht wohl gefühlt. 
Abends gemüthlich mit Arthur 
im Zimmer gesessen, vorgelesen.
Gut geschlafen. Nervös.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  THUR. FEB. 24, 1898  Ther. 

Sehr kaltes, trockenes Wetter.
Ich Vormittag nicht wohl 
gefühlt. Mit Mama in 
die Stadt gegangen, beim
Advokaten gewesen (Herrn 
W. <underlined>Butler</underlined> gesehen und gesprochen),
bei Herrn Pietsch und
Eddi. Auch ich als Patientin 
bei Dr. Bluthardt. 
Sehr beruhigt und viel wohler 
von ihm gegangen. Mi
Eddi und Mama im <underlined>Bismark</underlined>
zu Mittag gegessen. Nachmittag 
zuhause gearbeitet.
Abends zuhause. Vorgelesen.
Wohl gefühlt. 
O.


Wea.  FRIDAY 25   Ther. 

Kaltes, aber schönes Wetter. 
Ich früh mit Arthur zu Fuß 
in die Stadt. In Eddie's
Fabrik und office. Einkäufe 
gemacht. Emil Eitel getroffen. 

Nachmittag zu Hause, genäht. 
Schneiderin Frau Scheuermann 
gekommen. -

Den ganzen Tag wohl
gefühlt, nur gegen Abend 
nicht recht: nervös, bald
vorüber gegangen. 

Abends Klavier gespielt.
Dann in unserm Zimmer 
gemüthlich gesessen, vorgelesen.
Geplaudert. Früh
zu Bett.
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  SAT. FEB. 26, 1898  Ther. 

Kaltes, aber gutes Wetter.
Ich Vormittag in die Stadt.
Bei Mandels Emma Ryckoff 
auf Verabredung getroffen. 
Mit ihr bei Rölling gewesen, 
Eddie Leicht, Frau Brucker getroffen.
Auf Arthurs office. 
Mit Arthur, Emma Ryckoff,
Karl Eitel im Bismarck zu
Mittag gegessen. Mama den
ganzen Tag zuhause. - Abends 
Arthur und ich zu Eitels. Surprise 
party zu Emil Eitel's Geburtstag. 
Arnolds, Rasters, Zeggels,
Ryckoff, Brands, Zeisler Günzel.
Rede von Arthur, sehr lustig.


Wea.   SUNDAY 27   Ther.

Um 2 Uhr früh von Eitels
fort. Zu Fuß nach der Hochbahn.
Um 3 nach Haus gekommen. 
O. - Morgens sehr spät aufgestanden. 
Arthur und ich
Spaziergang gemacht. Zu
Mittag wir drei allein. 
Nachmittag zum Kaffee 
Weber's bei uns; früh weg
gegangen. Trübes, wärmeres
Wetter. Ich gegen Abend 
nicht wohl: nervös. Später
all right. Abends Arthur 
und ich noch mal spazieren 
gegangen. Nachher vorgelesen 
Allein wir drei. Früh zu
Bett. Sehr gut geschlafen.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  MON. FEB. 28, 1898  Ther.

Dunkles, trübes, aber
warmes Wetter. Ich 
früh zu Fuß mit Arthur in
die Stadt, zu Fuß zurück. 
Mama und ich den ganzen 
Tag zuhause. Ich
Hausarbeit gethan,
geschneidert. Recht wohl
gefühlt. - Abends wir
drei zusammen zu 
Hause, Klavier gespielt, 
gelesen. Früh zu Bett.
O.  Seit lange keine
Briefe aus Ungarn; Arthur 
deshalb sehr verstimmt 
und aufgeregt. 


Wea.   TUES. MARCH 1   Ther. 

Schmütziges, kaltes Wetter. 
Nachmittag Schneefall. Morgens 
lange geschlafen, 
ich Hausarbeit gethan,
genäht. Wohl gefühlt. 

Nachmittag mit Mama 
erst in die Stadt, 
dann zu Frau Brucker's
Empfangstag. Frau Kramer,
Toni, Emma Ryckoff dort.
Wir zum Abendbrot bei 
Bruckers geblieben. Herr 
Brucker, Eddi, Arthur auch dort. 
Abends wir alle im Royalklub 
in der Germania.

Schwach besucht. Auseinandersetzung 
mit Lily Brand. - Um 1/2 1 Uhr zuhause

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  WED. MARCH 2, 1898   Ther. 

Schneewetter, Schmutz.
Vormittag zuhause geblieben,
genäht. Wohl
gefühlt. Nachmittag ich
zur italienischen Stunde 
zu Mattie Arnold. Emma 
und Maria Eitel, Clothilde 
Schmidt, Frau Mels dort.
Ich auf dem Wege 
unwohl geworden. 

Abends Arthur, Mama 
und ich zuhause. Gelesen.
Frau Scheuermann gekommen. -
Arthur müde, sehr
früh zu Bett. Ich erst später. 
Gut geschlafen. 


Wea.   THURSDAY 3   Ther.

Wunderschönes, warmes 
Wetter. Mama nicht ganz
wohl. - Ich Vormittag zu
Hause geschneidert.

Nachmittag auf Eddie's
Office. Günzel gesprochen.
Toni dort auf Verabredung 
getroffen; mit ihr und Arthur 
in Brand's Geschäft gegangen. 
Dort Stundenlang Bilder 
und Kunstsachen angesehen. 
Toni und ich mit Brand zurück.

Eddie und Toni zum Abendessen 
bei uns. Nachher 
Graf Contin bei uns; nicht 
gespielt. Mit Ed und Toni um
11 Uhr fort. Unruhig geschlafen

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.   FRI. MARCH 4, 1898   Ther. 

Wunderschönes, warmes
Frühjahrswetter. Mama 
den ganzen Tag krank im
Bette. Ich früh mit Arthur 
zu Fuß in die Stadt, zu
Fuß zurück. - Den Tag
über geschneidert. Rückfall
in meine Gemüthsverstimmung,
namentlich gegen
Abend. Mama wohler. Briefe 
aus Budapest. Abends 
Arthur und uch zu Ryckoffs. 
Alle Woltersdorfs und Zeggels 
getroffen. Bei Ryckoffs noch
Eddie und Toni und Günzel.
Gutes Essen. Um 1/2 1 Uhr zu Haus. 


Wea.   SATURDAY 5   Ther.

Wunderbar schönes Frühlingswetter.
Mama mit Migräne 
den ganzen Tag in ihrem Zimmer.
Ich zu Fuß mit Arthur 
in die Stadt. Hut[?]ger gesprochen. 
Zu haus geschneidert. 
Nachmittag ich zu 
Toni gefahren zum Kaffee.
Zwei Amerikanerinnen dort:
Misses Holmes, Bekannte von
Toni von der Schiffsreise. Sehr
lustig und nett. Arthur schon
Nachmittag zu Hause bei Mama.
Mama abends wohler. 
Ich wieder meinen "blues" gehabt. 
Abends gemüthlich zuhause:
gebrannt. Ich gebadet. 
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.   SUN. MARCH 6, 1898  Ther. 

Wunderbar schönes, warmes
Frühlingswetter, aber schmutzig. 
Lange geschlafen, Mama 
krank und schwach, in ihrem
Zimmer geblieben. Arthur nicht
ganz wohl. Zum Mittagessen 
Arthur und ich allein. 

Nachmittag wir beide zu
Beil's gegangen, ein Weilchen 
geblieben. Mit ihren zwei
reizenden kleinen Mädchen 
gespielt. - Abends gemüthlich 
zu dreien zuhause. Arthur 
nicht wohl, früh zu Bett. Ich
erst sehr nervös, aufgeregt. 
Später wohler. Auch Mama besser.


Wea.   MONDAY 7   Ther.

An Arthur's Vater geschrieben 
Nachts Schmerzen gehabt, aber 
gut geschlafen. Wunderbar
schönes, sehr warmes Wetter.
Schmutz. Ich früh mit Arthur 
in die Stadt gefahren. 
Erst Mittag nach Hause gekommen.
Frau Dr. Bluthardt 
getroffen. Mama wohler.
Arthur schlecht gefühlt, ich 
Kopfschmerz gehabt. - Hausarbeit 
gethan, genäht, geschrieben. 
Nachmittag ein bischen
spazieren gegangen. Ein 
halbes Jahr verheirathet. 

Abends wir drei zuhause 
gesessen. Arthur krank, Mama 
Kopfweh; ich <underlined>ein wenig</underlined> "blues" gehabt.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.   TUES. MARCH 8, 1898   Ther. 

Wunderschönes, heißes
Wetter. Schmutz. Mama 
etwas wohler. Arthur 
Schmerzen gehabt (00). Ich 
Vormittag Hausarbeit 
gethan. Nachmittag 
Mit Mama zu Fuß nach 
Halsted-Strasse. Dann 
ich zu Maria Eitel gefahren. 
Zum Kaffee eingeladen.
Wunderschönes flat.
Clothilde Schmidt, Mattie, 
Tonie, Janina Zeggel dort. 
Ich recht nervös, aufgeregt. - 
Abends zuhause. 
Arthur sehr früh zu Bett. Vor mir. 


Wea.   WEDNESDAY 9  Ther.

+++  +++

Sehr schönes, heißes
Wetter. Abends Regen. 
Arthur den ganzen Tag 
arge Schmerzen gehabt. 
Ich früh mit ihm in die 
Stadt gefahren. Zu Fuß
zurück. Mittags krank
geworden, ein wenig Schmerzen. 
Nachmittag mit Mama 
spazieren gegangen,
zu Woltersdorf's. Frida
Petersen angekommen. 
Arthur schon zum Kaffee 
nach Hause gekommen. 
Abends in unserm Zimmer. 
Beide nicht wohl. Früh zu Bett.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.   THUR. MARCH 10, 1898  Ther. 

Trübes, kühles Regenwetter. 
Arthur Schmerzen gehabt,
schlecht gefühlt, aber früh in 
die Stadt gegangen. Ich 
zuhause geblieben, ganz wohl
gefühlt, geschrieben, gebrannt. 

Nachmittag Mama und ich 
in den Columbia Damenclub 
(erst auf Arthur's office). Musikvorträge
im Club, Vortrag von 
Frl. Böttcher über Don Carlos. 
Viele Bekannte dort, Kaffee getrunken. 
Arthur, Mama, ich Abendessen 
in der Germania. Dann in 
Merker's Stück <underlined>"[Tantz?]"</underlined>, Turnerhalle,
mit Eitels gewesen. Ich schlecht gefühlt.


Wea.  FRIDAY 11  Ther.

Furchtbarer Regen. Um
1/2 1 Uhr nach Haus gekommen. 
Arthur morgens wohler; ich 
auch. Trübes, schmutziges Regenwetter. 
Vormittag zuhause 
geblieben, geschrieben. 

Nachmittag Frida Petersen 
einen Augenblick bei uns. 
Dann ich zu Woltersdorfs 
gegangen: Martha Petersen, 
Luise und Olga W. gesprochen. 

Gegen Abend nicht ganz
gut gefühlt. Geschrieben.
 
Arthur wieder wohler.
Abends wir drei gemüthlich 
zu Hause. Klavier gespielt. 
Vorgelesen. Spät eingeschlafen. 
Ich wohler.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.   SAT. MARCH 12, 1898  Ther. 

Trübes, warmes Wetter. 
Früh Arthur,  Mama und
ich zu Fuß in die Stadt. 
Einkäufe gemacht. Bei 
Allegretti. 

Nachmittag zuhause,
genäht, geschrieben, Ziemlich
wohl. Gegen Abend 
Martha und Frida Petersen 
gekommen. Zum Essen
und bis spät geblieben.
Musicirt, geplaudert. 
Strömender Regen. Arthur 
die beiden Mädchen nach 
Hause gebracht. Mama 
sehr nervös. 


Wea.   SUNDAY 13  Ther. 

Wunderschönes, warmes,
sonniges Wetter. Sehr 
spät aufgestanden. Zum
Mittagessen Eddi und Toni 
bei uns. Alle zusammen langen
Spaziergang gemacht. 
Zum Kaffee Brands bei 
uns. Nachher Günzel und 
Frida und Martha Petersen gekommen. 
Brands, Günzel, Ed
und Toni zum Abendessen geblieben. 
Nachher Ed & Toni ins 
Theater. Wir drei mit Brands 
und Günzel ins Bismark. 
Den ganzen Abend (bis 12 Uhr)
gekneipt, geknobelt. Nachher 
auch Ed, Toni, Brucker.
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.   MON. MARCH 14, 1898  Ther. 

Wunderschönes, warmes,
sonniges Wetter. Vormittag 
zuhause geblieben, Hausarbeit 
gethan. Nachmittag Mama und 
ich zu Fuß in die Stadt;
dann ich zu Clothilde Schmidt. 
Zur Verlobung gratuliren.
Dann bei Frl. Böttcher; Emma 
Eitel dort. Verse vorgelesen. 
Beim Nachhausekommen Frida 
P. vorgefunden. Sie zum Abendessen 
und abends geblieben. 
Mama mit Migräne in ihrem 
Zimmer. Arthur Frida nach Haus 
gebracht. Im Parlor gearbeitet. 
Ich gebadet. Spät zu Bett. 
O.


Wea.   TUESDAY 15  Ther.

Lange geschlafen. Regenwetter,
Schmutz. Mama wohler.  Vormittag 
Hausarbeit gethan. 
Frida P. ein Stündchen bei mir. - Frau
Scheuermann. - Nachmittag Mama 
und ich Visiten (in der Kutsche gemacht.
Wetter wunderschön. 
Bei Clara Grommer Rehm, Vockes, 
Bopps, Else Madlener, Leichts,
Frida Restraht, Julia Hessert,
Frau Dr. Matthei und Herrn Rothbart. 
Bei Letzterem Kaffee getrunken. Sonst
nur Frau Matthei und Else Seipp 
zuhause. Bei Else Frau Hotz mit 
Clara, 2 Frau Seipps, Frau Lehner. 
Abends ich mit Arthur bei Zeggels 
Ed & Toni dort. Um 1/2 1 zuhause. 
O

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  MON. MARCH 28, 1898  Ther.

Kaltes, klares Wetter. 
Sehr schön. Vormittag 
mit Frida zuhause geblieben, 
Hausarbeit gethan.
Mama Kopfweh gehabt. 
Nachmittag Frida und 
ich Besorgungen gemacht;
Ich auf Arthur's Office.  

Abends Arthur, Frida 
und ich mit Günzel ins 
Theater: Schillertheater. 
Operette: "Die Geisha" gesehen.
Brillante Aufführung. 
Gleich nach Hause. Mama 
noch auf. Frida bei mir geschlafen.
Ich Arthur besucht.
O.


Wea.   TUESDAY 29  Ther. 

Wunderschönes, kühles
Wetter. Mama den ganzen 
Tag krank im Bett.
Frida Vormittag allein Besorgungen 
gemacht. Zum
lunch Bei mir. Louise Woltersdorfs
Geburtstag. Frida Nachmittag 
und Abend bei ihr. 
Ich Nachmittag bei Frl. Böttcher 
zur Probe für Narrenkaffee.
Frau Leeb, Frau
Stern, Emma Eitel, Frau 
Kaufmann zum Kaffee dort.
Herrn Schmidt getroffen. - Abends 
Dr. Lee bei uns bis sehr spät. 
Mama Fieber gehabt. Vom Dr.
behandelt. Frida bei mir geschlafen.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  WED. MARCH 30, 1898  Ther. 

Sehr kaltes, trübes, trockenes
Wetter. Mama den ganzen 
Tag krank im Bett. Frida 
Vormittag in die Stadt. <underlined>House 
cleaning angefangen.</underlined>

Nachmittag Millie Freund,
Martha Petersen, Emma Ryckoff 
Clara Petersen zum Kaffee 
bei uns. Abends Arthur,
Frida und ich allein bei Tisch. 
Dann musicirt. Hugo
Petersen gekommen. Sehr 
lustig zusammen gewesen.
Frida nicht wohl gefühlt. 
Mama recht krank. Ich
Arthur besucht. O. Frida bei mir
geschlafen. 


Wea.   THURSDAY 31   Ther.

Schönes, sonniges Wetter. 
Mama noch immer
krank im Bett. Frida 
Vormittag nicht wohl, zu
Hause. Nachmittag Frida 
auf die Nordseite gegangen. 
Ueber Nacht weggeblieben. 
Mama und ich gemüthlich 
zusammen zuhause; Mama 
wohler. Laura Kranz bei 
mur. Abends Arthur und 
ich Eddie und Toni abgeholt,
zusammen zu jungen 
Madleners (Else Seipp) gegangen. 
Erste Visite dort gemacht. 
Früh nach Hause. Dr. Lee 
inzwischen bei Mama. Arthur bei mir
geschlafen.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  FRI. APRIL 1, 1898   Ther. 

Wechselndes Wetter. Regen 
und Sonnenschein.  Frida P.
krank zu uns gekommen.
Sie und Mama den ganzen 
Tag zuhause recht krank.
Ich schon Mittags zu Emma 
Eitel gegangen, zum Helfen. 
Nachmittag dort großer 
<underlined>Narren-Damenkaffee</underlined> von
Frl. Böttcher und Emma Eitel. 
V[?]gericht. Narrenspossen.
Viele Vorträge. Ich mit Emma 
und Frl. Böttcher viele Knittelverse 
vorgetragen; großer Erfolg.  
Abends Frida gepflegt: sehr krank.
Mama wohler; bei mir geschlafen. 


Wea.  SATURDAY 2   Ther. 

House-Cleaning
Schönes, sonniges Frühjahrswetter. 
Frida krank aufgewacht. 
Dr. Dorsch bei ihr.
Martha Petersen gekommen.
Gepackt. Mama, Frida
Martha und ich in der  
Kutsche zum Bahnhof. Frida 
mit Frau Gercken nach 
Rowden abgereist. Viele 
Verwandte am Bahnhof. 

Nachmittag zuhause. Mama 
wieder wohl. Teppiche 
aufgenommen. Arthur zum
Kaffee nach Haus gekommen. 
Mit mir Spaziergang gemacht.
Abends wir drei gemüthlich 
zu Haus. Sehr früh zu Bett.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  SUN. APRIL 3, 1898  Ther.

Wunderbar schönes, sonniges
Wetter. Spät aufgestanden. 
Arthur bicycle gefahren, zu
Melzers um das baby zu sehen. 
Eddie und Toni zum Mittagessen 
bei uns. Mama gar 
nicht wohl gefühlt. Nachmittag 
gemüthlich in unserm
Zimmer gesessen; Eddie viel
Klavier gespielt. Zum Kaffee
auch Frida Gugler gekommen. 
Alle drei zum Abendbrot geblieben, 
dann bald nach Hause.
Eddie Arthur Klavierunterricht 
gegeben. All unsere Teppiche aufgenommen. 
Mama krank. 
O.


Wea.   MONDAY 4   Ther.

Wunderbar schönes, sonniges
Wetter. Hausreinemachen.
Anstreicher, Tischler, Tapezierer.
Mama krank, sehr schlecht gefühlt.
Ich gleich nach Tisch 
in die Stadt gegangen  
Besorgungen gemacht. Bei
Arthur auf der office. (Mauch 
von Deutschland zurückgekommen). - 
Ich zu Fuß 
nach Hause; recht kalt.

Mit Mama gemüthlich 
Kaffee getrunken. Mama 
wohler. Abends wir drei zusammen 
zuhause. Ich Arthur 
Klavierstunde gegeben. Champagner 
getrunken. Ma bei mir geschlafen.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  TUES. APRIL 5, 1898  Ther.

Briefe aus Ungarn. 
Sehr schönes, aber kaltes
Wetter. Mama recht 
krank mit Darmleiden. 
Den ganzen Tag im Zimmer. 
Dr. Bluthardt mittags 
gekommen. House-cleaning:
painter, Tischler, 
Tapezierer. Ich den ganzen 
Tag zu Hause gearbeitet. 
Nachmittag Hagel
und Schnee. Abends 
Arthur und ich längeren 
Spaziergang gemacht. 
Klavierunterricht. Mama 
bei mir, Arthur im Hinterzimmer
geschlafen. Früh zu Bett.


Wea.  WEDNESDAY 6   Ther.

Schönes, aber kaltes Wetter. 
House-cleaning: painter, 
Tapezierer, Tischler. Mama 
krank im Bett. Mittags 
aufgestanden, aber sehr 
schwach. Ich Vormittag zu 
Hause: gearbeitet. 

Nachmittag Besorgungen 
in der Stadt gemacht, 
dann zur italienischen Stunde 
zu Emma Eitel. Frau Arnold,
Mattie, Frau Dr. Mels dort.  

Abends Arthur mit Ed und
Toni im Theater: "Cyprenne"
von Agnes Sorma. Ich bei
Mama zu Hause. Sie bei mir
geschlafen, krank. Ich auf A. gewartet.
O.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  THUR. APRIL 7, 1898  Ther. 

Wunderschönes, sonniges, aber
kühles Wetter. Mama krank
im Bett. - House-cleaning.
Ich Vormittag zuhause gearbeitet. 

Nachmittag zu Toni 
zum Kränzchen gegangen. 
Stella Leicht, Laura Kranz,
Jani Blocki und Polly Andersen
dort. Gemüthlich wie immer.
Arthur und ich allein beim
Abendessen zusammen. Mama
wohler. Ich abends bei ihr zu
Hause geblieben. Arthur in 
<underlined>"Versunkene Glocke"</underlined> von der
<underlined>Sorma</underlined> gegangen. Um
zuhause. Mama bei mir geschlafen. 


Wea.  FRIDAY 8   Ther. 

Wunderschönes, warmes
Wetter. Mama wohler; aufgestanden. 
House-cleaning. 
Mama's Zimmer fertig, parlors 
angefangen. Ich früh mit 
Arthur in die Stadt, zu Fuß
zurück. Nachmittag Mama 
und ich kleinen Spaziergang 
gemacht. In die Stadt: bei
Burnell Günther Einkäufe 
gemacht. Aus Pesth ein ungarisches 
Kochbuch bekommen. 
Abends wir drei gemüthlich 
zusammen in unserm Zimmer 
gesessen, gelesen. Arthur stark
erkältet: Er im Hinterzimmer 
geschlafen, Mama bei mir.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  SAT. APRIL 9, 1898  Ther.

Abscheuliches Regenwetter, 
greulicher Schmutz. Mama 
wieder wohl. House-cleaning. 
Ich früh zu Fuß mit Arthur
in die Stadt, Besorgungen 
gemacht. Auf der Bank
Eddie Willie Hüfner, Beil
getroffen. Nachmittag Mama 
und ich nochmals in
die Stadt. <strikethrough>Bei [?]ehre Kaffee
getrunken.</strikethrough> Arthur früh nach
Haus gekommen,  zuhause 
Kaffee getrunken; dann ich 
mit ihm an Madison-Street 
Besorgungen gemacht. Abends 
alle drei zuhause. Arthur bei mir
O.


Wea.  SUNDAY 10  Ther.

<underlined>Ostersonntag.</underlined> Himmlisches 
Wetter. Arthur früh
bicycle gefahren, zu Beils.
Mama und ich großen 
Spaziergang gemacht. 
Gegenseitig Ostereier geschenkt.
Zu Mittag Eddie und 
Toni bei uns: Ostereier 
verschenkt. Nachmittag 
im Hof gespielt. Zum 
Abendessen Willie Hüfner
gekommen. Alle zusammen 
Spiele gespielt.
Sehr lustig. Mama 
Kopfweh gehabt. Früh zu 
Bett. Arthur bei mir geschlafen.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  MON. APRIL 11, 1898  Ther.

Himmlisch schönes Wetter.
House-cleaning: Panter
Tapezierer. - Ich früh mit ♡
zu Fuß in die Stadt, Besorgungen 
gemacht. Klärchen 
Lynch getroffen.

Nachmittag Mama 
und ich in die Stadt, Einkäufe 
gemacht, bei Günther
Kaffee getrunken, zu Fuß
nach Hause. - Abends Mama, 
Arthur und ich in's Columbia 
Theater gegangen: von einer
ausgezeichneten italienischen 
Truppe die Oper <underlined>"Bohême"</underlined> v. Puccini
gehört. Tenor Agostini. - 
O.


Wea.  TUESDAY 12  Ther.

Himmlisch schönes Frühlingswetter:
<underlined>House-cleaning.</underlined>
Vormittag Mama und ich 
nach Graceland gefahren,
dann in der Stadt Besorgungen 
gemacht. Im
Bismark mit Arthur zu 
Mittag gegessen: Brand,
Eitels. - Nachmittag Günzel
zu uns gekommen, zum
Abendessen geblieben, 
mit uns geknobelt, früh 
nach Haus. - Arthur 
und ich noch einen
langen Spaziergang gemacht;
sehr warm. Früh zu 
Bett.

title: Anna Sophie Raster diaries [German], 1898
transcription:
Wea.  WED. APRIL 13, 1898   Ther.
