2000 RUSTIC CANYON ROAD
PACIFIC PALISADES, CALIFORNIA

July 30, 1963

Dear Jack:
It hardly seems possible that it was more than
four months ago- over a third of a year- that we
had lunch together in Chicago. It seems quite recent.
I began reading "The Disinherited" before I got home,
and finished it soon afterward. Before I had finished
it, my wife had begun it. We both wondered how
much of it might be autobiographical. I think it is well
to keep people reminded of the bleakness and hopelessness
of Depression days. Young people of course know nothing
about it, and I doubt whether they believe what older
people tell them about it. I hope every reader bears in
mind that at the time your book was written the various
relief agencies had not yet been founded. Charlie Rogers,
the assistant director here (a painter) told me how in Kansas
City in 1931 a girl of about 17 came up to him on the
street and offered him you-know-what for 25c. And
Charlie didn't even have 25c!
Conditions here are really ideal for work. I think you
should put in an application. The Foundation is open
all year, and since you are not a teacher you could
avoid applying for summer, which is the busiest time. Remember
that out here winter is not really "winter." I find
that I cannot only get a lot done here, and at my own

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
sweet time, but that I can spend a lot more time perfecting
details that what is possible ordinarily.
The deer are no longer here. The pet deer was killed by a
mountain lion. But the raccoons are still very much here.
Every night they come to my door to beg for crusts of bread
I save out from my lunch sandwiches or from the breakfast
or supper table.
Meals are fine. A Mexican dinner is promised for tonight.
Sunday there was a curry, and another time [??]
with potato pancakes.
The total number of fellows usually runs from 17 to 20.
My cottage has four rooms. In addition to the st[?] room
there is a bedroom, kitchen (in case you are in a mood to do
your own cooking), and bath. Here are the furnishings,
not to mention a work table and grand piano: 4 tables, 
dresser, 5 lamps, water cooler, book case, pencil sharpener,
coffee table, davenport, easy chair, 5 ordinary chairs, sink,
and refrigerator. And again if anyone is in the mood to
do his own cooking, there is a hot plate and dishes, silverware,
and kitchenware.
A fellow here who has been at Yoddo[?] recently told me
that vandals got into my old town studio in the woods and
smashed it completely, piano included. Just a group of
wholesome (?) teen-age kids (?) expressing themselves (?) you
see.
Esther did not come. After all, there would be nothing for
her to do but stare at the [?] walls of a motel room and pay
rent in two places. At home she can at least visit friends.
Thanks again for the autographed copy of the novel.
Sincerely,
Bill

Oct 21. [1950s]
Dear Bud-
I have been transferred to
the 21st floor, South, that is, the County
Jail, and am awaiting trial. The food
is good, and I am as happy as anybody
can be confined in jail, but it is
really hell to be without the dough
necessary for cigarettes and the other
small incidentals. If you want to,
you can either mail me some money
or leave it at the Sheriff's office on
the nineteenth floor. Visiting hours

Dear Jack:

Dave
Yoddo
S. Springs, N.Y.
Dear Jack:
I greet you from an old haunt.
Somehow I managed to finagle my
way into a two-month stay here. If
no one has told you about my other
good luck, allow me to do it now:
Harcourt-Bryce bought my novel
and will bring it out in August.
Furthermore, I'm on leave of absence
from Penn State. Have been winding
up revisions here. The book won't sell.
Alas and alack, The Sportsman's
Bar and Grill is no more. It is
under new management, is closed
now, and is for sale. How the 
mighty are fallen. The ghost of
Clocken[?] Conroy will lift his foot
to the bar-rail in vain.
Only three other people here now,
rather quiet souls. Plly Hanson
and Elizabeth think of you always
with fearful affection. God, I'd
love to lift a stein with you. I had
the good luck to spend six evenings this
fall with Dylan Thomas before he died. / Dave

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Dave

March 28, 1956
Dear Jack:
Thanks for the plug and the news and the tracts.
It's always a delight to hear from you.
You probably haven't heard that Bob Jones died.
He was that friend of mine we went out with once and
went to John Woods' party with: short, good-looking,
curly-haired, about thirty. They found him at the foot
of the basement stairs in his father's home in Peoria.
He had apparently fallen down by accident, and he died
an hour later in the hospital. He was really a nice
guy, a bit uncertain about what he wanted to do and
be; but lost or not, he was a good friend and a well-
meaning man. What a pointless way to die.
I don't know whether I'll be able to take part in
any festivities when you come West or not. I'd surely
like to, but there are a number of imponderables: I'm
sweating out a Guggenheim at the moment (I'll know
in a few weeks) and I'm also waiting for word from
Yoddo. If I get the Yoddo invitation, the term will
begin on July 1st, and since I won't be through here
till about June 12th, I'll have to head right for home
if I'm going to see my parents at all (it's been two years).
However, if I get the Guggenheim and not the Yoddo bid,
I'll have both enough money and enough time to sport
around the coast for awhile. I'll just have to wait
and see.
I've been working hard at poetry lately and have four
pieces coming out in Poetry- either April or May issue- and
one in New World Writing, due next month. I think I'm
getting a whole lot better.
Saw the movie version of Man with the Golden Arm, and
was disgusted with the way they emasculated it. Now I
see why Nelson was angry. What became of the play?

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
If I get the Guggenheim, I plan to spend a year in
Italy- I've never been abroad, and I'm sick of feeling
provincial.
Glad to hear about your activities (the recording
with Algren, Terkel, and Blum sounds fine), but 
I hope you'll be able to convince the boys at the
Sun-Times someday that book reviews should make
some evaluation, not just relate plots. What else is
reviewing for?
And thank Gladys for being a fan of mine. She's a
member of an extremely small group.
All my best,
Dave
P.S. I'm beginning to feel like Yeats at 70:
"All that I have said and done
Turns into a question"

45 Cambridge Rd

July 9, 1950

Dear Jack,
Have been wanting to write you
for the last six months but with our
work in school and the heavy demands
in trying to combat at least some of the
local madness in the weird "Days of
the Tood[?]", I have become guilty of personal
negligence on more than one hand. Ever see[?],
who can understand on an ideological basis,
the devotion to the principles of preserving
mankind as a working species or more
aptly as a species of working people, does
not appreciate the personal sacrifice and
endless requirement of time included. But
I keep obstinately bulling[?] my way along
and sometimes see slight signs of
encouragement even in these dark days.
One of the reasons that has been 
constantly needling em to write you is
about your book, "The Disinherited." See

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
was finally able to trace or run down a
copy of it and bought it as a Christmas
present for me. A month or two later we
received a card from the book store (in
Buffalo, N. Y.) that they had two or three
more copies on hand, quoting their price.
I contacted Ralph Peterson and he ordered
one, a new copy still in its original newspaper,
and I meant to write you immediately
about the others- I also asked Ralph to
give you the name and address of the place
just as a double check to be sure you
received word. Perhaps T[??] Cay may  [??]
as it probably allowed me to unconsciously
rationalize that if I failed to write promptly,
he would be letting you know anyway.
As I recall, they had three copies- the
new one that Ralph ordered at about $5.00,
one (used) which had some slight discoloring of the
corners (or something) and one second hand
copy in first class condition - listed at
$2.t and 3.t respectively. My own copy is a 
used one but it hasn't a mark or
a blemish in it & I think Lu paid

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
about $3 or $4 for it. So you see my conscience
has been bothering me because I know you
would want this information immediately. Ralph
told me you had paid some pretty high prices for
some copies and I know from the effort Lu
spent checking book stores in various cities &
advertizing, that it is nearly impossible to
find any copies of the books anymore. I
did have a card with the listings of price
and condition of the books but have mislaid
it- in fact, i do not now have the
street number but the store is a large one and
a very old established place in Buffalo- the
name of the place alone (Ulbrichts Book Store) would
be enough. I will check with Lu and postscript
a more definate address.
Lu completed her Phd prelims this
spring and is now finishing up her minor
requirements and preparing to write the thesis.
She wants to write on modern American drama.
I have been exerting every effort to keep
her as close as possible to our "People's Drama"
- even took on a special assignment in
writing up a paper on Federal Theatre and
thus held the greater part of her interest. But she
(over)

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
has to write something that can get the O.K. of
the Dept., here. So she and one of her profs
have tenatively compromised on something
on Paul Green. This narrows the field a little
but keeps her in active living drama. If you
have any opinions, comments, or advice on the
subject we would be extremely grateful to hear
them. Being an Agricultural economics major,
I am not too well grounded in literature & arts.
We have driven thru Chicago a number of
times on our way back & forth to Buffalo,
but are always pressed for time- or come thru
in the middle of the nite, etc. Will be
thru that way again in the later part of 
August and can plan ahead to definately
stop in and see you. Lu won't actually start
on her thesis before fall and I am very anxious
that she have a chance to talk with you again
no matter what she writes about. The short time
spent with you a year and a half ago has left a life-
long impression with her and if you do not mind
spending the time, we would like to repeat the experience
in the near future.
Best wishes to you and family,
Don
Haven't see much of Ralph & Claire lately tho Ralph still comes to Madison for
Sun afternoon broadcasts. Their papers are pretty well established now. They wanted me
to take off & help on a sub-drive this summer but it was impossible. At any rate,
from what they tell me & I hear, they are doing a pretty good job.

Main & Eagle Sts.
Buffalo, N.Y.

That is a beautiful little project
-- the metamorphosis idea. I hasten to answer
your welcome letter in order to get across my
few reactions before they are forgotten. Antiquity[?]
will furnish a good bit of it. There is much
of that to be found in Simplified English
form in Hawthorne's Tanglewood Tales. e.g. The
Philemon and Baucis[?] tale, the transformations
of Circe's victims etc. I think the former comes
from Ovid if I remember correctly. Let me suggest
another possible source for this sort of story:
Fraser's Golden Bough where much of it may
appear in the religious, superstitious and
otherwise interesting practices of peoples. Fraser's
Golden Bough is of course a long work of several
volumes but one volume abridgements exist. Fairy
tales like Grimm Brothers and Anderson's come
naturally to mind.
One very excellent example is in Hiawatha,
the story of the struggle with Mandarin[?]. I am
sure that Indian legends are rich in examples
like this episode of Longfellow's. A man for
information of that sort might be John Joseph

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Matthews whose Talking to the Moon you may have
reviewed. I am sure he is versed in the lore of
the Osage. His publishers you recall were Univ.
of Chicago Press. I enjoyed his books a great deal.
One of the curious things that Fraser brings out is
that these stories and traditions of Antiquity are
frequently enough paraphrased int he lore of
barbarous or semi-barbarous peoples. In
the old French Tristan[?] of Ber[?] there is a
curious circumstance- a metamorphosis that
is arrested so to speak. After certain things
take place King Marc grows asses' ears on
his head. I think E.A. Robinson used Beroul's
version for his poem, Tristan, in English. In
the Arthurian legends there is probably more
of the sort. The Celts were strong for such conceits.
As its the fantasy in current or contemporary
literature there must be a great deal of it. Some
that I recall is not exactly to the point but
I should say mean enough. For instance did
you ever read Saki's[?] (Munro) Tabermary?
The irony of it is superb. However the transformation
is here taken for granted. We are
presented with a cat that can talk much to
its misters' consternation. Then there is Penguin
[??], a whole race of penguins which are
really men, Frenchmen, if I remember correctly.
You probably have read that Gulliver-like [?]
I must refer to a little-known novel translated

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
from the originals. A search through an English
translation of the Welsh Mab[?] would
undoubtedly reveal some of your desideratum.
A good work on the Celtic influences like
Laura Hi[?] Loomis' book (title escapes me) might
point the way. I think you would have no
trouble finding an English version of the Mab[?]
in any of the big libraries. I believe Tennyson
and the English generally used the Mab[??]
sources either directly or indirectly. In
this particular the legend of the Chevalier
du Cygne[?] or Au Cygne is a good example
of the genre- The Swan Knight. I read a
very nice version of it this summer in that
Belgian bulletin which comes from New
York- a propos of a statue or painting.
It is a genuine metamorphosis theme, old
and common place but delightful. There
are of course many versions.
If I think of other things I'll drop you a
line about them. I'm glad your book is
receiving recognition. your remark about its
reception in the South is significant. Some
of the best people in the world live in
these lattitudes. it would be unjust not
to recognize it. The [??] is working but

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
from French which is very whimsical. It is
K. B. Saintaine's Picchola[?]. I have never read
it in full, only a selection or two. So I don't
know how nearly it fits your purpose. The protagonist
is a man in a solitary prison
who walks daily in his courtyard for
exercise and falls in love with a little plant
which grows up between the flag-stones. The
name he gives to his vegetable sweetheart
is Cicclola[?], the title of the story. Then of
course there is the famous Don Juan theme,
the versions of Moliére, (Le Festin[?] de Pierre), of
[?] de Molina (Don Juan Terrorio) in which
the metamorphosis is into a statue of stone.
I don't remember how Byron treats the theme.
I have read a good many of the fairy tails
of Oscar Wilde; they are excellent bits of art.
I should not be surprised were you to find
grist for your mill there.
The old Celtic material, especially
the Breton in France, contains many of
these metamorphosis conceits. Marie de France
and [?] de [?] and other wrote
them. The metamorphoses where they exist
in the Middle Age material or often
inspired by Ovid but gracefully varied

it is bound to be slow. Temple Graves is

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991

I may be in the Windy City around

Dear Gladys & Jack -
Hope you are all well and enjoying the weather - we get Mo. weather reports - we are about frozen to death - & my God, the snow! Everyone has, or has had, the fly - Mother had it & was hospitalized, she hasn't really re-covered yet. I guess at her age one doesn't snap out of things so quickly. She will be 81 in July.
I haven't been out of the house since before Christmas - first Christmas in my life I haven't spent with my mother. I was sick in bed in Hammond & Mother was sick in Elkhart. What a terrible holiday season - I got my tree up but was too sick to trim it. Arnold cooked a turkey & dropped the pumpkin pie (a bought one) all over the rug - it is still in the rug - probably never come out. Well, as soon as I can I'm going to visit Elkhart for a few days - I feel much better.
I'd love to hear from you all. How is Jean - also the boys?
Love
Eve

Dear Reverend C:
The laconic brilliance of the above 10-word books review
I felt certain would interest you both as a reviewer and a book-man.
Advantages of such reviews are numerous- some of which
occur to me:
1- Saves paper in war time.
2- Makes it possible to review a whole 5-foot shelf on one
page of a literary section.
3- Makes the job of you reviewers much easier.
4- Book reviews can be sent by wire- even Cablegram- when
10 words or less.
Ask Max Siegel if he doesn't agree with me.
Reverend D is 23-months on the water-wagon today
-and within "stumbling distance" of a 2nd Anniversary- Oct. 10.
Of course I spent an extra-fervent quiet time today- as I do
every 10th of the month- and thought of my chauvinist god-son in the
"apostolic" AA, Barnie Abelle[?]- and of my 2 [?] in
"AA" (Schism)- yourself and brother Russell. Several
questions came to mind, Jack, which I wish you'd answer:
1. When was AA (schism) founded? As the Holy founder
or "Emancipated Bill Wilson" of our movement you must recall
the precise date- and we'll have a festivity on that dday every year.
2. How long are you now on the beam? This data too will
be important when we seriously tackle the problem of getting
some new adherents.
(over)

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
2.

3. How are we to get some new adherents(?). 
Surely just 3 of us- with 1/2nd of our roster on a continuous
"bat"[?] isn't strong enough to withstand the Persian Hordes of
Wilson and Co.
You will be happy to know I am popularly
known as "Reverend" in the Battery now- and since I gave
out a full candy box load of AA leaflets to our outstanding
member[?[ I am rarely called by any other "handle." Even the
Battery Commander- a boy of 24 (Capt.) called me "Reverend"
the other day. With this fine title established maybe I can
make one or two "converts" before the War ends in the Pacific.
One [?]- Cpl. OKane from Brooklyn- is my most serious
and se[?]-minded prospect. In the past, tho, OKane had
trouble remaining repentant after the hang-over dissolved.
In civilian life he is a Railroad man- fireman on the
Perusy[?]- so his conversion must be miraculously firm to
withstand the tidal waves of whiskey which will flow around
him if he returns to his own job.
Here is an authentic little story about
your fellow evangelist: When officers' wives eat in our mess
hall the sergeant goes out on the steps outside and asks
the men to "watch their language." This is a good precaution-
as many of the men use language which shouldn't be 
heard in a s[?]men's shanty, let alone fall upon the
ear-drums of our gallant officers' beauteous women's [?].
Yesterday I was "dining room orderly"- and the sergeant
went on the porch and and cautioned the men to "watch your
language- the "Reverend" is on duty inside." Be sure
to use this, Jack, if you ever become my hagiographer!
The Army post office of this outfit is
some 360 miles from here- at San Luis Obispo- and

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
3
about 1/2 of the 97th Division (my Division) is here at
Callau[?] going thru amphibious training. The San Diego papers
have observed in their columns that we are here for training
to fit us for war in the Pacific- so just why our mail
cannot be delivered directly to us instead of to San Luis
Obispo 360 miles North is a "G.I. Mystery." This
G.I. life is just as full of mystery as any mystic could
desire- Tho most of the mysteries are "sad" rather than
"joyous" or "glorious".
In spite of the over-cast future which
apparently awaits us of the "97th" I expect to get another
10 days at home in late October. If and when I do, Jack,
be sure we'll have an evening together- and I'll solemnly
turn over to you the entire responsibility of the C[?]
development of AA (schism). [?] I will assume the
huge task of spreading our saving Doctrine in the armed
forces.
I have given the [?] "Orientation" Course 3 times
of late (1 hour per week). It will amuse you to hear that [?]
"Army Regulation" governing orientation talks is not to criticise
any citizen by name! I lambasted Hearst in one of my
talks- and the B.C. told me this was against "AR" (Army
Regulations)- tho he agreed with me. Think of it, Rev.- we

Well, Jack, I await your book- and want an autographed

copies. Also give my love to Gladys and Margaret and the
boys- and do phone Chesapeake 1475 and tell Mary I
am both "faithful and sober"- and find both easy and pleasant
as well as dutiful!
Fraternally, Rev. D. F.A. A.A.

Enjoyed it and sent it on to Mary. -ICR

Dear Jack,
I constantly remember feeling last New Year's that
1965 would be a good year for me. Felt like something
would come across. I'm not sure if it has or
not. I'm in Iowa City enrolled at the Iowa Writers
Program. Read in the paper last year that the students
here had 12 novels published, and after Kim (who
wrote it here) hit the N.Y. Times list with The [?]
I thought something must be going on out there.
If something is going on out here I can't put my
finger on it.
Donna says we got a card from you in London,
but I haven't seen it yet. What are you planning,
travel books?
Write and let me know if you are still on Jeffery[?],
I would like to stop and see you when I get back
in Chi. I'll be in for Thanksgiving.
I am sipping Burgundy and it is very late-
a fine activity and hour for writers. I've just
been going over Hem's A Movable Feast again.
It is like a shot in the arm. I have been teetering
over S.S's and a novel, wanting to do the latter,
and even got two chapters of one finished here,
but think I've [?] for S.S.'s. Write the very best
shorts I can. I think I'm learning things out
here: I'm suspicious of so much of the way I've
written up to now, and now only wanting to write
well, which means simply and honestly. And with
that sort of an idea a novel is too long a run to
make without building up some wind. Did your
They Seek a City come out yet.
Read the Starrett[?] review and looked up to see
who did it and was pleased. Maybe you can give
up that tedious rag the Trib has called a "book
section". Also happy to see that you got that too-much
ignored Jack London [?] in print.

for 2 months. Christianson is slow as money.

same as usal round moberly
got a [?] letter J.B. he
says How factor do, hot as hell
round Her hope it cool off so
a body can sleep. what a gal
eh? my regards to gladys
& kids
Adois

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Fred
Dec. 21. 1938

Dear Jack
This is the kind of stuff chemists
used to, and still do, publish in Journals
at let-down times. These poems, I
picked up in the Lab. today. They evidently
came from some [?].
This stuff might come under the
heading of Industrial-hemical-Lo[r]e!!!,
which is a far cry from what you are
looking for, but may be of some interest
to you.
You might use the attitude in some
of your stories in which a chemist
figures. They are also highly suggestive
of technician-worker-relationship
in plants. Or, at least, used to be,
for the majority, before
'29. Seventy five % unemployment
and the 
F.A.E.C.T. have
done much to
remedy the situation.
Fred.
Back to work
for fear the
presses might
break down.

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Fred
Dec. 4, 1937
1530 Upshur St. S.W.,
Washington, D.C.
Dear Jack
Just received your letter of Dec. 2 a few moments
ago. Will write you in pencil, trying to make it clear
as I can write more and faster this way than
with typewriter or ink.
To get down to your problem at once, while
I am not at all familiar with the "human fox
hunt" type of story, I will give you some impressions
that flew to mind when I read your
sentences dealing with requirements for background.
Going over to St. Catherines, Canada, I passed
a paper mill which was pouring its
waste liquors into a stream via a sort
of concrete viaduct. The appearance of
the stream, and surrounding soggy
ground, was that of a mad dog:- white
froth and foam all over the water.
As the bleaching agent used in paper mills
is sulfurous acid, undoubtedly the waste
was largely this in water. Perhaps some paper pulp also. This acid
which is a solution of sulfur dioxide (SO2)
in H2O, yielding H2SO3 (not H2SO4 which is 
sulfuric) is highly oxidizing. It is a problem

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
2
to handle in the plants and tears hell out of
iron and steel pipes. Brass will not stand
up at all and modern plants use the
chrome-nickel (18:8) stainless steel. Lead
would be all right except for structural
weakness. (The foregoing to give you an
idea of the nature of the beast).
In short it is a powerful oxidizing
agent and hence its use as a bleaching
agent for paper. How it acts on the
human skin I don't know but I would
hate like hell to be thrown into a bath
of it or even into a stream of waste from
a plant such as your negro might conceivably
fall or jump into in escaping
detection. (Perhaps he is seeking the
entrance to the concrete viaduct or conduit
at the head of the stream.)
To make sure of the visciousness of
the fluid, the stream could also serve
as open sewer to other plants in the
neighborhood and then (due to the
other acids) you would be sure to
have sulfuric acid as well which burns the
hell out of any skin. You may have

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
3.
seen men burned this way. Skin is white,
wrinkled, features distorted. But I wouldn't
go too much into the details of this, say,
he suffers tortures and is burnt outwardly
(skin) and inwardly (from swallowing the crap).
Further evidence for severity of the
sulphurous acid. poisoning and burns:
Antidote for acid swallowed:
mustard plaster on chest, narcotics, expectorants
Skin burns:
wash in water, and lime water, or, lime water
and raw linseed oil mixed together,
baking soda, water and soap solution.
--
A paper mill is located near convenient
source of supply of logs- hence piles of cut
logs around factory, heavy sulfurous
smell in air from bleaching agent inside
factory.
There are paper mills in South, undoubtedly.
Other plants are steel, with blast

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
4.
furnaces manufacturing phosphoric acid
as by-product; there are sulfuric acid
plants and soda plants, as well as
phosphate manufactures. But all
these do not hook up in same locale
so would not necessarily feed your
paper mill stream.
--
Well Jack I wouldn't want to jeopardize 
your reputation so don't take too much of
a chance on this if the thing you have
in mind is important. There is no way
that I have now of definitely ascertaining
whether a paper mill will discharge waste
capable of taking the skin off a man. The
foregoing is purely suggestive but I would
not hesitate to stretch a few points-
without giving into too much detail, as you
say- if I were writing a pulpish detective
yarn. And no one's reputation but my own
was at stake.

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
5.
To summarize:-
If I, personally, were reading a story about an escaped
convict in the South, stumbling out of the woods
onto a foaming, ill-smelling (sulfurous) stream
running by a paper mill, and diving into the stream
and making his way toward the mouth of a concrete
viaduct from the plant, I would certainly find
no fault. And if the man experienced
burning of the skin, which rapidly became
unbearable, and eyes lungs and mouth
were burned so that he suffered the torture
of the damned while in it, I would still
find no fault. If the writer hinted that
sulfurous acid was coming out of the plant
at time contaminating the already
fouled stream, and that the man was so
badly burnt there was doubt as to his
recovery, I still wouldn't [?] (I wish
you could check on this with somebody
else for credulity.)
Well I guess this is not much help after all.
But I judge your problem is urgent, and it
would take me considerable time the way
things are now to hunt up a technically certain
background for your needs.
[OVER]

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
6.
I was in Pgh.[?] and Yo[?] the last few days job hunting
but no soap. Am in very low frame of mind and
must hit up my old boss at Niagara Falls for
a reopening of my former job. Fancy that!
and with the slump and all. I had put
off answering your former letter until, I had
hoped, this business would be settled. And
I will yet postone writing in detail re. that
and your present letter until I can do them
justice. Jack, I see eye to eye with you
on your present financial difficulties.
They are the shit. You may hear from 
me in a day or two perhaps later. Hope
this [?] gives you a lead. Don't hesitate
to drop me a line at any moment re. further
discussion of matter or other like it.
Will now start writing some more futile
epistles re. job, I suppose.
Sincerely
Fred

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Freda
Moberly Mo-
Jan. 26- 1954.
Dear Jack & Gladys-
rec'd card, yes I remember Gertrude[?]
and husband well, had quite a conersation
with her, I can't help but remember how
odd she was dressed, am I right or not
Mary says I'm wrong. I understand he
(Frank) was really a Jewel thief or a
burglar and that is why he has written
the book, maybe I took it wrong.
I sure do want to read the book
and here is hoping that he will send
one.
How is the weather in Chicago, we
have really had a touch of winter here,
Had a very bad plane crash Mon. nite
The pilot missed the Moberly airport and crashed
in the new memorial cemetery and
finally ended up at the edge of the
Drive in theatre. They were all from

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
are injured pretty bad, then there was
a couple with them the woman was
dragged as she was the only one strapped
in, of course she was killed the others

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Dear Jack
Lincoln Way is the south boundary
of Golden Gate Park. It begins sat Arguello
Road and ends at Great Highway. The
address, 1645 is between 17 & 18 Avenues
(not 17 & 18 Streets).
What's this about Paris[?]? Not so
much doing in San Francisco but the
climate is better, the atmosphere more
relaxed and prices a lot lower.
Since any rich reactionary from the
Middlewest can retire to California and,
though he or she contributes nothing to
the state, be granted the franchise, there
is little hope for anyone who is anywhere
left of the John Birch Society.
Had Pat Brown not been bent o his
[?]lomaniacal Feather River Project, he
might have suggested splitting the state.
Or so he says.
But now water will be diverted to
make the fertile North a barren waste
and the barren South an urban
barnyard where all the animals are
equal.
over

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Except for the grape eating foxes
who will be more equal. Now there
is a mixed up metaphor for you.
Some day I must show you around
Los Angeles. To see everything would
take months but a single day can
encompass to send you running
after the lemmings.
Lots of fun, bon voyage and
all that jazz
George
O tempora, [?]
O Orwell

KIDDIE KORNER: At St. Francis Hosp, the
nurse at the desk tried several times to communicate
with four-yr-old Johnny via the intercom over
his bed. At last she said in some exasperation:
"Come on, Johnny, answer me--I know you're

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
George
Dear Jack
I'm not watching Dudley Dwight
of the Canadian Mounties do battle
with S[?] Whiplash. But I
can't turn it off because I work at
Channel 7. Summer replacement 
in the engineering department.
Mostly the work is rather dull,
sitting and waiting for station breaks.
As I told Alice[?], we get a 28 1/2
minute break away every half hour. And
there are few days when I work
a full eight hours. Yesterday I put
in seven hours but will be paid
for nine and one half as scheduled.
There are times when we do
get busy and $4.00 per hour is 
small pay for the needed skills.
Of course the senior guys get
more than that. But there are 
others who get less.

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
would you believe it takes a director,
a technical director, an audio man, a
video man and a projectionist plus a
standby announcer to handle a 63
second station break? There's so
much money in this business,
something should be done about it.
Meanwhile, I'm pulling strings to
try and get a job at Channel 9. The
educational station. Things are a
lot busier there and the program
content is generally not quite so
dull.
Poor Alice, after a long drought,
she sold some paintings. This had
her all cranked up to paint some
more this weekend. But, Thursday
she aquired a cast on
her right hand.
The only consolation is that two
office visits, two courses of X rays,
consultation of the radiologist and
the cast cost only two dollars
for the whole [?]

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
The only other information I have
to pass along is that we've had mucho
rain and snow. Floods are expected
when the snow melts.
For my part, I've been spending
42 hours a week in school and
another 20 to 40 hours a week on
my homework. But it's beginning to pay off.
Alice and I have discussed your 
problem and believe we may have an
answer here in San Francisco. You
saw the apartment we got for
managing a building. With something
like that going you'd need very little
cash income.
I can help you with any repairs
you'd have to make and guide you
past the pitfalls of dealing with owners.
Think about it, meanwhile send
love from both of us to both of you.
We think about you often
George

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
George
Feb 17 & 18 -'62
Having just finished my italian
salami & wine lunch, I thought
it appropriate to write you. No,
that is city glibness, actually as
I looked out over the distant
mountains & thought of the people in
the valleys, my mind flit from
Frank to Charlie & Lee to Jack & Kathy
-- to you & the Mrs. It settled there
-- so I write. Another sip of vino.
I appreciated your brief
but hesitant note about the Mrs.
Brown bit. Yes, it was off-beat &
yes it was scant. Perhaps a
clumsy beginning, but worse-
an inearnest one. Thank you for
inviting me to join you at one of

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
those readings, but it would be
difficult living in the mountains.
(again the glibness.)
The encyclopedia quarterly 
was also a pleasant gesture & I
scanned through it, with special
consideration to the literature section.
God- do you have to read all those books
-- it takes much gusto & enthusiasm
for me to read just one per month.
Another sip of vino.
Yes, looking through the
gnarled bare winter branches of a
California live oak tree, to the tumbling
hills, upwards a wild austere sky,
& earthward in the greater distance,
the jagged steel-blue silhouettes
of the Santa Lucia Mountains- I realize

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
3
The barrenness of words & books in
my life. To me, they seem
incidental to mountains, a valley
perspective, a sunrise striving
to praise.
Praise must be lived, like
a hymn. I have always felt
there was such a life where song
is grateful endeavor, where thought
& action are one- like a flexing
muscle, where the mind is subservient
to the hand, praising it- where
words are instincts.
The mountains are before me
& I am trying. I work in a 
vineyard at 2000 ft. elevation.
I live long here, caring for it-
In these winter months, I prune

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
the vines. Another chap comes
two days a week to supervise.
We make superior wines!
No electricity, no communication,
except for mail which I have
to go for to a town post office 10 miles
below. Last week, however, the
heavy rains washed away the dirt roads.
So- only mountains & fierce clouds for
company. And vino- 'nother sip.
Jack- I saw your friend
Art Carlbon[?] about a month ago-
He thinks highly of you & we got drunk
& talked & bullshited.
Jack say hello to Ken & Sanka[?]0
Jack Jack goodbye- the mountains-
Mucho Vino
George
!Write!

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
George
Morning Jack- 
May as well do the complete
rounds of the meals. Just finished
my breakfast of Oatmeal & blackberry
jam. And coffee to get me
warm. We don't have deep
freezing temperatures here, the lowest
period this year was about 25*.
But I sleep with my window off,
it's detachable, & my room reaches
the same temperature as outside, about
40* today. So hot coffee serves its purpose
in the morning.
My first morning chore is to
close the winery doors & windows
- we let it stay open at night to get
the cold at the wines, needed to clarify
them.

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
2.
I rarely drink our wines, perhaps
once a week. They're too dear-
- costing $2-3-&4 a fifth bottle.
Very exclusive stuff. We make
dinner wines- two white wines-
Chardonnay & Chenin Blanc, &
one red- Pinot Noir. Although
this vineyard has been here since
1919, this year will be the first time
that the wines will be sold. Formerly
the grapes were sold to larger wineries.
As a matter of education, wine which
is made on the same premises where
the grapes are grown is entitled to
 a very exclusive designation on the bottle
-- Estate bottled. There is only a
handful of vineyard-winery operations
with this feature. So you can
realize the quality & expense.

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
3.
I feel very fortunate in acquiring
this job, even though there weren't
many takers. My boss- an awkward
word- rather, the winemaker is an
englishman, about 35, who learned
his trade in France, attending a
wine school in Bordeau, & working
in the vineyards of France, Algeria,
& Chile. He's very exacting, a
perfectionist, & keeps me on the mark.
It's a dying tradition- craft- &
more obsolete is the genuine master-apprentice
relationship. Basic values
are dying with mass production,
unionism & city complexities.
I felt dissipated into petty
activities in the city, crowds made 
my perceptions mere blurs. Of course

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
4.
cabdriving wasn't the most serene
vocation, but whatever I thought
about doing forced me to consider a
basic division in my life, my body
& soul were schizoid antagonists.
Most people do not have a unifying
structure, a central focus, in their
lives- the hand works at ditch digging
or filing sales reports while the
mind day dreams about the cocktail
hour or pinching the comely ass passing.
The only reward for their labors is The
Dollar, & somehow in their total frustration
& unfulfillment, the dollar must be
spent. Thus[?] compulsive consumption
of Americana.
Shit, this sounds like some
sort of tract- but anyhow I wanted
unity, a concrete manifestation of
my endeavors, a worthy object towards

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
5.
which my energies were directed.
I have no illusions, I am still very
much the distracted, impotent
intellectual, day dreaming in
abstractions, I am not yet tangent[?]
to earth & flesh. But every morning I
awake to see more clearly only one image
in the mirror, each day my gesture
becomes more precise, more firm & eloquent.
Each night I understand that love is
really blood.
And so the basic things of life
reaffirm their significance. To work
hard & ache means to sleep soundly
as the slow moon, to eat deeply, simply.
Life has appetite. In the next few
days I am going to walk a mile over
to my nearest neighbor. She has a
milking cow & I want to bargain
for fresh milk & some of her hand-churned
butter. I am going to learn

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
to make bread as coarse as earth,
that makes the jaw work &
the teeth glisten with white power.
Then beer. Gallons of the stuff,
heavy & non-carbonated, weighty
as a German's stomach.
But today, after I finish this letter
I am going to plant my first garden
& in a couple months- harvest fresh
carrots, corn, squash, peas, cauliflower,
onions, broccoli, tomatoes. And on.
Last month we poached a deer. With
the next one, we're going to
smoke it.
What else is there- beer,
coarse bread, creamy milk, fresh vegetables
& wine?
A woman. Yes I am alone,
but I realize in this ridiculous chasing
game of hide & seek of the sexes that a
woman is not caught by grabbing.

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
7.
No, I have to steady myself & be
sure inside & the woman will
come as if drawn by a magnet.
I have chased enough. There are
flowers aplenty in my heart
for the woman who can see them.
Let her come, I will wait.
So Jack, I must keep occupied
to make this dreaming actuality.
It wasn't long ago I felt that
a dream could harden to artifact,
that faith could be as firm as the
calloused hand, now my chores
await me.
Love,
George
If you & the Mrs. decide on a westward
trip- mi casa es su casa.
WRITE

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Send home address- misplaced it-
Geo.

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
George
Again- dear Jack,
My gas lanterns are burning
fiercely, I've just finished my 
hamburger & boiled potato dinner
with lettuce salad, shut off the dripping
faucet & refilled my pen. Poured
some wine from the jug & sipped.
This was my day off yet I
worked a half a day. I straightened
my clothes out, scraped the week's mud
off my boots, & looked at the sky
as leisurely & powerfully as a
mountain lion contentedly
sitting on his rocky butte.
Everything moves slowly but 
fully here, a slow twisted country,
every twist is a struggle for life, every
gesture a direction. it is a barren

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
2.
tough land with jagged rock outcrops
as gripping fists of earth held
high skyward. The live oak tree
is the only tree able to grow here,
and it writhes & contorts itself in 
singular spasms of time to live. Life
is a daily struggle, the live oak
tree outside my window is about 400 years old.
The vine also illustrates this earth
- a contorted, cut & seared stump
stretching its sinewy shoots towards
the sky- the sun, the rain. Many
of the vines die for lack of rain, others
from rabbits, hungry drought-parched
birds eat many of the grapes.
We were fortunate this year-
for the past week we had a constant rain,
7 inches, giving us a 13 inch total
for the year. Yet the wind is drying

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
3.
& strong, & while working this afternoon
the soil was firm under my boot.
Only yesterday while pruning,
I would sink above the ankles in
an oozy mud.
But today, my face was flush
with sun & wind, my back was
bent earthward over the vines, my
hand squeezed the shears, my eye
surveyed the future shape of the vine.
A meadow lark whistled in a
nearby wood, occasionally I replied.
A hawk glided in a lazy potent
spiral overhead. The barley cover crop
stirred restlessly in the wind. My hand
kept steadily coiled, the soil yielded in
soft reluctance under my boot.

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
4.
Occasionally, I would stretch
my back & look skyward, then
sweep towards every horizon.
I was high & everywhere horizons.
The most immediate horizon to the
east was Mount Chalone, a lazy
sloping mountain reclined in slumber,
yielding in a slow angle to
The Pinnacles, a monument of rocks
that stands boldly & precariously
upright, a half mile of blunt skyward
thrusts. Hills, the humbler mountains,
bowed & crumbled to the north, then
west & south above & beyond the 
hills, misty gray silhouettes of
eternity: mountains. And always
overhead, fractioned by the width &
depth of earth, glimpsed with such

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
5. 
a dim perspective by eyes, ungraspable
with earth-hewn hands- the dome of sky.
It is the earth which I stand on,
I work the vine, I drink the wine:
These words ring from the bell of the sky,
echoing deeply, resounding in my
arched back, articulate with my
cuttings, meaningful with my
scanning surveying eye, enjoyable
with my lips of wine.
My answer to life is reverence,
reverence is the stance of love. My back
is bent over this slow earth, my eyes smart
with the green eager shoots, my lips
divine their offerings. My hands
are poised, latent with task.
With wine & love-
George

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Gertrude & Frank

The 1st Mrs. ROBERT I. LIVINGSTON
5728 DORCHESTER AVENUE
CHICAGO 37, ILLINOIS

March 20, '63
Dear Jack.
How really dandy to get your
book! I tried to call you but they said
you weren't there today. i hope you ain't
got the flu. We had it really for a month.
I am so happy for you that the book
is reprinted. And I hope beside the
glory that you receive that you receive
a lot of money too.
Cat Koko had 2 kittens on St. Patrick's
day. Sweet. Do you want one?
I read one tract and I promise never
to dress in Franks clothing ever again.
He gets into my sweaters. Is that allowed?
Can't wait until Jesus starts hugging me.
Do you think he kisses too?
Please call us up. Thanks just ever
so much.
Love from your old pals
Gertrude and Frank
Hello to Gladys!

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
Gracie?
in jail
at squaw lake
dere Jack,
i am in a terrible fix and only you can help
me i hope. read the enclose and you will
no i am hoples but don't tell no one or i will be
dis"grace"d. O it is awfull! they put me in this
dreery jailhouse i don't no when and they even
took evin my lipstick away from me. then the
sherif ask questions for hours. at first he
was nice and only cuffed me twist[?] then
he asked did i have a character wit[?]. i didn't no
what he ment so he got m-a-d and yelled did
i have anyone to stand up for me so i said
yes my buddy "Jack Conroy" back in chicago.
that seamid to make him sore and he run
out and whispered to the others. they all come
in and looked at me like a dangerous criminal-
they took my shoelaces and earrings
and said in a snear thats her that's gashouse
gracie. i don't like it. it may mean i'm headed
for the gas chamber. if i don't come back
you can divide my books iwth the others. they
don't no the irish. i will go on a hunger strike
the food aint safe. they had some suspicious berries
in the soup. i think its poison so i picked them
out and threw them on the floor befor i ate the soup,
then the sherif acted nice again and wanted me
to sneak out to a square [?] with him but

title: Jack Conroy letters [22], 1924-1991
transcription:
i ignored him. (i'm too wise see!) he caught me upping my
nose at him so now hes sore again. im
writing in the dark with my eye brow pencil
so excuse it. im suppose to be in bed but
who can sleep on a [?] plank and only my
mooted mink cape for cover just like the poor
little babes in the woods you hear about. if the

Cleveland 6, Ohio

Sept 28

Dear Jack:
 I just returned from Europe to find your very welcome letter. As one of your admirers, I was tickled to get a copy of The disinherited and wrote to Emerson Price, book review editor of the Press, to be sure to give you a review. He is almost impossible to get by phone because he does his work at home in a distant town.
 Thanks for your comments on my work: This month two of my anthologies appear: One is Slavery Since The Civil War (Farrar, Straus, 4.95) which includes some hair-raising accounts by Nat Turner, the insurrectionist, and others of both races. The other is The Negro Since Emancipation (Prentice, Hall, Spectrum Series) covering Frederick Douglass to Elijah Muhammed, your fellow-townsman.
 I shall certainly try to locate you in my next trip to Chicago where I transfer to the J.C. for Urbana where I have a daughter, Dorothy, married to a graduate student-instructor in Sociology, and a grandson.
 Cordially,
 Harvey Wish

21 Oct 1982
New York City

Dear Jack -
 Suzanne and I were very saddened by the news of Gladys' death. The Chamiers called us - we are still "en voyage" on a month-long odyssey of Eastern archives.
 We are thinking about you and hoping all is as well as can be.
Betty C. said the sermon was lovely and appropriate, and she was very moved by the tribute the minister paid to you and Gladys.
 You took extraordinary care of Gladys during these past few years. You gave her the absolute best, your loyal and selfless devotion.
 We hope to pass through Moberly again on the 31st and will pay a call on    -over-

title: Jack Conroy letters [21], 1924-1991
transcription:
you then.
 The trip has been very rewarding and included a visit with Maxim Lieber as well as others you will want to hear about, I'm certain.
 We have sore feet from marching the streets of Manhattan all day. We have heard many strange tongues, seen men with purple hair, women with four dogs, and shall leave with the most favorable impressions of a Lexington Ave - bar where the pianist played Gershwin, we felt, for us.
 Larry Hill says The Disinherited will be in press this month.
   Amities and our love,
      Doug & Suzanne

August 6 - 1955
Dear Jack -
It's difficult for me to write this but I must tell you that Howard died Thursday. He slipped away in an instant while he were at the breakfast table. You can understand in an instant what this means to me. It's as if the whole world had ceased to have any meaning. But I know I have to pick up the pieces and start over again.
The funeral services were last evening. And I made them just as he would have wanted. None of the funeral trappings - no viewing, no flowers - the playing of one of his favorite records, Berlioz requiem. And the reading of two of James Weldon Johnson's poems.

January 12, 1977
Dear Jack & Gladys,
 It was sad to hear of the death of your daughter, and to know what your recent life must have been like. I guess your family and my own have been picked for too much of death. There's nothing I can say that wouldn't be awfully inept, except I'm feeling for you both and wish to God it hadn't happened.
  My mother died ^ this Dec 31st, in Oshkosh. (It was also cancer.) I had gone back to see her at Thanksgiving, and then returned to help my father to care for her (he is 80 yrs. old and was tending her round - the - clock at home, as she was unwilling to go to the hospital). After mother's death, we brought my father back to San Diego. We're hoping he'll remain here and so far he seems content to do so. I think you'd like him, Jack; he's a former foundry-worker and has a pretty keen sense of how things measure up for the working people. Maybe we'll all be able to get together soon.
  I'll close for now and write more when I get my brain cleared up a little. Meantime, stay well and keep punching!

Dear Jack:
I wish I shared your consideration as one who replies quickly to correspondence - even in adversity.
Was so sorry to hear of your family troubles - worries - financial pressures and mostly, I presume, the concern for your daughter left widowed with young children and still so young herself.
Hopefully, some adjustment to the loss is in vew. Living with illness of a chronic nature is sad and yet, I have met some who hang on - hopefully - preferring to have life with a beloved invalid than bearing the loss. I hope this is not so in your daughter's situation.
Sanka & Kenny speak continually of a Chicago sojourn and yet place obsticles in their way - such as assurances of a fine, adequate - reasonable and interesting apartment. They have not renewed insurance on their car - as a costly & unnecessary expense in view of returning to Chicago & so goes the self conviction.
They are a fine couple and I believe down deep - he agrees to Chicago to Please her & she helps the delay to please him and so it goes.

vintage.

She did not want a publisher - I know of your enthusiasm for new talent and of your reputation in encouragement to young writers. I sent it as a brag since I thrill at finding people - any people - who are creative. And in one so young as she my response was more than usually enthusiastic, especially since she is so unspoiled and modest and yet so capable.

3.
At least Millie's time hasn't been wasted. She showed the stories and her illustrations to friends as a sort of one man effort to get reaction to them. As a result she's been asked to do similar illustrations for a movie on children.
If you think these stories can be used in any collection in relation to the conference, would you discuss your ideas with Millie? I'll comply with what you both think though I would like to earn something on them. You can find Millie in the phone book listed under her husbands name Morton Goldsholl.
Incidentally I had a very long letter from her in which she enclosed her invite to the conference hoping to lure me back to Chicago as a result. I wonder if that means she plans to attend? She's interested in Childrens problems and as am I. In fact I have the pediatric service in the hospital where I work.
Most of what I get is from their acting out their feelings so that I can fairly well get at the inter-family relationships and the problems contributing to these youngsters illnesses. So many of their illnesses have a psychogenic base and others, where organic basis exists, are greatly aggravated by what goes on at home.
Its fascinating when, a subsequent interview with parents during which time factual background information is obtained, bears out what these children tell by gestures behavior and general acting out of their problems.
You know a good ploy is timely on the psycho-somatic approach to illness.

title: Jack Conroy letters [18], 1924-1991
transcription:
4.
So many stories plays etc. have been written which explain the effect of one's background on mental breakdowns. None has been done on medical conditions and believe me, from the facts I have on hand, the stories that can be written would be equal to Snakepit and others such stories.
Have you ever considered doing a play? If your interested - suppose you spend some time reviewing the play form and I'll send you a bibliography on the psychosomatic approach to illness. If your interested - when I get to Chicago I can give you some real life histories and we might collaborate on a play. Let me know how you feel about this idea?
I know for example, the way people prone to certain illnesses behave and why - that's called the dynamics - that in addition to the real histories, which would give the plot; together with your ability to know how people from certain walks of life would talk in addition to your marvelous skill at writing should help make these stories alive. I can say with enough assurance that I'm considered fairly well oriented psycho analytically as well as having a fairly good fund of knowledge about the psychosomatic approach to the study of treatment of illnesses.
If this scheme is a success it would be the 1st of its kind. Please consider it and let me know.

I had a short note from Theo recently. Shes not fareing too well.
How have you been? What are you working on now? And whats happening in the literary field generally in Chicago? I have so many ideas for books I consider timely. Unfortunately I'm unable to express myself through writing and I guess writers have their own compulsions as to what they want to express.

Rose Randall

Dear Jack,
We have been saddened to hear about your stroke, but it was good to learn from Doug Wixson that you are recovering. We often think of you, and simply wanted to take Valentine's Day as an appropriate time to tell you that we love you, and we treasure the works you have so generously inscribed in the past. Sapphina also delights in looking back at your books, particularly The Fast Sooner Hound, and the playful drawings and tender wishes for her happiness — she has taken those words seriously, and benefitted greatly from them.
But the main thing is just to say we love you!!
Doug has been in touch about your papers, and there is certainly no need to worry about them — I am sure Doug will find an appropriate place and one that you can give your blessing to. You should not be too selfless in this, of course, as this would be an appropriate source of income to pay for your medical expenses. Whatever some institution gives you, it won't be a fraction of what your fantastic collection of literary treasures is worth. Over the years I was playing with the notion of coming up with some thousands to offer you, with the idea of merging these works with my collection, but I think Doug is pursuing the right course, which is to bestow them outright and create a Jack Conroy room where scholars will devote themselves to an understanding of your immense contribution to our literature. By the way, I have found them well aware of that contribution both in India and in New Zealand and in Australia.

title: Jack Conroy letters [18], 1924-1991
transcription:
These days, when my manuscripts are off at ZIFF-DAVIS, and I am suffering the hinges of hell with simple waiting... and waiting... and waiting... my nerves are raw, and I feel futile.
Ah, God Almighty, you subtle Irisher, what a nerve you've got to be reminding me of those days when all the world in Missouri was green... and the spirit was fierce and unflinching. And one argued with every singing bird and every crack in the sidewalk and praised every common flower in the roadside because of the terrible joy of realizing that one was alone against xall the odds of humanity. And now, comes the xday when I realize I xam becoming,more xand more, one of humanityx, subjectx to all its failings xand futilities. Oh, blessed mither of God!t h e world was, indeed, green as green around Moberly!
And now, to cap all my tribulations, my blessed old type-writer is busted.
Ah, Jack, we are safely past more than we dream — I remember the time I hung by my fingertips to the ladder of a reefer in a freight train pounding out of Utah into Colorado. And all my future and all my life depended on the strength in my fingers. And I hung there, seared, and determined to hold on. I think the flame from those days must be the fire that sustains me, now. Sure it is!
For, in spite of all my temperamental inconstancy, and all my failure, and all the rejections and rebuffs, in spite of my present despond — the ignorant, savage spirit of those green days, when I could cheerfully butt my head against any stone wall, has placed a determination in me that now becomes patience and endurance.
You know, Jack, that day I bought candy in that Moberly store with my final 50 ¢ents, candy for the kids who, now, are grown men, I never dreamed you'd be the one to point me out as one of the supreme poetsingers of America — For that was my whole desire, in those days: to become recognized as an American, not as a representative of any section — and it always will be that way with me — I have asked Frank to send me a copy of Volume One of the Encyclopedia —but, so far, no reply. I wish you were still in the office, so you could urge him to send it —
—OVER—

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991

6 Gransden Rd
W.12.
23rd June:
Dear Mr. Conroy,
How lovely to hear from you again. Thank you for the cuttings enclosed with your letter, and also the dollar, which was completely unnecessary. It was kind of you to think of me, and I appreciate that, but I can assure you that I didn't mind getting the book for you, and am only too pleased to be able to help if I can.
I enjoyed your letter, especially the firey paragraph about Vietnam. I'm afraid I don't know enough about the war to voice any real opinion but I agree with you, and have thought

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
2
for a long time that the U.S.A. should put her own house in order before organising everyone else's. I do think that it is such an appalling waste of men, time, and money. Apart from the loss of life, the money being wasted there could be used in many other directions e.g. instead of blowing the place to bits money used on ammo. could be used to build and generally develop the place. If the money were not used there I'm sure the Indians dying of starvation in Bihar would be grateful for the food it would buy.
Getting back to "Anyplace but here" I am glad you are inclined to agree with me that the English are more tolerant on the question of racial

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
3
relations. I'm sorry you saw some prejudice while you were here. You don't say what it was, but I hope there were no ugly scenes. You mention unemployment as a source of irritation but I would say more bad feeling is caused over housing (or rather the acute shortage of it) than anything else. But now we're getting on to another social problem; one which should have been solved a long time ago.
Fancy Burl Ives being a friend of yours. Of course we know his records — Ugly Bug Ball, etc. On Saturday we have a programme on the radio called Children's Favorites, and Burl Ives' records are among the favorites such as Teddy Bears Picnic, Four legged friend, assorted top records etc. and usually they play one of his each week.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
4
I like his opinion of the British Isles but hesitate to agree (although I do, wholeheartedly) in case you think I'm just plain biased.
Nelson takes the last of this year's exams on Tuesday morning. We have a bonfire of notes etc. on schedule for Tuesday afternoon. Seriously though I think he will be really glad when they're over although he'll be a nervous wreck until the results are through. Only one more year after this!
Nelson's Mum flies out to the U.S. a week today, and she's so excited about it. I certainly wish I were coming with her.
I hope you enjoy the summer, and I expect you & Mrs. Conroy are

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
5
looking forward to your son, and his family's, visit. We are hoping to get away in August; we shall need the rest after decorating for the best part of July.
My parents send their regards to you both. Please remember me to Mrs. Conroy. Nelson sends his regards and said something about writing, but with all due respect to my other half, I shouldn't count on it.
Thanks for the book you have posted. I look forward to receiving it; it is sweet of you to remember us.
Sincerely yours,
Gay.
24.6.67.
P.S. The letter was just waiting to be sealed & posted, when the book arrived this morning. Many thanks once again for your kindness. I am looking forward to reading it. Gay.

Dear Jack,
Many thanks for the clippings (how do you all of that reading?), the autographed copy of New Letters, and most of all, your letter. Yes, I was "frisked" in London — and it's very unpleasant.
I do subscribe to New Letters and I've just received the last issue with Michel Fabre's article. I'm looking forward to reading it. How does it feel to be a "sage"?

You mention my doing a book on the Fitzgeralds. After the Dreiser

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991

As ever
Ruth

Primm, Sandy
7 23 88
Dear Jack —
Doug recently told me that you're taking it easy this summer at a relatively friendly hostel. I hope you found something to cheer you up in the Democrat Convention, a few of the faithful seemed to have fair command of the English language and some well grounded idealism. My only beef was the lack of emphasis on the environment; too much of politics as usual.
I haven't had a chance to do much writing lately, tho have gotten a small grant to do oral history video tapes in the Ozarks. Our fivist is focusing on some of the old-time river rats and tie rafters.
The only writing I've done lately that is in any condition to share is an eulogy I did for my father whose heart unexpectedly gave out a month ago. The piece I wrote for him isn't too schmaltzy or grisly. I think that by the end of his life my father treasured much more the works of nature than those of the business world that took so much of his time. He often tried to write, but usually only got as far as making lists. I hope that you find inspiration to keep a sharp pencil nearby and put it to good use. With the hope of seeing you soon —
All good wishes —
Sandy

June 6, 1949
Dear Jack,
When I first saw "Phoebe Snow" it was "blithesome Spring" and I made a sketch for you. Now, "Summer is a cumin in" and — going too, and I have not had a chance to send it to you.
It is the knowing, all consuming, ATOM — how to use it, where to hide it, where shall we hide, and "No Place to Hide", — just bogging a poor mortal.
I often wonder about my work. Even though I love it, trying to eek out coherent facts and sentences out of great scientists takes a lot of cudgeling of the mind, and is very exhausting. The only satisfying thing about it is that I

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
am in a position to tell the "great" they are wrong and they don't know what they are talking about — in writing of course.
I have not written a line of my own since I enlisted with the Government. The reason is primarily due to my disagreable experience with the area highway man of the publishing field.
The publisher's lawyers were stabling, and the case was postponed for a Fall hearing. How long this can go on I don't know. But, I have a hunch long enough for the publisher to sell a second edition, and even have someone with a second book on the remaining material from my book.
That is where the atom bomb comes in, and I sign off.
My best to Mrs Conroy and the boys.
Sophia

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
January 6, 1950
Dear Jack:
There was no "Merry Christmas" nor a "Happy New Year" from the Priors this year because the sudden death of my sister Edith.
I had, however, put in an order in advance for a happy and successful year for all the Conroys. I couldn't forget.
One of my pleasantest surprises was a card from Jim, and I shall tell him so one of these days.
What is everyone doing? I have often thought, and wondered, but have still to find out.
The tomorrows are not ours, but why don't we gamble and plan to get together sometime.
Remember me to the boys and especially to Mrs. Conroy.
Sincerely,
Sophia

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991

I have been waiting to thank you for your letter, but I have been in an incoherent frame of mind and feel the results might be startling in writing.
Somehow, in the daily

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
Sometime when the chill wind forgets to blow we'll have to plan an evening. I hope it will be soon.
My regards to the family — special for Mrs. Conroy.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
whirl of living one forgets that it is all to end; so, the blows are overwhelming
I keep remembering some lines I read in Dryden, once upon a time:
"When I consider life, 'tis all a cheat;
Yet, fooled with hope,

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
men favor the deceit.
Trust on, and think to-morrow will repay.
Tomorrow's falser than the former day —
Lies worse, and, while it says it shall be blest
With some new joys, cuts off what we possessed."
....
But one must carry on, and not think too hard.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
8 October 1950
Dear Jack:
I am sending you an "old times" I found at the book store because it reminded me of a communication we once had — a "once" that has now become so long ago.
It seems strange that this whirpool of existence should have such a grip on our very own time that we cannot even be alloted a tiny bit for seeing, and enjoying our friends.
But, of course, you are among the chosen who is allowed such pleasures by an annual trip to Yaddo where one meets not only old and new friends, but can also commune with nature — (and even bet on horses).
My life seems to have become narrowed down, by time and distance, to the group that split atoms, neutrons, protons, and keep their irons not in fire like our forebearers, but in "hot stuff."
I did have a visit with Jack Conroy, the author, and stood gazing at your fine portrait and thought, "I knew him well." I tarried some minutes longer hoping to hear you coming with some celebrity on personal tour. No one came. And so, I left, and boarded a bus for home.
Now, I have graduated from bus to

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
to car — a Plymouth that takes me each day on my long journey more leisurely. I am in basic training as taxi driver trying to keep in step with the race track locally known as "Outer Prior."
Who knows? Maybe sometime the motion of my chariot will propagate stresses that might direct me to your neighborhood to see all the Conroys.
Sincerely,
Sophia

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991

Sophia
13 August 1951
Dear Jack:
Just in case you were planning to point a finger my way when the bombs start "bursting in air," I want to inform you that I have terminated in that service.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
In fact, my boss took it into his head to resign sud-denly, and my chair was just whisked from under me — quickly, and painlessly.
And so, now I am sounding "the happy hunting horn" —

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
not "hunting for mice", but another job. Keep your ears peeled for sweet sounds.
Sincerely,
Sophia

Dear Jack:
I tried to get you on the phone to tell you that so far I had won a moral victory.
Schuman and C[[?]] admitted in court that they got the idea from my book, and that they had had access to my material when they got their book together.
I was very lucky in having Judge Samuel Kaufman, who tried to Copland case.
I wish you had been there! It was a wonderful session.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:

When he dismissed the court he said that the case rests entirely on facts — and, fortunately I have all the facts in writing. But, one never knows about the final verdict. Here's hoping.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991

24 November 1952
Dear Jack:
By now you must think me a most unreliable person.
Strangely enough, my life has become crowded with obstacles, and all sorts of unacceptable interferences.
The thing that has really shelved me is one of these "unknown" virusses. It cannot even be solved by "X:"
I have had to get up with this "unknown" and struggle along with a recurrent fever which almost finished me up.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
The doctor tells me that there are a lot of cases like mine, and that it takes six months to a year to overcome this infinitesimal monster. (I think the REDS are spraying bugs around.)
I was very sorry to hear abut Gladys's brother and would have written her a note had I not been carried away with the idea that I was going to see you soon.
I thought of you often during the trying election hours and wished I could have heard

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
some of your comments on the skittering, sticky, moss that crawled into Washington.
I managed to write a short story for children as an example for some job. I didn't get the job, but I would like you to see the story sometime. It is called "Moçeno", and is about a Cuban boy — pre-Hemingway. No influence at all.
A merrie Thanksgiving to all — especially to our Korean hero.
Sincerely,
Sophia

12 August 1963
Dear Jack:
Here's an answer to a "gentlemen's" prayer. Half price — just as you wished.
I was sorry to miss your lecture at Northwestern. I had gone to Hinsdale for an interview and I was too tired to make it.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
3 April 1966
Dear Jack:
I have been saving these clippings for you and thought I had better lend them now so that you could use them.
I can see that you are really keeping busy — what with reviews and your books.
If you ever do come "North," as you said you might, be sure and let me know. We could at least have a short chat over a cup of coffee.
Moody and Carlene returned from Bangkok. A great experience!
Regards to Gladys —
Sincerely,  Sophia

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
3 March 1967
Dear Jack:
Everytime I pick up something to read, I find a reference to your work or some association that makes me want to tell you about it.
When I saw the last ride of "Phoebe Snow" on TV I had hoped that you too were viewing the historical ride. The reporter quoted:
"My gown stays white from morn till night
Upon the road of anthracite.
Now, rest in peace to Phoebe Snow."
I also heard the fine discussion with Bontemp on your latest book. And, just last night (2 March) I found the enclosed announcement in the "Daily News." The ABC summer programs will include a program on the migration of the Negroes. Are you in on this? I hope so.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
And, speaking of TV, I saw Nelson Algren running down the steps of the Courthouse trying to avoid the anxious reporters who were trying to get the "dope" right out of the horses mouth. Disgraceful man! And then — in an article in the "New Yorker" by Edmund Wilson there is reference to Simone de Beauvoir's new book about which Wilson say: "It is embarassing to read her account of her relations with Nelson Algren and Sartre." Aren't these people repulsive?
When I last saw you, you had told me that you had nothing to do with Algren anymore. How could a respectable human being tolerate such company!
You and Gladys should be very happy in that charming "Conroy Manse" — with fireplace.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
Is there really a brook near your home?
We were about to buy some eskimo dogs and a sled but the snow is beginning to go. Yesterday was the first time I was able to move my car and drive away. There is a mound of ice and snow, at least ten feet, high near the street. Even the weather got mixed up in this messy world.
Moody is being asked to go back to Thailand this summer. Actually, they want him to stay three years but that is out of the question.
Remember me to Gladys.
Sincerely,
Sophia

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
Sunday September 12
