New York. August 4, 1932
Dear Jack,
My typewriter is on the bum, so please forgive this scribble. I purposedly delayed my reply to your last letter in order to be able to report to you — in full — the new developments. I think this meeting was the most vital and constructive we have held, and, frankly, it seems that the group is coalescing into an harmonious working organization. The antipodal attitudes of Spier and Miller are gradually being submerged in the stress of new tasks and ideas. Provided we can keep up the distribution work, the mag will grow into a real fighting working-class organ. The Negro issue presents a very good appearance — the cover is swell. I am glad you cut out the three-columned pages, for the typography of the poems was badly mangled by the exigencies of space. We are, by degrees, doing away with the lowbrow tone and the stale conventional rhythm of much of the poetry that used to appear in the RP. As I have written you once, lowbrow and proletarian are synonyms to the bourgeoisie, but not to us. I particuraly liked Kenneth W. Porter's review — it is brilliantly written. Rogers' poems are also good. He exhibits an artistic sensibility of a high order. Stacy's poem, too, strikes home. Gerome's are excellent.
We are going to make a gallant effort to finance UNREST 1932. It was decided to arrange a symposium, with prominent speakers. I am going to try to get Joe
(over)

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
Freeman, and it's up to you to entice Porty and Cousley; John Herrman will also be appealed to. I suggested the truly inflammatory topic, Is Bourgeois Literature Dead? and it was immediately accepted by the group. If we succeed in getting the speakers named above, we shall certainly draw a huge crowd, as well as get ourselves a good deal of valuable publicity. The speakers will have to be inveigled into doing their bit for the good of the cause, as we want to keep expenses as low as possible. You will get the rest of the details from the minutes.
Various methods for improving the mag were discussed. We decided to cut out the book reviews, inasmuch as the publishing houses don't send us any of the important books for review, and we are certainly not going to buy them. Instead (of course, with your approval) we thought it would liven up the contents to run a magazine-review section, something after the order of the Criterion & Hound & Horn, but from an analytical Marxian angle of course. My idea is, as I was delegated to write the first sample of the new product, to call a spade a spade and take bourgeois

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
2
pig-stys like the Hound & Horn, the New Review, for a ride. I intend to review five or six magazines, such as the above mentioned, and the New Masses and Left, in one lump, link them all up into a good-sized essay shoving the trend of letters on the two fronts, the proletarian or the bourgeois. If we succeed in goading some of the esthetic die-hards into heated rebuttal and vociferous contempt for the culture-wrecking Bolsheviks, we shall have accomplished our purpose, not to mention the publicity for the RP. We can't make the public aware of our existence, unless we go in for some real hot battles and throu gentlemanly manners to the winds. What do you think of the idea? Here in NY the bourgeois critics, being in sole command of the book-pages in the newspapers, are hitting right and left at the "Communist intellectuals and generally doing their damned best to get such new converts as Hicks and Arvin fired from their jobs. Almost daily they pour kettle-fulls of filth on the heads of the leftist writers. The radical advance on the cultural front is evoking a counter
(over)

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
revolution, so to speak. George Jean Nathan is leading the black army (or is it the white army?) with Harry Hansen, Kirstein and Roscoe, as his lieutenants. Nathan is editor of a new magazine, "that will shun politics" and and reassert the good old virtues of Neroinesque fiddling to the roar of a starving America.
The negotiations with the Party have now been shifted to the National Committee of the JRES, with Komorowski in charge. I will be present at the faction meeting scheduled to take place this week, where the question of the RP will be discussed. Of course, the RP will remain an autonomous organization. However, the actual form that our affiliation will take has not been worked out as yet. After they arrive at some conclusions, the conditions will be sent to you for consideration.
I read your story in the Mercury. I think it is the best prose you have ever written: your style is gaining in sensitivity and psychic tension. The figure of Mike is drawn full-length by means or a few keen strokes. The end is not precipitous, but significantly abrupt, plastic, and fertile with implication. You succeed in evoking the atmosphere of a toiler's family — life, the gnawing form of unpaid bills, debts, and constant physical danger.

title: Jack Conroy letters [17], 1924-1991
transcription:
3
However, keeping in mind the rigid attitude of our leftist editors, I don't believe Left or New Masses would have taken to it, seeing that the administration of the mind — the bosses, are not being fried on the fire of proletarian indignation. But, no doubt, they will learn in time not to demand "PROLETARIAN literature" but "proletarian literature."
I am enclosing a translation from a well-known Soviet Yiddish poet. Xarik strikes here a subtle note; a more or less philosophical one. He spiritualizes the personalities of revolutionists, which is a welcome relief from the general harshness and stridency of most revolutionary utterance. The last two lines are really good. Tell me what you think of it. STORM — but we must know why! Let the storm be purposeful, not blind, anarchic.
Yrs,
Phil
P.S. With regard to magazine review: since I would like to review the proletarian issue of Contempo and Left 3, in the first inning, I think it is best We let the matter slide till October. —

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription:
4-11-72

Dear Jack:

Received your letter, postcard, &yesterday the mags. only scanned them in moberly so it was a delight to read them through last night. Christ, what powerful stuff! Am going to go to millville saturday & go over them with Kack Miller then will mail them back next week. By the way Jack is talking about having the first issue out by 5/21. I will discuss your piece with him & get a fast note off to you with the mags.

Questions:
1) How big were your press runs?
2) How did you distribute the mags?
3) Did any issue ever show a profit - or break even?
4) Where did the writers & poets come from?
5) Who read them (workers, academics, lit people - or who?)?
6) How close to the c.p. were the mags - were they sold only in party bookshops, etc.?

The thing that struck me the most about all 3 of the mags was their nitty-gritty worker-level approach (without being patronizing like a lot of the c.p. stuff was) without any of the doctrinaire mindbusting about Hegel, Feuerbach, etc that turns workers off faster then the 'ol sonner hound could run. A good job, Jack - something you can be proud of long after the "Readers Digest" has replaced northern tissue in the nation's latrines.

As for Chris Suggs displaying his negro baby in the pubs of wheeler (incidentally there are 3 - to match the 3 churches - with 212 people I guess you are either in church or a joint!) I would say, with some degree

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription:
of certainty, that the baby's brains would probably be dashed out on the bar & Chris would be hung from the nearest sour-apple tree. According to the local bar talk "welfare-niggers" are responsible for all of society's ills - you can take it from there. Needless to say, we have had some interesting discussions up here over our brews. Which brings to mind a piece I have been toying with - "The Biggest Snow-job in History" - pointing out what a piker Goebbels really was compared to the job that has been done on the workers here. The tragedy of it is, is that marx was right, workers aren't dumb - they know something is wrong & that they are getting fucked, but are just having a little problem in identifying the enemy.

In the suggs baby vein, we got a call from a group of our friends (all black) in L. a. on New Years Eve - they were concerned about us living here with all the "honkies & crackers" & wanted us to come back out there (L.A.) with "our people". Had to point out we've lived with "honkies" before & guess we can do it again - after all they are 85% of the people & 2/3 of the poor & someone has to look out for them. Oh well, someday we won't have to concern ourselves with this kind of shit - they'll be just people . . .

salud,

Harlan

p.s. - wrote a slashing attack on the "movies of the 30's" for the next December - think you'll enjoy it - "of Bread & Circuses"

3/27/72
Dear Jack:
Exciting news from the frozen north - am working with a group (north country alternatives) that is planning a new radical mag in Minneapolis - title: "North Country Anvil". The editor (Jack Miller) is a young (33) man of considerable talent who used to be a feature writer for the Mpls Tribune & then chucked it all two years ago to take a crack at free-lancing. Jack wanted me to ask you two things:
1) Would you like to do a short piece for the pilot issue (current projection - June 21) along the lines of what the old anvil & rebel poet were - sort of a nostalgic passing-the-torch type thing?
2) Do you have any extra copies of the anvil and/or Rebel poet that you could send us to look over? Would return them of course.
Our mag (physically - not editorially) would be a 7 1/4 x 9 3/4 along the lines of the New Republic - slick cover & rough stock inside. You'd be in good company in the 1st issue - planning an attack on the steel trust (the pissant & the elephant), a stab at the Mpls Mayor (a brainless ex-cop - low & [[?]] demagogue), a look at communal living, & a few other sallies at assorted windmills.
Enjoyed your last postcard - & your piece in latest December - a gem.
(over)

Curt sent me B. Traven's "Jungle Novels" the other day - Christ, what powerful stuff!

Harlan

12-13-77
Dear Jack:
How's the "foolkiller" of Moberly - & his trusty companion Gladys?
Thought about you the other day - was browsing used bookshops & finally (after 35 years) found a copy of "Germinal" so now I won't have to steal yours (the only one I've ever seen outside of the library copy I read when I was 14). Reread it last night - God, what a powerful book! Also read "Main Street" and now I know why I left Minnesota 25 years ado. Interesting; books such as "Main Street" & anything else by Lewis, Faulkner and Hemingway, Sinclair, Steinbeck, etc are stocked separately in book stores under the heading of "classics" while the fiction sections are full of Vonnegut, "Jaws", "Starwars". & all the tripe that passes as literature nowadays - where will it end? To have witnessed the death of literature, art & music in my short lifetime is amazing - I can hear the stormtroopers boots around the corner!
Amusing, one of the tenants in the apartment we manage (old Jewish people from N.Y.) have a photo of Lenin on their wall - they were terrified when I commented on it; now we are the best of pals & he brings me all is daily workers, etc. when he's done with them.
Elsinore (oddly enough in a small town of 4000) is a radical hotbed - cast 27 votes for the CP candidate in the last election.
Took in the SOVIET NATIONAL EXHIBITION in L.A. a couple of weeks ago, awesome! over 300,000 people attended and a lot of eyes were opened - if "letters to the Editor" of LA Times a[[?]] any barometer.
Enough of my radical musings - Keep in touch & stay healthy - the world needs you!
Salud,
Harlan.

Sept 2, 1954
Dear Jack,
The world has done it again - though I guess I should be grateful that its ironies stay smaller than the worst. I was in New York one day of the five I had figured my mini[[?]]um when I received news that Miriam, my wife, was seriously ill. There's been a dread thing in the offing for several years & the doctors said this was it. So I flew back. Now, thank God, it turns out they were wrong & she is recovering nicely. - So I have no right to complain at being here instead of in a tub of sour mash at Conroy's Folly, .. but I can't help a small bitterness anyway. I had been looking forward so damn much to seeing you again, & other friends in both NY & Chicago, Looks as if I'll have to save up & come out over Christmas or next summer. Harvey Webster & I got to be good friends & talked of you a great deal - so much so that it will be a long, sad day until we do get together, old Pappy. But do not give up hope. Even as I write I am scheming ways. I will yet drink up all the whiskey [[?]]

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription:
you have. - As you may have heard, I concluded my training at Yaddo by falling into the fountain in the hall one night. I was only trying to warm up that shy Psyche there, but I seemed to fail in some was. Googly Harvey pulled me out ( actually I was carrying a chair which got much wetter, though less bruised than I), aided by Daniel Curley - a good-hearted friend & writer of short stories I hope will meet you & vice versa some day.My splash was kep rather quiet, I am led to believe, however.
Did have a splendid summer, Got a great deal of work done, which seems - most of it - to move a good bit ahead. But maybe this is part of my optimistic grief for les temps perdu, now I am back in my unfinished cave & again condemned for an uncertain term to walk the scaffolds, carrying picks, shovels, hammers & my usual [[?]] of shit.
- Well, I should treat my present aches lightly, perhaps, but more seriousl the time at Yaddo which really was an important

experience for me. - Except I expect you know all the nightmares & their values - provided by two really free-from-the-wolf months, with nothing but yourself between you & the great american poem or whatever. What also counted for a good deal was the sense of a real community of letters, which I suddenly feeel I've joined, & which I was never very sure existed before. It is at once reassuring & alarming - as, I guess, all communities of all kinds must be. But probably better (for mortal frailty) with than without.
Scribners turned down my book of poems - which may be just as wekk since I did send it prematurely. But now it is nearly ready &and I'll fire it off in another month or so. When I type it up anew I'll shop off some recent things for your perusal. Have only sent out a few individual poems recently, & so far have heard only from Harper's and New Yorker - the former yes, the latter no. But that's something, anyway.
Give my best to Dave Waggoner &

Take it out of those bible tracts. - It's true that if you're going to stop with what you've done that's still a lot to stop with, but it's just because it's a lot (you know?) that you ought to do more now.

Dear Mr. Conroy,
  Thank you very much for your interesting letter about Mike Gold. Actually, I found your address in the "Who's Who", though I am sure that Michael Folsom, whom I am going to see next week, will suggest that I write you.
 I do have a few queries, but I'm afraid not all specific. Firstly, could you tell me what qualities you admired in [underlined] 120 Million, and what your views were concerning [underlined] Jews Without Money a year later? I know it's a terribly hackneyed term, but in what sense did you find them 'revolutionary'?
 Part of my thesis will concern Gold in relation to other left-wing writers with whom he had differences of view over the requirements of revolutionary or proletarian literature. I have been in touch with John Howard Larson, and asked him to try to define areas where his and Gold's views converged

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription:
or contrasted with regard to the New Playwrights Theatre and the 'revolutionary' drama. In general, I am interested in the problem of the aesthetic forms of 'Tenderz', and I hope to examine [[underlined] The disinherited and Gold's reaction to it so that his own position, at a certain point in time, may be roughly defined. It would be most valuable for me if you could tell me something of the spirit in which your novel was written, precisely how it was intended to be tendentious, and what problems you encountered in writing it. I really believe that the 'mechanics' (if that isn't too crude a term) of left-wing literature has been largely overlooked by commentators, and I hope to explore this more fully - my thesis.

August 24, 1974
Baring, Missouri
Dear Mr. Conroy;
I am writing to you again for several reasons; one of which is to thank you again for putting me in touch with the 'Foolkiller' magazine. They were very prompt about sending me the special issue I requested for which I am grateful.
Mr. Conroy, I know you are a very busy person and I know you might not be able to answer this letter, but you are the only one I know who might be in a position to give me some answers to some questions I have had going around in my mind since I finally accepted the fact that Bill Mason was dead. Those questions include how, where and why. You interviewed Bill. Did he seem to you the kind of young man who would take his own life?
As for me, I am married now and have a family, but I first met Bill in 1953 in the early spring. I don't believe, at that time, he had been home from military service long and he was still very nervous from that and from the fact that he had been on the same boat that had brought his older brother, Johnny, home. Johnny had been killed in action and Bill, himself, had been wounded by shell fragments in his leg and a head injury. At that time, he also found he had family troubles and, when I  met him, was in the final phases of getting a divorce from

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription:
his first wife who he had married about three weeks before leaving for service, What made things worse he found he had a son by her. Of course, for some reason known only to himself, he didn't tell me himself about any of this. I guess he thought his troubles were his own and he had no right to bother anyone else with them. I was eighteen then and Bill sang his way right into my heart. That's why I told you before he was very special to me. This probably sounds rather bold since I married my present husband in late 1954 but I am only trying to explain why I can't accept that Bill killed himself. I love and respect my husband, Mr. Conroy, but Bill will always be with me.
I got to know him well the year and a half we went together. One of my best girlfriends schoolmates met her husband through Bill. 
As I mentioned before, when I first met him he was nervous and couldn't stay in one place very long at a time but as we got better acquainted and he found that I was willing to listen to him when he felt like talking he told me about his family, but mostly about his love of music; how Tonney Burton had taught him all he knew about it but there was one thing Tonney couldn't have taught him. No one could teach him to sing the was he did, putting his love and sorrows all to music that came from his heart. No one who heard him could fail to hear it and he could make you laugh or cry just as easily with music. That

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription: was his life, what he'd been born for and the longer I knew him the more convinced I was that if Bill ever had to stop playing and singing he'd just as well stop breathing. We spent a lot of happy days with Tonney and Anna Burton at their home in Moberly; Tonney and his violin and Bill with his guitar and singing. He really relaxed and enjoyed himself and as more time passed I knew Bill was healing on the inside as well as on the outside. He had a respect and a lve of life that nothing could put down. He left Moberly and I never saw him again for about 8 months. In that time, never heard from him either. I was heartsick and, I must admit, when I met my husband I think at that time I agreed to marry him out of hurt and loneliness. We had been married in November of 1954 for exactly one week when Bill came back, his divorce final and apparently expecting me to be still waiting. To make part of this shorter, we tried to make the most of our mistake. I introduced him to my new husband and to say he and my husband hit it off great is putting it mildly but it really didn't surprise me to much. When Bill tried he could charm anyone. My husband was the real surprise to me. He knew Bill and I had dated before and he didn't generally take to anyone I had known before because he was, and is, a very jealous man although I have never given him any cause to be since we were married twenty years ago.

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription:
Bill finally remarried a girl named Orma and they had a boy and a girl. Orma played banjo when the were married and the two kids could really sing a wonderful duet. Bill had taken a steady job with the railroad and seemed pretty settled then. He still played and sang and he had been writing some of his own songs. We didn't see much of his family; Orma worked at the telephone office and Bill and I saw each other several times alone. At first, he talked as though he was happy but there was something wrong and I could feel it so I finally asked him to talk to me about it and it seems Orma had stopped playing her banjo and she wanted Bill to give up his music and just be satisfied with his family and the railroad. He asked me what I would do if I were in her place and I told him that, had I been in her place, I couldn't and wouldn't ask him to give up his music. He and Orma apparently were having other problems, too, and soon after that she took the two children and moved back to Kansas City. We didn't see much of Bill after that. His visits grew less frequent until they finally stopped altogether.
Tonney Burton's granddaughter married one of the friends Bill brought down from Kansas City and we were close friends. Marie was like a sister to Bill and she and Ken kept in touch with him by letter and telephone.
The first we heard of Bill's death was trough a friend in Huntsville, and this is another reason I am writing to you. This

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription:
friend of Bill's had been working in Boulder, Colorado for sometime and this is the story he told: Bill came to Boulder to visit this friend and talked to him for about an hour and when he left Bill said he would see this friend at supper. This friend, Keith, said Bill was going to his apartment to wait for him and he said when he talked to Bill there was no sign of strain or worry about him at all. He was just like he always was. Three hours later, Keith says he arrived home found a suicide note on his kitchen table and then found Bill in his bathroom where he had shot himself in the head.
This story came to us about two weeks after Bill died.
A month or so after that I was lucky enough to meet Marie and Ken who were still a little shook up over the news but they were completely surprised by this story I have just written down. Now here is their version:
The first they had even heard of Bill's death was when Marie's mother had called them in Tucson, Arizona where they lived and told them. Ken immediately called Bill's younger brother in Kansas City who told them that Bill and his new bride of four months had been moving back to Kansas City from Rifle, Colorado where they had been living. They had already moved most of their belongings to K.C. but Mrs. Mason still had a few personal things in Rifle and they had gone back to Rifle after them and Bill

title: Jack Conroy letters [15], 1924-1991
transcription:
killed himself.
Apparently no one except his wife, his brother and his sister knew anything  about his death until after he was buried a week or more. Why wasn't Marie, who was nearly a sister to him, and Ken notified so they could attend the funeral. There were others who loved Bill, too, and would have attended his funeral had they known or, if the couldn't attend then, they could have sent flowers and their sympathy to his wife. Another question is this. Why, if it was his wish to be buried beside Tonney and Anna Burton, wasn't his wishes carried out and his body brought back here for burial. And one other question. Why would a young man with a new wife, a bright, wonderful, rising musical career ahead of him, and who loved life and loved living it to the full all of a sudden come to such a tragic end.
Mr. Conroy, I know this is a long letter and there are many questions that perhaps only Bill, himself, could answer but that doesn't keep me from wanting to know why he would do it. It just wasn't something that Bill Mason would do. I knew him and he just couldn't do such a thing unless something terribly drastic had happened to him.
I don't really expect an answer to this letter because I know that you are a very busy man and [something is crossed out] no doubt have more important things to do than answer letters which almost are long enough for a

DEAR JACK:
God, but you're a lousy correspondent! I wouldn't feel so bad about it, but I haven't heard a word from you since 1957 - and then only because Joy and I were there to see you. You even missed a divorce. And now there's a sixth Mrs. Ralph Peterson, which only proves that being 52, I'll never match Tommy Manville, but it isn't because I haven't tried. And I don't have his money...

The intervening 11 years has been split between Yukon Territory (Whitehorse, where I now own half a daily paper and starve) and the twin cities. Along about 1959 or 1960, I wrote you several times at Green Street - No response until the third time - "unclaimed". Last week I saw Herman Kogan and finally pinned you down.

So, for Christ's sake (I missed you, you bastard) fill me in on the Conroys and particularly Jack.. I got a host of questions i.e. samples: Did you retire at the Encyclopedia factory? How - and at what profit, I hope - did you dispose of Conroy's Folly? And did the neighborhood "go" like it was last time I saw you? What's with Jug-head? Nels? The Misses?

I'd love to hear from Jack, and will respond at length, when I'm near my typewriter, which I'm not now.  Warm regards
    Ralph

title: Jack Conroy letters [14], 1924-1991
transcription:
Dear Jack,

We often think of you and Gladys but never seem to think about you at the appropriate time for writing a letter.  However, now that school is over (it just ended last Friday) I do have time to send you a few lines.

This year has been a very difficult one at the high school.  All of them are difficult, but this one was, I believe, the most.  Even before the murder of Dr. M.L. King, our black students were very militant.  They weren't militant about learning or studying (except studying "black power"), but militant in a "get rid of whitey" way or "Let's don't let Whitey brainwash us."  The big hero of some--just how large a percentage I don't know--was the late Malcolm X.  So, you can see that things haven't been easy.  The murder of Dr. King, of course, gave the signal for burning and looting.  Most of this was on the West side, as you undoubtedly have read.  The local youth gangs in our neighborhood have been given much of the credit for keeping things cool on the South Side.  Yet they were some very rebellious and defiant kids in my classes for a few days or a week after the assassination, even though many of the students had turned away from King's leadership during the past year or two.  Then, RFK's murder bothered the Negroes, too.  He was a semi-hero to many of them--as much as any white man could be.

Of course, I was a very great admirer of

title: Jack Conroy letters [14], 1924-1991
transcription:
Martin Luther King—for some years—(and still was at the time of his death).  I was not an ardent admirer of RFK;  I have been for McCarthy before New Hampshire, and still am.  By the way, I hope that you will do your part in carrying Missouri for McCarthy.
In view of conditions, I have been thinking about looking for another job.  Not that I’m not sympathetic with the blacks or anxious to desert them.  But if they want to get white men out of the ghetto (and school teachers as well as merchants), there seems to be an end to my usefulness.  A teacher can’t teach students who reject him and don’t believe what he tells them.   But I haven’t taken any active steps towards a new job.  So, perforce, I’ll probably ne back in the fall at Hyde Park High, but what it will be like, Lord only knows.
In the meantime, in order to escape and relax, Anne and I are going to take a slow boat to Mexico.  (We always do go places in roundabout ways, and we love ships.)  Seriously, we are going to take the train this next Monday to San Francisco, get on a big round the world passenger liner (the Oriana), and ride just as far as Acapulco, Mexico.  
We’ll spend a couple of days there and a couple of weeks in Mexico City.  Then home over land, probably by train.  I have never seen Mexico; Anne was there briefly about 22 years ago—before we were married.  We’ll drop you a card if and when we get there and get used to the food and drinks.  (I understand the beer there is very good.)

title: Jack Conroy letters [14], 1924-1991
transcription:
The political picture is very discouraging to me.  You remember how much of a choice we felt we had in the election of 1964.  Well, Nixon and Humphrey won’t be a much better choice.  Perhaps we will be worse off than we were during the last four years.  
I like McCarthy, as I said before.  But  he doesn’t have much appeal to the working classes, the ethnic groups, or the blacks.  It’s hard to see how he is going to make it.  He gets very enthusiastic supporters among some groups, but how can he make it with the rest of the voters?  I have the feeling that he could perhaps get elected if he got the Democratic nomination.  But an even bigger obstacle is getting the delegates under the system we have.  Do you remember how Kefauver won all the primaries but still couldn’t get the nomination?   I like the way Eugene tries to talk sense and the way he sticks to the issues.  But can a man get elected here without making impassioned speeches and without promising things to all sorts of pressure groups?  Rockefeller would be an improvement over Nixon, but I don’t trust him too much.  Anyhow, he has little chance of getting the delegates.
One reason I’m writing to you now is that I thought I might look up your friend Charlie Miller if you could send me his address and if he lives in or near Mexico City.  I seem to recall hearing you say (or perhaps writing) that he got married recently.  
So if you feel like sending me his address, you might answer me very promptly, and I’ll get the answer by Monday, July 1.  We are leaving that same day but not until 6 PM.  Or, if that’s rushing you too much, you could

title: Jack Conroy letters [14], 1924-1991
transcription:
address it to us c/o the Mexican branch of American Express, Avenida Niza 22, Mexico City, to get there about three days after we get to the capital.  (We expect to get to Acapulco on July 8, and Mexico City on July 10th or 11th.)
In any case, we hope that later in the year we get to see you and tell you about our experiences in Mexico.  (We’ll write you and tell you some of our adventures in any case.)
We hope you and Gladys are both well
Write when you can, and if you want to send us Charly’s address or any other person’s address in Mexico, please do so.
Best regards,
Warren

Dearest Jack,

title: Jack Conroy letters [13], 1924-1991

Light, Jim
Dec. 15, 1982
Dear Jack + Gladys: The Light report this year has a couple of items worth mentioning. The most important — shown on the reverse side — is the product of my son Sheldon + his wife Maureen. The Brendan is obviously not as pretty as I am, he is, from what I've seen, a trifle smarter + a good bit nicer.... The second item is my daughter Jama's engagement marriage scheduled in July — to a young man who's a doctoral candidate in the Yale Divinity School. I like him — he seems to have common sense — even tho he may turn out to be parson, or even more frightening a professional musician (he has undergraduate + graduate degrees in music).... Otherwise, not much. The state of Illinois is in poor shape financially — which translates into the same sort of problems I fled from at CUNY: budget cuts, losses of positions, higher teaching loads, + general faculty discontent. I try to cope by pursuing, every month or so, my alternate career in numerical analysis at Vegas, Tahoe, + Reno. Occasionally I even do do a little reading + writing, as well as too much eating + drinking. Wish I could do some of it with you. Love,
Jim L

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
Light, Jim [1983]
Southern Illinois University
CARBONDALE, ILLINOIS 62901
College of Liberal Arts and Sciences
June 4
Dear Jack:
Just as note to tell you how much I enjoyed seeing you + visiting Moberly on Jack Conroy day. I wish I'd known exactly what I was supposed to do on that panel prior to sitting down, so I could have done more than talk off the top of my head — maybe even have said something intelligent — but as your old friend Archie says, "toujour gai, toujor gai." I wish also that I'd been able to stay for "Banjo Dancing," but I just had to get back in Carbondale the next morning to discuss with the President here, a lad named Sumit, the need for our Russian program — a fairly costly program that he'd like to destroy. In any case I truly enjoyed seeing you, more than I can say, + I hope to see you again + again + again before our last shirts wear out.
All goes much the same as usual here in Carbondale. A couple of weeks ago I wandered to the local race track to squander my substance + what should strike my eye in the first race but a horse called Hy Jamie. A miracle I thought — but then to check the validity of the miracle I scanned the racing form and of course concluded that I couldn't believe in this miracle because the facts implied it

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
wouldn't happen (or to put it another way, the pedigree + past performance proved the horse was really a dog). Of course the dog won — paying 53.00 + proving that miracles transcend facts; if they didn't they wouldn't be miracles — + I didn't have penny one on him. Alas!
Another adventure occurred last week when Amy + I went to one of those places called dinner-theatres. The play was called The Second Time Around, + it proved to be a very cutesy switcheroo about how an elderly pair shook their children + grand-children by their desire, for purposes of social security benefits, to live together outside the bonds of matrimony. The only thing of significance (for me) came during intermission when I saw that the audience were all elderly folk who had been ha-ha-ing + he-he-ing throughout the cutest parts of the play. And there it struck me that they were all my own age, give or take a year or two, + I began to cry. But Amy comforted me.
Tomorrow New Jersey + California hold their primaries, along with a couple of other lesser states, + I don't care. The only thing the interminable process proves is that it is costly + idiotic — + that Mondale will promise anything to anyone in pursuit of votes, + that Hart would do the same thing if Mondale hadn't got there first. The best of the lot is Jackson — who at least is intelli-gent + witty — but he's a bit of a bigot + I don't like all of his agenda. What do you think?
Love,
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
Dear Jack + Gladys: Hope both of you — + all those you love — are thriving. As for me, I'm a year older + no better morally intellectually, or financially. My life at S.I.U. goes on pretty much as usual, which means that I'm frustrated more often than not by the reality that more + more of the University's students + resources go into the Colleges of Business + Engineering + the like + fewer + fewer into the College of Liberal Arts. Alas!... My kids are now all married (two of them this past summer) + scattered over the country (Detroit, New Haven, Berkeley) + thriving well beyond their just desserts. They all threaten to come to Carbondale for the holidays and Amy is terrified at the prospects.... Amy + I still enjoy Carbondale, but every month or so we wander away for a long weekend of meditation (+ occasional prayer) at the tables of Vegas + Lake Tahoe. We also managed this November to spend a couple of weeks in England — mostly London, Oxford, Bath, + Keele — trying to recapture our Lost Youth. Didn't succeed too well — our feet kept aching — but did have lots of fun. Wish you'd been with us at the pubs. Best, Jim L
1983

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
Light, James F (Jim
Southern Illinois University
CARBONDALE, ILLINOIS 62901
College of Liberal Arts and Sciences
August 14, 1985
Dear Jack:
My guardian angel sent me a marvellous book called The Weed King + Other Stories, + I've been enjoying it far more than I can say in words. You were — are — a master of humor + pathos, and the book is a treasure for which the world should be grateful to you + to Wixson. Certainly, reading some of the pieces that I'd never seen before brought back anew how remarkably fine a talent you have — and how fortunate I was to have known you, if only for so short a time. In any case, few stories have ever moved me more than The Weed King, whose fight against weeds — + his defeat by their strength + his frailty — reminded me of the struggle against dirt fought so valiantly by Maggie's mother in Crane's Maggie. And the folk narratives capture so remarkably the folk wisdom + language of The Workplace (whether it be that of Slappy Hooper or a typesetter shop or whatever) + transforms them, through the folk narrative, into folk lore that can't be forgotten because it captures life itself, only magnified and bigger than life can ever be. And Uncle Ollie's hatred of stupidity + bigotry — so fine a person, so human a man.
The book is great, in other words, + I

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
think everybody involved in its production — most of all, the author — but also Wixson + Hill have much to be proud of. I hope it sells beyond your fondest dreams, + I'll try, as best I can, to spread the word.
Otherwise:
As of mid-August, Amy + I will be leaving Carbondale, at least for a while. Until October We'll be seeking El Dorado in Europe, gallivanting in London, Paris, Rome, Venice, Florence, Amsterdam, + other assorted places of high couth. After October 1, or at least for a few months, we'll be at the following address:
Watergate
5 Commodore Drive, #B 207
Emeryville, CA, 94608
The charm of the place is it's equidistant (about 5 minutes) from the Berkeley Library + the Frisco race track, with a very nice view of the East Bay (which the condo is on).
Right now we're moving mountains of furniture, records, + books, + storing even more, is spasmodic surges of activity. Wish you were here to watch + laugh.
What else? I got new eyeglasses, + found the world a brighter, though not better, place. I got all the cavities in my teeth filled again — + rejected the doctor's invitation for another root canal and tooth cap (despite his dire predictions) because i wanted to have a few teeth left without caps of one kind. Most important, I got a thorough physical exam, + the doctor said I was in pretty good health (even my heart, which showed, he said, few of the kinds of irregular rhythms it had been prone to since my heart attack of a few years back) + might live to be a hundred. Not sure it's worth it — but anyway — Best, Jim Light

Southern Illinois University
CARBONDALE, ILLINOIS 62901

June 28, 1985
Dear Jack:
I send on a memento. It's most valuable for the chubby portrait of some imposter who claims to be me.
I'll be sixty four years to Heaven in No-vember. As of mid-August I'll be free from administrative chores here (+ with a leave of absence until January 1987), so I'll have a fairly extensive period in which to read + write + gamble, as well as to continue with my commit-ment to root-canal work, followed by caps, for all of my teeth. All this forthcoming freedom, with all the attendant options, has left me in a kind of paralysis. The only thing I've done recently to cope with this is to apply for a teaching Fulbright to New Zealand for six months in '86. Why there? I think it's because the natives speak English, but it may be because there are 75 million sheep + only three million people in residence. In any case I have no idea whether I'll really force my poor wife to go to N.Z. (the truth is, she likes the idea better than I) if by some miracle I were invited there. What would Conroy do?
One of my friends here, the Dean of the Law School, Dan Hopson, died a short while ago. The two of us had decided a couple of years ago, for much the same reasons (none of them to do with health), that we wanted to give up administrative chores for other joys. But he died. Now, some of the faculty
(over)

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
look appraisingly at me + ask, "How you feeling, Dean?" I answer, "Pretty fair, considerin'." And no one asks, "Considering what?" For no one's really listening.
So I've got some questions to answer soon, one of them being where I'm going to light + for what purpose for the next few years. I wish I knew the answers, but though you learned me plenty (one of the few that ever learned me anything), you never learned me that. For now, I only know that Amy + I are going to spend a long 4th of July weekend in Vegas + will be spending a month or so in the Fall wandering around the parts of Europe that I most love. After that, the void. Maybe Frisco (where I have a son in Berkeley — who wants to be a writer — and a condo on the East Bay); or Connecticut (where I have a daughter in Ridgefield and a house in Westport); or Detroit (where I have a son + two grandchildren in Grosse Pointe); or Vegas (where most of my gambling friends alight most often); or the Bronx (where most of my academic friends parse their texts). In any case, my kids say I should write something immortal, + maybe I will write something. Plan to try anyway.
Writ by hand,
With love,
Jim Light

Dear Jack: On the whole, despite far too many aches + pains + root canals, '85 has been a good year for Amy + me + our kids + grandchildren. Amy + I spent the first six months or so in Carbondale (winding up my tour as Dean) + then i nAugust we went to Europe (mostly Amsterdam, London, + Paris, but lots of sights also in Rome, Venice, Munich, + elsewhere) for a few weeks. Along about November I accepted a Fulbright award to New Zealand, + since then I've been involved in the torture of planning another move -- what to do with the furniture (much of which we just bought), the cars, my so-called investments, other trivia. But I can't resist the thought of all the sheep in New Zealand (where I'll be at the University of Canterbury, Christchurch) because N.Z. is another chance at adventure, even life, if only for a short time. So we're lighting out for the territory come February. Wish you were there — but absent that, wish all the best for you in the New Year.

Dear Jack:
Amy + I are back in Westport again -- I remember you visited us here after one of your raids on New York -- + we're enjoying being here even though the pace in everything is faster (especially the driving) than it was in Carbondale. We got here in July + then spent months working like dogs trying to repair the damages of time (+ renters) to our new (but old) home place. Now it's done + I feel like the Lord (retired) of the manor. I find that I like loafing + feel that I have a talent for it that I should have discovered earlier. I can spend the entire day reading — the N.Y. Times + listening to classical music. Occasionally for real adventure Amy + I drive in to N. York for dinner + a show, but I have come, over the years, to discover that Amy's cooking is better than that at most restaurants, + the sound amplification at most plays (especially musicals) distorts reality enough to make me furious -- so I don't seek adventure too often.
We enjoy Westport most of all, I guess, because we're near two of my children + three of my grandchildren, + we see a good bit of all of them. Recently my son Matthew's son James took his first steps, + I was as pleased as if I'd taken them myself. All of the children have copies of "Slappy Hooper" + "The Fast Sooner Hound" + we're hoping they grow up well under the right influences.
I went to my dentist here -- he remembered me fondly after some eighteen years -- + he began dreaming of a new Mercedes. He sent me to a specialist, an oral surgeon among other things, +

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
he tore up my mouth + then started sewing it together again. After that he started talking about problems + solutions + miracles -- all at great cost -- + I began to weep while he kept ringing up the cash register.
I hope you're enjoying the political campaign. I despise Bush for the hypocrisy + lies of his campaign, but I fear that someone has bribed Dukakis + his staff + they're throwing the game. Nevertheless, I've registered to vote even though I will do so in despair. Maybe I can become fond of the phrase "President Bush," but I still find it difficult to like hypocrites even though I've spent much of my life in close proximity to them.
I hope things are going better for you. For me you are one of the best + most important men of my time, certainly one who influenced me, for good or bad, in all I've done since I first met you + you taught me, or tried to teach me, to write something worth reading.
Love,
Jim Light

All goes well with Amy + me. We spent the summer in California, with occasional raids on Reno + Tahoe, + then wandered around Portugal + Spain for a couple of weeks in September. Occasionally I remind her of her various pills + she reminds me of mine, but what's life without a few pills?
Since we got back from Spain we've been having fun in Connecticut. The weather was beautiful + the colors remark-able this Fall, but it started to get cold + very, very windy along about November -- even had a tornado close by -- + right now the branches on the tree outside my window are blowing madly about. Next week we're going to Vegas for a few days; then we're going to spend the Christmas season here in Westport; + then in late January we'll probably go to our condo in California for a few weeks. Amy whimpers occasionally about earthquakes, but I say to her, "Baby, it's cold outside."

Amy Light, was added a short while back) + those when added to the two in Michigan, make a total of six -- ranging in age from about four months to about six years. They're all beautiful + bright -- three boys, three girls -- and deserve a cleaner + better world.

Dear Jack:
It seems a long time since I was in Chicago — almost a myth — but I still remember it happily, + I'm still appreciative of your kindness — as well as that of Gladys — while I was there. Sure wish you could get to Terre Haute, so I could do a little to repay you.
Since Chicago, I've attended the MLK meetings — which also are receding toward the land of myth — + come back here to [[?]] illiterate horde of students. Lately I've been working like a dog. I'm teaching 3 classes (2 Junior composition + one Freshman class) + I've also gotten two other chores. I'm faculty advisor to 30 entering freshman (+ they're always hanging around my office so I'm afraid to go there), + I'm also chairman of a library committee, which is terribly time consuming. Despite this I've managed to get another West article done (which I sent to PMLA) + I've been plugging along in the task of accumulating biographical information. (Would you have the slightest idea of the addresses of any of these people: George Milburn, Jerry Cody, Dalton

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
Trumbo, John Herrmann, Max Lieber, or Mike Gold?) I've also submitted an application for a fellowship to the American Council of Learned Societies. I asked for $7,000, + I'm enclosing a copy of my proposed project. I have no real hope, of course, of getting anything, but I do have a dream — + teachers of composi-tion courses need a dream. Finally, I'm thinking of applying to Yaddo — + if you would tell me to whom to write I'd again be indebted.
I read Somebody in Boots, + thought it was pretty good. I mentioned it to my best friend up here — whose specialty is also American Literature — + he asked me if he might read it. So I took the liberty of loaning it to him — which I wouldn't have done for just anybody. I hope you don't mind. I'll return it — with the West newspaper ma-terial — as soon as my friend returns it.
Yesterday I was talking to my son Shel — who has just entered first grade — + to make conversation I asked him if he's met his principal. "Oh, yes," he said. "When?" I said. "Yesterday," he said, "My teacher said I hit another kid in the belly + she took me to the principal's office." I said, "Did you hit the other kid?" Shel said: "No." "Well," I said: "you should have told the principal the whole story." "I tried to," Shel said, "but she wasn't caring what I said; she was only caring what she said." — I thought the statement was amazingly perceptive, al-most suggestive of man's essential egocentricity + his difficulty in communi-cating with the rest of mankind.
Again, thanks for everything — + try to get to Terre Haute some time soon.
Love, Jim

Dear Jack + Gladys:
Beginning August 23, I get a vacation, one which continues until September 8. I have decided to spend a couple of days of that vast period in Chicago. (Rowena + the children are leaving tomorrow — the 9th — for Maryland, where they will be seeking peace + strength through the soil.) I was hoping that I might be able to spend the evening of August 24 with you — + if you have a cot, to spend the night there, with subsequent breakfast + coffee the following morning. So drop me a card about the 24th + if it's not agreeable to plans of your own — then, for goodness' sake, tell me so.
Up here things go on as usual. I've been teaching a graduate course in Hemingway, Fitzgerald, + Faulkner — +

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991

that's fun. (It may not be when I get to Faulkner next week.) I've been trying to write a short story (the first one in over five years) + trying to plan an anthology which I'm supposed to present to a couple of publishers in Madison, Wisconsin (where this year's Modern Language Association meetings are being held — from Sept. 8-11). I've been buoyed up by the fact that a couple of West articles of mine have been accepted — by Prairie Schooner + Modern Fiction Studies — + even more buoyed up by Modern Fiction Studies actually requesting me to do an article (on Katherine Anne Porter) for them. It's rather interesting — as commentary on scholarly publishing — that the West article for MFS is scheduled to appear in December, 1958.
I guess that's about all except I do hope you're free on the 24th for I'm looking forward to seeing both of you again.

What I'd like to keep the article a little longer for is, possibly, to use the picture upon it. I'm going to write the San Francisco Chronicle + see if I can get the original. title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
Up here, things go on. My review of The Collected Works came out in Prairie Schooner, + I'd send you an offprint except for the fact I wasn't given any myself. I also sent another article off to American Quarterly; it was probably the best article I've ever done so I have high hopes for it.
Primarily, I've been writing letters madly, trying to dig up as much biographical information as I can. I've gotten a good deal of help, + even without Perelman's help the biographical sections shouldn't be too bad. Apparently there is considerable interest in a study of West right now, for I've gotten queries — without my instiga-tion — from a couple of other publishers — neither of them commercial. With such interest, I'm beginning to wonder if I shouldn't try a commercial publisher. Of course I don't wonder long, for certain-ly what I'm doing can't have much of an audience.
Recently I had a boost to my ego. I got a query from Who's Who — who said they wanted to put my name in their reference files + add my name to their current Who's Who in the South + Southwest. I was flattered no end, but told them I wouldn't look appropriate in that par-ticular regional Who's Who. As I wrote down my accomplishments on their form, I wondered if I'd look appropriate in any Who's Who.
Love, Jim

I think this is a really fine piece of criticism, perceptive, intelligence, well phrased. If there is anything that I could quarrel with — + it's pretty presumptuous of me to even say it — it is the slight tendency to a lack of connection between the parts. The connection, of course, is always there, but I think it might be wise in spots to make the links for your readers; + probably even a brief anticipatory paragraph — immediately preceding James T. Farrell (on page 1) — might be wise, a paragraph in which you briefly suggest the various aspects you plan to cover.

well be appropriate to the Socialist magazine you mentioned, but I think The Reporter or any of the little magazines (Prairie Schooner, Accent, Sewanee, etc.) might dislike such a tone. And these are the places I would conceive of as the smart obvious ones for publication.
These quarrels are, of course, trivial ones, + certainly — revised or not — I think the piece should be published. Of course, once again the question of timeliness comes in. How long has Rideout's book been out. If it's over a yera, then I don't think this should be even presented as a critical book review. Instead, I think the whole should be a methodical treatment (1500 words or so) of Rideout, Kempton, Wechsler, et. al., + then another final 1000-1500 words upon you + your attitudes towards the fiction of the thirties (that is, how you today feel about what you + your fellows did in the thirties — trying, of course, for the judicious tone). Such a piece would be a valuable contribution to the criticism of the lit. of the thirties — done by one who was really there.
Love,
Jim

Dear Jack:
I have written the Guggenheim people, + I put everything I had into it. I pray that you get it, not so much for your sake (though that means a great deal to me) but for the sake of American letters. You have much to say, not only about your own life (+ i think that life has major import far over time) but about the lives and letters of all the great + near-great writers whom you have know. Be sure to let me know.
You mentioned on your last letter that Henrietta Weigel may settle in this area. If she does, I most certainly would like to meet her. If she'd like to teach an evening course in Creative Writing, I'd like to talk to her about that kind of possibility.
There is not a great deal i have to report. I finished a little book over the summer on J. D. Salinger, + I do some reviewing + such, but for the most part I teach + try to run the department here. One of the courses I'm teaching is in Mod. Am. Lit., and it's given at an extension section in Greenwich. One of my pupils is a former editor of the Sat. Evening Post (his name is Clay Blair), + recently he had to give a report on Hemingway's Big Two Hearted River. It was a fascinating

title: Jack Conroy letters [11], 1924-1991
transcription:
report, but the intriguing thing is the way he prefaced it: "I didn't have time to get up to Michigan to re-live Hemingway's story (I had to work on the last chapter of my novel), but I did talk to the postmaster in the area for an hour or so. Now, when I was on the phone..." Some people are different from you + me — that's my conclusion.
One of the most intriguing of recent events (for me) is a letter I got from Carnegie Tech. The Dean there noted that Carnegie Tech + Mellon Institute were going to merge soon into Carnegie University (with a combined endowment of 200 million) + the University was going to be offering a doctorate in English in the near future. At any rate, the Dean wanted to know if that bait might induce me to consider the Chairmanship at Carnegie. I wrote back + said "maybe" + they've asked me to come down + visit the place on the 14th, 15th, + 16th of December. At the worst I'll get royal treatment + I'm looking forward to the sparring session with the President + assorted deities.
The family is well. Amy learned to drive recently, + I bought another car — second hand. Now Amy buzzes around Westport as if she owned it.
The children are all doing well in school. Shel got straight A's on his last report card, + the other children did equally well. Shel is not yet a master on the violin, but he is improving vastly, + the same is true of Matt + the cello.
Love,
Jim

He learns that unions are good organizations as long as they have people to stir them up and make them worthwhile like his father had with the coal miners. At any rate I'm trying to decide on something to do next. I'm going to try a novel again, but at the same time I'm going to put most of my energie into some fairly easy scholarly piece (which won't be the literature of the 30's, for that would not be easy + would take a full year at least of full time work) upon some single person + his work. Dear Jack,
The typewriter's upstairs, so I'm scribbling this - so as not to delay telling you how much I appreciated all your suggestions for Dublin, London + Paris.
In Dublin, Moran's was fine - including whopping breakfast as you predicted. I went out to see Jim Powers, who sends his best regards. His wife Betty will soon have a novel out - being published by Farrar, Straus, Giroux.
In London the Glendower was fine, complete with fireplace in the lobby which my son enjoyed greatly. We liked Schmidt, the night, + the people who lived there. I left a copy of Mask of Glory with Tony Mills, the editor at F. Muller, who published my Gorky book in England. It got a huge batch of big reviews - but not much in sales. They're not sorry they published it; a consolation.
Mike Weaver + I exchanged letters but couldn't manage to meet. He'll soon be a father, + didn't want to [crossed out] come to London, + Exeter was a bit far for me this time. He sounds O.K. - friendly.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
In Paris, I'm at the Hotel Nicolo, 39 Rue Pierre Nicolo, Paris V - where I lived 15 yrs ago when living in France. It's as charming as ever, + rates - for Paris - are very modest. I recommend it to you.
Michel Fabre was very gracious + very open + friendly. He had me out to a big gathering, + again for dinner with his wife Guenevieve + small sons. He gave me a copy of his book on Les Noirs Americains - seems very well researched. I think I've made a friend, thanks to you!
He + I agree that Disinherited stands up, over the years, in a way Grapes of Wrath does not!
By the way, I went to Collect's in London. They were out of Disinherited but I ordered two copies + arranged to have them mailed to you. Hope they arrived, or will soon!
Paris just as fine as ever, but awful traffic + high high prices.
I'll write again from the Pays-Bas. Best to Gladys. Dan
Some news - about LBJ, etc.!

433 Bayville Ave. Bayville, N. Y. 11709. [1970]
Dear Jack -
So I got hold of a pen with red ink!
Kathaleen and I were warmed by the card from you + Gladys, that was so thoughtful. (I'm beginning to appreciate thoughtfulness - and hope some day I can start being thoughtful of others; never have been very good at it.)
My sabbatical leave starts in January, + I want to make it a fruitful year (get paid till September). I've been struggling to rewrite my old (first) unpublished novel of the Depression + the Old Left, trying to interweave it with a contemporary story (student rebellion, student problems). The two editors I've queried - Bob Amussen at Bobbs-Merrill, + a guy named Quinn at at Mcgraw-Hill - both expressed interest; the theme's attractive today.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
But whether I can pull it together, I don't know. It's hard to summon the enthusiasm, + a string of books that have failed - though all lack of quality - seems to have set up hurdles internally that are hard to jump.
Also trying to finish a play (or script for a movie or TV, more likely) based on my Gorky book - The Last Play of Maxim Gorky. No idea where I'll go with it, but I think it's valid. I'm afraid you'd find it too disillusioned - although I know how tolerant you are toward all views.
I'm applying for a Chapelbrook grant. Hope it's OK, to use your name among references, if they want them. If I got it, I could extend my leave or else take another leave in 71, and see what I really can produce in an extended stretch.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Not sure where I'll go to live + work for part of the sabbatical. Ireland attracted me, London has always been a place that inspired me - + I sure need inspiration. If I got to Jerusalem, the mayor there has promised me a chance to do some useful work, building some bridges for living between the two peoples.
Or I might just work by the beach here on Long Island. I've got to find a new theme, and that's to be found inside, really, if at all; place is somehow incidental.
I know we'll see one another in '71. Have a good Christmas, and may the coming year be a strong + fulfilling one.
Dan

You once mentioned, I think, you could put in a word for me with the people who run Yaddo. Can you still? I ought to at least know the inside of one of those places. The Authors Guild sent a bulletin inviting members to apply to the MacDowell Colony (with it), so I did - but it turns out they want to have questionnaires filled out, etc., etc., + it sounds like more of a Social Club than anything else. But I do need to be closer to the swing of things, know what others are doing, etc. Even for future effectiveness on the campus, this would be useful. So tell me anything you can about Yaddo.
I got a note from Michel Fabre, with thanks for the Spinoza book. I've been derelict about writing him - what a fine guy, and how friendly he was to me in Paris!
Keep a date open, if you can, for early October, to come out to Post + talk to my Writing Workshop. I'll get together at least $300, and will try for more. You'd also meet some of the Confrontation editors. (I still want that mag. to amount to something!) Warm regards to Gladys. We'll meet this year for sure! - in Moberly, or on L. Island. Dan

[1973]
Dear Jack,
I enclose two papers by graduate students, evoked by their reading of our discussion of The Disinherited. I felt they'd interest you, and the young people were quite pleased - thrilled - at my gratuitous offer to let you see their papers. If you communicate with readers (+ enthusiastic critics) in such cases, they'd be honored; but they don't really expect it. (By the way, the marginal comments are mine)
There were other papers, too. In general, the book made a strong impression, Jack. It was important reading for them - and as more than one prorated out, it is valid history as well as literature. Anyway, you can be assured the book lives. Our graduate students, by + large, will rate with any adult students anywhere, without exception - even those who preferred Zola's Germinal - they took your book damn seriously: a work of enduring literary meaning.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991

I think nearly all - including me, on rereading - felt that the first section, Monkey Nest, is the great one. But the assembly-line expose, and other sections, won their faces also.
I will use The Disinherited again - I know that now, just make 'em keep it in print!
Aside from that, how've you been? And Gladys? A fun young gal - a graduate student - will be coming to Missouri this summer, searching for her own themes, her background for future writing; and I'm going to send her to see Jack Conroy, if you don't mind.
Jack, I've had a hell of a time getting down to that article I penned the Nation, centered on your book. [crossed out] And from my personal despairs, which slow me down, of the novel I'm struggling to finish, I haven't gotten the handle I want, yet. One thing that I think would help - and that I wanted to ask you some time, anyway - is: assuming Disinherited is autobiographical, what was your family background? Was your dad "educated"? What "profession", before being a miner - if any? (My tentative point being that you may be virtually the only really proletarian writer! ?) Please write me about this, Jack, if only because I'm interested. As ever, Dan

Levin, Dan [1978]
I don't know how else it'll be possible.
I lost two friends recently to death. One a close college friend with whom I'd lost touch for many years: became a doctor + went to a very small Ohio town (his dream) as its one doctor; died suddenly, on his way to a patient. The other my brother in law, a noted physician (one of the [crossed out] pioneers who made the Cleveland Clinic what it is), a terribly hard drinker, + a brilliant man - greatest reciter of poetry I've ever heard.
I'm in the process of gently trying to extract my novels from the agent who isn't doing me any good + trying another one. It's tricky - human feelings involved.
And corresponding with some small British theatres to see if one may want to do my play about Gorky. I think it's terrific, but like my novels it needs to find the right outlet.
I'll be happy, + reassured, to hear from you Jack.
As ever, Dan Levin

transcription:
[Maxim Lieber]
East Hartford, Ct 06108
May 10, 1984
Dear Jack — My wife and I are indebted to the Wixsons for sending us an invitation to your birthday party. Believe me if my old bones, gone rusty after 87 years of wear, could take the haunt, I'd love to give you an old-fashioned abrazo. But I dare say, what with all those friends to greet you, you wont miss me.
Practically none of my old friends miss me. The only one who telephones me from time to time is Albert Maltz. He is like Old Faithful in Yellowstone.
Do you recall that seminar on the Thirties at the U. of Conn. which our dear friend, Mickey Stern, arranged for my account? One of the pleasures I had on that occasion was to snub Caldwell who had behaved like a louse when I asked him to contribute to an anthology I was preparing during my stay in Mexico. But the world contains many Caldwells — for instance a John Cheever for whom I worked as hard as for any of my clients (he who married my secretary). On the other hand there was Langston Hughes who inscribed all of his books to me; or Nathanael West dedicated his Miss Lonely Hearts to Max.
Our best wishes to you for Auld Lang Syne.
Maxim

147 Woodland Ave
Lexington, Ky
June 8, 1948
Dear Jack:
I am alive and well. To calm all fears, to soothe all doubts, I am alive and well. Yesterday I was even mellow — the light of old. Yesterday I was in Cincinnatti, drinking at the D[[?]] bowl. And while there, I and Ze[[?]] reminisced about Chicago, and most of all remembered the hellion of Green Street, the seducer of youth. Remembered him so fondly that Ze[[?]] insisted that he should come to the D[[?]] mansion some weekend, bringing with him all the old ballads, all the charm that made him beloved of all who knew him. And why not? Why can't you come down to Cincinnatti for a weekend? The fare is only about fifteen dollars, both ways. The food for the weekend will be free. There will be a bountiful board, and a full wine cellar. And most of all you would bring a spot of joy into Ze[[?]]'s life — and even more into mine. For, fear you not, I would be there — not drinking as in my youth — glasses on the grass, alas — but, still, smiling, smirking, + simpering, all in the fashion you remember. How about it, Jack? Any weekend you say (and, if you could persuade him, I think Ze[[?]] has — I'm sure Ze[[?]] has — room for Tommy as well). So, write and name the weekend, either to Ze[[?]] or to me.
Transition, to be inserted at will.
I; I become respectable. Now, I have all the

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
respectable accoutrements. The wife you know about (and she's a wonderful person; you really would like her; even considering my poor taste in women I think you would approve of her); to her I've added (perhaps I told you before — but it's worth repeating) a second hand car, a 1939 Buick, which is gradually impoverishing me, eating of my substance, and withering of my marrow. Today I got my driver's license and both my wife and I have been in mortal terror ever since. Even the car groans + whimpers when I sit at the wheel, and when I start the clutch (or is it the brake?) it bucks in deathlike agonies + rattles — but I have no pity for it. For I must keep up with the Joneses — 1940 Buick — and if Jones can drive, so can I.
Today also I handed in the grades for the last quarter. Nineteen failures out of 81 students — which is less than my 2.5% of failures last quarter, thank heaven. Now I am waiting to know whether I will be allowed to teach during the summer quarter or not. Before I got married, I haughtily rejected an offer from the head of the department, saying smugly that I intended to be in New York City writing my memoirs, but then, after marriage, I humbly crawled from my office to Brady's, making obeisance every thirteen feet, licked the sacred spot, and begged to be allowed to impart wisdom to the beauties of Kentucky. Now I'm waiting to know the result of my petition. Starvation sits at my doorstep, howling interminably. I wouldn't mind if it were only I — but my wife is too young to die.
There is really nothing more to say. Occasionally I dream of writing — but I only dream. Occasionally I read a book — but only

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
casually. For the most part I sink into the soil, grow roots — grow respectable. You would weep to see it, I weep to think of all the missionary work you wasted on me. The pupil outstripped the master, but now all the effort is only wasted — and the pupil is a teacher, with inertia in his footsteps, and his roots in the soil. I weep to think of it — you weep, too.
Friend always,
Jim
P.S. Come to Cincinnatti
P.P.S. Yes, you would like my wife. She just stretched out on the bed, reading a book. The book? The Disinherited — Moscow edition. By Jack Conroy.

Dear Jack:
We miss you, we miss you, we miss [[?]] — We love your letters, but somehow they're like [[?]] cigarettes: there aren't enough of them, + the more you get the more you want, so that you're irritable when they aren't always on hand, in full supply. Dear Jack:
Got your recent letter + it warmed the cockles of my heart — but nowhere near as much so as those few days at Christmas time, all the moments of which I remember fondly — lovingly, gradually working up total recall. Of course I can't begin to thank you for the get together of all the beautiful Chicago people — [[?]] I won't even try, not in words; I feel it [[?]], I do.
Life in Radford drags [[?]] The climate remains the most fabulous thing I've ever known — no snow, practically no cold, little rain, mostly blue skies — + the rest of the atmosphere remains provincial + even foolish. A recent story in the New Yorker, called A Stranger in the House + written by Ogden Nash, symbolized Southern hospitality to me, as well as the heights + depths of Southern conversation. This deadness [[?]] anything else, [[?]] want to [[?]] dispute its many [[?]] Illinois State been in [[?]] job [[?]] Col[[?]] to Ill[?]] whether

Anyway things have been so drab here that I've even began to write again, after my fashion. I'm trying to do a novel about a man who, very sanely, m[[?]] the philosophic conclusion that in the present world only the insane can be happy. The problem, then, is for him to break the mind, to get into an insane asylum + not only get there but to belong there. The idea of course is Westian, but the style, I hope, is not so deri-vative, even if not as good. October 25, 1958
Dear Jack and Gladys:
The news about Jimmy was of course, shocking — the more so because he was so young + Margaret Jean + the children needed him so. I imagine things are going to be pretty rough for all of you for a while. I wish I could help. Do you think maybe it might help Margaret Jean to spend a little time away from Chicago? If so, we'd love to have her spend a while in Terre Haute; it wouldn't be exciting, but I doubt if Margaret Jean wants any excitement.
Things up here are pretty much as they always are. Most exciting thing was that I was involved in a car accident and my car was a total loss. So now I've got a 1956 Plymouth — in-surance paid — + slowly am getting over a sprained back that hurt pretty badly for awhile.
Next news: Rowena is pregnant again — a miscalculation — and we're hoping for another human being.
Next: Columbia sent back my West manuscript. They had no comments except for regrets. Said the decision had been hard to make but they felt the study couldn't have much long-term appeal. I felt like writing back + saying that that depended on how well West's reputation stood up, + that was conjectural and they knew that to begin with. — At any rate I've made a few changes + additions + shall send the manuscript somewhere else, I guess.
A short while back I did a review for PS on Motley's new book. I said some pretty nasty things — all deserved — but I told Karl Shapiro I'd just as soon — even would prefer — that the review not be seen. I thought that would end the review — which I felt obligated to do since I'd accepted the assignment — but it didn't: the review is supposed to appear in the [[?]] Schooner.
That's about it. The teaching goes on as always, + I [[?]] [[?]]ing — less + less hopefully — that Haward will call someday. The [[?]]st [[?]] I got last year though were from Purdue + Michigan State, both of which jobs I turned down. Have nothing interesting in prospect now, but I'm going to New York — the Modern Language Association meetings — after Christmas + see if anything turns up there. Something of no worth [[?]]
