Light, Jim
1724 Crawford
Terre Haute, Indiana
January 30, 1959
Dear Jack + Gladys:
Just a note to let you know how things are up here. The most important news is that Rowena was operated on at John Hopkins — on December 6 — for a recurrence of the brain tumor of two years ago. It was a pretty terrible operation — much worse than earlier — but R left the hospital a short while ago, + I'm hoping that she will be able to rejoin me — Shel another month or so. (Matt + Rowena are with R's parents now.)
I myself spent six weeks or so in Baltimore. I got to know the city — or at least a part of it — pretty well, + I also got a lot of reading done. Didn't do anything else of any worth, but I'm hoping soon to resume a little productivity. One thing I've got to do — is some revising of the West study. (I imagine you're sick of that subject, but no more than I am.) Apparently the University of Nebraska Press — which I submitted the manuscript to after Columbia rejected it — is going to publish the work; but they want some revisions, + I didn't have the courage to say no (though if I had, they might have published the study as it is). At any rate the Press is going over the study chapter by chapter + making suggestions for revision. The Press wants the revision by June 1 + hopes to publish the book in either the fall or winter or 1959. So do I.
One other thing. I attended the MLA in New York in December + was offered a job at the University of Missouri. It was pretty attractive in many ways — only literature courses + an Assistant Professorship — but I turned the job down because I didn't want to move at this particular time + also because I didn't think very highly of the U of M location. I'm of course hoping that the publication of the West book will lead to a really decent offer next year.
I'd hoped to go back to Yaddo this summer — I actually have a good novel partly done — but the illness of November ruined those plans. Without Yaddo, I don't know how I'm going to get any time — I get more + more committee work anyhow — to do any writing; but I'm going to try a little. I get discouraged a little though, + I keep thinking how much

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
more easily things could be if only there were just a little bit of genius to go with the little talent + the little work. (I've been sending a sample of recent stories out + getting nice rejections, but even nice rejections now are terribly discouraging.)
I miss you a great deal + wish I could talk to you both.
Love,
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Light, Jim
1724 Crawford
Terre Haute, Indiana
May 23, 1959
Dear Jack + Gladys:
Just a few lines to let you know the news. About two months ago Rowena gave birth to a beautiful girl. We named her Jama (Rowena wanted that) Rowena (I wanted that), + we were both pleased to have a girl. A few days after the birth Rowena died of brain cancer. It, of course, was inevitable, had been so for the last three years, but was nevertheless hard to accept.
For a while after Rowena's death her mother stayed here + helped with the children. Recently she returned to Maryland, taking with her the two younger children. Sheldon + I are now alone, + we are planning to come to Chicago on the evening of June 13. I'd like to see + talk with you, + if you have room stay over with you — maybe through Sunday the 14th. After that Sheldon + I will go to Maryland, + the entire family — me, Shel, Mattie, + Jama — will return to Terre Haute sometime during the latesummer. I plan to get a housekeeper then.
The other news briefly — more development when I see you.
1) I got promoted promoted to Associate Professor, so that with the raise in pay I'm no longer a pauper, only impoverished.
2) I finished the revision of the West book + Nebraska turned it down, just a few days ago.
3) I do have four pieces to be published sometime — on West, Schulberg, Salinger, + Motley (a review) — + I sent two pieces to that magazine Contact which you were so kind as to put on my trail. I don't really think either piece was really suitable to Contact; it seemed directed to a more popular audience than my pieces would satisfy. Nevertheless, I hope they'll

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
be interested; but I don't hope much. Anyway, thanks for mentioning my name; it was truly kind.
More when I see you.
Love,
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Light, Jim
1724 Crawford
Terre Haute, Indiana
August 8, 1959
Dear Jack + Gladys:
I got back to Terre Haute a few weeks ago, + though I had a good time in South Dakota, Maryland, + New York, I was glad to get back to my own small town. Since I returned I've been teaching four hours a day, + preparing to teach most of the rest of the day. The Contemporary Novel course is the course: lots of work. You may be interested to know that one of the students (a girl named Mary Youman) is writing a term paper on — guess what — Jack Conroy. Another student (Bill Lowes) is writing on Existentialism in Nelson Algren. Both students are excellent; I know, for I had them in their undergraduate days + they know more than I did then. (Don't say it wouldn't be hard!)
A week or so ago I got a long distance phone call from California. Couldn't imagine who it was. Wondered who I knew well enough there, so that some-one would call to tell me about his death. (To me long distance phone calls — the influence of the thirties — are to tell about death; telegrams to tell about sickness; letters for everything else.) Turned out to be W M Ryan, or some such name — the Contact man — + he wanted to tell me Contact was going to publish a West piece I had sent them. It's to appear in the September, 1959, issue, + it's to be entitled, rather flamboyantly + not my idea, Genius on the Campus: Nathanael West at Brown.
While I was in New York I wrote to Algren asking his permission to do a profile on him. He never answered, so I assume he was irritated by the request. I can guess why (one should never trade on friendship + I was — that is, I was if I know Algren well enough to have the right to call him a friend), + I felt wary. At any rate I shan't do — or rather finish, for I had it started — any profile on Algren. I'll return the ma-

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
terials I borrowed from you (+ there, too, I had traded on friendship, + I felt — + still feel — guilty about it) when I come to Chicago. That should be in another two or three weeks. I'll let you know, + I hope you'll still be at the same address, for God knows how I'd ever find Midlothian.
I'm enclosing a piece that appeared in Modern Fiction Studies + that you said I'd never sent you. I think the content is pretty good, but the style is pretty heavy.
Love to all,
Jim
P.S. A piece of mine upon Motley's Let No Man is in the current Prairie Schooner.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Light, Jim
Indiana State Teachers College
Terre Haute, Indiana
DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH
October 12, 1960
Dear Jack + Gladys:
I've been wanting to write you for a good while, but I kept waiting for something to happen worth reporting. Nothing did, + I fear nothing is. So bear with me...
The closest thing to new is the fact that my book on West was accepted by Northwestern University Press and is scheduled for publication around February or March of next year. I went up to Evanston for a hasty visit a month or so ago (called you at your office for lunch but you'd already left) and had a gay old time. Off it, I keep thinking I've already made money on the book. The editor feted me in lavish style, including liquor, + then the following day I went with him to Arlington Park and won $30 on the races. So I'm content if I never get another penny. The people at the N. U. Press though keep telling me the book should sell well (it's unique, they say) and that they plan to advertise it well. So I'm dreaming of royalty riches already — + while I'm dreaming I know I'm a damn fool.
Last summer I spent in the East largely — doing work on John William De Forest. I don't think the world is panting for such a study, but it's the best thing I could think of at the time (and Indiana State gave me a handsome research grant to pay my summer's expenses). I hope I can get the De Forest thing done a little faster than the West (which by publication time will have taken some eight years) but I doubt it (at least I doubt it if I've got to keep teaching full time).

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
The children are all well. Sheldon I am especially proud of — because he was the most trouble. At least, he was the most trouble last year, when he disturbed everyone in school (most of all teachers + principal) + eventually had to have psychological + mental tests made of him. He did well on the tests (nothing wrong with him except maybe a little too bright) but kept driving his teacher mad. (She's left for another job — another school — this year.) Now, this year Shel is causing no trouble at all + is doing well in his school work, as well as in his music lessons (he's taking violin). I attribute the improvement to two things: a better teacher and my new wife (who loves all the kids + is good with them and for them). As for Jama + Mattie, they're both becoming a little more individualistic and so a little more demanding of their rights and wishes; they're not becoming bothersome yet in that respect and they're still lovable in all the others.
I've been reading Snow a little and think he's pretty good. I find Darrell a terrible bore. That's about all my outside reading. Have you made any exciting discoveries? (You know you were the one to first mention West to me, a fact I note in the indebtedness section of my book.)
Otherwise nothing except
Love to all
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Light, Jim
509 Spruce St.
Marshall, Ill.
October 15, 1961
Dear Jack:
Thanks for sending me the "extra mileage" on the West book. I'm truly grateful.
I was sorry to hear of Bobo's troubles with the police department but was glad to hear he is going to try to reform. I was even more happy to hear that you were doing the article on Dreiser. Seems to me that your research would certainly lead you to Terre Haute. No really authoritative piece on Dreiser could be done without a visit to Terre Haute. I'm sure of that, + I think you should persuade Inland of that. In other words, expenses. Even if you can't get expenses, I'd think you'd want to come to Terre Haute to see your old pal. That's me.
Me, I'm doing an article for pay too. The Encyclopedia Brittanica article on West: 250 words, 10 dollars. Makes me think of good old Purple's Encyclopedia: — I've also got an article coming out in Minnesota Review that I got 50 bucks for. So I'm getting rich too. But no one's offered me $500 for anything. Maybe someday.
I've been teaching a course in Comtemporary Prose this term. Fun and games with Kafka, Joyce, Mann — lots of people. The course is rather insane in concept; contemporary prose is everything published anywhere in The 20th Century. That gives me lots of latitude, too much to make me think I can teach such a course. But I'm learning a little bit about a lot of things.
I've been wondering what to do next year. I've got a sabbatical coming up + don't know whether to spend it in Europe or here; whether to take a full year with half pay or a half year with full pay. We really don't have enough money to take a whole year; but if we take a half year we'll have to have the children change schools twice in a single year. It's all very difficult.
I'd be glad to add something to The [[?]] for the republication

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
of The Disinherited, but could you help me a little? Whom especially might I write to?
Best,
Jim
P.S. The current Kenyon + Va. Quarterly have some nice + some not so nice things to say about The West book.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Indiana State College
Terre Haute, Indiana
DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH
March 3, 1963
Dear Jack + Gladys:
The most important news here (for us anyway) is that I was recently given a Fulbright grant for teaching in England. I don't know yet what University I'll be teaching at, though I suspect it won't be either Oxford or Cambridge. I'm pretty sure though that I'll be teaching courses in "The American Novel," and according to the grant I should have considerable time for research. I am looking forward to the year, and I hope to have the chance to squeeze in some travel in Europe. I sure would like to be cosmopolitan, though I despair that well-known Conroy savoir fairé.
I'll be glad to get away for another reason: because we recently hired a new Vice President at ISC and he has some weird ideas about administration. One of his recent desires is to keep our students in college, and to do this he is advocating that we lower our grading standards (a student failed is a teacher failure). I haven't bumped into him yet (thank Heaven I was on sabbatical last term) but he's been trying to terrify some of our non-tenured staff. I'm afraid there's going to be a real mess eventually (because that's just one of his ideas; another is that an administrator should administer and the faculty should tremble) and I'd just as soon not be here when the explosion erupts. I'm also grateful that I'm still relatively mobile (probably the only full professor here that is) and that I can go elsewhere if need be. (Though I doubt if I will be offered again any of the chairmanships I've turned down recently.)
I'm teaching a graduate seminar this term in Eugene O'Neill and Tennessee Williams, as well as the Am. Lit. Survey, and the course in "The American Novel." I had planned to use a really fine book called "The Disinherited," but the publishers inform me that it is still not available. When will it be? I shan't be teaching the novel course this

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
summer — I'm teaching a course called "Contemporary Prose" and a graduate course in "Henry James" — but I would like to use it in England if I can.
I've read little of any merit lately, save possibly for Uncle Tom's Cabin. Edmund Wilson's Patriotic Gore had its points, but I have the feeling he's getting by on other people's scholarship (largely unacknowledged by him) and a willingness on the part of publishers to let him quote at length. (Well over half the book consists of quotes.) I'd like to read Phillip Roth's Letting Go if I ever get the time, but I'm too busy reading such things as Little Dorrit + I Promessi Sposi. I am, however, coming fairly close to the end of De Forest and maybe will have the time soon to read something for pleasure.
I have no literary gossip. I might have if I'd gone to Yaddo for the month of January (as I planned to), but at the last minute I decided I'd rather be with my family than slave for scholarship. Maybe I was foolish but I've decided it's just not worth it, what I'd gain from that kind of work, wondering what I'd lose.
The children are all fine, though Sheldon is having some trouble with his teeth. He's had braces on for over a year, but new teeth seem to be coming in very slowly and not coming in as they should. The dentist says maybe he'll have to extract four teeth, one upper + one lower on each side, in order to provide room for the new teeth. I'm not happy about it.
Nothing more to write.
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
(It was a beautiful inscription, + I appreciated it.)
P.S. Vainly I note that I am to be honored at a Recognition dinner to be given by the President of ISC on May 5. Wish you could be here to see my peacock spread.
Indiana State College
Terre Haute, Indiana
DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH
April 29, 1963
Dear Jack:
Please forgive me for not writing earlier. I deserve curses + brimstone, but I hope for Paradise.
I have received two copies of The Disinherited, one from you and one from the publishers. The publishers sent me a desk copy because I planned to use the novel in The American Novel course instead of Steinbeck's In Dubious Battle. However, the book (TD) was not available at the time the book order for my course was sent in, and after the bookstore heard that the book was not yet available I had to give a title that was avail-able. What I did reluctantly, after stalling for a couple of weeks in hopes TD would come through, was to return to In D. B. I have, of course, ordered a copy of the book for the Library here and have put it on the Recommended reading list The Am. Novel. I shan't be able to use it in the summer because I'm teaching two graduate courses ("Henry James" and "O'Neill and Williams") and the book couldn't be forced into either of these courses. I well may be able to use it in England, for I'll be teaching a course

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
in "Naturalism in the Am. Novel" (not my idea) + TD could be fitted in such a course I believe. Whether anyone here other than me would use the book, I don't know. Dick Bash, who teaches a course ("Midwestern Prose") where the book might be fitted in, is in Morocco at the moment (though he'll be back for next academic year). I hope to see Dick for a few days in the East (I'll be going, he'll be coming) and I'll mention the possibility of his using the book. — As for the Aaron intro, I would have done it better, but he did a competent job.
As for England, I'll be teaching at the University of Keele, in North Staffordshire, England. The U is in the midlands, near a town called Newcastle Under Lyme. I'll be teaching two courses — the one I mentioned above and a survey of Am. Poetry + Fiction. I'll be leaving on Sept. 4 (the Queen Mary), + I imagine I'll return about July 1 of the next year. I've rented my house, furnished, to an incoming member of the English faculty here, and I thank Heaven nightly that that burden is off my back.
No news of great important here. I've re-cently turned down an offer, a flattering one, from the Library of Con-gress to be a Manuscript Specialist in Am. Lit. because I wouldn't give up my Fulbright, + they wanted the appointment to begin in September, 1963. I'm in-volved in a battle for survival with the newly appointed Dean of Faculty, an imbecile who thinks he can run Indiana State with the kind of dictatorial tactics he used in his previous posts. I'm drawing near the end of the De Forest book. The West book is to be published in paperback by McGraw-Hill in six months or so. I'm busy as a bee, buzzing around foolishly. I wish I could get to Chicago or you could get to Terre Haute.
Love
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
At sea,
Sept. 8, 1963
Dear Jack + Gladys:
We left Terre Haute on August 18, went to Maryland, where I worked on De Forest + finished all save the last chapter of that book, then went to New york + spent a few days, + finally boarded the Queen Mary on September 4. Life since then has been a round of eating, drinking, going to movies, + sleeping. I know I should be working on the last chapter of De Forest, but I can't get up the ambition to do anything. We're supposed to land on the tenth and then go to London for a week. After that we're going to tour Europe for a couple of weeks, pick up a car (a VW) in Frankfurt, + then in early October return to England + go on to the University of Keele. My address will be University of Keele, Staffordshire, England, U.K. — My mind has been a complete blank ever since I got on board the Q. M. All I know that's new is that I'm not affected by sea travel — and our voyage has been a cold, rough one — while Amy has been seasick a good deal of the time. The kids hold up well, except Jama whines a good deal. Shel + Matty are having a ball.
Love,
Jim
Cunard Line
R.M.S "Queen Mary"

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
March 23, 1964
Dear Jack + Gladys:
I have been planning to write to you for weeks — months really — but I've kept waiting in hopes I'd have something eventful to tell you. I'm afraid though that no really exciting things are going to happen, + so I'll have to be content with telling you of trivia. A couple of weeks ago I finished teaching the Spring term here, + I'm now on Easter vacation until April 27. The teaching here has been quite a surprise, + in nothing more so than in the laziness of the English students. At times I think the laziness is encouraged by the faculty, for the greater the student laziness the greater the possibilities for faculty laziness. The whole thing is rationalized by the pretense that the students are adults + should, therefore, not be required to do anything save at the end of their college career pass the appropriate exams. Since the students have studied so little, the exams have to be made up with vast leeway in the choice of questions to be answered, in the hopes (on the part of faculty) that there will be at least one area in which a student can write competently. The fact that most students have studied one area in a course fairly comprehensively (while ignoring 9/10's of the course) means that they do do fairly well on exams + so the faculty are encouraged in the smug belief that they are doing a good job of education. The truth is, so I see it, that the glory of English education is the grammar schools + public schools (comparable to our best high schools), so that students come to college well prepared + then do little afterward.
I haven't done anything in the way of original scholarship since I came here (save for finishing the De Forest manuscript, which I sent to the publishers in December + which still hasn't been read by the editors there). I have written out numerous lectures, both college + public, + I've learned to speak loudly if not well. Maybe I'll be able to use some of the lecture material eventually in an article or two.
Most of my other writing has been of letters to second rate colleges that need a chairman for their English departments + want to add my name to those that dream of accepting their chairmanship. Among those I turned down were Southern Methodist University, Wyoming University + San Bernardino State College. I indicated interest in the Univ. of Kansas (but didn't get the job) + Bridgeport University (where I may be offered the job). You would have been proud of what I wrote to SMU — which is in Dallas. I said, among other things, that I doubted if I could be happy in a place — the city — so noted for religious bigotry + political intolerance.
They only other item that excites me is the vacation I'm planning

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
for the next couple of weeks. The family is going uo to Scotland for a week or so, + then Sheldon + I are going to Paris for another week. Sheldon keeps talking about going to the Folies Bergere + drinking champagn out of slippers, while I keep telling him of how he'll enjoy the Louvre + Notre Dame. We'll see where we wind up.
I wish I could tell you how grateful I was for the article on Dreiser you sent me, as well as the extra copy of The Disinherited. I used the Dreiser material in teaching the course in naturalism, + I loaned The Disinherited to a student who wanted to do a compari-son of In Dubious Battle with The Disinherited. He thought your book, by the way, was the better one — but he spent most of his time on In Dubious Battle. I suggested in my criticism of his paper that there seemed something illogical about his proportion of space, + he defended the proportion by suggesting that strikes in American apple orchards were more common than labor troubles in American mines or factories. I suggested that he was nuts + that he should learn something about American history. That was his major interest, he said.
Love
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
April 26, 1964
Dear Jack and Gladys:
I have been getting a kick out of the human parade, as Harry Hansen would say, but I left terribly embittered when I got your last letter. The reason is that we are leaving perfidious Albion on June 30 and so can't walk down Picadilly with you, or even worship at Dove Cottage by your side. Damn. The more damn since I decided to leave England early because I expected I'd be needed at Indiana State — and I now suspect they could get along quite pleasantly without me. Damn. The more damn since I quit smoking a week ago, + though my lungs are now pure lily-white and my tongue is tasting things I hadn't tasted in years and my nose is less stuffed-up than in decades — I'm all on edge. Damn, damn, damn!
You're right to want to see the Lake Country. It has the most beautiful natural scenery I've ever seen in my life — so much so that even I begin to talk in meters. And if you do get to the Lake Country, you should keep on going until you hit Edinburgh — which I enjoyed vastly because I felt I got to know the town in the week or so I spend there. It's a town worth knowing, too, for it has the feel of history about it. The Castle overlooking Princes Street is an unforgettable sight. What is more, the food is better in Scotland than in England, + living is cheaper there too.
I haven't done anything worthy of reporting since I got to England. I've travelled a bit, talked a bit up and down this little isle, + read + taught a bit. In my reading I've tried to catch up on some of the contemporary writers, but I can't find anyone that excites me very much. Have you any hot tips? Better yet, do you know any work of scholarship the world is panting for? I finished the De Forest in December — though the editor, Sylvia Bowman, still hasn't read it — + have been trying to dream up something worth doing. Everything seems flat, stale, + unprofitable though — or worse yet, unpublishable.
What else? I turned down half a dozen jobs since I got here. I got a raise at ISC; I did like your Dreiser piece — even to the photograph; and I shall, of course, use The Disinherited when I get back to ISC — that is, if I'm still teaching the Novel course at any time. (I'm not during the Fall term, I do know that, for I'm stuck with something called The American Renaissance instead.) The reason I'd teach The Disinherited is that it's worth teaching, not that you wrote it; it should be taught — though it would seem a little strange to me to have it mixed in with Sophocles + Aristotle.
Love, Jim

June 29, 1964
Dear Jack and Gladys:
We are leaving England tomorrow, and I have been thinking — between visits to the Stafford hospital (nothing serious) — of what I can tell you to make your voyage happier. All I can think of really is bon voyage. In truth, summing up all I've learned from my jaunt here, I come up with nothing but clichés. Drink wine in France, + never try to get Bourbon or coke. Buy your gifts in Amsterdam, + don't think you can get anything cheap anywhere — least of all in France (though you can get a 20% discount if you use Am. Express Traveller's Checks). Get the Prix fixe meals in France + don't be shy on asking for them. Go to the jeu de paume gallery (impressionist painting) in France + see Versailles + (in England) Hampton Court. Eat roast beef at Simpsons (in the Strand) in London. Expect to pay high prices (despite what you've heard) for lodging, meals, all other things, in Ireland. Don't go to the Folies Bergere; Clark Street is better and not so greedy. — Jesus, I wish I could tell you something really worth while, but I've only learned the clichés, only learned how to avoid being stung, only learned what I liked + what I didn't and most of what I liked, the guide books say you must see. Be sure to see Paris (the lights of Paris) at night, and if you can, see something at the Opera Comique and wander around the place. Love + kisses + have a good time — + save some money.
Yours
Jim

Indiana State College

DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH
Jan. 26, 1965
Dear Jack + Gladys:
I saw your mention of me, Jack, in the review you did of Comerchero's book, and I was grateful. I should add that other people around here also saw what you had to say of my West book — "brilliantly perceptive study" — and in their eyes my stature jumped a foot or more. Thanks.
The most important news from around here is that I have taken a new job. It is at the University of Bridgeport, + the title sounds impressive: "Bernhard Professor + Chairman, Department of English." The job carries an endowed chair with it, + so the salary is fairly decent, but the real reason I decided to go was the location; 55 miles from N.Y. and twenty miles from the New Haven library. I will miss my friends in Terre Haute, for there could not be better people anywhere, but I have a number of close friends in N.Y., and I hope to see more of them than I have hitherto been able to. I would say that I also would miss my Chicago friends, but I suspect New York in turns of number of visits is no farther away than Terre Haute. At least I haven't been to Chicago since before I went to England. Middle age lethargy? I suspect you're right.
Indiana State keeps growing. It is around 7,500 now (slightly larger than Bridgeport) and it will have a new President in July. The new man is presently Vice President at Univ. of Pittsburgh (Rankin is his name), + when he takes over this place will be called Indiana State University (a name change recently approved by the

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
legislature). In some ways I regret leaving now, for the English Dep't here is embarking upon a doctorate program (while Bridgeport only offer a M.A.), and I think I would be happy working with doctoral students. The Administra-tion here offered me that as an inducement (plus a thousand dollar raise and a nine hour teaching load), but Bridgeport still sounded better to me. I suspect — I fear — that next year I'll be begging to come back — but I hope not.
Of my own work I don't have much to say. I'm presently in the midst of semester exams, + next term I have four course — + four preparations — to teach. One of the courses is a graduate course (American Realism) + another is a mixed upper class and graduate course ("The American Novel"), + I suspect I'll do less than justice to these courses in order to save some time for my self. That's an injustice to the students maybe — but in this business nobody cares much about the students, + certainly no one gets ahead by trying to be a good teacher.
What else? The book — reprint — on West + the one on De Forest should be out around March or so. Aside from these all I have done is a review of the Comerchero book for Am. Literature. I thought the book was atrocious.
The family is all fine — though Sheldon had more trouble with athlete's foot for awhile. Amy is thinking of painting the inside of our house in order to sell it at a profit. I expect to take a whopping loss. The difference, I guess, is that between an optimist + a pessimist.
Love,
Jim
P.S. Come + see us.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Indiana State University
Terre Haute, Indiana 47809
DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH
April 28, 1965
Dear Jack + Gladys: 
Between trying to do justice to my teaching chores at Indiana State, trying to aid Bridgeport in some of the areas — like recruitment of faculty — in which I'm vitally interested, + trying to attend to all the business that attends to a move like this — such as selling one house, renting another, + buying another — between all of these things I'm barely managing to retain my sanity. Over Easter, for instance, I flew down to Bridgeport, attended to some chores at the University, looked at fifty houses or so — + bought one — and then flew back (after a week of mad rush) just in time to meet a clan of mine. Then, to make things worse, the house I'd bought had termites, so, at considerable expense, I had to un-buy it and buy another (which I pray doesn't turn out to have termites too). At any rate I do think I now have an address to move my junk to — it's in Westport, Connect-

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
icut but I forget the exact address — + if I can sell one of my houses here (I've rented one on a two year lease) I'll be content. Or relatively content, save for my worry about where I'm going to bed my family down between June 15 (when I've rented my home here) + September 1 (when I get possession of the Westport house). And that dilemma was caused by buying a house + then having to un-buy it and so give up an early possession date.
I enclose a note on the West reprint. It's self-explanatory, the De Forest is finished + should be published soon. I signed a contract to write a book for Twayne on Thorstein Veblen — critical + biographical — + maybe I will. At any rate I'm supposed to have the book done by August of 1967.
I don't know anyone in the West that would be of use to you in arranging some lecture stop-overs. I do have a friend — at least an acquaintance — who books talent on tours around the West + Middle West, + I asked him if he could be of any use to you. He said "maybe" + I gave him your name + address. The guy's name is Steve Eisner, so if you've heard from him, or do hear from him,

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Indiana State University
Terre Haute, Indiana 47809

I've been getting in term papers for the novel course + numbers of papers have been written on a little classic which we're using this term. It's called The Disinherited + one paper, by an elderly woman called Susan Cummings, runs 61 pages.
Considering that the papers were supposed to be around 20 pages or so (and graduate students, of which she's one, have to write two such papers) you at least inspired her to female flow. favorite author.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
UNIVERSITY OF BRIDGEPORT
BRIDGEPORT, CONNECTICUT 06602
Feb 27, 1968
Dear Jack + Gladys:
I hope you're happy in your retreat in Moberly, but every time I think of you there, I think of Napoleon and exile + Elba. When are you coming to the East. I'll rouse the peasants — for we need you.
As for the news of the Lights, there is not a great deal of it, but what there is is all good. Amy, for instance, went back to work a few months ago, and a couple of weeks ago she was promoted to Head Nurse (whatever that is). Ever since she started working she has been singing like a lark, + now her cheerfulness is so extreme as to be slightly obnoxious. I drew two morals: One is that women prefer many things to housework; the second is that women enjoy being appreciated, + the men who marry them often fail to give them the promotions they need to make them feel their [[?]]t. Summary'ed my wisdom runs like this: Kids + kisses aren't enough.
About the children, all is well. Most of the news worth telling — save for the repetition of their uniform beauty, charm, + intelligence — concerns Sheldon. He recently became 16, and now he has his driver's license, + I have two additional headaches. One is that my car insurance has soared into the stratosphere. The other is that he insists we need a third car. Imagine, me — who grew up in the thirties, full of fear + poverty — forced to think of a third car. I'm hardly used to indoor plumbing.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Sheldon is also nagging in another way. He wants to begin college — though he hasn't finished yet his junior year in high school — and in furtherance of his campaign he's applied to Chicago (+ been interviewed) and taken the Scholastic Aptitude Tests. In the latter he scored in the 99+ percentile, + he keeps flaunting those scores in front of me to prove that he's ready for college. I keep telling him I don't want him to go to college yet, not so much because it's damned expensive but because I want him — with Vietnam the way it is — to fail a couple of grades in high school before he even starts college.
As for me, the most important news is that I've quit smoking — at least I've quit for over a month — + I look in the mirror each day + am awed by the face (noble + strong) that stares back at me.
I've also inveigled $1500 annually out of the administration — you'd be proud of me — to give annual awards (at an annual Banquet) to the Connecticut Writers of the best work of fiction, non-fiction, + poetry for the year. The Banquet is to be held in May, at which time the Van Wyck Brooks Awards will be announced. Why not come?
Beyond these facts, nothing much. For a while I was toying with the idea of leaving Bridgeport, for a couple of rather attractive offers were thrust at me — one as a Dean, the other as a Provost (or Vice-President-Academic) — But Bridgeport bribed me with money (beyond my wildest dreams of avarice) and with departmental concessions (which should please my senior staff) and so I'm rather content to remain here. Who wants to be a Provost. I really don't. As a matter of fact — save for the money — I don't want to be a Chairman. I'd rather teach.
Come + see us —
Love,
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
to be be a football player, and complains bitterly about the fact that his braces — teeth — keep him from being a star on his Junior High team. Jama is in the fifth grade and grows prettier (to my eyes) every day. I'm reading galleys for a college text for Holt-Rinehart (entitled The Modern Age) and doing a little reading for a book on Sinclair Lewis that I'm doing for Crowell. In addition I quarrel a good bit with Assistant Deans + sulk in my office.
Come + see us,
Love —
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
HUNTER COLLEGE
OF THE CITY UNIVERSITY OF NEW YORK
695 PARK AVENUE
New York 21, N. Y.
Department of English
Aug 26, 1969
Dear Jack + Gladys:
I finished summer teaching at Hunter (thus the stationary) a few days ago, and aside from reading page proofs for the teacher's manual of The Modern Age, I've done nothing since the term ended save to loafe. It has been great fun, + I think I'm going to do more of it. Wish you were here to loiter on the beach + watch the mermaids with me.
All of the family are well. Sheldon hitch-hiked home from the University of Chicago last June + arrived with hair a yard long + opinions to match. He did condescend to get his hair cut (slightly), and a week or so later he got a job doing computer programming at the social science research center of Columbia University. He's been working quite hard, + he now knows a number of computer languages. He + a friend of his at Chicago have dreams of doing some kind of computer programming on a contract basis — they've already done some programs on private contracts — after they return to the University. It seems rather weird to me — I'm no enterpreneur — but no more weird than Shel's decision (after his early orientation toward science) to major in English.
Matt + Jama are growing like weeds. Matt, at the age of thirteen, is already approaching six

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
feet. He's also been inspired by the art of J. R. Tolkien, and he writes stories constantly if not well. Lately he's been submitting his "art" to magazines — such ones as The Evergreen Review — and though I keep telling him that he should at least read the magazines to which he submits his work, he feels (I think) that would be cheating.
Amy is in good health + spirits. She is still working but has given up her teaching chores — primarily because they became too much of an emotional strain.
Aside from the fact that I've quit smoking — I think — I have no personal news of any significance. I do an occasional book review, and I spend a little time every day on the book I'm doing on Sinclair Lewis for Crowell. I've also seen a few plays lately (I liked The Prince of Miss Jean Brodie), gone to the race track a few times, bet a little on the stock market — all in all nothing very exciting. What about you? How's the autobiography shaping up? Are you planning any more trips? Tell me all!
Love,
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Dear Jack + Gladys:
I've been working like a dog and doing nothing of any scholarly importance. I have, however, received the undergraduate English curriculum, and I've attended innumerable obligatory social binges, where I've drunk like a fish and held my tongue like a gentleman. I wish you had been there. — Incidentally, I've been rather friendly with a fellow named Bert Gilden (Hurry Sundown) + he remembers you fondly from a short period he spent with you in Chicago.
Best,
Jim
Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year
Jim + Amy Light

June 28, 1972
Dear Jack + Gladys:
I just finished my "Annual Report" to the President (of Fresno State University, that is), and felt I should also send you some kind of report about the Lights. Basically, I guess you might say that we survived, but more specifically —
Well, Amy has a job as Director of Nurses at a convalescent home, and she is working far harder than any human being should be asked to. She does enjoy what she is doing, however, and in a sense the work paid off when the State Inspector of such hospitals visited her hospital + praised it lavishly for the improvements she had made in the personnel + the procedures of the hospital. That made Amy beam — really set her up — but she's still working ten hours a day sometimes, plus trying to keep a house running, + she shouldn't be doing all that much. She seems to thrive on such burdens, however, + doesn't desire either to quit her job or get any significant household help, + I'm not strong enough

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
to force her to do either.
My son Sheldon (age 20) graduated with an English major in June from the University of Chicago + is working as a bookman for Dell. He seems to enjoy the job fairly well, + I don't mind him doing it for a while until he decides upon some permanent career objective. I hope, however, that the urge to travel — + he gets more than enough traveling in his job — declines a little in the future, or that he'll desire to go to graduate school (which he has no inclination to do at the present time. At any rate I'm grateful that he's got a fairly decent job, for it's not easy for young people (especially those with majors in such useless subjects as English + History) to find a job nowadays. I'm kind of sorry though that he had to cut his hair — despite the fact I'd told him innumerable times that he looked stupid, as well as unkempt, with hair down to his shoulders. He did get to keep his moustache though — a reddish, straggling, untidy thing, + I'm grateful for that (though I wish he'd cut it off because it looks so miserable).
My son Matt (age 16 + scheduled to

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
be a senior in high school next year) is taking a couple of courses this summer at the University of California, Santa Barbara; he's fairly pleased with that since the University only allows a few honors students from high school to enroll in summer courses. In addition Matt seems to be enjoying himself immensely in California. He's made a vast number of friends at his high school — primarily because he's been extremely active in dramatics at the school — + the phone was ringing constantly until he left.
Between his calls, and those of my daughter, Amy + I felt we were running an answering service. Now he's happy — the bliss of independence! — and we have a little peace for a few weeks.
My daughter Jama (age 13) is serving as a teacher's aide this summer in an elementary school nearby. I don't know how much she's learning — or of how much actual use she is to the teacher — but the job keeps her off the sheets all morning, + I'm grateful for that. I'm especially grateful for her job because she's discovered BOYS — they now excite her far more than the violin does — + she's become a little hysterical, as well as a bit wild, over this

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
new world that's scrum into her ken. I hope she can be tamed, but meanwhile Amy + I are plotting on finding a way to send her to summer camp — a fate she abhors.
As for me, I'm well. I've discovered a little more than I really wanted to know about the paranoia, the provincialism, + the egoism of some faculty members, but I've discovered even more about the solid merit, the real humanity, of most academic people. Probably my most difficult moments this year came in trying to cope with some of the eccentrics (really, the madmen) in the art department, but I've even learned to tolerate their fondness — their obsession — with the obscene; their tendency to feel they alone can judge art while at the same time they admit they have no standards by which to judge art (unless it is that art is something which artists do); their wild + somewhat chaotic imaginativeness (we've got one faculty member who's preoccupied with the image of the American flag stuck up the ass, yet waving bravely, of

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
a black man or woman; we've got another artist whose dream is to be America's foremost baloon sculptor, so he's constantly taking pictures of his sculptures as they float upward on the mid-day breezes; we've got still another weirdo who insists on putting live animals into his "art" — so that when he put on a show in our very modern, + very lavish, gallery, we had to find a live cow, plus straw + attendant, + I had to try to justify that kind of expense to the beady eyes of the sovereign state of California); + finally department is totally insane in its meetings, so that what they decide they want me doing is exactly what they'll be evidently opposed to on the following day. On the other hand if I didn't have the art department to keep me entertained, I might not have had much to do, for such departments as English + Philosophy are so well run that I suspect they don't really need me, or the Vice Presidents (of which we've got four), or the President.
Physically I'm in pretty good shape now, though for a while I was somewhat ill. The illness

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
began with a chest cold a couple of months ago, which then weakened me so that I reacted more easily to my innumerable allergies, which then escalated to asthmatic attacks which left me unable to be down much less to sleep, which then led to total exhaustion + black despair. I finally, however, managed to get out of the hands of an allergist + a G.P. who didn't know what they were doing (+ didn't much care either) + into the hands of a chest specialist who did. He made a lot of lists — all of which showed nothing organically was wrong —, gave me some shots in most of the more private parts of my anatomy, put me on a diet (which allows me to eat almost anything I dislike + forbids almost everything of which I'm fond), + within a week I was as chipper as ever. As a bonus I managed to lose fifteen pounds + to stop smoking, + I hope those losses are permanent. On the other hand I haven't had a drink in over two months, + I plan to remedy that as soon as the doctor will allow it.
I could especially use a few drinks for the next few days, for I have a rather difficult decision to make — I was offered the position of Dean of the Faculties at Lehman College of the City University of

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
New York — and I've always depended on liquor for guidance in such matters. Now I have to try to think rationally. On the one hand I have a good administrative job here with harmonious working relations with the faculty + the higher administration. On the other hand, the position at Lehman would give me greater academic authority to do some things I want to do (my only adminis-trative superior would be the President of Lehman), a much higher salary (the salaries in the city university system are absurdly disproportionate to academic salaries elsewhere), + possibly ulcers. Five years ago, or even a few months ago I wouldn't have hesitated at all, but in the last few months I've discovered that I'm not as strong either physically or emotionally as I once thought I was. For that reason the prospect of entering the maelstrom of the New York system — with its ethnic problems, its union demands, its student aggressiveness — makes me wary. But then, there is the challenge, and maybe even I could be of some use...
Not much else. I haven't done any real writing — though I did do some work on the revised edition of The Modern Age which came out a couple of months ago. The only exciting thing I've done lately is to buy a new house (shortly before — the

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
day before — I got a letter from Lehman asking if I might be interested in the position of Dean of Faculties at Lehman; but we've never lived in the house, the only real pleasure we gotten from it (save for the pleasure of buying it) has been from a few dips in the swimming pool.
Otherwise what: well, I have taught one course here and used The Disinherited, to which the students responded with vast enthusiasm. One other teacher here also uses The Disinherited, and he was quite impressed with me when I said I knew the author.
How goes the autobiography? Any idea when it'll be published. From the few things I've seen it should be an impressive book — and even may sell well if the Conroy curse can be pacified.
Thanks for sending me the Anvil (which I got in today's mail) + curses on you for sicing that M.A. student, with a thesis on Josie, onto me.
Love — to both —
Jim

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991

Dear Jack + Gladys:

August 12, 1974
Dear Jack + Gladys:
It's been good to see the renewed output of you, Jack, + I'm really looking forward to seeing the completed autobiography. With the renewed interest in the thirties, I would think there might be a good chance for considerable sales. At any rate, I hope so.
As for the Lights, we are all together now + in good health. Jama finished her first year at Greenwich High School + eventually managed to make some good friends, so that she's relatively happy (she'll never be very happy, I fear) until we move again (which isn't likely until she's finished high school). She's still crazy about animals, + we sent her off to a riding camp a couple of days ago. I hope she finds a horse there that she can love.
Matt finished his first year at the Univ. of Connecticut, taking most of his courses in English, most specifically in creative writing. This summer he's spent between working at McDonald's (frying hamburgers) + writing. Tomorrow he + a friend of his are setting off to hitch to Fresno. It's not a plan I'm fond of, but there's not much I can do about it since there are girls in Fresno + he's eighteen years old. I assume I'll get a phone call from somewhere in Wyoming in a week or so, + then I'll respond as I must.

title: Jack Conroy letters [10], 1924-1991
transcription:
Sheldon quit his job with Dell a couple of months ago, then got married + took a honeymoon trip to Ireland. Now, Ireland behind them, Shel + his new bride are in Greenwich. Since they got here, they've managed to find an apartment in Hartford, not too far from the University of Connecticut Law School (where Shel will be going come fall), + they're doing a good bit of painting + such to make the apartment beautiful. I don't think it will ever be beautiful, but then I think of how I started married life — in a one room rental with a sagging bed — + I don't worry too much. I just hope the two of them can see the wisdom of scrimping (without babies) until Shel gets his law degree.
Amy still is working as Director of Nurses in the Greenwich Municipal Hospital. She's not as happy with the work as she was earlier, for she's had to do some of the things an administrator has to do, + not all of her decisions have made her beloved. I keep telling her that that's the price she has to pay for the job she has, but since everything she's done (she says) is eminently just + reason-able, she can't see why anyone would find fault with it. Telling her that justice is not what everyone seeks is no answer to her problem.
As for me, I still find considerable variety + excitement in my work. Sometimes I think I should try to write something again, but I'm usually so busy I don't have time for such thoughts. Mostly I worry about inflation + the stock somewhat, but Nixon's resignation makes me see some hope for the future.
Love,
Jim

Dear Jack,
Thanks for your card which has been received for some time. We went to St. Louis unexpectedly and being away more than a week, much works and quite a bit of correspondence piled up. On the way up we stayed overnite with Clay + Mabel. They had heard from you meanwhile.
Later I learned that you are a friend of Rhoda + Jerry Nedwick. A mutual friend has written Rhoda several times without receiving an answer and this is the first Xmas that no card was received. My friend is afraid that something may have happened - especially considering Rhoda's state of health. I met her about 5 years ago when Jerry was in England. As I recalled the address was 2013 Prairie. If you know about her please tell me next time you write.
We go to Mexico again in a couple of weeks. We make forays out into the world for money: sell Mexican sterling silver handmade jewelry + art objects. Don't work much + just get by. Will tour the northern resorts (Wisc. + Illin.) this year, having never made them.
Be sure to advise well ahead of time if you plan to come this way - I'd hate to miss you. We make the Ill. State Fair every year - booth in North end of Grandstand Aug. 14 to 23. Write when you can.
Sincerely,
Dick

May Day '59

Dear Jack,
  Back home & preparing to take off again - this time     north. We will be in St. Louis for a week or two. Will stop over nite with Clay & Mabel staying in a house trailer we are hauling - a rather old one belonging to a friend in Mena.
 If you come down this way, why not go by [[Neasho?]] for Clay & Mabel, then to the Gilberts at [[Trk?]] (old Land Colonists) get Billy Gilbert to give you the keys to my house & stay here awhile & enjoy the place. I'm afraid we will be working this summer. I want to start construction on the community building this fall which will have about 8 rooms in it for "singletons." We will try to earn a little dough for the project. Also will make Ill [Illinois{ State Fair in Aug.
 Saw Willard & aside from passing quickly under a flour sifter he hasn't changed. Still shy, mild & controverted. He seems to have only O'Leary there now plus the boy he adopted in Cuernavaca while I was there. do you know his brother Archibald? I don't. He's a painter.

title: Jack Conroy letters [09], 1924-1991
transcription:
Mexico is modernizing fast & I suggest you try to see it before too long. It is beautiful at Rancho Chico now. All is bright & expectant looking, flowers blooming & birds singing - things growing like mad. I hate like hell to leave it for those damned cities!! We plan to do a little work in St. Louis - a matter of a week or ten days & then go into the resort area of Minn - Mich, Wisc - don't really know just where as yet, merely that general area. We will be peddling our art objects & sterling silver jewelry - all handmade - Mexico.
 First address will be our "Ancestral" home in St Louis - 5738 Maple Avenue St. L.ouis Mo. - where my mother still lives. Mail will be forwarded from here or there. Don't know if we will get to Chicago but may. I'll take your address along just in case.
 Hope you are well & everything OK.
  Best,  Dick.

Rancho Chico
R.F. Keaney
Route 2
Mena, Arkansas
December 27 1963

Dear Jack,
 Thanks for your note of some little time ago. Hope you both had a nice Xmas. The Silferts were over here and we had a lovely day (70 degrees F) leaving the poor turkey carcass somewhat maulled but as always some survives for the next day (or week!)
 Last time we talked you were not far from retirement. As you know I was once interested in a community; (that's how we met) well I still am. About five or six couples - all intelligent people altho not necessarily holding the ^ same ideas, A sort of retirement idea for the kind of people you would choose to be with. Non-profit, completely. The wives will balk at the idea, thinking they will be stuck out in the woods - which isn't so - and it would have to be a going concern before they would accept it. The rub is it can't be without the people. Basically, one would have a life-lease; non-tranferrable, non-revocable

title: Jack Conroy letters [09], 1924-1991
transcription:
for $1.00 per year. We would all pay into a Maintenance fund a nominal sum, $15 or $20 per month. Each would furnish his own abode, house, housetrailer - whatever  he chose. If he becomes disenchanted he could leave & take his abode with him or sell it to the group. He could not sell it to anyone else, give it away or bequeath it. The group would buy it & sell it to a successor. The idea of 5 or 6 couples is - no factions - no politics
 I maintain it is the only answer to the goofy society of today - a partial escape. We have pure air & pure water & a pretty good "poor man's" climate.
 I will also write Bryan Fulks who moved to Phoenix, then to Calif. & wrote me that  "if they didn't like that "they'd" move on to some other place."
 If you prefer to live in Moberly (where they haven't even asked for your book in the library) my friend Mary Christian has a house for sale on east Rollins with a new gas furnace. She says Moberly is no place for you. If you have some nostalgia in line with Oliver Goldsmith's "Deserted Village" then read George Crabbe's "The Village" & get the low-down. Mary would be glad to sell all their property & lease.  I think people should commit themselves only on the basis that we would have enough to start off with to make some communal life - say 4 couples.
  We sill leave for Mexico before the middle of next month. Hope you & Gladys are both well & that all is going well for you. We'll be in Chicago around May 7th for a week & see you then. Best to both from both of us.   Sincerely
  Dick

Mr. Jack Conroy sir,
Dear Friend,
Again I venture to send you a line I had a blue time down on The Loop Tuesday morning looking for work. Got wet and cold. Looking for a job in a place like that is Hell and its hard to smile when your cold & wet I came to your LaSalle st address, rapped on the Fire Escap door but found you had either got-away or hadn't got down town. I felt so blue I came home but probably should have waited a little longer. After returning home I met a laundry man in a few rods of my rooming place who has given me what one might call a job soliciting for new laundry work. He brought me to this address where I eat & sleep. It brings me in contact with people and has builded a back ground for a good Short Story entitled "Finding a Job in Chicago," where I went to apply for work, what they said and all would

be interestingly told if I could contact with you would enjoy seeing a copy of your "New Anvil which might some day tell a Story to some reader about the grindstone of Life . Gosh! it does hurt, don't it? but yet the sunshine this morning seemed to me to be the brightest I ever seen so also was the rain this afternoon, really cold & wet. Yet, I think of How our Hoosier poet put it what he said "When God sorts out the weather and sends down the rain, Rain is my choice." Really a country without rain would be nearer Hell than Chicagos pile of Stone and Bricks many will tell you that world is cockeyed but I can't think so. However there are people who look that was at a world that's been here for sometime and will remain here after quite a few of us are gone would like to see you very much and believe me yours very Friendly

[1972]
Dear Mr. Conroy
Joe's passing has been such a shock to us. Its even worse because we were together 24 hrs a day during the last 4 1/2 years since retirement and he was such a home body and enjoyed just staying home. Joe was going on a short shopping trip and had started the car, came in while it warmed up & went in the bed room. I heard a strange noise & rand in but he was unconscious. I called the Emergency Squad who was stationed just down the street. They were here in about 5 minutes but he was gone. He had been feeling fine.
Joe has never kept his writings together. We have kept after him to gather it all up and he was going to but never got around to it. The boys are just sick about this. They have never even read but a few of his poems and want not to try & get them gathered up. Joe had boxes of magazines, books, etc. in the attic,  cabin, basement. I take for granted his writings are in them. Can you tell us the names of what magazines or what books to look in? I will go thru every [[?]] but it would help to have some idea. I do hope they are here

Saturday, 28 May, 1949 8:20 PM
I am writing this aboard S.S. "African Pilgrim," being in charge of her at the moment. An 8-day job, & then I wonder when the next work will show up. Things are tight in the shipping industry. Too many [[?]] have lost or abated what union spirit we had, the phonies are riding high, & the future is dim. The ships of the company I work for are beautiful & well maintained, I love them & am happy working on them, even in port. And the outfit has promised to send me to sea.
Your letter, which I have been remiss in answering, calls up memories. Of course we have changed, with the shifting environment, like a chameleon; our outer hides, I swear; within, I rather think you & I believe as we did in the old days, & keep the torch of faith burning.
What has hurt me more than anything else is the reft between our daughter (our only child) & us, caused, from our point of view, by her marrying a fellow we detest. In the two years I knew him, I was never able to hold a conversation with him. Enough said, I think. Nancy & I were buddies until he came into the picture. Though I was initiated by what Columbia U did to her social & political outlook. You do not write as if any similar situation were disturbing you Didn't you have five kids? You mention only three. I am glad the elder boy came through the war all right.
Kitty and I read much of your book aloud, one or two selections at a time. Thank you, Jack, for the gift. What do I think of "Midland Humor"? I read it through, & liked "Sal Fink" & "Peck's Bad Boy" best. I respect the work as a point of departure into Americana. It shows evidence of the sweat you worked up while putting it together. You did the job you

title: Jack Conroy letters [07], 1924-1991
transcription:
set out to do, but too many of your authors were pedestrian; outstanding in their time, but somewhat flat to-day. To repeat, the glimpses into our past are valuable; I have formed the habit of seeking to link together what I read with a synthesis I can readily bring to the fore; your bits of mosaic were [[?]] in & "Sal Fink", I know, will stick with me.
Having said what I said in the above paragraph, I now want to tell you the best written, most telling, most interesting selection in your book was      your own story of the quarry man. Jack, that was excellent writing. Kitty & I both got enthusiastic as she read it aloud. Which leads me to remark that I look forward to reading your juveniles, as you say they are in the same vein.
Yes, I recall Hauser, but not as a very good poet. Where is Walt Snow Edith Snow was a fine person. I was interested in your news of Algren & Price. What happened to H.H. Lewis?
I am writing this in the saloon, to the fine music of WQXR. The big ship is quiet otherwise. I discount the chatter of the night Engineer, though he did serve aboard HMS "Tiger" at Jutland, in '16.
My poetry goes fairly well, I think. William Rose Benet has proved a good friend. I have a novel of our Civil War to peddle, a collection of sailor terms, & a half-completed novel of to-day in our borough. That was why I asked if you could suggest, or recommend me to a literary agent who will find the soft spots. I do gardening, for the first time in my life, so we may eat this summer; I like it; the old Dutch peasant blood coming out, I guess. I collect stamps. Increasing home library of 3700 volumes. Now you are partially up to date with me. Tell me more about yourself in your next letter, which I'll be eagerly awaiting. 
I do hope we can meet one of these days.
All the best, old friend.
Jack

Dear Jack:
Did you see the program about Yaddo on Public Television last night? Robert McNeil was the "host," and it really brought back memories. It was 37 years ago that I was there — 1949.
There was a view of my studio from down below and a view of the little bridge that led to the door. They have built some small studios in the woods since our day.
Once we laughed about Elizabeth Bishop and some of her poems, but I was recently embarassed to find that she won a Pulitzer prize a number of years ago with a collection called Poems North and South. I shouldn't have laughed about those drops of coffee falling off the balcony.
I have been looking through the New Standard Encyclopedia a lot lately. A fine work. I have you to thank for recommending me as music adviser and authenticator.
As ever, "Bill" Grant

13 February 74
Dear Jack -
I ordered & received your Anvil anthology and have been reading it - much of it - and recalling names / faces / times. The big bulk[[?]] of it, physically, is hard to handle, but then the writing is a bellyful: tough and punchy.
Your introduction is vigorous, informative if informal, with news of other times seeming still relevant in many ways. The poetry as a whole has dated much more than the fiction. Maybe political, tendentious poetry is harder to write. The stories woke sharp points, draw on character, deliver live dialogue. Most of the stories I read - those by authors I remembered personally or by name - hold up remarkably well, language direct and hard hitting. The Caldwell pieces are really something!
A good job - congratulations.
Best!
You
Louis
GIOP

April 23, 1964

Dear Jack,
Hello, there! I finished "The Disinherited" yesterday, Jack, and I want to tell you that I enjoyed reading it very much (and I'm not conning you, either). The book has a vitality which sustains interest and an honesty which I found very moving.
I don't think I could add to Prof.Aaron's review, so I won't try. I'm sure that you are familiar with the points he cited (p. xii). I thought that Warren Beek's review was excellent. One point, though- I think the "awkwardly hitched eposides"(Aaron's [[?]]) could be remedied by a simple typographical technique. For example, refer to p. 12. At about the middle of the page you shift from a discussion between Larry and his father to a description of [raining], with no "bridge" in between. My idea is this- would it be possible to insert a series of asterisks across the page, like
* * * * * * * * * *
after the line "Maybe you can be a doctor or a lawyer" to denote the end of an episode and the beginning of another statement? In this way, the continuity is clearer. What do you think? Of course, this technique is not new- by any means.
A few ideas occur to me in terms of promoting the book. The colleges, universities, and labor unions are the likliest sources of demand. In the schools, interested department would include Amer. Lit., Amer. Hist., and perhaps sociology or the social sciences, in general. What about contacting the professional educator societies?
By the way, Jack, have you read John O'Hara's introduction to the

title: Jack Conroy letters [05], 1924-1991
transcription:
2
paperback edition of "The Cape Cod Lighter" where he really pours it on the phony book reviewers and critics? If you haven't read it as yet, I recommend it highly. Also, I am enclosing a clipping which refers to The Disinherited.
In closing, Jack, I want to that you for the copy you sent and I'll talk it up every chance that I get. By the way, was Ed a real person or an invention? If a real person, what happened to him? And to Bonny Fern, if real. Here's hoping we meet again - if not at Nate's perhaps elsewhere. If you happen to be on the North Side, my phone number is Li9-6780. Perhaps we can run out for a couple of beers to Old Town, the site that Slim Brundage deserted like a fool (remember the old College of Complexes?)
Very truly yours,
Bernard Gordon

Miami, Fla.
Dear Jack --
I had a letter from Blake from the county jail at Clearwater, Fla. He faces, with [[?]]ing up low to and poise that seems unnatural, 5 to 10 years. There is hardly a chance that he will be released since his record in this state is so bad. It's all very depressing to me. Dear Jack:
I hope your anthology of Midwest humor is finished and in press.

When I finish I shall worry about a publisher. Will probably end up at the Hopkins Press where I'll have to invest $2000 and hope I get it back. Comment: excellent; would be proud to publish it; but it won't have large sale; consequently could I "finance" publication? What do you know of the Packard firm? Dear Jack -

Jan 19th 1935
Dear Jack Conroy: -
I have yours of the 16th and I am sorry that I bothered you with the stories at this time. I surely do understand and I can appreciate just what you are up against. Working against time. I feel as convinced as a mortal can be in this funny old world that I have something in those two stories or else I do not know beans when the bag is open. I somehow feel a deep interest in you and I want to see the ANVIL succeed. If it does not naturally any defieit will necessarily come out of the proceeds of your novel writing. I am also thoroughly convinced unless you get better writers than some of your contrivutors that it will not make a go. I do hope and trust that you will not take offensce at this for I swear by all that is holy that I would never say this if I did not have your interest so deeply at heart.
I do not want ^you to get the impression that my mouth goes like a machine tiring out lying words and that I am full of gossedom in those two stories the words are the out-pouring of a troubled soul. I am not trying to be swellheaded and I hope you will not set me down as a preeminent goddam fool in setting out to advise you. I know its looks flukey for an amateur to advise a professional but I have always appreciated advice no matter what the source.

[Written Vertically: Just a lot of wise cracking? Dick]

title: Jack Conroy letters [02], 1924-1991
transcription:
I want to hear the ANVIL on everybody's tongue and not spoken of as ^just so-so.
In a way I suppose I am a stop-at-nothing fellow but at heart I am no giver-inner and any kindest shown me hits the spot and I am always ready and willing to be hit twice in the same place and I will take my shirt off for anyone I like.
Maybe if you would estimate the words in the last half of your book and divide by the days you have left to finish it and then set for yourself a daily stint of say 2000 words that might be the answer.
Don't run yourself ragged or get hairs in your palms. I had rather be the daddy of a nice heifer calf. We can't all be Cole Porters, or Alexander Woolcots.
Tighten your circingle and say "my diet from now on will be a diet of human gizzards. Why ^it is not worth while to try to live on the giblets of hell.
Get out on a rail and see if theres not something for the lizzard 
Buck-up and give them both barrels. Make the last part of the book as hot as the hinges of hell and water then eat it up. Hey nonny-nonny. Hot-cha-cha! Don't let them catch you with your pants down. You don't have write to Congress about it. Your output is the proof of the pudding. What you did once you can do again. Drink While Mule in a goblet as big and tall as joint of stove pipe. Don't get the jitters but walk like a cat on gutter spout. Make your tummy a rummy tummy until you get through, why rabbits come out of hats and storks.

title: Jack Conroy letters [02], 1924-1991

600 E 21st

and have babies. Nothing is impossible. Why are you realer than the real thing. You don't have to roll your eyes like Houptmann who is on trial for his life or you don't have to make a living as a gum shoe artist and that is something. Things could be worse. You'll pull through if you don't get the hi-gulgum-filps. Use highly combustible words and let them explode on the paper right in front of your face. Pad the seat of your pants to keep from getting corns on your ask me no questions and I'll tell you no lies. Smoke a handful of nickel cigars a day ^and drink a dozen cups of black coffee. Be as stubborn as a mule and reach your goal. You can't quench your thirst ^entirely just drinking at a literary trough. Your job is word juggling and your ideas are as sound as a dollar. The turkey shot the buzzard and the buzzard shot the crow. Don't be goosey. Your last friend hasent died.

title: Jack Conroy letters [01], 1924-1991

May 6, 1962
Dear Jack,
Sorry to hear of your mishaps guess the jinx has been put on the Conroy's for the past two years have been torture for me. As you know, I have been drinking for years, but really put on the steam the past 2 years, going to 3 different hospitals for help, losing a procession of jobs, having divorce papers served on me a few weeks ago, and doing very little writing.
When it reached the point where I was thinking of suicide, I knew that something had to be done, so I had myself committed to the county jail for 60 days, I'll come out around June 18th. Muriel really doesn't want to divorce me, but in desperation she tried anything to make me do something constructive about my problem. All prisoners should write. It would be good for them and good for society. Some of the greatest literature hav been written by prisoners, among them, Sir Walter Raleigh, Bunyon, Dustoewusky and even Chessman. Prisoners suffer, think, and are lonely, so have much to say. Their creative yearning and power is shown by the fact that their is much demand for great literature in prisons. I work in the library and know this to be true. Aside from the westerns and mysteries, the most popular authors here are: Caldwell, Yerby, Chessman, Algren, & Motley. A few months ago, Ne[[?]]on sent me a fine autographed photo. Same one that appeared in "Nugget."
The Evergreen Review is using my poem "Skid Row" The Negro Digest is using "Slight Advantage" and A.A. is going to use my poem "The Local Bar." I will contact Mr. S[[?]]gal.
Before coming here, I was taking a course in writing, for purposes of stimulation. The teacher, George Kauffman has appeared in "The New Anvil" --- Remember?
Every thing is under control, Jack If you could send me a money order for $2.00, I would be most grateful. All that we have here is smokes.
Nice hearing from you Jack. Don't remain such a stranger.
Tom
