title: W.S. Drummond diary, 1830
transcription:
Left to my own thoughts immediately on my Fathers departure. I took up a pen and wrote a few things, of which the following is a true and litteral transcript: I am sorrow to say I have not even noticed these from that time to this: (29. Nov. 1830) Sunday 19. Sept. 1830.
I arrived in Steubenville and immediately proceeded to I.G. Wright's where I was received a student of Law. It seemed but a small thing, when the Profession was only in prospect, to enter upon it: but when the reality was at hand a feeling of dread came over me. Why? That in a time, when so many and such excellent men, were engaged in it with bare success, I should be sure to fail. Yet, not withstanding my humble intellect and purse scantily* supplied
*Only because from a scanty source.

title: W.S. Drummond diary, 1830
transcription:
with lowly dependence on Him who is the Father of the fatherless and needy, I commence a two year's study in a profession which treats or showed treat of the formation and regulation of society — the laws which are between nation and nation — between a Gov: and its subjects and between one subject and another. It is an extensive study and well prosecuted may benefit my-self and my fellow creatures (how sanguine!) I trust in God such may be the consequence. For the better attaining to such a desirable end, I propose the following rules to be guided by:
I. I will, those God being helper, engage in all outward exercises, which shall be for the bringing on of thy kingdom and also cultivate as far as in me lies a mental

title: W.S. Drummond diary, 1830
transcription:
mental holiness towards thee.
11. "That honesty is the best policy" Shall be my attempt to prove; encouraging good feelings is all I shall hurt no body designedly by word or deed.
111. I shall endeavor to treat myself honorably: [[?]] 1 I will drink nothing, not even wine,* besides water;
2. engage in no association but such as is conducted by genteel men and besides genteely managed; 3. treat all kindly and make intimate acquaintances with but few; 4. be as disinterested as possible. 
Here ended my code and tho' many things may be omitted in it which ought to find a place there, yet I do not now choose to add to it and thus destroy it
*This law has been repealed

title: W.S. Drummond diary, 1830
transcription:
February 5, 1831.
To-day returned from the Federal City, wither I had been on a visit to my parents. The City at first appeared beautiful, more so than ever. But it was too much for me. To see (myself an idle spectator) so many engaged in public antics, so many distinguished for their talents and their looking in to myself, to see a young man near 21 years of age, and as yet unfit to be called a student in any profession, was insupportable. Steubenville soon again received me. In heaviness I left home so rotten; but all were well. I entered this place a second time with strange feelings.

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
(11)
In the morning Gabriel a half breed, and leader of a small band of half breeds who today have established their camp at the wagon road crossing of the upper fork came into the Fort. He does not know of any report in regard to hostile Sioux on the Porcupine, except that five Tetons had been in the Yankton Camp. I should have stated that the half breed Scouts said that Medicine Bear had ordered his camp to move further north to avoid the hostile Sioux.
[margin note] Medicine Bear orders his camp to move-

To day in the afternoon Grovon Jerry came into the Fort bringing his lodges and reports that the camp will all be here in two or three days. He has heard nothing of hostile Sioux. He reports that they have killed plenty buffalo, and that they have plenty of meat. 
The half breed camp will remain for some days on the Fork and will then proceed to Carroll, in the mean time a party of them will go to Jeauneux to trade for supplies. 

[margin note] "Gro Von" Jerry came to the fort with his two lodges-

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
(12)
Sept 24th 1876
Caheen, Long Soldier and a small party of Assinaboines came to the Fort today Gev them a very little sugar and coffee, a few blankets and some tobacco. They have no information of hostile Sioux-
[[margin note: Caheen and Long Soldier came to camp]]

A part of the men form the half breed camp on the upper Fork started to Jeauneax this morning. I sent a letter to John A Culbertson asking information in regard to the Sioux Weather cool, windy and cloudy
[[margin note: Sent later to John A Culbertson]]

Sept 25th 1876
Indians came to the Fort this evening who say they came from the camp on their way to Wolf Point, They say that they have heard no report of Hostile Sioux Swan the Half Breed, says while hunting yesterday that he discovered a trail of about forty horsemen, which he thinks were made a Gros-Ventres war party, supposed to be the same party reported by Bent, below here just after the Gros Ventres were here Swan saw the trail several miles below here on milk river, The Indians who came from Jackson and Bobtail Bear's camp report that most of the camp had scattered, and that, but few are still on their way to Wolf Point -

[[margin note: Report of Gros Ventres war party by Half Breeds]]
[[margin note: Report from Bob Tail Bear and Jackson camp]]

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
(13)
(13)
Sept 26th 1876
[margin note: Half Breed Messenger Sent by OHanlon returned from Jeanneaux]
The messenger sent by OHanlon to medicine Lodge arrived this evening, bringing letters from Jack Culbertson, saying that Sioux are reported to have crossed the Missouri river at Half Point and that the soldiers had followed them from the Yellow Stone that far, and then went to Ft Buford also a report that the Yanktons had [[served?]] with the hostiles, and were expected to join with the hostiles against the whites which report was from [[Saunter?]] Joe Joe Larry, that Major Mitchell had gone to Bismark and was daily expected to return. Jack does not feel any apprehension of danger,  The messengers brought Helena papers to the 10th of Sept from the first

Wed - Sept 27th. 1876
[margin note: OHanlon started to Benton]
Thos OHanlon and Chris Hawley started to Benton, Crow Chief came in from the Assinaboine camp, on the Fork, no news 
[margin note: Joe Butcher and Valentino came in from hunt -]
Joe Butcher and Valentino came from their hunt, Butch says he was at Clagett, They had several won skins a few antelope, and deer skins, Report Buffalo plenty in the little Rockeys -

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
(14)
Sept 28th 1876
Weather fine, and clear, except being Indian Summer and smoky. Charles Perry arrived from the Marias -
Sept 29th 1876.
[margin note: went to mountains and hunt]
Went to the mountains to hunt, with Charley Ingram, Joe [[Butoh?]], "Gros Ventres Jerry" and "Hig" - killed two Bulls and found [[?]] few buffalo, Camped near to mountains. 
[margin note: Capt Buck arrived from Ft Peck]
Capt Buck, Joe Culbertson and Jimmie Boyd about ten Oclock.

September 30th 1876
[margin note: Returned from hunt]
Arrived at Fort 11 o'clock. 
[margin note: Recd Instructions from Agt Mitchell]
Recd instructions from Agent Mitchell saying that the Government did not oppose his recommendation to make this a place of distributions for the Gros Ventres and Upper Apinaboines and directing that when teams should arrive from Ft Peck to load evrything and transport it to Ft Peck
[margin note: Little Chief arrived and met in Council -]
"Little Chief" the head of a number of Lodges and some 12 or 15 other Assinaboines came to the Fort today, and met in Council, Little Chief said that he and his lodges did not want to go to Half Point, that they would starve there, that he was not strong enough

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
(15)
to work and make a living in any other way than by hunting, that this was thier country now, that they had been driven from below many years ago, that they had allways been friendly to the whites and that they did not know why the Great father should wish to do them harm, that is they had to starve they might as well starve on their own country, that they wanted to receive their supplies and annuities at this place, that the Government might deduct, our amount for the transportation of their subsistence supplies from their annuity goods to pay for the transportation of the same to this Fort, He concluded by saying that they would not go below, and thought that some evil [dispased?] whites must have talked against them to their Great Father -
[margin note: Capt Buck departed for Benton-]
Capt Buck, Jimmie Boyd and Joe Culbertson started for Benton this afternoon. Capt Buck to go to Helena before returning

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
(16) 
Sunday October 1st 1876 -
Weather clear and warm, Indian Summer -
Monday - October 2nd 1876 - 
Weather Cooler, cloudy and very smokey, 
[margin note: Half Breeds came from their camp this morning. Say they are going to build houses, warned them not to do so]
Half Breeds came from their camp this morning, [[Levan?]] said that they were going to build houses at this present camping place. I told them that I should inform the agent, and would not give my consent for them to build Had an interview with "Gros Ventres Jerry" He is very made incensed at the Half Breed's [[locating?]] on Milk river near this fort. saying that they will destroy and drive out the Buffalo as they have done before, and asks that they bee, ordered not to build houses, to winter in this winter.
Tuesday October 3d 1876 -
[margin note: OHanlon returned from Benton]
O'Hanlon returned from Benton bringing mail, but little news, Weather cool and cloudy
Wed, Oct 4th 1876
Cal Culbertson and Gros Ventres Jerry started to the Gros Ventres camp this morning -

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
17
[margin note: speech by Lance Bull]
Lance Bull a Gros Ventres says that the Gros Ventres do not want to go to Fort Peck for they will be among their enemies the Sioux, and that they are afraid of them, and want nothing to do with them. He says that they have lived on Milk River a long time and they like the country, and do not want to leave it. That there is plenty of game here and if they should go to Peck there would be none. They do not want to be located on the Missouri River for liquor sellers would come among them and sell them whiskey and make trouble in their camp. He says that milk river is so far away that whiskey sellers rarely come among them, That they want two traders, alleging that they are better treated when they have two - and that they are better supplied with such articles as they need - Complained of the Half Breeds, that they were killing and destroying the game and causing them to be poor - and wants them ordered out the country - when asked what they would do to live when the buffalo were all gone, he answered  he did not know -

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
(18)
Thursday - October 5th 1876 -
Weather cool, windy and cloudy
Friday - October 6th 1876
[margin note: Gros Ventres camp in three miles]
Hunted for cattle, could not find them, saw the Gros Ventres camp about three miles above the Fort on the north side of the Milk River, Found a lodge of Cree Indians encamped on the [[same?]] ground, with two Red river carts.
[margin note: Cal Culbertson returned from Gros Ventres camp -]
Cal Culbertson arrived from the Gros Ventres camp, 
[margin note: Joe Culbertson Mrs Fraidick ad son, Indian girl - Ed [?] and Pete Grinnell arrived -]
also Joe Culbertson Mrs Fraidick, and Charley and Ed [[?]] and Peter Grinnell, Cal Culbertson reports seeing the cripple handed man described by the Indians, whose name is Frank Robinson, with a two horse wagon and team. He said he was hunting the Gros Ventres camp to get a squaw, He is one of a party whose property was seized last spring by H Beidler and Grinnell - Joe Culbertson reports that H Beidler and Marshall Wheeler will come in a day or two going to Peck
Cal Culbertson brings intelligence obtained from the Gros Ventres that a young Gros Ventres named White Wolf was killed on the Maria River in a whiskey and horse brawl and that the whiskey was sold by two white men for a saddle the killing was the result - The name of one of the white men is Chas Perry

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
19
Saturday October 7th 1876 -
[margin note: Report that a party of white men are selling whiskey to the Gr venres]
Indians report to day that a party of white men are selling whiskey on the Box Elder in the Bear Paw Mountains also ammunition, This report comes from both the Gros Ventres camped above here and Caheen's camp out north on the fork - Indians come in daily from the camp - Thos OHanlon closed up his store yesterday, as reported by notice given by Capt Buck to do so -

Sunday - Oct 8th 1876
[Margin note: Caheen came to camp and makes a speech]
Caheen from he camp on the Fork came to the Fort today, and says that the report of the Half Breeds that he had agreed that they might build winter houses below the Forks on Milk River was false and that he had told them he did not want them in the country and that they must leave. In regard to this place being abandoned, he said that he was glad that we were going to see the Father and hoped that we would tell the father how they are situated, and hoped that they would have somebody kept here to give them a little sugar, coffee, flour & c - He says that the English wanted him to take goods on that side of the line, but he told them that

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
(20)
he had a father on this side of the line and was satisfied with him and dodged not want another - He says that it is too late to go below this winter, that the [[horses?]] are too poor and that the winter is too cold, that when spring comes he thinks he will go, that he wants to do right -
Joe Culbertson and Ed Annible went to the Assinaboine camp at night in a spring wagon. He took the Indian called [["Hig"?]] with them
Monday October 9th 1876
Joe Culbertson and Ed Annible arrived from Little Chief's camp this morning and report the camp some distance 30 mls above the crossing, and consisting of about forty to fifty lodges - 
[Margin note: "Gros Ven Jerry"]
"Gros Ventres Jerry" came in from his camp and gives the particulars of the killing of a young Gros Ventres near the Coal Mines. He says, that about the last of September a young Gros Ventres left Milk river and went to a camp near the Coal Banks of eight lodges, and when he arrived there two white men had been selling whiskey to the camp and

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
that the Indians were drunk, and during the night this young Gros Ventres whose name was "white wolf" was killed, He says that an old man named Freundir was an eye witness to the selling of the whiskey and the killing, and the two white men both had whiskey and they took in exchange a horse and saddle, and that Charles Perry was one of the two white men, and that the saddle in his possession here recently was the saddle received for the whiskey, the other white man lives in Benton. The Indian who committed the murder fled across the river with his lodge after committing the murder - and the others are now on Shield river in this viacity"

He says that the white men are now on the Bax Elder selling whiskey and thinks they have Sugar coffee and ammunition, and are frorsevaning wolves.

He says that the Gros Ventres are more than ever appeared to going on the Missonve River, and that "they have a fear of like if they even going to be driven into a big fire". that the whiskey sold among them is causing the death of their best young men by drunken brawls and fights.

title: Lemuel Burke diary, 1876
transcription:
[22]
Continued
He asks on behalf of the Gros Ventre that these white men engaged in selling whiskey be arrested and punished or that they turned over to the Indians to be punished in their own way -
He says that he is not going to the Missouri river this winter and will remain near this place in the mountains to hunt elk, and Big horns for their skins, until he can hear from the agent, He says that Big Beaver will remain in the mountains (Bear Paw) to get lodge poles for awhile and will return here and will return to milk river about the first of November.

on Mr + Mrs. Wilkinson, at Edith's
request. Prof. Wilkinson came
to my 1:30 class. I brushed and
dusted room.
Sunday Quite warm. Went to church and S.S.
Jan 11 taught Lillie Johnson's class again
the boys were not on their good behavior,
to speak mildly. Prof. Bourne preached
at the College. Mrs. Caswell, of the
North Bennett Mission, Boston. Spoke
this evening. Very interesting.
Rain in the evening, so I went not to the village.

Mrs. Wilkinson gave
jilly to the whole college
for dinner.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [02], 1883-1889
transcription:
Monday Rain and wind all day. I did
Jan 12
not take my tooth out in it.
Mended 6 pairs of stockings +c. At-
-tempted to sleep some- had a 
meeting with the Comm. of the section
on prayer meeting subjects- Went
to Dr. Wilkinson's lecture on Geo. El-
-iot, in the evening. Letter from
Harl. Pater had a fainting fit-
on Saturday- Wrote short letter home.
Read Archibald Malmaison by Julia
Hawthorne. Studied Bible lesson.
Tuesday Studied and taught Chemistry and
Jan 13 Bible - Neither of my classes knew
anything. (I did not know much). Went
down- to village- to take my velvet
waist to Mrs. Irwine- Letter from
John. Read Tribune. Made Bible
topics.
Wed. Jan. 14 Cool, clear- beautiful weather. Classes
as usual. No mail. Read some vainly
on Electricity. Went to teachers' prayer meet-
ing- Tired- Early to bed.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [02], 1883-1889
transcription:
Thurs. Snow first- then rain - did not
Jan 15
go out doors. Classes as usual.
Did Quantitative experiment.
Went to prayer meeting - Studied Bible.
Letter came from Caius Cassius
to the Peterkins.
T. W. Higginson was here today with
his little daughter Margaret.
Friday Snow and rain. Studied Bible and
Jan 16 taught Bible class. Letter from Pater
and one from Uncle George. Made out
Bible topics. studied some for my
scientific temperance address.
Went to prayer meeting in the village this
evening with Miss Cooley. And afterward
made and ate lemon snow with her at S.H.
Saturday Cooler. clear in evening. Classes 
Jan 17 as usual. Went to South Natick
to talk about alcohol to the Saturday
Night Club. Helen Howard was called
home by a telegram this evening.
Letters from Pater and Annie.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [02], 1883-1889
transcription:
Annie Stephens started for home
Sunday
this afternoon - her sister is very
Jan 18 ill with pneumonia-
A beautiful day. Went to church
in the village, but stayed not to
Sunday School. Edith Wilkinson
came in this evening, also Miss Home.
We had a very good prayer meeting-
17 were present. Miss Wild led it-
Monday Wrote letters to John + Ethel - sent statis-
Jan. 19 -tics to Miss Newell for Alumnae Regis-
-ter. Met with Committee to arrange topics
for section prayer meetings. Mended and
cleaned red dress. Went to Boston at
1:53, and out to Electrical Exhibition
about 5:30- Where I had a delightful
time, on account of meeting Mr. Morse
of Oberlin '83, who explained everything
patiently and persistently. Came back
at nine and walked up from station with Eliza-
-beth Eliza. A beautiful day - cold.
Tuesday Another fine day. Bible class +
Jan 20 Chemistry as usual. Went to village
with Cassius Caius in P.M.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [02], 1883-1889
transcription:
Faculty meeting in the evening-
Spoke to Dr. Speakman about Miss
Noble's frequent absences.
Wed. 21. Classes as usual. Went skating from
4 till 5. Examination at 1:30. Written
lesson at 10:55. Printed prayer meeting
topics on hektograph between dinner and
silent time. Went to prayer meeting.
Looked over papers. loitered where Cassius
Caius + Miss Winfield were making O.
Letters from home + Dora Freeman
Thurs. 22 Cold. Finished correcting papers-
reclined on bed most of day-
Miss Noble came to see me. Studied
Bible lesson in evening- Could not go
with Miss Cooley to sewing society at
Mrs. Corran's as we had planned-
Miss Eaton met the 1:30 class and told
them to rewrite their examination papers.
Friday 23 Studied + taught Bible. Went not
to breakfast. Went to see Miss Corley
in afternoon + to prayer meeting in the

title: Marion Metcalf diary [02], 1883-1889
transcription:
Wrote letter to Annie-
village in the evening- Edith Wilkinson
brought her baby sister to see me
just before dinner. Letter from Annie-
Saturday A very busy day- Classes at 9:50
Jan 24 10:55, 1:30 (oxygen experiments)
and 4:00 (Chlorine experiments) -
Mr. Root appears to have come in vain
to see me at sometime this afternoon-
and left a nice book. I did not go to
dinner- the 10X1 Club met here this
evening and read "Laddie"- while
making pillowcases-
Snow, followed by rain-
Ethel Stanwood went home, sick-
Sunday Did not get up to breakfast- felt ray-
Jan. 25 -ther slim all day- Went not to
church- only to section meeting at
Stone Hall in the evening- Jo Peass
came to see me before dinner, as al-
-so did Amelia Hall and Nellie
Pendleton - and Elizabeth Eliza-
Read Missionary Herald in P.M.
Monday. Mended clothes- wrote to Dora Freeman,
Jan 26. 
Mr. Root, Pater + Nettie. Went to Reception

title: Marion Metcalf diary [02], 1883-1889
transcription:
this afternoon and really had quite a 
good time thereat- Rev. Harry A. Met-
-calf was there and was very agreeable.
Studied Chemistry and Quantitative
this evening while there was a Piano
Concert in the chapel-
Tues. 27. Classes as usual. Geography lesson
in Bible. Went to walk with Miss
Whiting and Miss Sumack. called
on Miss Wetherbee and Miss Worusreley
between dinner + silent time-
Wed. 28 Classes. Went to walk with Edith
Wilkinson- had lemon ice in evening
with Misses Knox, Aumack, Marsh, Dar-
-ling, Roberts + Grace Marsh- Went
to prayer meeting + teachers' prayer-
-meeting- Letter from Mr. Root.
Thurs. 29 Day of Prayer for Colleges- Dr
Meredith preached in the morning and
conversed in the afternoon. Miss
Talcott, of Kobe, Japan, and Miss Proctor
of Kessab, Turkey- spoke at the pray-
-ermeeting this evening- Went to see

title: Marion Metcalf diary [02], 1883-1889
transcription:
Solomon John and went to walk
with him- Had orange ice with
Miss Knox and Cassius-
Wrote to Annie-
Friday Studied and taught Bible. Went
Jan 30 down to Stone Hall in P.M. Walk-
-ed a little with Miss Home. Met
Miss Fisher of Elyna with Miss Ful-
-ler and a friend of hers- and was
with them until dinnertime-
Went to prayermeeting in the
village- accompanied by Emma
Shaw- At 9 there was a party
in No. 102- at which Miss Knox
and Cassius appeared arrayed
in fine feathers- Swept room -
Saturday Dusted room - taught
Jan. 31 classes- did Quantitative
experiment - mended clothes
wrote letter to Mr. Root - 2 letters
from home this morning and two
more this evening - including one
of Dismission from the Church and a
funny one from Mayo-

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription: [front cover]

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
Jan 1 1883
Miss Mary Monroe of Oberlin, Ohio, late of Brazil, and still later, the delight of the elite of Washington circles will essay to receive her friends in the Reception Room from 4 to 10 P.M. and will be assisted by Dr. E. H. Jones, Misses Hawes, Chandler, Morgan, Foster, Shafer, Metcalf and Mrs. McCoy. Dr. E. H. Jones of Oxford, more recently of Cambridge assisted by the distinguished writer, Mrs. Anna Il. McCoy and a coterie of literary stars of the first magnitude among where we may mention Misses Foster, Morgan, Monroe, Hawes, Chandler, Shafer and Metcalf will be glad to receive her many friends in their vicinity at No. 1 Centre Sq. College Place, Wellesley, from 4 to 10 P.M.
Professor in Anne Eugenia Felicia Morgan of wide European reputation, will be in a state of receptivity for the good of proximate beings especially her own. From 4 to 10 P.M. in the salon adjacent to the parlor environment in fellowship with the following parties Mrs. McCoy, Dr. E. H. Jones, Misses Hawes, Foster, Chandler, Monroe, Shafer, and Metcalf.
Miss Harriet Hawes, well known among us as the guardian of pedagogical bibliography will close her classic alcove from 4 to 10 P.M. in order to receive her friends with Misses Morgan, Shafer, Chandler, Metcalf, Foster, Dr. E. H. Jones and Mrs. Anna Maria McCoy and Miss Monroe at the grand entrance to the Appian Way.
Professor Helen Almira Shafer, the constant factor in our delightful circle, will receive incalculable pleasure from the convergence of her friends near the north focus of the Palm ellipse from 4 to 10 P.M. Washington time. She will be assisted by a quaternion of friends, Miss Hawes and Morgan, Mrs. McCoy and Dr. E. H. Jones also by the well known

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
triad Misses Monroe, Chandler, and Metcalf, and the incomparable unit Miss Florence Foster, a relation of the Dr. Foster who went to Gloucester in a shower of rain"-We cannot help remarking that this distinguished combination our Professor is certainly no cipher.
Mrs. Anna Maria McCoy of Belvidere, whose recent literary productions have attracted the interest of young and old from the sounding shore of the Atlantic to the Golden Gate, from the cities of the Sandwich Islands to the palms of the Zulu Land and from Greenland's icy mountains to India's coral strand will hold a coversazione at Abbotsford, Sir Walter Scott being present on a bust, Dr. E. H. Jones, the distinguished homeopathist in attendance - Mrs. McCoy will be assisted by her circle of close friends Misses Shafer, Chandler, Monroe, Foster, Hanes, Morgan and Metcalf.
Miss Eva Chandler, the fair resident of Diamond Cottage, who is spending the gay holiday season in our midst has consorted within a circumscribed sphere to radiate the infinite witcheries of her youthful charms on all who come within the zone of her attraction. Though attracted to many other points she has finally decided to receive at the same locus and temples as Prof Shafer and her coefficients and exponents, Dr. E. H. Jones, Mrs. A.M. McCoy, Misses Hawes, Metcalf, Monroe, Foster and Morgan.
Miss Marion Metcalf, B. A. N20, who has recently arrived from Waban Hall is also spending the holiday season in our city, her old home, and will be glad to remember affinities here. The addition of such an element to the constituents of our society will set in motion our social molecules and precipitate some of them at her feet. She prefers to receive her friends in

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
her old haunt, the reception room of Wellesley College, from 4 to 10 P.M. where she will be assisted
by Misses Chandler, Hawes, Monroe and Foster, Profs. Helen Almira Shafer, and Annie Eugenia Felicia Morgan, Dr. E.H. Jones and Mrs. Anna Maria McCoy -
This reception, with the preparations for it, occupied most of the day - A box from home arrived at night, containing this book, among other things - especially a box of butter scotch.
We had a little watch meeting in the reception room Sunday evening from 11:30 - 12:10.
Jan. 2 - Another bright, beautiful day. Miss Chandler and I put No. 102 in order, preparatory to leaving to leaving it. Carrie Cummings arrived at 2:43. I went to see Miss Hattie Townshend and Marion Sheldon at the village school. Marion Marsh returned. I wrote letters to Annie, Karl and Harry - received letters from Annie and Alice Leonard. card from Cora Harlow. Emily Murdoch stays with me tonight in No. 102.
Jan. 3. Fine weather still. Lottie came back this morning. We finished our gifts for the domestic workers and hung them on their doorknobs. Studied some in the Cl compounds. wrote to Alice Leonard. Went to prayer meeting in the village in the evening - At Waban Cottage again - nearly all the family back, and in good spirits. Rec'd an Etiquette Book from the Department - also "Choice of Books" and two soap images. Miss Emerson returned tonight.
(on left margin) Read from the morning Chronicle at breakfast or the morning of Jan. 1. 1883. received with loud applause.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
Jan. 4. Fair Weather. Cold. Ben. F. Butler was inaugurated Gov. of Mass. made a very long address. College opened. girls nearly all back.
Went to sewing society at Mrs. Shattuck's and had a very good time. rode home with some South Natick people, reaching here about ten oclock. The lady who brought me home is Mr. Edwards' daughter. Received a letter from Pater this morning. Prof. Niles gave his first Lecture at the College this evening.
Jan. 5. Snow. Taught three classes today and began my Qualitative Analysis work. Attended Prof. Niles' Geology lecture in the evening. Miss Chandler and I did not read Oliver Twist together at 2:05 as we had planned to letters. Read 'Scientific Philanthropy' and 'Gospel of Recreation' in Popular Science Monthly. We took the Etiquette Book to the lunch table and endeavored to follow its directions.
Jan. 6. Snow all day. After 9:50 class, went to Boston to Annual Meeting of Intercollegiate Alumnae Association, at the Vendome - a pleasant meeting and a good lunch. Left there soon after 2:00, a went to see Edith at 170 W. Brookshire St. found her well and enjoyed a visit with her. Came out on the 6:30 train. Dean Huntington, of Boston University, who preaches at the College tomorrow, rode up in the coach with me. May Ellis arrived this afternoon. 
Jan. 7.  Sunday - Snow has stopped. Clear towards night. and warmer. Mr. Cowan's text was I Tim. 2.5. "One mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus." My five boys were all at Sunday School. The third Sunday that Will Tailby has been present. "L[[ouie?]] H[[u?]]ig" seemed quite interested. Miss Hodgkins was here to dinner and talked of her own and Delia Lyman's European experiences. Spent most of the evening singing hymns with May Ellis and Cora Harlow.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
Jan. 8. Monday. Clear and warm. Sent off letters to Pater, Ralph, Ethel and Nettie, Reed letter from Annie and Temperance Leaflet from Miss Guernsey. Spent most of the day at work in the Qualitative Analysis Laboratory doing four unknowns. Concert this evening by the Boston Glee Club, assisted by two ladies and one Baritone. I enjoyed the concert very much as a whole, though the Soprano squealed and wore a very marvelous costume, of blue silk, pink silk and black velvet, not to mention pink artificial flowers. Lizzie Wallace is sick today.
Jan. 9. Colder. A Tuesday like other Tuesdays, hard. M. Marsh and I got out the things for the Cl Experiments this morning. I attempted to give my 10:55 class a thunder and lightning quiz, and found out that they did not know anything, so to speak. We tried to make Prussian blue with various Mn compounds after3:45. Went up to the College this evening for gymnastic appointment and afterwards to prayer meeting. Went to bed very soon after 9 oclock.
Jan. 10. Snow Blow 6 degrees below 0. Drifts. Addie Emerson and Carrie Wheeler both married today. Four letters this morning. From Annie, John, Pater &c, Marie Olmsted (acknowledging Christmas card) - also invitation to Mr and Mrs Horton's golden wedding, next Tuesday. We missed the first coach this morning - rode to the depot & had to wait until the 8:25 coach, losing chapel. I rode down tonight also. 3 classes today and practised Electrolysis of HCL. Wrote a letter to Jack this evening. Annie is elected for Latin Oration for Junior Ex. Three cheers!.
Jan. 11. Thurs. Clear and not very cold. Taught classes this morning- quizzes on H1H2O and H2O2 - as severe as possible. spent the afternoon in practicing the Cl experiments, without a very large measure of success, but with an abundance of suffocation. Mr. Peloubet gave a talk this evening, instead of the regular prayer meeting. After it went to Prof. Niles' lecture. No letters today. Mary Beattie's friend, Miss Potter, arrived at the College today. I have not yet seen her. 
Jan. 12. Friday. Cold. We performed the Chlorine experiments today, at 10:55 and 2:55. They were quite successful, but rather suffocating & the room was very cold. Went to prayer meeting.
Brought up my new waist from Miss Townshend's this P.M.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
Mrs. Joseph Cork spoke in the chapel at 2:05. I could not go being occupied with Cl. Subject. Pompeii and Athens re. At the College but lost Prof. Niles' lecture through carelessness thinking it was at 8 instead of 7:20. 
Jan. 13. Wind. Snow Drifts- 8 degrees below 0 in the morning. thawing rapidly and raining in the evening. 
Cl again at 11:45 - M. Marsh taught this division and I assisted. The room was close and warm. Did qualitative analysis laboratory work in the P.M. Led the prayer meeting at the College, and went down alone to that in the village- after which I spent some time in May Ellis' room. It is thawing & raining. January thaw. The drifts between here & the College were quite serious. I went to the greenhouse this morning for flowers to bleach, as he said, two beautiful camellias. He says they have succeeded in making fragrant ones in France. 
Sunday- Jan. 14 January thaw, Freezing towards night.
A theologue from Newton preached at the College today - I did not go to church, but tried to sleep instead. Went to Sunday School and to U.C.C. meeting in the afternoon. They did not come for me to go to Charles River Village. We have had a sing this evening from Gospel Hymns. One of the boys in my Sunday School Class,  Will Wills, is a Christian. 
Monday Jan. 15 Swept in the morning and had a call from Miss Darling and Stella Stickney. Spent about four hours on my Chemistry paper, and went up to the College in the afternoon. Prayer meeting in the village in the evening. Prof. Leotsakos, of the University of Athens, Greece, gave an illustrated lecture at the College. Letters from Annie and Flo today. 
Tuesday. 16. Slippery.  Usual work at the College. Went to Miss Hill to be measured &c at 10:30. Also at 2:05 to learn hour to use chestweights rowing machine &c for back and arms. Lottie came down here to dinner and we went together to the Golden Wedding. It was very pleasant indeed. Mr and Mrs Horton are lovely old people. Miss Horton was not there- she is with a sick friend, Mr. John Horton was there. The presents were very pretty. Much gold money. There were some interesting exercises and very nice refreshments. Back at the Cottage at ten oclock.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
Wednesday Jan 17. Classes as usual. Went to the depot with Lottie, also to the post office where she obtained a registered parcel. Went to prayer meeting in the village in the evening in a pouring rain, the remains of a beautiful afternoon snowstorm.
Letters from Lorne and from Annie-
Thursday Jan. 18. Taught classes, did laboratory work for Qual. Anal - practiced experiments. H A Fountain, K CLA's fireworks &c- Read Wagner's Chemical Technology-and the Christian Union's remarks upon Joseph Cook's first lecture. In the evening, went up to prayer meeting, where Miss Krebs told something about the terrible suffering from floods in her sister's town - afterwards, to Prof Niles' lecture Now I shall take a bath and go to bed. No time
yet to practices with the chestweights - No letters -
Friday -19. Snowstorm. HCl Fountain in class today - not a perfect success - Did Qual Anal. work. Went to Mrs. Dana's to tea, with Emily Clark and Carrie Cooke. Miss Lord could not go on account of "meeting of Heads". Mr. Dana came for us, and his man brought us back, in a sleigh- I missed Prof. Niles' lecture by going to Mrs. Dana's-
Saturday, 20. Rain in the evening, freezing as it fell - Taught class, tutored Miss Wardlaw- attended M. Marsh's class. We all went to lunch together. Worked in Lab. with M. Marsh - did not have good success. Went to the College in the evening to write the absences and study the Sunday School lesson. Beetho[[?]]e Soc. were having a meeting. The door was open and I heard Miss Trumbull sing twice - Took from the Library "Adventures of a Am. Consul Abroad," by Luigi Monte - After return to the Cottage, read the Tribune and made some equations in Qual Anal- Letter from Alice Leonard came this morning-
Sunday, 21 Thawing in A. M. Freezing again in P. M. Slippery and wet- A very good Sunday, though disagreeable weather and very bad walking- Church, Sunday School, and two meetings in the evening- all good- Joined the U.C.C. in the village- Read Congregationalists, Gospel in All Lands &c. in the afternoon. Had a short sing in evening after my return from prayermeeting. Mr. Smith walked up here with me. Pauline and Harry were at meeting also-

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
Monday. 22. A beautiful, cold, slippery day. Went to College in the morning and did my Qual. Anal. unknowns. Called at the farmhouse on my way back. Kitty Jones and her mother were here to dinner. This afternoon and evening I have spent on the bed. Finished Martin Chuzzlewit, read "Adventures of A Consul Abroad," by Luigi Monti, and studied my Chemistry Lesson more or less. Letter from Annie this morning.
Tuesday. 23. Did not get up to breakfast, nor go to chapel, but did hear all my classes today, besides going to Qual. Anal. class. Finished letter to Annie and made up equations for my unknown substances. I am getting behind in the Chemistry classes. I went across the lake twice today, and did not slip down. 
Wednesday. Went to lunch early with Lottie. did Laboratory work. acid tests in Qual. Anal. Had pretty fireworks in the 1:15 and 2:55 classes. The children have struggled terribly over the problems given out yesterday. Went to the village with Minnie Wiggin, and paid my debts. Went to prayer meeting at College in the evening, stopping on the way to see Miss Stratton and Miss Patterson, whom I did not find at home. Spent the rest of the evening, after coming down, in looking the Chemistry problems handed in. Took John Halifax from the Library.
Thursday.25. Day of Prayer for Colleges. Sermon by Dr. Alexander Mackenzie Cambridge. Text "Not by weight, nor by [[power?]], but by my Spirit, saith the Lord of Hosts." We may have the Spirit by welcoming Him, and letting Him have His own way, yielding to His leadings always. At the evening meeting Dr. Mackenzie talked about the young ruler who came to Christ and was told to go and sell all that he had and give to the poor. The point is that we must do whatever He commands. There was a meeting at seven to talk over plans for a Reading Club or some such thing, among the factory girls at South Natick. A social meeting has been appointed for Saturday night, in a room which Mr. Edwards offers us. Wrote letters to Jo Cass and Miss Mary Hosford.

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
the Board of Visitors, on Mineralogy- and sup-
-posed he was coming to Lottie's class when he
came to mine- Spent some time in looking
up scientific items for our meeting. After
dinner, went up to prayermeeting, Stopping
on the way to carry some birthday cake to
Miss Chandler and Miss Cummings- I led
the prayermeeting- Went to Hattie's Pierce's
lecture on Sun - Lit -at four- Postal from
Annie Capron, thanking me for the questions I
answered for her about printing of Class History-
Friday. 4. Classes as usual. This afternoon a new organization
was formed in No. 144. The Royal Geographical Soc. or
the Red Indian Geog. Soc. Present membership - Misses
Roberts, Kendall, March. Alice Hazeltine and Metcalf
meetings to be held Wednesdays at 8:45 A.M. and Fridays at
4- P.M. Greek Play of Electra at Jacob Sleeper Hall to-
-night by Boston Univ. students. We were offered tickets
ot at least admittance but did not go-
Saturday 5 Taught class. studied Geography. Received invitation
to wedding of Lee Twiss and Waldo Shepard.
Reading of Twelfth Night by Prof. Raymond of Bos-
-ton School of Oratory- did not like him as well as
I had expected to. Maggie Hell's friend Miss Deton
has come to stay on Sunday with her. Brushed
up and dusted my room-
Sunday-6 Cloudy and cool in A.M. Clear in P.M. Went to Ch
with Lottie Roberts- Louis Eade was at Sunday
School. I told Mr. Stevens that I thought I must
give up my class. Mr. and Mrs. Clark from the
village, came up to take Miss Hill and Miss Dunton
to ride, but, on account of my representations,
they did not go- Miss Eusiger is here with Jen-
-nette Carpenter- Went to meetings in P.M.
Read Memoirs of Old Bull, and a little in Duties
of Women, which latter is rather disappointing to
me, I fear -am quite tired and will go to bed early-

title: Marion Metcalf diary [01], 1883-1889
transcription:
30
Monday May 7- Letters from Annie and Edith. Wrote to the family and
to Jack, also sent Ethel's letter to Jennie Bullock.
Made a few Chemistry questions. Walked to Cochituate
and back in the P.M. with Miss Kendall. and found
a little Asbestos. Lake Cochituate is a very beauti-
-ful place. We must have a picnic here sometime.
Came back, pretty tired, had a late supper, by kind-
-ness of Miss Dennison and some of the girls, then
went to Horace E. Scudder's lecture on Childhood before 
and after Christ. Was too tired to enjoy it much-
took the coach home. Mrs. Durant was in the coach
part of the time and talked to me very pleasantly.
Tuesday-8- Letters from Annie + John, with accounts of the Junior
Ex. wrote to Annie. R.I.Geog.Soc. met at 4:30 or
even and considered the U.S. I staid to dinner
at the College, then went boatriding with the girls to
the cottage, and a young man who was with them
from Princeton.
Wednesday Not very well today. Marion March quizzed my 2:55
class on O, O3 + CO2. Had no letters, but received the Oberlin
Jubilee Notes. Went in evening to a rehearsal at South
atick of the Entertainment to be given by the Satur-
-day Night Club tomorrow night. Mr. Bailey is very
kind to us. Returned about 9:45 and sat up till
11:15 finishing my examination questions.
Thursday Classes in A.M. Qual.Anal.in P.M. Studied Geography some-
read paper. The French Deputation now in the country on
behalf of the McAll Mission spoke at W.C. this P.M. Was
Berger,Sec. Mr. Sailleus and Mr. Greig. They were very
interesting, especially Mr. Sailleus. I have in some way
taken a bad cold. Am hoarse and have sore throat. Am ta-
-king some of Dr. Jones' pills- Alice Dow gave me some
KCCl3+ Maggie Hill gave me some honey-
Friday- 11 Have been quite hoarse all day, but managed to teach my three
classes. The R.I.G.S. met at 4 P.M. The bad Miss Kendall being
absent, cause unknown. Letter from Flo - sent postal to
Edith. Went to Entertainment of Saturday Night Club in

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [6], 1844-1865
transcription:
Foxcroft Dec 18th 1846
Dear Friend Sir -
I hardly know how I may commence a letter to you. So long a time has elapsed since I received you last and as you may know very welcome letter, that I fear you will not forgive my long delay to answer it.
I have as usual many very good excuses yet I fear they are scearcely sufficient to justify me in delaying to answer a letter from a friend.
I beleive I have been hitherto nearly, perhaps I ought to say quite, as punctual in answering your letters, as you have been in replying to mine.
Therefore as this is the first time that I have really neglected to answer your letters, as you were not always prompt, do you not think you ought justly to pardon me? I will give you my excuse

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [6], 1844-1865
transcription:
although I fear it will be of little use to me, and then leave the subject to your mature judgment to decide, whether I may be forgiven or not.
Since I received your last letter most of my time which I generally devote to writing, has been spent either in making or attending parties, therefore I have had little time to write to my friends - I suppose you would say that my time had been very badly spent.
I cannot say that I enjoy myself much in such large assemblies, neither, do I think them beneficial.
I have attended several large parties, and I am quite tired, and disgusted with them. The first thing that is introduced after the company are assembled is a play which is generally termed [[?]], I beleive, or some other play and, is kept in action during the evening - For little children such amusement will do very well, but for yong gentlemen & ladies to spend their time in such a manner I think it is I had almost said, wicked, at least permit me to say wrong. Forgiv me if I am to severe, perhaps I have said too much! I was much surprised to hear that you had concluded to spend the fall in Topsham instead of Turner. I should think from your description that you have a very pleasant situation, but yet, should have judged that you would have prefered to have gone to Turner. I beleive you wrote me that you liked the people in Turner very well and had a very pleasant school and some very interesting scholars. My cousin Freland is now teaching
[text continues on side of page]
For your kind words in your [[?]]dis[[?]] please to accept my most sincere thanks and in return, may you be attended withe same degree of prosperity which has accompanied you thus far, may your most fond anticipation be realized is

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [6], 1844-1865
transcription:
in this town. He has a very pleasant school but rather
short, but I believe he complains that it is too long,
a general complaint among teachers I think.
Your friend Mr Clark has returned home I have
understood, and is teaching the school in Dover
Village- Mr Tash has quite a full school this
term about 30 scholars I believe. I have not commenced
to go to school yet, but think of going soon.
Your sister Lucy has been in Foxcroft this fall
I have been told. I did not see her or at least did not
know her if I saw her. She was here at the time
of the dedication of the Masonic [[?]] Sons of Temperance
Hall. Mary saw her and spoke with her.  I have not
seen Lucy since the spring we attended school together
and I have grown so tall since, that I suppose she
would not have known me if she had seen me.
Speaking of attending school with your sister
reminds me that you have, or once had two pieces of
paper, called "compositions" that once belonged to me.
I really wish you would destroy if you ever again
meet with them; if they are worth keeping I would
be willing that you should retain them in your possession,
but as they are not, I think it would be better
to destroy them, do you not think me to be wright?
You asked me if I thought the "Count" would ever go
to college, really: I cannot say that I think he ought
to but rather that he feels competent. He likes music
much and may conclude to prepare to give lessons
in music, there will then be a chance for you to learn
if you wish to, if he comes to Brunswick to teach.
the wish of your friend, Sarah.
Hoping you will forgive my delay without imitating my negligence. I will close my letter, you will think I have not much order if I
write further. If you please I shall be hoping to hear 
from you again soon. As ever I remain your friend,
Sarah E. Homes

My school closes tomorrow

Officiating in a large, village

to go, is enough to wear out the soul
of a saint and the body of Hercules.
I hope the Lord will grant me better

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Brunswick June 29th, 44
Friend Metcalf.
I suppose you will not feel particularly rejoiced to learn that I have taken up my pen for the ostensible and avowed purpose of writing you a long an borous letter. Do not tremble. I recd your letter in due time. There is nothing so pleasing as to received good full letter from a friend. I do not know as my letters are so acceptable to others, but theirs are to me, and as I can get them by no other means than to write I do it. I have been walking this evening: it is very pleasant: the moon shines brightly. I must confess that I feel rather sentimental to night Metcalf. I beleive you never feel very much so: at any rate I should judge so by your last, I shall take your letter up in course and write a review of it; I am very much interested in your letters whether you are a letter writer or not. They seem full of the generosity of spirit and soul. It seems like sitting together upon the end of a sofa resting our heads upon each other's shoulder, pouring real thought and secret feelings, without fear of disclosure and in confidence, telling our stories of love and danger, and all our scrapes; that you rather let out my confessions where you let those fair ones read that letter. But I will forgive you this time. What pleasure is there in talking with some stiff old fellow on some stiff and dry subject? When you cannot pour forth your whole heart. You will find students here free and willing to converse. I can not help remarking the beauty of the evening, Metcalf, I should like to walk round the "square" to night with some "fair" red haired maiden of Foxcroft or some black haired one. All have their preferences. And I am not an exception to that rule, I think you are not. Who knows but that at this very moment while I write this line you are looking over the railing of the bridge pretending to look at the waters below? But Ah! where are your thoughts? On that fair one by your side. Metcalf I seem to see you blush. I have done the same thing, or things as bad. But Ah tis happiness, tis life. You will think I am smashed. You are mistaken. to be sure have felt a little curious time and again in my life but it soon over. I was happy behind the curtains that night. And those times are past. There are no such chances here. I have been introduced to but one young lady since I came from home, I do not wish to be to any more. They are tremendous homely in this place. But few students have any thing to do with

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
the ladies of town and those force themselves into company. Stevens may be called one of them but he does not succeed very well. He is rather soft in some of his actions: He went to Augusta and scraped an acquaintance with some of Rice's cousins without an invitation: he is going again on the Fourth. But I will not say any thing against Stevens, although he is not very popular in College, he has not had an election to either of the secret societies. I would never have joined the Atheneau Soc. if all had been like Stevens he is very overbearing. I roomed with him last term but do not now, and never shall again. He is very quick of temper. I think that he will try to get the school at Foxcroft, when he graduates: The Trustees do not know what he is. Almost every one thinks that he is a prime scholar down at Foxcroft. They (the Trustees) ought to know all about it for he will make the attempt and he would ruin the school. He will be at home in the fall and deliver lectures on Grammar. A fine lecturer he will make. He brags a great deal of his scholarship but I have seen him [[rawed?]] up several times by Rice and Kilby on points of Gram.
There is on thing of which I wish to speak you must not let him know that I spoke of it. He is practising deceit upon Miss Dennett which is too bad. For him to have one or two girls in town six or seven others somewher else and Miss Dennett in Milo and being on so serious terms with her as I know him to be, is not right. He cannot live without he has a dozen or sixteen girls here and there with whom he must correspond: He is trying to such her in in order that she may be his plaything when he is in Milo and Rice's cousins when he is in Augusta. I have nothing against Collins myself. We are on first rate terms but folks down here are very much mistaken about him and he will attempt to "come the game" over them yet. He feels nicely because Tash and Jerusha are likely to make a bargain. As I said Stevens be at home in September I suppose and Also Rice will study at Foxcroft this fall I expect. He will read Horace, I suppose, as we shall only read Excerpts this summer. You can easily make that up in the fall. I will send you book by Rice if you would like. We are reading Horace now (the Iliad) about 25 lines at a lesson: is is easy In the morning we read a page of Excerpt and have a lesson in Hedges Logick which is pretty hard. We shall finish the Algebra this term. We review regularly every week. We have exercises in Elocution three times a week For text book we use Comstocks System of Elocution

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
which is a late work and said to be far superior to any other. It ought to be introduced at Foxcroft. It is of far more importance than I thought, But I should advise to introduce. that at Foxcroft Academy and more pains ought to be taken with it. Tutor Boody has the charge of that department. The principle consists in strengthening the organs of speech by constant or frequent and violent practice and uttering the vowels sounds in a clear and distinct manner and also the consonants by a violent action of those organs which are used in coughing and also in giving the inflections which rules are entirely different from those laid down in Porters Retorical Reader. I should advise you to obtain a coppy of it. It will be of great assistance to you in declaring 
I am glad you are not so lazy that you will not hold the plough: and I am extremely glad your mother sent you back to school, for I wish to have you come here and then we will have first rate times. But if you do not wish to remain here in the fall term I would not advise you to come here for the sake of being examined, as it wou cost you about fifteen dollars, and would do no particular good. besides it will answer just as well if you come her in the spring to be examined then
[[I?]] Rice is there in the fall you may have rather pleasant times. But it will never do for me. Alas the Girls! they have wasted many an hour for me which might have been spent to better advantage: but they will never get the chance again according to my humble beleif. Recolect do not stop out in the entry a few minutes after the bell rings. if you do you will wish to stop an hour the next day with the fair charmers. I would not advise you to study more than six or seven hours per day or eight at the most. but then study. The best scholars do so here, by all means study those grammars thoroughly, that is the thing that makes a linguist.
I am glad to see that you have such a fine school. Hope you will make the best of it. And now sir to come to the point how do you think it looks for you to ask me the meaning of "smashed" "Technical terms." "Who is it" are you crazy Metcalf. Look at some fair maiden and you will find out the meaning, I presume my ideas in my last were not quite so clear as yours are you being in habit of thinking on that subject more than I do. But my letter meant something about the girls. I am at loss to know what you mean by the terms "smashed "broken" "cracked" in the sense in which you use them in

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
your last. You acknowledge that you felt a little queer once when you were a smaller boy. could you not have well said twice when you were a large boy? "You guess you never told any one." I guess you had better guess a little straighter. As regards "some pretty little girl" that does mean a good many in particular.
I see that you are a little romantic owing to your ride to [[Monson?]]. I do not blame you. Enjoy yourself while you can I say. I must close. Write soon. fill your letter first with news. then with sentiment and then with nonsense. Give my respects to all. Rice sends his respects. And I remain your freind J. G. Clark.
J. G. Clark

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Enfield Aug 6th, 1844.
Dear Friend
I was very happy in receiving your letter of the 10th Ult. which was duly received, but as I have been very busily engaged I have not found time to acknowledge the receit of it. It is ever pleasant to correspond with friends: it awakens those feelings of love and sympathy which would otherwise slumber within our breasts.
I have been engaged this season as usual, in farming, lumbering &c. I agree with you in thinking active employment the most natural, healthy, and pleasant occupation for man. When employed with our hands in labor we may have our thoughts placed on God, the source from which all our blessings flow. We have an unusually cool summer: vegetation, however, looks very well. The hay crop comes in very plentifully. You wrote that you thought of leaving school awhile, and go at the pleasant business of haying. You did not say where you was going at work, but I suppose at home, and shall therefore direct this letter to Milo

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Haying will soon be over and you will return to your studies. I do not expect to enjoy the pleasure of attending school this fall, but shall endeavor to visit Foxcroft, sometime during the fall, and hope to see you there. Politics do not excite a very great interest in these parts. I think the contest will not be so great as it was in -40. There is, however, some interest felt. We expect a meeting of the friends of Clay here sometime near the last of this month. The Hon George Evans is expected to address the meeting on that occasion. I am opposed to slavery in any form, but as I beleive without doubt that Clay or Polk will be our next president, and as I like the principles of Clay much better than those of Polk, I prefer him. If Polk should be elected Texas would, doubless, be immediately annexed which would add a large slave holding territory to the union This I think would give the slave holders a majority, and would be more injurious to the welfare of the slaves than having Henry Clay for president.
On the whole I think I shall go for Clay 
Please write again soon
Respectfully Yours
E H Great
I S Metcalf

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Levant, August 15th
Friend Metcalf -
You left Foxcroft a little sooner than I expected; but perhaps no sooner than your own intention. The school closed on Friday noon, after a tedious examination, at which no one was present, save about a dozen students. I started for home on Saturday, at 7 o'clock A.M., on foot, and arrived at 3 P.M. - pretty well tired out I assure you. I have worked at haying two days, - and studied a little. Our folks finished haying yesterday; so I have nothing to do now but to review the Greek Reader, Cicero, Sallust, Virgil, &c. &c.!! - a small job, you know.
According to our arrangements, I have concluded to go to Commencement with you, and offer myself for admission to "Old Bowdoin"; if they choose to accept me, well and good - if not, there ends my efforts for literary fame. - I shall return to the plough, and end my days as a yankee farmer. Our plan you know, was, to take the Boat at Bangor on Monday morning, go to Portland, and walk thence to Brunswick. I shall either do that, or go to Thomaston on the Thursday before and meet you there on board the steamer, on Monday. I want to make a short visit at T., and perhaps I shall not have a more convenient opportunity. I suppose you will go to Bangor on Saturday; if so, I want you to call at our house on the way - If I do not go to Thn. I shall wait for you, at home - (I don't mean at your home: - I am such a Paddy I can't tell my meaning the first time.) I see no reason why we may not have a very interesting time at Brunswick - the journey will undoubtedly be pleasant and profitable - not in the

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
matter of cash, but in the "feast of reason" which we shall enjoy; and perchance it may have a tendency to remove a moiety of the "greenness" that may yet cling ad corporatua - give me credit for the Latin -
Mr. Tash passed through Levant on Sunday last, in his way to the city, but I did not see him. He sent up by Tuesday's mail, some documents for us - one for you to Professor Smyth - one for me to Prof. Packard. I will take yours with me, should I start before you, or leave it, as you may direct.
I don't know how far Mr. Tash 'brand' goes at Bowdoin: I presume we shall be obliged to undergo re-inspection, befor we can "pass muster," and call ourselves the matriculated sons of "Old Bowdoin" -
Perhaps you may see Smart during the vacation; if so, you must try to pursuade him to return to Foxcroft and prepare to enter college in the spring.
I wish you to write soon after the receipt of this, and say whether the plans proposed will be convenient for you - If not, propose others -
Yours Truly
Isaac W. Case
PS
Give my best respects to Miss Dennett, when you see her

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Foxcroft, October 23d, '44
Friend Metcalf, -
I received your very acceptable letter, accompanied by a bundle of catalogues, last night, for which you will please accept my thanks.
I am glad to hear that you are so well settled, so contented and happy - and only wish that I could be with you; for, though I am pleasantly situated here, I should much prefer being at Brunswick. - You wish me to give you an account of matters and things at Foxcroft - Well, in the first place, we have a fine school, numbering, all told, about 110, great and small, male and female. - They are about equally divided with regard to sex. Of those who attended in the summer there are Misses Foss, Holmes, Farnham, Edes, &c. Miss Tash attended about half of the term, then returned to N.H. on account of the decease of her mother.
Of the males there are Oakes, Stephens, Johnston, Smart Clement & Case. We have a Literary Society, called "The Students' Association," which holds its meetings on Wednesday evenings, at which times all the genius, talent, spirit and eloquence of the school are displayed in the discussion of the great questions that are agitating the Nation at the present day. Among these are the "Annexation of Texas," the "Tariff," the "Abolition of flogging in common schools," the "relative influence of the sexes," &c. &c. - important questions you

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
must acknowledge!! On the question of "Annexation," the disputants were Oakes & Greely, in favor, Clement and Case, against. The question was decided - friget me dicere, on account of the school being exceedingly loco-focoish, and by the assistance of the ladies, in favor of Annexation! - "O! Tempora! O! Mores" - O! Temperance! O! Moses! The question of the Tariff was discussed by Smart & Clement in favor, Oakes & Gray against. It was decided in favor of the anti-protectionists by a majority of one vote. Besides the discussions, we have quite a number of declamations at our meetings, and a "Paper," conducted by the Ladies, for which there have been, thus far, no contributions! - but that it the fun of it, I suppose. 
Thus much for the Students' Association, a society certainly not quite equal to your "Peucinian," and "Athenaean, "yet a society by no means to be "grinned at." 
I don't think of much else connected with the school that will be interesting to you - I might add though that Mr. Tucker occupies your place, as 'Assistant,' so far as he is needed. He hears only two or three classes, I believe. Smart and I are getting along pretty well in our "college course" - We shall finish the second book of the "Anabasis" to-morrow, which is all that is required the first term, I believe. We shall read no other Greek this term, as we did not receive the "Memorabilia" till we had nearly finished the portion of the Anabasis that we were to read. We read about two pages per day in Livy, and shall finish the 2nd book next week We shall then have three weeks for review - We were not expecting

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
to go over more than 6. Sections in Algebra, but shall now have to put on a little harder in order to keep pace with the class - By the way, I should like to know the object in driving Algebra so - In addition to the college studies, I have the remainder of the preparatory course to make up - I am now reading the "Georgics," which I shall finish this week. The Greek Testament I shall not trouble this term; but if convenient, shall probably read some in it during the winter - it not convenient, I shall trust to the "inspiration" of the moment when I come to be examined. At any rate I have little fear of failure on that score, unless the examination should be worse than the other, on that part - I believe each read one verse of the Latin, which answered all practical purposes - I shall not take advantage of that course, however - You need not inform Professor Upham of this though!! - 
You Sophs. seem to have a great antipathy to the old Chapel. I hope it will not be entirely demolished till another shall be erected - I would seem that some of the Freshmen are a little green - according to the Sophomoric notions - now, making all reasonable allowance for the medium through which you, as a Sophomore, would look upon them, perhaps we must acknowledge that there may be a shade of the green, but I presume it will wear away before another term - and then you will have to beware how you [[crowed?]] bah!
Now, Friend Metcalf, I have nearly filled my sheet with just such matters as first occurred to my mind; whether It will be in the least interesting to you I do not know - be assured yours was to me, and I hope you will again lay me under obligation for another favor of the same kind - and rest assured it shall not long go unanswered -
Yours Truly
Isaac W. Case

I have some doubt whether he will do so though.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Foxcroft, Nov. 30th 1844.
Dear Sir
Your letter was received and with true pleasure. If your former letter was unexpected the latter truly was; for I had come to the conclusion that you had seen a sample of my letter-writing, and thought me a worthless correspondent, as indeed I think I am.
Yet as you have taken the trouble to write to me again, I will try to pen something (though in my inelegant style) in return. The account you gave me in your last of the College and the proceedings there was welcomed truly. I am glad to learn that you like so well, but am sorry that J. G. C is in no better a way. He has, I understand returned home, accompanied by his Mother, and is agoing to teach our school this winter.) I like system, too, and think the ringing of the bell an excelent plan, particularly at dawn. Surely, when you said that 'one is sometimes almost disposed to rebel, especially if he happens to want to sleep a little longer in the morning', you could not mean so early a riser as Mr. I. S. Metcalf. Since my return from Enfield I have been at "Home," busily engaged (except when idle) in the various duties of a farmers daughter. I have not heard much about the school the past term. I was in one afternoon and heard quite a number of gentlemen declaim. For

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: instance, Charles Chandler, George Sawyer, and if I recollect rightly Mr James Bush. I then listened attentively while the themes were read; but did not hear the truly excelent piece of I. S. M. or the sweet production of his sister's Muse, nor yet friend Sarahs piece upon 'Order'. On the Friday after the close of the school, there was a Pic Nic at the Academy. There were about 70 present. I was there but did not enjoy myself at all. I certainly do not think there is much pleasure to be enjoyed in such parties at any time; and on that evening the death of a friend and schoolmate, Elizabeth Augusta Edes, made the scene a mournful one to me. I have not heard the particulars of Miss Edes sickness. Her health was not good last spring, and it has continued to decline until last Friday when she sweetly resigned her spirit to the God who gave it. She was, I believe, a true Christian and has gone to that blessed clime "where life is not a breath, where parting is unknown'. I mourn, but not for her. She enjoys the bless company of the redeemed around the throne. There, and in the anticipation of that 'Heavenly Home alone, can true happiness be found. If 'friendship is eternal; if, sometimes there is 'pure, disinterested friendship' formed on earth in the minds of those who are, through the merits of the Redeemer, anticipating a happier home in Heaven may we not hope to meet her again? This is indeed a glorious thought; a theme on which I love to dwell. If I am indeed a true Christian, I love to think of [[meeting?]] many beloved friends in a better world, where

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
friendship must be pure.
Sarah Holmes is at home and I see her every week. I believe she intends to attend Clarks school this winter. Miss Caverno has left; she does not think of returning again. I feel quite disappointed, for I fear they will not obtain a better instructress, or one who will be generally so well liked. Miss [[Treap?]] left on Saturday accompanied by Joseph and Sarah. She was my roomate last summer and we have been together so long that I feel quite lonely now that she has gone.
I am extremely gratified to hear that you are teaching this winter (or what will be Monday) and I am when I hear of any one who is. For I expect to teach, and there is some gratification in knowing that there are others who are engaged in the same employment, Who are placed in a room full of human natures, all looking to one for an approving smile or a frown. There are certainly many trials as well as pleasures experienced by those who teach, which others cannot fully appreciate. But I will haste to close this epistle which I fear is destitute of interest. I am glad to write for the pleasure of receiving, yet I fear my willingness will prove troublesome to you. I mentioned that I expected to teach this winter. I have a small school engaged, about two miles from home and commence in 2 weeks. I have taught the school one summer, and as I am acquainted with the most of the scholars I hope it will be an easy task compared with my school last summer.
With great respect,
Your friend,
Mary W. Tower
Mr. Issac S. Metcalf.

Bowd Coll Sep 30 1845
Friend Metcalf
Your letter of the twenty third came to hand yesterday on my return; was glad to hear of your success and that your are so well pleased: But I am sorry! sorry!! you were not here yourself; for the interest of [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon], as well as many other things. I thought you had abandoned the idea of going there this fall. but you are there, and I am here; came yesteday Monday; expected to have the pleasure of rooming with my new chum.  Well as I must be in a hurry since [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] meets at 8. this evening and I have a lesson in mechanics to get, I will just say I have taken up my quaters at 24 M. H. with S M Merrill pro tempore. He has things in good shape this term; a carpet &c. While I think of it Perry took 1' prize for themes, Rice 2d, Holt Knight & Crosly's are to be put in the Library. Not so bad for [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] as it might be!! Your ("Our s'il vous plait) furniture I have moved. I can sell the carpet for $7 or 7 1/2. Think I better sell. It will be dead money till spring if I do not.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
I would like to know your opinion as soon as you receive this epistle. Please send a paper the 1' mail after this comes to hand If I better sell write 'Carpet; yes': if not: write "Carpet, no"

We clapped him when he informed us mechanics we read over and [[Ferox?]] asks questions Have had but one lesson of 6 pages: Tomorrow morn, we go through pre. remarks. How then non possum dicere. German: well yesterday Prof. Goodwin gave us a lecture upon the sounds of the vowels: letters I mean. Today we had to answer questions as to the sounds & decline the dif. [[arb?]] [[?er]] the Tomorrow the pres & imp. tenses of the verbs to be & to have Juvenal about 50 lines at a lesson 7c I will write soon again & give you more information Did you buy Grover's curtains? if not would I better? My health pretty good Where do you teach this winter? I must go to the meeting, excuse all mistakes for I shall not review it Write again soon Dont forget to send the paper instanter

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Foxcroft Academy Oct. 11th 1845.
Friend Metcalf.
You must pardon my want of promptness in answering your kind letters knowing my labors as you do you will not fail to do so. I am ony happy to hear of you & of your prosperity. I think in Turner you must have a very pleasant school & must among ladies & Philosophy enjoy yourself finely. I wish you could have remained in College all the time for I am expecting from you an oration & have no doubt I shall have my expectations answered if you can be there most of the time.
I think so far as I hear most of our College boys are getting along finely - I am sorry to hear of Clark succeeding no better. A great pity he is inconsiderate. Rice is at home now, but I should think doing but little. - Mr Snow of Waterville had, I think from what he told me a few days since, concluded to commence the study of medicine without pursuing his College studies farther - Messrs Smart & Philbrick have started or are about to start for Kentucky, and so our students get scattered -
I presume if you could come into our school room now you would not recognise more than 1/4 of of the students We have now about 160 & the most regular & quiet school I ever had - Mr Holbrook who fills your old place is a very fine young man - has taught in Washington City & is a thoro' going Whig. I judge our school for this first

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
half term has averaged at least 140 scholars & we have now 10 music scholars but the Drawing class is very small - our classes in the Languages are very good & there are a larg proportion studying but the Philosophy & Astronomy & Algebra classes are not so good as sometimes. The Chemistry class is very good & large and the surveying class also - I have too a very large class in Bookkeeping - Miss Ca[[verno?]] has very large French classes -
Mr Harlow is not here this Term but I have a number of lads from Bangor & some of them rather wild such for example as Mr Maltby's son whom you possibly have heard of - I have them boarding with me - some 8 or 10 boys at Mr Stevens where we have some 15 boarders - His house he has made very commodious by the addition of another story &c - young Stevens is here [[?]] yet & I doubt whether he is ever better - I have the rheumatism in my right hip ever since vacation but it is now somewhat better - It has been very similar in kind to Stevens' but much more favorable in degree I doubt whether I get entirely free of it before spring but hope now to have but little more trouble from it. The Parson Parker has been quite unwell, arising from a fall his carriage. He has not preached for several Sabbaths & I am uncertain whether he will tomorrow - I [[?]] occasionally very favorable reports of your brothers in B. I have no one here to school from your town I believe I have quite a number from the Towns below near the river - I have a number from Ellsworth also and Orono - I think I may have a very good school for winter -

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
I should like to drop in & see your school & make you a short call if I had but Hassan's tapestry. Oh! our locomotion now notwithstanding steam & Electro M. is far inferior to what we would sometimes like & yet I presume we move about as much as moraly profitable - They have connected with the school a noble Lyceum & in it some very spirited debates. - The room is filled every evening to the overflowing - I have been in one evening & heard the subject of foreign emigration discussed - There was more debate than argument & there would be likely on that question -
Mond. Morn - Altho' rainy yesterday, we had two very good sermons from Mr Parker who looks rather paler than usual - He does not appear very well -
Metcalf have you any good potatoes up in your County? Oh they are horrid down here - not fit to be eaten & I miss them much more than I do the Ladies - I am a real Irishman on that point! But really I dont see what Maine is going to do without potatoes -
I had [[some?]] idea awhile since of going to E. Machias to teach in their Academy but conclude on the whole to stop here -  There school is entirely run down & they want to get some one likely to give it a start. I am not sure but they will remove it entirely from E. M. on account of the entire want of interest in the school in that place. They can give a very good salary & I think that far preferable to getting what one can catch. - But I must close this curious letter. It will make no difference where you commence to read it - Please let me hear from you soon - I remain your friend T. Tash
