Bowd. Coll Nov 15 '45
Bro Metcalf
You must pardon me for my delinquency and I will endeavor to do better for the future. Your writing me immediately on the reception of this will prove your disposition to do better than I have. I have not written because I have not commenced I know of no other reason. The exhibition came off Tuesday Evening 11' - a very good performance Edwards played - the eve'g was delightful - The salutatory by Pickard was superior to any thing of the kind performed here for some time. So they say!! He was much cheered in his performance. In speaking of the present Junior class he held this language Umbrae hominem (a laugh) While complimenting the ladies & speaking of their charms he turned round to Pres and said it is  not good for man to be along. It took well. There was a laugh at the old man's expense His face was soon suffused (covered) with blishes. Fred Sewall holds such language as this grand climacteric of the anti-psicological monomania! Big words for a little man
[cross writing:]
My address will be Bowdoinham and now Isaac write me as soon as you receive this & tell me where youll teach how much wages how long a school when you begin &c. &c. Send me papers often

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
The Juniors did credit to themselves at least they suffered nothing in comparison with the Seniors - There have been two very powerful rains here lately 13 inches as Prof. Cleav informs us. Has done but little damage  - carried off a part of one dam. Students a leaving fast some one or more daily. Baker today (& Newcomb) I go tomorrow Jordan yesterday &c. We are now reading Spanish. I like it because there is a precision in it, which we do not find in many if any of the other languages Par Example the vowels always have the same sound with only four exception The con's have the same sounds in the same situation We have three lesson in a week. As to German it is hard to say where we are reading. We have about two pages a day. We (the class) will read this term all the poetry as far as 211 page in the reader. We are also studying the [[sweet?]] Calculus, have got thro' first chapter, & shall advance one week longer. What we get in this is no part of the review - We shall read the 1, 3, 38, 11, 13 & 14 Satires. I do not think of any
[cross writing:]
I shall leave what things I have here now, using where they are till spring. They will safer here than in S. Coll [[for?]] [[?erril?]] [[stops?]] till the close of the term. I here [[enjoin?]] a secret and as a Bro of [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] you will not disclose. I think of writing for my own improvement a communication for the Forrester My signature is "Solon" and when you see any articles under this signature criticize them freely and

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
thing more on this point. I would say learn the declension of the nouns well in German. Learn the declension of the adj. also, for Prof. Goodwin drills us on this. You understand the rules for declension of adj's & nouns? If not you just write & I will lend you some aid.
Our prospects now in the [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] Society are better than when you were here. We have initiated 6 good fellows since you were here Jones Picard [[?]] Humphrey Hawkins Thomson & Harson I think we stand as good a chance now as any society in Coll. We had an anniversary party at Mr Jackson's last week. Nearly all of the society were there and some twenty of the fair sex. I wish you had been there. We were entertained with music vocal & instrumental (Piano) conversation and a collation. How the grapes vanished I am going home tomorrow My school will be 3 or 3 1/2 months, may not be here to first of the term I will leave the key at Prof Boody's room Yours in the bonds of [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]  S. W. Hatch

You can appreciate them or you would not avail yourself of the privilege My first is already out & I will send you a paper Friendship is the subject. There are faults in the punctuation tyographical faults. What are the most striking faults? are there any excellences Enough. Write I say S W H

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Levant, Dec. 24, 1845
Dear Brother Metcalf -
"Video, proboque meliora - Deteriora Sequor." - I acknowledge my error - I have been a very unworthy correspondent and deserve at least, all the reproach that you may in your wisdom pour on my devoted head. But I should have written to you ere this, had I known your "whereabouts." Your very acceptable letter of the 17th inst. was received yesterday, for which, as well as for other similar favors, you have my warmest thanks. I am glad to learn that you have got into another good place. Truly you are a "lucky fellow." You always get a good situation when you are teaching - find a pleasant home - an abundance of pretty girls - enough to eat of the best that the land affords; and finally, everything to your mind. What an enviable situation you occupied at Turner! - Teacher of the 'High School' - Junior in Bowdoin College, and holding a high rank as a Teacher. How I wish that I could get into a place where I could be looked up to with the respect due to Sophomore dignity! - where merit and 'science' are appreciated!! Alas! - such is not my lot. May I not in allusion to myself, with reason exclaim with old Anchises - "Heu, miserande puer! si qua fata aspera rumpas, tu Marcellus eris." As you are aware, I am again teaching "at home." I commenced my school on the Monday after

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Thanksgiving - have about sixty scholars, of all kinds - good, bad and indifferent - some, the very best - some, no better than they should be. I dont rule them with "a rod of iron," but with an article of not less virtue, - a long maple "ruler," and the way some of 'em have to take it is a caution to idlers. The school is much the same that it was last winter, and like most village schools it is rather noisy, and irregular. But I get along as well as I can, and have the prospects of my pay when I get through, which is a comfortable idea. I am not a teacher by profession, and could I get the same wages at almost any other business, I should not teach many more winter schools. I shall keep about eight weeks longer, and shall close in season to go to Brunswick very near the first of the term. I want to get in as early as possible, on account of society matters. We shall have to keep our eyes open, and improve any opportunity to advance the interests of our two societies. We seem to have obtained a very fair delegation from the Freshman class to our secret society, and the Athenaean prospects look favorable. I think we shall get a majority of those who are to join in the spring, and perhaps of all who will join during the year. Our [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] society will be pretty well represented in the spring, as there will probably be twenty badges to be seen on college ground, - more than any other society will be able to show.
I made a short visit to Foxcroft before I began my school, and called on some of our old friends there. I stopped with Mr. Tash one night, and had a very pleasant visit. We took a ride up to the Captain's, and saw Jerusha and Clara,

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: who seemed very much as of yore, when you and I were students in the delightful village of Foxcroft. I also saw our old friend Susan O., but did not get a chance to speak with her, which of course I very much regreted. Blake and Holmes are fitted to enter a term in advance, and Holmes has concluded to go on in the spring; but Blake told me that he had not determined whether to go then, or wait till the Soph. year. I advised him to go in the spring, and hope he will. We shall want his vote in the next Ath. election, and I suppose there would be no difficulty in securing it. We must claim and assert our rights at that election, - and, if we give proper attention to the subject, shall be able to maintain them. We ought to have the President and Secretary - and must have the former. Stevens is trying hard for the Secretaryship, and no doubt is very confident of obtaining it, though there is room for some doubt whether he will be able to carry the election. It is an office in which much can be done for a secret society if the Secy. is disposed to use his influence in that way. If the [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]'s would put some one forward for the office, I think they might elect him. You mentioned Weeks in your letter. He is teaching in Brewer, and thinks some of going to Brunswick next term. If he goes we will make him an Athenaean, and I think he might make a good member of the secret society. If he should prove a desirable fellow, I can get him, as he will room with me. I wish I could go down and make "Susannah" a visit some Sunday night, but [[marks?]] wont let me! - aint it too bad? My brother stays at home this winter, and as he has just become "of age," I suppose he will not teach much more, since he can now have his own way about it. I have rec'd letters

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
from our friends Hayes, Hawkins and Packard, who all seem to be enjoying themselves finely. Hayes is at Farmington, Hawkins at North Bridgton, & Packard at N. Auburn. Now I think of it I learned at Foxcroft that our old schoolmate B. F. Smart, has fixed his residence in Nashville, Tenn.! You must write to him. He would rejoice to hear from you. I did not learn what business he is engaged in.
John G. Clark is teaching in Dexter - A. H. Rice, at "Great Works," above Oldtown - Bro. Metcalf, I have filled my sheet - with what material you can judge. But dont be ashamed of yours again - Let me hear from you at your convenience, and I will write you in return -
I am your friend and brother - Issac W Case

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Levant, Jan'y 29th 1846
Friend Metcalf,
Your letter of Jan. 7th was received in good season, and would have been replied to ere this had any thing happened down east here, on account of which would have filled a sheet - but one day here is so like another, and none remarkable, that there is nothing new under the sun. Nobody gets married - 'taint leap-year, and the girls wont go a courting - and the 'fellers' are all too "bashful" to go themselves, - so on the whole 'tis rather a still time.
For my part, I am progressing pretty much after the old sort - each day brings the same duties - a little flogging of dull scholars, - and considerable instruction to the bright ones. - so much reading, writing, "'rithmetic" grammar, geography &c. &c. - and "school's done!"
My school consists of about the usual number, and is 'exceedingly pleasant.' My classes in the classics are prospering finely - I think of sending several to Brunswick next fall, one or two to Yale, and some to Thomaston! for which places I think they will by that time be qualified. But my class of young ladies is doing the strongest business. They have gone clean through "the Grammar," and made considerable progress in the spelling book. If you hear of any inquiry for a female teacher in any academy up west there,

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: tell 'em to send to me - I can furnish one to order, no mistake! You sey you hate small scholars. Now I can't say so much - dear little innocents how I love 'em. What tho' their noses are regular "pugs" - and dirty withal! my affection for them is none the less strong, but perhaps shown in a manner a little different from yours. I have, you know, some scores of the little "varmints," and I get along with them after the following fashion: - I have rings put in their noses of every one under six years, (somewhat after the manner of bull calves), and all I have to do is to slip a 'cod line' thro' each one's ring, when he enters the room in the morning, and he is perfectly secure! The line hangs coiled up on a pin in the desk, and on the least uneasiness among the "cattle," I give a slight jerk to it, which brings every one into a proper state of discipline again; and, as each jerk affects the whole, is it for the advantage of each to set an example of patience before the rest, knowing his liability to be 'brought up all standing,' even for the fault of another. This method I find most salutary, and I would advise you to give it a trial. The expense is slight - a line of sufficient length may be had for ninepence, and any common blacksmith will ring the "critters" for a shilling a head! As the thing was a new one here, and all were not satisfied of its success, the expenses were defrayed by subscription; but I think you may persuade your people to ring their "cattle" at their own expense! Do try the plan.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: I rec'd a letter from Bro. Grover some weeks since, and was very sorry to learn that I intends to be absent from college the rest of this year. He thinks of staying out till next fall, and then entering the present Freshman class. I regret this very much; for as I had not heard from him for some time before, I thought he must be making up with the intention of returning in the spring. Grover is a noble fellow, and one that will be missed by us especially. There is no better society man in college than he, and we need his assistance in our [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]. But he is 'with us, if not there,' and can do something where he is. You pretend to think that we can't have the President of Athena next year. I don't agree with you. I think, that with sufficient attention, and seasonable attention to the matter, we can - and we are going to try our best for it. It belongs to us, and we must assert and support our claims. I think we may get the help of the [Greek letters chi, psi]'s if we work the card right. I will depend on old Southworth whether we do or not, and I am not without strong hopes that he will come into the arrangement. It will be well for us to keep on good terms with him at any rate. We can carry the neutrals almost to a man, with care enough. With them, and the [Greek letters chi, psi]'s we might bid defiance to [Greek letters psi, upsilon] & [Greek letters alpha, delta, phi?], and carry any thing we chose. But when I begin on society matters, I can't stop at once. I don't know but I shall become a "Fisher," if I don't guard against it. I shall try to be in Brunswick soon after the term begins, and hope to see you there. I shall want the Ath. celebration to come off in good shape, and long for the time to come. I have seen

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849

Tuesday Feb 17' 1846
Dear Chum
Pardon the appellat[[ion?]] Yet I must confess I prefer it or one equivalent to any other - The name seems to recall our past associations as classmates - fellow students united by still stranger bonds - the fellowship of [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] and finally the hope of being associated again soon as roommates. Would it were today! It is not therefore I am again writing! Isaac I am sick & have been for some four days am better design to commence school again this morning which I left some four day ago: I close next week sometime. I wish it were done now You are now no doubt in the sha[[de?]] of Old Bowd our common Alma Mater I feel I nee[[d?]] her kindness But I must be brief - You will find our things in No 24 M.H. There is some bed clothing in my High Desk. Take it. A large bed sack a new one there somewhere! take that

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
and perhaps you better order it filled We shall want it -
That Carpet! It ought to have been beaten. But dont scold! Can you light the north end of S.C. or cause it to be lighted for me till I come? -
I have much I wish to write but my head & back & time all fail Write me anon if you wish any information on any point
How are you getting on How are all things prospering there My respects to all who enquire
Pardon all mistakes
Yours in the bonds of [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Sebec Feb 28/46
My Dear Friend,
I rec'd yours of the 16th ultimo and read it with the greatest pleasure; and sincerely thank you for your favor. It gives me unfeigned satisfaction to see a person enjoying and improving such talents and advantages as you possess. Tis then man seems to aim at those stations of usfulness and honor for which Heaven designed him, and to which, his own temporal Happiness most alluringly invites him. This is the brightest side of human nature. The unfortunate [[alone?]] can appreciate such a favor or tell how much it serves to reanimate and encourage a person in my condition. It is like an Oasis to the weary traveller, on the scorching sands of Sahara buffetted by the withering blasts of the Simoom. It inspired the not altogether latent desire to arise and stem the current of adversity, and reassured my feeble resolutions. It gives me pleasure to hear that you have advanced so far under so happy auspices. Is is no misfortune to you

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: that you are learning the practical part of life as you go along. Although you should not "take rank in your class" you are fitting yourself to take rank among men. Recollect "Pigmies are pigmies still though perched on Alps and pyramids are pyramids in vales" How often this recurs to my mind when I see some witless wight attaching a great deal of importance to themselves on account of some temporary, trancient, and even accidental advantage which he happens to enjoy! And how often I am pained and sickened by the churlish heartlessness and even insolence of those who from their pretentions and advantages [[should?]] be well bred! I was glad to hear that you had so pleasant a school in the fall; also that you were succeeding so well in your town school. There is more practical benefit to be derives from acquitting yourself well once in such a situation as that in which you found yourself placed than we are apt to estimate. "Suaviter in modo et fortiter in re" is a very efficient motto if well adhered to; and it should be the "Dirigo" of every indigent student. You have returned to your "Alma Mater" O, what exquisite pleasures are yours if you estimate your advantages as you

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
should!
How I envy your lot; at the same time that I would help or encourage you on tho' I could add but the might of an emmet! But you need it not. But you cannot form a just estimate of your advantages unless you are deprived of them as I have been. Although I am happy in the consciousness that I have well improved all my advantages yet an undefinable feeling of regret at so much time worse than wasted haunts me continually. But I hope soon to console myself with the consideration that I am making all the atonement in my power for my past delay. I closed my school 25th Inst. I had, all things considered, quite as pleasant a school as I expected I had a small school and quite a pleasant one at Milo village in the fall. I used to be acquainted with a Mr. Hatch at Readfield who I suppose is the same now your Chum I congratulate you on having so pleasant a Chum & Classmate Please squeeze him well by the hand for me and give him my respects. I expect to commence studying Law in Sebec in about two weeks.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
I shall be very happy to hear from you whenever you can get time to write me; and hope I shall have the pleasure of seeing you when you visit Milo Please direct to South Sebec. And call there and see me when you visit Milo. It has been very sickly in Sebec and Milo John: my brother next older than myself died 16 January: disease: Chronic inflamation of the stomach. I do not know that you were personally acquainted with him He was the kindest of brothers the most dutiful of sons and a most affectionate friend. Death loves a shining mark!
My health has been very good this winter.
With Sincere Respects
E. Barker

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Woolwich April 24th/46
Friend Metcalf:
I have just received your letter and take this early opportunity to answer the same, as I received one from the "rebel Wheeler" also.
I always have a strong sympathy for the downtrodden and oppressed, and you can better imagine than I can describe my heartfelt sympathy for the vanquished Faculty of the time honored Bowdoin College.
Wheeler wrote that he & Boody had to take the blunt of the battle: I presume they were able to bear it and their knees did not shake quite as bad as Belshazzars. I hope you will leave as much as a greece spot of the Faculty, for one of them owes me a little, and if you annihilate them I fear it will be a bad go for me. Do spare Prof Packard, and for the sake of an old friend, leave the radical part of Ferox, the true champion. And I would especially enjoin it upon you to do nothing to wound the feelings of that truely great, but unassuming gentleman "H H Boody Professor of Rhetoric and Oratory, Bowd College," lest he take wings and fly away, and old Bowd be reconed only among the things that "have been.' A word to the wise, is enough: so I will say no more untill I see you, and then you shall have my fatherly advice verbatim, and see my abominable abhorence to every innovation upon equal rights & equal privileges.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Wheeler wrote that if he was sent away, he would leave a lock of his hair: tell him to get Prof Packard's bosom pin to seal it up with, or two & a half inches of Prof Boody's dignity. Please hand the inclosed note to Mr. W. as soon as convenient, and you will do me a favor. He was to send me a bundle, next Monday. I was very much surprised that Mr. S. should say he had paid any money to me, on account of the Society, for he never has. I asked him for some in the Library last fall term. He said he would pay within a short time, and I left him to pay it when most convenient, and that time never came, for he left without paying any thing. The records are perfectly correct, so far as I had any thing to do with them, and he is mistaken, if he says or thinks he paid me any thing.
If I remember right, he said, when I asked him for it, that he was collecting money of his class (their subscriptions for books) and he would pay his bill when he paid in the money for these subscriptions: but he never paid that money to me, and I do not know to whome it was paid.
My school closed the last day of March, and as I was behind in my studies, I thought it would be better to make up here than at college. Have a first rate boarding place (the same as during the winter) have my board lights &c for instructin the family about two hours per day.
Oh! those Junior parts! I should like to see them come off!
Yours
S. N. Merrill

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Bowdoinham May 26th, 46
Friend Metcalf
You wished me to write you at Milo This I undertake with all pleasure tho my epistle must needs be rather barren of interest. There is but little here to break the monotony, if it be proper to speak of monotony when we can enjoy the endless variety of objects that Nature presents to those who will take the trouble to pause & contemplate But you know chum I am no poet and but a sorry proser; ergo, there might be much to interest & instruct one of more lively imagination or acute observation than myself. True I almost daily enjoy the privilege of watching the gallant steamers as they course their way up & down the Kennebec; sometimes two in near proximity - even to colision. This sight once would have been a prodegy. The novelty is long since gone by, & with upon such scenes with but little emotion Then I am at home!! Can one be lonely amid the scenes of childhood & youth?
There are times when we feel we are but pilgrims in a foreign land having no abiding place on earth: then we sometimes

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
feel a sense of loneliness; other causes also may augment this feeling of depression. I need not explain; every poor student, whose spirits are more or less affected with bodily infirmity & pecuniary embarrassment can apperecite all.
As to news I hear but little that I can trust. O! Texas (tempora) O! Mexico. (mores) When shall we go I wonder? I think M[[?]]sy chose's will take place before I go! But for News! what we hear one day is contradicted the next. If they know themselves what they are fighting for it is well I dont think much of fighing anyway - much less for Texas. If you have any late despatches as authentic as the [Greek letter psi] [Greek letter upsilon] annexation please forward I am ever happy to hear from all who hold connection with our Alma Mater; and it not strange that I feel a peculiar interest Hatcher's welfare! I have had some acquaintance with him from his infancy He has many faults yet I myself for some reason have taken considerable interest in everything that affects his interest or character. I would resent an insult offered to him as soon as to myself!! And he is reported married! I cant hardly beleive it. Do you Isaac? This is not the first time; therefore I think it less strange and am disposed to question it No less than three times within three

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
years this same Hatch has had similar reports to repell and I am sanguine in the opinion that in about two weeks from this time That he will answer this grave charge in person[[a?]]
Seriously; all a humbug!! I dont say it is a libel: there is to much of the ridiculous for that. I married!! O! tell it not in Gath publish it not ye [Greek letters psi, upsilon]s in old Bowdoin.
I have [[weaugh?]] some on the farm and some at mechanical work, loafed some studied little. health decent. I expect to be at Bowd Coll at the 1st recon The fare to [[Boston?]] raised to $2,00 again, one boot left. Hold up your head up high with your new hat Isaac! What do you think of the coming election Be on hand to sustain the honor [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] and your own The [Greek letters psi, upsilon] are desperate and will have every victim they can sacrifice; & every office too. If this is to be the ultimate contest between the private societies (remember what the Fac say) [[let?]] [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] acquit herself manfully. Did you stop to the examination? Please write anon et multum. Where are you - what doing &c Did you see Perry for me? When you are Governor of Oragon shall I saw wood for you? Bon nuit, Meine Bruder,
Votre ami S. W. Hatch

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Old Town June 22d/46
Dear Sir
I received from you, (a few days since) as Treasurer of the Athenaean, a somewhat short & cold letter, putting me in mind that there was something still due Athena from me. Shall I say that my remembrance needed not quickening in the form of an official Dun?
It was hard for me to leave those hallowed grounds, without having first paid "the uttermost farthing." - But it was not "the unkindest cut of all" - Athena shall not suffer for my having belonged to it. I shall not send the money now - shall probably be there at Com - if not, before a long intervening time, & will take my name from among the long catalogue of the names of those who still stand indebted to "the Athenaean."
You say, "I write as an Athenaean" but if so, I am still unacquainted with Athenaean character - your official duty has been respectfully & properly performed. But silent upon all else, you have not even stated the standing of "Athena," in comparison with her neighbor, supposing probably that, "He that is guilty in one point, is

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
guilty in the whole," that all feeling or interist for her prosperity must be wanting. If the Athenaean has no worse members, or those who feel no less pride in contributing to her support, she will soon not only equal but far outstrip a rival society.
Notwithstanding your strictly formal official letter, I could not refrain from departing somewhat from a formal reply, though I have endeavored to confine myself to it somewhat. Yours in bonds &c
I. S. Metcalf                                               Elbridge Smith

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Bowdoinham Nov 28th '46
Br. Metcalf
I received a letter yesterday from my quondam chum, and I am now down to answer it in part at least before going to my School. I am much obliged for some information your letter contained.
You want to know what reasonable excuse I can offer for not not writing before? You forgot Br. that I could return the complement. I did not know where you were -whether at Turner, Topsham or some wheres else & more you promised to write me after going to Turner I believe. Who then is the delinquent?
You have quite a school! Mine is in the bill only two months of which 5 weeks are now gone. Have 60 scholars some as ugly as you please have a skuffle occasionally. This is good for exercise - Told one fellow to give me his hand! I wont was the reply! So I pounced upon him instanter!

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Gave him the raps of dardy over his shoulders! Damn you says he, if you touch me again I will prosecute you Upon this he retreated to his seat up the aisle. I upon his trail putting on the raps. He seated himself. "Come out here! said I." I wont! So I just laid hands on him - he planted both hands & feet against the benches! But the way he came out - wont - slow! Round & round I set him a going, make him dizzy & down he went crash upon the floor and I on top of him! He sung out, you have hurt my head I jumped & told him to get up & give me his hand? He obliged & cried - and promised to be obedient. and hence I did not punish him any farther. He is a pretty good boy now (comparatively).
When I finish this school I commence another upon the Foreside where we went one day - two or three months more. I went to work after I came from Br'k at [[joinering?]] & continued it nearly a month, made $20. Have studied but little yet. Must do something ab it soon I intend to be in Brunswick ab the commencement of the Spring Term Shall you be there?

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
How long a school have you? How much are you making per month? -- My health is good - tho' my school taxes me some. I boarded at home 4 miles for two weeks after I began. Quite a walk!
The Bonfire! It shone afar, I tell you. It was over where I live! A nefarious concern anyhow - Hope the rogues will be found out.
The Bills of the [[Stanwark?]] Club are not settled yet - That is too bad My bill was settled before I left - and the others were left with Case But Center write me yesterday say[[ing?]] he had not received a cent & that Case could not collect it! Case wrote me the same! Center calls on me to come down & settle! That I cant & 'shant' do en present. Am I responsible for all this busines? If so it will be a fine affair! Has Case left - Who was third on the committee Write me all the news Come up this winter and stop over the Sabbath. How is J G Evelette going it? O! that poem! My love to all the brethren? Where is Jackson & Upham too?
Your Brother
S W Hatch

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Bowdoinham, Dec. 14th 1846
Friend & Brother
I received a letter a few days since was very happy to hear from you, both of your personal affairs and other matters of importance and interest. The tour you speak of to Yale would be very congenial to my feelings but incompatible with my business. I closed my school in the bill last Saturday and commence this morning in district No. 9. Brick School house Foreside where you and I went one day where I shall be engaged till the commencement of the spring Term or later and if I am absent a week I shall lose Prof Cleaves Lectures!! And the "Means" as you say! There's the rub! I suppose if the Society send a member his expenses will be defrayed? so you will be to no charge Perhaps you will say I think too much of the money: Well you will allow me to make the same excuse you make yourself without charging me with avarice! Poor me: I shall come out minus from Coll, but this dont trouble me?

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
The affairs of the Club! burn my eyes As the negro said another time I shall say I 'ant there Who are there and who have paid I you can conveniently pay over your bill to Center and have it endorsed upon his bill Your bill I gave to Case. You know the time and the rate is $1.61 per week Where is C. A. [[Spof.?]] the quondam ex Pres who retires from the chair under so flattering auspices? Has he paid over?
Do you know what Case did with Bills? What is the case of the Bon Fire? Who have been expelled? any? Will you send me Paley's Evidence's and show me what is omitted if anything? Direct to the care of P. M. Merrow P. M. and thus accommodate an old friend?
I got my coat torn the other day in a spree with one of my scholars but I put him out of the house and then put him on his good behavior. Collared two or three others and flagged them Done! Good! You know about this business! More of this when we meet!
Write me soon. Give my love to all the brethren I must go to School In haste
Yours respectfully S. W. Hatch

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
East Thomaston, Decr. 26th, 46.
Brother Metcalf
In looking over my file of letters, I find yours of the 5th inst. remaining yet unanswered. Remembering that its reception and perusal gave me much pleasure, and knowing that "one good turn deserves another," I now seat myself to get you in debt for another letter - I was glad to learn of the prompt action taken by the remnant of the [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]'s in the matter of the Yale convention, and happy to be informed of the wise selection of the delegates; but somewhat disappointed to hear that our enthusiastic and enterprising Brother Wheeler, was not one of the number - This was a strange oversight - Is it possible that the society were so blind to their own best interests as not to choose the young gentleman in question for one of their representatives? How he would have shone within the time-honored walls of old Yale - and with what envy would the delegates from the other chapters have looked upon that of Bowdoin, at possessing so able, talented, & "personable" a representative! Truly, honest merit stands but a small chance now a days!!

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
But I suppose by the time this reaches Topsham, that you will have started for New Haven, and I shall receive no return till after your mission shall have been accomplished - I hope you will have a pleasant and profitable visit at Yale, as I doubt not you will. I should be very glad if I could have the pleasure of accompanying you; but 'tis not my good fortune.
With regard to school-keeping, I can inform you that I have my hands full six days in the week, though my school is not more difficult than I expected to find it.
I have had, all told, about 140 scholars; but 124! is the largest number that I have been honored with at one time! The average attendance is about a hundred, of all ages, conditions, and characters - Some are first rate scholars, - some are worse than Arabs. But I get along very well, taking all things into the account, and contrive to wear away the time pretty comfortably. While in school, I am constantly on the drive, and full of work; but when out, I calculate to enjoy myself to the best of my ability, which is sometimes, pretty well - For amusement, I spend one evening a week, in trying to acquire the Terpsichorean art, of which, as you know, I have hitherto been

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: ignorant. But this fact I communicate to you, not for the purpose of spreading it, but for your own satisfaction - Though by no means ashamed of attending dancing school here, I am aware that in many places, I should never dare to commit such a gross outrage upon morality and good manners! Bah! Besides this amusement, we have several bowling alleys here, where I have spent one afternoon with some profit, but which I do not intend to patronize to much great extent. For companions in my vices, I have our quondam Foxcroft friend,  I. A. Bartlett, now a member of Wat. college, who is to take a school a short distance from the village, next week, - and two other Waterville students, by the names of Bailey and Sandford, who are also teaching in town - We four make a pretty strong team, and make things go pretty lively, when we meet - But you needn't think I am getting unsteady - not a whit - I like to be merry, but not at the expense of "good habits." Then, you know my position - so we'll say no more about it now - I hope you are prospering well, and "little Wheeler," ditto - Give him my kindest regards, and remind him that a letter would not be unacceptable - Give me a full account of your journey to Yale - and your doings and [[thinkings?]] while there - Remember me to Hinkley, To[[?]]po[[?]] and the Topsham ladies - Your true friend Isaac W. Case

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Waterville College Jany 22d/47
Bro Metcalfe:
Your letter was duly recd, and I am happy in having an opportunity to assure you that your companionship was by no means so uninteresting as to be so soon forgotten, or your letter of such a nature as to be undeserving of a reply. Make no apology then for your communication, but be assured that I should wish it to be the beginning of a more extended correspondence Those who belong to our society should never meet as strangers And indeed they are not strangers; for there is at least one tie in common, and they who possess the token of that tie are sure to find a friend, where they find anyone who is able to interpret the mystic initials, [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]. The date of my membership is so recent that I am yet but a tyro in the craft, but I think from what little has come under my observation, that the society is destined to prosper and to take a high rank. We are yet in our infancy, while some of our opponents are evidently in their dotage: We have as many chapters as could be expected from the date of our origin and the obstacles to be overcome in the formation of a new society And I consider it some token of my attachment to the [Greek letters delta, kappa] to say that, I would not exchange my share in its interests and its Brotherhood, for a like share in any other society I have yet seen, though they may be able

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: to present a far more extended list of names, and to boast a somewhat more ancient pedigree. You ask me how on the whole I was pleased with the chap at Yale: In truth I can hardly put my opinion in a tangible form, or at least in such a form as to be comprehensive: I acknowledge that it did not square exactly with what had been my previous conception though I am far from supposing it to be below what I had supposed. There are indeed, as you suggest, many circumstances that should have their due weight in the formation of an opinion of our Parent chap: It was term-time when we visited them, and their college rules in regard to punctuality are of so stern a character, as to influence very much the attention which otherwise they would have paid to us personally: And again our members there are very young in years, and when free from the restraint of college discipline, are somewhat more boisterous than would characterize the deportment of your chapter or ours, where to a greater extent "age makes venerable." But after all, there is one thing for which the Yale chapter is preeminent, and for which it deserves the "crown and laurel" and that is, the interest which they take in the welfare of the Society generally. Amid all their mirth and pleasantry I believe they have the progress of our order steadily and heartily in view, and also I am of the opinion that they are those with whom its interest can be safely entrusted. Such is the estimation in which I hold the

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: parent chap: I found it different from what I expected, but though different, yet not less meritorious I think, after making due allowance for unfavorable circumstances. - I heard from N. Haven about a week after we returned: The message contained a copy entire of the new constitution, accompanied by a letter from Bro Hitchcock: You probably remember him; He is the one who graduated at a college in Tennessee, and the one who read the proposed constitution to the convention. He writes like one who possesses feelings and knows how to communicate them too. - If I rightly remember the name of the Cor Sec'y at Amherst, it is L. P. LeDoux:  As for myself, there is but little to be said: I employ my time in reading, very pleasantly and, I hope also, usefully to. Students are too apt to be deficient in general reading, and I am glad to embrace an opportunity to do a little to remedy what I know to be a very great deficiency on my part. Bro Gamble is my only compatriot on the premises: the others are scattered in every direction. - Just say to Bro Wheeler, that if he can find it in his heart to write I should be very happy indeed to hear from him [[?]] [[?]] also, Bro Metcalfe, if you think it will pay the way, I should be abundantly glad to receive another favor from you, and I would not wish you to accompany it with any more apologies. It would be very agreeable to know now what is your opinion of our friends at Yale: Truly & sincerely your Brother [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]. D.S. True

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Bowdoin College March 26, 1847
Friend Metcalf:
With a full sense of Senior Dignity - a phrase too often unappreciated - I spend a small part of to-day's [[show?]] in writing thee. Prof Upham is absent this week soft-soaping rich specimens of humanity with an eye all the time on their gold.
But my ear is this moment arrested by the clamor of the Junior Class, holding a meeting to take into consideration the expediency of a rebellion. The circumstances are as follows - At the late public declamation in the chapel several of the Juniors "aided and abetted" by some of the other classes, kept such a confusion as to make it almost impossible for the speakers to proceed - At the close, Boody asked Merrick and Hollett to stop - they did not comply with the command - were "called up" - and this morning it is reported that Merrick is suspended. Hence the class meeting.
Our class attempted to get up a cut yesterday to the Pres. but the rebels amounted to but 1/3 of the whole; conspicuous among whom were O'Brien and Peters. Seniors should never be radicals - they hold the conservation power
concluded on page third

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: Friend M   Jordan has just come into my room and given me an opportunity to address a few lines to you which I gladly improve. He tells me that you write that you are very pleasantly situated and have fair prospects of remuneration. I am glad to hear of your prosperity but I warn you to be careful about the "Gals" although I suppose my warning will be unheeded. At least however I have the satisfaction of having done my duty. We are getting along here about after the old sort with a full allowance of the famous Senior Dignity which you know no class can support better than ours. We have all of three recitations this week besides Cleaver's which seeming to the class too much of an infringement upon the rights of man, and to have a tendency to crush the rising genius they tried to get up the "cut" that Jordan has told you of. I have been here 3 weeks and in that time we have had 4 recitations in Butler and a week in Upham. So we go. Do you or do you not feel more of a man than when you first entered College and we had our windows broken and chased the rowdies. We have gotten our "diapers" almost off and are

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
just aspiring to the dignity of "jacket & trousers." Well well when 'we are growed up what we'll do wont we.' I am afraid however we shall find many trials in our youth which we escape in our infancy, and shall often wish ourselves back again in old Bowd's lap. Excuse this "hasty" scrawl, (not soup) pardon my presumption and answer.
Your Friend and Classmat
Wm M Baker.
You wish to hear about the anniversaries. Ours was May eve, yours Thurs eve. Subject of John Cotton's Oration "The Relation of Christianity to the present Life" It is highly spoken of. The audience was very kind after having listened an hour to the oration, to give me their undivided attention.
Richardson's Oration was well written and is highly commended. Prof. Boody expressed much admiration in respect to it. The subject of it "Art" He said there is a principle of Beauty, underlying all things - a substratum beneath material existence which it is the province of Art to detect and present to the common mind. It was tinctured with Germanism. The old Scottish caution which Prof. Upham adopts is too stale and cold for him. Pike's Poem was witty - Courtiers at Washington were ready to cry with a loud voice "Thy ways O! James K. Polk are just." 
Respects of all Bowdoin and of my chums in particular.
Yours E. S. Jordan

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Bowd. Coll. Apl. 1st 1847.
Brother Metcalf,
How shall I begin after just reminding you of the commencement of your letter, or rather of that beautiful exordium, in which you didn't know whether you were invited to write me or not!! I say how shall I begin to give you a thousandth part of the news you ask? - But first let me just say I wonder not at your thinking the time long since you left, Time moves slowly from many causes. Since you left, it has moved so here and still continues thus to move. One reason for this may be that dim, stern shade of Butler, which three times a week stalks triumphant through Old Bowdoin's Halls. Then only are seen "sights of woe" and heard wild shrieks of heartrending anguish. But for all this who that has ever entered these "Classic halls, can forget them till his latest hour,' - and even after that we know not but that numary may survive the shock of death and fondly

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
linger o'er the scenes of olden, by-gone time. You may well say, as every body else can, that you know not that you have many friends, as each one needs but few, yet you do wrong at least to a certain portion in saying that you don't know that you have any very warm friends. There are a few of us that should be friends in the strict sense of the term, and we should look upon each other as such, until we have strong evidence to the contrary. - Just think of the comparative merits of Lucretius and Bishop Butler, or Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress and the Almanack!!!! - But enough of this - 'Sed tamen amoto quaeramus seria ludo. Things are all right in Topsham, they have the "Circle" as usual. In regard to the aniversaries of genl societies, the parts were all of the best kind. Both evenings passed pleasantly. At the election of officers of [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] Society we had no poem, but listened to a fine oration by Hawkins on Poland. The following were elected officers,
Hatch P.P.
Ware P.S.
Case Sc.
Humphrey 2nd S.
Pickard T.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
We did find some difficulty in regard to the by laws but none very serious. I don't know exactly how the matter was disposed of. We have had the most splendid lectures imaginable on electricity, the most beautiful experiments. At present we have them on galvanism, experiments in this branch also of the finest kind, Prof Cleaveland as ever full of fun. Prof Upham has been absent two or three weeks, since you left, but we gained nothing by it, for we had - Hail Horrors!! - a double lesson in Butler. But when he returned we had no lesson in Butler for the s[[?]] time, but a double lesson in Upham. The Juniors & sophs have had 3 or 4 hold-ins which together with some other little things make business quite lively among the faculty. - excuse my boring you any longer with this horrible epistle and accept the best wishes of yr. friend and brother in [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]
(in haste) H. J. Ware
P.S. Write whenever you can. Chum will write you soon, and I suppose Wheeler will.  H.J.W.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Wm. C. Pond
Bowd. Coll.
Apr. 8th 1847.
April 12th 1847
Orono
Bowd. Coll. April 8th 1847
Friend Metcalf
It was with much pleasure that I received your kind favor of the 27 ult. I do, indeed, like very much to turn my eyes back upon last winter's residence at Orono. I find now that I enjoyed myself very much there. We are not apt, while we are in the possession of happiness, to think how we do enjoy ourselves, but after this happiness is gone, and we see ourselves entirely destitute of it, then we begin to feel its value. Though I knew at the time that I was enjoying myself highly, yet I have no idea how I should miss the pleasant times which I had there, and I longed to be back again to Brunswick. I now find myself looking back very often upon Orono, and wishing myself there. But all my wishing will do no good, and I have begun to make up my mind to rest contented where I am, till I can go where I shall enjoy myself better.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: I am happy to hear that you have so pleasant a school. I think that you could not well have had one of a different character, and as to your liking the place and people, you need not have told me that, as I knew you would before I proposed to you to go there. Dr. Ricker's family, I doubt not, you find very pleasant; I became somewhat acquainted there, and as far as my judgment will go, I think you could not have had a better place. Mr Palmer who boarded there last winter, was very much pleased with his boarding-place. Mrs. Ricker, I think it likely, you may find a little nervous, but that is all, and that accounts for many things which you would not expect in so intelligent a woman. She has been insane once or twice. As to your third item, that the people up there like me, I am very much obliged to you for the news, and to them for their good opinion; you may give almost any one there with whom I was acquainted, a similar compliment from me. You ask me in relation to Miss Ring. I do not know whether she would consider herself a scholar of mine or not. She attended school about a fortnight a the beginning of the school, and then left and went to a town opposite Oldtown, Milford I believe is the name, and taught school. Does she attend your school? And do any of her sisters? I believe, she is a fine scholar, as also are her sisters, one, especially, Elizabeth, whom I consider very superior for her age. Miss Weeks who is, as you say, a very fine scholar, and a fine girl too, has a brother who, perhaps, attends your school, whom I considered a very good scholar.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: But I have been talking all this time in relation to Orono, and have given you no Bowdoin news at all. The anniversaries passed off finely, with one exception, - there was no music. Richardson's oration was very much superior to Smith's, in the general opinion, though they were both very good. Smith's was on the connection of Christianity and art, Richardson's on the Artist especially the literary artist. Some passages in the latter are among the most beautiful I ever saw or heard. It is somewhat remarkable, that they both quoted the same poetry in connection with a portion, of their orations, on a similar point. It was quite a long extract and being the same in both attracted a great deal of attention. The poems were also very good, and, what cannot be said of all the poems delivered before the societies, very apropos. The exercises before both were good, but, I believe, it is universally acknowledged that ours were decidedly the best. Since then the college has been in a turmoil of excitement, on account of a declamation which Boody undertook to impose upon our class. The class went in at the time of declamation, but no sooner had the speakers begun, than, the whole chapel was in an uproar; stamping, clapping, hallooing, was the order of the day. The poor Tutor's soul was sorely vexed; what to do he knew not, and so he did nothing till afternoon, and then the calling up began. And ever since then it has been nothing but a succession scrapes from one day's end to another. At this rate,

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
the Faculty will have business enough to keep them till commencement, at work, and then the heap will be only larger. I am not certain but we shall have a rebellion yet, but if possible it will be prevented. There are some students who are very much excited and I think would join in such a thing with pleasure.
Give my best respects to all my friends in Orono. Let me hear from you very soon, and tell me how your school flourishes, and how matters are going on in Orono.
Yours truly, W. C. Pond
P.S. By the way, in relation to Johnson's book, tell him, or them, that in the first place I had no table on which the book could be lying, in the second place, if I had one, I never borrowed or had in my possession one of Mr Hamblin's books to lie there, and in the third place, I carried no books from his house but my own. Tell him more over that if he will write me, and tell me what it was, if he will prove that I took it I will pay for it. And, now, if you choose you may tell people there that I have never read three words in any of Mr Hamblin's books, and then they may believe Mr Johnson or myself as they choose. Do as you please about this last. Yours &c W. C. P.
Excuse chirography.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Bowdoin College, Apr. 17th, 47.
Dear Metcalf,
I have before me a letter which I received from you just before I left Thomaston, but whether I then answered it I do not now remember. If I did, why when you get this you will owe me one - otherwise you will not.
Be that as it may, I shall go ahead, as I have seated myself for the purpose of scribbling you a letter. Well then, what did you mean, Sir, when in a letter to my worthy chum some weeks since, you said 'that you should like to have a letter from Case, if he could keep steady long enough to write one?' Did you mean to hint even, that I am ever, on any occasion, under any circumstances, unsteady? If so, Sir, please have the goodness to retract, or meet me as a gentleman of honor to support your base accusations, at the pistol's muzzle! These, Sir, are your only alternatives - Retract, fight, or be ported as a coward and a calumniator!! My wrath will not permit me to fill this page, so turn over -

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: I expect you are so agreeably situated at Orono that you will scarcely care about hearing anything about college matters - If you were disposed to hear, I should not be able to gratify you with any news, as "we don't take the papers," and no such thing as news ever reaches these barren sands of Brunswick. Things in college go on about the same as ever - We have no scrapes now, but we all attend most strictly to our studies - or rather, we have till quite recently; but since the Junior parts have been given out, the chief motive for study has been removed. Those who are honored with  parts, settle back upon their lees, having attained the height of their ambition; and those who were passed over, have nothing to gain by further study! The parts came out on Wednesday of this week - Those for the Senior class are, Baker, Boody, Eveleth 2d, Hatch, Lomand, Pike (Salutatory) Spinney, Stinchfield, Wheeler 1st, Wheeler 2d, and Whitcob - The Juniors are Case, Hawkins, Humphrey 2d, Pickard and Stevens. So you see that [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] is not so far behind other folks after all. The following mathematical diagram, for which I am indebted to our friend Hawkins, gives a very distinct idea of the relative situation of the secret societies in our class - as there is not room on this page, you may look upon the next:

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Junior Parts - 1846-7.
[drawing of an inverted triangle showing Greek letter societies, with the Delta Kappa Epsilon society at the top, and descending levels: 4. Psi Upsilon; 3. Alpha Delta Phi; 2. N; 1. Chi Psi]
N.B. - N. stands for Neutral or Newcomb.
The diagram takes up considerable space on the page, but I think you will be willing to pardon it - Fales and Stanton have been looking pretty confidently for parts; but they are doomed to disappointment. Stanton bears it very well; but Fales is all down in the mouth, and unless he gets some relief soon there is no knowing what the result will be. You will doubtless be somewhat surprised to hear that Case was thought worthy of a Junior part - To confess the truth, I was surprised at it myself, and yet I have pretty good evidence that he was not the lowest on the list of ten-
I suppose you are doing fine business in the way of teaching, at any rate I hope so. From your letter to my chum I judge that you have quite a profitable school. You ought to have to justify you in staying out at this time of the course - I presume you will be back at the first of the summer term -
I have nothing of interest to communicate with regard to society matters, except that Perkins of the Sophomore class is pledged to join us.
Write soon, and let me know what you think of Orono, of school-keeping &c &c.
Yours sincerely - I. W. Case

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
C. H. Wheeler
May 25th 1847
Topsham
May 28 1847
Milo
Topsham Me, May 25th 1847
My Dear Friend,
Were I to defer answering your letter as long a time as you did mine, you would not hear from me so soon as this: but in point of Procrastination you acknowledge no superior, and I cheerfully award you the palm of excellence. Your letter, which was duly received, not being this moment at hand, I may not perhaps return answers to all your questions - The Exhibition of the 18th inst. passed off very well although the audience was smaller than usual on account of the rain. I enclose you an "Order of Exercises." Immediately after the Performances at the vestry - the ([Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon]) Society repaired to their homes where "they partook of a splendid collation prepared for the occasion, and amidst the feast of fat things literary and convivial, the bonds of brotherhood were knit more strongly together" - I quote the above from Bro. Stinchfields account of the Supper Commencement eve, 2 years ago, as contained in the 1st vol. of Records - We did however really have a very fine time - The Yale Chapter, it is true have proposed quite a number of Amendments, but they have merely offered them to us for adoption or rejection, and without the vote of two thirds of the Chap's. - they cannot go into effect - I am now going to tell you a "story" Metcalf - a true one too - and as I presume you have not heard it - perhaps it may interest you somewhat
see next page

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription: As our respected Bro. Hawkins was returning home from the village, pretty late at night (near the close of last term), stopping beneath the windows of the [Greek letters psi, upsilon] Room, he thought he heard the "sound of revelry by night," very distinct. Climbing up on a wood-pile near the building - applying his ear as near as possible - he distinctly heard the sound of voices, of knives and plates. He was able sometimes to distinguish the speakers and to hear the jokes &c. Fales stood preeminent upon this occasion I believe - Well suffice it to say, he went and aroused our notorious (I am afraid Case will see this letter sometimes) our notorious friend Case, who had long since retired - and they two, after the [Greek letters psi, upsilon]'s had retired, went and got a long pole, applied it to the back window of the building which was left partly open, raised the window - entered the building and found themselves in the "Sanctum Sanctorum" of Psi Upsilonism in this College. The room as you must know is quite small - there were no curtains to the windows no desks - very ill-looking paper upon the walls - no tables - with the exception of one 10 ft long and covered with the remnants of the evenings  feast, and a closet in one side filled with dishes and eatables. Well after having examined the Room as much as they wished, Hawkins did up a few figs and other dainties, in a paper as a memento, and Case possessed himself of a stick which was probably made use of to prepare the lemons and which was covered with quaint devices - and ancient too withal - having belonged to Isaac Wadsworth - as we infer from the initials on it. They then covered the stove with nuts, took a Pail, turned it bottom upwards, put a Pitcher into it, put a Lamp into the pitcher, put a plate full of nuts on top &c. and then retired the way they

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
entered, letting the window fall down on the shutter --
I have given you but a poor account of this memorable exploit, but it went off well, Case or Hawkins when you see them will give you a much fuller and more extended account The Stick is labelled and together with the [Greek letters alpha, delta, phi] Circular is put into the [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] "Cabinet of Curiosities" - where you may see it next term. But the best thing is coming now - A short time since I received a letter from Henry Hitchcock informing us that they had found out the [Greek letters psi, upsilon] motto viz [two-word phrase in Greek letters] (Yours in heart) - Immediately - we sat down and examined the Dictionary and found that they were absolutely the only words which we could make any motto of at all under these letters - We then wrote them down - as I have in this letter -  simply the two words - in all the 4 Recitation Rooms, and watched the countenances of the [Greek letters psi, upsilon]'s as they first saw it - We saw at the first glance that we were right - I needed but one look at Spinney's face in our Rec. room to convince me - others also manifested the same emotion - so that now there remains not a shadow of doubt that we are right - of course it was over College in a few moments, but after the 1st shock was over the [Greek letters psi, upsilon]'s took no notice of it - It remains there on the wall however to this time. Hitchcock sent me also the [Greek letters alpha, delta, phi] motto - [three-word phrase in Greek letters] differing only from the one we supposed to be correct here, in the 1st word viz [first word of the three-word phrase in Greek letters] instead of [one word in Greek letters] as we supposed - I have written you a very long and unintelligible letter, but I thought you would like to hear of these matters which

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
I have told you - and they are absolutely everything I have to tell you, or I would not have devoted my letter almost exclusively to them as I have done - I shall expect to hear from you very soon - write me when you are coming.
Miss Hall has inquired after you, and I will according to your request hand her $2.00 which is equivalent, I believe to a doubloon, and that will cancel my obligation to you - I would thank you for a receipt in your next letter - if you please.
I am with much respect,
Your obedient serv't.
Charles N. Wheeler
Hon. I. S. Metcalf M.P.
For the borough of Orono.
P.S. I have forgotten whether or no I told you that my youngest brother - Henry broke his leg - a few weeks since - in the ship-yard - he broke it in the same place as William - My turn comes next I believe. Do I beseech you pardon this Chirography, on account of my extreme haste - although I confess I could'nt were I in your case - I would just say with regard to Stinchfield's piece, that it was very finely written - and delivered very respectably - much better than we anticipated. Our Junior parts all went off well - Case had a very good piece and spoke it very well - Pickard spoke remarkably well and had a fine Latin piece, Hawkins & Humphrey's likewise were very good. I think Stinchfield's piece was the best original one on the Stage - Your obed't serv't C. N. W.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [5], 1844-1849
transcription:
Warwick July 1st, 1847.
Mr. I. S. Stevens,
Dear cousin, I recd. yours of June 28th this morning, in which you ask my advice what you had better do with yourself when you are through with your college course. I am not able to advise you in this matter. I came to the conclusion many years ago that school keeping would soon become the best and most profitable business, that people had become so waked up about schools that teaching would soon become one of the most honorable and profitable of all the professions but it has not turned out so yet, and I dont know as it ever will, perhaps it will continue to be for many years to come, such a thankless and disagreeable business that none will engage in it except from necessity and will then quit it the first opportunity. I am inclined to think the business of engineering is looking up, and that it may continue to be good. You say your mind has not turned very strongly towards either of the professions Divinity, Law, or Medecine and I do not think very inviting at this time. As to the best mode of getting into the business of engineering, I think you have started right and I would continue it. I would write to every freind with whom I had

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [4], 1878-1897
transcription:
Elyria Ohio
Nov 17th, 1889
Mrs A. S. Root,
Dear Anna,
I want to advise
you about your baby.
Do not worry about him.
You have a strong healthy baby- proof
positive, he grows, increases in size, grows
strong and hearty, increases in wisdom
and stature and favor with God & Man.
Evidently. Let him cry if he wants
to. It will not hurt him. Healthy children 
frequently cry about all the time. I heard
Mrs. Orville Root of Elyria say that her Fanny
a strong healthy and now remarkably
amiable child "cried all the time the first
year of her life."
But what I wanted to say to you is Do not
worry over the child. Take care of yourself, of your
own health spirits and feelings and the child

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [4], 1878-1897
transcription:
will be all right. Eat, drink and sleep for
yourself and not for the baby and baby will
come out all right. I repeat it, Eat and 
drink what you want, what tastes good, what is
best for your own health and strength, and
the baby will be all right, happy and strong
all the quicker.
Respectfully & especially,
Father

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [4], 1878-1897
transcription:
Elyria, Ohio,
April 3, 1890.
Dear Anna
We are sort of lonesome
here without you and your baby.
Your word from Miss Avery came as
soon as you got away.
I enclose it herewith.
I hope young Francis will like his new
home, and be tractable.
Sincerely
Father.
P.S. The Mother & Paul H. arrived in good condition.
Keyes slept most of the forenoon, and has
gone to sleep again this P.M.

are soon to have a short vacation in

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [4], 1878-1897
transcription: The small Eliah [[?]]ight Metcalf said "If I ever fall out of the wagon again don't tell any body."

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [3], 1878-1897
transcription:
Elyria O Mar 23 1878
Anna
My very dear
If I should be away next week, will you not try to have every thing get on smoothly with the children in my absence.  It seems to me you had better stay at home mostly. You might watch over and care for the children mostly.  And leave Lou chance to sew and work.  The children ought not to be permitted to stray about to the neighbors etc. especially Ethel; it will need some care and kindness and skill in finding pleasant employment to keep at home.  Remember a drop or two of syrup is better to call or keep  flies etc than a pint of vinegar.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [3], 1878-1897
transcription:
Keep at home yourself and you can the children; or go with them.  They might go up to Uncle Charles sometime, or down to Aunt Annas.  And Anna, you and Lon ought to keep up with the children the regular morning Bible reading.  Do not neglect this reading.  If nothing else you might repeat the Lord's Prayer often.  Remember, Labor on self denial for the good of others is really better paid for in the end than any other labor or pains of this world.
Sincerely,
Father

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [3], 1878-1897
transcription:
Elyria. Aug. 12th. 1878.
Anna Dear,
Guess you better come home.  Very glad you have had a good time. The Mother and the Marion want your help to make button holes &c.
Marion wants you to go our with her to Mr. Luiss' tomorrow to meet Helen Luiss.  
They are expecting Wilder and Mary every day.
Sincerely
Father

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Mr. J. M. Metcalf
Bowd. Coll. June 9th 1847
Dear Brother,
Your last letter was by me received upon the highway from the hand of a traveller whom I did not at first recognize. Your letter I think had been a good while due; at least, I had written to you several times after receiving a previous one from you. However, I do not know as there was any thing in any of my letters or communications which required an answer, or which would be worthy of any subsequent reference.
Sacred Poems By N. P. Willis, of the merits of which I suppose my opinion differs very little from yours; at least, most of the writing of N. P. W. I do not like and never did. I do not much admire the man himself. As for the proem to your criticism, it appears to be written is such perfect fashionable style, that I suppose we may fairly take it for granted that it does not mean any thing. N. P. Willis is perhaps the best specimen of a literary 'spoilt child.' Some of his first poems, written while he was quite young, in College, or about the time he graduated, were really very good - 'considerin' - with the defects to be sure of such circumstances, of precocious genius &c &c. But to be pardoned in first efforts.
But the undiscriminating, injudicious, almost unmeasured and undeserved praise which they received fairly turned the

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
poor fellows head. It showed thereby that he was not a really strongminded man; and made him, as you say, a conceited fop. In some other circumstances, such, for instance, as Genius usually meets with, he might have grown up a healthy vigorous writer, perhaps passed all his days for a man of sense. Wills' Sacred Poems are perhaps the best of all his poetic writings; his later poems show a repetition or increase of all their defects, without any more of real excellence.
I bought the volume on a certain occasion merely because it was the one I happened to see of the proper cost, appearance &c.
On the whole perhaps you & I should agree better upon N. P. Willis than upon Aesthetics in general, truth, beauty, utility, &c. or upon the real relative value of a book and a peck of corn
"An extremely malign disposition, when long denied any rent, will sometimes when circumstances are favorable thereto, produce a somewhat uncontrolable itch for scribbling which can be thoroughly relieved only by giving it free course." Pray what is the meaning, object, tendency, or point of all that? Or is it itself its own best illustration?
Words of counsel - for what young man? For [[?]] Senior? You had better take it all back
Question of Division & Settlement of Property at Milo. First, - how did you come to the idea of the sort of arrangement of thirds &c. a few years ago? You know I had & would have nothing at all to do with it then, & knew nothing at all of it. Whether that make it easier or worser now, I do not know. Was it like this. Charles W. Rich Cr. $1000,00 and compound interest for seventeen years. also Seventeen years labor at $400. per year and boarded, annuity at compound interest, after deducting

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
$100,00 per year as expenses. Mrs. A. M. Metcalf Cr. $1500, money & household [[furnt?]] with compound interest seventeen years; Also seventeen years labor at $150,00 per year and boarded, deducting $50.00 per year expenses. Annuity of $100,00 for seventeen years. To this last partners amount to be added or subtracted the value or cost of "broughting' up" sundry younger members of family
[next portion diagonally lined out]
As for instance I. S. M. Dr 9 years board at $50 interest annual per year, 13 years clothing & expenses at $50, interest annual per year. Cr. 1st year - 2d yr 50, 3d yr 50, fourth year 100, 5th yr 125, 6th yr. at school. 7th yr 150, 8th yr 200, 9th yr 200, 10th & 11th At school mostly 12th & 13th yrs 600 (200 of it cash earned elsewhere) all with annual interest, or any other reckoning However I guess it is generally allowed that the broughting up of so remarkably smart industrious hardworking & good natured young people as some I could name was not very expensive.
[end of diagonally lined out portion]
II However, supposing that matter all settled, and the exact relative proportions of the property rightfully belonging to each all definitely fixed upon there still remains to tell how much those proportions are now really worth - no very easy task either. Then if its value can be decided or determined, to tell what to do with it, is the next question.
There seem to be large difficulties in the way of almost any way of settling it I can think of at present. Some many be better than others. Think over the matter, if you have not already, and write to me about it. Is is the duty of all to counsel the parties, and keep them out of trouble, if it can be done. In counsel is safety & wisdom

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
As regards Charles & Almeda there is certainly danger, almost danger of a real quarrel. Charles, I know is willing to do and to do a good deal to assist Almeda, he has done much. he would be willing to do almost any thing if she would ever be willing to show or confess an obligation. She is certainly strange about that. I do not believe that she ever did really confess herself under an obligation to any one.
Now Chas. has certainly done a great deal for her, and he would feel a great deal better towards her, if she did not so curiously contrive to get round acknowledging it.
Not to have one's virtues appreciated and acknowledged is perhaps about the hardest of all trials for poor human nature
Charles I suppose is absolutely established & fixed as to how he will take back that East field & will not do it on no other conditions. Almeda wants him to take it back, and upon [no - crossed out] other conditions. She never did give up her will they say & does not mean to. Almeda says to frighten him, she will lease it out Chas. I suppose would rather give up the whole concern and all the other property he has in the world.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I did think I would get along a spell without that $40.00, pay my other bills and let the term bills go a spell longer but they have just lighted upon me for my bond which I am determined not to give, & perhaps I had better pay up what I can as soon as you can send that money convenently
Yr. br. I. S. Metcalfe
Write soon
Mr J. M. Metcalf
Bangor
Maine
