title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Bowd. Coll. June 25th, 1847
Brother Joseph,
I received a letter from you June 13 containing money, $35.00. I forget whether I have yet acknowledged its reception. I believe not, suppose I ought to have done it before now however.
Your last letter I received about one week since: and it probably deserves some what of answering. Some of it had become rather old for these time. Some things though ever improve by age.
As for "Jeremy Bentham," I believe you advise me to read more before I judge of him. I do not think I am very likely to read him much. There is a deal of truth in the old minister's remark that "it is wrong to read a good book; - there are so many better ones." If I should undertake to read every book which is really twice as [[truly?]] valuable as Bentham, I should have the work of more than one lifetime laid out. I guess that Bentham's warmest admirers do not think of denying his infidelity or Atheism. As to reading for ones self so as to judge, it is very plain that it will no do in all cases. Testimony is as valuable in the literary as in the physical world I am no more obliged to read "Paul de Kock" and "Eugene Sue" in order to determine they are not worth reading, than I am obliged to cross the Atlantic to determine the existence of such a city as Paris. One must have opinions upon books he has never read, as well as upon things he has never seen. Another thing - the guilt of Bentham in giving the utterance, the mighty 'bodying forth' to the great unspoken Atheism of the depraved human heart. Think it over again. It must be so - it is but just too. If Genius must have its glorious reward for its great and good, it must also

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
have its corresponding depth of degradation and punishment, when it violates its high responsibilities, and employs its mighty powers & influences in giving utterance to the evil and the bad of that humanity which its is its "mission" to elevate and purify. What is the guilt of Napoleon, of Jereboam the son of Nebat, of Voltaire, of Byron, of Bentham? Or rather, compared with theirs, what is the guilt of the very worst this world has ever seen of that class "Who never had a dozen thoughts in all their lives," Which shall be beaten with the most stripes.
As to your "objections" to my view of "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed." I do not take the passage out of its connection. It is its connection, not only the context, but the whole connection, the time, the place, the circumstances, the motives, the objects, the effects; it is this, it is all this, and all these, which convinces me that the passage can have no other rendering or meaning. 
2d I deny that the language is dubius - in the original - or even in their version of it, which could not be improved.
3d. There is a slight difference between "Whoso sheddeth &c." and "Multiply & replenish &c" "Whoso" is individual, particular, definite, pointed & could not be clothed in language more so. "Whoso" do eth so, shall be punished so. The other is general, universal, but not particular. In its true sense, it is undoubtedly a command, and as absolutely binding upon the human race as any other. A nation or a people refusing it entirely; doing like the "Areoi" of the Pacific, would probably perhaps be as guilty as a nation of idolaters, of pirates, or of murderers. It is one command, not to be sure the only one, wherein, the Antichrist, Mother of Abominations, has, in part, at least, set herself against the will of the Highest.
What were Prof. Goodwins great arguments? and what were his "chips and cobble stones." I believe I never heard Prof. Goodwin mention Cap. Pun. I have Rex Woods though & Prof. Upham, I did not call your "dust" argument; still it is worth minding.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
What shall I do when I get through at old Bowdoin? I have applied for a situation of some kind upon the "Lewiston Falls and Waterville Rail Road" survey. Am all ready to go into any thing any time on or after the twenty eighth day of July next (July 27th, 1847)
Shall I go West? What shall I do any how?
Where shall I get some money this summer? $100.00.
I like much our studies this term. One is "Smellie's Philosophy of Natural History," but we do not depend much upon the text book. We have some lectures upon Anatomy, Comparative Anatomy, Natural History, Physiology &c. scientifically considered; also plenty of anatomical subjects, specimens, cabinets and preparations; together with the most valuable & extensive and expensive, plates, books and so forth.
Also Lectures & examinations upon Mineralogy and Geology by to say the least I suppose one of the two greatest mineralogists on this side of the Atlantic at least. These lectures are in the Cabinet itself as a lecture room. Our other studies are "Wayland's Moral Science," and "Upham's Philosophy of the Will." I am most interested in the former. I am reading considerable upon Anatomy, and intend to somewhat upon Mineralogy and Geology [overwrites Botany]. Shall make some mineralogical excursions hereabouts I think.
It is somewhat exciting seasons here nowadays; Election times. Peucinian Election last Wednesday, Athenaean next Wednesday, the Theological was yesterday. The great interest is upon the Athenaean, next week. My own interests in it are very great; that is, for my friends.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Have you seen or read Headley's new book, "Washington and his Generals"? S. W. Furber presented the first volume to Lucy, the day I was in Bangor. I have not read the whole; interesting, but I guess hardly equal to "Napoleon and his Marshals"
Is Godman's Natural History in your Library?
What is the reason that Lucy, and Eliah, and Anne do not write to me? I have not even heard from that Milo Celebration, Pic Nic &c. yet. I do not understand why they do not write.
I heard Rev. Wm. S. Sewall of Brownville preach in Topsham, last Sabbath. Mr Swan Lyman Pomroy is to preach here next Sabbath.
Arthur Swasey has preached here four Sabbaths lately. He is certainly rather a good preacher for a youngster, he knows it far too well himself though.
I have heard something said of him as thought of for the Third or Central Church of Bangor. I may be prejudiced against the man, and against his intended wife; but as I think of them, I certainly hope A. Swasey will not be settled over that Church. I regard that that as likely to be a very important situation. It ought to be filled by a superior man, and a powerful man.
I suppose you have heard him preach somewhat. How? Is he the best of his class, as a preacher? I judge they do not have a great many great men graduate at that Institution nowadays; do they? Have you heard G. M. Adams [George Moulton Adams], J. H. Merrill, and H. M. Stone? Adams & Merrill are superior men. Adams is the very tall long necked fellow. Stood very high here. Drummond of the Junior Class, will come up. B. G. Snow is good, not very great

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Isaac
Engineering, Teaching, Bankers of Exeter
Settlement of property at home
Bowd. Coll. July 8th, 1847
Dear Brother,
Your letter of the sixth inst. was by me duly received this morning. As I happen just now to feel like it, I will endeavor to reply to it.
Engineering, "Plan may be a good one," damn with faint praise &c. rather cool at any rate
A college course may not be the best and most economical training for any occupation; it is certainly not the most economical one; but still is a good one for any business whatever, except that of a day laborer, is perhaps of no use for that, except as far as one's own happiness is concerned that is if one never wishes to rise from it; and may render one lasy, which is its usual effect.
Your idea of the duties of an Engineer, are perhaps a little erroneous, as far as overseeing Paddies &c. &c. is concerned. All that sort of thing is the business of the contractors, of those who build the road, and not of the engineers. Engineers find out, decide and direct, where, how, the road shall be built, and see that the contractors so build it, or cause their Paddies to.
I. S. M. "ought to be able to do something else equally as good quicker and easier" Do for pity's sake tell me what that ""something else" is - any thing - any where - any how - and I stand ready to "pitch into it." immediately, and just as if I meaned something too.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
My estimate of pay of Assistant Engineer was founded on personal knowledge. My friend Moses Leland Morse, who graduated here last year, with no sort of preparation, less fitted perhaps both by nature, habit, and education for the business than myself, obtained a situation as Assistant on the Lewiston & Waterville Rail Road. He received $1,25 per diem as Green hand for a few weeks. As soon as he learned the business a little, received and now receives $1,50 per diem, is Rod man in the levelling party.
E. Merrill Talbot of Turner, an acquaintance of mine, begun a few years ago on the Hartford & New Haven I believe. Had I suppose $1,50 per diem, at first, 2,00 per day summer & winter before he left there. Now has probably $1000, or 1200, per year on the Portsmouth and Concord R.R.
Engineers are employed by the year, (or by the job - till the road is done usually) two or three years) rather than by the month.
However, I suppose likely that there is not much of a chance of my getting any sort of a such situation in the business right away. These matters go not by merit, education or abilities) but by favor, the influence of rich relations, in which you know I happen to be especially poor I suppose it is much as Talbot wrote to me "Kissing goes by favor." 'every man who has a good situation in his power has also a relative to give it to."
I received Tuesday a letter from Uncle Joseph Stevens to whom I had written upon this subject. He seemed to approve of my views and course, and of my method of getting into the business.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
He said that as the Conn. River Road is completed, the Engineers with whom he is most acquainted are away. He knows some of the Engineers on the Vermont & Mass. Road, and also the Cheshire Road. and promised to make inquiries there and write to me.
They had lately received a letter from Mother, stating that Charles had been married three months. He wrote "they all had neglected to report the matter, I conclude they put it off till they could see whether he lived"!
Humphrey has returned from the West, and is expected at Warwick in a week. Maria is at home, &c. Want I should "come and see them "as soon as I am dismissed." &c.
As for teaching I have pretty much made up my mind never to teach any more. I do not like it. It is not my "calling." While in College, I was not my own man, must do whatever I could for money. I am so near through now that I begin to feel quite independent; even if I am a hundred or two in debt. I may be obliged to teach this Fall. If I go West probably shall; but, if not, I rather guess not.
As for the Waterville & Bangor R. R. I wish you would keep me constantly informed of every thing you can learn about Is this "Moor" of Waterville, or where?
Allow me to congratulate you upon your success in SOT Election, not however that I think that 'P. W. P.' or 'J.G. P. W. P.' or "J. G. N. P. G. W. P.' or any more of them are comparable to "Pres. of Ath. Soc."
What do you mean by "Rich Man's preacher"? I think neither Adams or Merrill very great men.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
The "Barker" of whom you speak was probably not (Lewis) He is a little lawyer (or doctor) at Stetson, small potatoes, and been crazy at that. If it was a little lame fellow, it was "Mark." If a very long tongued, polititian &c celebrated abolitionist and temperance man, it was David, rather a shallow fellow I say. rather smart naturally, but been sick and perhaps insane some, and slightly weakened. If a rough old farmer, it was Nathaniel. If the best one of the lot, both physically & intellectually a smart, fine fellow, it was my friend "Daniel." I liked him much.
The other brother "Noah" I have hardly seen. He is a regular old rough woods surveyor, and wears leather trousers come up to his shoulders, and is probably a smart and capable business man. I went to Stetson Pond with "Nat,", "Dan," "Mark," &c. in Nat's hay waggon, and saw "Lewis" at Stetson Mills.
Who is Robert Fernald? Where knew you him?
Presume you had a fine time at Milo, wish I had been there
Property settlement
$50, per annum, 25 years is at compound interest $639,167 1/2, is it? It seems small does it not. However, I think likely it is all right and for the best that it should be settled at some rate, not much matter how. Is the household furniture &c. &c. reckoned in that arrangement? or what & how of it? What does Mother do with the Line Cow. The keeping &c. will not be running behind hand, will it?
Is Charles likely to help me to any money anyway? You see, I must have some, at some rate, and that in about a fortnight. If there is no other way can you or Eliah contrive to get some to lend me a spell? Write me
I hope you, as well as some other folks will write to me again very soon. 
Aff. I. S. Metcalfe

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
It is well those shingles of Charles are Cedar; they would rot before the reach Bangor. What does the man do for Provisions and taxes, I should like to know.
Is he, or are they, likely to do any thing towards getting some money for me this summer? It certainly ought to be done.
Suppose I can, what do you think of the expediency of my getting upon the Rail Road anywhere? of intending to make myself an Engineer? Should I be fitted for such business, or likely to succeed in it?
I know that I can do better in something else than I can in School teaching, for I dislike it too much ever to take sufficient interest in it, to reach extended success. The whole heart must be in any thing to ensure success in it. Mine, I believe could not be in teaching as a permanent profession.
As I do not intend to follow it as a profession is it not, the quicker I give it up entirely the better for me every way? If I can earn say from twenty or thirty to fifty or sixty dolls. per month besides board & expenses, to begin with, as an Engineer's assistant, had I not better go into it? that is if I can get the chance. and why can I not? and succeed in it? An active, able bodied, rugged young man, familiar with labor, and exposure, professed of mind, and of education, with a disposition to do. What hinders
Please to write again soon as convenient
Aff. I. S. Metcalfe

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Brother J. M.
I did expect to intend to go to your city and conference with you by the words of our mouths on, or rather, upon the very next day after this same day. of Lebec Ric Nic.
You did advise me I believe that I should do something, or labor, somehow, "to profit." Well I have been laboring every essentially upon this poor man rich his haying. By the way, permit me here to commend this man, who will probably be the bearer of this epistle, to your kind and respectful consideration; he being as I do fully consider, a very first rate good sort of a man, in fact a very clever sort of a man;
Well, I must forgot what I begin to write, but there is an old and very venerable proverb, one, by the way, in which I take much comfort often time, which positively affirms that "The Lame & the Lazy shall be provided for." Well so it happened in this case that I being at the time diligently laboring in the vineyard, I mean the hayfield, that is on the cart pitching [[of?]] the hayton in the Barn, of this same man of whom I hereinbefore spake

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Foxcroft, Sat. March 23, 1844
Dear Brother
We are all situated very comfortably here together, with pleasant rooms, and very near the Academy.
We have got a rather large school for spring term, nearly a hundred now, and many more coming in yet.
The school is however of hardly so high a character as last fall; a great many new scholars, especially from round these two villages, a rude as well as ignorant set many of them.
Every thing goes on smoothly however. I am considerably more occupied in school, hearing recitations, at least. I have one very good class in Algebra, 12 or 15. Lucy is in it & Miss [[Bash?]]. All the Arithmetic in school. 2 pretty large classes. 1st Arith. contains more than a dozen ladies, besides boys; 2 classes in Eng. Grammar One of my Grammar classes contains between 30 & 40, the other a dozen or so. One recitation too at my room, at present, besides some occasional assistance. I generally study about 3 hours in the day, besides studying or writing in the evening, when not otherwise engaged. I get alonge finely in study for time spent. Study in own room entirely, and in the Academy only teaching.
I have paid $5,50 to Mr. Briggs, by borrowing some of Joseph I dont know but I shall have to borrow some money, before I can get my school money.
I have had to buy two or three dollars worth of books, lately. I think it would be a good plan to haul some potatoes to Bangor, if you can get 2/s. per. bu. for them. The cash would be much better than work or promises! What is the prospect of a market for hay?

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I have been looking over some of my last summer's records. I find we got in of your part of the hay about 23 loads or so what we considered as much as 15 or 20 tons. I suppose I ought to have as much as 4 or 5 tons of good hay from it. at least. The Peas and the Wheat would amount to little any way. As to the potatoes, there were, according to Joseph's account, 322 bushels in all, on that which I cultivated. I dont know whether there would be 100 bu. for my share after paying for the digging & loss by frost. I did 48 days works exactly upon the potatoes; the oxen did 12 or 13 days; & the digging was 23 days work, says Joseph. The seed was about 55 bushels, & 84 days work, would make dear potatoes, without reckoning the manure or soil. If I had a hundred bushels for mine, it would make about two bushels per day for my labor, and 'pay in taters,' 48 days. Joseph says the digging took 23 days in all. 10 out west 8 1/2 on intervale, & 4 1/2 in the corn field. It was agreed you know that you should do the digging & take it out of the potatoes at the winter or spring prices. I believe.
It would seem that I ought to have something from my last summers work, to help me along this summer or spring. I. S. Metcalfe
[written at bottom of page, upside down:]
I have bought a half ream, of just such paper as this sheet for only $1,12 1/2 or so. less than 12 1/2 per quire. So it is better for you to take of this than to give 25 or 33 for that about as good, by the quire. (This paper is good enough for any common purposes. Cheap. 
[written along top of page, upside down:]
I believe it is a great deal better way to sell hay or potatoes or anything else you sell, right off in a lump for cash or something like it, at much less prices, than to sell, a little here & a little there, for that poorest of all pay, promises.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Foxcroft March 24th 1844.
Dear Brother Charles, & Sister "Meady"
If it would do any good I would apologise for not writing before, as I intended; but since it is past and I can't help it I will say nothing about it. I have thought considerable about you Charles, and the way you get along "keeping house"; but when you marry an Irish lady from the "old country" who knows very little about housekeeping, all the knowledge which you may gain on the subject this winter will come in requisition, I assure you. Our good friend Bush, where we board is an Englishman; - his wife an Irish woman, who, I suspect, from appearances, was rather ignorant about domestic affairs when they "came over" eight years ago; for Mr. B. seems to help considerable about household matters, - chopping up the hash, making the cof[[fee?]] &c &c. She has four children to take care of however, besides we four boarders, so that she needs some help. We are quite pleasantly situated here all together with a parlor and two bedrooms - mine has a fire in it - . We are very near the Academy which is a good thing, especially in such stormy weather as we have had for a few days past. We step from the back door into the Academy yard. Isaac is digging into Latin & Greek as usual, - and "dipping occasionally" into an "extended mathematical course" as he says; viz. Smyth's Algebra, (the one used in College.) Joseph studies Algebra, Chemistry & Surveying; - and I study Algebra, Uphams Mental Philosophy (which is outrageous h[[ard?]]) and French. I get along pretty well in Algebra, much better than I expected. Isaac bought one new French book (price 33 1/3 cts.) and the rest I borrow. If Ann comes home long enough before the close of the term, to make it worth while, I desire her to send me her Dictionary, - (Boyer's) When you

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
get a letter from Mother you must send it to us. We sent a letter to her last week. Almeida you & Charles must write us a good long letter with lots of good sage advice; for we need it, you may depend. Love and kisses to the little folks. Tell Lucy & James I remember them & little Siery & want them to be good children, and I will tell them all about little roguish "Thomas & Caroline" Bush when I come home. I have had a bad cold since I have been here, but I think I feel better for going out every day. In haste - from Sister Lucy.
Mr. Charles W. Rich
Milo Maine
Isaac & Lucy
Mar. 23d/44
Foxcroft

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Richmond, Jan. 24th 1846
Dear Brother Charles
I have for some time had it in contemplation, to write a letter specifically to you. I believe I write an abundance of letters to you all, more than I ever receive, I guess; and I usually write to you all together there at Milo, all directed to Mother, perhaps. This time, however, I mean to write a letter, and direct it solely to you, hoping, if it be possible, to call forth an answer from you. Really it is no more than fair. I was about to say I hardly ever received a letter from you, very few, certainly, and those on business, or when there was no one but yourself at home to write.
I know just how it is, how one feels when they are at work all the time, & rarely never write any. I know how it is, for I have felt the same; my experience you know, has not been confined any one method or habit of life. But I do not think it is a good plan. The advantages of writing letters to friends are not small, advantages to the mind; it tends to draw the mind a little away from the constant care & attention to the little things in one's own peculiar sphere, 'a care which tends to narrow the mind down to itself'; to enlarge & liberalize the sphere of thought, & thus the mind. Any thing which tends to divert the continual current of thought from the here and the now, to the distant, the future, or the past is a benefit to the mind. The more any one writes, the easier they find it, and the more they realize its advantages &

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
the contrary; but a disinclination to write in any one, only shows that they need to write the more. You do write business letters. Now the amount or number of letters one writes makes not much difference. It is about as much work, and more trouble to write a letter once or twice a year, as once or twice a day. I do hope you will, according to the advice Mother writes in a letter I received today, that Uncle Joseph sent to you 'bow yourself with a mighty effort & strain out at least one letter'
I see by what Mother & Lucy write that you are sort of discontented, and want to go west. Now I hardly know about such policy. The time to move about is before one settles at all. I think, generally, when one has once settled, it is better to stick, even if it happens not to be the very best place. A moving man, is always poor; and perhaps never contented If I were you, I think I would settle down contented, and enjoy myself, take the comfort of life. You have, 'from circumstances,' taken every thing by the hardest, long enough. It is not worth awhile. Man is made to enjoy himself, in this life too. It is best to do it, when one can. You have, ought to have, -have property enough to get along comfortably; are old enough to enjoy the comforts of life, by & by if you live, you will have lost your relish for them; your character is formed; your reputation established, true perhaps it is not, at Milo, so high a one, in all respects, as you really deserve, but it might be easier raising it there, than forming a entire new one somewhere else Now why not, get married, settle down, see your children grow up around you, with prospect of quiet & happy old age, when it comes, in short, enjoy life, as it passes along? But if you cannot so do, and be so contented, I advise you by all means to go

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
take a trip west, and see the country there; determine to go, if go you must, and go; not let little obstacles hinder you. It will cost something, but you have something. You can go if you want & must But be cautious. Every country has its advantages and its disadvantages, and the disadvantages of moving are very great. if you should settle somewhere else, and in the end not get suited any better, you would be, all things considered, ten fold worse off than before. Farming, you know, has been very much worse than usual the past year.
Lucy wrote to me about your trouble with Everett for Josephs money. Everett is little mean puppy, and Macomber a fool. but what a miserable thing the law is. You must look out that being dragged into it so much, does not make you quarrelsome it must vex one to death almost. I believe it is usually best, both [[in?]] pecuniary & moral view, to give up a case, first thing rather than to go to law & gain it. Lucy wrote she thought likely you would join the 'Sons of Temperance.' I suppose I am a little prejudiced against those secret societies. To be sure I belong to one or two secret societies, but of a different character, purely literary. The S.O.T. I know very little about whether it is any better than the Odd Fellows I know not, its advantages would be less, cost less, are on a smaller scale. At any rate I should prefer to join a lodge or tent, better off than one there would probably be. Odd Fellows initiation fee is $20,00 & a constant weekly tax of ,06 1/4 or ,12 1/2. If any member is sick unable to work they have a regular weekly allowance of $5,00 per week & every attention. A young man near here, has been sick all winter Typhus fever; belongs to O.F. & S.O.T. both and has received regularly $8,00 per week some months! I have been solicited to join I.O. of O.F. but have no such intention. I do not know enough to decide. It is probably advantage to men in business making money, but not saving kind of Life Assurance. Your Brother I.S.M.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I received a letter from Joseph the other day. He was then unwell & commanded by Dr. McRuer to abstain from the counting room a few days. I hardly know what to think of him & his health. If the business thus disagrees with him, he better quit it. Perhaps he has been more hurried than usual lately. In reply to a query of mine, as to his line of conduct towards the 'fair sex' he says. 'it is a straight line, but so distant can't tell whether divergent parallel, or convergent!
Mr. Charles W. Rich
Milo
Maine
My school is 2 weeks longer I shall go to Brunswick in a few days after.
Isaac
Jan'y 24th/46
Richmond

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Bowd. Coll. March 29th '46
Dear Brother
Mr. James Newton, of Adrian Michigan, formerly of Bangor, Maine; for four years past a member of Bowdoin College, and graduated therefrom last August, now an Alumnus of Bowd. Coll. and member of the 'Class of '45' having spent 7 or 8 months past in Teaching School in the Town of Brunswick and vicinity, having been also for nearly a year past an Assistant Clerk in the Post Office Department of said Brunswick, by which operations and occupations, it is supposed that he has acquired several dollars more of less of lucre, is now about to visit your worshipful city of Bangor, with intent to put himself to a regular course of Theological Study, under the teaching of Rev Dr Pond assisted by Rev Messrs Sheppard and Smithe of said Bangor - therefore, I will try and write some letters unto you, and certain other members of 'our folks, to send by him, as he has kindly offered to take charge of any such affair, and you will probably receive such letter or letters in about 8 or 10 days from this present time.
There are several rather important faults in the introduction to this letter, as you will readily perceive, but you can perhaps pardon them. An apology for its length may possibly be found in the substance of the 'main body' of the letter.
I do not know as I have much or any thing to write that will prove at all interesting to any of you. But as my letters have all that reproach, I will not insist upon it as a reason

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
About as much of interest as any we poor mewed up students have attached to the various developments of 'Society matters.' But - as you know little about them, you would understand little, and consequently would be little interested in such matters. You may, or may not, be aware that, the rivalry between these societies is very great, and apparently increasing. I mean the secret societies. - Also that am a member of the DKE [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] a new society, but a very flourishing one, and which bids fair soon to stand almost without or above, a rival. The [Greek letters psi, nu] to which Thomas Tash belongs, and to which he intended I should belong, which perhaps I might then have joined, if I had come here first a little better dressed, and which I should have joined finally, if I had chosen the [Greek letters psi, nu] I was quite very favorably inclined to at first. They have some advantages, firmly established, and a high reputation; but now degenerated and at the same time, swollen awfully. The [Greek letters psi, nu] were good as pie to DKE [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon] at first, very friendly, but, behold - the little child has assumed the voice and stature of a man, their equal, and ready & able to cope with them on their own ground, constantly prospering. Ah! they feared the young giant to late, crush him while his strength is yet green. Ah! they cannot do it! As soon as I returned to College this spring, it commenced last fall, I was aware that a great effort was being made to crush DKE [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon], in every way, by abuse & slander personal & social, smeering & scorn, &c., all open politeness though of course - but meanness will fail
The Sophomores had their yearly class election of poet & orator Mar. 13 [Greek letters psi, nu] made every effort, all classes influence, to elect their great man of the class, attached much importance to it, but all failed - My friend and Brother I. W. Case of Levant, you have seen him, was elected.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
The elections of the other classes have turned out somewhat similarly. [Greek letters psi, nu] are failing. They are making great efforts though, directing their attention already to the Society election, which takes place at the beginning of the summer term. It is rather doubtful which way it will eventually turn.
You know there are two literary Societies in College the Athenaean & Peucinian, commonly called 'General Societies All the students belong to one or the other. Each posses a fine library, about 4,000 volumes each, & every thing to suit. They are very much alike, meet weekly or two. Exercises are regular declamations, discussions, original dissertations and declamations, and a paper. They are truly valuable Societies Every graduate of Bowd. Coll. and there many illustrious names, is enrolled among one or the other General Societies.
Each of these Societies has every spring term an Anniversary, (they were this will) An orator & poet, from the Sen Class, elected the year before, deliver an oration & poem public, to a crowded audience, And then the Society X adjourns to Commons Hall - - 
The rivalry between Athena & Peucinia, the Parthenon and the Pine, has always been very great, but lately the new secret societies attract so much attention, it is feared the General Societies lose interest.
Besides these there are two Societies, the Theological & the Christian Union, Unitarian affair, have considerable libraries Also the Caluvian & the Phi Alpha have two valuable cabinets of curiosities, Natural History &c.
X The Athenaean Peucinian General societies have also a celebration at Commencement

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Isaac Mar 29 -
/46
Bowd

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
The Athenaean Society of Bowd. Coll. celebrated its 28th anniversary in the Baptist Church, on Monday evening Mar. 30th, 1846, at 7 oclock. Music by the Brunswick Band, Chaplain Rev. Mr. Wheeler of Topsham.
The Oration by Jairus Ware Perry of Sweden Oxford [[Me?]] familiarly called by many in College the 'Oxford Bear' A great stout man, with a mind like his body powerful and well developed, perhaps not so polished as some.
Subject of Oration was the Reciprocal influence of Religion and Government.' A strong, well written argumentative oration, displaying deep, sound original thought, well applied.
The Poet regularly chosen was Albion Paris Spinney of Elliot, but he is absent and a few weeks since sent word that he could not be here. As substitute, Robert Hartly Dunlap Esq. now of Boston, graduated in 1842, being in town, delivered a poem The poem was a beautiful affair, the most elegant poem I ever heard, full of wit and gems of sparkling beauty. It cannot be described, any more than forgotten. 
After the Oration & Poem, the Society moved in Procession to Commons Hall where an elegant & substantial supper had been prepared. Roast Turkeys in abundance and every thing else to match. Then an abundant dessert of all kinds of fruit nuts &c & lemonade, after which came the 'feast of reason & the flow of soul' Speeches sentiments, jokes, joy, & songs, till 12 or 1 oclock Then after 9 cheers for Athena, more for her Library & then for her

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
President, most throw themselves upon their uneasy couches to be called thence, dull & haggard enough, by the hated prayer bell. For myself the excitement and the digestion are not very good to go to sleep upon, and I sometimes walk and talk an hour or two, till the mind is cooled and the body relaxed, and then a little sleep refreshes one somewhat.
The Peucinian Society of Bowd. Coll. celebrated its 40th anniversary, at the Congregationalist vestry, on Tuesday eve, March 31st. Same music.
Chaplain Rev. Elijah Kellogg of Harpswell. Oration by William W. Rice of Winchendon Mass. Subject, The Ideal World as distinct from the Material and manifesting itself in the Works of Art.
A very highly polished, poetical, ornamental oration more elegant than the other but lacking in its deep sound, original thought, polish not strength
Poem by Edwin B. Webb of New Castle. The man is perhaps not a natural poet, you know the proverb 'Poeta nascitur, non fit,' 'The poet is born, not made' and was elected by Society intrigues, instead of a true Poet F. L. Knight a DKE [Greek letters delta, kappa, epsilon], who should have had it. However Webb is a man of most indefatigable study and application. He has spent months upon his poem, every line was evidently elaborated almost painfully, and smelt of the midnight oil, still the poem showed how much could be done by laborious application, and was by no means a failure, had considerable sound thought, and many smooth lines.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
The New Great Church here was dedicated on March 18th It is a magnificent affair, but I could hardly give you any idea of it. How I wish you could see it. When I graduate you may some of you come and see how I look in it! The great gothic windows are of stained glass, and, and the 'dim religious light' that streams through those old columns & gothic arches gray, is certainly splendid.
At the Dedication the big house was filled and crowded with people, many extra seats, too in the aisles and platforms. The audience was probably somewhere near 1500 in number.
The dedicatory sermon was by the pastor Rev. George Eliashib Adams, and was his master effort.
Psalm 93.5. Holiness becometh thy house, O Lord, forever.
It described the object of a church as differing from other buildings, and what it should be in every respect. Architecture & all, vindicates this church. Holiness its object, means of promotion. There were very many misisters present, of whom took part in the exercises. Rev. Mr. Clement of Topsham Rev Messrs Palmer & Fisk of Bath. Rev Mr Parsons of Freeport and Rev Mr Drummond of Lewiston, besides Rev J. W. Chickering of Portland, who made the dedicatory prayer, which was truly splendid. The said JW Chickering is a great man, and no mistake He preached here one Sabbath two of the best sermons I ever heard
The Church is beautifully painted inside, all imitation of oak, very skillfully done by some of the best painters of the U.S. N.Y men, and looks splendid

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Isaac Bowd
March '46
2

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Bowd. Coll. March 1st, 1847
Dear Brother,
I was very much gratified a few days since by receiving a letter, or rather part of one, from you. It was so long since I had seen any of your hand writing, that the very sight of it seemed to do me good.
I really think you ought to write more, the only reason you do not like to write is that you are not enough in the habit of it. However you succeeded so well in this effort that I hope you will try it again, and that frequently.
I am very much obliged to you for your kind invitation to the wedding. I hardly know of any thing which could give me so great pleasure as to be present upon that interesting occasion; but I fear I shall be compelled to deny myself the wished for privelige.
Besides the fact that I am out of funds and so much in debt that I ought to avoid the expense of a journey; it is now right in perhaps the most important part of the most important term of the whole fours course; Prof. Cleaveland's lectures.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
We do not have to study so hard now as sometimes in the former part of the course, but it is more important to be here, on account of the lectures, which one cannot well get any where else, if one wishes to keep along with his class, he might about as well lose the term, as a single week of it.
So, I suppose, if I stay in College the rest of my course, I must, or had better at least, keep close to it, the little while longer I have.
My compliments, best love and deepest respect to the bride that is to be. All happiness and all blessings make for you both an Eden here, and -
"Like summer's beam,
And summer's stream
May you float on in joy to seek
A calmer sea, where storms shall cease -
A purer sky, where all is peace."
As for that taxing affair, I really cannot help thinking it rather a dirty business in the selectmen of your town of Milo. In the first place, as a general thing students are not taxed at all, even where they have a regular residence. Then it is very different with me from what it would be in case of a young man who has a father living, is supplied with his funds &c. &c. from a home. Moreover, I have been in Milo just about

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
seven or eight weeks within four years past; and the last place in which I had a strictly legal residence, was not at any rate in Milo; Mr Tash's paper would prove that.
I do not know but it is best to pay [[the?]] [[?]] it is such a small affair, rather than have just now the trouble about it: but, it may not be two years before they have a lawsuit upon them for repayment.
If I study Law, that will probably be my first case, after I am admitted to the Bar. If I do not, there are enough that will. It ought to cost them a few hundreds for their dirty meanness.
I wish you would just ask them how many years they intend to keep it up; how long while I am teaching an Academy in Wisconsin, engineer on the Rocky Mountain Rail Road, or after I am Senator from Oregon! Let me calculate upon it.
If I know who I believe I would write them.
I am right glad to hear of your temperance doings; hope you will kill out Monroe, at any rate. Is he the only one?
I hope you will give me the pleasure of hearing from you again. I should like much to know all about your business, farming affairs, &c.
Your Affectionate brother
I. S. Metcalfe

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Chas. W. Rich Esq.
Milo
Maine
I. S. Metcalf Bowd
Feb. 29 '47

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Jonesboro, Union Co, Illinois
Sabbath March 7, 1852
Dear Brother Charles
Your letter came safely to hand last evening. How long the time it takes for letters to go, especially in the winter season. My time is so fully occupied that I believe I must write today; especially as we have here no afternoon meeting. Meeting are always at eleven oclock and in the evening; never in the afternoon. So, for one who has no other leisure the afternoon is a fine time to write letters home.
I wish I could visit you & spend some of these Sabbaths or winter evenings, or even help you get up a wood pile a day or two. I am quite comfortably situated here in most respects, very much so for this country, but it seems to be a great way off. - a great ways in fact from every where that I care any thing about.
I am very much obliged to you for writing of all the news at Milo. You can hardly imagine how good it seems to one so far off, to hear every thing from about home. I presume that before this time you have had a good time to get up your wood. Probably though there is lots of snow there yet. Here it has been what we should call spring weather at the East for a long time

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
In fact ever since the last week of January. The grass & grain have started considerable. The fruit trees were injured by the extraordinary cold weather, so they say there can be no fruit this year at least, even if the Peach trees, are not killed entirely. They do not look as if they could have any leave at all this year. Some of the earlier forest trees are in full bloom; the hazel bushes long ago, &c.
It seems you are likely to have quite a brood of Partridges in Milo. Is Mr Partridge pretty popular there? does he really improve as a preacher?
Did you sow any winter wheat last summer or fall? I think you would do well to try it thoroughly, put it on your best land, and give it a fair chance. There seems little use in trying spring wheat anymore there.
I do not know but your people will all go off to California yet from that region. That is all that are able. Here they are going and coming all the time. The journey is not near so great from here. A great portion at first from all this region went overland to California, by thousands. And this emigration still continues somewhat, but very many are going this winter by N.O. & Panama. And every month great numbers are come back with all degrees of success from a fortune to sickness & death.
I hardly see why Everett should want to go, well situated as he is, lately married, & not fond of hard work either. If he really wanted to go, he would do better to go to remain, take every thing with him & never come back. I would if I went. It is a good chance for any one who wishes to more to go into a new state prospering as that must & prosper with it

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I have about concluded not to go East this spring. I will be very difficult for me to get away at all. The journey is a long and difficult one at this season. And moreover the expense is not a little. If I do not go this spring, I shall attempt to have a longer time at my command in the summer. I mean to be away quite a long time this summer.
Did I write to you about my horse? I bought a horse awhile ago or a colt which I think will make a fine horse, and which I like very much. 'John' is not yet three years old, very large, finely formed, high spirited, courageous, but kind & gentle as you please. He has cost me $55.00, and I could have sold him for 70. at least since I got him. As long as I stay he here he will be earning money for me all the time, and if nothing ill happens to injure him I may sell him for 100, some day. I have become very fond of riding hose back. It is almost the only way of riding here. I ride a great deal of the time and like it very much. I have got so that I am entirely at home in a good saddle, and it does not tire me in the least even to ride all the time. I should enjoy nothing better than to ride horseback across the country from here to Maine if I had only time for it. It would be quite a ride would it not? If I had another horse like my John, riding first one then the other, making an easy journey and then selling the pair at the East for three or four hundred dollars! how would it do?
I am quite pleasantly situated here now, or shall be this summer, I think. I have charge of 30 miles of Road from Jonesboro south. There is a good deal of heavy work on it, enough to keep me riding pretty busily upon it, I expect.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I shall live at Jonesboro, which is perhaps the most pleasant place in Southern Illinois.
My greatest difficulty is like to be the lack of suitable assistants. It is hard getting good sub engineers here
I consider Kossuth the greatest man of the age, and regret my being away here almost ore than any thing else because it deprives me of the opportunity of hearing him. As for France, it seems as if the whole nation were almost below contempt for suffering themselves to be so used. However I suppose there are many circumstances which we can hardly understand, which should moderate our judgment.
What a great thing that Maine Liquor Law is I have been very proud of my state since that Law is carried out so well.
Probably other states will soon follow the example Even Illinois had taken one step. A law prohibiting all sales of liquor in less quantity than a quart, passed a year since. Some thought, one would think, understand it that they must drink a quart!
However perhaps it does some good.
Well I must stop. Kiss Charley & Josie for me &c
Please write to me often Sincerely I. S. M.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Isaac Jonesboro
May 52
Illinois Central R. R. Office
Jonesboro, Union Co., Illinois
Monday, May 9, 1852
Dear Brother Charles
It is sometime since I have heard from you. Letters seem to be scarce from all directions lately. I suppose you are just getting busy about your Farming. And I should like to know how you are getting along with it. Here putting the crop in the ground is nearly through with, though as this spring has been unusually backward, cold, and wet, some are still planting corn. In about one month from now the farmers will be harvesting wheat. before you will get done sowing perhaps.
Here wheat is sown in the Fall, August to November, oats &c. in February & March. Corn any time after the first of April. Wheat harvest is in June, oats July, and corn about all the year round. The farmers in their shiftless improvidence, often let their corn crop remain in the field gathering it only as they want to use or feed to cattle all winter. The length of the season is certainly some advantage to the farmer, if he be only industrious enough to avail himself of it. It is worth something to be able to plough and sow all the year round as the farmers can almost here. If they would or could only work how fast farmers could get rich here. I know one man from Vermont on the Prairie 40 miles north of here who when I was there in April had sowed 170 acres of oats, doing all the work himself except the help of a boy 12 years old. By this time I suppose he has big corn fields planted too. And probably all the help he will have will be to hire the oats cut down at 30 or 40 cents per acre. Such farming must be profitable. It is land that produces good crops too.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
This country looks splendidly now. There is an exuberant luxuriousness in the vegetation, and a rich fullness in the forest foliage which is never seen I think at the north.
They are lately commencing raising wheat here in this hill land, and with fine success. The wheat fields look extra well now I think, about waist high, very thick & high colored. 
Have you got any winter wheat growing this year? I think you do well to give it a fair trial upon your best land. You have, it seems, very little encouragement to try spring wheat much more.
I wish they could get the Flax Culture started well in Maine. I believe or hope it would do well.
What have you done for orcharding this spring? I am inclined to consider that one the best things for you. How do our little trees of last spring from Uncle Natty prosper? And your young nursery. You know I feel an interest in everything there.
We are doing not much here nowadays, just keeping along, doing a little, waiting, and getting our wages. There is some delay in getting the work under contract. Some great London Capatalists are trying to get the whole road to build & equip. They want no money, only the Companys land Bonds. It is a great job. I think very likely that they will get is. Their agent, a Mr Fitzgibbon from London passed through here a few days since looking at the country. He is the best looking English business man I ever saw. This delay keeps us here lying on our oars. I want to go East and perhaps shall before a great while.
I wish you and Almeda would write to me oftener than you do. I want to hear from you all all the little ones, to whom much love.
Sincerely
I. S.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Steamboat Golden State, Ohio River, Sand Bars & Fog Banks
Monday Sept. 27 1853
Dear Brother Charles
We have written several letters to the rest of the folks while on our Journey. But if they were at Bangor, you may not see them, and might like to hear from us. We had a very pleasant time, both at Bangor, at Brunswick, and at Dunbarton. We left Dunbarton Sept. 15, and arrived at New York City the next morning, where I called upon Cousin Caleb Metcalf, who is very pleasantly situated there. He has bought a beautiful place just out of Town, very handsome Chateau Cottage, very finely situated, partly overlooking the City, and a beautiful Pond; Eleven acres of land, with, I believe, more than a thousand Fruit Trees. On the whole, a very eligible situation I judge, one of the finest, in many respects about Worcester, It is a little more than a mile out of the business part of the City. Caleb Metcalf I judge is thriving; is head of one of the Worcester Grammar Schools, you know, which gives him a pretty good salary. He talks of going down to Maine some time.
We stopped at New York City a day or two, then went up to Troy, and stopped awhile, then to Cleveland and stopped over the Sabbath, then to Cincinnati, where we were obliged to wait awhile, and after we did get fairly upon a

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Steamboat for St. Louis, we have been waiting along, progressing very slowly. The River is very low, the boat is liable to be stopped on a Sand Bar occasionally The nights are very foggy so that we are obliged to lay up most of the night, and I do not expect hardly to reach Jonesboro even tomorrow.
The Ohio River is a beautiful place to travel, always some thing pleasant & interesting to be seen, and one can but enjoy journeying on it. It is less pleasant however when the water is so very low, as it now is, so that from the boat one cannot see over the banks for most of the way, even from the upper decks; the same banks that at some seasons are all overflowed.
What is the story I heard about your being about to sell your farm? Is there any thing in? If you can sell it advantageously, where will you go, or what will you do? Milo certainly does not seem a very good place to stay. But upon the principle that when things are at the worst they must mend, it is a bad place, and now is a bad time to leave it, or at least to dispose of property there. I presume you have consulted Eliah & Samuel and they are  much better judges of property matters in that region than I could be of course.
Would you in any circumstances come out West if you did or could dispose of your property there? I suppose your farm is about as profitable one for its saleable value as you could have thereabout.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Monday morn Sept. 20 - Isaac just came to me and said "Do you wish to write anything to Mrs. Albina Rich? I was certainly very glad of the opportunity, and embrace it with pleasure. We have hardly heard anything from you since we left you - have been moving about so much that letters could not reach us very readily - We shall hope to find some at Jonesboro, when we reach there. It is difficult telling when this will be, - we are obliged to stop so much every night there comes a dense fog. But we are having, on the whole a very pleasant journey. I never enjoyed any method of travelling, I think, so much as this steamboating on the river. There is never so much motion to the boat as to occasion sickness, and the scenery is fine - the banks on both sides are very beautiful. We sit on the deck a good deal, watching them. The forests all along our way, are magnificent - great tall trees, and no underbrush.
My thoughts very often wander to "Cedar Grove" and I love to live over again those happy weeks we passed with you. How much you did do for us - It is very pleasant for me to think of that visit - How I should love to see Charlie and little Josie - dear little fellows - Tell Charlie Aunt Nettie never will forget him, and hopes he will be the very best boy in the world, and make his mother happy every day. I suppose he has no Lizzie to play with

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Ohio River Sept 27th/52
him now. You must miss Almeida very much. We take it for granted she is married, and gone to a new home, though we have heard nothing about it. The boat is going quite fast now, and shakes my table so effectually, that this writing is certainly not the better for it - but you will excuse it. Hope we shall hear from you very soon. You have so much to attend to, that I hardly dare ask you to write, but I should most happy to receive even two or three lines from you -
Most truly yours
Antoinette.
I suppose your harvesting is about completed ere this, and it is now cold frosty weather at Milo I would much like to hear how your crops turn out, corn, oats, potatoes, and whether you succeeded in receiving them successfully. Do you sell off any of your stock this Fall? Is hay really likely to be so very high there? What is done with Almeda's place there?
I hope you will write to us frequently, and we will do our part of the correspondence. How prosper your P. R. D. S. of T.?
Love to Charlie & Josie. Sincerely, I. S.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Du Quoin, Perry Co. Illinois
Aug. 13. 1853
Dear Brother Charles
It seems some time, really a long time, since we have heard from you directly. I wish, we wish, you would write to us oftener than you do. It would seem to be quite a comfort just to hear from a cool place this warm weather that we have here. We are said however to be very much favored with cool weather this summer. June was very warm, thermometer about 100 in the shade regularly day after day. but nearly the whole month of July was quite cool, astonishingly so to the natives.
But now for a week or two the heat has come back in full force. Down in Maine you can hardly have an idea of the enervating effect of such weather, when the only effort that seems possible, and that a great one, is to sit in the shadiest place or coolest side of the house to be found. I tell you Maine seems almost a Paradise to one here nowadays, and one good full breath of that bracing air worth a small farm. I expect to have to come Down East to live one of these days. By the way, I should like to swap

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Farm with you, I expect I have got plenty of land here that will yield better crops without any manure or without ever seeing a hoe than yours will with all manure & cultivation.
I am investing all the money I can raise in lands about here, and think I can make it profitable, even if I do not like the country myself. There are some fine things about this country though - for instance the peaches. How I wish you and your children could help us eat a few bushels of them. I expect there is no of finer Peach country in the world. In some spots apples do just as well as far as great growth & perfection are concerned; but they are only summer fruit like the peaches. Most varieties ripening from June till September: and the latest, such as in New England might be good the next summer commonly decaying before January 1st. In some places however a singular disease attacks the apples just before ripening, the Bitter Rot, and renders them entirely worthless for any use. But oh the Peaches! We almost live upon them nowadays. And I suppose they can be had here in perfection from July 1st to perhaps December. They are hardly as good as usual this season on account of the extreme drouth which has prevailed all spring & summer. It is injuring all crops somewhat.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription: I suppose you take the New York Tribune, and get in that as well as elsewhere pretty full accounts of the Great Exhibition, or World's Fair at New York. I should have liked to be there at the opening; though, doubtless much less to be seen then than in the Fall sometime when the Exhibition will be much fuller. I expect I shall be unable to visit it at all. I am a good ways off; and too am where I cannot get away, confined by business. I may get a leave of absence sometime, but hardly expect to for a year & more. But I advise you, by al means, to go to New York sometime this Fall, and spend a few days in seeing. You will never regret the time or the expense I think; and neither are very great nowadays, if one be careful. The greatest danger is perhaps to health from change of diet &c, especially if in very warm weather. My advice is always to go to really respectable houses not the "Astor" or the "Metropolitan" or the "Irving"; but some really good respectable, and Temperance Public House if possible, even if the cost is a little more. It is the best policy in the end. And a few dollars is not worth the while of risk of inconvenience, health & comfort. Unless careful a stranger is pretty sure to see only the worst & most disagreeable side of all things and persons.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I am lucky enough to lose my saddle Horse, the "Glorious Old Whitey" who has carried me so bravely these 9 months past. He was worth I suppose $150. to me. He was in high condition fat, sleek & proud, full of health & spirits, take suddenly sick and died in a week, of one of the malignant diseases of the country, which seems to be a very bad one for horses. I am afraid I may never get another such a saddle horse as Old Whitey - certainly not at any reasonable price.  However the old horse has well paid for himself in the service he has already done me.
We hardly know yet whether Mother has gone or is going West this summer. I hope she will. It would surely do her good. Try to persuade her. You must tell Charlie & Josie about the little bird we have here in the cradle. How we want to see them all. If you could only bring all yours here to [[sat?]] Peaches; or better still we could be down there in Maine this hot weather. Do write to us sometime. Sincerely I. S.
I have not time to write much today, but I must simply send love to you all and tell you how much we should enjoy seeing you - wish you could come and help eat peaches - such large rich, glorious ones, I never saw before - Our dear baby is well, & growing finely - Nettie -

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Bangor Jan 19th 1855
Dear Brother Charles
I believe I have written one letter to you since you left Ducoign. I received one letter from you written at Elyria, for which I was much obliged to you; and intended to have written again long before this. I had very good fortune in every respect about getting away from Illinois. I left Du Quoin the 28th Dec. but did not reach Chicago until the 30th.
I had extra good luck at Chicago. the Bookkeeper after puzzling over their books a while concluded that my accounts was exactly right just as I had it; and so I was not delayed there at all. I went to Elyria Jan. 2d and stopped there one day. Then went to New York City and appeared before the Illinois Central Directors: who received me most graciously; complimenting me and the Second Division very highly, even at expense of all the rest almost. It almost frightened me to be puffed so much by all these big folks there assembled.
I presume their favor or influence may sometime be of some benefit to me, in getting business, or succeeding in business.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I reached Dunbarton on Jan. 6th; and staid there until 21st. Part of the time because of the great snow storms which prevented us from getting away. Found Antoinette and little Mayo very well; Mayo was afraid of me - I was glad to see them all though. Then we went to Massachusetts, and spent last week visiting at Antoinettes' relatives (Brigham's) in Westboro & Northboro, Worcester Co.; and finally arrived here Saturday night in tolerable health, though considerably tired out. Visiting is rather hard work especially for little folks. In fact Mayo is nearly sick today; but I guess he will be well in day or two.
The folks here are all pretty well, and everything going on about as usual. To day is a great Rain Storm; and I judge will leave no sleighing here. We are intending to go up to Milo & Brownville - sometime - but can not yet tell just when it may be. I want to see you: and am anxious to hear how the Maine cold weather agrees with you this winter
Sincerely
I. S. Metcalf
Love
T. S.
This love is put in by Nettie

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton N. H. Dec 3d '55
Dear Brother Charles
I suppose you would like to hear of our safe arrival here. You know we left Bangor last Tuesday Nov. 27th and got as far as Lawrence that night about 11 hours ride, and quite comfortably though Nettie & Mother as well as the little ones I suppose got some tired. The children were very good, hardly cried at all - did not five minutes in all; and Mayo did himself credit as an old Traveller.
We stopped at Lawrence till one oclock the next afternoon so they got finely rested, and then had only about two hours ride in the cars on Wednesday, and five miles ride in a covered carriage. So we got here about 5 oclock Wednesday night Nov. 28th just in season for Thanksgiving the next day. So we have had two Thanksgivings this year, one at Bangor the 22d, and one here, the 29th. The journey from Bangor here was full as easy as we expected, and I believe none were worse for it. Nettie tired herself some some the next day or two, and has not been quite so well.
Mother appears to be enjoying herself finely here, and I guess will be contented for a week or two two or three weeks.
You have heard the news from Bangor, of Eliah's boy, born the very day after we left there. It must do Eliah good.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription: I wish you would see if there is a stray number of Putnam's Magazine for 1855 anywhere about that we left at Milo; and if there is save it & send to Lucy whenever you have opportunity There are two numbers for 1853, but they are spare; and not wanted. It is one number for 55

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Mother is very anxious to have you write to her; so are we all.
Sincerely
Isaac

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton. N. H. Dec. 17, 1855
Dear Brother Charles
Have you any snow away Down East? Here there have been two or three fine snow storms, but they all end with a rain storm which carries the snow off without leaving a single day of sleighing. This is unfortunate for me you see; I want to get up 10 or a dozen cords of wood, and have got it all cut and wait only the snow to haul it. This lack of snow is some thing quite unusual here. Last winter there was 21 weeks sleighing.
I wish you could see these twin babies now. You would astonished to see how they have grown since they left Milo. It was about the time they left Milo, when they were two months old they weighed exactly 9 1/2 lbs. each. A week ago today when they were just three months old they weighed each a little over 12 lbs; the youngest one an ounce or two the most nearly 12 1/2 lbs. It is now supposed that they may be named Willis Putnam, & Wilder Stevens. They laugh & crow nowadays at a great rate.
Mayo weighs about 35 lbs. He sits at the table regularly like folks, & behaves tolerably:
It is supposed that we may, Mother & I, remain here for two or three weeks longer, and then perhaps go around by the way of Brattleboro & Warwick perhaps and spend a week or two of visit before getting to Elyria. So we may not get to Elyria before towards the middle of January.
In the meantime we are anxious to hear from you. Why do you not write to us? We want to hear all how you get along, & how all the children are this winter.
Have you sold the Grey horse?
Horse flesh may fall next year
Sincerely
Isaac S. M[etcalf]

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Nettie thinks ever so much about you all and would dearly love to see you - Mayo talks of Mary - says "she has gone away to she's home." Do you not have a nice time, Albina, with just your own little family? Some time to read and to think as well as to do housework and sew - I am busy as usual with the little ones - They are good as babies generally I imagine - feed them four or five times a day now - they are hungry all the time. some of their dresses are too small already - The waists to their skirts I have enlarged.
Love to the children - Write soon
Lovingly Nettie.
I am having quite a comfortable easy time here - was not expecting to say so long I want very much to hear from home do write so that I may get it before I go further have you found out what became of the bundle. It is very strange it did not get there - I fear you did not take pains to label it properly - Do you have a good school &  do the boys go to school - I hope they study & learn nicely at home as well as at school - I am very glad they are such good children tell Mary I want he should learn to sew some before I come home - Tis a very pleasant place here more so than I expected Do write soon I will write again when I get to Elyria and write more & better I hope
much love to you all from your
Mother
P.S. I should think it worth while to enquire & try to find the bundle

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Ducoign, Jan 21 1856
Dear Brother Charles
Here I am at the old place, just about where you left me when you went from here nearly 14 months ago. Abram Mitchell you know makes his head quarters now in the upper story of the Passenger House here; and I stop with him. One of his brothers, Jacob, is the station agent here; another George, who was also with me in New Hampshire is here too, on a visit; and talks of going to farming here. The house is plastered and pretty comfortable. George Smith's new house is finished, a fine house, looks a good deal like the one he lived in at the Old Town. Mr Keyes new house, quite a fine one, is unfinished, though they live in one end. The new doctor has built a new house &c. Dr. Wall will probably build & move up this spring. G. S. Smith & Co.'s new store is not built yet; is to be this spring. There is a large new building for a store near the Passenger House. There is a Telegraph Line, up, in operation, and the office down stairs. It seems curious here, where I once rode horse back so laboriously through the mud, to sit

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
sit at ease by the fire, and converse with a person fifty miles off, getting answers as soon as the words are out of one's mouth, as if talking with one in the same room.
Up as Ashley's place they have really got well underweigh with the coal business, and are sending to Cairo 100 to 200 tons of coal per day. Considerable is sent north too. This coal is valuable for gas purposes, supplies even Dubuque for Gas Coal, where the freight is $8.00 per Ton, the cost of the coal here being only $2.00 per Ton or less.
Just here there is nothing doing mining. Half a mile east they are doing considerable on small scale, mainly for country use: though they haul some to the R.R. A great company are proposing to go into it on a large scale with side tracks run out from here down on to the coal level; and also to go largely into the coal oil business. I cannot tell yet what they will do.
Jos. McCoy the Blacksmith has moved away to Iowa. John Williams the other blacksmith from the old Town has moved up here; and another blacksmith too. Guitteau & Horace Smith still work here. Adam Yearian

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
works carpentering at the Mines. John Yearian is car oiler at Centralia. Mitchell has most of the same men on the Track.
I arrived here Saturday night 19th. Mother I guess wrote you about our journey from Dunbarton, accident at Albany, and delay at Buffalo for the snow. We arrived at Elyria safely on Friday the 11th. Mother had a bad cold the next week, but was getting over it when I left. I left there Wednesday the 16th; was hindered one day between there & Chicago by slight accidents staid at Chicago most two days.
I can yet tell nothing what I shall do this season. The Minnesota project is yet all undecided. And no conclusions seem yet to be made any where for the coming season's business. I shall not go back east until I look about some; though I do want to see those babies. Given is well married.
Mrs Sprague of old DuQuoin died two weeks ago. It is an extraordinaryly cold winter here. has been unusually cold weather for four weeks, ground is frozen more than a foot every where. The rivers are frozen up, and this Rail Road is

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
is now doing a very heavy business. Two or mor great freight Trains, all the engines can draw, every day. Most of the year the business is light, over this part of the road.
Mr Ashley has quarrelled with the coal people & moved back to Jonesboro. I have written off every thing here some of it may interest you, and some not. You ought to write to us. Write to Mother at Elyria and I shall see it when I get back there sometime.
Much love to all of you
Isaac S. M---

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Office of the Illinois Central R. R. Company,
No. 48 Michigan Avenue,
Chicago, Feb. 2 1856.
Dear Brother Charles
I wrote to you once from Du Quoin, I think, and do not know as I have any thing further to write today. But as I have nothing else to do, I may as well write letters. I arrived here from the south last Wednesday Jan. 30th, intending to go north to Milwaukie the next day; but ever since then there has been a great wind, and the northern cars have not been able to get through the snow drifts; so that I stop here until Monday, and mayhap longer. It is here a very interesting - excessively severe winter - very cold, very snowy, and very windy. All the Rail ways are more or less impeded by snow especially by snow. So here I spend these three days, rather impatiently, for I am getting anxious to see the Babies; part of the time loafing in this office; part of the time walking about this great mushroom of Chicago, spying it out &c. and partly in reading & writing.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription: Last evening I found my way in to a lecture by the Editor of the Prairie Farmer, the great western agricultural newspaper, upon Agricultural Tools. It was rather interesting, an examination and comparison of the agricultural implements of all ages and nations, from the forked stick ploughs & hoes of ancient times, and those very little better of many modern nations, to the magnificent tools of this country, and especially of Chicago. He asserted that, within a few 15 years, Chicago and this state, has done more for the improvement of agricultural implements, than all the rest of the country or the whole world together. It seems quite an assertion - but the magnificent steel plough of the Prairies, the Reapers, the Mowers, the Threshers, the corn shellers - I do not know as it can be denied. He examined too, very fairly, the questions of the real benefit of these great labor saving machines; and acknowledged that they, were narrowly considered, no saving of money. It costs as much to sow with the drill, to reap with the Reaper, to thresh with the Thresher, as to do it by hand. But the great saving was that of time. The work could be done by machinery which it was impossible to find manual labor to do.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
All the manual labor which could have been obtained, could not have cultivated & secured, one fourth of the past year's crop of Illinois.
The difference then was the same as in mercantile affairs; the merchant nowadays is contented to sell a great many goods at a smaller profit than before. So the Farmer nowadays must [[find?]] his profits in the extent of the crops which his machinery enables him to cultivate secure and market. The Railways even may be called improved agricultural machinery, as they market the crops.
The Lecturer finally declared that the next great agricultural improvement must be that of a new 'motor'; some less costly force to wield the machinery than that of horses, and more easily managed than that of steam.
I propose to wait here for the snow till Mon. or Tues. as I want to go to Milwaukie & Madison, Wis. I did hope to start east next week; but cannot now tell when I shall be able.
You must write to Mother at Elyria; I shall be there on my way East; and also to me at Dunbarton -
Yours Sincerely
I. S. Metcalf

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton, Merrimack Co.
Feb. 25th 1856   N.H.
Dear Brother
How do you get along this cold winter? Or is it not so cold up there as it is farther South? It has been a very cold winter most every where.
In Southern Illinois all frozen up for two months, and about a month of good sleighing.
I got home here Sat. night 16th and found all very well here. The Twins weigh about 16 lbs. apiece, and are very healthy. I wish you could see them. The look more exactly alike than they did. Few can tell them apart. They are very good natured, sit in a chair, or lie on a sofa & laugh and talk to themselves or Mayo

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Prospects for New Rail Roads at the West are rather dull as yet. The great Minnesota & North Western R. R. Co. question has been before the Supreme Court this month. Their decision confirms the decision of the Court below in favor of the R. R. Co. as far as the test question is concerned, but does not, if I understand it, make the decision general, covering the whole question. What the result will be I do not understand. Perhaps it has got to be all tried over again. I could find no chance to suit me on other roads. Some think though that business will take a new start in the spring. At present there is little doing.
I do not know yet what I shall do. Probably wait a while longer. I have been a little inclined to go right to Du Quoin, and establish myself there permanently, and go into the coal business. I believe I could

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
could make a fortune there. But I hardly like to have my family there. They did have a dreadful time there with sickness last fall.
Mother seems very comfortable and happy at Elyria: I stopped there a few days on my way back. I suppose Mother writes to you frequently. It is really a very fine place there. You can hardly tell how much they have improved that house since you were there. The Rooms are very fine. Sitting Room is 16 X 24 ft. very high; and on the end of it, with door on one side of the chymney & glass window on the other, another room, Boudoir you may call it 8 feet wide; a sort of Library. The two together, or the choice of the two is very pleasant. The whole house you know is warmed by a furnace.
I think Mother enjoys herself finely. When she will come back, I can not tell.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I rather think I shall go West again in April or May whether there is chance of Rail Road business or not.
How does your Grey Horse get along this winter? Do you have any chance to sell him? Is he improving finely? Do you find any thing for your great team oxen & three horses to do? How do your sheep bear the cold winter? Is there much sickness in Milo this winter? 
Did you intend to farm much this season coming?
I wish you would write to us frequently
Sincerely
I. S. Metcalf
Nettie sends love to all

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton Merrimac Co. N. H.
April 15, 1856
Dear Brother Charles
Looking over my portfolio I find your letter of March 2d, and cannot find that it has ever been answered, I fear therefore that I shall not get another from you till I do write to you again. We were were quite amazed at your account of your night's work on Mrs Rickess' account; though it was really altogether too bad to be very ridiculous. We were quite anxious to hear whether you had the same trip again the next snowy night. How long did it take your horse to get over it? Has the red horse got over his fright yet?
