Are you going to sell any of your horses this spring? Horses are very high here this spring. You have a pretty strong team of your own now; a good yoke oxen & three large stout horses. I want to hear how you make out with your hauling Bog Mud. I should much like the chance to help you some with that & the wood pile. I am doing very little here except some reading & taking care of and playing with the babies. I just about cut wood &c. enough for exercise. While I was here the first part of Winter I cut 10 or 12 cords

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
cords of wood in the woods, the minister's wood lot, a mile and a half from here. I have hauled it up with the minister's horse and cut it about all up one foot long. Wood is very high here (Rail Road on every side and only 10 or 12 miles from either Concord or Manchester, where wood is some six dollars per cord.) and good wood land is worth much more than good tillage land. I do not like to saw wood quite as well as to chop, but it is better than nothing. There ought to be a chance for gardening before this time; some farmers have already begun to plough & sow peas &c. on Southerly slopes; but the snow is still near a foot deep in the minister's garden. It was above the tops of the fences the first of April.
What I shall do with myself this season, I do not know. The prospects for business are rather discouraging. I do think of going west again within a month, but hardly know surely.
We are all very well here, and enjoying ourselves considerable. Mayo is as rosy cheeked as ever, out of doors a great part of the time. There is a fine common here, on one corner of which is the Parsonage, and around the other sides the Church, school houses, Church sheds, Store, half a dozen dwelling houses, and the great old Town House in the centre. This makes a very fine Play ground, and there is no lack

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
lack of little playfellows for Mayo.
The Twins, Willie Putnam & Wilder Stevens, seem very healthy, and good natured. They weigh about 18 lbs a peice, and are called model babies almost; many say they are no more trouble than one often is. The sit up in a chair, or lie kicking on the bed, or on the floor, taking care of themselves, a good deal of the time; perhaps with Mayo to hand them play things.
If the season is as backward with you, as it is here you may be sledding wood nowadays. There has been no rain here yet, and really no thaw all winter till April 1st; since then the snow has melted gradually away. There was not near as much snow here as farther South. Here barely two feet in all, and very little water in it at that. In Massachusetts & New York, I suppose, there has been at least three feet & much heavier.
The Great severity of the winter has been South and West. At St Louis the Mississippi closed by Ice from Christmas till about the first of March and at Du Coign the month of March even was still quite cold. They had near or quite 2 ft. of snow in all, and the ground frozen very unusually hard. And then a very cold March in addition to that!
I am inclined to think you usually, perhaps always, miss it in not beginning your farm work early enough in the spring. The farmers here I perceive are taking time by the forelock.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
There are now plenty of snow drifts 2 or 3 feet deep in the roads, and fence corners; but the farmers are busy at work hauling manure some on dry roads, or in the mornings while it is frozen, and on their dry lands ploughing & sowing as rapidly as possible - even before the frost is all out. Now some of your land - the river side of the Intervale, and part of that West Knoll is dry [[?]] enough to work just as soon as the snow is off of it; though you often wait a month for it to dry before you begin [[C. Ch.?]] to work much. 
I suppose you do not have much hay to spare this spring, keeping all your horses, and the winter has been unusually hard for hay. Does your mare have a colt?
How do your Nursery apple trees bear the winter? Do you have them grafted this spring? Try do do it in season.
Love to all the children.
Hope you will write to us often.
Sincerely
Isaac I. M.
Love from Nettie - she wants to see you ever so much - If we were only a little nearer, I know you would come & see us

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton Merrimack Co. N. H.
June 18, 1856
Dear Brother Charles
I have been wishing today to hear from you. I fear I shall not unless I write to you. I have very little to write though. I had a comfortable journey from Bangor with Mayo. He is quite a traveller I assure you. It would amuse you to see his anxiety for the carpet bag & umbrella, & lest we should lose the train at a stopping place or change of cars. We went to Lowel and stopped half a day. Saw Uncle Enoch Metcalf & wife, who live with Isaac [[?]] who is appears very pleasantly situated; has a fine house with about two acres of land just in the edge of city; fine garden, & lots of fancy poultry. (A pair of Seabright Bantams about as large as doves valued at $25.00 His business you know is music. Teaches music in the city schools, gives

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
gives concerts &c.
Charles the youngest son is in a store in Lowel & boards with them. Mr. Hunt, Nancy Metcalfe's husband lives near them; I judge he is wealthy. Young Enoch Metcalf is separated from his wife. She lives in Boston. He is a mercantile agent, or something of the sort: travels at the South & West. Uncle Enoch's health is pretty good; appears to have mainly recovered from the shock of Palsy he had two or three years ago. Isaac has three children, lost one, one of a pair of twins, last year, 3 yrs old. We have had some very hot weather since I got back here. Before that it had rained about all the time, & very cold; corn rotted in the ground &c. Crops all looked very backward, except hay. The warm weather has brought them forward very rapidly however. Prospect of fruit is very good.
How do your fruit tress? Have

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
You had a lot of grafting done? I did not think so much of it but those Harlow Grafted Trees need manure. The great numbers of young nursery trees near them steal away all the nourishment from the soil.
[arithmetical calculations crossed out]
Does your corn come up well? Do you be likely to sell any of your horses this summer? How much wood do you shear? Do you hoe those young trees set out in the garden occasionally this summer?
What do you do about your cultivator or Horse Hoe. I almost wished I had sent up one or the other at any rate. You certainly ought to have one.
I suppose they save considerable work in hoeing. And you have considerable to do including carrots

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
The prospect is here of very early haying. The grass is unusually forward, and the hot dry weather for a week or two past is ripening it off very rapidly. This afternoon it is trying to rain some. A good rain now would probably set the grass to growing again and retard its ripening. 
I did think of going West this month, but as I do not so well like July & August at Du Quoin, I have about concluded to put it off till about Sept. 1st. Another new Coal Co. are just commencing operations close to the station. They have bought the McElvain farms and 10 acres of ours to give them an opening to the R. R. and shaft as near the Depot grounds as possible. This bids fair to start things there rapidly at once. Dr Wall has put up a large Drug &c. store there. 
Isaac

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton Merrimac Co.
New Hampshire
August 2d, 1856
Dear Brother
Your letter of July 25 came to hand by last mail; and was exactly what we had been for some time wanting to see. I was very glad to see so good account of your farming this summer. The Prospect for Crops there must be better I think than it is here. Here the spring was very wet & backward until about the first of June. Then very suddenly & completely dry The corn though planted ever so early did not begin to grow any till July; but since then has come forward very rapidly, and now looks tolerably well.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
The Wheat & Oats are only about a foot high, and thin and poor at that. The Potatoes have grown up finely for their vines; but they say there will be no potatoes unless there comes rain.
When I came back here the first week in June there was the heaviest show of grass on the ground almost ever seen. But it did not seem to grow any more after the dry weather came on; and ripened off all at once. All seemed ready to be cut early in July, and all is now as dry as usual the first of September.
There was a very unusual demand for labor about here in haying. $1.50 per day was regular wages, as it has not been here heretofore.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
I worked out haying 12 days, and to the great acceptance of my employer; who called me the best mower he ever had in his field! And more than that I found I could rake or pitch with any of the New Hampshire boys. And I did not get tired either; so I think it will hardly do to say that my constitution is entirely ruined by engineering or by life at the west. There are comparitively few who are not injured more merely by getting through College.
You enquire about our going West. I believe the only answer can be "I dont know." I propose to go West in Sept. It is possible that Antoinette and the babies may go with me as far as Elyria: and they may remain in New England

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Whether or where I shall go on a R. R. this fall is still uncertain. There is little doing or immediate prospect of much doing, this season any where except in Iowa There there is considerable activity, partly on acc't of Kansas, and partly because of the late Land grants in that state.
I am less acquainted there or with those R. R. Projects than most others. But I think, if nothing else offers to [[?]] me I shall go around there this Fall for a while
Abram Mitchell was east in July spent one day here at Dunbarton. There is some progress at Du Quoin. A new Coal shaft commenced on our Land in connection with the McElvain Farm, new stores &c.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton N. H. Sept. 6 1856
Dear Brother Charles
Mayo is dead. I got back from Bangor last Saturday night or rather Sunday morning, found him sick with the Dysentery. The disease proved very malignant and reduced him rapidly, though we did not entirely give up hope until a few hours before he died; which was this (Saturday) morning at 15 minutes before Four oclock.
The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away. He has been comfort and joy to us for which we should be thankful. But the blow is severe The Lord hath taken away the pride

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
pride of our strength
May we feel that 'He doeth all things well, and may all the dispensations of His hand be sanctified to our Eternal good.
The funeral is to be tomorrow morning, probably at the Church.
We expect to start for Ohio in a week or two.
I cannot write more
Isaac

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton, N. H. Sept. 15 1856
Dear Brother Charles
I wrote to you I guess the 6th inst. telling of our dear Mayo's death, at 3.45 A. M. the 6th inst. I thought then to write to you again within a few days; but I had not had much time.
When Mayo died Father Putnam was complaining. Monday - a week ago today he was sick with Dysentery. He has not got off his bed yet, though we hope the disease has reached its height, but the Dr.s say he will be long recovering. The next day Mother Putnam was taken with the same disease, and is not able to sit up at all. Monday 8th Little Willie had a diarrhea. Tuesday it was severe, & we called in the Doctor. He called it severe Teething Diarrhea. Other Doctor since says it was Cholera Infantum. He was at once very sick. Thursday morning he was so much reduced we feared he would die at once, but he seemed to revive a little & we thought he was better, until Friday, when he grew worse. I suppose [[that?]] Dropsy of the Brain, or an effusion of blood on the brain commenced

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Friday night he was in great distress, Saturday morning he had convulsions, suffered extremely all the forenoon, and breathed his last at 1.30 P. M. Saturday 13th.
Little Willie was never healthier, stronger or fatter, than one week ago, on Sunday 7th. Neither of them went along, but pushed chairs every where. How full of life & play he was, running across the floors on all fours like a little dog, so fast you could hardly see his feet move, & looking over his shoulder to laugh, for every one laughed to see him run so. then perhaps springing up to a chair so quick to push that about. He was sick so little while that he did not lose his flesh at all. How beautiful he looked in his little coffin, so plump & fair & white. He was a very beautiful child. Little Wilder has been most sick diarrhea &c. but the Doctors now think him about out of danger.
Nettie was tired for a week or two and most sick. Friday, 12th. She was attacked with Dysentery. Saturday by the time Little Willie was dead she was abed, and has not been up since. But the Doctors say now she is doing very well, though the disease must have its course, and she must keep her bed for eight or ten days.
How lonely we are without those children. I cannot write about it.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
My own health appears pretty good, though I was somewhat worn out with care and watching. When little Willie died, I guess I had not slept more than fifteen minutes at a time since Tuesday night. Wednesday night I hardly slept at all, Thursday & Friday nights I did not take off my clothes or lie down at all. Sleeping only as I could lean my head down by the side of the child when it was quiet.
Mayo was buried Sunday 7th. The Coffin was carried to Church, and after service the whole congregation, some 300, followed to the grave. All knew him you see - the Minister's Grand child, and he had been at meeting regularly, almost every service for six months.
Little Willie's funeral was yesterday, Sunday 14th, at 5 P. M. and very many were present. 
It has been a very sick family here. But we have got along. The neighbors have been very kind to us, and we have excellent help.
I have much to do, both in care of sick, for I am Nettie's nurse, and looking after the household.
I cannot stop to write more.
Sincerely
Isaac S
Please write to us.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
C. W. Rich
Milo Maine

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dunbarton, Merrimack Co. N. H.
Tuesday, Sept. 23d 1856
Dear Bro' Charles
I suppose you would like to hear how we get along here in this house of sickness.
I wrote you a week ago, telling of Little Willie's death, and how the rest were sick.
Nettie is still sick abed; though the Doctor pronounces her "getting well." She has got about over the Dysentery, and begins to gain strength in fact has set up more than half an hour this morning. We hope she will now gain health and strength very fast.
Little Wilder is very well.
Father & Mother Putnam are both still very sick, though we hope now improving. But in their feeble

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
feeble condition, and worn constitutions can neither of them be considered really out of danger. Mr Putnam was taken last week Friday with his coughing very severe and painful, as his throat is very sore with bronchitis or Canker in the throat. It grew worse, and Saturday morning the Dr., finding he could not check it in any manner, even by ether, grew quite alarmed, and wanted advice. So Sat. afternoon we had three doctors here from Goffstown, Weare, & Concord. They all did not seem to effect much, but the hiccough appeared gradually to wear itself out, & stop, though leaving him much exhausted. But he seems to be better since.
My own health has been pretty good. Saturday though, in the hurry, fatigue & excitement, I was pretty strongly threatened with the Dysentery, but I have kept pretty still since them, been careful of my

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
my food & exercise, and now seem to have pretty much, as our Doctor says, "got it over."
It would not very well do for me to be sick. Though Eliah writes that he will come and take care of me, if I am sick. Still I think it would hardly do, that is, if it can be avoided.
We should like to hear from you very much. How you are all well. There is a good deal of sickness about here. And it has some of the time been rather difficult to get help to take care of our sick folks. The neighbors though are very kind.
Please write
Sincerely
Isaac

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Du Quoin, Perry Co. Illinois
Jan 12 1857
Dear Brother Charles
I sit here writing by my same old desk just as in years agone. Mitchell has still made it his head quarters here; and about the R. R. Buildings every thing is still very much as I left it.
There has been a good deal of change here in a year past, probably three or four times the worth of buildings here there was a year ago and lots bring more than double.
The Southern Illinois Coal Mining Comp. J. Carville Stoven, Agent; own the McElvains farm, we sold them the coal under 80 acres west of that farm, and ten (10) acres of land, on our north line between that farm and the R. R. Line, for a base to begin on. They have commenced at the R. R. Land Edge, a little north of the switch, and are commencing, on a considerable scale, though they have not yet got out more than 1000 Tons. The coal is there about 40 feel from surface at the Ashley, or St. John Mine it is 80

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Another Coal Mining Company, Winters & Co. propose to put in a R. R. Track from the station here, just north of our Public Square right east about half a mile down into the ravine where they have commenced mining only 15 feet below the surface. Moreover the R. R. Co. talk of commencing this spring right at the station or just south of it, to mining on their own hooks get out the coal for their own use themselves, so as not to be dependent on other companies. The R. R. Co. are now trying to get me to take charge of their mining operations here, as General Agent - not miner, They offer me $1500.00 salary, which for that business, a permanent situation, is large. They could have plenty of managers doubtless at $1000.00.
I must tell you about the people you know here. Mr. Keyes has a very fine house here, by side of the hollow, just north of the old Log farm house. Mrs Keyes & Chetty spend the winter in Ohio. Mr Keyes has a brick office near the R. R. Line, opposite the new coal works. Geo. Smith the Trader has a large new double store, quite a fine one; His new house, on the flat South of Keyes', is very much like his old one at the Old Town. Edwin Smith has also a pretty good house. Bradford Skinner boards with them. Horace Smith who had nothing when he commenced on the R. R.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription: R. R. Buildings, has worked steadily ever since, and now has $1200.00 to put in a house this spring. Dea. Benj. Sprague of the Old Town, lost his wife a year & half or more ago; has just married again, & moved up here, will build a house worth 2000. or 2500. this spring. He has gone into the Lumber business and is likely to do well. He has considerable capital. McCoy has gone north. Williams the blacksmith at the old Town is here, doing first rate. There will probably be three churches built here this spring, or in course of the season A Campbellite, (for which Schwarts, Ab. Williams and these country people about here give $100.00 apeice), a Regular Baptist, (Mr Peter Hagler's people, who will also have their religious newspaper established here this spring) and a Presbyterian. They will all be cheap buildings, probably costing only 1500. to 2000. each, though very likely built of brick. These churches are all to be in a row, where the school house now is just north of and facing the Public Square. They will show finely I think. McClure still trades where he did. Frissell has a large store near the Papenger house. There are two drug stores just back of it.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
The old R. R. Boarding House is sold, there are wings added to it, & it is Vancils Farem. Mrs Fulton keeps a large boarding house here. Dr Wall lives here, and practices largely, besides a drug store. Mrs Wall is east this winter. The Dr. will build a large dwelling house in the spring. Mr Mitchell is about leaving here He is appointed Assistant Superintendent Outdoors Assistant, from Centralia north on the Branch to Urbanna, some 125 miles. He will have I suppose $1500.00 a year Geo Watson has left, Jan 1st. Pease is Superintendent from Centralia South.
Well I have written considerable news I think. Hope to hear from you frequently.
Sincerely
Isaac S.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Ducoign Perry Co. Illinois
Feb. 16, 1857
Dear Brother Charles
I have written to you once since I have been here, and perhaps more than that since I have received a letter from you.
But I believe I must write again before I leave here at any rate. I believe I wrote you about most all the folks you used to know here. There has been a good deal of change here since you were here. Suppose I try to describe some of it. Beginning at the Passenger House; On the nearest corner, R. R. Lot, stands a two story white house Drug Store in front, Doctor's Family is back part & above. Doctor's Partner's house is on next lot south. On the other corner from lot across Main St, is Frizzell's Store in front, dwelling in rear, The whole 80 or 90 ft. long, two stories, 24 wide Back east of that is Dr wall's office, whe he now lives boarding at the [[Farem?]], his wife being away this winter. He is going to build a nice house this spring; next lot east is the other Drug Store, late Wall & Newberry's, now Paddock & brother's. Across the street from that is the new store of G. S. Smith & Co. right in front of their old building The new one is really a very fine store - would be

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription: in any village, or any where. I guess there is not a finer salesroom at any rate in Dover Village. South of that old Boarding house is now "J. Vancil's 'Du Quoin House." It is painted cream has two wings, one of them longer than the old part; and is quite a house; two or three lots neatly fenced in for yard & garden. Its stables &c. are twenty rods south. Vancil the Landlord is the same old chap you remember lived in the timber towards old Dick Taylor's. Old Vancil is now quite a Villager, a speculator in lots &c. The other Hotel - the "White House" is about ten rods east with half a dozen shops &c. between. The best Dwelling houses are on the east side of Town, where too Dr Wall & Benj. Sprague are going to build this spring. You know where Mr Keyes house is - in the broken ground falling off into the hollow north of the old Atkin's Farm house. G. S. Smith's Ed. Smith's & others are just south of that. John A Sprague is just north of Mr Keyes'. But Mr Keyes has just sold his house - House & the land with it, his half of the 40 acres on the north east of ours which we divided for $6.000.00 to a coal operator. Some of the best houses to be built this spring are on the extreme north; Horace Smith's for one. We reserved a tier of lots next north of the Public Square for Public purposes. The school house looks rather solitary there alone now. But the prospect now is that there will be four

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
four churches built there in the same row this season coming; Campbellite, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Methodist.
Keyes' office a brick building one story, with a ware house back now used for a carpenter's shop, is west of the north part of Public Square, next to R. R. line & Land. Two stores are building north of that. There are but two houses west of the R. R. Line, except at the mine lands. The "Tetley Coal Mine" Co. bought the McElvain farm, (where you used to board you know) bought ten acres on the north side of ours to get out to the R. R. Line, sunk their shaft & put up their works in the S. E. corner of it 150 ft. from Track. A long side track round it. The coal they find 40 ft from the surface, at the Ashley mine it is 80 ft. And which is the best think for the place they pump out 3000 to 5000 gallons of water per day. The R. R. Co. have put up there the best Tank house on the Line. It is the only place where there is a supply of water. At the Ashley mine there is hardly water enough for their own machinery. The Old South DuCoign well is the next best supply; at Centralia after boring near a thousand feet, they have to bring water for the Engine house & all from Crooked Creek two miles, much of the year. I have laid out lots here North South East & West - lots of them.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
And we are selling them at the rate of about $2000.00 per month.
The Du Quoin Property cost Keyes & Metcalf $3500.00) We have already sold about $12.000.00 and I made an estimate of the balance a few days ago at $24.000.00. It may be some time before we realize it though; and our sales are mostly upon time.
I want to hear how you all get along this frightfully cold winter. Colder than ever before known, reports call it east. Can you keep fire enough to keep warm. How are the little boys & Mary?
Do they go to school?
I suppose from last accounts, it is doubtful if Mr Ryder is alive yet. It is a dreadful death. And yet I presume he can triumph over death itself. How do your neighbors get along this winter? Is Albina's health good? Do you any cough this winter?
Love to all,
And Please write to us,
Sincerely
Isaac

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Isaac to Charles
Elyria June 8 57
Milo
Elyria Lorain Co. Ohio
June 8, 1857
Dear Brother
I believe I have received a letter from you since I wrote directly to you through we have perhaps written more than once to Mother since that time. I have written to Mother about my purchase of a place here in Elyria; and also about my slight prospect of a situation in Minnesota, on the Min. & Pacific R Road perhaps. I got Mr. R. B. Mason to write to St Paul recommending me for the situation; but have not yet heard from it.
I was much obliged to you for your account of the great freshet on the Piscataquis, and glad of your account of your farming operations this spring.
Milo seems to have been very fortunate not to lose any of its Bridges. It is very well for taxes there are enough already they always have been.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
How is your garden this spring? It seems to me it is hardly worth the while for a farmer not to have an earlier garden than yours ever is. The thing is perhaps the nature of the soil; it needs an under draining; but ploughing it up in high ridges in fall would help it much. And fall ploughing would not injure that soil as it does so badly the intervale. If that garden spot was ploughed thoroughly into ridges in the fall, you could plant Peas, lettuce, &c., such things as are not injured by frost, in March. Potatoes too. It has been a very late backward season here; but my early peas are all in full bloom for some days, they stand about 3 feet high. Tomatoes about ready to bloom. Early beets onions & turnips, getting pretty sizeable and lettuce & such things abundant for I do not know how long.
All such things are very convenient in a family.
The place I have just bought here is pretty thoroughly under drained throughout.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
How contented with Milo are you this summer? I suppose if you wanted to leave there ever so much you could not sell your farm for any decent price could you. It is too bad that farm should be in Milo instead of somewhere it would be worth fifty or a hundred dollars per acre.
I cannot see what makes Milo quite so bad a place. Some towns in Maine are improving considerably.
Hope you will write soon and frequently.
We are all well. Wilder is very hearty and happy, out of doors most of time
My principal business nowadays is gardening, and very little of that.
Nettie if she does not write sends much love.
Sincerely
Isaac S. M.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [2], 1844-1857
transcription:
Dear Albina -
I do not know if I have written or not since you wrote, and no matter; for I mean to write when I have time, at any rate. Wilder takes more than usual of my time just now, for he is getting his eye teeth & feels fretful, especially in the forenoon. He is usually very well & very full of mischief. It is hard to know what to do with him sometimes, just because he makes fun out of all one does to punish him. But we think him a pretty nice little fellow, after all - What a dear, good baby you have got - What does Mary say and do about it? O, I wish I could see you all - Love to you all, from Nettie -
Dear Mother, how do you and Percis, these summer days? We are having some very warm ones. Have just had a delightful shower, and the air seems cooler for it. You can perhaps imagine how things grow. Wish you could see out garden, grape vines &c. Have you got established now, so that you feel at home again? The Dr. is getting well now quite perceptibly - I was over there with Isaac an hour or two this morning - Isaac was trimming a large tree in front of the house, that shaded a cherry too much. Anna had been making & baking bread - Probably she has written to you of Mary's going away - She has for a week or two, a smaller girl, who needs instruction particularly in the art of cooking; so Anna is more in the kitchen 
We are invited to a party to night. Isaac will go, but I shall  not - He does not love to go without me but I try to have him. Anna & the Dr. are company for him - Lovingly your daughter Nettie.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
Page 1s.              Bangor May 2d 1839
Dear Mother, Brothers, & Sister,
When I got home from school to day, I perceived a pr. of shoes being by the door which looked as if they would fit me pretty well, so the girl told me that a man left them for me, a little while before. Well after supper Charles came in, he gave me a rale good letter! I went down town with him. I did not hardly have time to speak to him was not with him half an hour barely.
Ergo, I now sit down to answer your letter, as I had nothing written when C. was here, and did not have time to tell him 1/2 as [[Joe?]] said. First, I guess that there is not much danger of my hurting my health to work as I am used to it and good for it “to boot.” As for work I guess I am to work as erly in the morn as you are. Play, cought no fish! Lambs I (very straight) was not there to take care of them. As for jobs all I have done is to split up a little wood for C. Harris, next neighbor, about 1 1/2 hour: Mr. W. And I had a takl about board etc. last week and he concluded that as he had got the stump [[pied?]] bush hole as Joe says, that he should have enough for me to do to pay for my board spell at least. I get up between 4 et 4 1/2, make fire, milk &c. go out to work 5, breakfast 7 or little after. It does not [[?]] agree with me very well to work so long before break-fast I dont go out at noon, or after breakfast, commonly 3 or 4 I take care cow, get water, wood, do errands et cetera. [[?]]er &c. etc. So I study most of the time at noon, in eve, and morn sometimes I get along well in Virgil, Algebra, &c. I have not caepit Greek yet as there is no class and I could not do anything alone

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
Office of the Du Quoin Coal Mining & Mfg. Co.
Du Quoin, Ills. Dec. 7 1863
Dearest Nettie
I most always write to you when I am here on the Sabbath Day, whether I do other times or not. Yesterday I did not happen to have any pen & ink. But, Oh how I did want a letter from you. I really expected one Saturday but it did not come.
Yesterday was Episcopalian day. The Presbyterians have preaching but half the time, and the other half an Episcopalian Clergyman from Jonesboro, Mr Brittain, holds forth. You remember perhaps the three curates in "Shirley," I think this must be one of them, though I am not quite certain. It seemed almost ridiculous to see the little pompous, rather scanty brained Irishman come in there; (no vestry or dressing room you know) and dress himself in his white robes right before the audience, and then go through with all the minutia of the service, so almost absurdly, trying to intone in the fashionable high church style. Well it was almost laughable, and quite tiresome - to me at least.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
At church there were 40 or 50 for audience At the Sabbath School at 3 P.M. there were nearer a hundred & fifty the little church crowded full. and apparenly quite interesting. Damon Shing, you perhaps remember him, is very sick, apparently about to die. No Keyes says he has starved himself to death these six years. "It might be all very 'well leaving off Tea and coffee & all meat. 'if he had eaten any thing else good. But 'Bran & sawdust alone dont answer." 
Dr Wall has branched out. Times are so good every body so well off he cant get two percent a month for his money. So he has just put up a brick 3 story block on Main Street. Stores offices &c. I hope you will write to me often I shall feel bad if I do not get a letter today. Sincerely Isaac
Du Quoin
Dec. 7 1863
No letter today

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
Would it not be the best way for you to make out your visit alone this year, stay as long as you like, if we are all well, perhaps come back with Samuel, when he comes - of if that does not suit, get George to come to Boston with you - you paying his fare - and frm there you could come alone well enough couldnt you? And I will make my visit alone next year. I shall want to be at Old Bowdoin at commencement next year at any rate - Twenty years class meeting you know.
It is not just the thing to leave such a family as ours alone with any body a great while. Elisa is just as good as any body could be, perfectly faithful & trustworthy; would take any pains or inconvenience what ever to do every thing just right and care for the children the best she knows. But after all I guess you would a little rather trust them with me here, and I know I should with you here. The best way after all is to travel enmasse the whole family, children & all. I think we shall eventually have to adopt that plan. when the children get a little bigger perhaps. What do you think of the whole matter? Call for the previous question?
I was going to send you some money in this letter. If you go to Pembroke Wednesday, this will not get to Yarmouth before you leave there. Perhaps I had better direct it to Pembroke
Especially Isaac

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
July 17. 1866, Elyria
Tuesday Eve.                                                                                          
My Dearest
I have just written a letter to Rev J. N. Newton in reply to one from him asking for coal.  Last night wrote one to L. L. Jenkins in reply to one from him.  He is established at Boston you know.  Your letter of the 13th came to hand this evening.  The Boys and myself wrote a big letter to you Sunday night, mailed yesterday morning, which after some hesitation I directed to Pembroke; thinking it would not get around before Thursday, and that by that time you would be there rather than at Yarmouth.  I wrote much about going east, or rather not going, and mostly concluding it was hardly best to try to go.  If I went I should hardly feel like staying more than the fewest possible days to go and come in, and perhaps it would hardly be worth the while if you could come back alone or with Samuel or somehow
There would seem to be no difficulty about the Children, or about any one of them in particular at any rate.  Wilder could go up to Charles' or over to Mr Twiss, Charley to Dr DeMitts or half a dozen other places; he has a first class invitation to go down to Boyds' on the Lake Shore.  Geo Boyd you know is an especial chum of his.  Anna could stay at Twiss's or anywhere else; would be good and slight trouble any where; and Little  Don John, could go to Eliah, or Eliza could take

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
the best of care of him here. And yet somehow collectively I do not feel a bit like leaving them. Perhaps however I may start off in a hurry some day, but it is very doubtful
Glad to hear of May's well doing. I must write to her dear self specially, I think.
Took Anna tonight over to Mr Twiss by way of experiment. Do not know how it will answer. Little John wanted "Nanny" "Nanny" very frequently after she was. I suspect he will be sort of lonesome and fretting for her.
You speak of dry weather for our wet. You need not say much now on that score. It cleared off here on Monday July 9th. Since then a cloudless sky, the heat well the Thermometer any where but in the ice houses has ranged from 90 to 100, and the Drougth already begins to be severe! Tonight a few cloudy minutes and a bare sprinkle seem to have cooled the air a little.
Undeniably Isaac

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
Isaac 
July 29 1866
Elyria, July 19 1866
Very Dearest
Your letter to Charley came to hand tonight. Charley & Wilder had gone over to Mr Twiss' to see [[Emma?]] to carry her some clothes or lead her home as might be. She went over there on Tuesday P.M. I should not see the boys, (as it was meeting night) until tomorrow morning. So I thought I might as well read the letter myself. And now perhaps I may as well answer it. Though I do not know as it needs especial answer, except that we are especially glad to have you write to us often and particularly.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
It is very comfortably cool for a day or two past, cloudy though with very little rain, just enough yesterday afternoon to wet my hay; the three acre meadow beyond the Henson house was mowed by a mowing machine yesterday morning. The sun did not come out and it did not dry enough to rake up and it got wet before night. Today the boys & myself, have worked over it most of the the afternoon & Charles & his three boys two or three hours and it is now nicely in a little less than 150 cocks. (on which there is nice smart rain now 
The cooler weather is nice for the children, John feels much better for it and sleeps like a top, besides needing hardly any care all day. During the very warm weather he was red & itching all over Other people I guess feel better too judging from the meetings. Prayer

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
meetings last week & week before quite thin. Tonight the room quite full and a very good meeting. Just six prayers and six exhortations, besides a few remarks of Mr Wilbur. Charley will be greatly pleased at his letter, and Wilder will make a comical face because he has not one. Rev Geo A Perkins I very well remember. Though seeing his name occasionally of late I hardly knew if it was the same, slender, pale faced hard student.
Do I understand that you wanted another picture of John tried for? We thought that was about right. When are you going back from Pembroke & Dunbarton?
Samuel left here this morning. I was sorry it happened so you were gone from Yarmouth, the last part

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf letters [1], 1839-1866
transcription:
of this week and first of next.
Samuel might have called at Yarmouth if you had been to be there. I might have sent some money to you by him. You might have gone on with him to go to Brownville to visit a little there. As it is so doubtful about my going on at all, or if I should about my stopping to visit. And judging from a letter Charles received from Almeda yesterday there is little or no prospect of her coming west this fall. She said she could not at any rate come with Samuel for she could not at all travel in hot weather.
And the state of Hattie's (James' wife's) health was such it was very doubtful if she could leave at all. She is [[threat?]]ened with consumption I guess.
Sincerely Isaac.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [11], May-June 1852
transcription:
Stopped for the night on the North Bank of Grassy at Wiley's. Parker Wiley, I believe. Rather a wealthy man for this region. 
Large farm.  Store &c.
I suppose really rich, but live only as well as they know how.  Big Barefooted Girls.
Ox with a big sore on head.
Abundant Barns &c. 
& Mr. Barber of Town Mound Prairie, 3 miles east of Frankfort, with wife & child horse & buggy going home stopped there.
They raise much Tobacco & Castor Beans in this region in which Fat old Wiley, who resembles Sam. Anderson of Mud Prairie, profitably speculates.  Double money on horses sent to Chicago, many.
Very Coarse rough bed.  slept ill.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [11], May-June 1852

Abner Gardner W. Cambridge. Carrying a little boy across brook (not girl)
Bainbridge Village in a pretty little prairie.
Marion (do) Court House
Williamson Co
Between Wiley's & Bainbridge crossed the Crab Orchard by bridge, quite a stream at Marion.  The Marion Fork I suppose.
Five or six miles above Marion stopped at a little Farm house. dinner & sleep rain some hours.
Horse Buck not very well, trouble by the distemper. Fear consumptive

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [11], May-June 1852

Dr. Sams who lives there has large practice From Frankfort descending the hill North.  Cross Ewing's Fork, a principal branch of Muddy by Bridge, beyond which, road for Benton  & Mt. Vernon left McLeansboro Right.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [03], 1847-1848
transcription:
1847, Thursday, Nov. 25th. Thanksgiving Day. 7 A.M. Went out to Warwick on Worcester Stage, Uncle Joseph Stevens'. Humphrey S. arrived Wednesday P.M. Went up to Aunt Conants'. Spent three hours there. Returning, ran down across to the Old Brick School House, where I can remember going to school a little. I could remember the inside, but like other old remembrances, it now looked extremely small. If these scenes are interesting to me, how much more so would they be to my Mother, or even to my older brother and sisters!
Uncle Joseph's at Thanksgiving Dinner. All hands. After a walk, games &c. Humphrey, I think has left his Boston employment. Wishes to get upon the R.R.
Nov. 26th. Friday. A.M. Returned to Northfield. Walked part. Rode with Cousin Joseph partway. Found "Blake's" in all sorts of disorder from effects of the last night's Ball. Office drawing Plans. Mr. Field & men had gone to Vernon. Eve. Office & P.O.
Nov. 27th. Saturday. Office. Calculating areas of Ex. Em. Bradley R.R. Director. Northfield Town Meeting on the Road business

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [03], 1847-1848
transcription:
Nov. 28th. Sabbath
Northfield
Rose late. It is a bad practice of Sabbath mornings: the whole day appears to go worse for it.
Heard Rev. Mr. Jones preach. A. M. the History & Character of Daniel; why he was "greatly beloved." P.M. - Eve. Went down to Parson's. Joseph A. just from Warwick Read Ster[[n?]]e! Chilly day. Snow squall towards night.
Nov. 29th. Monday. A very cold day.
I'm R.R. Office all day. Calculating Areas principally. All who are out of doors complain bitterly of cold. Mr. Field at Vernon. I shall feel the cold worse for being in the house this weather. No one in Office but Irishmen. Oysters with Smith.
Nov. 30th Tuesday. Another cold day.
A bitter cold morning: up rather late. Found I was to go out up to Vernon. Rather hard to be kept in the office for three weeks, and then called out such a day as this. However, I dressed up a little warmer, though with no overcoat, and went off. Expected to suffer considerably, but believe I did not so much as the others. Regular drunken set at Whitheads. Bradley. R.R. Director with Dr. Washburn & Mr. Stebbins had a Gin to close a bargain. Field cut Bradley

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [03], 1847-1848
transcription:
pretty hard, as Director of a R.R. Co. allowing no ardent spirit on their works! It is too bad for men like those to set such an example to such a set as Whithead's. Noyes Streeter's land damage referred to Dr. Washburn & Stebbins 4 Acres & 40 Rods, poorish land, but lot cut badly. $110.00. Streeter would not Gin! A Temperance man in Vernon! Office in Evening. Plan of County & R.R. & River. Between How & Pratt. Lovett. carrying off old Greenfield surveys &c.
Dec. 1st. Wednesday. Cloudy growing Warm In the office all day. Slate Landing Road plan. Calculating &c. Messrs. Odell & Young arrived A.M. Paying off Irishmen &c all day. Messrs. Crocker & Johnson arrived in the evening.
Dec. 2d. Thursday. A Rainy Day. Vt. Thanksgiving Office. Crocker about. Johnson, making Plans of the Bridge with Birnie. Odell & Young paying off Irishmen &c. Chas. Fay with Kinin & Flynn in R.R. Office.
Dec. 3d. Friday. Rainy. The day passing very much like the previous one.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [03], 1847-1848
transcription:
Dec. 4th. Saturday. Snow squall. Pleasant. With the whole company, with Johnson & Mr. Birnie, laying out the foundations of the Conn. River bridge; the Eastern abutment. to be first commenced.
The rest muffled up with two coats on, complaining of cold. Myself with one coat & no vest perfectly comfortable, at work, gloves off, coat open &c. How much in these things depends upon habit. Moreover, it would seem that I must have a very good constitution or at any rate very robust health; or is it only because I am a "Down Easter"! Latter P.M. & Evening Office, calculating Areas &c.
Dec. 5th. Sabbath. Snow Squall. Cloudy Rather late. Waiting about &c. Shared by old Brockway Church. Rev. Mr. Jones. Subject A.M. & P.M. Gen. 2d. 17th. "In the day thou eatest thereof thou shall surely die." What was this death?, not natural, but moral. [[?]] What is this moral death? subject fully considered. Discourse written out entire: I did not like it any better. Collection for warming the house, repairs &c. I contributed a little. hardly knew whether I ought or not. The fact is Smith is partly right, that this people are too shiftless to help themselves.

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [03], 1847-1848
transcription:
Dec. 6th. Monday. Pleasant. 3/4 in snow night A.M. over on 45th section. Roads, earth estimates &c. P.M. Down by Smith's altering the line somewhat. Stratton & Grover to Vernon early. Holton at night. Evening office, estimates. Letter from Bangor [[?]] Anne mailed Nov. 28th! Has it been in this office so long, or mislaid elsewhere? Former I think. 20cts. postage.
Dec. 7th. Tuesday. Very Pleasant. A.M. George Smith, completing Curve, estimates &c. P. M. Office. Plan of Smith's Land, and Plan of pile[[s?]] in River abutment until near midnight, when I found myself locked out! Ed got up in his sleep, and let me in, never remembered it.
Dec. 8th. Wednesday. Quite pleasant. A. M. Office. Plans &c. P. M. Went to survey a peice of land down on Pine Meadow four or five miles: for Erastus Field, by him sold to Lanman Nye & Son. I should be a prime Land Surveyor. It was amusing to observe the solicitude of Mr. Nye about it. Meadow Land sold for $45.00 per acre

title: Isaac Stevens Metcalf diary [02], October-November 1839
transcription:
Isaac Stevens Metcalfs
Journal
Bangor October 5th 1839
Saturday October the 5th Rose at 5 1/2 or so A clear cold and windy day. Very frosty night. Some Ice made Potatoe. by mash on other such things, have not been entirely cut down by frost yet, before today. very flat indeed now.
My hands were quite cold in turning out the cow; I must write home for some mittens and other cold weather apparatus. 
There is no school at all to day. Studied my Greek a while
Went down town, helped Mr. W. [[?]] down a keg. Enquire about how I could wool; at Wood, they wont buy wool and pay cash
I dont see as there is any chance to sell it for any thing: I guess the folks made a mistake about wool selling for $ 50 and 60 at Exeter. Bought this of Smith and Lenno for $ 06 1/4
Came up about 10 A.M. up stairs, fixing and puttering Col. down stairs - 11. studied Greek a spill. Went and [[?]] wool 15 or 20 min. got warmed by virtue of the  [[?]]ble sa[[?]]. Up stairs at 12 trying to finish [[?]]om. till dinner. most luckily succeeded.
P.M. Getting in Pumpkins, Squashes etc. digging potatoes in front yard, finished, and sawing wood till 5 then after the cow and milk till supper 6. Upstairs to write etc. Writing letter to Milo till past 8 then studying Greek Reader to bed at 9 1/2 or so

April 1839 Me.
Wednesday
April 10th Arrived here last night from [[?]]lo about dusk it was rather bad traveling, the roads not being settled.
Went to Mr. Worcester's where I expect to board, they appear to be very agreable folks they have 2 children Joseph   years old and Sarah the babe. 3 or 4 months
9 o clock Went to be examined for admission to the City High School, passed a good examination but the Committee made an objection of m coming from another town and appointed a sub committee to enquire about it and see Mr. Worcester, keeping me in suspense
In the afternoon went with Charles [[?]]onn to Hampden to see if Joseph arrived in the steam-boat but he did not.
Thursday
Apr. 11th Charles got the money for his oxen at last, he gave me $ 5,00 of it. I had but 30 cents before He did not get started home till most night
The committee have not decided yet whether I can be admitted or not
Good Luck to Mee

Dear Mr. Shuman,
      It has been my opinion, for some time that an abnormal situation exists within the State of Illinois with gives a creditor, ability to attach the wages for labor of his debtor. A direct outgrowth of this situation, peculiar to our own state and to states which permit easy attachment of wages, is the overcrowding by wage earners of the bankruptcy courts with petitions for "restraining orders" and bankruptcy by these same debtors.
     I maintain further that, this forum is ill-equipped to grant the relief sought, that the wage earner who seeks help from the bankruptcy court does not get the help he seeks. Further, he almost invariably finds himself deeper in the morass of debt entanglement at the conclusion of his bankruptcy hearing than when he started.
      The initial and continuing purpose of the Bankruptcy court was to take custody of the property of a man whose debts exceeded his assets, to divide this property equitably subject to rules of priority among his creditors, and then to give the man a fresh start, free of any obligations he had earlier incurred.
             Bankruptcy generally contemplates that necessaries of life are not subject to its orders, and the business man bankrupt rarely changes his way of life after filing a petition in bankruptcy. But for the wage earner bankrupt, virtually every item of household article, down to clothing and even eyeglasses, is subject to conditional sale or chattel mortgage. The wage earner bankrupt cannot even take advantage of the few items he may by law claim as exempt.
      He may surrender his household furniture, clothing or such items, and go into debt anew to "refurnish" his house, or may "reaffirm" the obligation.
    In either case, bankruptcy has given him little releif; his ages, the one single asset he had sought to

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
1-1-1
You may know that I had hoped for many months to discuss with you personally the subject of housing financing in Chicago, and its place in the coming national campaigns.
Several months ago, in response to a telephone call I made to your office, a secretary stated to me, "Governor Stevenson is always seeking suggestions of imaginative people, and we should know what suggestions you do have that could be specifically adopted by the Governor."
Since that time I have studied and have written almost continuously upon this single subject and I do believe that it is of a consequence to merit your careful study and attention.
I ask in great part that you consider my expression and suggestions within the framework of your own oft repeated statements that "the wealthy nations become wealthier and the poor get steadily poorer."
The housing, FHA, BANKING and financing policies of the Federal government are directly responsible for the creation of a financial jungle among would be minority home owners in our larger cities.
These policies, together with the

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
2-2-2
rulings by our courts on the general subject of usury, the actions of our Federally insured savings and loan associations, and the emergence of a new and ruthless band of real estate speculators in our Cities, has made a housing jungle in our major population centers.
And the one single effect of all these factors, be they benign or cancerous, is that minority peoples, particularly Negro, pay for housing two and three times the honest cost of shelter, and in return get for themselves one third to one half of the housing they need.
As secondary effects, the practice I have (shall) describe (d) is the drawing from these same minority communities of vast sums of money to the enrichment of the wicked speculator and the consequent deterioration of a once stable part of our city. It is as though our Negro people carry on their backs two communities; one, the community in which they live and two, the ghost community occupied by the real estate speculator.
   It is not accidental that very deteriorating areas and the factors which bring about this deterioration is accompanied

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
3-3-3
by the costliest housing in Chicago.
I submit that a definite relationship of cause and effect between the finance practice of the Federal government and the Federally insured savings and loan associations.
Our Federal FHA practices have established loan standards which are known to the FHA officials to be beyond the peoples and structures of our cities. Our Federal FHA officials must know that the standards they have set up are such that leave vast areas of our cities in a financial desert so that there is no place the minority peoples can turn for help in necessary housing.
It should be remembered that these same areas are those which for years and generations were occupied by frugal working peoples. These are sections which were well financed and which required of their people an honest cost of housing and shelter.
The areas were stable and clean and healthy, and were not subject to deterioration. In fact, they made a strong part of the living and growing city.

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
4-4-4
But these were financially as well as culturally breathing communities. Contemporary with the healthy social phase was a ready availability of mortgage money, consistent with the ability of the people to pay.
An examination of the records when the homes are occupied as I have said, would show that the same local mortgage companies are helping all the peoples to finance and pay for their homes.
But no sooner do minority people come into the neighborhood, but these same mortgage lawyers immediately withdraw all their proposed and necessary help. In all ways the minority peoples  are equal in ability to buy and pay for and maintain the communities into which they come.
But they are cruelly deprived of the financial life Blood necessary to maintain any neighborhood.
Two other factors enter here to complete the vicious circle which these minority peoples encounter. The first is a tragic lack of education in even the most basic elements of

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
5-5-5
economics. Pathetically illiterate in matters of economics, they have no earlier arrivals to turn to for help. They are utterly unable to learn or evaluate the costs in which they face the purchase of homes.
They are likewise subject to prey by a profession dedicated to speculation in real estate who are economically expert in real estate values, and who take advantage of the combination of these factors. These men, and too many of these are lawyers, brokers, and other professionals connected with real estate, have made a practice of buying up properties in changing areas, getting mortgage financing from their own sources, and making sales to minority, particularly Negro peoples, at the fantastically high prices I have mentioned.
The heavy costs and resultant overcrowding speeds these processes of decay and destroy the cohesiveness of our communities.
A most necessary change in this situation is the ending of the financial anarchy that now exists in the matter of housing, much as this did exist in the matter of banking half a century ago.

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
6-6-6
The Federal government has the direct responsibility of ensuring that the funds held by insured loan associations are available to all peoples, regardless of race. Those mortgage practices which drain away mortgage financing as soon as Negro people enter a community must be stopped by Federal action.
To do this two steps are necessary. First, the loan companies must learn that the insurance under which they operate will be denied them if they continue in their discriminatory lending practices.
Secondly, I believe it is necessary that the Federal agency itself award its standards so that loans to minority peoples will profit from the same program of government insurance as is available to general loans. In other words, the government insurance policy now acts to make loan companies fearful of investing money in minority neighborhoods for fear of criticism by government auditors.
The very agency set up to help provide home financing now acts as a bar to the honest distribution of money.

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
7-7-7
As I see the first problem, it requires a public examination of this entire question. We should by way of Senate Banking Committee Inquiry, conduct hearings to learn the flow and the shortages of good money.
We should study openly the relationship between the changes in mortgage practices and the deterioration of once stable communities.
We should study the role of the housing speculator in minority areas.
All these offenses will give way to a searching examination. I submit that there rests with you an obligation as well as opportunity to restore to our cities the necessary money life blood needed for their continuous growth and development.
We need also a determined effort to restore the standards of frugal incentive to small homeowners in the heart of our larger cities.
It is an affront to our middle class people that the opportunity for small home ownership not be

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
8-8-8
extinguished. [[struck out:]] It is to no one's advantage that the gap, even in our own city between.[[End of strike out]]

We must avoid the circumstances that bring about major cities composed mainly of deteriorating slums alongside giant redevelopment projects consisting of government subsidized high-rise apartments, also owned by absentee real estate speculators.
These speculators are of course, sold the property under terms very much to their advantage, and very much underwritten by our government.
This practice continues to widen the gap between the people and the growing millionaires in our midst.
We must widen instead of contract, the opportunities for home and property ownership, and the resultant social contributions of people of all races.
I do hope you will see fit to further examine these problems with an eye toward your own contributions to their eradication.

You know that I stand ready to meet with you at your pleasure and further bring to you my own detailed examination and evidences of the existence of this practice.
I do not believe this problem will have the needed attention from any American but yourself.
Very truly yours

England alone was fighting on, grimly, almost without hope, but determined to go on to the end.

     There is a lot of sentimentality about the contract between the American situation this holiday time and that existing in beleaguered Britain, fallen France, devastated Poland, Red Russia, blockaded Germany, conquered Holland.

On the Scene
                                       The Coalition Ticket

  For many years the Chicago Bar Association has offered the coalition ticket for judges. This year the Ass'n has again issued a strong statement disapproving of "the nomination by both political parties of a single ticket some times called a coalition ticket."
  The political leaders like the coalition ticket because it saves the expense and the labor of a real campaign in an off-year. This feeling runs from the top clear down to the bottom of the organization. A G.O.P. precinct captain said he wished the Republican party ad Stuck to coalition. There is nothing in it for the party worker, he says, judges have no patronage and few favors can be expected of them, at least of the kind you can talk about. It only means that the organization has to put in a lot of hard work for very little tangible returns.
   The argument is sometimes set forth that it helps to take the judges out of politics. Of course the exact opposite is true. In case of a showdown only the judge who has been "regular" stands a chance to get on the ticket. All others will have been

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
smeared by backstairs innuendo, even discredited by unfair newspaper stories. Unless he has unusual backing he will lose out in the process of political bartering which precedes the selection of the "coalition ticket."
    The result is that this process of political bartering, by which the candidates are put on the slate, is actually the election. The voters rubber stamp the party selection at the polls. The public generally is so disgusted or uninterested the only a very small vote is cast. The whole thing certainly does not add up to the democratic election of judges.

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965

On the Scene
                                     This is It.

  There are many reasons for believing that the impact of war is only now beginning to be felt in force, and that in another year the hard blows of war will have struck again and again.
   We have an army today of perhaps 3,500,000 men. We now begin to envisage the probability of more than 10,000,000 men in our armed forces. That is going to remove from civil life, just about all the men of military age. Physical standards will be relaxed to the minimum. A man with a bad eye or ear or some deformity that does not prevent him from holding a civilian job may be set to doing a similar military job. A man with a dependent or even two or three dependents may be told his family will be provided for - he must shoulder a Garand.
   The vast needs of such an armed force in weapons, food, clothing, transportation, and shipping will keep the rest of the population working long hours.

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
II
   Women and older men will do most factory work.  There will be plenty to eat but we may not be able to buy new clothes. Automobiles, of course, are out; and so is nearly every thing else people generally buy in large quantities the sum of which we call the American standard of living.
   Meanwhile, industry, as well as employers of all kinds will be calling for help.  Wages will be good and money plentiful. There will be little you can buy except war bonds. For that little there will be many bidders.
   The willingness of those bidders to shoot the works adds up to inflation. That is a problem with which Congress has been struggling. It looks as if Congress both wants and does not want inflation. It voted the president the power to stop it, but refuses so far to vote him the money he says (this from Henderson) it takes to stop it.
   Inflation must be stopped before it really starts.  If the situation really gets desperate the president, under his war power, will no doubt find a way. [[struck out: FDR you remember once closed all banks. He could do it again. End of strike out]]

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
III
   Inflation essentially means the cheapening of money. One way to increase its value is to make it hard, or even impossible, to get.
   People will then say the FDR is at last a real dictator. It will be true - and our Constitution provided for it as early as 1789.
   With such a large army and navy deploying into action, casualty lists will become longer and more frequent. Many a family will give the last full measure of war  - in dead and maimed.
    When those bitter and hard days come as to some they have already, it is well to remember the lesson of Europe - which is that the end of war does not and will not end slaughter. The lesson of Lidice is that it is only the beginning

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965

On the Scene
                                    Unity for Times of Danger
   The sudden catastrophe of Tobruk, and the probable early fall of Sevastopol remind us of a fact that was temporarily observed in the rosy glow of our naval victories at Midway and in the Coral Sea.
   Hitler is still a dangerous foe. A disastrous winter in Russia has not finished him. By "dangerous" we mean he could still whip us.  If such a statement is treason make the most of it.
   The public mind is again suddenly filled with the thot that things are not going well. WE hear again that the British are incompetent or worse - even that they don't care whether they win the war or not. We hear that our leaders are incompetent too. They forget the miracle of production whereby we have armed our forces in an incredibly short time and, to boot, supplied Russia, Britain, Australia, even some for China.

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
II
In these desperate times it behooves us to hang together. WE are under the literal necessity of having faith in our Allies - The United Nations.  Our own leaders deserve our full support.  Any other attitude is by way of strengthening the hand of the enemy - of claiming the lives of more of our soldiers is the price of victory.
    For the trend of the war indicates that in this year of 1942, the stage could be set for Armageddon. Let it be said of none of us that he shirked his duty or gave the enemy the least comfort, even in the most indirect way.
   In the terrible days ahead, let us be of one mind and heart.

On the Scene.
                           Roosevelt and Peace

    What are the issues facing us?
Rationing? Senator Lucas reminds us that all of the inconvenience suffered by everybody in Cook County does not amount to as much as that suffered by five American boys spending 20 minutes in a foxhole on Guadalcanal.
    To him the great issues are bringing the boys home and winning the peace.
   There are signs that a little group of isolationist senators are preparing to sabotage the peace. They plan to follow the lead of Henry Cabot Lodge, who 25 years ago destroyed the effectiveness of the League. It is fair to say that on the conscience of Senator Lodge is a large share of the guilt for the present bloody struggle.
     Senator Bell of Minnesota posed two questions to the presidential asperants. These were in substance : 1- Will you support a world peace organization with teeth? 2. Will you oppose nullifying reservations?

He weighed the answers of the two candidates as thus far given. He found that Dewey had unclearly answered that he had dodged the issue. He found that Roosevelt had answered there questions squarely. Therefore he will support Roosevelt.
   We have the same choice before us. The time is growing short. WE, the American people must on November 7th next, answer the greatest question of our time.
    That question is not rationing, the fourth term, bureaucracy, high taxes, big city machines, or states rights. We are called upon to answer for our own sons and brothers, and for generations to come. The generation's Peace.

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
On the Scene

 The General Welfare
   Aside from the immediate goal of winning the war and bringing the boys back home our greatest interest is in what they will find when they return.   
      Congress has passed the G.I. Bill and it is already in operation. Its purpose is to install veterans as members of the community on equal terms. Those who have been disabled are to be cared for. Those whose injuries prevent them from following their prewar occupations, are to be retrained.    
     Provisions are made from those who wish to continue their education. Tuition and expenses will be provided. If a veteran wishes to buy a home, or a farm, or go into business he can get federal help in borrowing money.
    Both the federal and state laws provide a list of benefits, aids and preferences that will help the serviceman get a new start as a civilian.
      The veteran, however, will obtain little permanent advantage from these things alone. Far more important is a high level of prosperity for the country as a whole. If the general economic condition is good the soldier will be well off. If there is another severe depression he will suffer with the rest of us. This is not to suggest that

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
the G.I. bill is unwise or unnecessary. Generous and specific help of money kind should be available to the G.I. Joe's when they get their discharge papers.
     But they must be under the umbrella of the general welfare.

   Five gentlemen of the R.A.F. came to our house to spend leave. Each day the went forth to see the sight of the great city of Chicago.
    Three were from Manchester, one was from Cornwall, and one from Lancaster. When their people learned they were to go to America for further training, tearful mothers warned them - not of wartime dangers of the deep sea, nor of the hazards of flying - but to stay away from Chicago if they might be so fortunate. To the uninformed Englishman, it seems Chicago is a place scarcely safer than the average battlefield. Indeed it is visualized as a city that is a combat zone for gangsters.

     What was even pleasanter was the discovery of our broad city beaches, the fine parks, and great public buildings. Chicago as a vacation and pleasure spot soon captivated them
   Never had they imagined that in the heart of the North American Continent might be found massive universities such as Chicago and Northwestern, miles of galleries filled with old masters and precious art objects or vast department stores.
    Our Museum of Science and Industry interested them most. Their great regret was that they could not spend days studying the scientific exhibits.
     What they appreciated most of all was the friendliness with which they were greeted every where. Each one answered us that they would never forget the hospitality they found in Chicago. A week was not long enough to enjoy it.
    From these fine lads was learned a little of the true nature of Englishmen.  It was not only the gallons of tea they drank for breakfast, their eager interest in life, the extreme

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
pleasure one of these bomber pilots found in driving a car on the right (wrong) side of the road, or the quiet restraint of their manner.
   It was a little in their curiosity about how English cities look since the blackout has been lifted, and a little in their reserve about speaking of their families. And there was a good deal in the songs they sang one night when we were riding together.
   They were not ashamed of a tear or two, when at the moment of parting, I proposed a toast "To England, and happy days in Blighty."

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
In the Scene.

   A Chicago Motor Coach takes its place in history next to the slot machine as one of the smartest little money-makers in town. At that the gamble is almost as great.
    You step up to the curb and stand at what you think is a likely spot. After a while, along comes a bus operating on a schedule it completely disregards. You move frantically, the driver looks at you critically and if you pass inspection, he brings his vehicle to a halt. After the manner of a pre-Roosevelt speak-easy some doors unfold and you enter, if possible.
    If you get in and are able to put your dime in the slot the game of chance has only begun.  The odds are against you. Favorite bit is that you will not get a seat. A sudden lurch may land you in  some ones lap, but most likely not in a lap you'd care to be photographed in. Not getting a seat, you stoop to keep from bumping your head. You cringe on tip-toe to prevent any one from stepping on your feet. The chances are about 100 to 1 that some one will make a

title: Mark J. Satter letters, 1951-1965
transcription:
mad dash for the door, knock off your spectacles, and maybe even rip off some of your clothes.
    In any event you inhale fumes guaranteed to shorten your life, and get every known type of germ blown into your face.
   There are federal laws about how many hogs, sheep, or cattle may be loaded into a single freight car. But no ordinance protects the bus Rider. Profit is the motive, and the motive all you get for your dime. You can hardly call it transportation.
   That isn't all there is to the gamble. One thing is sure - there will be no tea served on board during the trip. Also you generally get to where you were going but more than likely you are in no condition to do what you intended to do there.
   The Commerce Commission seems to have woke up to the fact the Company is making too much profit, and proposes to reduce fares. For my money it's a standoff whether I'd rather have a lower fare or a less crowded bus. If the number of passengers were limited to double the seating capacity it might reduce the take and increase the pleasure of the trip.

In a special edition on the Tokyo government, supposed to be strongly Fascist, contemplates no alliance with the Rome-Berlin Axis, tho it does expect to bring about closer political ties with the two European Dictators. The editor sees the principle of an Asiatic Monroe Doctrine as the guide for action in the East.
     At that point, as we know there is definite danger of a clash with the U.S. Right now our Navy is carrying the burden formerly shared with the British, the Dutch and the French in staving off Jap expansion to the East Indies.
Only the threat of our Pacific Fleet is preventing the realization of this dream of Asia for Asiatics. The new cabinet is expected to take a stronger attitude here.
     On page one, is a story to the effect that a vast oil supply will still be available to the Nippon war machine, even if the U.S. forbids the sale. A Standard Oil (California) chief is quoted as saying that his company stood to lose $50,000,000 in annual sales if the ban is ordered.

While the American branch is particularly making a good profit selling our army the sinews of war the foreign branch may do the same thing nullifying American foreign policy. Meanwhile stockholders, even as you and I continue to get our dividends.

(1)
Ye may talk about your Fishing Clubs
By mountain, rill or stream-
Of Trout and bass and Red horse-
That large to vision seem-
But the Club down at Ignacio
Where bright Pine river flows,
It's a dandy! don't forget it,
And they line the bridge in rows.
(2)
As the sun behind the Mesa
Sinks to rest, when day is done-
And fishing rods are waving high
Where swift cool waters run.
The Ladies fish with might and main
And whip the stream with glee-
And chat about the wonders
That in its depths they see-
(3)
Now just you wait! I've got a bite-
Swish: now ain't that just too bad-
Twas such a great big [[stunner?]]!
Twould drive an Angel mad-
To think I had him almost out
And now he's got away-
I'm going to fish right in this spot
So! They'll know I've come to stay.

4
Ah! There they are, just see how thick!
They go in great big bands.
So many! You'd think to take your pick
and scoop them out with your hands-
Well! There now! Pshaw! I had him sure!
But the mean old thing let go!
I'll try once more, that fish to lure,
Then straight for home I'll go.
5
And so it is with the devotees
Of good old Isaak Waltons art-
They do their best from the waters to wrest;
The [[finney?]] beauties and play their part.
But 'een though luck may seem unjust-
What all had wished for in the fight,
And tried for too! As Anglers must,
And was failure! cause they wouldn't bite.
(Paghaghet)
Chas. S. Stobie
Ignacio Ute Agency= Colo
June 24th 1902
