title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(1)
The Scalp Parade-
The Scalp dance as practiced by many of the tribes of American indians has been often described by writers who have witnessed these celebrations at or near the villages of the red-man-
There is a custom among the Utes which is not so familiar to our people. And many whites who have been born and raised on the frontier know nothing of this picturesque and imposing Spectacle.
In the summer of 1866 I had the first opportunity of witnessing "The Scalp parade of the Utes"-
The scalp dance being performed on foot requires but a small space- The Scalp parade is participated in by greater numbers and they are all mounted. The actions of both riders and horses, together with the brilliant display of color and glitter of Arms and orniments make an impression on the beholder which it is useless to say once seen is never to be forgotten.
It was a beautiful summer day not to warm, and the clear invigorating breezes from the pine and fir covered mountains were most refreshing- All nature seemed to rejoice- It was evident that something out of the ordinary was going on in the Village of the Utes

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(2)
Many of the men and women were attired in their best, and the young men and boys were bringing in the pick of the ponies from the herd. The scalps on the scalp-poles were brought out from the lodges and were resting against the Medicine poles near the lodge entrances- The ponies were brought in among the lodges and both braves and squaws were soon engaged in saddlling up, and arranging the quaintly ornimented bridles, saddle-cloths and saddles. The latter with high pommels and cantles plentifuly studded with brass headed nails.
Then singley or in groups the indians rode out of the village and crossed on the ripple or fording place to the east side of Grand river. Here opposite the camping ground there was a tract of tolerably level ground, at least sufficiently so for their purpose. Slightly elevated, and surrounded by mountains, and high buttes with great level mesas at the tops- on this clear space several miles in extent, the parade was formed.
The warriors were drawn up in a long straight line all faced to the front, like troops on dress parade, with their war-paint on tricked out as if for battle-many stripped to the waist and their breasts and arms painted

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(3)
as well as their faces. Bows and arrows, riffles, pistols, battle-axes or war clubs and shields being born, as if ready to charge upon a foe. All along in the rear of the front line of warriors who have taken part in the late fights, many othe bucks have stationed themselves, forming a second line. Then still behind these, the boys and squaws, relatives and near friends of the members of the victorious war party, bring up the rear.
In the centre of the front line of braves a single squaw occupies the place of honor. She is generaly the daughter of the Chief who has led the command in the late successful foray-
Dressed in her finest costume of beaded buckskin and wearing on her arms massive armlets and bracelets of silver. Her long black hair sweeping down her back to the cantle of her saddle. She sits erect and as proud as a young queen holding aloft a light pole from which hang the scalps taken in the late fight- these are afterwards stretched on small hoops being previously wel tanned, and preserved as trophies, and highly prized, not only by the braves who took them, but by all the tribe-

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(4)
When the parade is formed a number of the principal warriors from eight to twelve, sometimes more- gather at the end of the line. They are often stripped to the waist all painted in various ways, as may suit the fancy of each. and all wear the war-bonnet of Eagles or Hawks feathers-
At a given signal, a shot from a rifle or pistol. The whole body moves forward at a walk, keeping their places and [[dressed?]] from right-to-left- as perfectly as a command of well drilled troops.
Now, right down along the front of the advancing column the principal warriors who have waited at the end of the line Start off one after the other at short invervals. They are mounted on their war-ponies and plying quirt-lash and heels they charge at furious speed down along the front of the advancing line the full length. Then whirl and come back to the starting point and again turn- Thus a string of continualy charging from one end of the advancing column to the other on a [[keen?]] jump, firing their rifles and pistols and yelling their war-cries like so many demons broke loose.

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(5)
When the parade begins, so does the singing. The drumers are stationed on each side of the squaw with the scalp. Thus being right and left of centre The singing is all in time with the peculiar tapping or pounding of the drums and is continuous. The long war-cry is repeated at intervals and almost constantly the short yelps and I-ya's sound sharply out above all the other sounds. The drums are about the shape of a tambourine but a little deeper and from ten to twelve inches in diamiter. The are opperated upon with a single drum-stick, resembling those used by our bass-drummers but smaller-
The ponies of both bucks and squaws are often handsonely caparisoned. The buck-skin and red and blue indian cloth trappings heavily beaded in beautiful designs peculiar to the tribe and strung or fringed with the hoofs of the Antelope or with deers dew-claws- and in many places with innumberable small tin tubes larger at the base than at the top and looking seperately like small elongated tin pincil sharpeners- Thear by the movement are kept in a continual rattle or jingle-
The horses appear to enjoy the affair as much

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(6)
as the people and are as proud and spirited in their actions as their riders- Rattling their Spanish bits which are strung with steel chain-work and pendants that jingle and clatter with every motion of the ponies head-
Eagle and Hawks feathers flutter from Head-stall main and tail and the long fringes of the leggings of the men nearly reach the ground and flutter and flaunt with the motion of the rider-
On elevated spots near at hand are clustered groups of indians, men women children, intent on witnessing the performance. Some mounted, others on foot, often two astride one poney just as they have crossed the river to the parade grounds many have been brought across the stream by their friends, seated behind them on the ponies and then scatter out afoot and find suitable places on which to stand, sit or recline while witnessing the manueveres of those taking part in the parade- The excitement after an hour or more calms down and the column moves off toward the fording place on the way back to the village, preceeded by the bold riders who with their horses have begun to show the effects of their wild and exciting [[exercises?]], arriving at the lodges the ponies

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(7)
well rubbed down and allowed to cool off gradually and get down to their normal condition before they are again turned loose on the range across the river
The warriors adjurn to the lodges to rest and swap experiences with their friends. or entertain them by relating incidents in the late fight or to speculate on the effect of the repulse or defeat of the enimy and study up what moves to make next-
The scenes about an indian village are most interesting and novel. In the morning many men and women are to be seen making their toilet. Some down at the banks of the stream. others at or near the lodges entrances- It would be well if some of our ladies in civilized communities would adopt the indian method of dressing the hair at least so far as the combing is concerned. Instead of drawing the comb forcibly through their locks as they will at times. The indian woman first loosens out the hair by throwing her head on on side so that the tresses fall straight down. The whip the hair with the side of the hand held edgeways toward the perpendicular line of the drooping locks commencing at the lower ends or points

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(8)
the hair and by so whipping it and gradualy moving the stroke of the hand upward against the hair. The whole mass on one side at a time is not only ridden of dust, or water after washing it but now hangs perpendicularly and so free from tangles that a comb may be run through it with the greatest ease and without tearing the hair out or breaking it-
Then a light application of bears grease and the hair is combed smothely on each side- The men plait their side braids and assist each other or have the squaws plait the scalplock behind in the regulation manner.-
Great care is sometimes taken to keep the saddles, bridles & etc in good order, and may show good workmanship. The straps forming the head-stall were often covered with silver (Real silver gotten in trade from the mixicano-) bent around the leather. The saddles are their own manfacture, strongly built and covered with raw-hide and with high pomel and cantle, often plentifully studded with brass headed nails such as upholsterers use. These are procured from the white traders. Brass wire is used in many ways also for orniment-among the men

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(9)
small locks of hair wound around closely in a spirel manner and a five or six inches long hang down beside each temple.
A breastplate from six to ten inches square, sometimes larger is formed of the tubular bones of large birds. But of late years they use white glass bugles nearly of the thickness of a lead pencil and these taper somewhat toward the ends. They are fastened one below the other in rows downward by the buck-skin strings which are run through them to perpendicular stripps of leather & hanging off on either side like small ribs-
The shields were made of raw-hide and painted on the outer side often in circles something like a target but with broader stripes and many had small tassels of hair arranged around the edge. A scalp being divided into small locks for this purpose.
The cases or covers for the bows and arrows, often of mountain lion skin, are made seperately and fastened side by side. Then a broad band or sling of the skin of the same animal is attached to the covers about two feet apart covered on the inside with red indian cloth. (A thick firm felt like cloth traded to the indians.) and often beautifully beaded and

title: Charles S. Stobie artist's journal and notes, 1866-1902
transcription:
(10)
[[Descending?]] from the mouth of the arrow case there's a pendant of the same skin lined and the lining beaded. This is broad at the top where the feathered end of the arrows some times protrude is over, 2 feet long and tapers to a point___
This quiver or arrow case is not slung under the arm but carried across the back, the sling crossing the breast and resting on the outer part of the shoulders- but in action, when the bow is brought into use, the left arm is thrust through the sling throwing the cases on an angle across the back and the ends of the arrows are grasped by the right hand as they are wanted by reaching over the right shoulder.-

Sept 11 1935.
My dear little friend
Arthur.
When I came home from your house all our friendly neighbors here - The big gray squirrels, the little chipmunks, the robins and the blue Jays, with a family of red cardinal birds were here to greet us around our porch.
Soon you will receive a book of pictures and stories of a funny horse & cow, like those you have. I am sure you will like it & your mother & father too. Here are pictures of some great big animals who live in the Zoo not far from us.

Graham Taylor.

transcription:
Keene Valley NY Aug 11 1918
Copy
Mr J. [[Merlin?]] Bardin
Clerk of the Fourth Church
Mr dear Mr Bardin
For the letter of appreciative Sympathy from the dear old Fourth Church which you sent us in our loss and sorrow we are very grateful. Mrs Taylor and I sought hard fields in which to invest our home life and our work together. She had the generosity and steadfastness to unite home and work without sacrificing the one to the other, altho at much cost to her retiring home-loving spirit.
No one but myself will ever know the life and love she put into lives that were lost and found again, and into the effort to let families and neighborhoods share the common good of the great Church and Community of which they had less than their rightful share -
Across the frontier in the rear she was as content to live and work these many years as she appreciated and enjoyed the cheer and privileges in the  more favored places and fellowships of life

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
So Self forgetful was she all the while that she would accept no credit for any of the work she did or for any achievement of the lives she inspired. Whatever may have been done while we were with you in Hartford, or in the far harder field of our home and work in Chicago, a large share is due to her Noble life
Your appreciation of her, across the intervening years and your considerate thought of me are treasured in my heart.
Gratefully
Graham Taylor

Mr Giovanni Capinille
c/o Chicago Commons
955 Grand Ave. Chicago
My dear Friend
Our Italian Community Meeting touched my heart in thinking of me on my birthday - It made me home-sick to be with you all as I hope to be soon.
It would make you all homesick for Italy to see the orange fig and lemon trees in our garden, and the roses and ivies growing over the walls and up to the roof just as they do in Firenze- Milan - Napoli and Palermo -
Your message named the things best worth working and living for, the good things of life have always seemed better to me when others shared them as their right -
Justice to every one of every race should be as dear to each of us as is our claim that every Italian here should stand for American law and  liberty so it is only just to Italy for every American to judge fairly the many great things Italy has done for the world, and the many good things our Italian American Citizens have done and are doing for America - We must all learn better to live and let live to give and take, to
The worlds fear is a victory better worth fighting for than that of any War None of the brave boys who went from this room to the last war wants to see any next war - We should all work and vote to get the United States into the Court of International justice and into the League of Nations           (over)

  Yours of the 11, forwarded from Atlanta and your letter from Geneva both reached me here. At Jacksonville your Chicago letter of the 12th awaited me.

 I arrived here just in time for my 3 oclock Women's Club appointment this afternoon & had a most responsive hearing. This is the prettiest place I have yet seen - further South

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
with Orange groves, palmettos and more tropical  verdure than about Jacksonville. I wish I could have seen something of the far South, but am rady [ready] to turn homeward Friday.
 Mr McCulloch of Nashville telegraphed me to stop over there an hour or two on Saturday afternoon. This will bring me home a little later Sunday morning. 9 40 Am.
 If you go home or are out when I arrive, leave my mail on my desk. I telegraphed Baldwin to wait until I got home for my answer, or[underline] better [/underline] count me [underline] out [/underline] now. I am glad nothing of importance came up - & am grateful to escape [underline] forwarded [/underline] mail.
 With good cheer to you and all
 Sincerely  Graham Taylor

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
THE CHICAGO DAILY NEWS
Victor F. Lawson
Publisher
Trafalgar Buildings
Trafalgar Square
Telegrams "Epinglage London" Telephone 2325 Gerrard
Visitors' Writing Room

London W.C.  8/12/1914
Dear Miss Hawkins.
 I meant to have written you on this paper. So I will write another letter for Daily News association.
 Its office here is fine in location, equipment and personal [personnel?]  The Bell is almost like Mr [[Davies?]], Miss Archer you would like very much. American tourists throng the place and are so cordially received. At ^ the Paris ^ office Miss Berkler is a Chicago girl. The Bell was on the Chicago Staff & returns there

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
when the War is over.
 Another Chicago reporter for the news started for the front and reached Belgium last week. I knew him and saw him off on his perilous assignment.
 When you come abroad you will get some compensation for overtime Daily News rights. You must come, but, as a lady allowed, "not when a peace delegation Kicks of [[off?]] such a row."     G T

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Harvard Club
27 West 44th Street
Aug. 23/14
My dear Miss Hawkins
 With two steerage passengers I joined in "My Native Country Thee" last night when the good American ship "St Louis" landed us [underline] home [/underline]. Glad was I that poor war crazed Europe is 3,000 miles away.  It was ten oclock when we

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
docked, but Graham awaited me. Neither he nor any one at home had received any of my letters & I have had no word from them though they wrote and called
 Daily News Cables Reported me at [[Me?]] Paris & London & as about sailing home. [[?]]inligation is Suspended indefinitely over there. One is bewildered by the unreason of it all. It is like a terrible night-mare, too awful to be

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription: ture, incredible tho seen and felt. I am so glad all's well there with you all. So I stay here tomorrow and Tuesday to write copy for The Survey & Daily News. Wednesday I hope to be Macatawa. It will be good to be at home a little while before plunging into the thick of things. It seems as though I [underline] must [/underline] think

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
myself [underline] to rights [/underline], after the rough, ruthless shock which this War gives to all one's faith and hope. I have much of interest to tell you, but must wait until we meet.
Trusting you are having a restful month with much fun and good fellowship, and with greetings to your parents Grandmother and Sisters, I am Sincerely Your Friend
  Graham Taylor

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
CLAYPOOL HOTEL
Henry W. Lawrence
President & Manager
The Only Fire Proof Hotel in the City
[image of large hotel]

Indianapolis
Sat Evg May 1916
Dear Miss Hawkins.
 Thanks for your note & inclosures There seems to be no time for me to write or even attend the Conference. Interviews, committees & speedifying [sic] almost all the time.
 I spoke last evg [evening] as a stop-gap to a great audience & heard ^ far more of it than of my presidents address on which I worked so long & hard.
 My report on change of name was adopted without dissent.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
John Dill Robertson appeared here - "to see what Graham Taylor was up to" as he reported.
 He demanded that I publicly retreat what I said about him with regard to [[St Bachs?]] "Not on your life" I said. Then he invited me to lunch and for 3 hours I had [underline] everything out [/underline] with him - in [[unparliamentary]] language! Yet we parted, with the way still open between us.
We have a Commons supper tomorrow Evg I go to Ill[Illinois] [[round up?]] now.
 Expect me to Breakfast Tuesday
 Cordially  Graham Taylor

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
William Penn Hotel
Pittsburgh
[image of large hotel]
June 7 1917
My dear Miss Hawkins -
 I appreciate your good letter received today, with is [sic] word that "all''s well."
 I really have had no time to myself - Incessant Committee sessions, reports, Survey Copy (to get one Conference story [underline] out [/underline] this week) At least a dozen speeches, luncheon & dinner

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Conferences and besetting personal interviews at every turn have as completely taken possession of me as I have been possessed for ten days.
 Tomorrow night I take the 10 ock [oclock] train for home due
 8 50 Wed. morning.
 Will you please get from [[Miss?]] Coleman the Examination papers of my Sen'y class & have them at the Commons for me? If she does not have them, Prof Robinson will know where they are.
 Now I must be off to dine with the Settlemt [Settlement] Federation officers. Its a great Conference. I wish you could have shared it.
 Sincerely  G.T.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Telephone Monroe 1030
Chicago Commons
Grand Ave. and Morgan St.
 Sept 25/17
My dear Miss Hawkins
 Glad to hear of your arrival home. The more so for your good [[farm?]]-outing. You will be welcome at your other home.
 Residents are at lowest ebb - Smith - Hassenstein Notzel - M. Collins & 3 little tailors!  Two of these tail enders have been here all the while, except Lea who was off at Macatawa 1 week & I 13 days which was taken in two "spells."
 Draft Work still exacts all both of us can do to tie up the ravellings & get the quota off - a big job in itself to [underline] land [/underline] the men in camp. I took [[entrainment?]] in charge & went to camp Friday - to muster in 169 men, but lost [[23?]] in the crowd at the Station. So I staid over night at camp to clear up the confusion & Lea staid on the job at this end of the line - Period. Continued by telephone - For Staccato Style
  G.T.  X his mark

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
HOTELS STATLER
Buffalo 450 Rooms - 450 Baths
Cleveland 1000 Rooms - 1000 Baths
Detroit 1000 Rooms - 1000 Baths
St. Louis 650 Rooms - 650 Baths
 Hotel Pennsylvania, New York  New Building 2200 Rooms - 2200 Baths The Largest Hotel in the World

[image of hotel] Cleveland 1000 Rooms  1000 Baths
This Letter Written at CLEVELAND
 Friday aft. Dec 6 1919
Dear Miss Hawkins
 [underline] Briefly [/underline] please my blatent? in S ory copy that chicago Fidectn of Lan, last Tuesday, demanded the destruction of the draft board documents by fire - Some one told me so. But I did not come see the [underline] report [/underline] of it. Frieda Maynard was there. If untrue, I can telegraph correction Monday.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
I am comfortably settled in a nice room here, where all the Com. Conferences are held on the 2d floor. Mornings & afternoons - I am [[sporting?]] away noons & evgs & 3 times Sunday - but tomorrow have no [underline] public [/underline] appointments  There are only 20 on the Com - all able men - I hope my girls acknowledge the [[Spencer?]] invitations or go
 It is cold & cloudy, & so good to be indoors.
 Thanking you for helping me off
  Yrs  G T
Please telephone Miss Chamberlin at the University that I cannot possibly prepare the article requested for publication Dec 15

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
The Grunewald
Best Hotel South
Natl Conf. & Social Work

New Orleans   April 15/20
My dear Miss Hawkins
  two letters, with their enclosures came without delay. It adds cheer and peace of mind to hear from home. While "no news is good news, yet something direct is better.
 I have stood the rather swift pace at Birmingham & Chickesaw well, without daytime rest or mid-meal re-plenishment, tho when you spoke of my morning egg-nog, I hankered for it right away.  My cold is disappearing, tho I cough a little yet. Appetite returns quite vigorously.  So I will build up some. I am taking the morning off, as I speak this afternoon ^ for [[Brancher?]] & again this evg at a Round Table Club of big wig men on "Outlook in Industrial Relations". The Conf Com. made the appointment, explaining that I could say

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
what they could not to that group so here goes!
 Twelve or more Commoners are here so far; the Burns', Vaile, Hyer Willis Ledward, Borsts' Hunter, Marshall Many friends from every where fnt one at every turn. I wish all of you could share the experience & see this unique city. Yesterday after [[tea?]] Miss [[?]] & I spent on the deck of a steamer touring this [[river?]] harbor which is full of interest. School of [[Ciris?]] d   comes Har  Kingsley House is a cordial & family comfortable with three of us men in one room. Dr Elliot, Kennedy & I. Miss McMan was awarded the [[hng?]] cup offered each year by the Times-Picayune "Morning Newspaper, as the one rendering New Orleans the most service last year. She knew nothing of the
 [[suprise?]] sprung at the opening meeting & in briefly responding gave all the credit to the Kingsley House [[group?]].

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
The Grunewald
Best Hotel South

New Orleans   April 15 1920

Alexander Johnson left his work here recently because of nervous exhaustion. Miss Johnson is running the School he started near here for feeble-minded children. The registration at conference is [[promising?]]. Late arrivals due to the strike will increase it. Lovejoy was not as "happy" as usual in his presidents' address - needlessly [[drawing?]] the lives in this very Catholic city, with the Arch Bp [[Bishop]] & other clergy on the platform. Illinois & N.Y. attempt to discredit the conference because of last year's row fails to keep officials & others from participating. I will send you the Bulletins & will "write up" something for next week's Daily News.
 Thanks for the papers. Avery Conley's death in mid-life is a great loss to the public as well as to his family. Please

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Send me their Washington address as I will write to [[Queene?]]
 The returns received from your letters is encouraging. I hoped for that kind of receipts - Not large but many. They may come yet. At any rate we have covered costs of printing & postage, if not of the toil you put into the speculation.
 Brother Howard Elting is a skyrocket for sure. Some "sticks" may fall from him upon us.
 My Daily News this week reports my impressions at Birmingham & Chickesaw. Wonderful work. Miss Collins has hers well in hand - much to her credit. President Crawford took me into his confidence amazingly for He is a [underline] whole
 [/underline] big man.   With [[?ertings]] to you and [underline] all - [/underline]    Sincerely   Graham Taylor

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
[underline[ Newberry [/underline]
1) * Letter from Graham Taylor to his secretary (1920) about transfer of School of [[Curies?]] & PhilanThropy to U. of C.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Santa Barbara May 26/20
My dear Miss Hawkins
  I do not seem to get time for letter writing even here. The family plans so many fine auto-drives and interesting things all the while that I cannot resist going with them. Being out so much in the Sun and air makes me so sleepy 
evgs [evenings] that I swiftly have to retire shortly after nine oclock!
 Miss Edwards seems to have revived from her physical depression following too hard work at the bank for two years, for she seems much brighter and stronger, so that she is up & about all day & evening. She is just as nice as ever & the family life is very fine in its fellowships. Ease and reality
 She wants me to urge for to visit her when

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
You came "out". don't miss it! Her father & good brother (unmarried!) are off with a friend to day for a Month's camping in the mountains. I leave in the morning for [[Saratoga? Sacatoga?]] - to stay over Sunday. Then I go in to [underline] San F - [/underline] for most of next week. Skirting about the Bay to Kentfield, Berkeley, & [underline] Alameda [/underline] for day trips to see friends. I have just written your Sister that I would telephone her about coming out to spend part of a day with [underline] the family [/underline], when I hope to enlist her in overcoming your work-a-day conscience sufficiently to give in to your [underline] duty [/underline] to take rest and leisure - So!
 Yesterday I was personally conducted through Montecito "Estates" surrounding the [underline] palaces [/underline] that crown every hill-top. The lady who knew all & everybody said she could fill every afternoon

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
+ in going through others there. General belong to Chicago Grandees[?]. Mr. Peabody as grand as any of them. I waited over today for his return hoping to renew my personal and bond with him + his helpful interest on the [?].
Mr Ryerson's place, while less pretentious, is very beautiful. But I can only tell you about this wonderland + am keeping memoranda to share with you all.
On days trip through the mountain passes was the long trail of beauty + pleasure. 
I spoke to the social Mr Ken + others here twice- the eighteenth city in which I have done so! I simply had to- to be decent to them + to [?] the rare opportunities to speak for the School + the C[?]. Wherever these mere [?] + better reciprocities, which together will [?] two treatment fees, go far to earning my way!

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
But I have no speaking appointments ahead + having just written Kent Hdquarters that I have done all I can here in the Southern towns, where Kent himself thought I could help more than in the North. He was with me at Los Angeles + Whittier. Please get 3 extra copies of [?] of May 22 + 29
I am seceding a parcel post package of some printed memoranda of my journey to deposit in those yearning vacant spaces behind my chain [?] I work them up with [?]stalks. I should start homes and the [?] of next week,- via yosemite, if I find time + hotel accommodations available. I may send a night letter by [?] advising when I leave + when I am due at Chicago. Any mail or telegrams addressed to Mr Kent R 213. 1st  [?] Bank Bg will reach me on or before June 4th Fri fore noon. Tho I may [?] this time- take [?] will let you know. Sincerely Graham Taylor

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription: G.T. to his secretary Mabel Hawkins - about transfer of Civics & Philanthropy to U. of C.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Telephone Monroe 1030
Chicago Commons
Grand Ave. and Morgan St.
[July - crossed out]  August 6, 1920   6/20
Aug 6/20
Dear Miss Hawkins
 I hope you had a comfortable trip and are enjoying your "Neck of the Woods."  Tell Mrs Parsons to exert her authority as head of the house to see that you let yourself down from the hectic high note on which I have kept the office lately.
 It is quite enough in its precincts now, with the click of your typewriter silenced and your up-roarious ^ (sic) self gone! 
[underline] Confidential [/underline]
 My center of gravity has been transferred to the School & will be there for a week or two daily. The transition was rapid. Wednesday Evg late L.P.B. (Breckenridge) called me up at [[Rainnia?]] to say that the University Com would not accept the School [underline] Com's [/underline] action in lieu of a guarantee by the trustees. So I went the rounds of the six again by [[mie?]] & got [underline] all [/underline] of them - just a quorum of the Board - to meet yesterday noon at the

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Union League. Mrs Blain, Aldis, & Ryerson coming in town for the purpose. They endorsed the [underline] Committee [/underline] communication to the University without change, appending a list of the guarantors, which with Mr Fold's addition of $3,000 was said by Mr Rosenwald to be satisfactory to the University.   Then I was authorized to end the service of all employed Aug 31 (with appreciation) retaining those necessary thru Sept. A Com. was appointed to dispose of the equipment an inventory of which I submitted. I inclose it to Lee if you think we should bid for any of it for the Commons.
I again presented the [underline] deficit [/underline]. It was assumed by Mrs Blaine for $2,500 Mr Ryerson for $2,000 & Mr Rosenfeld for the balance. & cheerfully! I urged the acceptance of My resignation to take effect at any date set by the Bd. It was held up again until the transfer is completed. Meanwhile Mrs Aldis had prepared & read an appreciation obituary which was also held, awaiting my decease. Adjournment immediately followed. When S.P.B (Breckenridge) dissolved in [underline] tears [/underline], with Mrs Blaine trying to find out why to administer comfort. Mrs Aldis returning to help her I dared not delay my retreat to inquire. I fear a nervous break impends. Must stop short.  G T  (I sent Survly (Survey) announcement to be released after [[Un?]] trustees act Tues.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Ye Claremont Inn
Claremont, California
April 15/21
Dear Miss Hawkins
 Thanks for your never failing thoughtfulness in sending me these checks.
 Tell Lea please that I have not yet drawn any check on my personal account.  The book & spectacle case arrived safely, likewise Lea's package of heavy underwear. It is still needed. Danger of frost is feared tonight. The Daily News arrives promptly & keeps me posted. I feared for Dr Brown. He has so changed the last time I saw him. I am glad I wrote

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
him a friendly note tho it was an appeal too. His check came did it not? I am writing Mrs Brown direct [crossed out - Please address in closed letter in C.C. envelope]
 After my public lecture last Evg [evening] which drew a good audience of towns folk & college people, the McKenna's who were in the front seat, asked me to their [[homes?]] here. He is a Steel co. chemist & his brother a Steel Co president. This one said he agreed with 9/10 of what I said, but wanted to put his side of the 1/10. So we had it out on hours, wages &c in a friendly tilt, with night [[lunch?]] added. We have two new friends!

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Ye Claremont Inn                              3
Claremont, California

The Pattons from Highland Park drove over from Pasadena to see me this afternoon. I go there to speak for Dr Fox at his next Sunday Evg forum. & preach here in the morning.
 I [[? aced]] it all well. These first two weeks have been the hardest. The two hours a week with each of three classes are left entirely to me, the professor sitting in the back row & offering not a word, tho friendly enough. My only disappointment

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
is not to have much chance to read, except in preparation for lectures. The immigration Course I have to work out as I go along, having no syllabus or even reference list on that subject, on which I have never lectured.
 Mrs Johnson, formerly Miss Burton who was a resident for a short while 2 or 3 years ago lives 2 miles away & wants me to "tea". Friends turn up unexpectedly here after learning of my speaking & lecturing. Family letters must follow. So good night. Has your father been ill, tho now "better?"   G T

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
HOTEL VIRGINIA
Long Beach California
[image of hotel]
Fri Evg [Evening] April 22/21
Dear Miss Hawkins
 who do you think introduced me to the Washington Gladden club at Mr Beveth's church this Evg? An old friend of yours from Geneva - Jas A. McDill. Now in charge of the YMCA boys work here.
What do you think he said in presenting me to the assembled multitude of men & women? Nothing less than these very words:

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
that he "Knew me better because he knew ^ so well Miss Mabel Hawkins, my Secretary, an old friend of his at Geneva." So! As news to send you he said: After returning from the War he "picked up" the ^Indiana girl he proceeded to marry 3 weeks after he got back, to whom he had been engaged. And so they were happy ever afterwards! His folks - old folks - are near here, as he said your father & mother knew.
 Mr. Booth is as fine as ever. He lives here at this fine hotel - having sold his home when his wife died. The young girl they brought up

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
HOTEL VIRGINIA                                         II
Long Beach California

is interesting for Nursing at Los Angeles.
 I had a wonderfully sympathetic leaning for this reactionary coast crowd ^ to [[give?]] anyone, tho I put the situation up squarely, as I have everywhere else. It has been a great opportunity to help balance them up - the "100% Americans." & "Better Americans" that so much more need to be Americanized than the people they

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
denounce & persecute. E.g. the YWCA. [W underlined twice]  I may be deported before I leave for their spies & threats are everywhere, especially among the School & College people. Therein I [[rapped? or rassed]] them in the Daily News for tomorrow.   I have just run across fine material for my next Ed'l ^ (to be written tomorrow) in a copy of the Long Beach [underlined] Charter, which was unanimously ratified [underlined] today by the State legislature.
 Mr [[Benet? Burnet?]] was one of its 13 framers. The Rotary Club presented him with money for a European trip as a birthday

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
HOTEL VIRGINIA                                         III
Long Beach California

present this week. so he is off early in June. Crowds continue to hear him, so that the church is to be enlarged to seat 2.300. I am proud of the try (45 yrs old!)
 The Methodist Minister at the dinner said he had followed me since I came West to speak at Crete [[M?b.?ork?]] Chautauqua & that Chicago Commons & I had "[[Casred?]] the Country." The

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
episcopal Minister also remarks that he had my "Religion in Social Action" & preached its doctrine. So!
I stay here for a day of rest & fellowship tomorrow. The sea is  almost under my window & the surf sounds sleepy as bed time arrives.  I run out to Santa Ana ^ 18 miles by Auto Sunday Morning to speak at 11 AM. Then by auto stage I go 80 miles to San Diego to Miss Marston's home, to speak in the Cong'l Church in the Evg. Monday I run down to La Jolla to speak to the Bishop's School for girls & to see old lady Miss Scripps. Tuesday I return to Santa Ana

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
HOTEL VIRGINIA                                         IV
Long Beach California

to address a County Ministers Conference & then return to Claremont to meet my classes Wed. Thurs & Fri. Sat, I go North to Ojai Valley to be with George L. Marsh. dear crippled fellow with a sweet strong spirit. I preach for him Tuesday Morng [Morning] & speak to the Thatcher School boys in the afternoon.  I am tempted to stop over to "rest awhile" at Carmel, near

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Monterey, on my way to Oregon. I do not expect to stay in S. Francisco tho I may stop long enough to meet [[Mr?]]  Kent who wrote me to do so. I will telephone your sister. Send me her address  c/o [[Marsh?]] He will forward. I am due, at Eugene Sunday May 8, Portland May 9th & at the University & College until the 12th. If I start homeward right away, I should arrive Monday May 16. But I have not planned so far ahead, nor looked up my route or time tables. Write me frankly if I should hurry home for any reason. I can do so & expect to. But might be tempted to be leisurely after keeping the pace so continuously
 Greetings to all.  G.T.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
574 Bellefontaine Street
Pasadena, California
 Aug 4/25
Dear Miss Hawkins.
 Your "three graces" are together today, just as my three are at Chicago! [[Int?]] for this day only. For KT starts West tonight & is due here Friday. She writes that The Baby is "So ensnaring" that she could hardly tear herself away from N.Y.!
 She also reports the arrival of Mrs Maynard & Frieda in N.Y. July 31, en route to Boston. I do  not know when they expect to be in Chicago. I hope not until October.
 Lea writes "contentedly" of her decision to stay by the Commons. While I expected it, yet I urged her to  feel free to decide as she thought best, but

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
My wits were at their very end in forecasting the bare possibility of her withdrawal - and I think the trustees would have been at their wits end, had they known of any such possibility - as only the McCullochs & the Ryersons did. I wrote the McCulloch's that the permanency of an experienced better paid staff is essential to the stability of the Commons, tho of course I insisted that they had done more than their share financially.
 Clara & Joe Hallinan called on us today for the first time. She is the "picture of health" &  he is has himself as well in hand as ever. They inquired often you, & took your present address. Her mother is ill with heart trouble. I hope your trip [[rounded?]] out as happily as it began & that your mother will be as young again as you three girls on your fine outing. With Mrs Taylor's greeting to [[n..?]] - Sincerely yours
 Graham Taylor - The End.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
574 Bellefontaine Street
Pasadena, California
Aug 26/25
Dear Miss Hawkins
 Thanks for your well-worded message. Mr Lawson's bequest is all the more appreciated by me because it was unsolicited & unexpected - a gift of his own free-will in token of his own appreciation of what the Commons had been & done & what it should & would continue to be & do.
 It [[universely]] relieves me of solicitude for its future. With the Reddington bequest our invested funds will amount to nearly $500,000, with a prospect of other bequests.
 This warrants my urgency of the need to raise the salaries of the permanent staff so as to assure the continuity of experienced heads of departments &

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
freeing them from unreasonable solicitude for their future, now  due to their lack of any scruples, about scant living expenses.
 I am so glad that Lea has this justification of her decision to stand by the [[MPC?]] & that she will not have to fairly live upon the ragged & sharp edge of financial solicitude as I have had to do so very very long. But I am glad to have been able to do it - especially since the future makes the past so much better worth while.
 I inclose the Tribune's sketch of Mr Lawson's life in addition to the D.N. reports for Thursday Aug 20 & Sat Aug 22d for you  all to read & to be filed at the Commons  KT will return to you the clippings of Thursday & Friday. [[?m]] be sure to secur[e] Monday's Aug 24 & Tues 25th (possibly in Oakland or SF)
With the text of the Will from our file & secure any letters from or to him you may find. My tributes appear, among many others viz [[Dr]] Aug 23 p 3. Col. 1 &2 - a brief one wired from Santa Barbara, a long one in my column Aug 29 - which you may get enroute.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
574 Bellefontaine Street
Pasadena, California

Until I see the text of the will I cannot judge of how the Dr & Mrs Davis may fare (my column also) under the trusteeship of the Ill [Illinois] Merchants Trust directors with John J. Mitchell at the wheel of their pilot house! But Mr Lawson doubtless did what he could to perpetuate his spirit & purpose in the management of the paper.
 What else could he have done? What other group could have been trusted to be self-perpetuating? So uncertain is the future to any one! So unavoidable is faith in one's fellows! I am glad Mr Davis was well remembered by $50,000 bequest - in token of Mr Lawson's appreciation of his past loyalty & [[worthiness]] of trust in the future. I am perceiving that Mr [[Dewald?]] will want

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
me to continue.
 There is a great empty space back there, where I always knew I had a friend & could get his sympathetic hearing. [[now?]] such is left me. Lonely indeed I feel without him whose friendship was as true in life as it was until death. That last hope of his to meet & talk over common interests cannot be realized as soon as he - & I - thought. - yet not so very long deferred after all -
K T enlivened as much. Mrs Taylor would love to have her "stay always." Her help on my book MSS has been very valuable & stimulating to m e. She is the only one who has really read it through. I am going at it again with fresh impetus & hope to finish the first rough draft before coming East. With our greetings to all & Love from both of us.  
 Cordially  Graham Taylor.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Letters - G.T. to his Secretary, Mabel Hawkins -
1935 - Money gift to her
1938 - during the last weeks of his life.

title: Graham Taylor letters [1], 1884-1938
transcription:
Chicago Commons
955 Grand Avenue
July 1 1933
My dear Miss Hawkins
 For a long while my Will has reserved this token of my deep appreciation for the large share I have had of your devoted friendship with [[Mr?]] Taylor and our whole family. I take it out now that you may receive it without any reduction levied by heavy taxes upon bequests going beyond kinships.
 Be assured of how gratified I am to deliver it myself as a very inadequate expression of what I owe to your helpfulness in serving the great human cause for which Chicago Commons stands, to which you have contributed so skillfully and devotedly through all these years of our cherished friendship.

January [[4th?]] 1909
Dear Mrs Kerr
Or have you droped the name? I am in a fog how to address you! Very many thanks dear for the lovely photo. What a quantity of hair. I guess you are proud of

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription: your girlie. I picture you quite ch[[?]]. It was good to spare me one. The Jap's seem busy. I have been alone as usual am so glad now we shall begin to look forward to

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
Albert Villa
CartBridge
Woking
Feby 23 - 1909
Dear Mrs Kerr,
I feel that I did not thank you half enough for Katherine’s Photo - it seems that it must be a good one, she seems likely to be a fine woman, and I hope a comfort to you. What a busy life you lead, and it will make you more so

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
having to attend C. C. Committee. Times seem very hard for many now. If something only could be done! I wonder dear if you have had three Photos from Pattie? I had this morning, one evening dress, one full length with hat - (which I like best). the other a laughing face. I have acknowledged them to C/O Henderson stock Co - Warsaw, Indiana - so I conclude
she’s gone on the stage, she appears smartly clad. Not one line with them. The life must be wearing, at the best

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription: but some folks seemed to like it; so many take to drink, that seems dreadful. I hope she will not; but one can do nothing, so it’s useless talking. We have had some cold, foggy weather lately, the frost cut off all our winter greens one misses them so. I think [[them?]] so wholesome. The snow drops are coming out, and the black birds and thrushes, begin to sing so soon garden work will have to begin, but I fear to venture if at all damp, it’s penny wise, and pound foolish

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
to take cold, which I am a good hand at, so far have not had a very hard turn. I hear theres a lot of Influenza about. I dread it. You see I have no particular news so will not take up more of your time. Trust you and K - are keeping well, Your Mother also. With much love to you both Believe me Yours affec ately
Jenny Ingham

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
Albert Villa
Cartbridge
Woking
Jany 23 - 1910
Dear Mrs Walden
It is such a long time since I had a letter from you (the end of July) I think I answered it after I came home from the Sea (I went to Eastbourne for 10 days to pick up strength; I sent papers and small parcel with letter to Indiana [[?]] for Xmas, and a P-C since to this address to thank you for pretty Calender - I trust you

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
are not ill - Do let me hear soon -
I have had P.C. and letters from Pattie - but you are never mentioned by me to her, she asked once if I heard from you. If she has been trying to make mischief, please tell me - She sent me a fancy [[?]] brush at Xmas, and seems to be getting on alright -
I have had one of my old friends daughters here

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription: a month, I fear its a case of spinal complaint, but am thankful to say she went to her father last week - We have not had very much cold yet - it does not seem to last longer than three days frost, then rain - The papers are full of election news - I hope the Liberals will get in - I suppose you are not for "tariff reform" I shall be glad when its all over, for it seems to make a great upset -

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
I hope this will find you well - With much love to you both
Yours affec ately
Jenny Ingham

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
Albert Villa
Cart Bridge
Woking
24 Feb - 1910
Dear Mrs Walden,
Yours just to hand so will answer at once or I shall be putting off as usual. I do hate writing I was so surprised to learn Ks hair was not dark, I thought both of you had brown hair, I dont know why I should, mine used to be

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription: but now its turning white. I expect K- is taller than you now, and could look after you at the Masque, I guess you both enjoyed it. How dreadful it must be to turn out of heated rooms into the cold. it would about finish me I think - So it seems you have given of up the people! I fear it must have been a thankless office, but I do hope this undertaking will be a success, and that you havent to be always on

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription: the tramp, you are a wonderful go a head people, what would you say to be here, the Gas, or Electric does not reach us yet! but it does not trouble one. I dont want to go out at night. We have had nothing but rain lately, its so damp - I have not been out for a walk for five weeks, had La [[?]] a fortnight in bed and dont seem to get up strength yet - but we must hope for better weather soon

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
So glad P- had not been up to mischief, its nice to hope she is doing better now. I had a P.C. from her to day. Perhaps this "Harry" will be able to look after her. How strange the paper did not reach you. It was lucky you got the letter - I suppose K- holidays are over now. What busy people you must be - Conclude you got over your cold right-
With much love to you both from yours ever
Jenny I-

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
Just a line from P - at Plattsburg, she seem doing well. I don't know yet if she as changed her name
Albert Villa
Cart Bridge
Woking
March 27th 1911
Dear Mrs Walden
I was so pleased to have your most interesting letter and think it's too bad of me not to have written before, but you know how it is when one starts putting off and I have been so lazy everything seemed to much trouble the winter, and spring does not suit me, only been out of the

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
garden about four times in as many months, but this last week have been brighter and feeling better. I think it's  hives and gout. So glad you are
feeling stronger. You need to with the busy life you lead. Its so nice you have K. at home in the evenings. I expect both you and her father are very
proud of her (he might have treated you to a set of furs also) it must be somewhat awkward for poor K--isn't it? but your life seems altogether less stiff than here, "[[Mrs?]] Grundy" is so much to the fore especialy

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
no country villages. The coat of arms belongs to this country. Children leave school at 14 here. We are only taxed so far as penny in the pound
or rent of house--but many have to pay more. It seems to me somewhat absurd how they try to teach the [[yokels?]] The Three Rs, well taught, surely would be enough unless for the extra sharp. I have not heard from Pattie lately. The photo was not very pretty of her!! she seems to stick to the life--It must be very trying--We have not had a severe winter much rain, little snow, but there

title: May Walden letters [1], 1904-1940
transcription:
was a fall last week to our surprise after two quite warm days. it's now blowing N.E. which I hate. We have got some peas in [[so?]] we want it warmer. Have not put a [[hen?]] down [[yit?]] are bothered with rats I wish we could grow tomatoes like you. Its to be hoped it may be a fine summer for the Coronation, doubtless London will be very full, but I don't suppose I shall see anything of it. It takes so much money to go about. Hoping this will find you all in good hands. With much love from
Yours ever
Jenny
