title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
16
111
The Red Rock Canon Fight
I
'Twas in camp we lay as you quickly shall hear
McKenzie came to us and bade us prepare
Saying saddle your horses by the setting sun
For the Indians were laying in Red Rock Canon.
II
We saddled our horses and away we did go
Over rivers of ice and mountains of snow
To the Red Rock Canon our course we did stear
It was the Fourth Horses who had never known fear.
III 
We rode all that night 'til the daylight did break
[[When?]] the herd from the Cheyennes the Pawnee did take
But the squaws they escaped papooses and all
For we wasn't in time to capture them all.
IV
The Indians formed up, the fight it began
They thought they could frighten the bold white man
With our glistening arms right at them we sped
They turned tail about, to the rocks they all fled.
V
We soon overtook them as frightened they fled
Cut off the long hair they wore on their head
"No Mercy" "No Mercy" so loud was our cry
Have vengeance for Custer brace soldiers or die
VI
'Mid snow on the rocks the Indians lay dead
Over thirty were scalped and the rest of them fled
Six hundred dragoons made thousands to yield
Their chief's sons likewise lay dead on the field
VII
McKenzie came to us and this he did say
"I thank you brave boys for your valor today"
Catch up your horses and feed everyone
For the fight it is over and the battle is done.

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
110
made me feel better. I then set there a while and goot up and started to find hed quarters. I met the Genral and he asked me if I had been shot I told him no and he sed no more. I went past the hospitle and a round the hill and hear I found the boys they had all had there dinner and the Pack trane had goot in. so I goot my self some thing to eate I fed my little horse for he was near gone up some of the boys were mity sick and I did not say mutch a bout my leg. the Indins had stuck up a White flag two or three times in the day but the Genral did not see it and the boys would shoot at it. a bout this time Frank Gurrard our scout come up and sed that the Indins sed if the soldiers would stop firring that they would so the Genlal gave orders to seeces firring now every thing was quiet and pooty soon there was a White flag stuck up and the Gen told Gurralde to go and se what they wanted. they told him if the Gen would give them there Poyenes that they would surrender. but the Gen told them he could not give them there Poyens. So they told him to come and take them that he had cild most all of them and he could cill the rest. I gess there had been a bout 1 hundrad cilld and I dont now how meny wounded. Well there was no more firring done to a mount to any thing and I took a walk down a mong the teepes our Indins had birnt a good menney of them I come to the teepe where I had goot the pipe in the morning. and hear I saw the old squaw shot all to peeces. I found out after wards that some of the boys in my company had done it for to git the Bufflow robe. I saw lots of ded Indins now laying a round all over. I went back and watched the boys Carring in the ded and Wounded some skelpt and striped of all their clothing. a mong them was 3 out of our company one by the name of Kellie was kild and two by the nams of Strick and Buck were wounded

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
9
109
us in a cross fire all day. When the Indins Broke the Squaws and young ons lit out for the timber and goot a way. the boolets come so thick that the Genral says you ordlys need not follow me a round any more so that left us to go where we wanted to, so I went down in a mong the teepes to see what I could find. for the Pawneys were plundering the camp. I went in to one teepe and hear I found an old squaw with a nice pipe Well thinks I I must have that and so I made moshens to let me see it. but she would not do it I could of shot hir but I did not like to do that so when the stuck it out a little to one side. I made a grab and caught it by the bowl and she hung on to the stem. She would of made at me now but I stuck my pistell in hir fase and she did not like the looks of it and she lade down and roled up in a nice Buflow robe I had a noshen to take that but I went out and left hire to hirr fate. I poot the pipe in me pocket and went over to a company that had there horses in a reven and left mine there and climbed up on a hill Where I could see all that was going on. I now thought I woild take a few shots at some Indins I saw a bout 1 thousand yards off. I fired all the shots I had in my belt and then as I was laying there on my belley. I fell a sleep I dont now how long I lay there but when I a wake Wright on my right side lay a fellow and his back ded with his mouth open. you bet I started to git a way from hear. but found I could hardley moove for my right leg was stiff. I limped off and found my hors and set there a while rubing my leg. I did not now what to do for I did not want to go to the doctor with a little thing like this. So I goot on my hors and started a cross a flat and I belive there was one hundred shots fired at me but I did not notice it for I was in sutch pane I did not care weather I goot shot or not. I now went down behing our company and bathed my leg in the crick and this

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
108
I saw an old Indin and a boy makeing for the hill. I took a shot at him with my pistell and he caught hold of his leg and limped off I dont now weather I hit him or not as I come to each company I told them what the Genrall sed and they dashed off at Lighting speed it seemed as if the horses had goot new life. When I goot to the last Company I turned back and I never hird such a thunder of horses in all my life for it was all rocks where we were. as I come in to the camp and looking for the Gen I looked up on a nole Wright over the camp and saw a man drest in a suit of Buckskin. I could not help but stop and watch him fireing in to the Indins it turned out to bee a scout that they call Little buck shot. 1 hundred of such men as him could whip more Indins than all the command poot to geather. Well I found the Genrall at last and saw [[777?]] company scatter off. I then hird some one say Leut Mckiney was shot. but not a word of lots of Privits that I could se laying a round ded. the Genral says go over and tell Capt. Davis to make a charge with his company and take a hill. jest as I goot there I hird some thing go pot and one of the men Wright by me throde up his hands and droped off of his horse. I goot out of hear and then watched this Company make the Charge it was nice for they all hung togeather like one man. they took a hill Wright where Leut Mccinney was shot and cild a grate menney Indins hear. I went to the Gen now and followed him a round. We were standing still once and the boolets were flying thick. Where a fellow by the name of Foster one of the ordleys Wrode up to me and says moove a round smith or you will git shot. this is some thing I had never thought a bout before for I was to much excited looking at some of the rest of the boys gitting shot and beeing carried down to the Hospitle. I for goot to say that When the Indins saw so meny soldiers comming over the hill they broke and run for the hills and this left

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
8
107
to git reddy for a dash for it was to late to surround the camp but not to shoot unless they shot first the Gen come a hed now and I hird the Genrall tell Leut. Latton how we would have to do it he sed we were to late to surround the camp and we would have to make a dash for it he says We will ceep the Indins right a hed of us and make them go in first and if there is any trap they will catch it first and then we can open on them from the rear. it was now I thought of the Custer Mascree and began to think what I was a bout to go in to. but I did not feel a bit shakey I dont now why eather. I never took off my over coat for it was to cold. it was now day light and we started. We had room in the Pass to go in colloms  of fours and the Indins at the hed We had not gone far when I looked up and saw a Indin on top of a big rock he firred one shot and that was a signal that the Ball had opend. he was up there as a sentinal for the camp I supose he [[waunted?]] his poney and lit out. it was now that our Indins set up the War hoop this was the first time I had ever hird it in earnest then I was Wild with excitement. We started now on the charge but just as we goot near the camp the Indins turned up on the side of the mounten and this left us right to the front. Well this did not stop the Genrall and we dashed on. now there was a bout 10 of us a way a hed of the collom. When the Indins saw the Indins on the hill they all turned out and commenced a hevy fire on them they had not seen us yet. When we were Wright in to the camp the Genral looked a round and saw we were all a lone. he goot a little excited and says go back and tell them companys to charge in hear. I went my self and went on the jump. I would of dashed in to the camp if he had of told me to jest now for the Bullets were flying every way and mity thick to I had my Pistell in my hand and felt a little Rattled I must say for this was the first time I had ever hird them so close. as I was going a round a hill

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
106
Satirday Nov 25th. 1876
if the hostils had of none we were a comming they could of cild every man of us in some of these places Well a bout 2 Oclock we come in to a nice valey they call it Sioux Pass it was the nisest place I ever saw a bout five mils long on one side there was a wall of stone just as thoe it had of been bilt and on the other side there was mountanes and they were covered with fine treas. and it was a bout one hundred yards wide and the moon shone in at one end and it was a splend site to see the boddy of horses moving a long and not a sound to bee hird to the ground was like a carpet I belive this Wall of rocks stood one thousand feet high. Well when we come to the end of this Pass we found the Indins all un saddling and saddling there War Poynes getting reddy for war and they changed thare close and pot on thair war dres and panted them selvs up and they did look wild a nuff some did look hiddius We mad a halt hear for 10 or 15 minuts and the Indin sed we were near the camp. We started a hed and past the Indins hear and marched over a worse cuntry than we had been in before as we were going up a offle bag mountane We hird a shot a way in the rear then you had out to hear the Genrall curse he was to mad for any youse. We donut out after wards it was a man shot his Plade out horse. When we goot to the top of the mountane we made a holt for there had not any Indins come a hed since we had mad the last holt and I thought the Genrall thought we were beeing drawd in to a trap and he mad all the in dins march a hed. Well we went down off of the mountane and went about 2 mils and the Gide says stop and come with me. We hosted and the Gen went a hed with the Indin and in a bout 10 or 15 minuts he come back and sed tighteng your saddels and git reddy for a charge it was now jest dawn of day and could jest see a little the Genrall now went back and told all the companys

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
7
105
Friday Nov 24th. 1876
Left camp 8 Oclock since we left the Wagon trane I had to stay with the Pack trane to look out for our muls for I was cook. We marched 10 mils and hear we met an Indin and he told us we were Close to an Indin camp. So we made a holt right at the foot of the Big horn mountanes and it was a nice place to. We were not a loud to bild any firs an so we had to eate our raishons raw fat pork and hard tack. We lay still till Nite and nobody was a loud on any of the hills a round We had not been hear long When a soldire came dashing in to camp and sed they were a comming Well that cosd quite a stompeed a mung the men and we all started for our horses in the hird but it was nothing but some of our Indins looking a round for signs. you can see now that they aught not to inlist boys to send out to fite Indins they air not the thing a tall in this cuntry they air to frade and not to bee on Post. I will ceep on till 12 Oclock at nite a bout sun down we goot orders to saddle up and have every thing straped [[tite?]] I now found that I was to bee left with the Pack muls but I could not stand that a tall so I went to the Genrall and told him that I wanted to a long with him for I wanted to see all the sits there was to bee seen so he told me I could and he left an other ordly with the muls. We started out and climbed the first hill on our rigtt and I dont now how we ever goot up and this cind of marching lasted all nite a grate meny horses gave out and some could not clime the mountains the Indines now began to pass us one and two at a time till they all goot by us We were not a loud to speak or lite a match in some plases We had to go in single file and that strung the colm out five or six mils

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
104
Wensday Nov 22td. 1876
left camp at seven oclock and made 28 mils and camped an crasy Wommans Fork it was the day that the Grate Sargent Mager began to think that there was a going to bee a fite soon and he goot the roomitize all at once and could not ride his horse. and had to ride in the amblance I was glad to git rid of him for I hatterd him warse than a snake. this was a very cold day
Thirsday Nov 23td. 1876
this morning a bout sun up we saw an Indin comming in with two Poynes and carring a White flag he come up to our Gen and shook hands and it turned out to bee two Bors that the Gen had sent out from Red Cloud to hunt an I camp and to meet us hear he had been out now 1 month. then he and our Genral went up to Genral Crooks quarters and they had a big pow wow the Indin sed there was a camp 45 mils to the north and he had been in the camp. then Gen Crook gave our Gen orders to take all the Cavelery and all the Indins and the pack trane with 10 days raishons and go and try and bring them in and not to have a fite if he could avoid it and this Indin two Bors would bee our gid. the Genril came back to our quarters and told us to pack our three muels as quick as we could and bee reddy to start and all the companys goot orders to the same affect. I had it a little better hear a gane then if I had of been in my company for I was alade to poot all my blankets on the muls and the boys in the company could only carry one and that on there hors. and we had all we wanted to [[late?]] on our muls. Well a bout noon we left and mad 11 mils and camped on annone Crick. We left the Wagon trane Correld with the Infratry with it and more men with poor horses beer cold to day

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
6
103
Sunday Nov 19th 1876
We lay over hear all day and goot pade this was the first Pay day I had ever poot any money a way with the Pay master I poot 18 dollars with him to start with I dont supose I would of done this only I had mad a strong resilution never to tutch Whiskey a gane. Well us boys thought we had to have some thing better to eate So we throde in and made up a nuff to bye a lot of corn stuff sutch as corn and tomatots. Well we did a feast while this stuff lasted and hear I had a fus with the Sadler Sargent a little dride up fist but I dare not tell him this he went to the Gen a bout me and the Gen cold me up and told me he did not want to realeve me and if I had any thing to complane a bout to come to him and this settled it all We wound up the day by cutting cotton Wood there were a grate menney drunk to nite
Monday 20th. Nov 1877
Lade over to day all day and run a round with orders last nite while one of the boys belonging to the 5 Cavelery  was on a drunk he goot so drunk that he fell in to the crick and goot wet and lad out on the bank he frose to death and his Company planted him in the after noon. I was up with the Gen to the Post and goot my super with the company there. there were a grate menney drunk up there to day
Tuasday Nov 2td. 1876
We broke camp and moved camp a bout 2 mils up the crick it was hear I was poot in to cook for they thought it was my turn Well I was satsfide and went at it and the first thing I done was to bake [[bred?]] and I burnt up the first pan. I finley mad a pooty good cook out of my self. and now it was that thay all let up on that handy name Smith they had near wore it out. I had fool swing now to do as I pleased the onley thing that botherd me the first day was carred watter a bout half a mile in camp kettles it was a very slopy day

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
102
Wensday 15th. 1876
left camp as usual and made 15 mils and went in to Camp on the South Fork of the Chyene River. and it was hear that the holl command camped to geather We were well up in the Indine cuntry now and pooty wild to
Thirsday Nov 16th. 1876
Broke camp earley for we had to pool the Wagons up a hill this camp was in an cind of a bason and it was nice and warm and had lots of Wood. The man that was cooking for the mes opend a con of lard and Gack Morrarety the buglar went to work and cooked some Donuts and made some tea and this was the best supper I had on the trip. We pooled the Wagons up the hill with roaps by hand
Friday Nov 17th. 1876
broke camp and marched 22 mils and camped on a unknown crick it snod all day and very cold
Saturday Nov 18th. 1876
We left camp at the usual time and after going a while the Gen says Smith come with me so him and me started out a hed on the jump We were going threw a nice valley and we did not stop till we goot in side of Fort Reno so we went in and up to the Commanding officers and found out where the best place top camp We went in to camp 1 mile below the Fort this Fort is bilt on a branch of the Padder river and is bilt of logs a bout 15 log cabins. that is all there is at this place and it is in site of the big horn Mountanes We had a hard time gitting the Wagons a cross the crick had to pool them a cross with ropes our camp was a nice camp. there was a big bank on the North of us and that ceep the wind off it was hear that we cut our first Cotonwood to feed our horses in sted of hay this cind of work lasted till we goot back. it was a grate bother

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
5
101
Monday Nov 13th. 1876
Still we lay over for orders to move on very cold all day this morning the frost stood out on every thing the Gen stade up with Gen Crook all nite and I took his horse up to him in the morning and we came back WE had not been back long when I hird that offle name Smith. I did hate to leave that little Sibley stove for it was nice and warm in the tent Well I went out and this Sargent Mager says saddle up your one and the Genrals horse so I done so and went to the Gen he came out and mounted and we started he says to me Smith how dose your little hors run Well I say he allways ceeps up with the rest of them. Well he says that is a good horse and we will have a rase Well we started We jest flew for a half of a mile I could of past him but I did not like to Well we stade there a bout an our and come back the old man felt his Bitters pooty well and we come back as fast as we went and I liked it for it was fearful Cold
Tuasday Nov 14th. 1876
It was very cold in the morning and the Ice was Flotting down the river we were all Wadeing a round in the snow and did not now weather we were going to leave or not. Well a bout noon we goot orders from genral Crook to pack up so we started and marched 18 mils threw a Worse cuntry than we had been in yet it was gitting from better to worse all the time this Nite We camped on Sage Brush Crick and there was nothing but sage Brush to Birn it was hear that an Indin came in and gave the Genral an half of an anitlope and the Gen gave half of it to us ordeles and that made is a good meal. We had more to eate than if we had of been in our Company

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
100
Saturday Nov 11th.1876
lay over all day a nice day We drawd our seal skin caps and over shoos hear to day
Sunday Nov 12, 1876
I woke with a shudder for I was cold for the first I node it was winter I peeped out of my tent and there before my eyes I beheld a foot of snow but I had to croll out and fed my hors and went to my brekfast I missed one of the boys now and asked where is Wilson. now then this Sargent Mager Welch had to poot in he says What the hell is that your buisness if you dont tend to your one buisness I will make you. it is. good thing for this rum sucker that I never drank as I would been apt to cill him one of those times. but I had to much sence to give back talk. Well I smelt a rot and walked up to his tent and looked in and there I saw my man with his nose split open and eye cut he was all over blud and pooty drunk yet. I goot some warm watter for it was offel cold and washed him off the best I could and then I goot it out of him how it come. he sed he was cold up in the nite to go up to the Fort with Leut Latton and they both goot drunk and started to come back and his hors ran a way with him and the started the Leut hors and as he come up by his side the Leut drew his pistell and struck him a cross the fase with it witch nocked him off and senless When he woke he found him self in the edge of the Plat River all wet and all blud but he went to Camp and went to bed before day Broke. the Genral gave the Leut quite a talking to but that did not a mount to nothing as I will hearafter show of course he felt sorrey when he goot strate and told Wilson if he wanted any thing he would git it for him. snode till noon to day pooty cold

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
4
99
Tuasday Nov 7th. 1876
We left camp at sunrise and it was offle dusty a way behind in the collom all day. marched 15 mils and went in to camp on Elk horn crick plenty of wood hear and pooty good watter
Wensday Nov 8th. 1876
Broke camp at 9 Oclock and marched 15 mils and went in to camp on Wagon hound crick We past eight or nine graves on the road suposed to of been kild by Indins. it was hear that the big supply trade come in site of us and they camped a bout 3 mils from us and the Pawne Indins eat up hear to for the first time
Thirsday Nov 9th. 1877
Broke camp at sun rise made 18 mils and went in to camp on Plat River 1 mile from Fort Fetterman. goot to camp earley and it was a nice day so I washed my close and it turned off cold a bout nite the Prayery caut fire and come near driving us out of camp. it was at this camp that the old gard had to report to poot up hed quarters tents and git wood this took a good deal off us ordleys it was hear that two men of the old gard come up and reported to the Genral in this manner. Hallo What do you want us to do hear the Gen says look hear my man who air you they told him and then he cald a sargent and told him to take them out and make them [[?]] a stump for 1 Our and a half. then some of the Gard was late and he made them carrey forrige a bout a mile for punshiment
Friday Nov 10th. 1876
We lay over all day and they had all the companys out drilling I lay in my tent and watched them twords nite I took a dispatch up to Gen Crook and saw some of the men pooty fool and some were lade out commenced snowing about 9 Oclock

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
98
Sunday Nov 5th. 1876
I had to jump up with the bugle and take care of my horse and git my brekfast and then I hird that name Smith from the Genrall. I began to think now that I was the only ordley that he had all thoe there was 4 more beside me. Well I went to the tent and he says git your horse and go up to the Post and give this dispatch to Gen Crook jest as soon as you can Well a way I went and dellivered it and started back When I goot near back I met the Gen all a lone he says come with me Smith so I followd him a round for a while and he sent me to comt with the order to pack up. Well we goot packed up and started on our march it was hear that Gen Crook first joined us with a nother Company of Cavelery and it was on the day we felt the first of Winter Snode some in the after noon, We narked 18 mils and went in to comt on North Plat river
Monday Nov 6th.1876
this day we made 18 mils all so and went in to camp near North Plat on some mud hols. hear some of the indins had found some muls and the Genral sent me over to see if they were Goverment muls or not there was an Indin with me by the name of Sharp nose and he started and poor me behind him. We jest flew over ditches and hols. I thought he was jest trying me to see how a soldier could ride. Well now I was not to bee bluffed of by an Indine and I cep wright on to him he cep looking back and when we goot there he says [[heep?]] ride. I then made signs that they were not Goverment muls and went back. I had not been in my tent long when I hird that Sargent Mager calling Smith Smith. I says What the hell do you want. He flew at the tent and says What do you mean by talking that way to me. he says if you ever talk to me that way a gane I will tie you up by the thumbs

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
3 
97
Saturday Nov 4th. 1876
We broke camp earley and made 28 mils and camped on North Plat River a bout 1 mile above Fort Larmie. We goot in to camp pooty late and goot our tents up and all fixed I went to bed earley and went to sleep for the nite as I suposed but that was not to bee  a bout 10 Oclock I hird that handy name Smith I jumped up and drested and went out only to meet that noted Sargent magor With God dam your lasy Sole it takes you longer to dres than it would a holl company now says he go and saddle up your hors and the Genrals to and report to him. of corse I felt good after beeing so kindly talk to and goot the horses and went to the tent then the Genrall come out and we mounted up and started to the fort it was a bout 11 Oclock now and the Genral jumped off and says look out for the horses. Well there I stood I guess about two ours then I saw some one come out the dore and come up to my. I now thought I would bee back soon in my tent under blankets but Alass it was not to bee so for in stid of beeing the genral it was one of Genral Crooks ordleys with a drink of Whiskey for me but I told him no I did not want it all thoe it went a gane the grone I was nearley frose by this time and I asked him how long he thought it would bee before he would come out God only nows says he they ais all potty fool We talk a while and then he went in and left me to think of the post I had after hird of nigers standing out side and holding the horses but I never node how it went before. time went by and finley yes after a while I saw what was a grate Genral but a few ours befor. but now Alass. yes Alass. Well we finley got started and I was so stiff with the cold I could hardly ride. but the way we went over that hill I soon goot warm we were about two [[mints?]] gitting to camp

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
96
Thirsday Nov 2st. 1876
our Wagon had come in by this time and we unloaded and goot our brekfast and packed up a gane and left this camp We were all to geather  now a gane and we were at the hed We marched 12 mils and went in to camp on Running Watter after the horses were all turned out to hird and our tents up the Genrall says Smith go over to Mager Mack and tell him to poot his hird over there pointing with his finger I went to the Magor and says the Genrall say poot your hird over there jest as the Genral had done. he says dose he mean over the crick I says I dont now sir then he say God dam your soul if you ever come to me that way a gane I will make you walk all the trip. my hair stood up strate i now but I dare not say a Word. and Walked a Way like a Whiped school boy. I now at the time I would gave fiver years of my life to Walked up to him and smaked him in the nose. there was no wood at this camp and the boys began to tore down an old stable that is at an ranch hear. It was here at this camp that the two companies of Indians first camped with us.
Friday Nov 3d. 1876.
Left camp at nine o'clock and marched 25 miles to Rawhide creek and camped. It was at the crossing of this creek that only three months before the Indians burnt the ranche, killed one man and two escaped. Not being much wood here I had to carry a log as heavy as myself for a bout one mile. the men had to come to hed quarters and git there forrige and you could hear grate growling for they had to carrey it a long ways to there companys

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
[pencil note: Gift 95. Norene Berry 2]
95 
of the Wagon train and tell him to git our Wagon in as soon as posibale to let it pass the rest of the Wagons if it was behind. I mounted up With out a saddle and started out on the jump I did not come on to any Wagon for a bout 3 mils I had as good a horse as there was in the command and I had not broke the [[lope?]] yet and I did not stop hear Went on a bout 1 mile and hear found one Wagon unloded for the muls could not pool up the hill. I was pooty warm by this time and the hors to so I stoped and hird the teamster cruse a While. I went on a little father and hear found a wagon broke down there was some dad boys around this wagon I did not think it was safe to stay a round this crowd for they were like made men and so I went on and found wagons in the same fox for a bout 2 mils I then come to the Leut and told him what the General sed he tell me to go back and tell the Genral he did not now what time he could got to camp and to tell him jest how things were a long the road he asked me how far it was to camp and I told him I thought it was a bout 6 mils he then aperd me a drink out of a bottle but I told him I never drank. I started back on the jump and never pooled up till I come to camp for it was moon light and could se well I told the Genral all I had found out and went down where the boys were and they had borrowd some flour and bacon and coffe from one of the Wagons that had come in so they had made flap jacks so I took the pan for they were all done eating and it was fun to see me late for I had not had a bite since earley int he morning. the sargent magor had to poot in and says you late like a [[dom?]]  [[?]] hog but I sed nothing. Well I goot done and made down my bed that is I roled up in my saddle blanket and took my saddle for a pillow and never woke up till the bugle soundded revilee

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
94
Winter Scout fr Nov 1st. 1876
I saddoled up in the morning and Went up to hed quarters a started to pack up the Genrals things in a Wagon When his things were all in our things had to go in the same Wagon Well We had an eight mule Wagon and the Geral say Pack it fool and after we goot every thing in We had no room for our tents and We had to strap them on the out side and it made a pooty big lode Well by this time the companys had come out and the Genral gave them orders to start out on our roade. Well we did not start till after all the rest had gone and then the Genral and all us ordeleys started 11 all told on the Staff. by this time it had goot to bee near 12 Oclock Well of course We had not had our dinner. Well we marched down through the White Earth Cannon passing the Wagons and then past all the command. Well we came came to the end of last 18 mils out there is a fine stream in this Cannon and we had to cross it 24 tims and that made it slow travling for the Wagons. Well it was sun down when we goot to [[comt?]] and it was after dark when all the command goot in, you see our command cossisted of 9 companys of cavalry 5 of Infantry and 4 of Artillery. Well then the Word Went a round Where is the Wagons no Wagons no super and so it Went on till 10 Oclock and the first wagon come in but it was not ours and the Genral began to walk a round for our Wagon had aut to be a hed. We had a fire for it was pooty cold. I was gitting all the comfort i could out of the fire when I hird the Genral call out Smith my name had goot to bee pooty common all reddy Well I goot up and went to him nearly starved he says jump on your horse and go back and do not stop till you find Leut Latton for he had charge

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
93
dreams I ever had I would think some times I was at home and was just a going to set down to a good meal and then the horse would stumble and the I would wake up with a curse to find it was all a lie. and then I would try to ceep a wake and watch the rest Some would foll a sleep and their horses would wander out of Colom and then then you could hear the officers cusing them Well we come to Camp Robinson a bout two Oclock in the nite and tirned our Prisners over at the Post and then went down to our quarters and the men that were left back had a cind of a supper reddy for us and some ate and some went to bed as for my self I ate till I made my self sick and it was near day broke When I fell a sleep sitting by the stove. I will not state what hapened between this date and the 31st. October I was orderd to reporte to him for Ordlay for the Scoute. We had muster on that day and so after it I took my bundel of bedding and my horse and went up to the Post and reported to Gen MaKinsey he asked me my name and some few more questions and told me to report to Sargent magor Welch as one of the ordleys. Witch I did I will now say this Sargent Magor was an grate big overgrown Irishman and I did not like the new thing much but I was cind of green a round hed quarters and did not have any thing to say. I waited out side for a little while and the first saloot I got from the Sargent mager was God dam you Soul bee a little lively a round hear. I node I was pooty lively on foot so I took it all in and sed nothing. I will not say any more hear but we drawd raishons for ten days: and then went back to the quarters and slept all nite
[pencil in side margin: Charles Atwood Smith [[farmers?]] & W Smith]

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
80
Monday Januray 1st. 1877
Left camp and marched 10 mils and went in to camp of horse shooe crick the Infantry past our camp on route for Medician Bow and this was the last of them
Tuasday 2td. 1877
Broke camp and made 20 mils and camped on North Plat River with plenty of Wood in camp
Wensday 3td 1877
Broke camp and mad 18 mils and camped on a fork of Plat River very cold
Thirsday 4th. 1877
Left camp earley and and made 12 mils and campted right at Fort Larme a good menney goot drunk here to day and I shiped my pipe home from hear that I had carried in my inside pocket ever since the fite
Friday 5th. 1877
Lay over all day and bought dome [[unclear]] stuff and had a good super, the 5 cavalry now left us and went to Ft Russel
Sunday 6th. 1877
Broke camp and left for our old home in Red Cloud this is the first time we were let now where we were a going We goot to now hide after going threw rane and mud all day. I had on a nuff close for two men and I was wet to the skin all over and my Boots fool of watter. this day I soy two soldiers stand off and shoot six shots a peace at each other and never tuched a hare then one mounted his horse and lit out and never come back a gane. Woth of them were drunk, durring the nite the Wind come up and Lord it did turn cold every thing frose [[still?]] tents and all and some of the tents Blod down and so did mine a long with the rest

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
79
Sunday Dec 31st. 1876
Left camp at the yousel time and marched 15 mils and camped on Elk Horn Crick, the boy in my tent were on gard and they mad a raid on a Whiskey Wagon that was near, some of the boys goot tide up to Wagons the boys in my tent come in some time in the nite and Woke me up and they had a coffe Pot fool of Whiskey and they would have me to take some. I took my tin cup and fild it and set it to my [[hed?]] and told them I would drink it in the morning. I went to sleep and in the morning I found the cup all right I did not titch it and went and bilt a fire in the stove. I now looked out and the Bugle had not gone yet. I looked down at my feet and hear I my Bunkey covered with snow I pooled him in to the tent and bilt a big fire and after a while he came to. he was near frose to death I now goot my cup of Whiskey and gave it to him Well he soon goot all right after drinking a quart of Whiskey. I told him if I would have drunk it it would have cild me and he says it just saved my life. Well the Leut When he found out how the Whiskey had worked the company he took a ax and stove in the heds of the kegs and let all the Poison run a way and I for one was glad of it. but a grate meny gave a loud sye a bout one half of the company was under gard this day and had to walk threw snow nee deep and so ended the last day of the year 1876

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
78
Monday Dec 25th. 1876
Left camp as yousel and spent my Crismas on the road walked nearley allday made 20 mils and camped on some watter holls no wood We had a reglar old Crismas Dinner a little peace of fat bacon and hard tack and a half a cup of coffe you bet I thought of home now if ever I did. but fate was a gane me  and I could not bee there my Bunkey bought some candy and we ate it
Tuasday Dec 26th. 1876
Left our camp at Pumpkins Butes and made 12 mils and camped at out old camp on Wind River cut cotton Wood till a Way after dark
Wensday Dec 27th. 1876
Left camp at 9 Oclock and made 17 mils and went into camp on South Fork of Cheyenne River Plenty of Wood hear [[?]] all day
Thirsday Dec 28th. 1876
Broke camp and 13 mil and camped on Sage crick and mity cold no wood and plenty of sage Briesh to birn
Friday Dec 29th. 1876
Broke camp and marched 19 mils and camped 1 mile from Fort Feterman
Saturday Dec 30th. 1876
Left camp in a hurry this morning snow storm lasted all day the road was fool of straglers all day in all sorts of ways nearley every Boddy drunk We went in to camp after marching 18 mils now the next thing was supper but where was the cook wagon it had tiped over and the teamster and quarter master [[?]] were drunk every thing was in a grate [[?]] and we had to go to bed with out any supper mitty hard luck

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
77 
Friday Dec 22td. 1876
Broke camp at day broke and marched 15 mils and every body feeling good We were on our back trale and Ward went a round that We were a going in off of the scout, snowing all dad and cold 
Saturday Dec 23td. 1876
the Bugle sounded at 5 Oclock and we up and frose stiff. We mad 15 mils and camped on some Watter hols and not a stick of Wood and the coldest day we had on the trip I was now deataled for gard and I never shall forgit it in all my life
Sunday Dec 24th. 1876
Well morning come at last yes at last and I never was as glad to see a morning in all my life for such a nite as I had poot in I had to ceep a wake to ceep from freesing to death corpral Hall was in charge of the gard and I can all ways see him sitting by that sage Brush fore a bout as big as a Wash pan with five Blankets eaped a round him. When I walked my two ours I run all the time around and a round I went and never stoped till my time was up. I was now pooty warm and thought I could sleep I lade down with 14 Blankets over me and a lot under me but it would not work for I frose out and had to git out and pool sage Brush and Rin a round We left camp a yousel and made 12 mils and camped on sage crick, and there was no wood heer neather but I had a stove in the tent and I and my Bunkey Pooled sage Brush a nuff to ceep warm with. this nite the thormometer was frose up and they could not tell how cold it was the same the nite before this Nite I went over to the Commeicires and bought one can of Peaches I gave 2 dollars for a can. I saw one man give 10 dollars for a bottle of Whiskey I ate the Peaches crismas [[?]] my bunkey helped

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
76
Monday Dec 18th. 1876
this day there was most all the Sargents and Corprals goot drunk and a privite by the name of Moore was drunk and was poot under gard, When we were after the hird at stable call Moore had to go allso he could not until a not was in his halter for it was one solid lump of ice the first sargent ran up to him and gave him an affle kick and a welt in the fase he did not say a word back and neather did the sentry When we led up to the Picket line Moore asked the sentry to let him go to the tent for his [[?]] come and Brush Witch he did, When he come out he had his pistell in his right hand behind him and the sentry did not see it. When the first sargent came a long the man that struck him at the crick he pooled down on him With the Pistell and as luck or bad luck would have it is mist fire, and he snaped down on three catcherrigs and none of them went off by this time the boys had grabed him and goot the Pistell a way from him and then the sargent ran up and punched him in the fase earn they held him, they now tide him up to a wagon the Leut told me to take a rope and help to tie him up I picked up the rope and walked over to the Wagon and throde it down and walked a round the Wagon, the sentry goot under gard too, nothing elce sed to any body elce [[?]]
Tuasday Dec 19th. 1876
mooved two or three mils down the crick Weather mity fine to day
Wensday 20th. 1876
Lay over all day and done nothing much
Thirsday Dec 21st. 1876
Law over all day and cut cotton Wood Weather fine every thing quiet to day

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
75
Sunday Dec 10th. 1876
mooved camp dow the crick. bout 8 mils and struck a nice camp the best we had been at in a long time lots of wood and watter, A large train left the comand to go to Fort Feteman for suplyes the command was string a long this crick for 2 or 3 mils
Monday Dec 11th 1876
Lay over all day and it was a fine day
Tuasday 12th. 1876
Still we lay over and fearful winday  and cold 
Wensday Dec 13th. 1876
moved camp 3 or 4 mils father down the crick
Thirsday 15th. 1876
I awoke in the moning and found to my suprise that I had no hors for the hird had stompeded durring the nite. I never saw the men in as good yoummer as they were this morning every boddy praying that they would never find them. for we had been worked to death cutting cotton Wood for them, I company was ordered out to look for them and brought them back tiwards nite Lay over to day
Saturday Dec 16th 1876
Lay over to day and some of the boys goot goot drunk it the setters lots of them Whiskey only one dollar a drink it was pooty hard for me to ceep a way from this now for I had mad lots of money renting my tent out at nite to fellows to gamble in one note I goot 10 dollars from one fellow he has Won 1,100 dollars I had quite a good stake saved up now over 40 dollars  I had saved in this Way
Sunday Dec 17th. 1876
Worked hard all fore noon choping cotton wood the suply trane come back to day a fine day

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
74
Saturday 2td. Dec. 1876
Broke camp a bout 9 Oclock and marched 28 mils on the back trail and camped on Powder River a bout 1 mile from old Fort Reno. I was poot on gard hear for the first time in a long while and I node we were hedding for home
Sunday Dec 3td. 1876
Left camp early and mass 15 miles and went in to camp on dry Fork and this was bad Water very muddy and not much of it
Monday Dec 4th. 1876
Lay over hear to day and all the wounded and all the sick and men with the worst horses left us and started for Fort Fetterman and hear they lay the Sargent of I company under the ground
Tuasday Dec 5th. 1876
struck camp and did not moove after all so I carred Wood a gane all day Went on hed quarters gard and got a good super there from the nigas 
Wensday Dec 6th. 1876
Left camp and a bout noon and made 15 mils and camped on some water holes the grass was proty good hear Weather Fine
Thirsday Dec 7th 1876
Broke camp early and mad 20 mils and went in to camp on some watter holes pased some miners on the road going to ded Wood city
Friday Dec 8th. 1876
Left camp [[coiled?]] and made 18 mils and camped on Sage Crick no Wood hear nothing but sage brush - brush very cold Was on gard
Saturday Dec 9th. 1876
Broke camp as yousel and made 8 mils and camped on hed Water of Belle Fourche there was lots of cotton Wood to bee cut hear for the horses

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
73
Friday December 1st. 1876
I had not had my Brekfast long when my old friend come to see me and sed the Genrell say you can Report Back to your company. I says all right. I node it was his dooings bocaus I would not cook, well this winds up my [[ordley?]] carrer I went to my company and reported for dooty. I now expected to git hell all a round for when a man is off a while they stick every thing on to him that there is to do. but they yoused me poty well this time. for I all ways tride to do right as near as I node how. I had not been back long when the first Sargent come to me any says you will be on of the Pall Bors at the funral this after noon. the Leut in charge of our company see me and cold me up to him and says how is your hors smith is he shod. I seys all right Leut he say you will bee one of the 25 me out of the company to go out to nite to jump another Indin camp. his name was Leut Shoomaker and was a fine man to. he told me he was glad I was back in the company you see this name smith was handey where ever I was. in the after noon we went to berrey the ded and it was the hardest looking funral I was ever at, well we goot done and went back. I jest thought then I would never like to bee left in the ground in this wild cuntry Whear no white man would ever see the place a gane the way they berrey in the cuntry they take and sow a man up in a Blanket and dont have no coffin. We had not been back long when stable call went and a Sargent in I company went to the hird for his horse and little did he know it was his last time for he had not more than goot on his horse than he fell with him and roled over him and he dead his last breath in a bout five minutes. and this wound up the first day in our company. I now went to bunking with a young fellow by the name of Deon and we stade till spring Broke us up

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
72
Tuasday Nov 28th. 1876
left this camp at day light and made 16 mils and Went in to camp on a branch of crasy Womns fork the nite the snow was a bout 2 feet deep on a level and I fell in to the crick and goot all Wet While gitting Water for super. I goot pooty dry before I went to bed it was so cold I could hardley sleep
Wensday Nov 29th. 1876
Broke camp and marched 10 Mils and come to our suply trane and was mity glad to get in our tents a gane I had for drather sleep in a tent than out doors int he snow. and hear it was that I saw my old friend Sargent Magor Welch and I told him I wanted to git out of the cooking for I had been in over my turn now for 10 days Was as long as were to cook Well says I will se and he says git super anyway I goot super and sed no more and goot Breakfast you see I turned out to bee such a good cook that he would not realeve me. after Breackfast I told him I would not cook an other meal and he says God dam your soul I will make your cook I says look hear dont you cus me any more now I have had a nuff of it. I would have shot him then in a minte. he sed no more and told a nother man to go the cook house and I would show him how to Bake Bred and this old Gaurd of a son of a B. went to the Gen and had a talk and I node it was a bout me. Well this nite I post in in my tent by a fire 
Thirsday the 30th 1876
Thanksgiving day I had a little longer to sleep now and I post it in Well had nothing do but git up and take care of my horse and go and eat my Breackfast. We had an reglar old thanksgiving dinner Bacon and Flap Jacks not much runnig around today and stade close to my tent nor had no words with this Sargent Magor

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
71
and a lot of the Gen things Were on it and all so my Blankets and that left me With only two I had on my horse, every thing was a mooving a round the hospitle makeing travose to carrey the Wounded on and stroping the ded on muls for the boddies were frose stiff we finly Broke camp a bout 11 Oclock and started out of  this dedly valley and I was glad to git a way We marched 7 mils and camped on Rock crick the some one the fite was on. hear our Indins had a skelp dance and I went over to see it they has a good meny and they made the valey ring with there shouts. the camp was Well garded to nite for fear of a surprise and the Wounded were resting well

Monday Nov 27th. 1876
Broke camp earley and made 15 mils and camped on a fork of the Powder river this was a hard day for the Wounded for they had to go over a ruff cuntry and hear We hird that Gen crook was near us with all the Infratry he had hird that we were in a place and could not git aut he had marched the Infrantry 35 mils over the cuntry and nearley cripled them all this nite jest after super there was a stompeed a mong the soldiers I had a nice big fire for I was Baking Breed and one of the boys wanted to poot it aut I told him to git a way dam quick to for I was mitty sick of Indins by this time for beeing up nite and day cooking and near frose to death. I went to my [[?]] that was locreted near the fire and my carbine was there saddle and all I poot my belt on and side linde my Poney and then set down on my saddle witch was on the Picket Pin and Waited to see what was comming I had 1 hudred rounds of shots in my saddle Pockets and I dont belive I could of been mad to leave hear of I had of been shot right hear. but I would of been a bad peace of meat just now to of took. it had been snowing all day and was very cold. the stompeed was cosed by some Indins shooting Buflow. and some of this we goot the next day. Baked my Bred

title: William Earl Smith diary, 1876-1877
transcription:
70
Nov 25th 1876

It was near nite now and the Gen says boys make down your bedds a long hear in a row for the Indians will atact yes agane to nite. This camp was in a kind of a bason and a fine stream runing threw it Wright in the senter of the Big horn Mnt. on both sids the mountane rase up 1 thousand feet high and all red rock at one end was a long hill covered with fine trees this is where all the Squaws goat out and we could not take the woods. they poot a strong gard on to nite and I went to bed more ded that a live, We were rite near the hospitle and I could hear the Wounded groneing all nite. I could not sleep mitch for my leg now was gitting worse and every tie I wake I could see the Generall walking up and down. I dont belive he slept a bit that Nite his mind must of been trubled a bout some thing I dont now what for he is the bravest man I ever saw; he dont seem to think any more a bout boolets flying than I would a bout snow balls, We had in all cilled 11 and wounded 28 this mad quite a lot. Will this ended the 25 of Nov and I was glad to see Nite
Sunday Nov 26th. 1876
I awake in the morning after my Restless nite sleep and goot Breackfast reddy for I had to bee up before any body elce. While I was cooking the Generall come to me and asked me if I was sick during the nite he sed I did not sleep much. I made by this that he had not slept a tall durring the nite. I asked him if he would have a coop of coffe  and he sed he would While I was drinking he talked to me a good deal a bout the fite a seemed to feel bad a bout the boys that had been hirt and cild now the bugal sounded for the first time in this camp and every body Was a stir Breakfast all over the Gen gave orders to birn every thing in the camp and pack up I for goot to say We had lost one of our Pack muls

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
Dear Slim,
6/21/70
Hon, just so you'll know that I really did send you a letter, look what came back to me?
Want to thank you very much for sending me the [[?]]. It's an excellent publication, and I read the issue with great interest from cover to cover.
And I also want to assure you that I am in no way upset with Slim - only sorry that you aren't 
2
feeling chipper. But just remember that things will get better tomorrow and don't be too mad at yourself.
Did you take the room upstairs with the Mexican woman or get yourself a better roommate? I suspect your spirits will lift when you have a decent pad, and you'll find yourself charging away on the book. The situation with Jamee sounds miserable, but then I couldn't have lived with that one to begin with. (up)
5
Think I'll go down to Baja with her next week and say "farewell, busy world" for at least seven days. The tip shouldn't be crowded at this time of year - or at least I hope not.
Take care doll, and don't let the little things bug you.
Luv, Esther

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
3
As for a report on the law school, I took my exams last week and think they may let me stay in for the summer term. My typewriter fell apart during the Criminal Law final, shooting pieces all over the room, and I fell apart with it, so I probably flunked it outright or got a D if he's kind. On Friday, armed with a newer machine & a spare typerwiter I borrowed just in case, I conquered
4
the Introduction to Law course and hope I did well enough to offset the other test. Will know in two or three weeks, after summer school starts.
In the meantime, my Mom arrived for a visit She tried to call you for help on the basement expedition, but you weren't there, so somehow or other she made it without you. But it must have been very hard for her.
(over)

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
Dear Slim,
So sorry to learn of Do[[?]]'s death. I tried to call you with condoloences on getting your letter last night, but of course coudn't reach you. Hope you are able to find a health and wealthy roommate, at least, wealthy enough to withstand half the cost of your pad.
I like your idea for Who Said That. Remember how many years Ripley had a good thing going with "Believe It Or Not?" Why don't you make up a couple of sample columns, dream up some kind of plan for doing it on a regular basis and try peddling it? If you could sell it to 5 or 10 papers, it would be quite worthwhile. You might have to break down and buy a later edition of Bartlett's, but that's about the only sacrifice you'd have to make. Do be sure there's a market, though, before you leap into it whole hog. And will on my end try to figure out who said "What's good for General Motors is good for the country" and when he said it. Must have been a secretayr of labor in times past, no?
Sure hope yu find your rent money. THat's really a sad situation, but be comforted by the fact that you have a lot of company in doing insane things like that. Would you believe that I've lost more than $300 since 1960 from

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
2
my own brand of stupidity — failing to take my purse with me when I leave my desk at work & finding the cash, entire wallet and once even the purse gone when I returned?
No, doll, I haven't been photographed much by a newspaper photog. On seeing the drastic results on a first try, I quietly hired said photog to take as many shots as necessary to get a decent one of me (think it took a role or two of film — I'm not very photogenic, so they have to try harder to get a good one). Then, I had prints made & distributed them as necessary. 'Twas NO trouble at all after the initial six were taken and I was spared the agony of being unable to face myself in the paper.
Washing shorts? Vacuuming? You put me to shame! Am hoping that my Inez can return to work BEFORE the drapes die from dirt—been over a year since I had them cleaned.
Hope you've worked up the energy to break the ice with someone new. I've always been terrified of strangers, so I know how you feel. Take care. I start school tomorrow night again.
Luv,
Esther

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
9/27/71
Hon-
Read your column material with great interest. I like it very much, but am not sure any paper would want that much detail.They may prefer only the first paragraph or so on each item. Am returning your good letter, marking the margins where I suspect an editor would cut. Do get some feedback from an interested party before you wear yourself out. As for the quantity, hon, I think a week's worth of items would be enough to show. Then, if anyone buys, you hustle! So much for the views of one E[[?]] as to what [[Slim?]] ought to do. But then, just maybe I'm right for once. Love ya, Esther
PS-saw Jesus Christ Superstar at the Hollywood Bowl-much to my surprise it was terrific! The "original" production-see if it comes to town.

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
Sat – 6/17/72
Dear Slim,
Please forgive me for not writing sooner. I was on an extended work week and trying to study for finals at the same time. I know that's really no excuse for not writing, but I just couldn't manage to do anything else. Didn't even pay the rent (until this morning), call my momma, or do any of the necessities in the interim.
Fortunately, that's now a thing of the past, and I feel like they took a monkey off my back. Now I'll have time to tend to the houses, eat regularly, and perhaps even live it up by going in the pool, using my bike (I still wave at them both every morning), and other good things.
Sorry to learn that you've been ousted from your flat. About all I can say in sympathy is that it is really no great loss. Am sure your new quarters will be better and at least the mean and cruel landlord didn't throw out your belongings. Am sending this to you on Melrose, since I have a hunch you'll get it. (The La Salle St. address you gave me has yet to be confirmed.)
Before I forget, Carl Spring says to tell you that he'll start a house search for the pix of you next

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
week when he returns from San Francisco. (He's off on a holiday and not know for keeping extensive catalogs of the many films he takes – but you'll get it.)
Love your idea of a senior citizen column. I agree with Louise that you should have takers. Let me know what kind of response you get, and in the meantime, I'll keep my fingers crossed.
Should have the word on exams in about a month – think I flunked out of school on contracts, and passed torts. But then so does everyone else in the class and the fact is that only half of us will be thrown out. Will have to wait and see.
At long last, here is my check for the lovely suede skirt and vest. Am now off chasing the right thread to try to sew the hem – their glue and press job didn't make it for very long. Were you ever able to make an arrangement for me to get one for my lady lawyer? Couldn't tell from your letter. Let me know. I like mine very much.
Really all the news for now. Will be hoping to hear great things from you in spite of my undue delay in writing. But I still love ya,
Esther

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
Dear Slim,
It was so very good to see you and have the pleasure of your company in Chicago.  I only wish that I had been able to figure out a way to see more of you, but I was kind of caught between only neice and only sister-in law (the Philidelphia contingent), my mother's family (the Oakland Calif. contigent), and the post wedding festivities I hadn't anticipated from the Chicago contingent.  And the way it was done -the bride and groom showed up for all, so everyone who came to town to wish them well did too. And I come from such a small family too!  Next time I hope to see more of Slim and more of my mother as well. Would you (up)

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
2
believe we had the great sum of one hour together? But it is good to know that I'll be seeing you in L.A. in December and will hope you do a better job than I did in getting to see you.
Returned to an avalanche of free lance (undertaken to pay a dental bill), finished it, and promptly got sick. Thus far, I'm undiagnosed - doc said if it keeps up, we try tests - so I'm using Esther's all-purpose remedy instead: a weekend in Palm Springs. It works about half the time, regardless of what's wrong. Hopefully, I'll return all well again.
Carl and Alice are vacationing in Lassen, near the Oregon border, which has become a busy spot for camping. I marvel that people can claim they enjoy mosquito-ridden sites sleeping on wet ground, cooking with an inadequate stove, and using an outhouse in the name of fun. Also driving forever to have the privilege. But then, I always was out of it. Take care and keep on looking as great as you did in August. Again, my apologies for not getting to see you again. 
Love,
Esther

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
May 13, 1971
117 W. Dayton St.
Madison, Wis. 53703
My dear Slim:
I hope you are well again and busy enjoying the College again. I assume you have arrived back in Chicago as you planned by the beginning of May.
I was angry with not feeling good so I tossed out the chairs and the gate-legged table. Bought 3 folding chairs and made cushions on them. Bought folding legs, plywood and plastic top and put them all together to make a table 24” x 30”. So now it’s very crowded but the chairs won’t fall to pieces as the others did and I have a table to work on. But it didn’t help a bit, I still feel like garbage. 
Last week Betty was in the hospital She had extra joints removed from 2 toes on each foot. After visiting her las Wednesday I walked home. When I reached State & Park streets there were thousands of students and lots of police in riot gear. Tear gas was all over the place but I still haven’t found out what it was all about. Several (4 or 5) students were arrested for ‘disorderly conduct’ which don’t tell me anything. Almost nothing was mentioned about it altho even the YWCA/YMCA on Park street was maced. I got home without any trouble but sneezing from the tear gas. That was the last of the May Day activities I guess. Now I don’t see any long haired students

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
for about 6 days. I hope they are not cooking up more trouble.
I find that all the ladies, except here in this house, that I’ve talked to have been in the mental Hospital. The conclusion I reach is that they are the only ones who can’t afford a car and so are stuck in the center of town.
There’s a tempest in a teapot over the arrest of a doctor who was performing abortions — was it legal or illegal! (It was against the state constitution to arrest him). Still in the courts. In the meantime no one can get rid of her pregnancy unless they go elsewhere and pay ten times as much.
The more I see and hear, the less it seems worthwhile to live. There is a built-in resistence to improve the lot of people and the cause is not money alone. I guess it’s Allah’s fault. —“The boy was ment to be sold.”
When my brain works again I will write a better letter. This is just to let you know I still love you and hope you will feel like dropping me a line so I won’t worry about you.
These 3 K’scopes forced me to take pen in hand. So you see I always think of you.
Sent with love, 
Alice

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
June 7, 1971
117 W. Dayton St.
Madison, Wi. 53703
Dear Slim:
Received your card from Calif. saying you were looking for your brother. I hope you found him well. Received a package of books June 1st and a new return address. I'm wondering why you moved. You seemed so happy with the other place. I don't know where 143 Armitage is. Thought the numbers started at 300.
How is the college doing? When your gone for a while I don't hear from you about the college. – Here there is no free open discussion anymore as far as I can find out. I wonder how much longer you will be able to have them without the police interfering. Isn't it wonderful to live in a free country. — I asked what freedom means and the only answer was we were free to choose any kind of  work and move wherever we want to. That sounds like well brain-washed people. That is because all children are taught to obey authority and if their brain says something else then their brains are wrong. Soon they can't even zip up their pants without someone telling them how to do it.
My son and family visited me Sunday and were proud to tell me another baby is due in October. Brrrr and also Grrrrr. —I gave them some literature

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
on birth control including male and female sterilization. Now they want a new car but have no money for it. They better not ask me for money.
Had a hard time reading the Military and Industrial State by Sidney Lenz and also the New Industrial State by Gailbraith but they, together, give an accurate picture of what is going on and how and why we are told to believe so many foolish things and I'm glad I read them. Now I'm reading the bible and actually the same things were told the common people even in 4000 B.C. right up to today. Instill fear by misrepresenting and create pride in something that should be hated such as war. Marriage! Authority! all in the name of a vindictive and jealous god. Phooey.
In a couple of days I'll send you a couple more Kaleidoscopes, as soon as the next one comes out.
I expect that I will stay physically less than able or capeable but if I can keep my brain active its still worth while.
Just heard how New York's bridges are up and all the trouble it causes. I think that is a wonderful thing to do. 
Thanks for the books. I do always enjoy who-dun-its. Glad you think of me. I love you much and hope your well again. Take care of yourself, make sure you get drunk regularly.
Many good wishes and much love from,
Alice

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
July 14, 1971
117 W. Dayton St.
Madison, Wi. 53703
Dear Slim:
Received your letter but was not feeling well enough to write. I'm afraid your visit here was not as nice as it should have been but I'm going downhill so fast I just don't expect to be able to do anything any more.
I told the chiropractor about your handy gadget and he got interested in the magazine that's going to print it. I don't expect him to tell me if he likes it or not. It would put him and me in an awkward position if he didn't like it. Hope you get some money from it. I thought your method of writing has improved very much.
When you told me Looking Backward had my ideas in it I thought you were just making fun of me but not that I've read it I agree that Edward Bellamy and I have the same ideas only mine are updated. So now I got the Decline of the West by Spengler like you told me to but I still have to read it. 
I'm reading The Wall Street Jungle by Richard Ney now and it tells all the things my mother and I used to wonder about how the Stock Exchange really made the price changes. Mr. Ney was on TV and he predicted a complete breakdown of Stocks and Banks in 5 years. Another big broker predicted 5 years or sooner! This book tells why the market cannot go on indefinitely.

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
I wish you had told me about Looking Backward and Spengler about 10 years ago. If you know any modern writers in this line please let me know and I'll read them. I'm real sorry Bellamy's book didn't up more people. It should be read instead of the bible. Most people still believe what the papers say about democracy. 
My son called me long distance June 30th to tell me you were on TV on chanel 44 and he said you were real funny, meaning humerous. I'm glad your still getting publicity. That should bring the people to the college.
We had an art fair here last week end but the art was not very good. They did sell quite a lot tho. Lots of people, several thousand. I had thought everyone had left Madison it was so dead till the art show came.
This drug trouble with Jamee bothers me. She has always been so disappointed with life and still she had so much ability that I'm sorry to see her go down hill so fast. — I don't remember Louise but she has the same problem so many parents have now. I hope her daughter returns to school this fall and finishes. 
This old society needs a big change and I think we will get it.
Your fat moron,
Alice
P.S. Dictionary says a moron lacks good judgment!

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
August 3, 1971
117 W. Dayton St.
Madison, Wi 53703
Dear Slim:
As soon as I read your letter I went to the used book store and tried to get Decline of the West for you but they didn't have any more copies. I bought one there last week for my reference library. Spengler is a son-of-a-gun to read if you don't have a good history background. Even what I have studied about history I can't remember. But that guy really had a lot to say that makes sense. If he could have written it in  today's manner I could have gotten much more out of it. Again I hope it will be written better. The book is not in paper back.
The Wall Street Jungle by Richard Ney is in paperback, published by Grove Press for $1.50. Mr. Ney is publishing another book. It may be out by now. Also about the stock market. I don't know the title.
Your letter was real good. It gave me a lift. I'm happy about you feeling so well. Your the only one I've heard of that does. I hope it lasts and lasts.
The Chicago TV stations don't reach here so we don't get to see interesting programs like Slim Brundage. All I do is hear about it and eat my heart out that I miss it. But let me know when your on anyway.
I'm worried about Doc. He needs his drink more than you do and that can cause both of you trouble. Tell

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
him I wish him the best of all things. I sure wish I had his storehouse of knowledge and his memory.
Your curriculum for August sounds real good. Any one of those subjects should draw a crowd. Hope it turns out that way.
I tried to get a Fling mag. but it isn't sold here even not in the pornography shop. Since they aren't publishing your story I'm not missing anything by not having a copy of Fling.
Being on Heroin is going to be bad soon. Several cities are starting to put a bounty on sellers or pushers. One city had several thousand tips but only 5 convictions on pushers. So that sity has dried up. The pushers left. Don't remember for sure what city but it could be Miami.
Just heard a program on the changes in the Catholic Church. The cardinal who was doing the explaining said among other things that "ritual ceremony calms the big fears that people cannot control any other way". That is I think a big truth. A ritual of course can be anything, even a morning cup of coffee first thing in the morning. I will have to think moe about that. 
By the way Spengler is in the library. You will probably have to order a new one and have to wait for it besides paying 5 or 6 bucks for it otherwise.
How are the grand children? and your Oldest son? Keep that receipt for good health or the simulation of it. — It's cold or rainy or very windy here but seldom nice weather. 
Affectionately yours,
Alice

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
Sept. 8, 1971
117 W. Dayton St.
Madison, Wi. 53703
Dear Slim:
It sounds to me like you are better off in Mexico as far as getting a place to live and nice people to live with. I have an idea you will go to Mexico this time and not come back.
I made a small trip into Iowa. The big building next door to me is being remodeled and is very noisy. Besides the weather has been so awfull I was going down hill fast. So I took a suitcase to the bus and went to Iowa for 4 days. Dubuque is a very beautiful interesting city but is dieing. The industry has moved out and the young people have to leave to get work. The humidity is 90% even when its cold and often its 90° temperature and 90% humidity. Then you really can't breathe. Next day to Cedar Rapids. I stuck my nose out the door of the bus station and found the stink so bad I took the next bus to Des Moines. There was some kind of trouble just outside my room in Des Moines and no one would tell me what happened. I saw police men and squad cars but was afraid to leave my room till things quieted down. The bed was so soft I slept on the floor. The room and bath with free TV and air conditioning was $7.50. But the little I saw of Des Moines is a dirty, greedy, corrupt city. So I left real quick and went to Marshalltown. That was perfect. 26,000 population, no crime, no unemployment, no graft, no slum section, wonderful library and everything good. Dinner of 2 huge porkchops with veg. potatoes, salad & coffee $1.50. Parking 5¢ an hour some places 5¢ for three hours. State sales tax 3%. Altogether

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
the best there is except that its much too humid. So that's why I won't go back. In a couple of weeks I want to take a trip to southern Illinois. Maybe that won't be too humid. I've never been there.
A year ago I couldn't ride a bus more than an hour but that seems to be getting better. Go without a suitcase and I think I won't suffer from my back because even in hotels no one will carry my suitcase. 
Madison is not liked even by the U. students this year. I don't blame them. It's noisy, crowded, rents too high, streets all torn up, good teachers have left, and much more that was not so 3 years ago. I guess I've jinxed this town. Now they are going to raise the State Income Tax again. It is higher than 46 other states now. So with the new increase I guess we will be paying more taxes than any other state.
I feel some what better but there is lots of room for more improvement. ——— I got a card from my brother Jake. He and wife visited Holland this summer. My sister wrote they have returned and had not enjoyed their trip. We have lots of cousin, Aunts & Uncles there yet.
Since its too noisy to think at my house I decided to write this in the library. I come here every day for several hours now. I read the history of China in the Encyclopedia Brit. and was surprised to find how up to date it is. It's well worth reading especially now that Nixon is going to give us a snow job about China. I expect war with China within 5 years.
There is so much to study and learn that I wish my brain would function better. My memory is getting worse but the enjoyment of reading is improving.
Take good care of yourself so that you will continue to feel good.
Much love, 
Alice

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
Sept 25, 1971
117 W. Dayton St.
Madison, Wis 53703
Dear Slim:
Was to Peoria, Bloomington (nice town), Springfield and Decatur, Illinois all in one week. The weather soaked me 5 of the 7 days. The $4 hotel rooms had such soft beds they broke my back. The buses completed breaking my back where the lousy beds didn't. The food cost us very high, much more than in Iowa. The people seem so depressed and poor and others sour and well off. Altho Madison leaves much to be desired I find it is as good as anything else. The humidity is high all over the midwest. All that rain and no heat in the rooms gave me a cold but since I had my back fixed by the chiropractor I'm in rather better condition than I expected to be.
I'm reading "The Rich and the Super Rich" by Ferdinand Lundberg. He wrote America's Sixty Families in 1937. This is a follow up published in 1968. This is of America's ruling multi-millionaires (75 to 100 million dollars each) who pay no taxes and rule the country through the politicians, lawyers, judges and military puppets. There are 200,000 of these wealthy people most of them are of 500 families. Like 250 DuPonts, 73 Rockefellers etc. It gives the background information for the things we always know about power in the U.S. Very interesting if I ignore all the statistics and figures except for 1.6% of the population holds all the power of wealth. I think you would like it if you skipped the figures. It's in Bantam Books for 1.95 The library has it too.
I've been looking for information on where Hitler got money to raise an army and make war materials. As far as I can find out Germany was broke, the mark was worthless and suddenly there was money for everything. Do you know anything about where Hitler got all that money from? It seems the money was re valued before he was

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972
transcription:
voted into office but it still was not worth much. So where did it come from?
It's Saturday and the building next door is quiet but Monday it will start again with the power hammers etc. It's going to be pretty tho. It will be called el Esplanade with a covered walkway to the parking ramp across the street. There will be a supper club in the basement, stores on the first floor and all the upper floors for offices. I think it will be a financial flop.
I was unable to find out anything about your TV show of Sept. 5th. How did it go? By the time they decide to put you on a regular show you won't be interested any more.
How's your book coming along. Does Paul Romaine, whoever he is, have someone on the line yet? I hope it is a humorous story you wrote. I can't see you writing anything depressing.
Haven't heard from anyone for about a month so I'm plum out of news. If I wrote more often to people maybe they would write back but most people hate to write letters.
Who was it, do you know, who said 'violence is the last resort of the incompetent'? I wrote that to my son when he said he beat his kid. I think those words were meant for war is because of government incompetence but I don't know. I heard it once at one of your C of C lectures. —— By the way what is coming up for Oct. curriculum?
Hope you are well and at peace with yourself and the world.
Sent with love, 
Alice

title: Slim Brundage letters, 1965-1972

117 W. Dayton St.
Madison, Wi 53703
Dear Slim:

I asked you what 'middle class' was some time ago. Thi is what I've found so far: (dictionary) composed principally of business and professional people, bureaucrats, and some farmers and skilled workers sharing common social characteristics and values (it don't say what or which social values). 
from (Japan's New Middle Class) — the "old middle class", the small independent businessman and landwoner ..... being replaced by the "new middle class" the white collar employee of the large business corporations and government bureaucracies."
This Japanese explanation fits in with what I read about American middle class also.
The curriculum was or is good for Oct. Did you learn anything worthwhile about whether using marijuana has any constructive vale? I've been wondering about that for a long time.
